en: May my intellect take the form of devotion toward the Supreme Brahman, Śrīnivāsa, who shines at the crest of the Vedas; whose play consists of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of all worlds; and who is solely consecrated to the protection of the multitudes of various beings who bow before him. (1)
The nectar of the words of Pārāśarya, extracted from the midst of the milk-ocean of the Upaniṣads,
which restores life to the self whose vital breath has departed due to the blazing fire of saṃsāra.

May those of noble mind from this earth daily drink that [work] which was well-guarded by the ancient teachers, which stands far removed from the contradictions of many opinions, and which is honored in its own letters.
The former teachers have condensed the extensive commentary on the Brahma-sūtras composed by the venerable Bodhāyana; following their view, the words of the sūtras will now be explained.
Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman (athāto brahmajijñāsā). 1.

The word *ataḥ* (therefore) indicates the causal relationship of what has preceded. For one who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and its esoteric portions (*śiras*), and who—having understood that ritual action (*karman*) yields only limited and unstable fruits—has conceived a desire for liberation, there necessarily follows the inquiry into Brahman, which yields infinite and stable results. "Inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*) means the desire to know Brahman; here the genitive case in *brahmaṇaḥ* denotes the object (*karman*), because of the specific rule: "The genitive is used for both the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows."

Although the status of [the word *brahma*] as the object (*karman*) is established because the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) requires an object even when the relation is understood in its general sense, nevertheless, since that which is directly expressed (*ābhidhānika*) must be preferred over what is obtained through implication (*ākṣepataḥ*), the genitive case is taken in the sense of the object. Nor should one suspect a prohibition of compounding for the genitive in the sense of the object, based on the rule "a genitive prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*) is not compounded," for there exists a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) stating that "a genitive connected with a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*) is compounded."

And by the word *brahman*, the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) is denoted, who by His very nature has all defects eliminated and possesses an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities. For everywhere the word *brahman* is used in connection with the quality of vastness (*bṛhattva*); and its primary meaning is that in which vastness is unsurpassed both in essence and in attributes. And He alone is the Lord of All; therefore, the word *brahman* functions in its primary sense only with reference to Him.

Therefore, in other cases, the term is used figuratively due to a mere trace of those qualities, because it is illogical to assume multiple meanings, as in the case of the word *bhagavat*. He alone is to be sought after for the sake of immortality by those afflicted by the three types of suffering; therefore, the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*) alone is Brahman, the object of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*). "Desire to know" (*jijñāsā*) is the wish to know; since in a wish the desired object is primary, it is knowledge itself that is enjoined here as the object of the wish.

Because ritual action (*karman*) known from the first part of the *Mīmāṃsā* yields results that are limited and unstable, whereas the knowledge of Brahman ascertainable from the subsequent part yields infinite and imperishable results, it follows that after the knowledge of ritual action—which has preceded—it is for that very reason that Brahman must be known. Thus says the author of the *Vṛtti*: "After the mastery of ritual action has occurred, there arises the desire to know Brahman."

And he will state the unity of the two systems of inquiry—into ritual action (*karma-mīmāṃsā*) and into Brahman (*brahma-mīmāṃsā*)—in the words: "This *Śārīraka* [Mīmāṃsā] is joined with the sixteen-chaptered [Jaiminīya] work; thus the unity of the scripture is established. Therefore, the distinction between the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā is based on the difference in the subjects intended to be explained, just as there is a division into six books (*ṣaṭka*) and a division into chapters (*adhyāya*).

The Mīmāṃsā Śāstra begins with "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) and concludes with "Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement" (*anāvṛttiḥ śabdādanāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*), following a specific sequence determined by particular logical connections. For instance, first of all, regarding the injunction "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied," there arises the expectation: what is the nature of that study of one's own Veda, and how is it to be performed? In response to this, [the text states]: "An eight-year-old Brāhmaṇa is to be initiated; he should be taught. By this...
Having performed the Upākarma ceremony according to the rules on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months.

Thus, by means of instructions on specific vows and observances (*vrata-niyama*) such as these, the required duties are enjoined. In this way, it is understood that *adhyayana* (study) consists in the repetition of what has been uttered by the teacher—characterized by the acquisition of the mass of syllables—and pertains to one who has been initiated by a teacher who is a knower of the Veda, endowed with self-qualities, and established in the good conduct born of a noble lineage; and such study is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *svādhyāya* (one's own portion of the Veda), because from the injunction "One's own portion of the Veda is to be studied," the *svādhyāya* is understood to be the object of the action. For a "refinement" indeed consists in making something fit for another purpose.

Furthermore, it is logical that the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is something to be refined (*saṃskārya*), because it provides knowledge of the four aims of human life—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—as well as their means; and because it serves as a means to those ends even through its own form, such as by means of recitation (*japa*). Thus, the injunction for study culminates merely in the acquisition of the mass of syllables, similar to the case of mantras, since it is observed that the Veda, once acquired through study, possesses by its very nature the capacity to provide knowledge of purposeful meaning.

Having perceived, at first glance, from the Vedic study already undertaken that it possesses a purposeful meaning, the person who has completed his Vedic studies spontaneously engages in the hearing of Mīmāṃsā—which consists of the investigation of Vedic sentences aimed at determining the specific nature and particulars of that meaning.

In that process, once the nature of ritual injunctions has been ascertained and the transitory, unstable, and limited nature of the fruits of those rituals is seen, and because an initial perception of infinite, stable, and immortal fruits arises from the Upaniṣadic passages within the Veda-study already mastered, he qualifies himself for Śārīraka-Mīmāṃsā, which consists of the investigation of Vedānta texts aimed at the definitive determination of that [immortal fruit].

And likewise, the Vedānta texts demonstrate that the fruit of mere ritual action is perishable, whereas the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is imperishable: "As here the world acquired by action perishes, even so here the world acquired by merit perishes"; "That of his becomes merely finite"; "For it is not by unstable things that the eternal is attained"; "These forms of sacrifice are indeed frail rafts"; "Having examined the worlds acquired by action, let the Brāhmaṇa attain detachment; there is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created; for the sake of knowing That... [he approaches a teacher].
"One should approach a guru alone, with fuel in hand, who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭha*).

To him, who has approached properly, whose mind is perfectly tranquil, and who is endowed with self-restraint—that wise one should truly proclaim that knowledge of Brahman by which one knows the Imperishable, the True Person. The word *provāca* means "should proclaim."

"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"; "he does not see death again, for he sees that One alone"; "the seer does not see death"; "he becomes self-ruling"; "knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here; there is no other path for the journey"; "having perceived the Self and the Impeller as distinct, being gratified by Him, one thereafter attains immortality"—and so forth.

But surely, from the mere study of the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-veda*), it is already known that rituals have heaven and the like as their fruits, that heaven and the like are perishable, and that the meditation on Brahman has immortality as its fruit. Consequently, one who desires liberation should proceed directly to the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*); what need is there for a preliminary inquiry into Dharma? If this were so, then one would not even proceed to the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā*, since everything would already be known through the study of the Veda and its auxiliaries.

If it is argued that while an initial impression certainly exists, nevertheless, because a sentence supported by reasoning is what determines the meaning, even an object of initial impression does not transcend doubt and error; therefore, for the sake of its determination, an inquiry into Vedāntic sentences must be undertaken—then please consider that an inquiry into Dharma must likewise be undertaken.

But surely, only that which the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) necessarily requires should be stated as the prerequisite (*pūrvavṛtta*). The inquiry into Brahman does not depend upon an inquiry into religious duty (*dharma*), because it is possible for one who has studied the Vedānta but has not yet mastered ritual action to engage in the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedāntic texts. If it is argued that meditations such as those on the *udgītha*, which have ritual action as their substrate, are investigated in this very [work], and thus cannot be performed by one who has not mastered ritual action—then you are ignorant of the true nature of the Śārīraka-śāstra.

In this scripture, the knowledge of the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva-vijñāna*) is intended to be established for the purpose of removing false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), which is the root of all suffering for one who is submerged in the ocean of worldly misery—such as birth, old age, and death—caused by the perception of various distinctions created by beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*). For what use could the knowledge of ritual action (*karmajñāna*), which relies upon duality, be for this? On the contrary, it is indeed contradictory.

The inquiry into the *udgītha* and so forth, being of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*), is indeed performed here as a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karma*); however, it is not directly relevant [to the main subject]. Therefore, whatever has preceded [this inquiry] that is required by the primary scripture must be stated. Certainly; and what is required by it is precisely the knowledge of ritual action (*karmavijñāna*), because liberation is heard of [in scripture] as resulting from knowledge conjoined with ritual action. And the author will state: "And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse."

Furthermore, when the action to be expected is unknown, it is impossible to discern the distinction as to which [action] is to be combined and which is not; therefore, that alone must be the previously established [subject]. This is not correct, because... [the whole] is...

For ignorance is removed solely through the realization of Brahman as pure consciousness, which is opposed to all particularity; indeed, liberation is nothing other than the cessation of ignorance. How could ritual action—which is the locus of endless conceptual distinctions such as the specific castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), the goals to be accomplished, the means, and the procedures—be a means for the cessation of ignorance, which consists in the cessation of the perception of all duality? Moreover, the Śruti texts demonstrate that actions have perishable fruits and are thus antagonistic to liberation, while showing that knowledge alone is the means to liberation: "Finite indeed is his world... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.15].

There are such [scriptural passages] as: "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes"; "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"; "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed"; and "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death," and so forth.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that knowledge depends upon rituals such as sacrifices—that is useful only for the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) by way of purifying the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), through both the contradiction of the nature of the reality (*vastu-virodha*) and a careful consideration of the words of the scripture; it is not useful for the actual production of the fruit [of knowledge]. For we hear in scripture, "They desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*); and once the desire to know has arisen, the scripture itself declares that tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities are the direct means (*antaraṅga-upāya*) for the arising of knowledge: "Having become tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, one should see the Self in oneself alone."

Thus, when the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) arises in one whose impurities have been worn away by actions performed over hundreds of previous births without aiming for specific fruits, ignorance (*avidyā*) is removed through the knowledge arising from such scriptural statements as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second"; "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite; It is partless, actionless, and tranquil"; "This Self is Brahman"; and "That thou art. Furthermore, hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are the means conducive to the knowledge of the meaning of these sentences.

*Śravaṇa* (hearing) is the grasping of the meaning endowed with logical reasoning from a teacher who perceives reality, according to the Vedānta texts which establish the knowledge of the oneness of the Self. *Manana* (reflection) is the stabilization of that very meaning taught by the teacher within one's own self through reasoning, such as "this alone is logical. *Nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) is the uninterrupted cultivation of this same meaning for the purpose of dispelling the beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of duality that contradict it.

For one whose latent impressions of all distinctions have been dispelled by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other means, the knowledge of the meaning of the Great Sentence (*vākyārtha-jñāna*) removes ignorance; therefore, the prerequisite for such hearing must necessarily be stated. And that is this fourfold set of means: the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, the perfection of the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*), detachment from the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter, and the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*). Since the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) is impossible without these, it is understood—by the very nature of the subject—that this alone is the prerequisite.

This is what is meant: the root of bondage is precisely the perception of difference, which is unreal and rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*) that veils the true nature of Brahman. Bondage is unreal, and because it is unreal along with its root, it is removed by knowledge alone. And the knowledge that removes it is that produced by such statements as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). Regarding this knowledge produced by the statement, ritual action (*karman*) has no utility either in the production of its own nature or in its result; rather, the utility of rituals lies solely in the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

And since that [desire for knowledge] occurs through the increase of *sattva* by means of the eradication of the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*, which are the roots of evil—it is with this utility in mind that it was stated, "The Brahmins desire to know. Therefore, because ritual action is not useful for that [knowledge], one must state that the fourfold qualification (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) alone is what has preceded [the inquiry into Brahman].

The *Laghusiddhānta* states here: Regarding what was said—that liberation is indeed the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā-nivṛtti*) and that this occurs only through the knowledge of Brahman (*brahma-vijñāna*)—that is accepted. However, it must be investigated what the nature of the knowledge intended by the Vedānta texts for the cessation of ignorance is: is it merely the knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-jñāna*) derived from the sentence, or...

Is that root [knowledge] of the nature of meditation (*upāsanā*)? It cannot be knowledge produced by the [Vedic] sentence, because such knowledge is established from the sentence even without an injunction, and because the cessation of ignorance is not observed through that alone. Nor should it be argued that as long as the latent impression of duality (*bhedavāsanā*) has not been destroyed, the sentence does not produce the knowledge that removes ignorance; for even when [that knowledge] has arisen, the non-cessation of dualistic cognition for everyone all at once is no fault, just as the cognition of two moons does not cease even when the oneness of the moon is known.

Even though it has not ceased, [the misconception] does not lead to bondage because its root has been severed. This is because it is impossible for knowledge not to arise when the causal conditions are present; furthermore, even when contrary latent impressions (*vāsanā*) exist, we observe the arising of subverting knowledge through authoritative instruction, logical marks (*liṅga*), and so forth. Moreover, you cannot maintain that even when the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence exists, a cognition of difference continues to persist in some measure due to beginningless latent impressions.

Since the causal complex for the cognition of difference (*bhedajñāna*)—namely, the latent impression (*vāsanā*)—is itself of a false nature, it ceases precisely upon the arising of [true] knowledge; for even when knowledge has arisen, if that false impression were not to cease, there would be no other means to remove it, and thus that impression would never cease. To claim that the cognition of difference, which is the effect of the impression, continues to persist even though its root has been severed, is the talk of a fool.

It has been said: however, in cases such as the cognition of two moons, even when a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) is present, the false cognition does not cease because its cause—the ultimate defect of cataracts and the like—is not destroyed, since it cannot be subverted by cognition. Thus, the non-cessation of the false cognition is not contradictory. Yet, the effect, such as fear and so forth, ceases because it is subverted by a powerful means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, for those who maintain that the arising of knowledge occurs through the elimination of the latent impressions of difference (*bhedavāsanā*), the arising of knowledge will never be established.

Since the latent impressions of difference (*bhedavāsanā*) have been accumulated since beginningless time and are therefore immeasurable, while the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) that opposes them is minimal, it is impossible for the latter to dispel the former. Therefore, the knowledge denoted by terms such as "meditation" (*dhyāna*) and "worship" (*upāsanā*), which is distinct from the knowledge of the meaning of the [Vedic] sentences, is what is intended to be enjoined by the Vedānta texts.

And thus the Śruti texts declare: "Having understood, let one cultivate wisdom"; "Having known [it] through inquiry, one understands [it]"; "Meditate upon the Self as 'Om' alone"; "By perceiving Him, one is released from the jaws of death"; "One should worship the Self alone as the world"; "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"; "That is to be sought; that is to be desired to be understood"—and so forth.

Because of the unity of purpose with such passages as "one should meditate upon [it]" (*nididhyāsitavya*), and because the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence—as seen in expressions such as "having understood, one realizes" (*anuvidya vijānāti*) and "having known, one should cultivate wisdom" (*vijñāya prajñāṃ kurvīta*)—is an aid to meditation, the text first restates "having understood" (*anuvidya*) and "having known" (*vijñāya*), and then prescribes meditation through the injunctions "one should cultivate wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*) and "one realizes" (*vijānāti*).

The phrase "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because hearing is already established as a duty; for a person who has studied the Veda with the intent of grasping its meaning perceives that the Veda conveys purposeful knowledge, and thus he engages in hearing by himself in order to determine that meaning. Furthermore, since reflection (*manana*) is for the sake of stabilizing what has been heard, the phrase "it is to be reflected upon" (*mantavya*) is also a restatement. Therefore, only meditation (*nididhyāsana*) is enjoined here. And the author will state later: "Repetition [is required], because of the instruction more than once."

It is understood that this very act of knowing (*vedana*), which is intended as a means to liberation (*apavarga*), is *upāsana* (meditative worship), because we observe the interchangeability of the roots *vid* and *upās* in both the opening and the concluding sections [of the texts]. For instance, in the passage beginning with "One should meditate (*upāsīta*) on the mind as Brahman," it concludes with "He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, renown, and the splendor of Brahman"; and in the passage beginning with "He does not know; for this Self is incomplete; one should meditate (*upāsīta*) on it as 'This is the Self,'" it concludes with "He who knows what he knows—he has been told this by me. Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "Teach me, O Venerable One, that deity... [it continues] "anu ma etāṃ bhagavo devatāṃ śādhi yāṃ... [and so forth].

"You meditate upon the deity. And meditation (*dhyāna*) consists of an uninterrupted stream of memory, like a continuous flow of oil. This is because of the scriptural teaching that constant memory is the means to liberation: "Constant memory; upon the attainment of memory, there is the loosening of all knots. Furthermore, that memory has a form identical to direct perception (*darśana*), as evidenced by its having the same purport as [the verse]: "The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted when He, who is both high and low, is seen."

This being the case, by the statement "The Self, indeed, is to be seen," the fact that meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) possesses a form identical to direct perception (*darśana*) is enjoined. And through the intensification of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), recollection (*smṛti*) indeed takes on the nature of direct perception. All of this has been elaborated upon by the author of the *Vākya* [Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya]: "Knowledge (*vedana*) must be worship (*upāsana*), because it is so heard in reference to that [Self]."

In all the Upaniṣads, it is stated that "knowing" (vedana), which is prescribed as the means to liberation, is "meditation" (upāsana). Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the argument, "One should perform the cognition only once, because the purpose of the word has been fulfilled, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings," the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was determined with the statement, "But [it is] meditation, because of the word 'meditation'"; thus, knowing is resolved to be the means to liberation when repeated. Furthermore, in the aphorism, "Meditation is constant recollection, because of the [word] 'seeing' and from etymological derivation," the nature of that very same knowing—which is meditation and repeated—as "constant recollection" (*dhruvānusmṛti*) is described.

This very *smṛti* has been established as having the nature of vision (*darśana*), and its nature as vision is the attainment of direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*). Thus, he qualifies this *smṛti*, which has attained the state of direct perception and serves as the means to liberation: "This Self is not to be obtained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing; only by whomsoever this [Self] chooses him is He obtained; to him this Self reveals His own form."

By this, having stated that mere hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are not the means for attaining the Self, it was said: "He alone by whom this Self chooses, by him is He attainable. For only one who is most dear is worthy of being chosen; he for whom this [Self] is the unsurpassed beloved becomes His most beloved. It has been stated by the Lord Himself that the Lord Himself exerts effort so that this most beloved may attain the Self: "For those who are ever steadfast and worship with love..."

"I give them that yoga of discernment by which they come unto Me," and "For the knower is dear to Me, and I am dear to him. Therefore, for one whose remembrance—which is of the nature of direct realization—is itself exceedingly dear because the object remembered is exceedingly dear, he alone becomes eligible for being chosen by the Supreme Self; thus it is said that the Supreme Self is attained by him alone. Such is this very *dhruvānusmṛti* (constant remembrance).

It is designated by the word *bhakti*, since the word *bhakti* is a synonym for *upāsana* (meditation). For this very reason, it is stated thus in the Śruti and Smṛti: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death"; "Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here; there is no other path for the journey. "Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice... [I am not to be attained].

"It is indeed possible to see Me in this form, just as you have seen Me; by means of unswerving devotion, O Arjuna, it is possible to know Me, to see Me in this way in truth, and to enter into Me, O scorcher of foes. And: "That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion. Thus, sacrifices and other rites are the means for this constant mindfulness (*dhruvānusmṛti*) of such a nature.

Regarding the phrase "rites," it will be stated [in the Sūtras] that "because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. Although sacrifices and other rites are enjoined for the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), nevertheless, because that very knowledge—which consists of meditation, is performed day after day, acquires excellence through practice, and continues until death—is the means for attaining Brahman, all duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) must be performed throughout one's entire life for the sake of its production.

And he will say: "For even there [in the intermediate state], it is seen until the departure," and "But the Agnihotra and so forth are for that very purpose, because of the scriptural vision," and "And as a cooperative factor," and so on. Furthermore, the author of the *Vākya* states that the perfection of constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) arises from discernment (*viveka*) and the other means alone: "The attainment of that [remembrance] occurs through discernment, detachment, practice, action, auspiciousness, non-despondency, and lack of elation, because of their possibility and because of the etymological definition. He also describes the nature of discernment and the others: "Purification of the body from food that is not defective due to its species, source, or cause is discernment (*viveka*)."

The etymological explanation here is: "From purity of food comes purity of being; from purity of being comes steady mindfulness. "Liberation is freedom from attachment to desires"—this is the explanation. "One should meditate in a state of tranquility"—this is the explanation. "Cultivation of the object of meditation is repeated practice"—this is the explanation. Furthermore, the commentator has cited Smṛti as the etymological source for the phrase "always permeated by that state," and for the phrase "performance of the five great sacrifices and so forth according to one's ability" as the definition of action (*kriyā*).

The scriptural definition is: "This one who is active in [right] action is the best among the knowers of Brahman," and "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, and through austerity consisting of fasting. Also: "Truth, uprightness, compassion, charity, non-violence, and freedom from covetousness are the auspicious qualities. The scriptural definition is: "He is to be attained through truth," and "For them alone is that stainless world of Brahman," and so forth. "Dejection is a depression of the mind characterized by a lack of luster, born of the unfavorable conditions of place and time, as well as the recollection of objects of grief and the like."

The opposite of that is non-dejection (*anavasāda*). Its etymological definition is: "This Self is not to be attained by one who is devoid of strength. "Exultation (*uddharṣa*) is the contentment born from the opposite of that. The opposite of that is non-exultation (*anuddharṣa*); the meaning is that excessive joy is its contrary. Its scriptural definition is also: "Tranquil and self-controlled. Thus, it is stated that for one endowed with such restraints (*niyama*), the perfection of knowledge occurs precisely through the performance of duties prescribed for one's stage of life (*āśrama*). And so says another Śruti: "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together..."

"Having crossed over death by means of ignorance (*avidyā*), one attains immortality (*amṛta*) by means of knowledge (*vidyā*). Here, that which is denoted by the word "ignorance" is action (*karman*) prescribed for the [four] social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*). By means of "ignorance"—that is, by means of action—having "crossed over," meaning having cast off, "death"—namely, prior action that is an obstacle to the arising of knowledge—one "attains," meaning reaches, "immortality," which is Brahman, by means of "knowledge. Ignorance, understood as the means for crossing over death, is none other than the prescribed action distinct from knowledge, as it has been said: "Even he, relying upon knowledge, performed many sacrifices."

"Having taken recourse to the knowledge of Brahman, one may cross over death through ignorance. Action, consisting of both merit and demerit, is opposed to knowledge. Because it obstructs the arising of the knowledge of Brahman and results in undesirable fruits, both types of action are denoted by the term "sin" (*pāpa*). Furthermore, its opposition to knowledge occurs by way of increasing *rajas* and *tamas*, which are contrary to the pure *sattva* that serves as the cause for the arising of knowledge. And the opposition of sin to the emergence of knowledge is expressed [in scripture] as: "He alone causes one to perform evil action..."

This is understood from the Vedic scripture: "Him He leads downward. Furthermore, that rajas and tamas are obstacles to knowledge of reality as it is, while sattva is the cause of such knowledge, has been established by the Blessed Lord Himself in passages such as, "From sattva arises knowledge. Therefore, for the production of knowledge, sinful action must be eliminated. And its elimination is achieved through dharma practiced without regard for its fruits. Thus says the Śruti: "By dharma one wipes away evil."

Thus, since the knowledge that is the means for attaining Brahman depends upon the duties of all stages of life (*āśrama*), it follows that the knowledge of the nature of those required duties, as well as the knowledge that actions alone yield results that are limited and impermanent, must be derived from the *Karma-mīmāṃsā*. Therefore, that very [inquiry] which is required by the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) must be stated as having preceded it.

Moreover, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities and so forth will not be accomplished without hearing the Mīmāṃsā, because the nature of ritual action, its results, their permanence or impermanence, and the eternality of the Self are difficult to comprehend without a definitive determination of the specific fruit, the instrument, the procedure, and the qualified agent. Furthermore, the status of these as means is to be understood through application (*viniyoga*), and application is derived from direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and other criteria; and that [application] belongs to the third book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra].

The meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth, although intended for the success of ritual action (*karma*), consist in the vision of Brahman and thus depend upon the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, they must be considered right here [in this section]. Furthermore, since those very rituals, when performed without desire for their fruits, produce the knowledge of Brahman, these meditations—which bring about the excellence of those rituals—are all the more appropriately connected right here. And it is universally accepted that these depend upon the comprehension of the nature of the rituals themselves. This concludes the great prima facie argument (*mahāpūrvapakṣa*). As for what others have said—that Brahman alone, which is pure consciousness devoid of all distinctions, is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and that there is no manifold knower distinct from it—[that is incorrect].

All distinctions, such as the object of knowledge and the knowledge produced by it, are merely imagined and false within that very [Reality]. Thus, the Upaniṣads declare: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second"; "Now, there is the higher [knowledge] by which that Imperishable is apprehended—That which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet, eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, and imperishable; that which the wise perceive as the source of all beings"; "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite"; and "Partless and actionless."

"Peaceful, blameless, and stainless. He for whom it is not known has known it; he who knows it does not know it. It is unknown to those who understand, and known to those who do not understand. You cannot see the seer of seeing; you cannot conceive the thinker of thinking. "Bliss is Brahman. "All this is that which is the Self. "There is no diversity whatsoever here."

"He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity. For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another; but where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see? By what and whom should one know? "The modification is a mere verbal handle, not substantial; 'clay' alone is the truth. For when he perceives even the slightest difference in this [Self], then fear comes upon him. "Even in its various states, the Supreme does not possess both characteristics (of cause and effect), for it is everywhere [one]."

"But it is mere illusion, because its true nature is not fully manifested. That which has all distinctions subsided, which is pure existence alone, beyond the reach of words, and to be realized by the self—that knowledge is designated as Brahman. Its nature is knowledge, utterly pure from the perspective of ultimate reality; yet, due to erroneous perception, it appears to exist in the form of external objects. "In ultimate reality, you alone are one; there is no other, O Lord of the world. This which is seen as a material form is, in truth, you whose essence is knowledge.

Those who are not yogis perceive the world through deluded cognition; those of unawakened intellect, perceiving this entire world as having the nature of external objects, wander in the flood of delusion. But those pure-minded ones who know gnosis see the entire world as being of the nature of gnosis.

O Supreme Lord, they behold Your form; for that consciousness which exists as one and the same within their own bodies and those of others is indeed the ultimate reality. Those who perceive duality are seers of untruth. O best of kings, if there were any other whatsoever distinct from me, then it would be possible to say, "This is I" and "That is another. Just as the distinctions known as *ṣaḍja* and so forth arise from the differences in the holes of a flute, while the air pervading it remains non-different, such is the case with the Supreme Self.

"I am he, and you are he; all this is the very nature of the Self—abandon the delusion of duality. Thus addressed by him, that best of kings, possessing the vision of ultimate reality, abandoned all sense of difference. When the ignorance that produces differentiation has gone to absolute destruction, who could create a non-existent distinction between the Self and Brahman?

This is because the scriptures, which are intent on teaching the true nature of reality through such passages as, "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, dwelling in the heart of all beings," "And know Me also as the Field in all fields, O Bhārata," and "There is nothing, whether moving or unmoving, that exists without Me," declare that Brahman alone—which is non-dual pure consciousness—is real, while everything else is illusory.

Falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in being sublated by the knowledge of a thing as it actually exists, preceded by its non-apprehension, as in the case of a snake [superimposed] upon a substrate such as a rope. For that conceptualization occurs there due to a defect (*doṣa*). In the same way, this entire world—divided into gods, animals, humans, and plants—is superimposed upon the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is pure consciousness, by means of defects; it is false in nature and is to be sublated by the realization of the true nature of Brahman as it actually exists.

And the defect is beginningless ignorance (*anādya-vidyā*), which conceals the true nature [of reality] and causes various diverse distractions; it is indefinable as being either existent or non-existent. [This is supported by such scriptural passages as: "For they are veiled by untruth" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.3.2); "Of those truths that exist, untruth is the covering" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.6.1); "There was neither non-existence nor existence then; there was only darkness hidden by darkness, unperceived in the beginning" (*Ṛgveda* 10.129.3); "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 4.10); "Indra appears in many forms through his Māyās" (*Ṛgveda* 6.47.18); "My Māyā is difficult to overcome" (*Bhagavad Gītā* 7.14); and "When the individual soul (*jīva*) is asleep due to beginningless Māyā... (*Māṇḍūkya Kārikā* 2.18).

From such passages as "it awakens," it is understood that Brahman alone—which is non-dual pure consciousness—having its true nature obscured by beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), which is indeterminable as being either existent or non-existent, perceives a multiplicity within itself. As it has been said: "The Blessed Lord is of the nature of knowledge, since he is the form of all things and not a material entity. Therefore, know that the distinctions of mountains, oceans, the earth, and so forth, are but the expansions of consciousness. But when, upon the exhaustion of all karma, knowledge is pure in its own nature and free from defects..."

For then, the fruits of the tree of volition do not appear as distinct entities within objects. Therefore, O twice-born one, there is never any collection of objects whatsoever apart from consciousness. Consciousness is one; it is conceived as manifold by minds divided by the differences of their own respective karmas. Knowledge is pure, stainless, free from sorrow, with all attachment to greed and the like cast out; it is eternally one, the supreme, the highest Lord, Vāsudeva, than whom nothing else exists.

"In this way, I have declared to you the true nature of existence; knowledge is that which is real, while the other is unreal. Furthermore, that which pertains to the realm of worldly convention (*saṃvyavahāra*)—which rests upon the world—I have also explained to you. Regarding this ignorance (*avidyā*), they declare its cessation through the realization of the identity of the Self with Brahman, which is pure consciousness devoid of distinctions: "One does not see death again; he who sees that One does not see death," for when he [sees] this invisible, bodiless, indefinable...

"In the abode he finds fearlessness and a firm foundation; then, having attained fearlessness, he becomes [established]. "The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are severed, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. "Having known Him thus, one transcends death; there is no other path," and so forth—these are the scriptural passages (*śruti*). Here, by the word "death" (*mṛtyu*), ignorance (*avidyā*) is denoted.

As stated in the words of Sanatsujāta: "I declare negligence to be death; I declare constant vigilance to be immortality. And the realization of the oneness of the Self with Brahman—the non-dual nature of Brahman as determined by purificatory statements such as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" and "Brahman is Consciousness and Bliss"—is expressed in passages such as: "But he who worships another deity [thinking], 'He is one and I am another,' does not know; for this Self is incomplete; therefore, one should worship It as 'This is the Self,'" "That thou art," and "Verily, O Venerable One, I am Thou."

This is established by such scriptural passages as: "O Devatā, I am indeed you; O Blessed Devatā, that which I am, that he is; that which he is, I am. And this very point will be stated later: "But they approach [the Self] as 'the Self,' and they cause [others] to grasp it as such. Likewise, the author of the Vākya states: "One should indeed grasp it as 'the Self,' because everything originates from that. And by means of this realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, the cessation of bondage—which is illusory in nature and accompanied by its causes—is logically established.

Now, one might object: how can the removal of all distinctions—which contradicts perception—be effected by the knowledge produced by the scripture? Or how is it that the cessation of the [perceived] snake, which contradicts perception, is brought about by the cognition "This is a rope, not a snake"? If it is argued that in those cases there is a contradiction between two perceptions, whereas here there is a contradiction between a perception and a scripture rooted in perception;

Or, if two [cognitions] are equal, how can there be a relationship of the sublated and the sublator? If it is argued that this is due to the earlier and later cognitions being produced by defective causes versus the absence thereof, then this is equally applicable to scripture and perception as well. What is meant is this: in the case of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator, factors such as equality, dependence, or independence are not the cause, because perception cannot be set aside by the inference of a difference in flames. For in that case, the identity of the flame is apprehended by perception.

This being the case, when there is a conflict between two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that one whose alternative establishment (*anyathāsiddhi*) is possible is the sublated; whereas that which is established as having no other possibility and leaves no room for the other is the sublator. Thus, in all cases, the determination of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is made in this manner.

Therefore, it is entirely logical that the cessation of bondage—which consists of various conceptual constructions established by perception and other means of knowledge that are subject to doubt and have room for error—is brought about by the realization of the identity of the Self with Brahman, which is pure consciousness alone, self-luminous, eternally pure, free, awakened, and devoid of distinctions; a realization produced by the Śāstra, which is beginningless, endless, of uninterrupted tradition, and free from even a scent of possible defects. Furthermore, it is reasonable to maintain that the defect called *avidyā*—consisting of beginningless tendencies toward duality (*bhedavāsanā*) and so forth—is the cause of perception, which grasps the manifold world of diverse conceptual constructions.

[Objection: But surely, even for a scripture that is faultless due to its beginningless, endless, and uninterrupted tradition, there would follow the consequence of its sublation by such [scriptural injunctions] as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," which rely upon duality. [Reply: True; in the case of a contradiction between earlier and later [teachings], the scripture of liberation (mokṣa-śāstra) sublates [the former] precisely because, like the earlier scripture, it leaves no room [for the latter]. This same principle applies even to those scriptural passages within the Vedānta texts that are devoted to the meditation on Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahma), since the supreme Brahman is devoid of attributes (nirguṇa).

But how can the authority of those scriptural passages—which are intent on establishing the nature of Brahman, such as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are innate," and "He whose desires are true, whose resolves are true"—be sublated? [The answer is: by the force of the passages concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa*).

We reply: This is what is meant. Passages such as "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long," "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and "devoid of qualities, stainless," establish that Brahman is the eternally immutable consciousness from which all distinctions have been eliminated. Other passages, however, describe Brahman as possessing qualities (*saguṇa*). When there is a conflict between these two types of statements, by the very principle of the "subsequent annulment" (*apacchedanyāya*), the statements regarding the absence of qualities are more authoritative because they are independent of qualities and thus superior. Therefore, nothing is lost.

But is it not the case that in the passage, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite," qualities such as truthfulness and so forth are perceived? No, it is replied, because through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) there is the perception of a single referent. If it is argued that even when denoting multiple qualified attributes, a single referent is not contradictory, [we reply: the "beloved of the gods" (the opponent) is ignorant of the meaning of words. "Single referent" means the identity of meaning among all the words; for if one denotes distinct qualified objects, a difference in the meanings of the words becomes unavoidable due to the difference between the qualifiers.

Consequently, the state of having a single referent is not established. If that were so, all words would become synonyms, because they would express an undifferentiated object. Listen with an attentive mind: even when expressing a single referent, there is no synonymy. One—

Because the purport (*tātparya*) is determined to be [the knowledge] of a single reality, all the words possess meaning, convey a single referent, and are not synonyms, insofar as they aim at the state of being the opposite of that which is contradictory to the respective meanings of those words. This is what is meant: Brahman, who is to be realized through its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), possesses a nature that is the opposite of every other category of entity. That entire nature which is contradictory to Him is effectively excluded by these three words. Among them, the word "Real" (*satya*) is most meaningful, as it makes known that the one and only Reality—though appearing as the locus of modification—is in fact of a nature opposed to everything else.

Therefore, it is stated that Brahman alone is self-luminous and entirely devoid of all distinctions. When the meaning of the sentence is thus established, there is consistency with such passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second. This is the statement of the essential nature of Brahman—which is characterized as the cause of the world by such texts as, "From which indeed these beings are born," "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone"—that "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."

In this regard, according to the principle of all Vedic branches supporting a single conclusion (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*), Brahman—excluded from all things of its own class and of other classes—is understood as non-dual (*advitīya*) in all causal statements. The true nature of that non-dual Brahman, which is indicated as the cause of the world, must be explained in a manner consistent with that [non-duality]. The scriptural teaching of non-duality does not tolerate even a duality in terms of qualities (*guṇataḥ*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such passages as "stainless" (*nirañjana*) and "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*). Therefore, this defining statement (*lakṣaṇa-vākya*) teaches nothing but an undivided, single essence (*akhaṇḍa-ekarasa*).

But surely, if words such as "non-existent" (*asat*) were intended to set aside their own primary meanings and instead establish the nature of a reality excluded from what is contrary to those meanings, there would be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is not a fault, because the function of intention (*tātparya-vṛtti*) is stronger than the function of denotation (*abhidhāna-vṛtti*). For it is universally accepted that the intention of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) lies precisely in identity. But surely, figurative indication for all words has never been observed before. What of it? It is not observed even for a single word when it does not contradict the intention of the sentence.

Once it is determined that this is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the collection of words uttered together, then—whether two, three, or all of them are involved—the figurative function (*lakṣaṇā*) applied to even a single word for the sake of avoiding contradiction with that intent is not a fault. This is accepted by those established in the [Mīmāṃsā] scriptures. Proponents of the theory that the sentence-meaning is the primary meaning (*vākyārthavādin*) resort to the figurative function of all words in worldly sentences; for since the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers have their primary denotation (*mukhyavṛtti*) only in the unprecedented action (*apūrva-kārya*), the action to be performed (*kriyā-kārya*) is conveyed by the optative suffix through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

If it is held that for other words, which denote their own meanings as connected with an action to be accomplished, the primary meaning consists exclusively in being connected with an apūrva (unprecedented) action, then the presentation of [words] as denoting an action connected with an action would be merely figurative (lākṣaṇika).
Therefore, even the metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) of all words is not a defect, provided it does not contradict the intended purport of the sentence.
Consequently, the Vedāntas are authoritative precisely because they establish this very collection of meanings.

It has been stated that the scripture (*śāstra*) possesses superior authority when there is a conflict with perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the like. However, such superior authority must be asserted only when a conflict actually exists; yet no conflict is observed here, because perception grasps only Brahman as undifferentiated pure Being (*sanmātra*). But an objection may be raised: since perception has as its object various things possessing diverse forms—such as "the pot exists" and "the cloth exists"—how can it be said to grasp only pure Being? If there were no apprehension of distinct characteristics, all cognitions would have a single object, and consequently, they would serve merely as causes for a single conventional usage, just like a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-vijñāna*). True; this very point is being analyzed here.

How so? In the expression "the jar exists," both existence (*astitva*) and its distinction (*bheda*) are being communicated. Yet it is impossible for both these communications to have perception as their basis, because they are the results of cognitions occurring at different times, whereas perceptual cognition lasts for only a single moment. Therefore, one must discern whether it is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or the distinction (*bheda*) that is the object of perception.

Since the apprehension of difference necessarily depends upon the apprehension of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*) and the recollection of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), it must be admitted that the object [of such apprehension] is the thing's own nature; thus, difference is not grasped by perception. Therefore, the conventional usage of difference is rooted solely in error.

Furthermore, no such category as "difference" (*bheda*) can be defined by those learned in logic. Difference is certainly not the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the object; for if it were, then just as the usage of the object's own nature occurs when that nature is apprehended, the usage of its difference from everything else would necessarily follow upon the apprehension of that nature. Nor can it be argued that even when the nature is apprehended, the usage "it is different" depends upon the recollection of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), and thus, due to the absence of such recollection, there is no usage of difference at that very moment.

For those who maintain that difference is merely the distinction of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), dependence upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) cannot even be imagined; for there is no distinction between the intrinsic nature and the difference itself, both being the thing's own essence. Just as the conventional usage of "intrinsic nature" does not depend on a counter-correlate, the conventional usage of "difference" would likewise be independent. Furthermore, "pot" and "different" would become synonyms, just like "hand" and "palm. Nor is difference a property (*dharma*). If it were a property, its difference from the intrinsic nature would necessarily have to be admitted; otherwise, it would simply be the intrinsic nature itself. And if there were such a difference, that difference would also have another difference as its property, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*): the apprehension of an object qualified by genus and so forth occurs when there is the apprehension of difference, and the apprehension of an object qualified by genus and so forth occurs when there is the apprehension of difference.
Therefore, because difference is difficult to define, perception is the illuminator of pure Being (*sanmātra*) alone.

Furthermore, in such cognitions as "the pot exists," "the cloth exists," "the pot is perceived," and "the cloth is perceived," all objects are seen to be constituted by existence (*sattā*) and perception (*anubhūti*). Here, in all these apprehensions, pure existence alone is observed to persist; therefore, that alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). The particularities (*viśeṣa*), however, being subject to exclusion, are not ultimately real, like the snake [superimposed] on a rope. Just as the rope, as the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), persists and is thus ultimately real;

Snakes, earth, leaves, streams of water, and so forth, which cease to exist, are unreal. Now, one might argue that in the case of a rope-snake and the like, the unreality of the snake and other such things is due to their being sublated by the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum—the rope and so on—expressed as "This is a rope, not a snake," and not because of their ceasing to exist. Furthermore, the reality of the rope and such things does not stem from their persisting, but rather from their being unsublated. In this context, however, how can jars and other such things be unreal when they are unsublated?

It is said: An exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is observed in the case of a jar and so forth. It must be investigated what the nature of that [exclusion] is. Is it the absence of cloth and other things in the statement "the jar exists"? In that case, it is established that by the phrase "the jar exists," cloth and other things are sublated (*bādhita*). Therefore, exclusion is the cessation of the object which results from such sublation. That exclusion establishes the non-ultimate reality (*apāramārthya*) of those things being excluded. Like a rope, only pure Being (*sanmātra*), which is unsublatable, persists. Consequently, everything other than pure Being is non-ultimate.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Existence (*sat*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because it persists, like the rope in the case of the [illusory] snake and so forth; whereas jars and the like are not the ultimate reality, because they do not persist, like the snake [superimposed] upon its substrate, the rope. This being so, only the persisting experience (*anubhūti*) is the ultimate reality, and that alone is existence. [Objection: But surely "mere existence" (*sanmātra*) is distinct from experience, since it is the object of that experience. [Reply: Not so. For difference has already been refuted previously, both because it is not an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and because it is difficult to define.

For this very reason, even the status of being an object of experience for that which exists does not follow the path of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, existence is nothing other than experience itself. And that experience is self-established, because it is experience. If its establishment were dependent on something else, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it being non-experience, like a jar or similar objects. Furthermore, it is impossible to conceive of experience as depending upon another experience, since it shines forth by its very existence. For experience, while present, is never seen to be unmanifest like a jar or similar objects, such that its manifestation would have to be admitted as dependent on something else.

Now, one might argue that even when an experience has arisen, only the object appears—as in "the jar is experienced"—for no one, while knowing "this is a jar," simultaneously experiences the experience itself as a non-object, devoid of the "this-ness" (idam-bhāva). Therefore, just like the contact of the eyes and other sense organs, the mere existence of the experience is the cause for the manifestation of the jar and so forth; subsequently, the experience is inferred by means of the mark (liṅga) of a certain occasional excellence in the illumination residing in the object.

If it is argued that, in that case, consciousness (*anubhūti*), being non-inert (*ajaḍā*), would incur inertness just like its object, we ask: what is this so-called "non-inertness"? It cannot be the non-deviation of its own existence from manifestation (*prakāśa*), for that is possible even in the case of pleasure (*sukha*) and the like; indeed, pleasure and such are never found to exist without being perceived. Therefore, consciousness is not experienced by itself, because it is as impossible [for it to experience itself] as it is for the tip of a finger, while touching another object, to touch itself.

This is merely the product of one’s own imagination, arising from a failure to grasp the full power of experience (*anubhava*), because no manifestation (*prakāśa*) exists as a property of an object distinct from experience itself—unlike color and other such qualities—and because it is illogical to postulate a property called "manifestation" when all worldly transactions are fully accounted for by experience alone, which is accepted by both parties. Therefore, experience is not inferred; nor is it established by another cognition. Rather, experience establishes everything while being established by itself.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: experience (*anubhūti*) has its own properties functioning independently of anything else, because it is the cause for the application of those properties to another object through its relation with that object. Whatever is the cause for the application of a certain property to another object through its relation with that object is seen to have that property in itself independently of anything else, just as color and so forth are in their visibility and so forth. For color and so forth, while producing visibility and so forth in earth and other substances through their relation with them, do not depend upon a relation with color and so forth for their own visibility and so forth.

Therefore, experience (*anubhūti*) itself is the cause for both the self’s being manifest and for the linguistic usage "it is manifest. This very experience, which is self-luminous, is also eternal, because its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and other such states are absent. And that absence [of prior non-existence] follows precisely from its being established by itself (*svatas-siddhatva*). For the prior non-existence of experience, which is established by itself, cannot be apprehended either by itself or by anything else. Experience, while making known its own non-existence, [cannot do so] as long as it exists...

It makes [the absence] known. Since its existence is contradictory [to its own absence], its non-existence does not exist; how then could it make its own absence known? Likewise, even if it were non-existent, it would not make [itself] known; how could an experience that is itself non-existent be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its own absence? Nor can it be known through anything else, because experience has no other object-domain. A means of valid cognition establishing its prior non-existence would have to establish that absence by taking "this experience" (*anubhūtir iyam*) as its object.

Because it is established by its own nature (*svatassiddha*), it cannot be made an object of cognition as "this is it"; therefore, its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) cannot be known through any other means. Consequently, since there is no prior non-existence of this [consciousness], its origination cannot be asserted; and because origination is thus precluded, the other modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*) are likewise absent in it.

This unarisen experience does not tolerate even multiplicity within itself, because of the perception of what is contradictory to its pervading nature. For that which is unarisen is never seen to be manifold. Furthermore, since difference and the like are objects of experience, it is impossible for them to be attributes of experience, just as color and so forth are not. Therefore, precisely because experience has the nature of being experienced, there can be no other object of experience that is its attribute.

Since consciousness is that in which all differentiation has been shaken off, for this very reason there exists no so-called "knower" as its substrate distinct from its own nature; thus, it is consciousness itself, being self-luminous by nature, that is the Self. Furthermore, because it is non-inert (ajaḍa): inertness is pervaded by non-selfhood, and as this inertness is excluded from consciousness, non-selfhood is likewise excluded from consciousness.

[Objection: But surely the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtā*) is established by the cognition "I know. [Reply: It is not so; that [state] is established through delusion, just as the nature of silver is [superimposed] upon a fragment of mother-of-pearl, because it is impossible for experience (*anubhūti*) to possess agency with respect to itself. Therefore, just like the identification with a body characterized by humanity and so forth—which is entirely external [to the self], such as in the thought "I am a man"—the state of being a knower is also superimposed. For the state of being a knower is indeed the status of being the agent of the action of knowing.

Furthermore, how could that which is of the nature of modification, insentient, and situated within the knot of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)—a substance subject to change—possibly exist in the Self, which is the unchanging witness and pure consciousness? Since it is dependent on the Seer for its manifestation, agency and the like cannot be attributes of the Self, just as color and other such qualities are not attributes of the seer. Moreover, because the Self is experienced even during deep sleep and fainting when the notion of "I" has ceased, the Self is not the objective referent of the "I"-notion.

If the Self were admitted to be the agent and the object of the notion of "I," then, like the body, it would incur the unavoidable consequence of being insentient (*jaḍatva*), extrinsic (*parāktva*), and non-Self (*anātmatva*). It is well known among authoritative persons that the Self, as the enjoyer of the fruits of actions such as heaven resulting from those deeds, is distinct from the body, which is established as the agent and the object of the notion of "I. Likewise, it must be understood that the inner Self (*pratyagātman*) is the Witness (*sākṣin*), which is entirely different even from the knower who constitutes the referent of "I."

Thus, although the ego (ahaṅkāra) is insentient, it manifests that very nature of experience which is changeless; it manifests it by being its own substrate. It is the inherent nature of manifestors to manifest that which is to be manifested by residing within themselves. For instance, a mirror, water, a fragment of crystal, and so forth, manifest the face, the moon’s disc, or the universal "cowness" by residing within themselves. This error—"I know"—is produced by that [identification].

Do not say: "How can self-luminous experience be manifested by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which is itself inert and manifested by that [experience]? For it is observed that the palm of the hand, though manifested by the rays of the sun, acts as their manifester. Indeed, it is commonly seen that the rays of the sun passing through a lattice window become even more clearly manifest when they strike the palm of the hand, which is itself manifested by those very rays.

For this reason, this "I-sense" (*ahamartha*), which is the knower who thinks "I know," is not an ultimate attribute of the self that is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); therefore, it does not persist in deep sleep or liberation. For in those states, the self shines forth in its natural form as mere experience, devoid of any reference to the "I-sense. It is for this very reason that one who has awakened from sleep sometimes reflects: "Even me, I did not know."

Therefore, it is precisely this supreme reality—the eternally stable, uniform consciousness that is pure being alone, devoid of all distinctions and free from every conceptualization of difference—that, through delusion, manifests as the manifold and diverse distinctions of the knower, the known, and the act of knowing. Consequently, all the Vedānta texts are commenced for the purpose of attaining the knowledge of the identity of the Self with Brahman—which is by nature eternally pure and liberated—in order to eradicate ignorance, which is the root of that manifestation.

Therefore, this [view]—which is fashioned from the dregs of various fallacious reasonings that cannot withstand scrutiny—is to be disregarded by those who know the true nature of all means of valid cognition, such as perception, as supported by logic; for it is devoid of those specific qualities that cause one to be chosen by the Supreme Person taught in the Upaniṣads; its entire intellect is defiled by the impressions of beginningless sin; it has not mastered the true nature of words, sentences, and their meanings; nor has it understood the correct path of reasoning, which consists of the operation of all means of valid cognition like perception, along with their respective procedures and applications. To explain: Thus, indeed:

Those who maintain that reality is devoid of distinctions cannot state that "this" is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding a distinctionless reality, because all means of valid cognition have as their object reality possessed of distinctions. As for the convention established within one's own circle—that [reality] is established by one's own experience—that too is refuted precisely by the fact that experience, witnessed by oneself, is always of a nature qualified by distinctions. This is because every experience has as its object something qualified by some particularity, such as "I saw this."

Even when an experience is being experienced as possessing distinctions, if it is extracted as "without distinction" by some fallacious reasoning, it must be extracted by means of its own unique essential characteristics (svabhāvaviśeṣa) that exceed mere existence (sattā). Thus, by those very unique essential characteristics that serve as the causes for extraction—which exceed mere existence—the object remains precisely as something possessing distinctions. Therefore, since other distinctions are merely excluded from an object already qualified by certain distinctions, there is no establishment anywhere of an object devoid of distinctions.
For the nature of being an intellect and self-luminosity belong to cognitions because they are perceived as having the inherent character of illuminating objects for the knower.

Furthermore, we shall establish more thoroughly in its proper place that experience during sleep, intoxication, and fainting is indeed characterized by specific qualities (*saviśeṣa*). Moreover, there certainly exist numerous specific qualities such as permanence (*nityatva*) and so forth, which you yourself accept. And it cannot be established that these are merely the thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*); for even when the mere thing is accepted, disputes regarding its various modes and distinctions are observed, and one's own position is established by demonstrating those very modes and distinctions as one intends them. Therefore, one must state that the object is indeed qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) by those specific qualities that are supported by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).

Words, however, possess the capacity to denote only an entity that possesses specific qualities (*saviśeṣa*), because they function in the form of words and sentences. For a word-status (*padatva*) arises through the connection of a base (*prakṛti*) and a suffix (*pratyaya*). Since the base and the suffix have distinct meanings, it is inevitable that the word itself conveys a qualified meaning. Furthermore, the differentiation of words is based on the differentiation of their meanings. Since a sentence, which consists of a collection of words, expresses a specific relation between the meanings of multiple words, it lacks the capacity to convey an entity devoid of specific qualities; therefore, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not a means of valid cognition regarding an entity devoid of specific qualities.

Perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is divided into the categories of non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*), does not possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to an entity devoid of distinctions. Conceptual perception has as its object that which possesses distinctions precisely because its object is qualified by multiple categories such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth. Non-conceptual perception also has as its object only that which possesses distinctions; for it is the cause of the subsequent synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) of an object qualified by those very categories experienced within itself during conceptual perception. What is called "non-conceptual" is the apprehension of an object as dissociated from some particular distinction, but not...

[It is] devoid of all specific qualities (*viśeṣa*); for such a thing is never observed to be apprehended, nor is it logically possible [to do so]. Indeed, every cognition arises in the form "this is thus" by means of some specific quality. Since it is impossible to apprehend any object whatsoever without a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*), such as triangularity or having sides, the first apprehension of an individual substance among objects of the same class is called non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). The apprehension of a second and subsequent individuals is called conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

In that process, the universal nature (*anuvṛttākāratā*) of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth is not perceived during the apprehension of the first individual (*piṇḍa*). It is only during the apprehensions of the second and subsequent individuals that the perception of recurrence occurs. Since the state of being qualified by the property of recurrence—namely, the universal "cowness" and so forth, whose nature is the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of the object as connected with the first cognition—is to be determined through the apprehension of the second and subsequent individuals, the apprehension of the second and subsequent instances is conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

It is not the case that the persistence (*anuvṛtti*) of the form of the configuration (*saṃsthāna*), the genus (*gotva*), and so forth—which are objects of the treatises—is not grasped at the apprehension of the first individual (*prathamapiṇḍagrahaṇa*); rather, the apprehension of the first individual is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) because of the absence of conceptualization, and not because of a failure to grasp the configuration, the form, the genus, and so forth. Since the configuration, the form, the genus, and so forth are no different from the object itself in being perceptible by the senses, and since the cognition of the possessor of a configuration (*saṃsthānin*) is impossible without the configuration, even at the apprehension of the first individual, the object is grasped precisely as possessing its configuration, in this manner: "it is thus."

Therefore, in the apprehension of the second and subsequent individuals, the cowness and so forth are always perceived as qualified by the property of recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), just like the configuration and its possessor; thus, these [cognitions] are necessarily determinate (*savikalpaka*).
Consequently, perception never has an object devoid of qualifiers (*nirviśeṣa*).

For this very reason, the view that things are both different and non-different is also refuted everywhere. In the cognition "this is thus," how could the identity of "this" (the substrate) and "thusness" (the attribute) possibly be apprehended? In this context, "thusness" refers to a specific configuration such as a dewlap and so forth, while the substance qualified by that is the "this"-portion; the identity of these two is indeed contradicted by experience itself. For instance, even at the very first moment an object is perceived, it is perceived precisely as excluded from everything else. And this exclusion consists in a specific configuration, such as "cowness" and so forth.

This is because they are understood as being distinct. In every case where the relationship between a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and a qualified (*viśeṣya*) is apprehended, their absolute difference is made perfectly clear by that very cognition. In that regard, objects such as a staff or an earring, which exist in separate configurations and are self-contained, sometimes stand as qualifiers of another substance in certain instances. However, universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*), being themselves established as categories (*padārtha*) precisely through their configuration as the substance, exist as qualifiers of that substance.

In both cases, the relationship between qualifier and qualified is identical, and from that very fact, the cognition of their distinction arises as well. However, this is the difference: staffs and the like are capable of being perceived as existing separately, whereas universals such as "cowness" are, by necessity, incapable of doing so. Therefore, the claim that there is a contradiction in the nature of things is stated merely to deny the manner in which they are perceived; for the manner of perception—namely, "this is thus"—is universally accepted. This very point has been clearly established by the author of the Sūtras in the aphorism: "Because [contradictory properties] cannot coexist in one thing."

Therefore, since perception has a qualified object as its domain, and since inference also has as its domain a relationship perceived through perception and other means as qualified by specific attributes, inference too has only a qualified object as its domain. Even in disputes regarding the number of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this very same domain belongs to all those means of knowledge accepted by everyone; thus, no means of knowledge whatsoever can establish a featureless reality (*nirviśeṣa-vastu*). One who asserts that the very same reality is "featureless" despite the specific attributes inherent in the nature of things does not even realize his own contradiction in speech, like one who claims his mother is barren.

As for the claim that perception, by virtue of grasping only pure existence (*sanmātra*), does not have difference as its object, and that difference is indefinable because it cannot withstand conceptual analysis—that too is utterly refuted; for it is precisely an entity qualified by universals (*jāti*) and so forth that is the object of perception, and it is the universal and so forth themselves that serve as the basis for the linguistic usage of difference, both with respect to the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) and with respect to the entity itself.
