Just as in the case of cognition and as with form and so forth, because it is the cause of specific linguistic usage regarding another, you yourselves have accepted that it is also the cause of such usage regarding itself; this is certainly possible for difference as well. For this very reason, there is neither an infinite regress nor mutual dependence.

Even though perceptual cognition occurs in a single moment, since the specific nature of the object, its configuration, and [universals] such as "cowness" are apprehended in that very same moment, there remains nothing here to be grasped in a subsequent moment. Furthermore, if it were to grasp only pure existence (*sanmātra*), the empirical cognition of qualified objects—such as "the pot exists" or "the cloth exists"—would be contradicted.

Furthermore, if difference—characterized by the form, genus, and so forth of an entity that is distinct from pure Being—is not apprehended by perception, why does one seeking a horse desist upon seeing a buffalo? If pure Being alone is the object in all cognitions, why are all the words associated with the objects of those respective cognitions not remembered in each individual cognition?

Furthermore, since the two cognitions regarding a horse and an elephant would have the same object, the subsequent cognition would lack distinction from memory because it would be grasping what has already been grasped; thus, there would be no difference between them. If one were to admit a distinction in each cognition, then it would necessarily be admitted that perception has a qualified object as its domain. If all cognitions had the same object, everything would be grasped by a single cognition, which would lead to the absurd consequence that there are no such things as the blind or the deaf.

Furthermore, pure existence (*sanmātra*) is not apprehended by the eye, because the eye grasps objects that possess color, as well as objects inherent in the same substrate as those possessing color. Nor is it apprehended by the skin, since the skin has for its object only things that possess tangibility. The ear and the other senses likewise do not have pure existence as their object; rather, they have only specific objects characterized as sound, taste, and smell. Therefore, nothing is observed here that can be the apprehender of pure existence.

If the pure Being devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa-sanmātra*) were apprehended by perception alone, then scripture (*āgama*) concerning that object would merely be a restatement (*anuvādaka*), as its subject matter would already have been attained. Furthermore, the pure Being-Brahman would then fall into the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameya*). Consequently, you yourself have stated that it would follow that it is insentient (*jaḍatva*), perishable (*nāśitva*), and so forth. Therefore, perception has as its object only that which is qualified by distinctions characterized by genus (*jāti*) and the like, which consist of the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of things. This is because nothing distinct from configuration—such as a single form perceived through a uniform cognition across multiple individuals—is ever observed; and it is sufficient for the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of a genus such as "cowness" (*gotva*) to be established by that much alone.

Furthermore, since shape (*saṃsthāna*) is universally accepted even in the theory of "excess" (*atireka-vāda*), shape alone is the universal (*jāti*). Shape is defined as a form unique to itself; thus, one should understand shape according to the actual state of the object. Since the linguistic usage of "different" (*bhinna*) is possible through the apprehension of the universal alone, because no other distinct category (*padārthāntara*) is observed, and because even those who maintain the existence of a separate entity [as difference] must admit this, the universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth is itself difference (*bheda*). But [it may be objected]: "However—"

If difference were nothing other than genus (*jāti*) and the like, then upon the apprehension of that [genus], there would be the linguistic usage of "difference," just as there is the linguistic usage of that [genus] itself. This is true; for difference is indeed expressed through the linguistic usage of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth. For cowness and the like are themselves the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from everything else; because when cowness and the like are apprehended, there occurs the cessation of both the cognition and the linguistic usage of what belongs to the same class as everything else. Indeed, by the very apprehension of difference, non-difference is excluded.

However, regarding the linguistic usage "this is different from that," since the mention of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) depends upon that [other thing], it was stated that the usage "different" occurs in dependence upon the counter-correlate.

Furthermore, as for the claim that particulars such as jars and the like are unreal because they are excluded [from one another], that is a fabrication of delusion by one who has not considered the specific distinction between exclusion and persistence, nor the relationship between the sublated and the sublator. For the relationship between the sublated and the sublator exists only when there is a contradiction between two cognitions; it is only the sublated that is excluded. In this case, regarding jars, cloths, and so forth, there is no contradiction at all due to differences in place and time.

If, in whatever place and at whatever time the existence of something is apprehended, its non-existence is apprehended in that same place and at that same time, then, due to this contradiction, the stronger [cognition] acts as a sublater and the sublated [cognition] ceases.

There is no contradiction in the cognition of the non-existence of something experienced as connected with a different place and time when it is perceived to be absent in another place and time; how, then, can there be a relationship of the sublated and the sublator here? Or how can the cessation [of an object] in one place be said to entail its cessation in another? In the case of the rope-snake and similar illusions, however, since the non-existence is perceived precisely as being connected to that specific place and time, there is contradiction, sublation, and exclusion. Thus, the property of being excluded from other places and times is not seen to be pervaded by falsity; therefore, mere "being excluded" (*vyāvartamānatvamātra*) is not a reason for ultimate unreality.

As for the claim that existence (*sat*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) because it persists [through all states], that is already established and thus does not require proof; therefore, the entity is not merely existence alone. Furthermore, since the distinction between experience (*anubhūti*) and existent particulars (*sad-viśeṣa*) is established by perception through their relationship as subject and object, and since this is uncontradicted, the view that "experience alone is the existent" is also refuted.

As for the self-luminosity (svayaṃprakāśatva) attributed to experience: that applies only in the same way to the knowing subject, the Self, at the very moment it illumines an object; however, there is no rule that it must always be so for everyone. This is because another’s experience is an object of inferential knowledge based on signs such as avoidance or pursuit, and even one’s own past experience is seen to be an object of knowledge in the form of the cognition "I knew. Therefore, it cannot be said that "experience, being itself, is established by itself."

The claim that "if experience were itself an object of experience, it would cease to be experience" is also poorly argued; for it would follow that one's own past experiences and the experiences of others are not experiences, precisely because they are objects of experience. Furthermore, if one does not admit the inference of another's experience, there would be no grasping of the relationship between words and their meanings, resulting in the total collapse of all linguistic usage. Moreover, one approaches a teacher after inferring his possession of knowledge; yet such an approach would be impossible [under your view]. Nor does being an object of another [experience] entail the loss of its status as an experience.

What is called "experientiality" (*anubhūtitva*) is either the state of manifesting to its own substrate by its very existence at the time of its occurrence, or the state of establishing its own object by its very existence. And these two characteristics do not depart even when the experiences are themselves experienced by another experience, because they are established by the experience itself; thus, experientiality does not depart. As for objects such as jars, their lack of experientiality is due to the absence of this intrinsic nature, and not due to their being objects of experience.

Likewise, even if experience (*anubhūti*) is not itself an object of experience (*ananubhāvya*), the consequence that it would not be an experience (*ananubhūtitva*) is unavoidable; for things such as a sky-flower, which are not objects of experience, are not experiences. If you argue that the non-experiential nature of a sky-flower and the like is due to its non-existence (*asattva*) and not due to its being an object of experience, then you must likewise accept that for a jar and so forth, the very fact of not being opposed to ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the basis for their non-experiential nature, and not their being objects of experience.

If it is argued that if experience were itself an object of experience, it would follow—just as in the case of a jar—that it would not be opposed to ignorance; [we reply: even if it were an object of experience, it would likewise follow that it is not opposed to ignorance, just like a sky-flower. Therefore, the claim that "being an object of experience entails not being an experience" is laughable.

As for the rejection of the production of consciousness—which is self-established—on the grounds that its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth do not exist, this is like a blind man handing a staff to another blind man. It cannot be said that the prior non-existence does not exist because there is no means of apprehending it, for it is indeed apprehended by consciousness itself. If it is asked, "How can consciousness, while being existent, perceive its own contradictory non-existence at that very same time?"—there is no rule that consciousness must only take as its object what exists simultaneously with itself, for that would entail the consequence that the past and the future could never be objects of cognition.

Now, if you think that because the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth of an experience are established, there is a rule that they must exist at the same time as that experience—have you ever seen this anywhere, such that you assert such a rule? Alas! In that case, since it is established precisely through that very perception, the prior non-existence and so forth cannot be denied. And what sane person would claim that its prior non-existence exists simultaneously with it?

For this restriction of the nature of sensory perception—that it apprehends an object existing at its own time—does not apply to all cognitions or means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since in cases such as memory, inference, verbal testimony, and the yogic perception of practitioners, objects belonging to other times are observed to be apprehended. For this very reason, the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) of a means of valid knowledge with its object does not consist in a connection with an object existing at the same time as the cognition; rather, it consists in being connected with that which possesses a specific spatial, temporal, and other such characteristics.

Whatever object appears, it possesses a counter-nature to the falsity of such a form. Therefore, this [objection] is also refuted: "Memory does not have an external object, because memory is observed even when the object has perished."

Now, it might be argued: "The prior non-existence of consciousness cannot be apprehended through perception, because it is not present [at that time]. Nor can it be apprehended by other means of knowledge, due to the absence of a probans (*liṅga*) and so forth. Indeed, no probans pervaded by the prior non-existence of consciousness is perceived here, nor has scripture ever been seen to have that as its object. Therefore, its prior non-existence will not be established simply due to the absence of a means of knowledge.

If this is so, then having abandoned the power of being self-established (*svataḥsiddhatva*), you have descended into the absence of a means of knowledge; thus, the non-existence is established merely through the non-apprehension of the perceptible (*ayogyānupalabdhi*). Let your objection rest.

Furthermore, perceptual cognition, while establishing its own object—such as a jar—as existing at the time of its own existence, is not seen to make known that object's existence at all times; thus, the existence of the jar and so forth in prior and subsequent times is not perceived. And this non-perception [of their temporal extension] is due to the fact that cognition itself is perceived as being delimited by time. If it were the case that the cognition of the object, such as a jar, were itself perceived as unconditioned by time;

Even objects such as jars, which are the objects of cognition, would have to be eternal if they were perceived as unconditioned by time. If cognition were eternal and self-established, it would be perceived simply as "eternal. Yet it is not perceived in that way.

Similarly, if cognitions such as inference were perceived as unconditioned by time, they would manifest their own objects as also being unconditioned by time; consequently, all those objects would be eternal, being unconditioned by time, because the nature of objects conforms to the nature of cognition.

Furthermore, there is no consciousness whatsoever that is devoid of an object, because such is never apprehended. Indeed, it is precisely through its illumination of an object that the self-luminosity of consciousness is established. If consciousness were to lack the nature of illuminating an object, its self-luminosity would remain unproven; moreover, since experience cannot be experienced by another experience, consciousness would become as non-existent as a barren woman's son.

Nor can it be argued that in states such as sleep, intoxication, or fainting, consciousness alone shines forth, entirely devoid of all objects; for this is refuted by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible. If experience were experienced even in those states, there would be a recollection of it at the time of awakening; yet no such recollection occurs. [Objection: It is not observed that there is an invariable rule of recollection for an object that has been experienced; therefore, how can the absence of recollection prove the absence of experience? [Reply: It is said in response: [The rest of the passage continues with the argument regarding the nature of memory and its dependence on prior experience.]

Even in the absence of powerful causes such as the destruction of the body—which effects the obliteration of all latent impressions—the rule that there is no recollection establishes nothing other than the absence of experience.

The absence of experience is not established solely by the rule of non-recollection; for it is established precisely by the retrospective reflection of one who has awakened from sleep: "For such a length of time, I was not aware of anything. Nor can it be argued that even when an experience exists, there is a rule of non-recollection due to the absence of a defining object or the disappearance of the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense); because the non-experience of one thing cannot be the cause for the non-recollection of another experienced thing, nor can the absence of one thing be the cause for the non-recollection of another. Furthermore, it will be stated later that the referent of "I" persists even in those states.

But was it not previously stated that even in states such as deep sleep, there is an experience possessing specific qualities? True, it was so stated; however, that is an experience of the Self (ātman), and it will be established that this too possesses specific qualities. Here, however, consciousness (saṃvid) devoid of all objects and lacking a substratum is being negated. If it is argued that pure consciousness alone is the experience of the Self, we say no; for it will be demonstrated that such consciousness necessarily has a substratum.

Therefore, it cannot be asserted that consciousness is unproduced due to the non-establishment of its prior absence (prāgabhāva), on the grounds that "being existent, experience does not establish its own prior absence. By demonstrating the possibility of experience being an object of experience, the non-establishment [of consciousness] through other means is also refuted. Consequently, the claim that consciousness is unproduced because its prior absence and so forth are unestablished is not logically tenable.

Furthermore, the claim that the exclusion of other modifications follows from its non-arising is also untenable, because it fails in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). For even though that [prior non-existence] lacks birth, its destruction is observed. If one adds the qualification "among existing things" (*bhāveṣu*), then one merely displays one's own proficiency in logic. Consequently, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding your intended *avidyā*, for it is unarisen yet serves as the locus of various modifications, and it is finite upon the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

If you argue that all its modifications (vikāras) are unreal (mithyā), do you yourself admit the existence of even a single modification that is ultimately real (paramārthabhūta), by virtue of which this qualification [of yours] would be meaningful? For no such [ultimately real modification] is admitted.

Furthermore, the claim that experience, being unborn (*aja*), cannot admit of division within itself is also untenable; for the very Self, though unborn, is indeed distinct from the body, senses, and so forth. Moreover, since ignorance (*avidyā*) is admitted to be beginningless, its distinction from the Self must necessarily be accepted.
If you argue that this division is illusory in nature, have you ever observed anywhere a real division that is contingent upon birth?
If there were no real division of ignorance from the Self, then in reality, ignorance would simply be the Self.

By establishing the difference between visible objects through the proof of their perception as uncontradicted, the difference in the acts of seeing is likewise established, just as the difference in the act of cutting follows from the difference in the objects to be cut.

Furthermore, as for the claim that there is no visible object whatsoever belonging to this vision which is itself of the nature of vision—and that because they possess the quality of being visible, those objects cannot be attributes of vision—that too is rendered inconclusive by both [propositions] due to the attributes of eternality, self-luminosity, and so forth, which are accepted by you and established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor are these [attributes] mere consciousness, because their essential natures are distinct. For consciousness is indeed the illumination of some object toward its own substrate by its very existence.

Self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatā*), however, is the state of being manifest to its own substratum by its very existence. And "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) is the suitability for practical transaction (*vyavahārānuguṇya*) common to all things, whether conscious or unconscious. Indeed, eternality (*nityatva*) is the state of existing at all times; and oneness (*ekatva*) is the exclusion of any other number.

Even if those [attributes] such as insentience (*jaḍatva*) are of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvarūpa*), an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) remains unavoidable, because they are nevertheless properties belonging to consciousness (*caitanya*). In the case of consciousness (*saṃvit*), however, its opposition to insentience and the like exists as something distinct from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*); thus, if one does not admit a property—whether of the nature of existence (*bhāvarūpa*) or non-existence (*abhāvarūpa*)—then by the mere statement of their negation, nothing at all would have been said.

Moreover, is consciousness established or not? If it is established, it would possess the nature of an existent entity (*sadharma*). If not, it would be a mere nothingness (*tucchatā*), like a sky-flower and the like. If you argue that consciousness itself is its own establishment, then it must be stated: of whom, and with respect to whom? If it is not of anyone with respect to anyone, then it is not an establishment at all. For establishment occurs only of someone with respect to someone, just as being a son exists only for someone with respect to someone. If you say "of the self" (*ātman*), then what is this self? Have you not already said it is consciousness itself? True, it was so said; but it was poorly said. And thus:
How indeed could that consciousness, which relates to some collection of objects for a certain person by way of being their established form, experience its own nature as a self?

This is what is meant: "Experience" (anubhūti) is a specific attribute of the experiencing self, synonymous with terms such as *jñāna*, *avagati*, and *saṃvit*; it is transitive by nature, consisting in the capacity to render some object suitable for practical discourse (*vyavahāra*) through its very existence toward its own substratum. This is well-known and personally witnessed by everyone in such expressions as "I know the jar," "I perceive this object," or "I experience the cloth. Indeed, it is precisely because of this nature that its self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatā*) has been established even by you.
For this [self], which possesses an action and whose specific attribute is that of an agent, agency—as well as objecthood—is difficult to establish.

For instance: the permanence of this agent, as well as the arising, persistence, and cessation of the attribute of agency known as consciousness—such as pleasure, pain, and so forth—are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Regarding the stability of the agent, first of all, the recognition "this very same object was previously experienced by me" is established by the perception of re-cognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Furthermore, the arising and other states of consciousness—such as "I know," "I knew," and "my knowledge, which belonged to me as a knower, has now perished"—are established by direct perception. How, then, can there be identity [between these successive states]?
Thus, if consciousness—which is subject to momentary destruction—is accepted as the Self, then recognition such as "I saw this yesterday" or "I see this today" would not be possible;
for it is impossible for one person to recognize what was experienced by another.

Furthermore, even if one accepts that experience (*anubhūti*) is the self, the impossibility of recognition (*pratisandhāna*) remains as it was, despite its permanence. For recognition establishes an enduring experiencer who persists through prior and subsequent times; it does not establish a mere experience, such that one could say, "I myself experienced this previously. Even for you, it is not accepted that experience possesses the status of an experiencer; experience is merely experience itself.

It has been stated that something called "consciousness" (saṃvit), being devoid of any support or object, is impossible because it is absolutely unperceived. Furthermore, the claim that consciousness itself—which is accepted by both parties—is the Self is contradicted by direct experience. And the fallacious arguments intended to establish that pure experience alone is the ultimate reality have been refuted.

[Objection: But surely, that which is the non-"this" (anidam) element in the cognition "I know"—the reality of consciousness whose sole essence is luminosity—that is the Self (*ātman*). Since the referent of "you" (*yuṣmad-artha*), characterized by its being manifested by the power of that [Self], is established as the referent of "I" (*aham-artha*) in the cognition "I know," the referent of "I" must be distinct from pure consciousness and is indeed the referent of "you. [Reply: This is not so; for it would contradict the perceptual experience itself, in which "I know" occurs through the relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharma-dharmitayā*).

Furthermore: "If the referent of 'I' were not the Self, selfhood would not belong to the Self. For the referent of the 'I'-cognition is distinguished from the objective (parāg) referent by the 'I'-cognition itself. Desiring liberation, one engages in hearing [the scriptures] and other practices with the thought: 'May I become one who has cast off all suffering, who partakes in infinite bliss, and is self-sovereign. If one were to conclude that liberation consists in the destruction of the referent of 'I', such a person would recoil even from the mere scent of a discussion on liberation."
"Even when I have perished, some other cognition distinct from me will remain; thus, no one will make an effort to attain it."
For its existence, its nature as cognition, and so forth, depend upon its relation to itself; however, when separated from that relation to itself, even cognition itself cannot be established.

Just as cutting and the like cannot be established in the absence of both the cutter and the object to be cut, it is therefore certain that the referent of "I" (ahamartha) is indeed the knowing inner self (pratyagātman).
The Śruti says, "By what, O Maitreyī, would one know the knower? and "He indeed knows. The Smṛti also says, "He who knows this, him they call the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).

Furthermore, beginning with the Sūtra "Not the Self, because of scripture," the author of the Sūtras will also state: "Therefore, it is a knower; thus it is established that the Self is not mere consciousness (jñaptimātra)."

For the referent of "I" (*asmadartha*) is established by the notion of "I," while the referent of "you" (*yuṣmadartha*) is the object of the notion of "you. In this regard, the statement that the knower—who is established in the cognition "I know"—is the referent of "you" is contradictory in meaning, like saying "my mother is barren. Furthermore, this knower who is the referent of "I" does not have its manifestation dependent on another, because it is self-luminous (*svayamprakāśa*). Indeed, self-luminosity consists in having consciousness as one's essential nature (*caitanyasvabhāvatā*). Whatever has manifestation as its essential nature does not depend on another for its manifestation, just like a lamp.

For it is not the case that a lamp or the like lacks luminosity or possesses a luminosity dependent on another simply because it is illuminated by its own radiance. What then? A lamp has the nature of light; it shines by itself and illuminates other things as well through its own radiance.
This is what is meant: just as a single substance of fire exists in the form of both light and its possessor.

Although light (*prabhā*) is a quality of its possessing substance (*prabhāvaddravya*), it is nevertheless a luminous substance (*tejodravya*) itself and not a quality like whiteness (*śauklya*) and so forth. This is because it exists even elsewhere than in its own substratum, and because it possesses color (*rūpavattva*). Due to these points of dissimilarity with qualities such as whiteness, and because it possesses illumination (*prakāśavattva*), it is indeed a luminous substance and not a separate entity. Its status as "illumination" arises from its capacity to illuminate both its own nature and other things. Furthermore, its conventional designation as a "quality" is based on its constant dependence upon its substratum and its subservience to it.

Nor can it be said that the very disintegrated parts of the substratum circulating as they are called "light," for that would entail the consequence of the destruction of gems, the sun-gem, and so forth.

Furthermore, there would never be any cognition of a whole (avayavin) [in the case of a lamp]. For it cannot be said that lamps, whose very nature is to disintegrate, necessarily rise upward as a compact mass measuring only four finger-breadths, and subsequently spread out simultaneously in all directions—horizontally, vertically, and downward—in a single form while falling apart. Therefore, lamps together with their radiance arise and perish at every moment; this is understood from the sequence of the occurrence of their abundant causes and from their destruction upon the destruction of those causes.

The greater intensity of illumination, the greater intensity of heat, and so forth, in light near its own substrate are established by perception; just as fire and other things possess heat and the like, so too the Self is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) and has consciousness as its quality (*caitanya-guṇaka*). For being of the nature of consciousness is indeed self-luminosity (*svayaṃ-prakāśatā*).

For thus say the Śruti texts: "Just as a mass of salt has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a mass of consciousness"; "It is indeed a mass of cognition"; "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous"; "For there is no loss of the knower’s consciousness"; "Now, he who knows 'I shall smell this,' that is the Self"; "Which one is the Self? [and so forth].

"This person who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart"; "For he is the seer, the hearer, the taster, the smeller, the thinker, the knower, the agent—the person whose self is consciousness"; "O, by what means could one know the knower?"; "This person indeed knows"; "The seer sees neither death, nor disease, nor even suffering"; "He is the supreme person... not remembering this body into which he was born"; "In this very way, for this seer, these sixteen parts have the Person as their goal."
"Having reached the Person, they set," and "Different from this self consisting of mind is another inner self consisting of consciousness," and so forth. He will state [this further].

And [it is stated] in the *Pāṇini Sūtra*: "The knower (*jña*) [is so called] for this very reason. Therefore, this self is self-luminous and is indeed a knower; it is not mere luminosity. For if it were merely luminosity, its light would belong only to someone else, like the light of a lamp or similar objects. Consequently, consciousness (*saṃvit*) cannot be the self. Furthermore, those who know the meaning of words maintain that terms such as "consciousness," "experience" (*anubhūti*), and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) are relative terms (*sambandhi-śabda*). Indeed, in neither common usage nor the Veda is the use of verbs such as "he knows" (*jānāti*) observed without an object or without an agent.

Regarding the statement that "consciousness alone is the Self because it is non-inert," this must be asked: what is intended by "non-inertness"? If it is meant to be "the state of having luminosity dependent upon its own existence," then in that case, there is the fallacy of over-extension (*anaikāntya*) to lamps and the like. Furthermore, since you do not admit any property of luminosity distinct from consciousness itself, there is both a lack of proof (*asiddhi*) and a contradiction (*virodha*). Even the definition of "having a luminosity whose existence is never non-deviant" is refuted, as it is subject to deviation in the case of pleasure (*sukha*) and other such states.

If it were argued that even though pleasure and the like possess an invariable luminosity, they are nonetheless non-self because they shine for another, like a jar or other objects, and thus are insentient—then does cognition itself shine for itself? For that too shines only for another, namely the "I-sense" (ahamartha) who is the knower, just as one says "I am happy," so too one says "I know. Therefore, the quality of being insentient, defined as shining for another, is unestablished in the case of consciousness. Consequently, since it is established for its own self by its very existence, the "I-sense" alone, which is non-insentient, is the Self.

Even the luminosity (*prakāśatā*) of cognition depends upon its connection with that [Self]. For it is precisely due to that [connection] that cognition possesses manifestness toward its own substrate, the conscious Self—just as pleasure and the like do—and non-manifestness toward others. Therefore, the Self is not mere consciousness (*jñapti-mātra*), but rather the "I" (*aham-artha*) which is the knower (*jñātṛ*). Now, as for what was stated: that experience (*anubhūti*), being in reality objectless and supportless, appears through delusion as a knower—just as mother-of-pearl appears as silver—since an illusion without a substratum is untenable.

That is incorrect; for if that were the case, the "I" as the experiencer would be perceived as being in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the experience itself—just as silver and the like are perceived when they take on the form of a bright substance situated in front, such that one thinks, "The experience is I."

In this case, however, this experience, appearing as something distinct, qualifies the "I" (the self) as a separate entity, just as a staff qualifies Devadatta; for indeed, there is the cognition "I experience. Thus, while the cognition "I experience" manifests the referent of the word "I" as qualified by experience, how could it be asserted that—like the cognition "Devadatta with a staff" which rests on the staff alone as a qualifier—it has as its object merely the experience that serves as the qualifier?

As for the claim that even the status of being a knower is false—since the appearance of being a knower occurs only to one who possesses the conceit of identifying the body as the self, such as in the thought "I am fat"—that is incorrect. For in that case, even experience (*anubhūti*), which is itself identified as the Self, would have to be false, since it is perceived by that very same [agent] who possesses the conceit. If it is argued that experience is not false because it is not sublated by the knowledge that completely destroys all other [notions], then, precisely because it is unsublated, the status of being a knower is likewise not false.

As for what was also stated—that since the Self is changeless, its status as a knower, consisting in being the agent of the act of knowing, is not possible; therefore, knowership is of the nature of modification, insentient, and resides in the knot of the *ahaṅkāra*, which is a transformation of the unmanifest (*avyakta*) that is the locus of change—and thus knowership does not belong to the Self, but rather to the *ahaṅkāra* in the form of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); for agency and the like are attributes of the object of perception, just like color and other qualities.

If it is admitted that the Self possesses agency and is the object of the notion of "I," then it would follow—just as in the case of the body—that it lacks selfhood, is external, and is insentient; therefore, this [position] is untenable. For the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which consists of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is associated with insentience, being a transformation of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), being an object of perception, being external, and being for the sake of another; whereas the state of being a knower possesses a nature that is unique to consciousness.

This is what is meant: just as the body and so forth are distinguished from the seer and the knower—qualities which are the opposites of [the body's] properties such as being an object of sight and being external—by means of reasons such as visibility and externality; in the same way, the ego (ahaṅkāra), which consists of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), is also distinguished from that [seer] by those very same reasons, precisely because it is a substance.

Therefore, due to this contradiction, the ego cannot possess the status of a knower. Just as the status of being an object of sight is not admitted for the ego—which is itself an object of sight—so too the status of being a knower must not be admitted for the ego, which is an object of that [knowing].

Furthermore, the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is not of the nature of modification. For the state of being a knower consists in being the substratum of the quality of knowledge (*jñāna*). And for this eternal [Self], knowledge is eternal by virtue of being its inherent attribute (*svābhāvikadharma*). He will state this in such passages as, "The eternity of the Self [is established] from scripture," and so forth. Moreover, in the sūtra "It is a knower for that very reason" (*jño'ta eva*), he will state by the designation "knower" that the state of being the substratum of knowledge is inherent.

It has been stated that for this very consciousness whose nature is knowledge, it is not contradictory for it to have knowledge as its substrate, just as gems and the like have light as their substrate. We shall demonstrate that knowledge, though inherently undivided, is capable of contraction and expansion. Therefore, in the state of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), its essential nature is contracted by *karman*, and it exists according to the varying degrees of intensity corresponding to those respective actions. And that [knowledge] proceeds through the gateway of the senses.

This is established. It is with reference to this expansion of knowledge through the doors of the senses that the designations "arising" and "setting" occur. However, agency does indeed exist within the expansion of knowledge itself.

And that [agency] is not inherent; rather, it is produced by karma. Thus, the Self is of an unchanging nature. Since such a modification consisting of being a knower belongs to the Self whose very nature is knowledge, the possibility of the insentient ego (ahaṅkāra) ever being a knower is non-existent.

If it is argued that the existence of the ego (ahaṅkāra), though insentient by nature, is possible through the falling of its reflection upon consciousness due to the proximity of consciousness, then what is this "falling of the reflection of consciousness"? Is it the falling of the reflection of the ego onto consciousness, or the falling of the reflection of consciousness onto the ego? It cannot be the former, because subjectivity is not admitted in consciousness. Nor can it be the latter, because, as stated, that which is insentient cannot possess subjectivity. Furthermore, neither of the two is visible to the eye; for the reflection of non-visible objects is never observed.

Now, [the opponent might argue] that just as a lump of iron acquires heat through contact with fire, so too does the apprehension of being a knower arise in consciousness (*cit*) through its contact [with the ego]. This is not so; for since knowership is not admitted to exist in consciousness in reality, there can be no knowership or apprehension of it in the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) due to such contact. Furthermore, since knowership is impossible for the non-conscious ego, it is all the more impossible for knowership or its apprehension to exist in consciousness through contact with it.

As for what was also said—that in neither case does cognitive agency (jñātṛtva) exist in reality, but rather the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is a manifestor of consciousness (anubhūti) that manifests consciousness as it resides within itself, just like a mirror and so forth—that is incorrect. For it is impossible for the Self, which is self-luminous, to be manifested by the ego-sense, whose nature is insentient (jaḍa). As it has been said: "Just as a glowing charcoal cannot manifest the sun, it is not logical to say that the insentient ego-sense manifests the Self, which is self-luminous."

Thus [it is said]. For all objects have their establishment dependent upon self-luminous experience (*anubhava*). In that regard, the knowers of the Self (*ātmavid*) mock [the opponent] who claims that the insentient ego (*ahaṅkāra*), whose own manifestation depends on that [experience], manifests the experience which has a nature of manifestation that neither rises nor sets and which is the cause for the establishment of all objects. Furthermore, because there is a contradiction between the natures of the ego and experience, and because it would follow that experience itself would lack the status of being experienced, they cannot stand in the relationship of manifester and manifested. As it has been said: "There can be no mutual relationship of manifester and manifested due to their opposition."

"If it were [merely] manifestable (*vyaṅgya*), it would lack the nature of self-experience, just as a jar does. Nor is it more correct to say that consciousness is manifested by the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), which is itself manifested by consciousness—just as the rays of the sun are manifested by the palm of the hand which is manifested by those very rays; for even in that case, the rays of the sun are not manifested by the palm. Rather, when their movement is obstructed by the palm, the rays themselves become much more clearly perceived; thus, because the palm is merely the cause of that increased intensity, it is not a "manifestor" (*abhivyañjaka*).

Furthermore, what is the nature of the manifestation of this Self, whose essence is consciousness, which is brought about by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth? It cannot be its production, because it is admitted to be self-established and therefore not producible by anything else. Nor can it be its illumination, because that [manifestation] cannot be experienced by another experience.

For that very reason, there is no assistance rendered to the means of experiencing that [object]. For such assistance is twofold: either by being the cause of the connection between the sense organ and the object to be known—as, for example, individuals, mirrors, and so forth are the causes of the connection between the eyes and other senses in the perception of universals (*jāti*), faces, and the like; or by the removal of the impurities residing in the knower—as, for example, tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth, assist the scripture which is the means for realizing the supreme reality (*paratattva*). As it has been said: "Because the [internal] instruments have no objective ground, they do not serve as the cause of connection with that [reality]."

Furthermore, even if one accepts that experience (*anubhūti*) is itself an object of experience (*anubhāvya*), it is not easy to explain how the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) assists in the means of that experience. For such assistance would have to occur by removing an obstacle to the arising of the experience of the object, just as a lamp assists the eye by removing the deep darkness that obstructs the perception of color and other forms. However, no such thing to be removed is conceivable here. First of all, there exists nothing residing in the self that obstructs the arising of the knowledge of consciousness and which could be dispelled by the "I-sense."

If it is argued that ignorance (*ajñāna*) exists, we say no; for it is accepted that ignorance is to be dispelled by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). Indeed, knowledge alone is the remover of ignorance. Furthermore, it is impossible for ignorance to have consciousness (*saṃvit*) as its substratum, because [ignorance] must share the same substratum and the same object as knowledge. Ignorance cannot exist in the pure Witness (*sākṣin*), which is mere knowledge devoid of both the state of being a knower and an object. Just as objects such as a jar cannot be the substratum of ignorance because they lack the possibility of being a substratum for knowledge, so too mere knowledge cannot be the substratum of ignorance, as it lacks the status of being a substratum for knowledge.

Even if it were admitted that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is the locus of ignorance (*ajñāna*), since it is admitted to be the Self (*ātman*), it cannot be the object of knowledge; therefore, ignorance residing therein cannot be removed by knowledge. For knowledge removes ignorance only with respect to its own object, as in the case of a rope and the like. Consequently, ignorance whose locus is consciousness could never be destroyed by anything at any time. Furthermore, it will be explained later that the very nature of this ignorance—which is indefinable as being either existent or non-existent—is itself difficult to determine.

Furthermore, since ignorance, which consists of the prior non-existence of knowledge, lacks the capacity to obstruct the arising of knowledge, there can be no assistance to the means of that knowledge by way of its removal.
Therefore, in no way whatsoever can there be a manifestation of experience through the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).

Furthermore, it is not the nature of manifestors to manifest that which is to be manifested by being its own substratum, for this is not observed in the case of lamps and the like. Moreover, both cognition and its means possess a nature conducive to the apprehension of objects as they truly exist, as does that which assists them. And this is established by the reasoning of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*). Nor is a mirror or the like a manifestor of a face and so forth; rather, it is the cause of a defect consisting in the reflection of ocular light. And the appearance there as something else is produced by that defect.

Light and the like are indeed the manifestors [of objects]. However, in this case, it is not possible to attribute such a defect to consciousness (*saṃvit*), which is self-luminous, by means of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*). For a genus (*jāti*) is the form (*ākāra*) of an individual (*vyakti*), and thus its cognition occurs as having that [individual] as its substratum; it does not occur because it is manifested by the individual. Therefore, since consciousness is perceived as residing within the ego—which is itself a product of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—there is no cause for this, whether real or due to a defect. Thus, the ego is not the knower, nor is there such a perception [of consciousness as belonging to it].

Therefore, it is the "I-sense" (ahamartha) alone, established as the knower by its very nature, that is the inner self (pratyagātman), and not mere consciousness (jñapti) alone. For it has been stated that when the sense of "I" disappears, even consciousness cannot be established as the inner self.

Even though there is an absence of a distinct and clear manifestation of the "I" (ahamartha) due to the suppression of the quality of *tamas* and the lack of experience of external objects, the "I-sense" does not disappear even in deep sleep; for until awakening, the Self continues to manifest with the single form of "I. Therefore, it must be admitted that your own favored *anubhūti* (consciousness) likewise manifests in that very same way.

Indeed, no one who has awakened from sleep reflects upon an experience simultaneous with their sleep in such a form as: "I exist as the witness of ignorance, a cognition whose nature is opposed to any other object distinct from the sense of 'I' (ahambhāva). For the reflection of one who has awakened from sleep is precisely this: "I slept happily. By this very recollection, it is understood that even at that time, the self, which is the referent of "I," possessed both happiness and the status of a knower.

Nor should it be argued that the realization [of the Self] at that time must be such that it is as pleasant as it is now; for such a realization does not possess that form. Furthermore, there is no impossibility of the self—the referent of the "I"—recalling its state of happiness at that time on account of its instability; because one who has awakened from deep sleep reflects upon what was experienced prior to the state of deep sleep, thinking: "This was done by me, this was experienced by me, and I said this (or that)."

If it is argued that one reflects, "For all this time I did not know anything," then what of it? If you claim that "nothing" is a total negation, we say no; for in the reflection "I did not know," the "I"—the subject who knows—persists. That negation refers only to the object known. If the negation "nothing" were to have a total scope, then even the "experience" (anubhūti) favored by you would be negated.

At the time of deep sleep, however, having reflected upon the self as the knower—the referent of the "I"—in the form "I," and then negating its cognition in the statement "I did not know anything," one establishes by this very reflection, "I did not know anything," the non-establishment of the knower who persists through that time as the referent of the "I," while simultaneously establishing the existence of the cognition that was being negated at that time; let him establish this point for the gods themselves!

If you argue that at that time there is also the non-apprehension of the object "I," expressed as "I did not know even myself," then you do not even realize the contradiction between your own experience and your own words. For the experience and the statement are: "I [did] not know me. If you ask, "What is being negated by the word 'me'? you have asked well; to that it is replied: [The answer follows: It is the "I-ness" (*ahantva*) residing in the substrate of the "I" that is negated. This is because the cognition "I am not" is produced by the absence of the cognition "I am. Furthermore, since the cognition "I am" is produced by the presence of the cognition "I," the cognition "I am not" is produced by the absence of that very cognition. Therefore, the cognition "I am not" is indeed produced by the absence of the cognition "I am. Thus, the cognition "I am not" is produced by the absence of the cognition "I am"; it is not produced by the absence of the cognition "I know myself. Consequently, the cognition "I am not" does not negate the "I" itself, but rather negates the "I-ness" residing in the substrate of the "I. Therefore, the cognition "I am not" does not negate the "I" itself. Consequently, the claim that the "I" is not apprehended at that time is refuted. Also, the cognition "I am not" is produced by the absence of the cognition "I am," and not by the absence of the cognition "I know myself. Therefore, the cognition "I am not" does not negate the "I" itself. Thus, the claim that the "I" is not apprehended at that time is refuted. Because the knowing subject, whose essence is the referent "I" (*ahamartha*), persists, its essential nature is not negated; rather, what is negated at the time of awakening is this referent "I" as characterized by caste, stage of life, and so forth. When it is said, "I did not know myself," the object must be discerned. The object of the portion "myself" (*mām*) is the referent "I" (*asmadartha*) as characterized by birth and other attributes, which is integrated with the waking state. [The object] is that which is known solely through the clear self-experience established in the state of deep sleep (*svāpyaya*).

And the "I" that is the substrate of the aspect "I am" is the object [of the ego-consciousness]. In this regard, the manner of one's own experience is precisely: "While asleep, I was such-and-such; I did not even know myself as 'I'."

Furthermore, according to your own system, the Self exists in deep sleep as the witness (*sākṣin*) of ignorance. And witnessing consists precisely in being a direct knower (*sākṣājjñātṛtva*); for one who does not know cannot be a witness. Indeed, in both common usage and the Vedas, it is only a knower who is designated as a "witness," not mere consciousness (*jñānamātra*). The venerable Pāṇini also records this in the rule "sākṣāddraṣṭari saṃjñāyām," whereby the word *sākṣin* applies only to one who directly knows.

And since this witness, being perceived as "I know," is indeed the referent of the word "I," how could it be that the referent of "I" is not perceived at that time? Since the Self, manifesting by itself, manifests precisely as "I," it is established that even in states such as deep sleep, the Self, while shining forth, manifests as "I."

As for the claim that the referent of "I" (ahamartha) does not persist in the state of liberation—that is untenable. If that were so, liberation would effectively be the destruction of the self (ātman), which would be asserted under another guise. Furthermore, the referent of "I" is not a mere attribute (dharma); if it were, then even upon its disappearance, the self’s true nature (svarūpa) would remain just as it does when ignorance (avidyā) ceases. On the contrary, the referent of "I" is the very essence of the self, while cognition (jñāna) is its attribute, precisely because cognition is perceived as an attribute of the referent of "I" in such cognitions as "I know" and "knowledge has arisen in me."

Furthermore, one who—whether from the perspective of ultimate reality or through delusion—considers himself afflicted by internal and other forms of suffering, thinking "I am suffering," and who has developed a longing for liberation (mokṣarāga), thinking, "How might I become free from agitation and established in well-being, having eliminated this entire mass of suffering so that it never arises again?"—it is precisely such a person who engages in its means. If, through the performance of those means, he were to realize, "I myself shall no longer exist," he would surely withdraw from the very discussion of liberation.

Consequently, due to the very absence of a qualified person (adhikārin), the entire scripture on liberation would lack authority. If it is argued that "mere luminosity, characterized by 'I', remains in liberation," what is the point of this? For no one acting with intelligence would exert effort with the thought, "Even when I have perished, some mere luminosity remains in liberation. Therefore, since the status of being the inner self (pratyagātmatva) is established only for the referent of "I" as the knower, [the self must persist].

And that inner self (pratyagātman) shines forth as "I" even in liberation, because it shines for itself. Whatever shines for itself shines as "I"; just as the transmigrating self, which appears in such a manner, is accepted by both parties [of the debate]. On the other hand, whatever does not shine as "I" does not shine for itself, like a jar or similar objects. This liberated self, however, shines for itself; therefore, it shines forth precisely as "I."

Nor does the fact that it manifests as "I" entail for it the consequence of being ignorant or a transmigrating soul (saṃsārin), because that would contradict liberation and because the notion of "I" is not a cause of ignorance and so forth. Ignorance consists either of non-cognition of one's own nature, or cognition otherwise, or contrary cognition. Since the notion of "I" is essentially the cognition of the Self's own nature—given that "I" is indeed the very nature of the Self—it does not produce ignorance; how much less could it produce transmigratoriness? On the contrary, because it is opposed to it, it destroys it entirely.

Furthermore, even for Vāmadeva and others who have completely eradicated all ignorance through the direct realization of the Self as Brahman, we observe that they experience the Self as "I. For it is heard in scripture: "Seeing this very [Self], the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I was Manu and the Sun,'" and "I alone existed in the beginning, and I exist now, and I shall exist in the future," and so forth.

"The conventional usage of the Supreme Brahman—which is opposed to all other ignorance and is the sole object of the notion and word 'Being' (sat)—is likewise [as follows]: 'Alas! I shall enter these three deities'; 'May I become many; may I procreate'; 'He reflected, "Shall I now create the worlds?"'; and similarly, 'Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable.'"

Thus, in such passages as: "Therefore, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama"; "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa"; "Never was I not, nor you, nor these lords of men"; "I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe"; "I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds"; "I am the deliverer from the ocean of the mortal cycle of birth and death"; "I am the father who provides the seed"; and "I know the past that has passed away," and so forth.

If the very nature of the Self is indeed "I" (aham), how then is the inclusion of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) within the field (kṣetra) taught by the Blessed One in the passage: "The great elements, the ego-sense, the intellect, and the unmanifest"? It is said in reply: Since in all teachings concerning the essential nature [of the Self], it is taught as "I," and since the nature of the Self is realized exactly in that way, "I" alone is the nature of the inner Self (pratyagātman). However, the Blessed One himself teaches that the ego-sense—which is a specific modification of the unmanifest—is included within the field. But that [ego-sense] is... [unmanifest].

In the self—that is, the body—it is called *ahaṅkāra* because it is the cause of the manifestation of the notion of "I. The etymology of this word *ahaṅkāra* should be understood by deriving the suffix *cvipratyaya* in the sense of "becoming that which it was not before" (*abhūtatadbhāve*). However, this very same *ahaṅkāra*, when it is the cause of insulting superior persons and is synonymous with pride (*garva*), is frequently taught in the scriptures as something to be abandoned. Therefore, the notion of "I" (*ahambuddhi*) that is free from sublation has the Self itself as its direct object; whereas the notion of "I" whose object is the body is merely ignorance (*avidyā*).

As stated by the Blessed Lord Parāśara: "Listen also, O delighter of your lineage, to the true nature of ignorance (*avidyā*): it is the notion of 'self' with regard to that which is not the self. If the self were merely consciousness (*jñapti*), then in the conceit of self regarding what is not the self—such as the body—there would appear only mere consciousness, and not the appearance of being a knower (*jñātṛ*). Therefore, the self is the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) which is the knower. As it has been said: "Therefore, because it is established through direct perception, and because it conforms to the aforementioned logic and scripture, the self appears as the knower, as 'I', due to its association with ignorance."

And thus it is said: "The Self is distinct from the body, senses, mind, vital breath, and intellect; it has no other means [of manifestation]; it is eternal, all-pervasive, different in every field, and by its very nature blissful.
"Having no other means" means self-luminous. "All-pervasive" means that, due to its extreme subtlety, its essential nature is to enter within all insentient things.

As for what was stated—that because it has its root in a defect (*doṣa*), there is the possibility of its being otherwise established, and thus perception which apprehends all forms of difference is sublated by scripture—it must be explained: what is this defect, by virtue of having which as its root perception is otherwise established? If it is argued that "the very latent impression (*vāsanā*) of beginningless difference is the defect," then one must ask: has it ever been known elsewhere that the impression of difference, like cataracts (*timira*) and so forth, is the cause of a cognition contrary to the object as it actually exists? If it is argued that "this will be known precisely through this contradiction with scripture," we say no.

Because they are mutually dependent: the certainty that the scripture teaches a reality devoid of all particularity depends upon the certainty that the latent impression of difference (*bhedavāsanā*) is a defect; and the certainty that the latent impression of difference is a defect depends upon the certainty that the scripture teaches a reality devoid of all particularity. Furthermore, if perception has a contrary object because it is rooted in the latent impression of difference, then the scripture would likewise have a contrary object for being rooted in that same impression.

Now, if it be argued that even though the scripture is rooted in defects, it sublates perception because it is superior as the cause of the knowledge that negates all distinctions apprehended by perception—that is not so; for once it is known that [the scripture] is rooted in defects, its superiority is of no avail. This is seen from the fact that when someone who is known to be deluded is afraid due to the cognition of a snake in a rope, his fear does not cease even when another person tells him, "This is not a snake; do not be afraid."

Furthermore, the fact that the scripture is rooted in defects was known at the very moment of hearing it. This is because reflection (*manana*) and the other stages consist in the repeated practice of the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, which sublates all differences understood through hearing. Moreover, by whom has this been understood by you: that "this scripture is free from possible defects, whereas perception is subject to possible defects"? Certainly not the self-evident experience (*anubhūti*), which is devoid of all distinctions, that can make this point known; for that [experience] is detached from all objects.

Furthermore, because they lack partiality toward their own scriptures, [their position is untenable]. Nor is there sensory perception (*pratyakṣa*), since it possesses a contrary object due to its being rooted in defects. Precisely because it is rooted in that [sensory perception], the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are likewise excluded. Therefore, since they do not accept the means of valid cognition that would establish their own position, their desired objective cannot be proven.

[Objection: Is it not the case that even for us, there exists the conventional practice of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*)? [Reply: What is this so-called "conventional" (*vyāvahārika*)? [Objection: It is that which is established by immediate cognition (*āpātapratīti*), but which, when examined through reasoning (*yukti*), is found not to exist in that way. [Reply: What is the use of that? For even if something is accepted as a means of knowledge, it lacks the function of a means of knowledge precisely because it is sublated by reasoning.

Now, it might be argued: even though both scripture (*śāstra*) and perception (*pratyakṣa*) are rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), we observe that the object of perception is sublated by scripture; whereas the object of scripture—the non-dual Brahman as Being—never undergoes subsequent sublation, and thus Brahman, which is mere attributeless pure experience, is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This is incorrect, because even that which is not sublated is determined to be non-ultimate if it is rooted in a defect (*doṣa*). This is what is meant: suppose there were a person suffering from ophthalmia (*taimira*) living in mountain caves inaccessible to others, who is free from all other defects such as cataracts, yet remains unaware of his own ophthalmia.

For everyone whose own darkness has been dispelled, the cognition of two moons arises without distinction due to the non-specificity of the defect of *timira*. Since there is no subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) in that case, it is not the case that [the cognition] is not false; thus, the duality of the moon—which is the object of that cognition—is also indeed false. For a defect (*doṣa*) is the cause of knowledge that does not correspond to reality. Likewise, the knowledge of Brahman, although devoid of a subverting cognition because its root is ignorance (*avidyā*), is false together with its object, Brahman.

And there are the following formal arguments (prayoga) in this regard: Brahman, which is the subject of dispute, is false, because it is the object of knowledge produced in one possessed of ignorance, like the phenomenal world (prapañca). Brahman is false, because it is an object of knowledge, like the phenomenal world. Brahman is false, because it is the object of knowledge produced by an unreal cause, just like the phenomenal world.

Nor should it be argued that, just as the unreal cognition of elephants and so forth in a dream serves as a cause for the apprehension of ultimate good or evil despite being rooted in ignorance, so too there is no contradiction in a scripture—though itself unreal—serving as a cause for the apprehension of Brahman, which is ultimately real, provided it is rooted in ignorance; for the dream-cognition is not unreal. In that case, it is only the objects that are false; for it is only those objects whose sublation is observed, not the cognition itself.

No one ever forms the conviction that even the cognition experienced during the state of dreaming does not exist at all; rather, it is the perception itself that exists, while the conviction that "the objects do not exist" is the sublating cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*). Furthermore, the illusory cognition produced by a magician through mantras, herbs, and so forth—which consists of illusion—is indeed real, as it is the cause of pleasure and fear; for in that case too, the cognition remains unsublated. Likewise, the cognition of a snake and the like regarding a rope and so forth, produced by defects in the sense organs and their objects, is indeed real and serves as the cause of fear and other such effects.

Even when one has not been bitten by a snake, the cognition that one has been bitten occurs due to the proximity of a snake; this is indeed real. Likewise, the cognition of the poison of doubt, which becomes a cause of death, is indeed real. Even in the case of water and such, the reflection of a face and so forth is a real entity, serving as the cause for the ascertainment of specific qualities belonging to the actual face. The reality of these cognitions is determined by their being produced and by their capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).

If it is asked, "In the absence of elephants and so forth, how can cognitions of them be real?"—this is not so, because cognitions are necessarily characterized merely by having an objective support (*sālambanatva*). For in the case of being an objective support, it is only the appearance of the object that is required. And that appearance certainly exists due to the influence of defects (*doṣa*). However, that [cognition] is determined to be unreal because it is sublated (*bādhita*); for it has been stated that an unsublated cognition is indeed real.

Even when a letter is understood through a written mark, there is no cognition of the real arising from the unreal, because the mark itself is real. [Objection: But surely it is the mark, as cognized in the form of the letter, that causes the cognition of the letter; however, its being the letter is unreal. [Reply: Not so; for that which is unreal—that is, lacking any designation—cannot function as a means (*upāya*). Indeed, the status of being a means is neither observed nor logically possible for what is non-existent. If, on the other hand, you claim that the mark serves as a means for the *cognition* of the letter, then in that case, there would be no instance of a cognition of the real arising from the unreal, precisely because the cognition itself is real.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the identity between the means (*upāya*) and the end (*upeya*), because both would be indistinguishable in being of the nature of the cognition of letters. Moreover, if a line were the means by virtue of its being the non-existent essence of a letter, then since it would be easy for a single line to possess the nature of all non-existent letters, the cognition of all letters would arise from the sight of a single line.

Furthermore, just as there is a convention of words such as "Devadatta" applied to a particular lump of clay, so too, by virtue of a convention where a particular line perceivable by the eye is associated with a particular phoneme perceivable by the ear, that particular line becomes the cause of the cognition of that particular phoneme. Well then, in this case, the comprehension of the real arises from the real itself, because both the line and the convention are real. Even the cognition of a real cow derived from a "cow-like" drawing (*rekhā-gavaya*) is based on similarity, and that similarity is indeed real.

Nor can the realization of the real arise from the unreal on the grounds that a single, unitary sound, though it serves as the cause for the cognition of different meanings through specific modulations (*nāda*), is itself unreal. This is because a single sound, manifested by various modulations, becomes the cause for the arising of cognitions of different meanings by virtue of its grasping of a relationship with those specific meanings through the forms manifested by each respective modulation. Furthermore, the claim that sound is of a single uniform nature is not tenable; for that which conveys meaning, such as the letter *ga*, is itself the sound, precisely because it is perceived by the auditory organ. Therefore, it is difficult to establish the realization of the real Brahman from an unreal scripture.

But surely, the scripture is not unreal like a sky-flower, because prior to the knowledge of non-duality (*advaitajñāna*), it is cognized by the notion of existence. Indeed, its unreality occurs only when the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) has arisen. At that time, the scripture is no longer a means for the knowledge of Brahman, which is pure consciousness devoid of all distinctions. When it is a means, the scripture certainly exists, because of the cognition "it exists. Not so; for when the scripture is non-existent, the cognition "the scripture exists" is itself false. What follows from this? This follows from it: [the scripture is unreal].

Since the knowledge produced by a false scripture is itself false, its object—Brahman—must also be false; just as the fire known through the cognition of smoke produced by mist (mistaken for smoke) is false because that cognition is false. Furthermore, the claim that no subsequent sublation is observed is unproven, for sublation is indeed observed through the statement "emptiness alone is the reality. If you argue that this [statement] is based on delusion, you yourself have stated that it too is based on delusion. As for the non-observation of subsequent sublation, it applies to that very [statement] itself; enough, then, with mocking such unstable, fallacious reasoning.

As for the claim that Vedic statements such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) are intended solely to establish a reality that is a single essence consisting of non-dual, attributeless knowledge—that is incorrect.

By means of establishing the proposition that through one consciousness all consciousnesses are known, [the text] demonstrates that the Supreme Brahman—which is denoted by the word "Sat"—is the material cause of the world, its efficient cause, its omniscience, its possession of all powers, its nature of having true volitions, its being the inner self of all, its being the substratum of all, its governance of all, and so forth; it further establishes that the entire world is of the same nature as that [Brahman], in order to instruct Śvetaketu with the words, "Thou art this very Brahman."

This is because the present context has already commenced; furthermore, this matter has been elaborated upon in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*, and it will be demonstrated even more thoroughly here in the section concerning "Originating from It" (*ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, in the passage, "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which the Imperishable is attained," having negated the natural qualities that are to be abandoned, the possession of auspicious qualities such as eternity, omnipresence, subtlety, all-pervasiveness, immutability, being the source of all beings, and omniscience is established for the Supreme Brahman. This is also the case in the passage, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."

The establishment of a featureless reality is not achieved through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), because the conventional understanding of coreferentiality is the denotation of a single object qualified by multiple qualifiers. For coreferentiality consists in the occurrence of words in a single referent despite a difference in their grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). In that case, when words such as "Being" (*satya*) and "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) apply to one and the same object through their primary meanings—either as qualities or as forms opposed to those forms that are incompatible with each respective quality—a difference in their grounds for application must necessarily be admitted.

However, there is this distinction: in one view, the words have their primary (mukhya) meaning, while in the other, they possess a secondary (lakṣaṇā) meaning. Furthermore, the nature of reality itself is not merely the state of being the opposite of ignorance and so forth. For if the essential nature were apprehended by a single word alone, the employment of further words would be redundant. Moreover, in that case, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) would be unestablished, because words referring to a single entity would not be based on different grounds (nimitta).

Nor does the multiplicity of meanings of words—arising from the difference in the qualified nature of a single object due to the difference in its qualifiers—contradict grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); for coreferentiality is intent upon conveying that a single reality is qualified by multiple qualifiers. For grammarians define coreferentiality as "the occurrence of words with different grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in reference to a single object."

Regarding what was stated in the passage "one only, without a second," the term "without a second" does not tolerate even a second entity by way of attributes; therefore, according to the principle of the uniformity of all Vedic branches (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*), it must be accepted that the causal texts have as their primary purport the teaching of a non-dual reality. This is stated as the definition of Brahman—which is non-dual and characterized as the cause—in the words: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."

Therefore, the claim that Brahman—which is intended to be defined—is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*) alone, lest there be a contradiction with such statements as "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*) and "stainless" (*nirañjana*), is untenable. This is because the term "without a second" (*advitīya*) aims to establish that Brahman, as the material cause of the world, possesses a variety of powers by precluding any other presiding agent distinct from itself. In the same way, the passage beginning with "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' It created fire" (*tadaikṣata bahu syāṃ prajāyeya iti tattejo'sṛjata*) makes known precisely this possession of diverse powers.

If it is asked how it is known that when it is stated without qualification that [Brahman] is "without a second," there is a negation of merely another efficient cause (*nimitta*); it is understood as follows: Brahman’s status as the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*)—desiring to emit [the world]—has been established by the text, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only. Since the existence of another efficient cause arises in the mind through the very nature of the production of effects, it is that [efficient cause] which is negated by the term "without a second. For if everything were negated, then even those qualities such as eternity and so forth, which are accepted by oneself and intended to be proven, would be negated.

Furthermore, the principle of the "corroboration by all branches" (sarvaśākhāpratyayanyāya) yields a result contrary to your position here, because it serves as the reason for the inclusion (upasaṃhāra) of qualities such as omniscience—which are inherent in the cause—in all the various recensions (śākhās). Therefore, even from the very nature of the causal statements, it is understood that Brahman is taught as being endowed with attributes by the passage, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite."
There is no contradiction between the statements concerning the qualityless and the qualified [Brahman], due to the distinction in their respective objects.

Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa*), for those passages—such as "without qualities," "stainless," "actionless," and "quiescent"—refer only to natural, discardable qualities. Furthermore, even those scriptures that proclaim the nature of Brahman to be pure knowledge declare that Brahman has knowledge as its essential nature; yet this does not mean that the reality is merely a qualityless knowledge, because it is the knower alone who possesses the nature of knowledge. It has already been stated that it is entirely logical for that which is of the nature of knowledge to be the substratum of knowledge, just as in the case of a gem, the sun, or a lamp. Indeed, all the scriptures speak only of the state of being a knower.

"He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving"; "Then He thought"; "That deity thought"; "He thought, 'Let me now create the worlds'"; "The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of the many"; "Two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Unlord"; "Him we know as the supreme Maheśvara among lords, the supreme deity among deities, the supreme lord among lords, the adorable God, the Lord of the world"; "Of Him no effect or instrument is known; neither is anyone seen equal or superior to Him."

"His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action, which are innate"; and "This Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolve is true. Such scriptural passages declare that auspicious qualities, headed by the status of being a knower, are innate to Brahman, who is of the very nature of knowledge, as well as its state of being entirely devoid of all that is to be discarded.
