By negating the qualities to be abandoned through the passage beginning with "free from evil" (apahatapāpman) and ending with "free from thirst" (apipāsa), and then prescribing the auspicious qualities of Brahman through "whose desires are true" (satyakāma) and "whose resolves are true" (satyasaṅkalpa), this very Śruti itself distinguishes between the subject matter of the passages concerning the qualityless (nirguṇa) and those concerning the qualified (saguṇa). Thus, since there is no contradiction between the passages on the qualified and the qualityless, one should not even suspect that either of them has a false subject matter.

Having begun with the qualities of Brahman in the passage, "From fear of Him the wind blows," and having described the excellence of the bliss of the individual soul (kṣetrajña) in the sequence beginning with "A hundredfold those [blisses]," this Śruti declares with great reverence the infinity of Brahman’s auspicious qualities in the words: "He who knows the bliss of Brahman, from which words turn back along with the mind, unable to reach it."

The statement, "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman," which makes known the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, declares the infinity of the qualities of the supreme, wise Brahman. Together with the wise Brahman, he enjoys all desires. Desires (*kāmāḥ*) are so called because they are desired; they are auspicious qualities. Together with Brahman, he enjoys all those qualities.

This is the meaning. In the Dahara-vidyā, the word "together" (saha) is used to express the predominance of the qualities, as in the passage: "That which is within it is what must be sought. The identity of the method for both the fruit and the meditation is established by the scripture itself: "In whatever manner a person acts in this world, so does he become after departing from here."

If it were said that Brahman is not an object of knowledge—as expressed in the passages, "He by whom it is not thought is [the knower],... and "...it is unknown to those who know it"—then the teaching that liberation results from knowledge, such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," would be untenable. Furthermore, the passage, "He indeed becomes non-existent, if he knows Brahman as non-existent; but if he knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as an existent being," declares both the destruction of the self and the existence of the self based on the presence or absence of knowledge regarding Brahman.

Therefore, all the Śrutis enjoin the realization of Brahman alone as the means to liberation (*apavarga*). It has been stated that this knowledge consists of meditation (*upāsanā*), and that the object of meditation is Brahman endowed with attributes (*saguṇa*).

From the scriptural statement, "From which words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it," we hear that Brahman—which is infinite and possesses unlimited qualities—is unfit to be delimited by speech and mind as being "this much. Therefore, for those who possess the knowledge that delimits Brahman as being "this much," it is said that Brahman is "unknown and unthought" (amatam), because Brahman is unlimited. Otherwise, the statements regarding its being thought and known—namely, "He by whom it is not thought is the knower of it" and "It is known by those who do not know"—would be contradicted in that very context.

As for the objection that the Śruti passage, "One does not see the seer of seeing... nor the thinker of thinking," negates a seer and a thinker distinct from seeing and thinking—that has been refuted by the following: having adopted the view, established through fallacious reasoning, that the knower is essentially ignorant because it possesses adventitious qualities such as consciousness, [the scripture] says, "Do not look upon the Self in that way; do not think so; rather, look upon the Self—even as the seer and the thinker—as being of the very nature of seeing and thinking. Thus it speaks.

Alternatively, the meaning of the sentence is: having negated the individual soul (jīvātman) as the seer of sight and the thinker of thought, one should meditate upon the Supreme Self alone, who is the inner self of all beings. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with scriptural texts concerning the nature of the knower, such as, "O, by what means could one know the Knower? As for the claim that the passage "Bliss is Brahman" indicates that bliss alone is the essential nature of Brahman, this has been refuted by the fact that it declares knowledge to be the very nature of Brahman, which is the substratum of knowledge.

For knowledge itself, when it is favorable, is called bliss. The statement, "Brahman is consciousness-bliss (*vijñānamānandaṃ brahma*)," means that Brahman is consciousness whose very nature is bliss. For this very reason, you maintain its state of being of one essence. Furthermore, it has been stated that this very consciousness-nature possesses the status of being a knower, as established by hundreds of scriptural passages. Likewise, because of the use of distinct grammatical designations in such passages as "That is the one bliss of Brahman" and "The knower of the bliss of Brahman," Brahman is not merely bliss alone; rather, it is the blissful one (*ānandin*). Indeed, the state of being the blissful one is nothing other than the state of being a knower.

As for what was stated—that the negation of difference is seen in many places, such as: "For where there is duality as it were," "There is not any diversity here at all; he goes from death to death who sees here as if there were diversity," and "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see?"—that is because, since the entire world is non-different from Brahman due to being its effect and having it as its inner controller, and thus being of the same nature as it, any plurality that is contrary to that unity is prohibited.
Furthermore, it has been refuted [by the opponent] that "the multiplicity of Brahman established by scripture—which is preceded by the volition 'May I be many, may I procreate'—is not being negated.

If it is argued that this negation of multiplicity concerns the non-ultimate reality (*aparamārtha*), we say no; for it would be laughable to first establish a multiplicity of Brahman that is inaccessible to all means of valid cognition such as perception, and then subsequently sublate that very same thing.

As for the statement that fear arises for one who perceives multiplicity in Brahman—namely, "For when he makes even a slight distinction in this [Brahman], then fear comes to him"—that is incorrect; because it is taught that such contemplation of multiplicity is a cause of peace, in the passage: "All this is indeed Brahman, born from it, dissolved in it, and breathing in it; therefore, let one meditate with a peaceful mind. For in this way, peace is enjoined here through the contemplation of the identity of the entire world with Brahman, by virtue of the world's being its very self as it is the object of its origination, sustenance, and dissolution.

Therefore, for one who contemplates the world—divided into the distinctions of gods, animals, humans, and immovable beings—as having Brahman as its essence, there is no possibility of it being a cause of fear, because it serves as a cause for peace and a cause for attaining fearlessness. If this is so, then why is it said, "Then fear comes to him"? This is explained: "For when he finds fearless support in that which is invisible, bodiless, indefinable, and without abode..."

Now, regarding the statement, "Then he becomes one who has attained fearlessness," this refers to the state of being established in Brahman as the cause for attaining fearlessness; when that establishment is interrupted, fear arises. As the great sages have said:

"If for even a moment or an instant Vāsudeva is not meditated upon, that is a loss, that is a great flaw, that is delusion, and that is a calamity," and so forth. An interval or opening within the state of being established in Brahman is precisely such an interruption.

As for what was stated—that Brahman is devoid of all attributes because it will be said, "Not even from the standpoint of place" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11)—that is not so; for in that very passage, he will indeed declare Brahman to be with attributes. Furthermore, by stating "But [the dream state is] mere illusion" (Brahma Sūtra 3.2.3), he declares that even dream objects possess the status of being mere illusion precisely because they differ from the objects experienced in the waking state; thus, he will imply that those objects experienced in the waking state possess ultimate reality (pāramārthikatva) just like [the objects of the waking state itself].

As for the claim that even in the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas* it is understood that knowledge of the attributeless alone is the supreme goal and everything else is non-ultimate, that is incorrect. For it is said: "He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds...

"All beings abide in Me, yet I do not abide in them; nor do beings abide in Me—behold My divine Yoga! My Self, the source of beings, sustains beings but does not dwell within them. "I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe."

"There is nothing else whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya! All this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread. "Supporting this entire universe with but a single fraction of Myself, I remain as the world. "But there is another, the Supreme Person, called the Supreme Self—the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them. "Since I transcend the perishable and am even superior to the imperishable..."

Therefore, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). O Sage! He has transcended the nature of all beings, their transformations, and the defects such as the qualities (guṇas);
having transcended all veils, he is the Self of all, by whom that which exists within the intermediate spaces of the worlds is pervaded.

He is the embodiment of all auspicious qualities; having brought forth the creation of beings by a mere fraction of his own power, he assumes vast bodies at will according to his desire, and has thus accomplished the welfare of the entire world.
He is the sole mass of qualities such as splendor, strength, sovereignty, great awakening, heroism, power, and majesty;
he is the supreme among the supreme, the lord of the high and the low, in whom no afflictions or other defects exist.
He is the Lord, whose nature is both individual and collective, whose form is unmanifest and whose form is manifest;
the Lord of all, the seer of all, the knower of all, possessing all powers, known as the Supreme Lord.

"That by which it is perceived—being free from defects, pure, supreme, stainless, and of a single form—is either seen or attained; that is knowledge, and what is other than that is called ignorance. "O Maitreya! The word *bhagavat* is applied to the Supreme Brahman, who is called the Great Sovereignty (*mahāvibhūti*) and is the cause of all causes. The syllable *bha* possesses a twofold meaning: *saṃbhartṛ* (the sustainer) and *bhartṛ* (the supporter). O Sage! The meaning of the syllable *ga* is likewise *netṛ* (the leader), *gamayitṛ* (the one who causes to attain), and *sraṣṭṛ* (the creator)."
The term *bhaga* is said to denote the sixfold aggregate consisting of complete sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion.

"Beings dwell therein, in that Self of beings who is the Self of all; and He dwells in all beings without exception, as their transformative essence; therefore He is the Imperishable (Avyaya). Knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor—in their entirety, and devoid of all qualities subject to rejection—these are what is expressed by the word 'Bhagavat'. Thus, O Maitreya, this great term 'Bhagavat' belongs to none other than Vāsudeva, who is the Supreme Brahman."

"In this context, this word is endowed with the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) used for denoting an object worthy of worship; it is not used figuratively (*upacāreṇa*), whereas elsewhere it is indeed used figuratively. "O King! That other, great form of Hari, which is both identical to and different from the universe, is that wherein all these powers are established."
O Lord of Men! He creates, by His own sport, all forms endowed with power, known as gods, animals, and humans, and possessed of their respective activities.
"For the benefit of the worlds, that activity of the Immeasurable One is not born of karma; it is all-pervading and characterized by being unimpeded.
"Such is the stainless, eternal, pervasive, and undecaying supreme state called Viṣṇu, which is devoid of all that is to be abandoned.
"The Supreme among the supreme, the Highest, the Supreme Self, established in the self, He is devoid of specific designations such as form, color, and other attributes."
That which is devoid of diminution, destruction, transformation, increase, and birth can be said to exist eternally as a mere "is-ness."
Since he dwells everywhere and everything dwells within him, for that reason he is recited by the learned as Vāsudeva.
That Brahman is supreme, eternal, unborn, imperishable, and immutable; it is always of a single nature and stainless because of the absence of anything to be discarded.

"All this is indeed that very same [reality], possessing the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest; likewise, it exists in the form of the Puruṣa and in the form of Time. "The Prakṛti which I have described, having the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and the Puruṣa as well—both of these dissolve into the Supreme Self."

"The Supreme Self and the Supreme Lord is the support of all; he is celebrated in the Vedas and the Vedāntas by the name Viṣṇu. That Brahman has two forms: the embodied and the unembodied; these are the natures of the perishable and the imperishable, abiding within all beings. The imperishable is that supreme Brahman, while this entire world is the perishable; just as the radiance of a fire situated in one place spreads far and wide."

"The power of the supreme Brahman is likewise this entire universe. "The power of Viṣṇu is said to be supreme; that which is called the individual soul (kṣetrajña) is the subordinate [power]; and another, known as ignorance (avidyā) and action (karman), is held to be the third power."
O King, by that [power] the all-pervading power of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is enveloped; thus it undergoes all the exceedingly continuous torments of saṃsāra.

"And because it is concealed by that [power], O King, the power known as the *kṣetrajña* exists in all beings according to a gradation. Both *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa*, O one of great intelligence, have the nature of taking refuge, being enveloped by the power of Viṣṇu which has become the self of all beings;
and that very [power] is the cause of their separation as well as of their union."

"Just as the wind, clinging to water, sustains hundreds of droplets, so too is that power of Viṣṇu, whose nature consists of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa. "Therefore, O best of sages, this entire world is imperishable and eternal, yet it possesses the conceptual distinctions of manifestation and disappearance, and of birth and destruction."

By such passages as these, having established that the Supreme Brahman is by its very nature free from even a trace of all defects, consists of all auspicious qualities, and performs the divine play (*līlā*) of the creation, sustenance, dissolution, internal entry, and governance of the universe; and having declared that the entire aggregate of sentient and insentient entities, existing in all their various states, is the body of the Supreme Brahman—which alone is ultimately real—and having expressed this through terms such as "body" (*śarīra*), "form" (*rūpa*), "limb" (*tanu*), "power" (*śakti*), and "manifestation" (*vibhūti*), as well as through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with those respective terms;

Having described the existence of the conscious reality—which constitutes its manifestation—in its own essential nature, as well as its existence in the form of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) through its association with the non-conscious, it is established that in the state of the *kṣetrajña*, there is a failure to realize its innate nature as knowledge due to being enveloped by ignorance in the form of karma consisting of merit and demerit, and instead there is a realization of itself in the form of objects which are non-conscious in nature. Thus, it is understood that the Supreme Brahman possesses attributes (*saviśeṣa*), and the world, which is its manifestation, is likewise ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).

Regarding the phrase "in which all distinctions have subsided," it is stated that although the Self is conjoined with specific transformations of primordial matter (prakṛti) such as gods and humans, its true nature—being devoid of the distinctions inherent therein—is beyond the range of words like "god" and so forth that denote those distinctions; rather, it is characterized solely by consciousness and existence, is self-cognizable, and is not within the range of the mind of one engaged in yoga. By this, there is no denial of the phenomenal world (prapañca).

If it is asked how this is understood, it is said in response: In this section, having described Yoga as the sole remedy for *saṃsāra* and having stated its constituent parts up to *pratyāhāra*, [the author] intends to state the auspicious support (*śubhāśraya*) for the sake of achieving *dhāraṇā*. To that end, he establishes two forms of the supreme Brahman Viṣṇu, denoted by the term "Power" (*śakti*), distinguished as the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*). Then, he describes the Kṣetrajña—the individual soul—which is enveloped by ignorance known as Karma, which is the third form of Power, and is characterized by non-sentience (*acid-viśiṣṭa*); this is the division known as the formed.

Having stated that [the body] is "impure" because it follows from the three types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), [the author] denies that the second [substratum], called the *kṣetrajña*, is a pure locus. This is because the *kṣetrajña*—which is devoid of karma, free from ignorance (*avidyā*), separated from non-consciousness, consists solely of the form of knowledge, and is designated as the "formless" (*amūrta*) division—is the object of meditation for perfected yogis; it serves as no objective support for the mind of one engaged in yoga, and it is naturally devoid of purity. Furthermore, this formless [aspect] is the nature of the supreme power (*para-śakti*), while the embodied [aspect] called the *kṣetrajña* is the nature of the non-supreme power (*apara-śakti*). And because it is of the nature of the supreme power, it is the Self (*ātman*).

The "auspicious support" (*śubhāśraya*) is said to be the formal, embodied form established by the Vedānta texts—such as that described as "having the luster of the sun"—which is the uncommon attribute of the Lord and the substratum of these three powers: the power called *māyā* (consisting of the forms of *avidyā*), which serves as the cause for the realization of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*). Here, in order to state that the nature of the completely pure Self is unfit to be the auspicious support, it is said: "That which has its distinctions cast aside. For instance: "O King, O high-minded one, that supreme state known as Viṣṇu, which is to be meditated upon by yogis, cannot be contemplated by one who is engaged in yoga because it is devoid of duality."
O King! That other, great form of Hari, in which all these powers are established, is both multiform and yet devoid of specific forms.

And so he says: likewise, because those within the world—such as the four-faced Brahmā, Sanaka, Sanandana, and others—are enveloped by ignorance (*avidyā*), they are unfit to be the auspicious refuge (*śubhāśraya*). Furthermore, since even those who are bound, and later attain awakening through yoga and assume their own true nature, lack inherent purity, the venerable Śaunaka has prohibited their status as the auspicious refuge: "From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, all living beings situated within the world are subject to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) produced by karma."
Therefore, those meditations do not benefit the meditators; for they are all encompassed by ignorance and remain within the sphere of saṃsāra.
"And those whose awakening has arisen subsequently are benefactors only through meditation; for even their awakening is not innate, since it comes from another.

And by such statements as, "Therefore, that stainless Brahman is by its very nature endowed with awakening," it is declared that the unique, inherent nature of the Supreme Brahman Viṣṇu alone is the auspicious substratum (*śubhāśraya*). Consequently, no denial of difference is perceived here.

Even in the passage beginning with “the nature of which is knowledge” (*jñānasvarūpam*), it is not being established that the entire aggregate of objects distinct from knowledge is false; for the statement merely asserts that the appearance of the Self, whose nature is knowledge, in the form of objects such as gods and humans is an illusion (*bhrānti*). Indeed, when it is said that the appearance of mother-of-pearl as silver is an illusion, it does not follow that the entire aggregate of silver in the world is false.

If it is argued that because the world and Brahman are perceived as identical through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and since it has been stated that the assumption of objective forms by Brahman—which is essentially consciousness—is an illusion, it follows that the entire collection of objects must be false; this is incorrect. For in this scripture, the Supreme Brahman Viṣṇu is established as being free from even a trace of defects such as ignorance, as consisting of all auspicious qualities, and as possessing great majesty; therefore, the possibility of His perceiving anything through illusion is impossible.

Furthermore, it will be demonstrated immediately hereafter that the presentation of identity through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is both incapable of being sublated and non-contradictory; therefore, this verse as well does not contradict the true nature of the object.

For instance, when it is established that Brahman is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world—based on the text: "That from which these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter at death; desire to know That; That is Brahman"—it is understood from the scriptural injunction:

"One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas; the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, 'He will deceive me,'" that the meaning [of the Veda] must be augmented by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.

*Upabṛṃhaṇa* (supplementation) means the clarification of the meaning of the Vedic sentences one has understood oneself, by means of the words of those who have mastered all the Vedas and their meanings, or who have directly realized the true essence of the Vedas through the power of their own yoga. Indeed, supplementation must be performed because the meaning of the sentences found across all Vedic branches is difficult to comprehend when heard only in part, and without that [supplementation], certainty cannot be attained. In this regard, Maitreya, desiring the supplementation of the Vedic meanings he had understood from the Lord Parāśara—who possessed knowledge of the supreme divinity of the Goddess obtained through the boons granted by Pulastya and Vasiṣṭha—questioned him.
"Therefore, O knower of dharma! I desire to hear from you how the world came into being and, O illustrious one! how it will come to be again."

"O Brahman, that from which this world, including all that is moving and unmoving, was produced; that in which it was dissolved; how it was dissolved; and where it will go to dissolution," and so forth.

Herein, the specific nature of Brahman, the distinctions among its manifestations (*vibhūti*), the modes of those manifestations, the nature of its worship, and the specific fruits thereof are inquired about. Among the questions regarding the specific nature of Brahman, by the phrase "from which this world of moving and unmoving beings [proceeds]," both the efficient and material causes are asked about; and by the phrase "consisting of what," it is asked what the essence of the world is—that is, what constitutes the world whose functions are creation, maintenance, and dissolution. And the answer to that is: "The world is He. This identity is brought about by His pervasion as the Self through the form of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*).

But this is not due to the identity of location between the pervaded and the pervader; for it serves as the answer to the question "Of what is it composed? through the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of "the world" and "he. Furthermore, the suffix *mayaṭ* here does not signify a modification (*vikāra*); otherwise, the separate question would be redundant.

Nor is [the suffix *maya*] used here in its own sense (svārthika) as it is in the case of *prāṇamaya* and so on; for the subsequent statement, "and the world is He," would otherwise be untenable. For in that case, the answer would have been "Viṣṇu alone. Therefore, it has the sense of abundance (*prācurya*). The suffix *mayaṭ* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of 'made of' or 'abounding in' that which is under discussion. And the entire world, being His body, abounds in Him alone. Consequently, it is determined that the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the response "and the world is He" to the question "of what is it composed? is based on the relationship between the body and the self (*śarīrātma-bhāva*) between the world and Brahman.

Otherwise, if a scripture intended solely to propound a featureless reality were accepted, none of these questions and answers would be consistent; indeed, the entire scripture, which consists of their exposition, would not be consistent. For if that were the case, there would be only a single answer—namely, "mere knowledge of the featureless"—to the single question, "What is the substratum of the delusion of phenomenal diversity?"

Furthermore, if the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the world and Brahman were taken to mean they are one and the same substance, then qualities such as the possession of true resolve and the state of being the sole locus of all auspicious attributes, as well as the state of being the opposite of all that is evil, would be sublated; moreover, Brahman would become the substratum of all impurity. Therefore, it is established that this coreferentiality is used in its primary sense only in the relation of self and body. Thus: "The world has emerged from Viṣṇu and remains in Him alone."

"He is the author of the maintenance of this world, and he is this world. Having thus stated the meaning in brief, [the author] begins with the verse "paraḥ parāṇām" (1.1) to explain it in detail. First, having prostrated before the Lord Viṣṇu—who is the Supreme Brahman—abiding in his own essential form with the verse "avikārāya," he then pays homage to that very same Lord as he abides in the forms of Hiraṇyagarbha, himself, and Śaṅkara (as the Trimūrti), and in the forms of the collective and individual aspects of Pradhāna, Kāla, and Kṣetrajña.

In this context, the verse beginning with "jñānasvarūpam" describes the essential nature of the Supreme Self as it exists in the form of the individual knower (*kṣetrajña*). Therefore, there is no perception here of a featureless reality. If the scripture were intended to establish the delusion that has as its substratum Brahman, whose nature is featureless knowledge, then the following objection would arise: "How can the agency of creation and so forth be attributed to Brahman, who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), immeasurable (*aprameya*), pure (*śuddha*), and stainless by nature (*amalātman*)?"

"The powers of all entities fall within the domain of inconceivable knowledge; therefore, O best of those who practice austerity, those powers of existence such as creation and so forth belong to Brahman, just as heat belongs to fire. This refutation, however, is not tenable.

For if that were the case, the following objection and its resolution would be possible: "How can Brahman, who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), be the agent of creation and so forth? and "The creation of Brahman is not ultimately real, but rather imagined through delusion. The objection is as follows: since effects such as origination are observed in those who possess qualities like *sattva*, who are imperfect, and who are subject to the power of karma, how can agency regarding creation and so forth be attributed to one who is devoid of qualities like *sattva*, who is perfect, who is not subject to karma, and who is unfit for connection with karma?

The resolution is that it is not contradictory for Brahman—which is seen to be entirely distinct from all other classes of entities and possesses the aforementioned nature—to be endowed with all powers, just as fire and other substances, which are distinct from water and the like, possess powers such as heat.

The statement, “You alone are the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)," and so forth, does not assert that everything else is entirely unreal; rather, it asserts that because everything has you as its essence, anything existing apart from you lacks ultimate reality. He establishes this very point with: "This is your majesty, by which this world of moving and non-moving things is pervaded. Since this world of moving and non-moving things is pervaded by you, all of this is indeed identical with you; thus, there is nothing whatsoever other than you. Therefore, as the self of all, you alone are the single ultimate reality.

Therefore, this is said: "This is Your majesty, which is the pervasion of all. Otherwise, it would have to be stated that "this is Your delusion"; furthermore, there would be a need for figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of such words as "O Lord of the world" and so forth, and there would be a contradiction with the context of the praise of the Blessed One, the Great Boar, who lifted up the earth as a pastime.

Since the entire world is your form (*mūrta*) by virtue of being pervaded by you as its self through your nature as consciousness (*jñānātman*), those who lack the yoga that is the means for experiencing their identity with you perceive this world merely as consisting of gods, humans, and so forth, due to erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*). Thus he says: "That which is seen here... It is not only the perception of the world—which in reality consists of you—as consisting of gods, humans, and so forth, that is an error; rather, even the perception of the selves, whose true nature is consciousness, as having the forms of objects such as gods and humans, is an error. Thus he says: "The whole [world] has the nature of consciousness (*jñānasvarūpa*)."

However, those who are wise, who know the Self as being of the nature of knowledge, whose supreme and pure minds are fit for the yoga that is the means for experiencing that everything has the Blessed Lord as its essence—they perceive this entire world, which consists of bodies that are specific transformations of the *prakṛti* of gods, humans, and so forth, as well as Your own body, as being of the nature of the Self, which is distinct from the body and consists of knowledge.

Thus he says, "But those who know through knowledge. Otherwise, there would be redundancy of verses, figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*) of words, contradiction of meaning, contradiction of context, and contradiction of the purport of the scripture.

Regarding the passage, "Though existing in the bodies of oneself and others, [the Self] is one and the same," it means that while all selves are equal insofar as they possess the single form of consciousness (*jñāna*).

It is stated that the perception of duality among selves in the form of gods and so forth—caused by contact with the physical body (*piṇḍa*), which is a specific transformation of the primary constituents (*prakṛti*) such as gods and humans—is unreal. However, this does not negate the duality residing in the body or even that residing in the self. The meaning is that the reality of the Self (*ātma-vastu*) is equal throughout all the diverse and manifold bodies of gods, humans, and others; as was said by the Blessed One: "The wise see equality even in a dog and an outcaste," and "For Brahman is faultless and equal," and so forth.

Because the division between self and other has been stated regarding the reality that transcends the body in the passage, "Even though He exists in the bodies of himself and others... Furthermore, even in the verse, "If there were any other who was superior to me," identity of self is not perceived; for it would be improper to employ both the words *para* (other/superior) and *anya* (different) with reference to a single entity. In that context, the word *para* denotes a self distinct from one's own, while the word *anya* serves to negate any difference in form, since [all selves] possess the single form of consciousness.

This is what is meant: if there were some self distinct from me, possessing a form other than the form of the cognition that constitutes my own nature, then it would be possible to designate, "I am of such a form, and this [other] is of a different form. But this is not the case; for all [selves] are identical precisely because they possess the single form of cognition.

In the phrase "by means of the distinction of the holes in the flute," it is taught that even here, the difference in form among the selves (*ātman*) is not caused by their essential nature (*svarūpa*), but rather by their entry into the bodies of gods and so forth; there is no identity of self. Furthermore, in the illustration, the portions of air residing in the multiple holes do not possess identity of essential nature; rather, they possess only identity of form. For those portions of air, which are identical in form as being air, the distinction in designations such as *ṣaḍja* and so on is indeed caused by their emergence through different holes; likewise is the distinction in designations such as "god" and so on for the selves.

Just as objects composed of portions of fiery, watery, and earthy substances possess unity only in terms of their respective substance-nature (*dravyatva*), but not unity of essential nature (*svarūpaikya*); likewise, a difference in essential nature among the aerial portions is also unavoidable.

By referring back with the word *tat* (that) to the previously stated fact that all selves have the form of knowledge—expressed in the phrase "I am he and you are he"—and by establishing grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meanings of "I," "you," and so forth, [the text] concludes that knowledge alone is the form. It then says, "Abandon the delusion of difference among selves based on differences in forms such as gods and others. Otherwise, if the nature of the self were something other than the body to be taught, the designation of difference in the form "I, you, and all this are the nature of the Self" would not be possible.

Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the statement "all this is the very nature of the Self," it is not even consistent for words such as "I" and "you" to function as mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*).

He also acted according to the instruction, as stated: "One whose vision is fixed on the ultimate reality abandons the sense of difference. If it is asked, "From what source is this determination derived?"—it is because the instruction concerns the discrimination between the body and the Self, as indicated by the opening statement: "Since the body, characterized by the head, hands, and so forth, is distinct from the Person (puṃs). Furthermore, the phrase "in the ignorance that produces differentiation" does not refer to the identity of the nature of the Self, nor to the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para). Identity of the nature of the Self has been refuted in the manner previously described.

Furthermore, the identity of essence between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) is not possible, just as it is not possible between the body and the self; and thus says the Śruti: "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree. Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. "The two drinking the *ṛta* in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the supreme, highest station..."

"The knowers of Brahman speak of shade and light, as do those who maintain the five fires and have thrice performed the Nāciketa sacrifice"; and "He has entered within, the ruler of people, the Self of all"—such passages as these; and in this scripture as well: "O Sage, he has transcended the nature of all beings, their transformations, and defects such as the qualities (guṇas)."

"He whose every veil has passed away, the Self of all, by whom the interior of the worlds is overspread"; "He consists of all auspicious qualities... the Supreme among the supreme, in whom no afflictions or the like exist, the Lord of the high and the low"; and "Ignorance, known as karma, is held to be another, a third power; it envelops the all-pervading power of the Knower of the Field, O King"—because of such designations of difference.

For both [schools] study this [Brahman] as distinct [from the individual soul], as seen in such sūtras as "And because there is a designation of difference," "And He is other than that because of the mention of difference," and "But He is greater because of the mention of difference. Furthermore, from the determination of the essential natures of both through their mutually contrasting forms, as in: "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, and who controls the self from within"; "Embraced by the conscious self (prājña-ātman)"; and "Mounted upon by the conscious self."

Nor is it possible for one who is freed from ignorance through the practice of spiritual means to attain identity of nature with the Supreme, because that which is capable of being the locus of ignorance cannot possibly be unfit for it. As it has been said:

"The union of the supreme Self and the individual self is held to be the ultimate reality; this [union] is false, for one substance does not become the nature of another. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Bhagavadgītā* that for the liberated soul, there is indeed the attainment of the attributes of that [Supreme].

"Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature; even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer. And here also: "O Sage, that Brahman leads this [individual]—who is dependent upon meditation—to its own state of being, by means of its own power of transformation, just as a magnet attracts iron. Here, "its own state of being" (*ātmabhāvam*) refers to its own essential nature (*svabhāvam*).

For [the Sūtrakāra] will not state that the one being drawn attains the very nature of the attractor; rather, he says: "Excluding the activity of the world, because of the context and because of non-proximity," "because of the mark of equality in mere enjoyment," and "because of the designation of being approached by the liberated. The *Vṛtti* also states: "Excluding the activity of the world, [he is] equal to the Light. And the author of the *Dramiḍa-bhāṣya* says: "From union with the deity, even for one who is bodiless, there shall be the accomplishment of all purposes, just like the deity."

And the Śruti texts state: "Those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds"; "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme... he enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman"; "Having reached this Self consisting of bliss, moving through these worlds at will and assuming forms at will, he moves about"; "He moves around there"; "For [Brahman] is indeed essence..."

"He, having indeed obtained that essence (rasa), becomes blissful"; "Just as rivers flowing toward the ocean disappear into it, casting off name and form, so the knower, freed from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high"; "Then the knower, having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, attains the supreme equality"—such passages as these.

"Brahman is the object of meditation in all higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), and the fruit is of one and the same form; therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*) among these knowledges. This was stated by the author of the Sūtras himself in such passages as "Bliss and so forth belong to the Principal" (*ānandādayaḥ pradhānasya*) and "There is an option because the fruit is not distinct" (*vikalpo’viśiṣṭaphalatvāt*). Furthermore, the author of the Vākya explained that only the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa*) is the object of meditation and that there is an option among the knowledges, stating, "It is appropriate because of the meditation upon Him as possessing those qualities" (*yuktaṃ tadguṇakopāsanāt*). And the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakṛt*) explained this with the words beginning, "Even though [the seeker] is possessed of a pure mind," and so forth.

In the passage, "One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," there is also consistency with such statements as, "Freed from name and form, he attains the divine Person who is higher than the high," "The stainless one attains supreme equality," and "Having reached the highest light, he appears in his own true form. Thus, for one who is liberated from natural name and form and whose distinctions caused by them have been eliminated, the state of being a mode (*prakāra*) of Brahman is described by virtue of having knowledge as its sole form. And when there is identity of mode, the usage of "thatness" (*tattva*) is indeed primary, just as in the expression, "This is that cow."

In this regard as well, [the text] states: "O King, consciousness is the attainer, and the supreme Brahman is that which is to be attained; likewise, the Self—whose residual mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) have been entirely destroyed—is that which is to be attained. Having thus declared that through meditation on the supreme Brahman, the Self becomes like the supreme Brahman—having its residual mental impressions (of *karman*) entirely destroyed—and being free from the three types of mental impressions, namely: the impression of *karman*, the impression of Brahman, and the impression of both, it is that which is to be attained.

"O twice-born one! The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the agent, and knowledge is indeed its instrument; having accomplished the task of liberation by means of that [instrument], it [the agent] should desist once its duty is fulfilled. Since this statement declares that the instrument—consisting of meditation on the Supreme Brahman—desists upon the attainment of one's true nature through the exhaustion of all residual mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) and the consequent fulfillment of its purpose, it follows that [this practice] must be performed until perfection is attained. Thus he spoke.

"Having attained the state of being that [Brahman], he thus becomes non-different from the Supreme Self; and his difference would be caused by ignorance. This describes the nature of the liberated one. "Tadbhāvaḥ" means the state (bhāva) of Brahman, its own nature (svabhāva); it does not mean identity of essence (svarūpaikyam), because the second occurrence of the word "bhāva" in the phrase "tadbhāvabhāvāpannaḥ" would otherwise be redundant, and because it would contradict the meaning previously stated. "Attaining the state of being that" (tadbhāvabhāvāpattiḥ) refers to attaining that which is Brahman’s state of having all mental impressions (bhāvanā) completely destroyed.

When one has attained this state, then one becomes non-different from the Supreme Self, that is, devoid of difference. Since this [individual self] is of the same nature as the Supreme Self by virtue of having knowledge as its sole form, its difference from Him—manifesting as a god or other forms—is based on ignorance in the form of karma; it is not caused by its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). That distinction of being a god or the like ceases when karma, which constitutes the root-ignorance, is destroyed through meditation on the Supreme Brahman, because of the absence of its cause; thus, one becomes non-different. As it has been said:

"But the distinction of a single nature arises from the activity of external karma; when the distinctions such as 'god' and so forth have been destroyed, that [nature] exists without obstruction. He explains this very point: "When the ignorance that produces manifold distinctions has gone to absolute destruction, who could produce the unreal distinction between the Self and Brahman? "Manifold distinction" (*vibheda*) means various distinctions consisting of gods, animals, humans, and stationary beings. As it was also said by Śaunaka: "This fourfold distinction is based upon false knowledge."

The meaning is this: when ignorance—known as *karman*, which is the cause of the various distinctions such as being a god and so forth within the Self whose nature is consciousness—is utterly destroyed through meditation on the Supreme Brahman, then, due to the absence of a cause, who will bring about the non-existent distinction of the Self from the Supreme Brahman in the form of a god and so forth? For it has been stated right here [in this very text]: "Ignorance is known by another name, namely *karman*.
*khḍhakhḍhakha* [End of section].

By the passage beginning with "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field," the oneness of all things is declared through the identity of being the Self in the form of the Inner Ruler (*antar-yāmin*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such statements as: "The perishable consists of all beings, while the unchanging is called the imperishable; the Supreme Person is another than these. That all things have Him as their Self in the form of the Inner Ruler was stated by the Lord Himself in that very same work: "O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings," and "And I am seated within the hearts of all."

And that very same thing is stated [in Bhagavad Gītā 10.20]: "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings. For the word *bhūta* here refers to the body as far as the Self. Since He is the Self of all, for that very reason the separate existence of all [beings] is denied on the grounds that they are His bodies, as it is said: "There is nothing that can exist without Him. Furthermore, this must be accepted as the conclusion of the Lord's manifestations (*vibhūti*). Therefore, this is said: "Whatever being is possessed of glory, or is majestic or powerful, know that to have sprung from a mere fragment of My splendor."
"I stand supporting this entire world with but a single fraction of Myself.

Therefore, in the scriptures, there is no teaching of a featureless reality; nor is there a teaching that the multitude of objects is illusory; nor is there a negation of the distinction between the essential natures of the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord.
(Thus ends the refutation of the doctrine of a partless Brahman in the *Mahāsiddhānta*).
The section on the inquiry (*jijñāsādhikaraṇa*), specifically the latter part concerning the demolition of the theory of ignorance (*avidyābhaṅgabhāga*), in the *Mahāsiddhānta*.

As for what is further stated: the entire world, consisting of endless conceptual constructions such as the Lord (*īśvara*) and those subject to His rule (*īśitavya*), is imagined through defects within a reality that is itself without distinctions and self-luminous. And this defect is beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), which is indefinable as being either existent or non-existent; it conceals the true nature [of reality] and causes various and manifold distractions. This must necessarily be accepted, both because of scriptural texts such as "For they are veiled by untruth" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.3.2), and because the identity of the individual soul with Brahman—known through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*)—would otherwise be untenable.

"But that [ignorance] is not real, because error and sublation would be impossible; nor is it unreal, because manifestation and sublation would be impossible. Therefore, this ignorance is that which is devoid of both alternatives—so say the knowers of reality. This is incorrect. For, depending upon what does it produce delusion? It cannot depend upon the *jīva*, because the state of being a *jīva* is itself imagined by ignorance. Nor can it depend upon Brahman, because Brahman, being of the nature of self-luminous consciousness, is the very opposite of ignorance. Indeed, ignorance is held to be sublatable by knowledge.
If ignorance—which is of the nature of falsehood and is to be removed—were to conceal the Supreme Brahman which is of the nature of knowledge, who would be the master capable of removing it?
If it is argued that knowledge is Brahman, [we reply: knowledge is the remover of ignorance; since it is luminous like Brahman, it too is indeed not something to be removed.

"If there exists the cognition that 'Brahman is knowledge,' then Brahman would be an object of knowledge (*prameya*). Consequently, it would follow—precisely from your own statement—that Brahman lacks the nature of self-manifestation (*ananubhūtitva*). If it is argued that the cognition "Brahman has knowledge as its essential nature" is the sublater (*bādhaka*) of that ignorance (*avidyā*), whereas the knowledge that constitutes its very essence (*svarūpabhūta-jñāna*) is not, we say no. For since both manifest the essential nature of Brahman, there is no perceived distinction whereby one is non-contradictory and the other is not.

What is meant is this: by the knowledge that "Brahman is of the nature of consciousness," Brahman is understood in its own essential nature; since Brahman is self-luminous, it shines forth by itself. Thus, there is no difference between the essential nature [of Brahman] and the knowledge that has that as its object, insofar as both are opposed to ignorance.

Furthermore, since Brahman, whose very nature is experience (*anubhava*), cannot be experienced by another experience, you have no cognition that takes it as its object. Therefore, if knowledge is the opponent of ignorance, it must be its own opponent; thus, it is impossible for ignorance to have Brahman as its substrate. Objects such as mother-of-pearl, however, are themselves incapable of manifesting their true nature and are not opposed to their own ignorance; they require another cognition to remove that ignorance. Brahman, on the other hand, has its true nature established by its own self-experience and is therefore inherently opposed to its own ignorance; for that very reason, it does not require any other remover [of that ignorance].

Now, it might be argued that the knowledge of the falsity of everything other than Brahman is the opponent of ignorance (*ajñāna*). To this we say: no. This knowledge of the falsity of what is other than Brahman—does it oppose the ignorance regarding the true nature (*yāthātmya*) of Brahman, or does it oppose the ignorance consisting in the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)? This must be examined. It cannot, first of all, oppose the ignorance regarding the true nature of Brahman, because its object is not that [Brahman]. For opposition between knowledge and ignorance occurs only when they have the same object.

The knowledge that the world of manifestation (*prapañca*) is false is opposed by the ignorance consisting in the notion of its reality. Therefore, it is precisely the ignorance regarding the reality of the world that is sublated, while the ignorance regarding the nature of Brahman remains intact. If it is argued that "ignorance regarding the nature of Brahman" is simply its being accompanied by a second entity (*sadvitīyatva*), and that this has been removed by the knowledge of the falsity of everything other than Him—while His own nature is established by one's own experience—the answer is no.

Since the non-duality of Brahman is its very nature, established by one's own experience, neither the ignorance consisting of duality—which contradicts that nature—nor its sublation could possibly exist. If it is argued that non-duality is an attribute (dharma), we say no; for you yourself have demonstrated that Brahman, whose nature is pure experience, is devoid of any objectifiable attributes. Therefore, because it is inherently contradictory to the nature of Brahman, which is consciousness itself, Brahman cannot be the substratum of ignorance.

Furthermore, by one who asserts that Brahman, whose very nature is light, is concealed by ignorance (*avidyā*), it would amount to saying that its essential nature is destroyed. For "concealment of light" must mean either an obstruction to the arising of light or the destruction of that which already exists. Since it is admitted that light is unproduced, the concealment of light is nothing other than the destruction of light itself.

Furthermore, it must be examined whether this defect residing in its own substratum—which causes this experience, though itself devoid of objects and devoid of a substratum, to experience the Self as having infinite substrata and infinite objects—is ultimately real (*paramārthabhūta*) or not ultimately real (*aparamārthabhūta*). It cannot be ultimately real, for that is not admitted. Nor can it be not ultimately real; for if that were the case, it would have to be admitted as either the seer (*draṣṭṛ*), the seen (*dṛśya*), or the act of seeing (*dṛśi*). It cannot be the non-seeing (*adṛśi*), because no difference from the nature of pure consciousness (*dṛśisvarūpa*) is admitted.

Furthermore, since direct perception (*sākṣāddṛṣṭi*), which serves as the locus of error, cannot be admitted as non-ultimate according to the Madhyamaka position, [the theory fails]. Moreover, because the seer, the seen, and the perception delimited by them are all conceptual constructs, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the requirement of further underlying defects. If, in order to avoid this, it is argued that the defect is simply ultimate experience (*anubhūti*) itself, which is of the nature of Brahman—then if Brahman itself were the defect, it would be the very root of the perception of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

What is the use of postulating another ignorance (avidyā) that is equal to conceptual proliferation (prapañca)? For if it were a defect of Brahman, then because of its eternity, there would be no liberation. Therefore, as long as one does not admit a real defect distinct from Brahman, delusion cannot be established.

And what is intended by "indefinability" (*anirvacanīyatva*)? If you say it is being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, then such an entity would be nothing but indefinable precisely because it lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is what is meant: the entire range of entities is established through cognition. And every cognition has the form of either the existent or the non-existent. Now, if it were admitted that a cognition having the form of both the existent and the non-existent has as its object something distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, then everything would become the object of every cognition.

Now, it may be argued that there exists a certain entity, denoted by such terms as *avidyā* (ignorance) or *ajñāna* (non-knowledge), which is indefinable as being either existent or non-existent; which serves as the material cause for the various superimpositions (*adhyāsa*) of internal and external forms that conceal the true nature of reality; which is sublated by the knowledge of the reality of things; and which is a positive entity distinct from the prior non-existence of knowledge. This entity is perceived through both perception and inference.

Furthermore, it is this [entity] that constitutes the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Brahman, whereby there occurs within the inner self (*pratyagātman*)—which is non-modifiable, whose essence is self-luminous pure consciousness, and whose true nature is concealed by that very [adjunct]—the superimposition consisting of the distinction between the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the knower, and the known.

In this very world, which is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) through its particular states, there also arises a superimposition in the form of various cognitions of objects such as silver, which are sublated by knowledge. Furthermore, it is understood through the force of reasoning that the entire false form must have a cause that is itself false, since only that which is false can serve as the material cause (*upādāna*) for what is false.

Perception would have the ignorance of the cause as its object, for there is an immediate manifestation in the form: "I am ignorant" and "I do not know myself or another. However, this [manifestation] does not have the prior absence of knowledge (*jñāna-prāgabhāva*) as its object, because that falls within the domain of the sixth means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); whereas this is immediate, like the experience "I am happy. Even if one were to admit that an absence can be an object of perception, this experience does not have the absence of knowledge in the self as its object, because at the very time of the experience, knowledge is actually present.

Furthermore, if [the self] were non-existent, the cognition of the absence of knowledge would be untenable. What is meant by this? In the experience "I am ignorant," is there an apprehension of the self as the locus (*dharmin*) of the absence and of knowledge as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), or not? If there is, then due to the very contradiction [between the existence of the self and the absence of knowledge], the experience of the absence of knowledge is impossible. If there is not, then the experience of the absence of knowledge—which necessarily depends upon the cognition of both the locus and the counter-correlate—is all the more impossible.

This same inconsistency applies equally whether the absence of knowledge is held to be inferable or whether it is the object of a means of valid cognition called "non-existence" (abhāva). Since there is no contradiction even when the knowledge of the locus (dharmin) and the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) exists if this ignorance is of a positive nature (bhāvarūpa), one must accept that this experience has positive ignorance as its very object.

But surely even ignorance (*ajñāna*), being a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), is opposed by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), which consists in the manifestation of the true nature of reality? Not so. Witness-consciousness does not have the true nature of reality as its object, but rather has ignorance itself as its object; otherwise, the manifestation of false objects would be inexplicable. For ignorance is not removed by a cognition that has ignorance as its object; thus, there is no contradiction. But surely this ignorance, even though it is a positive entity, becomes an object of witness-consciousness only as distinguished from its specific objects.

Since that object is established in dependence upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could ignorance—which is excluded from the "I" (*asmadartha*)—be made an object by the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*)? This is not a fault. The entire multitude of things is an object of the witnessing consciousness, either as known or as unknown. Among these, that which is established as known due to its insentience necessarily depends upon the intervention of the means of valid cognition.

However, for the non-inert inner reality (*pratyag-vastu*), which is self-established, there is no dependence on the mediation of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus, its manifestation as the dispeller of ignorance is always logically consistent. Therefore, by perception (*pratyakṣa*) reinforced by reasoning (*nyāya*), ignorance is perceived as being of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*). This very ignorance, being of a positive nature, is also established by inference (*anumāna*): "The valid cognition under dispute is distinct from its own prior negation (*prāgabhāva*)..."

[Objection: Darkness is preceded by another entity located in its own place which is removable by itself and obstructs the objects [of perception]; because it illuminates an object not previously illuminated, like the state of a lamp first produced in the dark. If it is argued that darkness is merely the absence of light or merely the absence of the perception of form, and not a distinct substance (*dravya*), then how can it be put forward as an illustrative example for proving ignorance (*ajñāna*) as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*)?

[Reply: It is said in response: Because it is perceived as possessing color (*rūpavat*) and because it is associated with states such as density and rarity, darkness is indeed a distinct substance; thus, [the argument] is faultless.

To this it is replied: In the statement "I am ignorant; I do not know myself or another," a positive entity in the form of ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*) is not perceived through either perception accompanied by reasoning or by perception alone. As for the contradiction that was alleged regarding its having the prior non-existence of knowledge (*jñānaprāgabhāva*) as its object—that same contradiction applies equally to the case of positive ignorance. Furthermore, whether the inner self (*pratyagartha*) is apprehended or not apprehended, it serves to distinguish ignorance by being its object and its locus.

If it has been realized, how can that ignorance—which is to be removed by the knowledge of its own nature—persist once it has been realized? If it has not been realized, how can ignorance, which lacks knowledge of its differentiating attributes, its locus, and its object, be experienced? Now, if it is argued that the manifestation of a clear nature is what opposes ignorance;

But since its own nature is perceived as indistinct, there is no contradiction with the experience of ignorance even when there is knowledge of the locus and the object; alas, in that case, the prior absence of knowledge (*jñānaprāgabhāva*) would also have a distinct nature as its object, while the knowledge of the locus and the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) would have an indistinct nature as its object—there is no difference whatsoever other than mere dogmatic insistence.

For even in the case of ignorance (*ajñāna*) as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), there is indeed a dependence [on something else] when it is established as "ignorance," just as there is in the establishment of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). To explain: "ignorance" must be either the absence of knowledge, something other than it, or its opposite. In all three cases, a dependence on the knowledge of its own nature (*tatsvarūpajñāna*) must necessarily be admitted. Although there is no dependence on light for the apprehension of the nature of darkness, nevertheless, there is certainly a dependence on the apprehension of light insofar as it is apprehended in the form of being "opposed to light."

The ignorance (ajñāna) favored by you is never established in its own nature; rather, it is established only as "ignorance. This being the case, its dependence on [the cognition of] knowledge is equal to that of the absence of knowledge.

Furthermore, since the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of knowledge is accepted by you as well and is indeed perceived, one must admit that it is precisely this prior non-existence of knowledge—accepted by both parties—that is experienced in the intuition: "I am ignorant; I do not know myself and others. Moreover, the experience of ignorance is impossible for Brahman, whose sole nature is eternal, liberated, and self-luminous consciousness, because its very nature consists in self-awareness.

If it is argued that ignorance experiences its own nature even while that nature is concealed (*tirohita*), then what is this "concealment of nature"? If you say it is the state of being unmanifest (*aprakāśita*), then how can that which has the nature of self-experience be unmanifest? If you argue that even for that which has the nature of self-experience, its nature may be unmanifest due to something else, then—since we do not admit a property called "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) and manifestation is itself the very nature [of consciousness]—it would follow, as stated previously, that there would be a destruction of the very nature [of consciousness] by something else.

Furthermore, this ignorance, which is the cause of the concealment of the nature of Brahman, conceals Brahman only after it has itself been experienced; having concealed Brahman, it then becomes the object of that very experience. This constitutes a circular dependency (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*).

If one argues that it conceals [Brahman] only because it has been experienced, then Brahman would have to experience ignorance while its own nature remains unconcealed; in that case, the postulation of concealment would be purposeless.

Furthermore, there is the postulation of the nature of ignorance itself; for, just as the perception of ignorance by Brahman is possible, so too is the perception of the phenomenal world—which is held to be the effect of ignorance—possible [for Brahman]. Moreover, is the experience of ignorance by Brahman due to itself or from another? If it were due to itself, then because the experience of ignorance would be inherent to its own nature, there would be no liberation.

If it is argued that Brahman, whose nature is the experience of ignorance (*ajñāna*), ceases to exist as the experience of ignorance through the knowledge that sublates it—just as the experience of silver is removed by the knowledge that sublates illusory silver—or if it is argued that its nature as Brahman, which is the experience of ignorance, is removed by that sublating knowledge; [we reply: if it ceases through something else, what is that "other"? If you say it is another instance of ignorance, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If you say that it becomes an object of experience itself by setting aside Brahman, then this ignorance would set aside Brahman by its own mere existence, like a piece of glass or similar substance; consequently, ignorance could not be something to be sublated by knowledge.

Now, it might be argued that this ignorance (*ajñāna*) is itself beginningless (*anādi*), and that it simultaneously effects both the state of being the witness (*sākṣitva*) of Brahman and the concealment of Brahman’s true nature; therefore, defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*) do not apply. This is not so; for it is impossible to bring about the state of being a witness for Brahman—which is by nature self-manifesting—without first concealing its own nature. If one were to say that it is concealed by some other cause, then its beginninglessness would be abandoned, and the previously mentioned infinite regress would follow. Furthermore, if the state of being a witness were brought about while the nature remains unconcealed, then Brahman could not be solely intent upon its own self-manifestation.

Furthermore, when Brahman is concealed by ignorance, does that Brahman not manifest at all, or does something manifest? In the former case, it has been stated repeatedly that if Brahman, whose very nature is pure manifestation, were not to manifest, it would fall into the state of non-existence (*tucchatā*).

In the subsequent argument: what portion of Brahman—which is of the single essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss—is concealed, and what portion is manifested? Since Brahman is partless, devoid of distinctions, and pure luminosity, the coexistence of concealment and manifestation is impossible, as two distinct forms cannot exist within such a reality. Alternatively, it may be held that Brahman, though its true nature is concealed by ignorance, appears as if indistinct.

What constitutes clarity or lack of clarity for that whose very nature is pure manifestation? This is what is meant: for an object of manifestation that possesses parts and specific qualities (*saviśeṣa*), the manifestation of all its aspects is "clear manifestation," while the manifestation devoid of some particular qualities is "unclear manifestation. In that regard, concerning the aspect that has not been apprehended, there is no lack of clarity in manifestation precisely because of the absence of manifestation in that part. And as for the aspect that has been apprehended, the manifestation directed toward that object is indeed clear in that part.

Therefore, lack of clarity (*avaishadya*) is not possible regarding the aspect of luminosity in any case. Even with respect to an object, when its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is being cognized, lack of clarity consists solely in the non-cognition of certain specific features (*viśeṣa*) belonging to it. Consequently, in the case of Brahman—which is not an [empirical] object, is devoid of specific features, and is pure luminosity—lack of clarity, defined as the non-apprehension of certain specific features while its own nature is being manifested, cannot possibly be an effect of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Furthermore, does this lack of clarity, which is an effect of ignorance, cease upon the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), or does it not?

If there is no cessation [of ignorance], there is an absence of liberation (*apavarga*). If there is cessation, it must be investigated what the nature of the reality (*vastu*) is. If it is said to be a clear nature (*viśadasvarūpa*), does that clear nature exist prior [to liberation] or not? If it exists, then the lack of clarity—which is the effect of nescience (*avidyā*)—and its subsequent cessation would be impossible. If it does not exist, then because liberation would be a produced effect, it would be non-eternal.

The impossibility of this ignorance has already been stated precisely because its locus cannot be established. Furthermore, for one who asserts that [ignorance] is rooted in a non-ultimate defect, it is difficult to maintain that an error without a substratum (niradhiṣṭhāna-bhrama) is impossible; for just as an error can arise from a defect that serves as its cause, so too can an error occur even if the substratum is not ultimately real. Consequently, there would result nothing but universal emptiness (sarvaśūnyatva).

As for what was said—that ignorance in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) is established even by inference—that is incorrect, because inference is impossible. Now, it may be argued that inference was indeed stated. True, it was stated; however, it was poorly stated. For with respect to ignorance, the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), since it establishes another, unintended ignorance. In that case, if another ignorance is not established, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). If it is established, however, that [new] ignorance precludes the very nature of ignorance as being the witness (*sākṣitva*) of ignorance. Consequently, the postulation of ignorance would be fruitless.

Furthermore, the example is devoid of the probans (sādhanavikala), because the light of a lamp lacks the quality of illuminating objects not previously illuminated. For in all cases, it is knowledge alone that possesses the power of illumination; for even when a lamp is present, there is no illumination of an object without knowledge. As for the sense organs, their function is merely to serve as the cause for the arising of knowledge, not to illuminate. The light of a lamp, moreover, serves only as an auxiliary to the visual faculty by removing the obstructing darkness while that faculty produces knowledge.

If it is argued that the lamp is conventionally designated as "illuminator" with reference to its being a causal factor that assists the visual organ when that organ is engaged in the production of illuminating cognition—and that we have not cited the light of a lamp as an example by accepting a mode of illumination identical to that of cognition, but rather by acknowledging that, like cognition, it possesses the nature of illumination consisting in the removal of the veil over its own object—then [we reply]: No, for illumination is not merely the removal of an opposing factor.

Rather, it is the determination of an object—that is to say, the rendering [of an object] fit for practical activity (*vyavahāra*). And that belongs to cognition alone. If you admit that even auxiliary factors possess the quality of illuminating an unilluminated object, then, since the sense organs are the most immediate auxiliaries, they too must be admitted to illuminate the unilluminated object. This being the case, because they lack the property of being preceded by another entity that is itself removed by them, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); so, enough of this.

And the counter-argument is as follows: "The ignorance under dispute does not have Brahman, which is mere consciousness, as its locus, because it is ignorance, like the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and the like; rather, it has the knower as its locus."

Indeed, it is so: the ignorance under discussion does not have Brahman, which is pure consciousness, as its locus, because it is ignorance, like the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and the like; for that [ignorance] is indeed a veil over the object. The ignorance under discussion is not removable by knowledge, because it does not veil the object of knowledge; whatever ignorance is removable by knowledge veils the object of that knowledge, just like the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and the like. Brahman is not the locus of ignorance, because it lacks the status of being a knower, like a jar or similar objects.
Brahman is not veiled by ignorance, because it is not an object of knowledge. Whatever...

That ignorance which is the object of knowledge is like a mother-of-pearl shell and the like; Brahman is not the ignorance that is removable by knowledge, because it is not an object of knowledge. That ignorance which is removable by knowledge is an object of knowledge, as in the case of a mother-of-pearl shell and the like.

The valid cognition under dispute is not preceded by an ignorance distinct from its own prior non-existence, because it is a valid cognition, like the valid cognition that serves as the means of proving the ignorance you yourself accept. Knowledge does not destroy an object, because, in the absence of being augmented by a specific power, it is knowledge; for that which destroys an object is seen to be either knowledge augmented by a specific power or ignorance, such as the knowledge of the Lord, yogis, and others, or such as a mallet and the like.

Ignorance, being of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), cannot be destroyed by knowledge, because it is a positive entity, like a jar or similar objects. If it be argued that the destruction of fear and other states produced by a prior cognition is seen through a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), this is not so; for their destruction is not caused by knowledge, since they perish of their own accord due to their momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), and because they do not arise subsequently once their causes have ceased. Their momentariness is understood from the fact that, like cognitions, they are perceived only when the causes of their production are present, and are not perceived otherwise.

Furthermore, if fear and the like were non-momentary, then since there would be no distinction within the continuum of cognitions that serve as the causes of fear and so forth, all cognitions would equally become causes for the arising of fear; consequently, it would follow that multiple instances of fear would be perceived simultaneously.

By employing the qualification "preceded by another entity distinct from its own prior non-existence," the proponent has revealed his lack of skill in formal argumentation. Therefore, even through inference, the existence of ignorance as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) is not established.
Furthermore, that ignorance is not established by scripture or by postulation based on it will be explained immediately hereafter.

The claim that the apprehension of a false object must itself be false is also refuted by the principle of the section beginning with the words, "Because of the difference in characteristics" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*). Therefore, there is no cognition whatsoever whose object is an indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyājñāna*). Even through the criteria of cognition, error, and sublation, such a thing cannot be accepted. For it is only that which is actually being cognized which constitutes the object of cognition, error, and sublation. It is not logical to postulate that the object of these cognitions is something unperceived by them or by any other cognition.

If it is argued that—because of the cognition of silver and the like in mother-of-pearl and such objects, because of the sublation (bādha) which shows that even at the time of cognition that [silver] does not exist there, and because it is impossible for one thing to appear as another—it must be postulated that this silver, which is neither existent nor non-existent and is unprecedented, is cognized due to the influence of a defect (doṣa)—we say no; for even in that postulation, the appearance of one thing as another remains unavoidable. Since the explanation of manifestation, activity, sublation, and the nature of error is fully accounted for simply by accepting the appearance of one thing as another, it is improper to postulate a thing whose form has never been observed and which lacks a cause.

For that which is being conceptualized as "indescribable" (anirvacanīya) is not perceived as "indescribable"; rather, it is perceived precisely as "the silver [of recollection]. If it were indeed perceived as "indescribable," then the occurrence of both error and sublation would be impossible. Therefore, since the perception, the inclination toward action, the sublation, and the state of being an error cannot be accounted for in the absence of one thing appearing as another, and because this [appearance] is unavoidable, you must admit that the mother-of-pearl and such appear in the form of silver and so forth.
