Moreover, even for those who maintain other theories of manifestation (*khyāti*), one must necessarily resort to a "manifestation otherwise" (*anyathābhāsa*), even if one goes as far as possible: in the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), it is by way of the nature of the existent; in the theory of self-manifestation (*ātmakhyāti*), it is by way of the nature of the object; in the theory of non-manifestation (*akhyāti*) as well, it is by taking a qualifier of one thing to be the qualifier of another, and by taking two cognitions to be one; and even in the theory that the object is non-existent, it is by way of its being present.

Furthermore, by one who asserts that an indefinable and unprecedented silver has been produced here, the cause of its production must be stated. It cannot be the cognition itself, because as that [silver] is the object of that [cognition], it is impossible for the cognition to attain its own existence prior to the production of the object. That a cognition, having arisen without an object, produces that very object and then makes it its object—this is a great feat of justification! Nor can it be a defect residing in the sense organs and so forth; for since such a defect resides in the person (the subject), it is unfit to produce an effect located in the object. Nor indeed...

Nor are the sense organs the cause [of such error], because they serve as the causes for [veridical] cognition. Nor are the defective sense organs the cause, for even they produce a distinction only within cognition itself, which is their own effect. Furthermore, the claim that beginningless false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) is the material cause has already been refuted. Moreover, how could this class of objects—neither previously experienced nor definable—be made the object of the cognition and the word "silver" and so forth, and not of the cognition and the word "jar" and so forth? If you say it is due to its similarity to silver and the like, then the cognition and the word would have to be "that which is similar to it."

If it is argued that this is due to the connection with universals (*jāti*) such as "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*), we ask: is that universal ultimately real (*paramārthabhūta*) or not ultimately real (*aparamārthabhūta*)? It cannot be ultimately real, because it is impossible for something ultimately real to be connected with what is not ultimately real. Nor can it be not ultimately real, because it is impossible for something not ultimately real to be connected with what is ultimately real. Furthermore, it is impossible for something not ultimately real to serve as the basis for the application of the cognition and the word "ultimately real. Enough, then, of refuting such immature sophistry. Alternatively, the view of those who know the Veda is that all cognition corresponds to its object, because the Śruti and Smṛti texts reveal that everything has everything as its self.
At the commencement of creation and so forth, preceded by the resolve "May I be many," it was enjoined by the Śruti itself: "Of these, each one became threefold."
For this very process of triplication is perceived through direct observation: that which is the red form of fire is [the form] of water as well.
The threefold nature of fire—consisting of the white, the black, and that which belongs to the earth—is shown by the Veda itself; therefore, all [elements] are present everywhere.

And it is stated likewise in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa at the beginning of the account of creation: "Possessing diverse powers and existing separately, they were unable to create offspring in their entirety without a collective union."
Having come together through mutual conjunction and being mutually dependent, the principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas [form] the Egg (aṇḍa), and so forth.

The author of the Sūtras likewise stated that the elements possess a threefold nature in the words, "But because they consist of three constituents and because of their predominance"; by this, the distinction of names is explained.
Experts in logic know that the scriptural injunction to take *pūtīka* plants in the absence of *soma* is based on the presence of parts of the *soma* within them.
And just as nīvāra grain is taken in the absence of rice because of that absence, so too that alone is similar to it which partakes of a portion of that substance.

The existence of silver and the like within mother-of-pearl and so forth is taught by the scripture itself; the distinction between the designations "silver" and "mother-of-pearl" is caused by their relative abundance.
Furthermore, this mother-of-pearl and the like is perceived as being similar to silver and so forth; therefore, its existence therein is not established even by perception.

Sometimes, however, due to a defect in the eye or other senses, the silver-portion is apprehended while the portion belonging to the mother-of-pearl is excluded; consequently, one who seeks silver proceeds toward it.

But when the defect is removed and the aspect of the mother-of-pearl is apprehended, that [error] ceases; therefore, the cognition of silver and so forth regarding mother-of-pearl and the like is in accordance with reality.

The relationship between the sublated and the sublator is also established by way of predominance, consisting in the perception of the deficiency or completeness of the predominance of the mother-of-pearl.

Therefore, the establishment of conventional usage is not based on the distinction between objects that have false meanings and those that have true meanings; for if everything were everything, such a systematic arrangement of conventions would be impossible.

During sleep, however, it is the Blessed Lord himself who creates for each individual person objects of such a nature—experienced by that person alone and lasting only for that particular time—in accordance with their respective merits and demerits. Thus, the Śruti concerning the subject of dreams states: "There are no chariots there, nor yoked chariots, nor roads; yet he creates chariots, yoked chariots, and roads. There are no lakes, lotus-pools, or rivers there; yet he creates lakes, lotus-pools, and rivers."

"For He is the agent. Although at that time those objects do not exist as being perceivable by all other persons, nevertheless, the Lord creates such objects so as to be perceivable by each respective person alone. For He is the agent. The meaning is that such agency is possible for Him, who possesses true resolve and wondrous power. "He who is awake among these sleeping ones, fashioning object after object according to desire—that indeed is the Bright, that is Brahman, that alone is called the Immortal."

"All worlds are supported in Him; no one transcends Him," so it is said. The author of the Sūtras as well, in the two sūtras: "For [the scripture] declares that there is creation in the intermediate state (sandhya)," and "And some [declare Him] to be the creator, as well as sons and so forth," [shows that] because the entire nature of the individual soul (jīva)—such as its innate power of true resolve—is unmanifest during the state of transmigratory existence, this creation, which is experienced by each specific person alone and is thus a marvel, belongs to the Lord Himself.

He offers this rebuttal: "In that [Self], all worlds are sheltered, and no one transcends it"—from this, it is understood that the Supreme Self alone is the creator therein. For one who is lying in a room or similar place and sees a dream, such things as traveling to another land, being consecrated to a kingdom, or having one's head cut off—which are the fruits of merit and demerit—are possible through the creation of another body whose form and configuration resemble the body of the one lying down, even though [the dreamer] travels with his own body.

Even a crystal gem situated near a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*) is perceived as red because it is overwhelmed by its luster. Furthermore, although the light of the hibiscus flower is diffused, it is perceived most clearly due to its contact with a transparent substance; this is established by such perception. Even in the cognition of water in a mirage (*marīcikā*), there is correspondence with reality (*yathārthatva*), because both fire and earth also exist there, yet due to a defect in the sense organ, fire and earth are not apprehended, while water is apprehended through the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

Even in the case of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*), such a perception is possible because the fire-brand, through its extremely rapid movement, comes into contact with all locations simultaneously, and thus the intervening spaces are not perceived. Even in the perception of a circle, it is simply the perception of various objects as they come into contact with their respective locations, preceded by the non-perception of the intervening spaces. The distinction is that in some cases there is no perception of intervening spaces due to their absence, while in other cases there is no perception due to rapidity; therefore, that [perception] too is real. Likewise, the perception of one's own face and so forth in mirrors and the like is also real.

For the visual rays, having been reflected by a mirror or similar surface, grasp one's own face and so forth only after first grasping the location of the mirror and such. Even in that case, because of extreme rapidity, there is no perception of the intervening space, and thus the cognition occurs in that manner. Even in the case of confusion regarding direction (*digmoha*), since another direction exists within this very direction, it is through the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) that a portion of another direction, separated from this directional part, is grasped. Therefore, the cognition of another direction is indeed real.

Even in cases such as the cognition of two moons, due to the obstruction by a finger or the presence of ophthalmia (*timira*), there is a divergence in the movement of the ocular light; because of this difference in causal conditions (*sāmagrī*), two distinct sets of conditions arise that are mutually independent and serve as the causes for the apprehension of two moons. Among these, one set of conditions apprehends the moon as qualified by its own location, while the second set, having a slightly curved trajectory, first apprehends the location near the moon and then apprehends the moon as separated from its own location.

Therefore, when two sets of causal conditions simultaneously apprehend the moon as qualified by two locations, there arises the specific cognition "there are two moons" because of the difference in the forms of the objects grasped due to the difference in the acts of apprehension, and because of the absence of an apprehension of unity. This qualification of the other location occurs through the continuous apprehension of the other location and of the moon that has not yet been apprehended in its own location. In this case, the duality of the causal conditions is ultimately real; consequently, the dual apprehension of the moon as qualified by two locations is also ultimately real.

Due to the duality of the apprehensions, the duality of the apprehended form of the moon itself is ultimately real. In that case, regarding the apprehension of two moons qualified by two attributes, since there is only one moon as the object to be apprehended, visual cognition remains fixed upon that very [single moon], because the mere eye lacks the capacity for recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Although both eyes are included within a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it is to be inferred from the effect that the visual light becomes two distinct causal complexes due to the presence of defects such as *timira*.

When the defect has departed, however, because the moon—distinguished by its own location—is cognized through a single act of perception, the cognition arises that "there is one moon. It is thus faultless to maintain that the duality of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is caused by the defect, the duality of the acts of perception is caused by that, and the duality of the forms of the objects perceived is caused by that.

Therefore, it is established that the entire collection of cognitions corresponds to reality (*yathārtha*). As for the refutations of other theories of error (*khyāti*), they have been elaborated by those very disputants themselves; hence, no effort is made here [to refute them].

(Alternatively, what is the use of this extensive method of demonstration? For those who accept the collection of means of valid knowledge known as perception, inference, and scripture, as well as the Supreme Brahman—which is accessible through scripture, free from even a trace of all defects, possessed of an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities, omniscient, and whose will is true—what [is there that cannot be established]?)*

It will be established; what is not possible? For by the Blessed One, who is the Supreme Brahman, the entire universe was created for the sake of being experienced by the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) in accordance with their merits and demerits. Thus, objects that result in the experience of pleasure, pain, or indifference are created as objects of universal experience; some are created as objects of experience for specific individuals alone, limited to specific times, and to be experienced in such-and-such a manner.
In this regard, the relationship of sublation and sublated is possible through being an object of universal experience and through being devoid thereof; thus, everything is consistent.

As for the claim that ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is both existent and non-existent and yet indefinable (*anirvacanīya*), is established by scripture—that is incorrect. This is because in passages such as "For they are veiled by the untrue" (*anṛtena hi pratyūḍhāḥ*), the word "untrue" (*anṛta*) does not denote something indefinable. Indeed, the word *anṛta* refers to that which is other than *ṛta* (truth). The term *ṛta* denotes action (*karman*), as seen in the statement "the two who drink the *ṛta*" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*). *Ṛta* is action devoid of desire for its fruits, taking the form of worship of the Supreme Person, with the attainment of Him as its fruit.

In this context, action that results in worldly fruits and is distinct from that [knowledge] is "unreal" (*anṛta*), because it is opposed to the attainment of Brahman; for there is the scriptural statement: "They do not find this world of Brahman, for they are veiled by the unreal."

In the passage, “Then there was neither non-existence nor existence,” the words “existent” (sat) and “non-existent” (asat) likewise refer to the collective manifestations (saṃhati) of consciousness (cit) and unconsciousness (acit). At the time of dissolution, even those two entities—which at the time of origination were designated by the words “existent” and “conscious” and constituted the collective manifestations of consciousness and unconsciousness—merge into the entity denoted by the word “darkness” (tamas), which constitutes the collective manifestation of the unconscious.

Because this sentence is intent upon establishing [the dissolution of the world], nothing here is stated regarding the existence, non-existence, or the inexpressibility of anything as being both existent and non-existent; for it merely states that both the existent and the non-existent become non-existent at a particular time. Here, the fact that what is denoted by the word "darkness" (*tamas*) is the aggregate of the insentient (*acit-samaṣṭi*) is understood from another scriptural passage: "The unmanifest dissolves into the imperishable (*akṣara*); the imperishable dissolves into darkness."

True; it may be argued that by the word *tamas* the subtle state of *prakṛti*, which is the aggregate of the non-intelligent (*acit*), is denoted, and since that [state] is designated by the word *māyā* in the passage, "One should know *māyā* as *prakṛti*," it follows that it is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*). But this is not so; for the word *māyā* is not observed to have the meaning of "indeterminable. If it is argued that the word *māyā* signifies the indeterminable because it is a synonym for "falsehood" (*mithyā*), that too is not the case; for the word *māyā* does not everywhere refer to what is false.

Because the word *māyā* is applied even to real things such as the weapons of Asuras and Rākṣasas, as it has been said: "By that swift-moving [missile], while protecting the body of the boy, a thousand of Śambara’s *māyās* were destroyed one by one. Therefore, the word *māyā* denotes that which produces a manifold creation of objects.

And the designation of *prakṛti* by the word *māyā* is precisely because it produces a manifold creation of objects; for [the scripture] shows that *prakṛti*, which is denoted by the word *māyā*, produces a manifold creation of objects in the passage: "From this, the Māyin creates this universe, and another, bound by *māyā*, is within it. Furthermore, the Supreme Person is called "possessing *māyā*" (*māyin*) merely by virtue of having that [power], not by virtue of being ignorant. For it is the individual soul alone that is heard to be bound by *māyā* in the passage: "And another, bound by *māyā*, is within it."

And [it is said]: "When the individual soul (jīva), sleeping through beginningless illusion (māyā), awakens. Also in the passage, "Indra, by means of māyās, moves in manifold forms," various powers (śaktis) are denoted; for this very reason it is said, "He shines forth abundantly like Tvaṣṭṛ. Indeed, no one who is overcome by falsehood shines forth. Furthermore, in the statement, "My māyā is difficult to transcend," because of the expression "consisting of the qualities" (guṇamayī), that same primordial nature (prakṛti) composed of the three qualities is what is being referred to. Thus, the Upaniṣads do not establish an ignorance (ajñāna) that is indefinable as either existent or non-existent.

Nor can it be [established] through the impossibility of the teaching of identity. For when there is the teaching of the identity between the individual soul and the Supreme Lord in the statement "That thou art," no inconsistency whatsoever is observed that could serve as a basis for postulating a contradictory ignorance in the context of Brahman—which is understood by the word "That," which is omniscient, whose will is true, and who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the entire universe. Furthermore, the teaching of identity is even more appropriately explained by the fact that the word "thou" (*tvam*) also denotes Brahman itself, having the individual soul as its body.

By the statement, "Entering by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms," it is indeed declared that everything down to the ultimate limit of the Supreme Self (paramātman) alone possesses name and form; therefore, there is no postulation of ignorance regarding Brahman. Furthermore, in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the doctrine of Brahman's ignorance is not seen anywhere.

Now, having first proposed that Brahman alone is the single reality in the statement, "The luminaries are Viṣṇu," and having then declared that this world—diversified by distinctions such as mountains, oceans, and the earth—is a manifestation of ignorance regarding Brahman, whose sole nature is knowledge, in the words, "Since the Blessed Lord is of the nature of knowledge"; and finally, having confirmed that it is indeed a manifestation of ignorance by demonstrating the absence of any real distinction between things at the time when Brahman, whose very nature is knowledge, abides in its own essential form, in the words, "But when [it is] pure and established in its own nature";

Having established the unreality of the various objects of the world even through the manner in which the world is perceived—by means of the two verses beginning with "vastvasti kim" and "mahī ghaṭatvam"—and having concluded the unreality of everything other than Brahman as promised in the statement "tasmānna vijñānamṛte," [the author] clarifies that one's own karma alone is the root of ignorance which causes the perception of difference in Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, by the verse "vijñānamekam"; and [finally], he describes the essential nature of Brahman, who is of the nature of consciousness, by the verse "jñānaṃ viśuddham."

Having purified [the mind], the instruction is seen as follows: "Thus has the true nature been declared by me to you"—meaning that Brahman, whose very essence is consciousness, alone is real, and nothing else; while everything else is indeed unreal, the reality of the world and so forth is merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*). This is the truth that has been taught to you.

This is not so; for after describing the vast nature of the cosmic egg (*bhuvanakośa*) here, another aspect previously unmentioned is now being set forth, beginning with the words, "Listen to the summary. In this world consisting of the sentient and the insentient, the sentient portion—whose distinct nature is self-evident and beyond the reach of speech and mind—is denoted by the word "is" (*asti*) because it is imperishable and its distinctions are untouched by material nature (*prakṛti*), being uniform in the form of knowledge alone. The insentient portion, however, whose distinct modifications are caused by the karma of the sentient portion and which is subject to destruction, is denoted by the word "is not" (*nāsti*).
However, since both are of the nature of that [Brahman] by virtue of being the body of Vāsudeva, who is the Supreme Brahman, this form has been described here in brief. For it is thus:

Regarding the statement: "O Brahmin, from that water which was indeed the body of Viṣṇu, the earth emerged in the form of a lotus, joined with mountains, oceans, and so forth," [the author] says that because water is the body of Viṣṇu, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which is a transformation of water, is also the body of Viṣṇu; and since Viṣṇu is its self, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—which serves as a reinforcement for the teaching of identity found throughout all the Śrutis, beginning with "The luminaries are Viṣṇu"—has precisely this relationship of body and self as its basis.

In this scripture, this has also been stated repeatedly previously: "All those are His body," "All that is indeed the body of Hari," and "He alone is the self of all beings, the universal form, because He is imperishable. This identity, dependent on the relationship between body and self, is designated through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in: "The luminaries are Viṣṇu. Here, it is stated that every object within the world—whether of the nature of existence or non-existence—is identical with Viṣṇu by virtue of being His body.

"This has the nature of existence, this has the nature of non-existence, and this is the reason for its nature of non-existence"—thus he says: "Because the Blessed Lord is of the very nature of consciousness. For the Blessed Lord, who exists as the self of all individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), consciousness alone is His natural form; He does not have the form of objects such as gods or humans. Since this is so, for that very reason, insentient entities such as gods, humans, mountains, oceans, and the earth are but the manifestations of His consciousness.

Although He exists as having the single form of pure knowledge (*jñāna*), His manifold nature as gods and so forth is rooted in the contemplation of His own self in various forms; that is to say, it is rooted in karma, which itself is rooted in the contemplation of the forms of gods and others. Since non-sentient matter (*acid-vastu*) is the locus of transformations according to the karma of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), it follows by implication that such matter is denoted by the word "non-existent," while everything else is denoted by the word "existent. He explains this very point with the words: "But when [He is] pure, possessing His own essential nature."

When this reality of the Self, which is of the single form of knowledge, becomes faultless, completely pure, and established in its own nature through the destruction of all karma—the root of which is the mental projection of diversity within itself in the forms of gods and so forth—then, because the conceptualization of the Self as one with the forms of gods and others has ceased, there no longer exist those distinctions between objects that constitute the fruits of karma and serve as the basis for experiencing them.

The meaning is this: among the various objects such as gods, humans, mountains, oceans, and the earth—which are conceived as the Self and serve as objects of enjoyment—these do not exist once the karmas that are their root have perished. Thus, because non-conscious matter (acid-vastu) possesses occasional specific states, it is denoted by the word "non-existent" (nāsti); whereas the other [the Self], because its nature is always established as consisting solely of knowledge, is denoted by the word "existent" (asti).

He states, "Is there any entity? because for an insentient object (*acidvastu*), which undergoes change at every moment and possesses occasional states, the very nature is that of being denoted by the word "non-existent. For an entity denotable by the word "existent" is one devoid of beginning, middle, and end—a reality whose form is eternally constant; since such an entity can never be the object of the cognition "it does not exist," no insentient object has ever been observed to be of such a nature anywhere. To the question "What follows from this?", he says, "And that which is subject to change... [and so forth].

Whatever entity undergoes change at every moment, it abandons each preceding state by attaining each succeeding state; thus, there is no reconnection of that which was in a prior state with its subsequent state. Therefore, at all times, such an entity is only denotable by the word "non-existent."

For this reason, he says: "The earth [attains] the state of being a jar. The meaning is that by their own actions—namely, through states such as those of gods or humans—those whose self-conviction is fixed perceive and experience insentient matter (*acid-vastu*), which has become their object of enjoyment, as changing at every moment. This being the case, is there any insentient substance whatsoever that is worthy of the word "exists," which is devoid of beginning, middle, or end, and which is perceived as eternally uniform? The intention is that there is no such thing.

Since this is so, he says, "Therefore, nothing other than the Self whose nature is consciousness ever exists anywhere as something denotable by the word 'is' alone," meaning that insentient matter (acidvastu), which is distinct from the Self whose nature is knowledge, is never at any time or place expressible by the word "exists" in its absolute sense.

The Self, however, because its sole form is knowledge, possesses a nature that is contrary to the distinctions of gods and so forth; yet, through the various cognitions of a self divided by the distinctions of gods and others—which are rooted in the diverse karmas performed by oneself and which serve as the cause for entering the bodies of gods and so forth—it is perceived in many ways according to those respective forms. Thus, he says, "Knowledge is one," to show that this perception of its divisions is not prompted by the true nature of the Self. The nature of the Self, moreover, is devoid of karma, and for that very reason, it is untouched by *prakṛti* in its form as impurity (*mala*).

Consequently, it is unattached to all qualities to be abandoned—such as grief, delusion, and greed—which are caused by that [material nature]; it is one, because it is incapable of increase or decrease; and for that very reason, it is eternally of a single form. And since it is the body of Vāsudeva, it has him as its essence; for there is nothing whatsoever that does not have him as its essence. Thus he says, "Knowledge is pure. The conscious aspect (cidaṃśa), being eternally of a single form, is always denoted by the word "is"; the unconscious aspect (acidaṃśa), however, because it undergoes momentary transformation, is always pregnant with destruction and is therefore always denoted by the word "is not."

He states that the true nature of the world has been correctly described by saying that this world, consisting of such a nature of both consciousness and non-consciousness, is the body of Vāsudeva and is identical with Him: "The true state..."

"So it is. Here, with the words "the real and the unreal," there is a conclusion of what was introduced as "that which exists and that which does not exist. He says, "But this which... to state that the cause for this—which exists as a single form of consciousness, yet possesses a distinction of essential nature beyond the reach of words, being a mixture of the conscious and the unconscious, dependent on the worlds, and appearing in the forms of gods, humans, and so forth, such that its distinctions are fit for correct worldly transaction—is indeed *karma* alone. He explains that very point with, "Sacrifice, animal...
and he states that the purpose of knowing the true nature of the world is the application of the means to liberation with, "And this which..."

In this regard, not even a single word is seen that is consistent with [the doctrines of] the supreme Brahman devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*), the ignorance (*ajñāna*) based upon it which is defined as being neither existent nor non-existent (*sadasadanirvacanīya*), or the fact that the world is imagined (*kalpita*) by that [ignorance]. Rather, the entire world, consisting of both consciousness and matter, which is denoted by the words "existent" and "non-existent," is of the nature of Viṣṇu—the supreme Brahman, the highest Lord—since it is His body (*kāya*) and thus identical with Him.

This is because it is established that for the Self, which is of the nature of pure consciousness, the cause of experiencing various forms such as gods and so forth, as well as the transformation of insentient matter (*acit*), is the very *karma* of the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) which is opposed to the knowledge of the true nature of reality; furthermore, because words such as "existent" (*asti*), "non-existent" (*nāsti*), "real" (*satya*), and "unreal" (*asatya*) lack the capacity to denote an entity that is both existent and non-existent yet indescribable (*sadasadanirvacanīya*). The terms "non-existent" and "unreal" are antithetical to the terms "existent" and "real"; therefore, through these [latter] two, non-existence (*asattva*) is indeed perceived, not indescribability (*anirvacanīyatva*).

In this context, regarding non-conscious entities (*acidvastu*), the terms *nāsti* (non-existent) and *asatya* (unreal) are not employed to signify insubstantiality (*tucchatva*) or falsity (*mithyātva*), but rather to signify perishability (*vināśitva*). Even in the cases of "Is there any real thing? and "The earth [attains] the state of a pot," it is indeed perishability that is established, and not a lack of evidence or sublation by cognition; for non-existence is established through the perception of something as otherwise at a later time due to a specific transformation, after it was experienced in one form at a previous time.

For "insubstantiality" (tucchatva) is the unfitness for connection with any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, "sublation" (*bādha*) consists in the perception that something which was previously perceived as existing in relation to a particular place, time, and so forth, is subsequently perceived as not existing in relation to that same place, time, and so forth; it does not consist in the perception that what was experienced at one time no longer exists at another time due to transformation or other changes, because there is no contradiction when the times differ. Therefore, [the world] is not false.

This is what is meant: the reality of the Self, whose nature is consciousness, being devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and possessing a single, constant nature, exists eternally by its own right and is denoted by the word "is" (*asti*). The insentient, however—which constitutes the object of experience for the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*)—undergoes transformation according to that [knower's] karma and is perishable; thus it always does not exist in its true sense and is denoted by the words "is not" (*nāsti*) and "unreal" (*asatya*). As it has been said:

"The wise accept that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is indestructible (*anāśin*). That [which is] destructible (*nāśin*) does not exist; there is no doubt about this, for it is produced from destructible substances. For an object that possesses both existence and non-existence depending on specific differences of place, time, and action, its being cognizable by the cognition of mere existence is called the "ultimate," while the other is called the "non-ultimate. Since the Self alone is cognizable by the cognition of mere existence, it is called the "ultimate. And for the listener, Maitreya—

And from the restatement: "Just as the three worlds are situated with Viṣṇu as their support, so has the ultimate reality been declared to me according to knowledge, primarily," it is understood that the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in passages such as "The luminaries are Viṣṇu" is based precisely on the relationship of self and body; furthermore, the primacy of knowledge—due to its being natural and not caused by karma—is the basis for applying the terms "existent" and "non-existent" to the conscious and unconscious entities respectively, while the non-primacy of the unconscious entity is due to its being subject to transformation caused by karma.

As for the claim that the scriptures state that the cessation of ignorance occurs solely through the knowledge of the undifferentiated Brahman (*nirviśeṣa-brahma*), that is incorrect; for it contradicts numerous scriptural passages such as: "I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness; knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here; there is no other path for the journey"; "All moments of time were born from the Puruṣa, who is like lightning"; "No one rules over Him; His name is Great Glory"; and "Those who know Him become immortal. Thus, there is a contradiction with many such statements.

Precisely because Brahman possesses distinctions, all scriptural passages declare that liberation results only from the knowledge of Brahman as possessing distinctions; it has already been stated that even the purificatory passages (*śodhakavākya*) establish Brahman as indeed possessing distinctions.

In sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not aim at the identity of a featureless reality; for the two words "That" (*tat*) and "thou" (*tvam*) denote Brahman as possessing attributes. For the word "That" refers to Brahman—the omniscient, whose will is true, and who is the cause of the world—since He alone is the subject under discussion in passages such as "He thought: 'May I be many'. And the word "thou," which is coreferential with it, establishes Brahman as having the individual soul, characterized by non-sentient matter, as its body; it is a single reality existing in two modes.

Because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is more fundamental [than the individual meanings]. If both modes [of meaning] were abandoned, coreferentiality itself would have to be abandoned, since a difference in the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) would be impossible. Furthermore, there would be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for both words. Even in the case of "This is that Devadatta," there is no figurative indication; for there is no contradiction in the cognition of a single entity as being connected with both past and present times. Moreover, the contradiction regarding the difference in location is resolved by the difference in time. And there is also a contradiction with the opening statement [of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*]: "It thought: 'May I become many.'"

Furthermore, the proposition that all consciousness is [identical] with a single consciousness is untenable. For one who is omniscient by nature, free from all defects, and whose essence consists of every auspicious quality, it would be contradictory for there to be ignorance or the locus of its effects—the infinite misfortunes of human existence. Moreover, if the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) were intended in the sense of sublation (*bādha*), then the very same defects previously mentioned—such as the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the substratum by the words "thou" (*tvam*) and "that" (*tat*), and the indication of cessation—would persist.

(However, there is this distinction: unlike the case of "this is not silver," sublation (*bādha*) must be postulated even for one who has not yet apprehended it, as there is no other way; furthermore, sublation would be untenable because the word *tat* does not bring to mind a property distinct from the substrate. If it is argued that the substrate, which was previously concealed, is presented by the word *tat* in its unconcealed nature, we say no; for if the substrate were not manifest prior [to the error], an error resting upon it and its subsequent sublation would be impossible. If it is argued that the substrate, which serves as the locus of the error, is indeed unconcealed;

Therefore, since the very nature of the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) is opposed to error, when that [substratum] is revealed, there can by no means be either the occurrence of an error or the sublation of one based upon it. Consequently, if one does not admit the concealment of the reality of the ultimate attribute—which is distinct from the substratum—it is difficult to account for both error and its sublation.

For when the substrate is perceived merely in the form of a person, while its ultimate reality as kingship—which transcends that [personality]—is concealed, there occurs the delusion of being a hunter. And the cessation of that [delusion] occurs through the instruction regarding kingship, not through the instruction regarding the substrate alone; for the substrate, being already manifest, is not something to be instructed about, and because it does not suppress the delusion.

The two words have their primary meaning when they refer to Brahman as the cause of the world, which has the individual soul as its body; and by establishing a single reality qualified by these two modes, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is achieved. Furthermore, the fact that Brahman—which is free from all defects and consists of all auspicious qualities—possesses the individual soul as its inner controller (*antaryāmin*) is established as another aspect of His sovereignty. This also accords with the opening statement (*upakrama*) and validates the promise that through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all.

Since Brahman, whose body consists of subtle sentient and insentient entities, becomes the effect by having gross sentient and insentient entities as its body, there is no contradiction with other scriptural passages such as, "Him, the supreme Lord of lords," "His power is indeed heard to be manifold," and "Free from evil, whose desires are true, whose resolves are true. If it is asked, "In the statement 'That thou art' (*tat tvam asi*), how is the distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*) to be understood?"—the answer is that here nothing is being predicated of anything else; rather, it is a case of identity.

This is because [the truth] has already been established by the very statement, "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*). For scripture is purposeful only with regard to what has not yet been attained. Having pointed out "all this"—that is, the world together with the living soul—as "having that as its self," it is demonstrated therein that "that" is indeed its Self. And the reason for this was stated: "O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support," just as in the passage: "All this is indeed Brahman, because it originates from it, dissolves into it, and breathes in it; therefore, be tranquil."

Likewise, other scriptural passages declare that the identity between Brahman and the sentient and insentient entities distinct from Him consists precisely in the relationship of body and self: "He has entered within as the ruler of people, the Self of all"; "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who rules the earth from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal"; and "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self..."

"He who controls the self from within—that is your self, the inner controller (antaryāmin), the immortal"; beginning with "He who moves within the earth," and continuing up to "He whose body is death, whom death does not know—this is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa"; and "Having created that, He entered into it; having entered it, He became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat)," and so forth.

In this context as well, by the statement, "Having entered with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms," it is established that the substantiality and the denotability by words of all things occur precisely through the entry of the living self whose essence is Brahman. Since this has the same meaning as the passage, "Having entered that, it became the existent (sat) and the non-existent (tyat)," it is understood that even for that living self, its nature as having Brahman as its essence arises solely from the entry of Brahman.

Therefore, it is understood that the identity of the entire multitude of things—consisting of both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*)—with Brahman arises solely from the relationship of self and body (*ātma-śarīra-bhāva*). Consequently, since everything other than Brahman possesses its reality only by virtue of being His body, even the word that denotes such a thing expresses its own meaning as culminating in Him alone. Thus, it is established that all words denote Brahman as qualified by their respective objects as known through worldly linguistic usage; hence, [the Upanishadic statement]: "All this has That as Its Self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*).
The conclusion regarding the specific meaning of the proposition is reached through the grammatical coordination expressed in "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).

Consequently, for those who maintain that the non-distinct reality is a single unity—namely, the proponents of identity-in-difference (*bhedābheda*) and the proponents of absolute difference (*kevalabheda*)—all teachings regarding the nature of Brahman as the Self, whether expressed through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or grammatical subordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), would be abandoned. For what identity could be taught concerning a single entity? If it is argued that it is the identity of that very entity itself, then since that is already understood by its own definition, there remains nothing to be established through the teaching of identity.

If it is argued that this [theory] is the refutation of imagined difference (*kalpitabheda*), we reply that this cannot be established by the teaching of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and identity (*tādātmya*), as has already been stated. Indeed, coreferentiality, by positing two distinct modes within Brahman, would only bring about contradiction. Furthermore, in the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābhedavāda*), because of the contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) within Brahman itself, the defects residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) caused by those adjuncts would manifest in Brahman itself; thus, the teachings regarding the nature of Brahman as consisting of all-auspicious qualities and being free from all defects would have to be abandoned precisely due to such contradiction.

Even in the doctrine of natural difference-and-non-difference (*svābhāvikabhedābheda*), since the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*) is admitted for Brahman by its very nature, defects—just like qualities—would also be inherent; thus, the teaching of identity with Brahman as being devoid of defects would be a direct contradiction. Furthermore, for those who maintain absolute difference (*kevalabheda*), since unity between two absolutely distinct entities is impossible in any way whatsoever, teachings regarding the identity of Brahman and the Self would be untenable, resulting in the total abandonment of all Vedānta.

For those who maintain that the entire universe constitutes the body of Brahman—a truth well-established in all the Upaniṣads—all the teachings regarding the identity of Brahman and the Self become perfectly justified. Just as genus and quality serve as qualifiers for substances by way of being their bodies, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) seen in expressions such as "He is born as a cow, a horse, a human, a god; he is a person through his actions" is observed to be entirely primary in both common usage and the Veda.

Indeed, even in the case of genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*), it is precisely their status as qualifiers (*prakāra*) of a substance that serves as the basis for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as seen in expressions such as "the spotted cow" (*khaṇḍo gauḥ*) and "the white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*). Since even in the case of individual bodies qualified by humanity and so forth, the self (*ātman*) is the referent of the word only in its capacity as a qualifier—as in "a human, a man, a eunuch, a woman, a self has been born"—coreferentiality is consistently observed everywhere. Thus, it is the status of being a qualifier alone that is the basis for coreferentiality; it is not mutually exclusive categories such as genus and the like.

Indeed, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is observed only in cases where substances established as independent entities occasionally function as qualifiers of another substance, as in "one with a staff" (*daṇḍī*) or "one with earrings" (*kuṇḍalī*); it is not used for substances that are incapable of being perceived or existing separately. Their status as qualifiers is to be understood solely through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

If, in the statement "the cow, the horse, the human, the god, the man, the woman, the eunuch, and the self are born through actions," one maintains that human and other bodies function as qualifiers (*prakāra*) of the self—just as "lumpy" or "hornless" qualifies a cow, or "white" or "black" qualifies a cloth—then there would necessarily be a simultaneous perception of the body and the self, just as there is between a genus (*jāti*) and its individual instance (*vyakti*). Yet, such a thing is not observed.

For it is not the case that human bodies and the like are invariably perceived as having the self as their substrate in the same way that "cowness" and other universals are perceived as inherent in their substrates. Therefore, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the expression "the human is the self" is merely figurative (lākṣaṇika). This is not so; for human bodies and the like also share with universals such as "cowness" the qualities of having the self as their sole substrate, having that [self] as their sole purpose, and being modes of that [self]. That they have the self as their sole substrate is understood from the fact that the body perishes upon separation from the self.

And its being for the sole purpose of the self is because it exists solely for the sake of experiencing the fruits of various actions. Its being a mode [of the self] is also due to its being perceived as a qualifier of the self—such as "god" or "human. This very fact is the reason why words such as "cow" extend to the individual (vyakti). It is precisely because of the absence of this nature that, when sticks, earrings, and so forth serve as qualifiers, possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) such as in *daṇḍin* ("staff-bearer") or *kuṇḍalin* ("wearer of earrings") are employed.

Because the aggregates (piṇḍa) such as gods and humans have the self as their sole substratum, have that [self] as their sole purpose, and have it as their mode (prakāra), there is a usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in both worldly and Vedic discourse, such as "the god is the self" or "the human is the self. This is because two universals (*jāti*) are invariably perceived together when both are visible to the eye. However, since the self is not visible to the eye, the self is not perceived at the time the body is grasped by the eye. Do not say that it is impossible for that which is capable of being perceived separately to have a nature consisting solely of being a mode [of something else].

Just as in the case of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, because the body also possesses the nature of being a mode of that [Self]—due to its having the same substratum, the same purpose, and being its qualifier—it is understood that the body likewise has the body-as-a-mode-of-the-Self as its sole essential nature. As for the rule of their simultaneous perception, it has been stated that this is based on their being cognizable by the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Just as the earth and other substances, though they naturally possess smell, taste, and so forth, do not have those qualities perceived by the eye, so too the body, though being perceived by the eye as having the body-as-a-mode-of-the-Self as its sole essential nature, is not perceived in that manner.

Because the eye lacks the capacity for grasping the self, the fact that the body has a nature consisting solely of being a mode of that [self] is not, by itself, the basis for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Rather, it is the word, which is capable of conveying [the body] as a mode of the self, that conveys it precisely as a mode along with [the self].

But is it not the case that even in verbal usage, by the word "body" (śarīra) only the physical body is grasped, and thus the word "body" does not extend to the Self? It is not so; because this is a defining term used to describe the body specifically as a mode of the Self for the purpose of demonstrating the discrimination of categories, just like words such as "cowness," "whiteness," "form," "quality," or "truth."

Therefore, like words such as "cow" and so forth, words such as "god" and "human" extend up to the Self (ātman). This very identity, characterized by the relation of body and self, is what will be stated [by Bādarāyaṇa]: "But they approach it as 'Self' and cause it to be grasped as 'Self'," and the author of the Vākya [Brahmasūtra] says: "One should indeed grasp it as 'Self'."

In this regard, the truth is as follows: certain Śruti passages declare the distinction between the essential natures of the non-sentient (acidvastu), the sentient (cidvastu), and the Supreme Brahman, [respectively] as the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the Ruler. They state: "From Him the Illusionist (māyī) creates this universe; and another, bound by illusion (māyā), is confined within it. "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti (primordial nature) and the Great Lord (maheśvara) as the Illusionist (māyin). "The perishable is Pradhāna (nature); the imperishable and immortal is Hara. The one God rules over both the perishable and the self (the soul). In the phrase "the imperishable and immortal is Hara," the enjoyer is indicated.

He is called Hara because he seizes the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) as his object of enjoyment. As it is said: "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses; there is no progenitor of him, nor is there any lord over him. "The Lord of *pradhāna* and the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the Master of the qualities (*guṇa*). "The Lord of the universe, the Self-Sovereign, the eternal, the auspicious, the infallible. "The two unborn ones—the Knower and the Unknowing, the Lord and the Unlord. "The eternal among the eternals, the consciousness among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of the many. "Having understood the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the Impeller. "Of these two, one eats the fruit of the *pippala* tree..."

"He eats the sweet fruit while the other looks on without eating"; "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct, being favored by Him, one then attains immortality"; "The unborn one, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form—another unborn one lies beside her, enjoying her, while yet another, having experienced his share, abandons her"; "On the same tree, a person is immersed and grieves, deluded by powerlessness; but when he sees the other, the Lord who is enjoyed, he becomes free from sorrow"—and so forth. Also in the Smṛti:

"This nature of mine, called egoism (ahaṅkāra), is divided eightfold. But know that there is another, higher nature of mine, O mighty-armed one, which is the life-force (jīvabhūta) by which this world is sustained! O son of Kuntī, know that all beings go into my own nature at the end of a cycle; again, at the beginning of a cycle, I send them forth. Resorting to my own nature, I project them forth again and again."
"This entire collection of beings is powerless due to its subjection to material nature (prakṛti). "Under my supervision, material nature produces the world of the moving and the non-moving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the universe revolves. "Know that both material nature and the spirit (puruṣa) are indeed beginningless.
"The Great Brahma is my womb; in it I place the seed. From that, O Bhārata, the birth of all beings occurs."

Thus: "My own Great Brahman, which is the source of the world—that insentient entity called Prakṛti consisting of the subtle elements of the beings—in that I unite the embryo called consciousness; from that conjunction of consciousness and matter produced by Me, there arises the birth of all beings, from the gods down to the stationary objects, who are mixed with the insentient. This is the meaning.

Thus, certain Śruti passages declare that for consciousness (cit) and unconsciousness (acit), which exist in the form of the enjoyer and the enjoyed and persist in all states, their non-separate existence from the Supreme Person is due to their being His body and being subject to His control, and that the Supreme Person is the Self. Beginning with: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within," and continuing until: "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose self... [is the Supreme Person].

"He who controls the body from within, he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. Likewise: "He who moves within the earth, whose body is the earth, whom the earth does not know," and so on, up to: "He who moves within the Imperishable (akṣara), whose body is the Imperishable, whom the Imperishable does not know; he who moves within Death, whose body is Death, whom Death does not know—this is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God."

Regarding the term *nārāyaṇa*: here, by the word *mṛtyu* (death), the subtle state of insentient matter denoted by the word *tamas* is expressed. This is because of the statement in this very Upaniṣad, "The unmanifest dissolves into the imperishable (*akṣara*); the imperishable dissolves into *tamas*," and also because of [the verse], "He has entered within, the ruler of people, the Self of all."

Thus, in order to make known this truth—that the Supreme Person alone, having the non-sentient and sentient entities in all their states as His body, exists as the mode (*prakāra*) of that [body] in the form of the world both in its causal and effected states—certain Śrutis declare that the world in its effected state and its causal state is indeed He: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone... (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1).

"In the beginning, this was indeed one only, without a second. It thought: 'May I be many; may I procreate. It emitted heat. Starting from there, [the text continues]: "O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. All this has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self; That art thou, Śvetaketu. Likewise: "It desired: 'May I be many; may I procreate. It performed austerity. Having performed austerity..."

Beginning with "He created all this," and continuing with "The true and the untrue became the True," and so forth; here too, the distinction between the nature of the conscious and the unconscious and that of the Supreme Person, as established in other Śrutis, is recalled: "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate name and form"; and "Having created that, He entered it. Having entered it, He became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat)."

And [it is said]: "Consciousness and non-consciousness, truth and untruth, became truth. Furthermore, by the passage "having entered with this living self (jīva-ātman)," the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman is established; and because the passages "having entered that, it became the existent (sat) and the non-existent (tyat)" and "consciousness and non-consciousness" have the same meaning, it is understood that this is based on the relationship between the Self and the body.

Such indeed is the differentiation of name and form (nāmarūpa-vyākaraṇa), as it is also stated here: "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated (avyākṛta); it was differentiated by means of name and form."

Therefore, since the Supreme Person alone possesses the gross and subtle sentient and insentient entities as His body—both in the state of effect and in the state of cause—it is most appropriately established that by knowing the cause, the effect is known; thus, through the knowledge of Him alone, the desired "knowledge of all" is logically attained.

"I, having entered these three deities by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), shall manifest names and forms"—by thus specifying the three deities as the insentient object and stating that the manifestation of names and forms occurs through the entry of His own self in the form of the individual soul (jīva), it follows that all words are denotative of the Supreme Self alone as qualified by the individual soul and the insentient matter. Therefore, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between a word denoting the causal state of the Supreme Self and a word denoting the effect is primary (mukhya-vṛtti).

Therefore, since Brahman alone—characterized by the modes of gross and subtle consciousness and non-consciousness—is both the effect and the cause, the world has Brahman as its material cause (*upādāna*).

Even though Brahman, whose body consists of the subtle entities of consciousness and non-consciousness, is the cause, it is even more appropriately established that there is no confusion of the natures of the conscious, the non-conscious, and Brahman, because the composite whole functions as the material cause.

Just as a variegated cloth, although it has as its material cause a collection of white, black, and red threads, its connection with whiteness and so forth occurs only where those specific threads enter; thus, even in the state of the effect, there is no confusion of colors everywhere—so too, although the world has as its material cause a collection of the conscious (cit), the unconscious (acit), and the Lord (Īśvara), even in the state of the effect, there is no confusion between the states of being the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the controller. Threads possess both causality and effectuality only when they are sometimes combined by the will of a person, even though they are capable of existing separately.

In this system, however, since both consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*) in all their states constitute categories of existence only as modes (*prakāra*) of the Supreme Person by virtue of being His body, the Supreme Person—who is the possessor of those modes—is always denotable by every word; this is the distinction. Furthermore, the difference in essential nature (*svabhāvabheda*) and the non-confusion (*asaṅkara*) between them are identical in that [Vedāntic] system and here [in Sāṃkhya]. This being so, even when the Supreme Brahman enters into the effects, its state of being unmodified (*avikṛtatva*) is more convincingly established, because there is no alteration in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Since the conscious and unconscious reality, which exists in its gross state as differentiated by name and form, abides as the Self [of Brahman], its status as an effect is even more appropriately established; for being an effect consists precisely in the attainment of a different state. Furthermore, the declarations regarding the absence of qualities (*nirguṇavāda*) concerning the supreme Brahman are justified by the fact that it has no connection with qualities to be abandoned (*heyaguṇa*).

Having negated qualities that are to be abandoned by stating, "He is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger, and free from thirst," this very Śruti, by prescribing auspicious qualities through the words, "His desires are true; His resolves are true," establishes that the negation of qualities understood generally elsewhere refers specifically to qualities that are to be abandoned.

Furthermore, the doctrine that Brahman is of the nature of knowledge is even more tenable, because it is accepted that the very essence of Brahman—who is omniscient, omnipotent, and the source of all auspicious qualities that are the opposite of everything to be abandoned—is definable solely by knowledge and is of the nature of knowledge due to its self-luminosity.

Passages such as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, as are His innate knowledge, strength, and action," and "By what, my dear, should one know the Knower? declare His nature as a knower; while passages such as "Truth, Knowledge... declare His nature as pure consciousness, since He is defined solely by knowledge and is self-luminous.

"He desired, 'May I be many,'" "He thought, 'May I be many,'" and "It was differentiated by name and form"—thus, Brahman alone, through its own volition, exists in various ways as the manifold forms of diverse moving and stationary beings. Therefore, the plurality of entities that are not of the nature of Brahman, which is opposed to that [unity], is denied as being unreal, in such passages as: "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity," "There is no diversity whatsoever here," and "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees the other."

He sees [this] through such passages as: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? By what and whom should he know? However, this does not negate the manifold nature of Brahman—consisting in its assumption of various names and forms—which is established by the scripture stating, "May I be many, may I procreate," and which is brought about by its own volition.

And that [non-duality] has been established in such negating passages as, "But where everything has become just the Self for him," and also by such statements as, "All this would forsake him who perceives all this as other than the Self; indeed, this Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and so forth, are the breath of this great Being."

Thus, there is no contradiction among all the Śrutis—those which declare the difference in essential nature and the difference in inherent character between the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord, and those which declare the relationship of cause and effect and the non-difference between cause and effect; for it is known precisely from the Śrutis themselves that the conscious and the unconscious are always in a body-soul relationship with the Supreme Self, such that when they exist in a causal state, they have entered a subtle condition unfit for the differentiation of name and form, and when they exist in an effected state, they have entered a gross condition fit for such differentiation.

No scope whatsoever is seen for the doctrine of Brahman’s ignorance (*brahmājñānavāda*), the doctrine of Brahman’s difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhikabrahmabhedavāda*), or any other theory rooted in fallacious reasoning that contradicts all the Śrutis.

Since the conscious (*cit*), the unconscious (*acit*), and the Lord (*īśvara*) possess distinct natures established by their respective scriptures, and since they are understood through the Śrutis themselves as being related as body and self (*śarīrātma-bhāva*) in the relation of the mode (*prakāra*) and the possessor of the mode (*prakārin*), it is not contradictory for another Śruti to establish the relationship of cause and effect between them, nor to establish the identity of cause and effect.

Just as the injunctional statement "By means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]" enjoins for the sake of one who desires [a result] the performance of the six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya—which have arisen separately through their originative statements (*utpattivākya*) and have attained the status of two groups by means of two subsequent statements of collective reference (*samudāyānuvāda*)—so too [the scripture enjoins] the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord, whose forms and natures are distinct from one another, as follows: "The perishable is primary matter (*pradhāna*); the immortal and imperishable is Hara; the one God rules over the perishable and the self" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 1.10); "The Lord of the universe, the Master of the Self" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 6.16); and "The Self is Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme" (*Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad* 10.4).
Having established these separately through such statements as, "He whose body is the earth," "He whose body is the self," and "He whose body is the unmanifest; he whose body is the imperishable."

By such statements as, "This is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, the divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa," the fact that both the conscious and the unconscious, existing in all their various states, constitute the body of the Supreme Self, and that the Supreme Self constitutes their very self, is established. Then, by means of terms such as *sat*, *brahman*, and *ātman*—which denote the Supreme Self as the embodied one—it is understood that the Supreme Self alone is one and the same, whether in its causal state or its effected state. Thus, the three distinct entities previously perceived [as separate]—in the passages "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1) and "All this has that as its self" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.8.7)—[are shown to be non-different].

It establishes such statements as "all" and "All this, indeed, is Brahman. For there is no contradiction in designating the Supreme Self—who has both conscious and unconscious entities as His body—by the term "Supreme Self," just as there is no contradiction in designating a particular self who has a human body by the word "self" in the expression "this self is happy. Enough with excessive detail.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the cessation of ignorance is logically possible through the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self alone—that is incorrect; for since bondage is ultimately real, it cannot be removed by knowledge. How indeed can it be asserted that this bondage—which consists of entering bodies such as those of gods caused by merit and demerit, and the resulting experience of pleasure and pain—is illusory?

It has already been stated that the cessation of the bondage of *rūpa* (form) is obtainable through the grace of the Supreme Person, who is pleased by worship that takes the form of devotion (*bhakti*). Since the knowledge of oneness (*ekyajñāna*) favored by you has as its object a reality contrary to the actual state of things, it is false in nature; consequently, its result is only the intensification of bondage, according to the scripture: "This is false, for one substance does not attain the nature of another."

Furthermore, from the teaching that the knowledge of Brahman—the inner controller who is of a different nature from the individual soul—is the means to liberation characterized as the supreme human goal, as seen in such passages as "But the Supreme Person is another" and "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct."

Moreover, since even the subverting cognition (*nivartaka-jñāna*) favored by you is itself illusory in nature, another subverting factor must be sought for it. If it is argued that this subverting cognition, having subverted the entire range of dualities opposed to it, perishes by itself due to its momentariness, we say no; because its own nature, its origination, and its destruction are all conceptual constructs, one must seek another subverting factor for that ignorance which consists in the conceptualization of destruction and its constructs.

If it is argued that its destruction is nothing other than the very nature of Brahman, then in that case, the arising of the knowledge of non-duality would be impossible; for as long as its destruction persists, the arising of that [non-dual] knowledge cannot occur.

Furthermore, who is this knower of the knowledge whose object is the negation of everything other than Brahman, which is pure consciousness? If you say it is of the nature of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), no; for since that [superimposition] is itself what is to be negated, it is the object (*karman*) of the subverting knowledge, and thus it is impossible for it to be its agent (*kartṛ*). If you say it is the very nature of Brahman, then [you must explain] Brahman’s status as a knower with respect to the subverting knowledge.

Is it the essential nature [of Brahman], or is it superimposed? If it were superimposed, then both that superimposition and its root—another ignorance—would certainly persist, as they would not be objects of the knowledge that removes them. If one were to posit yet another knowledge to remove that [second ignorance], then because that too would possess the three-fold form [of knower, known, and knowing], there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā) relative to the knower. If the essential nature of Brahman itself were the knower, then our own position would simply have been adopted.

To state that the nature of the subverting knowledge and its knower are included within that which is to be subverted by it—because they are distinct from Brahman—is laughable, like saying, "Everything other than the ground was cut by Devadatta," while the cutter and the act of cutting both enter into the very object being cut. The superimposed knower cannot himself be the agent in the subverting knowledge that causes his own destruction; for one's own destruction is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*).

If one were to accept that the destruction of that [bondage] is of the very nature of Brahman, then there would be no need for the conceptualization of the perception of difference, its root—ignorance (avidyā), and so forth; therefore, enough of this [objection], which is like striking with a mallet already shattered by fate.

Consequently, since bondage has its root in ignorance in the form of the beginningless stream of karma, its eradication occurs only through knowledge characterized as previously described. And the arising of that [knowledge] is obtained through the performance of duties appropriate to one’s caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), refined by a specific cognition of the true nature of the self in the form of the worship of the Supreme Person performed day after day.

In this regard, the fact that actions performed solely as mere ritual acts yield small and unstable fruits, whereas actions performed in the manner of worshiping the Supreme Person without aiming for their fruits yield infinite and stable fruits in the form of the experience of the true nature of Brahman through the medium of generating knowledge consisting of meditation—this cannot be known without knowing the true nature of action. Furthermore, the adoption of action in its aforementioned nature, preceded by the abandonment of its "mere" (mechanical) form, is not possible [without such knowledge]. Therefore, for this very reason, the inquiry into Brahman must be undertaken immediately after the inquiry into action;
thus it was said: "Then, therefore" (*athātaḥ*).
(Thus concludes the Great Siddhānta.

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that, since it is impossible to determine the expressive power of a word apart from the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), and since such usage is preceded by the cognition of an action to be performed (*kārya*), the authority of a word pertains only to what is to be done; therefore, the meaning of the Veda consists solely of things to be accomplished. Consequently, the Vedāntas cannot function as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the already established Supreme Brahman.

Furthermore, in the case of sentences concerning established entities such as the birth of a son, it is not possible to determine that they cause the cognition of a specific meaning by means of signs such as the expansion of the face resulting from the comprehension of a pleasant matter; for there is an infinity of objects existing in the three periods of time that could serve as causes for joy, and because there is the possibility of the occurrence of other joyful causes, such as an auspicious moment or a happy delivery.

Nor can the capacity of a word to denote an established entity be ascertained through the determination of the meaning of another word or the determination of the meaning of its own stem by one who has already mastered the meanings of the various case-terminations; for such [ascertainment] consists merely in the determination of a specific portion of a collection of words that denotes an effect already known. Furthermore, the fact that a person terrified by a snake ceases to fear immediately upon hearing the words "this is not a snake, it is only a rope" does not establish that the words are the cause of a cognition of the absence of the snake.

In this case as well, since there are many factors that cause the cessation of fear—such as the understanding that "this object is motionless," "it is non-venomous," or "it is insentient"—it is impossible to determine a specific [intended] meaning. Because it is understood through the force of the pervasion between the cognition of an effect and purposeful activity that a word conveys an object that prompts action, all words must have the effect (*kārya*) as their primary purport. Since every word thus conveys a specific effect, it is not determined that the power of a word lies merely in its own meaning as connected with another.

The cognition that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatābuddhi*) is the cause of activity only by way of the cognition of what is to be done (*kāryabuddhi*), not in its own form; for activity is not observed in the case of cognitions of past, future, or present means to a desired end. Indeed, one does not act as long as the cognition has not arisen: "This means to my desired end cannot be accomplished without my effort; therefore, it is achievable through my action."

Therefore, since the cognition of what is to be accomplished (*kārya*) alone is the cause of activity, and because only that which impels action is denotable by words, it follows that only the *kārya* is what is to be known through the Veda. Consequently, there is no comprehension of an internal, stable fruit characterized by the attainment of Brahman as an already-established reality (*pariniṣpanna-rūpa*). Furthermore, since passages such as "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices indeed becomes inexhaustible" demonstrate that ritual actions themselves possess stable fruits, it is argued that the commencement of an inquiry into Brahman—motivated by the knowledge that the fruits of action are insignificant and unstable, while the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is infinite and stable—is not tenable.

To this, it is replied: Logicians do not highly regard the determination that all words convey non-worldly (transcendental) meanings by setting aside the well-known worldly methods for determining the relationship between words and their meanings. Indeed, children determine the relationship between words and their meanings in this manner: when their mothers, fathers, and others point with their fingers at their mother, father, uncle, and so forth, as well as at the moon, domestic animals, humans, deer, birds, snakes, and the like, with the intention, "Know this one," or "Understand this one."

Having been instructed many times by those [instructors] using various words for those various objects, they gradually observe the arising of their own cognitions regarding those very objects through those very words. Then, seeing no other relation between word and object and lacking knowledge of a person who established the convention, they conclude that the capacity of those words to convey meaning in respect to those objects is based solely on the application [of the convention].

Furthermore, regarding words that are already established [in usage], people who have been previously instructed by elders that "this is the meaning of this word" come to understand the meaning of all words and employ various collections of sentences capable of conveying those respective meanings in order to inform others.

Moreover, it is quite possible for a person to determine the relationship between a word and its meaning through other means, such as hand gestures; for instance, someone sent with the command, "Inform Devadatta that 'your father is well'," proceeds to inform him and employs the sentence, "Your father is well."

Another person standing nearby, desiring to learn, who understands specific gestures like a mute, follows this man once he perceives that he is engaged in making something known; having heard this word employed by him for the purpose of making that known, he concludes: "This word is the cause of the cognition of that object. Thus, the insistence that linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) occurs only regarding an action to be performed (*kārya*) is groundless.

Therefore, since the Vedāntas teach the already-existent Supreme Brahman and its meditation which yields immeasurable fruit, an inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*), the result of which is the definitive determination of That, must be undertaken.

Even though the Veda has action as its purpose, the inquiry into Brahman must indeed be undertaken. How so?
