By such [scriptural passages] as: "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"; "That is to be sought, that is to be desired to be known"; "Having known, let him practice wisdom"; "Within this [heart] is the small ether; what is within that is to be sought, and that indeed is to be desired to be known"; and "Therein is the small sky, free from sorrow; what is within that is to be worshipped. Thus, by these and others.

Since the attainment of Brahman is heard of in such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," by virtue of being the fruit for one authorized in the performance of the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*), the nature of Brahman and its attributes are established solely through their utility toward that effect—just like heaven and other such states which consist of specific places unmixed with suffering, like the establishment resulting from the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice, or like the relationship between means and ends in the case of the hundred-fold torments resulting from threatening a Brāhmaṇa.

Even in sentences such as "Bring the cow," there is no acquisition of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) regarding a "task to be accomplished" (*kārya*); for the "task to be accomplished" as conceived by you is difficult to define. For you, a "task to be accomplished" is that which arises upon the occurrence of an effort (*kṛti*) and is the objective of that effort. Being the objective of an effort is being the object of that effort. And being the object of an effort is being that which is most desired to be attained through that effort. Furthermore, that which is most desired is either pleasure or the cessation of present suffering.

In this regard, it is observed that desired pleasure and the like are not accomplished by a person without his own effort; therefore, a person acts out of a desire for effort. Thus, nowhere is there found anything called "being the objective of an action" (kṛtyuddeśyatva) apart from the fact that the object of desire has its accomplishment dependent upon action.
Furthermore, the inciting nature of the object of desire consists precisely in its accomplishment being dependent upon effort, since it is from that alone that activity arises.

Furthermore, being "conducive to the person" (*puruṣānukūlatva*) does not constitute being the "object of purpose" (*kṛtyuddeśyatva*). For it is pleasure alone that is conducive to the person. Nor is the cessation of suffering conducive to the person. Indeed, the distinction between the essential natures of pleasure and pain is this: pleasure is conducive to the person, while pain is its opposite. Because pain is contrary [to the person], its cessation is desired; it is not desired because it is conducive. For the cessation of pain is simply abiding in one's own nature, in the absence of association with what is conducive or contrary.

Therefore, it is not possible for action and so forth, which are distinct from pleasure, to possess the quality of being "conducive" (*anukūlatva*). Nor can they be conducive by virtue of serving the purpose of pleasure; for they are of the nature of suffering (*duḥkhātmaka*). Even when serving the purpose of pleasure, there occurs only a mere desire to undertake them.

Furthermore, being the "principal" (*śeṣin*) with respect to an action does not mean being the intended object (*uddeśya*) of that action, because on your view, the nature of being the principal cannot be defined. Nor can it be understood that the principal is the correlate of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*), defined as the fitness to be pervaded by an action undertaken for the sake of another; for if that were so, since an action is not subsidiary, that which is to be accomplished by it would lack the status of being the principal with respect to it. Furthermore, one cannot claim that the other is the principal simply because subsidiarity consists in the fitness to be the object of an action undertaken for another's sake, since the very nature of being the intended object remains yet to be defined.

Furthermore, it is observed that even a master acts for the sake of his servant. If it is argued that the master acts with his own purpose in mind even while supporting his servant, we say no; for the servant also acts with his own purpose in mind while supporting the master.

Since the very nature of the "effect" (*kārya*) remains unestablished, the definition that "the subordinate (*śeṣa*) is that which is related to the effect, and the principal (*śeṣin*) is that which is related to it" is also incoherent.

Nor is being the purpose of an action (*kṛti*) the same as being the objective of an action (*kṛtyuddeśyatva*). For the purpose of an action's commencement is simply the purpose of the person; and that [purpose] is the object of desire (*icchā-viṣaya*).

Therefore, since it cannot be defined as being desired (*iṣṭa*) or as being the objective (*uddeśya*) of an effort (*kṛti*) that exceeds [the mere desire], the "task" (*kārya*)—defined as being both achievable by effort and having effort as its primary element—is indeed difficult to establish. Even in the case of a mandate (*niyoga*), because it is distinct from the pleasure or the cessation of pain that constitute its direct object, its being desired and its being achievable by effort exist only by virtue of its being a means to those ends. For this very reason, it is distinct from the action itself; otherwise, the task would be nothing more than the action.

In accordance with the syntactic connection (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), the *kārya* (task/obligation) denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth must be a means to heaven. Therefore, since the task is momentary, the *kārya* that is stable and distinct from the action (*karma*) is none other than the *apūrva* (the unseen potentiality); for it is precisely through the mention of being a means to heaven that the understanding of the *apūrva* arises. Consequently, it is laughable to claim that the *apūrva*—which is first understood as a task not for another purpose—later becomes a means to heaven in order to fulfill its status as a task not for another purpose.

For even by the word denoting the task (kārya) as connected with the term "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), there is no initial expression of being for the sake of nothing else; moreover, it is impossible to perceive that anything other than pleasure, the cessation of pain, or the means thereto is a goal for its own sake and yet achievable through volitional effort (*kṛti*).

Furthermore, what is this "status as a purpose" (prayojanatva) of the mandate (*niyoga*)? If it is argued that, like pleasure, the mandate is simply something favorable (*anukūlatva*), then is the mandate itself pleasure? For only pleasure is favorable. If it is argued that, like a particular kind of pleasure, there is another distinct pleasure synonymous with the mandate, then it must be stated: what is the proof for that? If you say it is one's own experience, no; for even by you, this experience of the mandate is not experienced as a pleasure in the same way that the experience of a specific object is experienced as pleasure.

If it is argued that because the scripture establishes the mandate (*niyoga*) as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), one will experience [the result] later, then what is that scripture which expresses the mandate’s status as a human goal? It cannot be an ordinary worldly statement, for such a statement has as its object an action consisting of suffering; by means of it, there is merely the establishment of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatā*) precisely by way of being a means to pleasure and so forth. Nor can it be a Vedic statement, for even by that, the "task" (*kārya*) is established only as a means to heaven and the like.

Nor does the scripture concerning obligatory and occasional rites [establish the self], for even that scripture’s capacity to denote those [rites] is preceded by the understanding of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) found in the sentence "one desiring heaven"; thus, according to the reasoning already stated, it too inevitably denotes an action that is a means to pleasure and so forth.

Furthermore, since no experience of the enjoyment of pleasure in the form of a *niyoga* (an injunction or mandate) is observed at that time—apart from the food, health, and other such things experienced as the fruit of a performed action whose result is restricted to this world—we find no evidence whatsoever for the claim that "the *niyoga* is pleasure. Even in the *arthavādas* and similar passages, we have never seen among you any mention of the nature of pleasure in the form of a *niyoga*, in the same way that the nature of pleasure such as heaven (*svarga*) is mentioned.

Therefore, even in injunctive sentences (*vidhivākya*), it is determined that what is expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is merely the fact that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is to be accomplished by the agent’s activity—a point established by the science of grammar (*śabdānuśāsana*). Furthermore, that the meaning of the root, such as sacrifice (*yāga*), consists in the propitiation of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) who dwells within the deities like Agni, and that the attainment of the fruit results from that propitiated Supreme Person, will be demonstrated in the section beginning with the sūtra, "The fruit [arises] from Him, because that is logical" (*phalamata upapatteḥ*).

Therefore, since the Vedānta texts reveal the supreme Brahman as the fully established reality, it is proven that the fruit of the meditation on Brahman is both infinite and stable. Furthermore, even regarding rites such as the Cāturmāsya, because scripture teaches that mere ritual action yields perishable results, the mention of imperishable fruits—such as in the passage, "The wind and the intermediate space, this is the immortal"—must be understood as being relative to those [other] terms. Thus, since mere rituals yield results that are both limited and unstable, whereas the knowledge of Brahman yields results that are infinite and stable, it is established that the commencement of the inquiry into Brahman, which aims at its definitive determination, is indeed appropriate.
Thus ends the Section on the Desire to Know (*Jijñāsādhikaraṇa*) in the *Śrībhāṣya*. To the question, "What, then, is that Brahman which is said to be the object of the desire to know? he says:
"That from which [proceed] the birth and so forth of this [world]. (1.1.2)

The term "janmādi" refers to creation, sustenance, and dissolution; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities are included in the meaning (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). [It denotes] this world, which possesses an inconceivable and manifoldly diverse arrangement, which is associated with individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) ranging from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, and wherein the enjoyment of fruits occurs according to fixed place, time, and cause.

The meaning of the Sūtra is: that Supreme Person—from whom, who is the Lord of all, whose nature is opposed to all that is to be discarded, whose resolve is true, who possesses infinite auspicious qualities such as knowledge and bliss, who is omniscient, omnipotent, and supremely compassionate—proceeds the creation, sustenance, and dissolution, that is Brahman.

"Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, approached his father Varuṇa and said: 'Teach me, O Venerable One, Brahman. Beginning thus, the scripture continues: "That from which indeed these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, and that into which they enter at death—desire to know that; that is Brahman. Regarding this, a doubt arises: can Brahman be understood through its definition from this passage, or not?

What is the conclusion? That it is not possible. To begin with, birth and the other [characteristics] do not define Brahman as a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*), because if they were qualifiers, Brahman would result in being manifold due to its exclusion from many distinct qualifiers; for a qualifier is by definition that which distinguishes. But surely, in the case of "Devadatta is dark-complexioned, young, red-eyed, and of medium stature," although there are many qualifiers, only one Devadatta is perceived; likewise here too, Brahman remains one. This is not so.

In that case, because identity is perceived through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is a synthesis of the qualifiers within a single entity; otherwise, even there, multiplicity would be unavoidable due to their function as differentiators. Here, however, since Brahman is intended to be defined by this very qualifier alone, its identity with anything else is not known through any other means of valid cognition; thus, a plurality of Brahmas would be unavoidable due to the difference between the differentiators. If it is argued that identity is perceived here as well because of the oneness of the word "Brahman" (*brahma-śabda*);

No; for when a person who does not know a particular cow is told, "The spotted one, the hornless one, the hump-backed one is a cow," even though the word 'cow' is one and the same, there is a cognition of a plurality of cow-individuals due to the distinctions of the qualifiers such as 'spotted-ness' and so forth. Consequently, the individualities of Brahman would also have to be many. For this very reason, it is also untenable that these qualifiers, taken together, constitute the definition (lakṣaṇa) of the entity intended to be defined.

Nor do they characterize [Brahman] by way of an indirect indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), because no other form is apprehended. For it is observed that indirect indicators serve as the cause for the apprehension of some other form in that which has already been apprehended through one form, as in such cases as: "Where this crane is, that is Devadatta’s field," and so forth. [Objection: But surely, the birth and so forth of the world are indirect indicators for Brahman, whose form has already been apprehended in the statement, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite.
[Reply: No, because both defining statements would be mutually dependent, since each would depend upon the form already apprehended by the other.
Therefore, Brahman cannot be understood through its defining characteristics.

This being the case, it is replied: Brahman can be understood through the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, which serve as its defining characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*). Nor does the failure to perceive any form other than that of the characteristic and the characterized imply a failure to perceive Brahman; for the characterized is that which is infinitely and unsurpassably vast (*bṛhat*), and it is "expansive" (*bṛṃhaṇa*) because the root *bṛh* has that as its meaning. And the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of the world are the characteristics by which it is defined.

By the demonstrative expression "from whom," "by whom," and "that which," the cause of birth and so forth is restated according to established tradition. And this established tradition—namely, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and "It emitted heat"—establishes that the single entity denoted by the word "Being" is the cause in the form of both efficient and material cause. Furthermore, having established its status as the material cause in the phrase "In the beginning, this was Being alone, one only," the term "without a second" excludes any other presiding agent.

Having refuted [other views], because it is established that the One alone is taught in the passage, "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'; It created fire," therefore, Brahman is that from which the birth, sustenance, and dissolution of the world proceed; thus, birth, sustenance, and dissolution define Brahman as the entity that serves as both their efficient cause and material cause.

Since Brahman is understood through its greatness of form—characterized by being the cause and material source of the world, and by the omniscience, true volition, and manifold powers implied by that status—the definition of Brahman as the source of birth and so forth does not entail the logical inconsistency of failing to apprehend any other forms [of Brahman].

Even though the birth and other states of the world function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) while serving as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there is no fault whatsoever. Although they are defining characteristics, qualifiers indicate a reality that is excluded from its opposites. Even when a single entity whose nature is unknown is intended to be defined by multiple non-contradictory qualifiers, this does not result in a division [of the object], because the qualifiers are perceived as having a single substratum and are thus subsumed within that one thing.

In contrast, properties such as "being broken" (*khaṇḍatva*) do indeed bring about a distinction among individual cows precisely because they are contradictory; however, in this case, there is no contradiction among birth and the other states due to their occurrence at different times.

The essential nature of Brahman—which is understood from the causal statements such as, "from which indeed these beings are born"—as being distinguished from everything else, is declared by the text: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite."

In this context, the term *satya* (Reality) denotes Brahman, which is endowed with unconditioned existence (*nirupādhika-sattā*). By this, the insentient world, which is the locus of transformation, as well as the sentient beings conjoined with it, are excluded; for these two, by virtue of their association with different states that require the assumption of other names, lack the possession of unconditioned existence. The term *jñāna* (Knowledge) denotes that whose sole form is eternal and uncontracted knowledge. By this, the liberated souls are excluded, as they possess knowledge that is occasionally contracted. The term *ananta* (Infinity) denotes the essential nature (*svarūpa*) which is devoid of limitations regarding space, time, and substance.

Because its essential nature possesses attributes, there is infinity both in its own nature and in its qualities. Consequently, the eternal, distinct nature and qualities—which are differentiated from the two extremes excluded by the first two words—are unsurpassed. Since qualifiers function as differentiators, the Brahman whose nature is understood through the statement "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and through its being the cause of the birth of the universe and so forth, is thereby characterized as being of an entirely different class from all other things; thus, there is no circular reasoning.

Therefore, it is established that Brahman—the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire world, which is faultless, omniscient, possessed of true volition, and omnipotent—can be understood through its defining characteristics.

However, in the view of those who maintain that a featureless reality (*nirviśeṣavastu*) is what is to be known, the [sūtras] "Inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*) and "From which [proceeds] the birth and so forth of this [world]" (*janmādy asya yataḥ*) would be inconsistent; for Brahman is defined etymologically as that which is unsurpassably great (*bṛhat*) and expansive (*bṛṃhaṇa*), and it is stated that this Brahman is the cause of the world’s birth and so forth. Likewise, in the subsequent groups of sūtras and the groups of scriptural citations adduced therein, since one observes the connection with [attributes such as] "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) and so on, neither the sūtras nor the scriptural citations adduced in the sūtras constitute valid authority for that [position].

Furthermore, reasoning (*tarka*) is not a means of valid knowledge regarding a featureless reality, because its object is a thing endowed with a probans that does not deviate from the property to be proven; thus, even under the view that Brahman is one's own imagination—namely, "Brahman is that from which the error of the world's birth and so forth arises"—there is no establishment of a featureless reality. This is because you admit that the root of error is ignorance (*ajñāna*), and that Brahman is the witness (*sākṣin*) of that ignorance; for witness-hood is indeed said to consist solely in the nature of pure luminosity.

Luminosity (*prakāśatva*), however, serves as the differentiator from the insentient by virtue of its nature of bringing about the fitness for practical transaction (*vyavahāra-yogyatā*) for both itself and others; this being so, it possesses specific qualities (*saviśeṣatva*). In the absence of that [luminosity], luminosity itself would not exist; there would be nothing but a void (*tucchatā*).

Thus concludes the section on "The Origin and so forth" (Janmādyadhikaraṇa). It has been stated that Brahman, the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, is to be known through the Vedāntas; however, this is improper, for it is not established by scriptural statements because it can be proven by inference. Anticipating this objection, the Sūtra says: || "Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source" (Śāstrayonitvāt) || 3 ||

That which has the scripture (*śāstra*) as its source, cause, or means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is "scripture-originated" (*śāstrayoni*); the state of being such is "scripture-originatedness" (*śāstrayonitva*). Therefore, because the scripture is the cause of the knowledge of Brahman, Brahman has that [scripture] as its source. Since Brahman is entirely beyond the senses and thus not an object of perception or other means of valid knowledge, the scripture is its sole means of valid knowledge; therefore, the meaning is that the scripture—through such statements as "from which indeed these beings are born"—does indeed make known Brahman whose nature has been described.

But is it not the case that Brahman cannot have the scripture as its source, because Brahman is cognizable through other means of valid knowledge? For scripture is purposeful only with regard to what is not already established by other means.

What, then, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that? It is not, first of all, perception (*pratyakṣa*). For that is twofold: arising from the senses (*indriya-sambhava*) and arising from yoga (*yoga-sambhava*). And that which arises from the senses is twofold: external (*bāhya-sambhava*) and internal (*āntara-sambhava*). External sense-faculties produce cognitions of their own objects that are capable of contact with what is presently existing; they do not produce cognitions of a specific person who is capable of directly perceiving all objects or of creating them.

Nor is it internal, because its activity with respect to external objects—which are distinct from internal pleasure, pain, and so forth—is impossible without depending on the external sense organs. Nor is it produced by yoga; for even though that [cognition] arising at the culmination of the intensity of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) possesses a vivid manifestation, it lacks validity because it is merely a memory of a previously experienced object. How, then, could it be perception? If it were to have an object distinct from that [previous experience], there would be no cause for it; and such being the case, it would be of the nature of an error.

Nor is there inference, whether based on perception of particulars (*viśeṣato dṛṣṭa*) or perception of generalities (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). Because there is no apprehension of a relation with respect to an object beyond the senses, there is no inference based on perception of particulars. Furthermore, even an inference based on perception of generalities—such as one restricted to a specific person capable of perceiving all things and creating them—is not found to possess a logical mark (*liṅga*).

But is it not the case that the world’s status as an effect is pervaded by its being produced by a creator who is cognizant of its material cause (*upādāna*), instruments (*upakaraṇa*), recipient (*sampradāna*), and purpose (*prayojana*)? Furthermore, the world’s being composed of non-conscious matter is pervaded by its dependence on a single conscious being. For every effect, such as a jar, is observed to have a creator who is cognizant of its material cause, instruments, recipient, and purpose; and one’s own healthy body, though composed of non-conscious matter, is seen to depend on a single conscious being. Thus, the world is an effect because it possesses constituent parts (*sāvayavatva*).

It is asked: what is this "dependence on a single conscious being"? It cannot mean that its production and subsistence are contingent upon that [single being], for in that case the illustrative example would be devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*). For one's own healthy body is not produced and sustained by dependence on a single conscious being; rather, the production and subsistence of that body are caused by the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) of all the conscious beings who experience it, such as the wife and others. Furthermore, the subsistence of a whole (*avayavin*), in the form of inherence in its own parts, does not require a conscious being beyond the specific conjunction of those parts.

However, existence characterized by "breathing" (prāṇana) is not possible in the earth, oceans, mountains, and so forth, which are intended as the subject (*pakṣa*); thus, we do not perceive a uniform existence that follows both the subject and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). If it is argued that "dependence on that" means "subordination to that," there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of heavy chariots, rocks, trees, and the like, which are accomplished by many conscious agents. If it is argued that [the dependence] is merely on consciousness in general, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

Furthermore, it is more reasonable to accept the agency of living beings (*jīvas*) alone, as this is the simpler hypothesis (*lāghava*), which is established for both parties in the debate. Nor is agency impossible for living beings on the grounds of their ignorance regarding the material cause (*upādāna*) and other factors; for all sentient beings possess the capacity to directly perceive the material causes such as earth and the instruments such as sacrifices. Indeed, at present, earth and the like, as well as sacrifices and the like, are perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*).

Even in the absence of direct perception of the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force)—which is denoted by terms such as *apūrva* and consists of the capacity for sacrifice and other rites that serve as instrumental causes—there is no logical impossibility of sentient beings being agents, because the commencement of an effect does not depend upon the direct perception of that [force]. Indeed, it is only the direct perception of the possessor of the capacity (*śaktimat*) that is useful for the commencement of an effect; however, with respect to the capacity itself, mere knowledge is sufficient, not direct perception. For potters and others do not commence an effect such as a jar only after they have directly perceived the capacity of their instruments, such as the staff and the wheel, in the same way that they perceive the instruments themselves.
In this case, however, it is not untenable for sentient beings—who possess specific capacities for sacrifice and the like understood through scripture—to initiate an effect.

Furthermore, whatever is capable of being produced and involves the knowledge of its accessible materials and so forth is seen to have an intelligent agent as its creator. If the earth, mountains, and great oceans were incapable of being produced and involved no knowledge of accessible materials and so forth, they would not have an intelligent creator. Therefore, it is only the "effect-ness" residing in things that are capable of being produced and involve knowledge of accessible materials and so forth—things belonging to the same class as jars, pots, and the like—that is capable of proving that they are preceded by an intelligent creator.

Furthermore, since objects such as jars are seen to be created by a non-omniscient agent who possesses limited knowledge and power, has a body, is subject to grasping, and has unfulfilled desires, this reason of "being an effect" (kāryatva), if it were to establish a conscious creator of that very same nature, would be contradictory because it would prove the opposite of the intended person's omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth. However, this does not entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference.

When the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) is within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), those contrary particulars presented by the force of the mark have their course obstructed by those other cognitions and thus recede. But here, in the case of the possessor of the mark who is beyond the range of all other means of cognition—him who is skilled in the creation of everything—all properties whose necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*) has been understood through positive and negative induction (*anvaya-vyatireka*) follow upon him without distinction; since there is no subverting cognition (*nivarttaka-pramāṇa*) to oppose them, they remain exactly as they are. Therefore, how can God be established (*setsyati/sidhyati*) except through scripture (*āgama*)?

On this point, they say: precisely because the world possesses parts, its status as an effect cannot be denied. And there are formal arguments (prayoga): "The earth, mountains, and so forth, which are the subject of dispute, are effects, because they possess parts, like a jar. Likewise: "The earth, oceans, mountains, and so forth, which are the subject of dispute, are effects, because, while possessing magnitude, they possess motion, like a jar. And: "The body, the world, and so forth, are effects, because, while possessing magnitude, they are corporeal, like a jar."

Regarding composite substances, we do not perceive any other characteristic besides "possessing parts" (*sāvayavatva*) that serves as the regulator for why this [effect] is produced and not another. If it is argued that "being capable of being produced" (*śakyakriyatva*) and "the capacity for knowledge regarding the material cause and so forth" (*śakyopādānādivijñānatva*), which are invariably concomitant with being an effect, are indeed perceived, we say no. Even in a case where an object is inferred to be an effect, the knowledge and capacity [to produce it] are themselves inferable from that effect; thus, in other cases as well, once "being an effect" is known through "having parts" and the like, those two [knowledge and capacity] are already established—there is no distinction.

For instance, when jars, water-pots, and the like have been made, a person who possesses knowledge of the creator’s capacity for their construction—knowledge inferred from the observation of the effects—upon seeing a royal palace of unprecedented and variegated structure, determines its status as an effect by means of its specific arrangement of parts, and at that very moment infers the diversity of the creator’s knowledge and power. Therefore, once the status of the body, the world, and so forth as effects is established, a particular person who is capable of directly perceiving everything and is skilled in their construction is indeed proven to exist.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—which are insentient and not presided over by consciousness—to serve as the cause of the experience of pleasure and pain for all sentient beings, one must postulate some [intelligent principle] capable of bestowing all fruits in accordance with all karmas; for we do not observe that an insentient tool such as an axe, when not presided over by a carpenter, serves as a means for constructing a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) even when various conditions like place and time are present.

To raise the objection of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) on the grounds of seeds, sprouts, and so forth being included within the subject (*pakṣa*), is merely the manifestation of ignorance on the part of those who are like *śrotriya*-zombies; for that very reason, the claim of inconclusiveness based on pleasure (*sukha*) and the like is likewise [invalid]. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to postulate that the *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls) admitted by both parties are the such controllers simply out of parsimony (*lāghava*), because it is certain that they lack the power to perceive what is subtle, concealed, or remote; for in all cases, a postulation must be consistent with what is actually observed.

Furthermore, there is no certainty regarding the Lord’s incapacity as there is regarding the individual soul (kṣetrajña); therefore, there is no impossibility of establishing Him through other means of valid cognition. Established by the reason that every effect is invariably preceded by a capable agent, He is established as being endowed with the natural power of direct perception of all objects and the power to govern them.

As for the inference that [the Lord] possesses qualities contrary to specific attributes—such as the production of non-sovereignty and so forth—that is based on an ignorance of the functioning of inference; for no properties whatsoever, whether observed in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) or not, nor even those effects that are not caused by the subject of inference (*liṅgin*), are established as present in that subject.

This is what is being said: when something is being produced by someone, it requires for its own production the agent’s capacity for self-creation and knowledge of its own material cause and instruments; however, it does not require the incapacity of other things or the ignorance of others, because those lack the status of being causes. Since its own production is established through its own capacity for self-creation and its knowledge of its own material cause and instruments, it is illogical to postulate that factors such as the ignorance of another object—which are irrelevant to the process—are causes merely on the basis of their being perceived in association with it.

Furthermore, is the lack of knowledge regarding objects other than the thing being produced, and so forth, applicable to all subjects and relevant to the action? Or does it apply only to some subjects? It cannot be the former, for a potter or similar agent does not fail to know anything whatsoever other than the object currently being produced. Nor can it be the latter, because among all agents there is no fixed rule regarding their respective ignorance or incapacity; thus, since ignorance and the like vary across all agents, they do not establish the probandum. Consequently, qualities such as non-omniscience, which fail to prove [the existence of] the effect, do not apply to the possessor of the mark (the subject), and therefore there is no "proving the opposite" (*viparīta-sādhana*).

If it is argued that the presiding over tools such as the staff and wheel by potters and others is observed only through the medium of a body, and therefore the presiding over the material causes and instruments of the universe by a bodiless Lord is untenable—this is not so; for we observe the removal and destruction of spirits, poisons, and the like residing in other bodies by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) alone. If it is asked how a bodiless being can have a volition consisting of the impelling of another, we say no; volition does not depend upon a body, because the body lacks the status of being the cause of volition.

The mind alone is indeed the cause of volition (*saṅkalpa*), and this is accepted even in the case of the Lord (*īśvara*), since the mind is established as possessing the power of knowledge simply by virtue of being an effect. If it is argued that mental volition belongs only to one who possesses a body, because only one with a body is endowed with a mind, we say no.

Since the mind is eternal, it exists even when the body has departed; therefore, the argument is inconclusive. Consequently, in the creation of effects such as bodies and worlds characterized by the specific arrangement of diverse parts, the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul), being subject to merit and demerit and possessing limited power and knowledge, is not capable [of such a task]. Thus, the Lord (*īśvara*)—who is a distinct Person, skilled in the creation of the entire universe, possessing inconceivable, immeasurable knowledge, power, and sovereignty, bodiless, and whose manifold expansion of variegated arrangements is accomplished solely through the means of mere volition—is established by inference alone.

Therefore, because Brahman is ascertainable through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this statement does not establish Brahman. Furthermore, since we observe that only two things that are absolutely distinct—such as clay and a potter—can function as the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*), and since it is impossible for a partless substance like space to be an effect, this [statement] cannot establish that a single Brahman is both the efficient and the material cause of the entire universe.

This being the case, we reply: the passage concerning the origin and so forth (*janmādivākya*) indeed makes known Brahman as characterized as previously described. Why? Because Brahman has scripture alone as its means of valid knowledge (*śāstraikapramāṇakatvāt*). As for the argument that the entire world is an effect because it possesses parts and the like, and that every effect is seen to be preceded by a specific agent suited to it—therefore, some person capable of knowing the creation of the entire world, as well as its material causes and instruments, must be inferred—that is incorrect.

There is no evidence to establish that the earth, the great oceans, and so forth were created by a single agent at one and the same time; nor do all these things share a single state of being an effect—like a single pot—which would necessitate a single creator for them all simultaneously. This is because, among distinct effects, we observe differences in both time and agent, and thus no rule is seen whereby the agent and the time must be identical.

Nor can it be argued that because individual conscious beings (*kṣetrajña*) lack the capacity to create the diverse world, an agent distinct from them must be postulated on the strength of the fact that the world is an effect; for such a postulation would involve the logical fallacy of assuming multiple agents when a single one suffices. This is because we observe a diversity of powers among those very conscious beings who have accumulated specific merits, and since it is possible for them alone—through the potentiality of their superior *adṛṣṭa* (unseen moral force)—to be the cause of various distinct effects, it is illogical to postulate an entirely unseen person beyond them. Furthermore, there is no simultaneous dissolution of all things.

Furthermore, the production of all things has not ascended to the status of being established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because such production is not observed; moreover, because production and destruction are observed to occur only sequentially, and because there is no contradiction in postulating the production and destruction of all things as effects in a manner consistent with observation, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) when used to prove that [the world] has a single intelligent creator. Furthermore, the subject (*pakṣa*) suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), and the example lacks the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*), since a single being capable of fashioning everything is unestablished.
If, however, the probandum were merely "having an intelligent creator," it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

Does this "effect-ness" (kāryatva), which is intended to prove the existence of a certain single being endowed with omniscience and omnipotence, reside in all things produced simultaneously, or does it reside in all things produced successively? If it resides in all things produced simultaneously, the property of "effect-ness" is unestablished (asiddha). If it resides in all things produced successively, there is contradiction (viruddha), because it proves a plurality of agents; furthermore, even if one were to attempt to prove a single agent here, there would be a conflict with perception and inference, as well as a conflict with scripture, since we hear [scriptural statements] such as, "A potter is born," "A cartwright is born," and so forth.

Furthermore, since all effects—such as the body and so forth—are observed to be permeated by pleasure and the like, which are themselves the effects of the qualities such as *sattva*, one must necessarily admit that they have *sattva* and the other qualities as their root. The specificities residing in the cause, namely *sattva* and the rest, serve as the causes for the diversity of these effects. The fact that these effects are rooted in those qualities occurs through the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) belonging to the Puruṣa who is associated with them.

Furthermore, since the soul's connection with that [body] is rooted in karma, it serves solely for the commencement of specific effects; thus, like the power of knowledge, the agent’s connection to karma must necessarily be accepted as the cause of the multiplicity of effects. Moreover, because the diversity of the power of knowledge is itself rooted in karma, even though desire is a cause for the commencement of an effect, its connection to karma is unavoidable, as that desire is characterized by its specific objects and is rooted in the impressions (*saṃskāra*) and so forth derived from karma. Therefore, the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) alone are the agents;
no entity distinct from them is established by inference.

And there are the following formal arguments (*prayoga*): 1. The body, the world, and so forth, have the *kṣetrajña* (the embodied soul) as their agent, because they are effects, like a pot. 2. God is not the agent, because he lacks a purpose, like a liberated soul (*muktātman*). 3. God is not the agent, because he is bodiless, for that very same reason [as the liberated soul]. 4. Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the *kṣetrajñas* regarding the governance of their own bodies, because even there, a beginningless subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*) exists. 5. The time under discussion is not devoid of worlds, because it is time, like the present time.

Furthermore, does the Lord perform his action while possessing a body or without a body? First of all, he cannot be bodiless, because agency is never observed in that which lacks a body. Even mental effects belong only to one who possesses a body; for even though the mind is eternal, its effects are not seen in liberated beings who are bodiless. Nor can he possess a body, as this position cannot withstand logical analysis. Is that body eternal or non-eternal?

It cannot be eternal, because if that [body] which possesses parts were eternal, there would be no contradiction in the world itself being eternal, and thus God would not be established. Nor can it be non-eternal, because at that time (the beginning of creation) there could be no cause for its body other than itself. If it is argued that the body is its own cause, we say no, because that is impossible for one who is bodiless. If it is argued that he becomes embodied by means of another body, we say no, because that would lead to an infinite regress.

Is He possessed of activity (*savyāpāra*) or devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*)? Because He is bodiless, He is not possessed of activity. Nor does He perform an action while being devoid of activity, like a liberated soul (*muktātman*). If it is argued that the effect—the world—is produced by Him through the mere activity of His will, then the subject (*pakṣa*) suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyahīnatā*). Therefore, an inference of God based on empirical observation is contradicted by the very nature of what is observed. Consequently, the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Person who is the Supreme Brahman, is known solely through the authority of Scripture (*śāstra*).

The scripture, however, establishes a Being who is of a nature entirely distinct from all things perceived by any other means of knowledge—a vast ocean of infinite, unsurpassed, and immeasurable noble qualities such as omniscience and the realization of true volition, whose very essence is the antithesis of every form of evil. Consequently, there is no possibility of even a trace of the defects associated with the similarity of an object established through other means of knowledge. As for the objection that the identity of the efficient cause and the material cause, as well as the fact that a partless substance like space is an effect, are unobserved and impossible to establish; [this is not so].

That too is not contradictory; this will be established in the sections beginning with "And [Brahman] is the material cause, because of the non-contradiction of the initial proposition and the illustrative examples" (BS 1.4.23) and "The ether [is not produced], because there is no scriptural statement to that effect" (BS 2.3.1).

Therefore, since Brahman is not an object of other means of knowledge and is thus the exclusive domain of scripture, it is established that the passage beginning with "From which indeed these... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1) sets forth Brahman as defined above.

Although Brahman is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), nevertheless, one might suspect that the scripture does not establish Brahman—which is established by nature—because it lacks the purpose of inciting activity or cessation; with this doubt in mind, he says:
"But that [is established] because of the harmony [of the texts]. (1.1.4)

The word "tu" (but/however) is for the purpose of removing a possible doubt; that is, it is indeed possible for Brahman to have the scripture as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Why? Because of "samanvaya. *Samanvaya* is the connection [of the texts] with Brahman as the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). This is because Brahman, being the supreme human goal itself, is connected [to the texts] as their denotable meaning (*abhidheya*). Indeed, the collection of words in the Upaniṣads is thus connected: "From which indeed these beings are born," and "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second."

"It thought: 'May I become many; may I procreate,' and it emitted heat"; "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman alone"; "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone"; "From that very Self, space was produced"; "Verily, in the beginning, Nārāyaṇa alone existed"; "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite"; "Bliss is Brahman"—such passages as these [are the source]. Nor can collections of words, which are capable of establishing a fully accomplished reality through established linguistic derivation, [refer to anything other than Brahman], for He is the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the entire universe, and is an ocean of immeasurable, noble qualities that are the opposite of all defects.

Since all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) terminate in the comprehension of their own respective objects, they lack a purpose consisting of engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) when directed toward Brahman, whose nature is the unsurpassed excellence of ninefold bliss; therefore, [the Vedas] cannot have another [worldly] purpose. Nor is the operation of a means of valid cognition dependent upon a purpose, for it is the purpose that conforms to the means of valid cognition. Furthermore, it is not the case that what lacks connection with engagement or withdrawal is devoid of purpose, because a connection with human goals (*puruṣārtha*) is perceived.

Likewise, even in cases where the words refer to their own primary meanings, such as "A son has been born to you" or "This is not a snake," we observe that they possess a purpose consisting of the production of joy or the cessation of fear.

Here [the opponent] objects: Vedānta statements do not establish Brahman, because a scripture that lacks connection with either engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) would be purposeless. Even though perception and the other means of knowledge culminate in the comprehension of the true nature of things, nevertheless, scripture must culminate in a specific purpose. Indeed, no usage of any sentence, whether worldly or Vedic, has ever been observed to be devoid of a purpose.

Furthermore, the employment of a sentence or its hearing cannot occur without aiming at some purpose. And that purpose is observed to consist in the attainment of the desired or the avoidance of the undesired, which are accomplished through engagement or desisting from action—as seen in such examples as: "One who desires wealth should go to the king's court," "One with weak digestion should not drink water," "One who desires heaven should sacrifice," and "One should not eat *kalañja*."

Furthermore, as for the statement that even in the case of statements concerning established facts—such as "A son has been born to you," or "This is not a snake, this is a rope"—the attainment of human goals in the form of joy or the cessation of fear is observed; in that regard, it must be discerned whether the attainment of the human goal consists in the birth of the son and so forth, or rather in the knowledge thereof.

If it is argued that even an existing object, if unknown, is not a human goal (puruṣārtha) and therefore [the scripture] aims at its knowledge, then a human goal would be accomplished through knowledge alone even when the object does not exist; thus, because the scripture would lack a focus on an actual object, it would not possess authority regarding the existence of an object, even though it culminates in a purpose.

Therefore, since every sentence culminates in a purpose by aiming either at engagement (pravṛtti) and withdrawal (nivṛtti) or at knowledge, and since no sentence can have its purport (tātparya) directed toward an already established entity, the Vedāntas do not propound an established Brahman.

Regarding this, someone says: even the Vedānta statements attain the status of being authoritative with respect to Brahman only by having as their purport an action. How so? It is argued that Brahman—which is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*), non-dual, and of the single essence of knowledge—is perceived as possessing phenomenal expansion due to beginningless ignorance; therefore, by means of the dissolution of the phenomenal world, Brahman becomes the object of an injunction, such that one should "make [Brahman] devoid of phenomenal expansion. Thus, it is said to be the domain of an injunction through the medium of the withdrawal of the world.

What is this injunction whose object is Brahman—the single essence of the knowledge to be accomplished—by means of the dissolution of the phenomenal world consisting of the seer and the seen? It is that which begins with: "One should not see the seer of seeing; one should not think the thinker of thought," and so forth. The meaning is: "One should make [the self] into Brahman, which is pure consciousness devoid of the distinction between seer and seen. For it is not contradictory for Brahman, though self-established, to be something to be accomplished in the form of its state as free from phenomenal expansion (niṣprapañcatā).

That is incorrect. For one who maintains that the meaning of a sentence is an injunction (*niyoga*), it must be stated what the object of the injunction (*viṣaya*) is, its qualification (*niyojya-viśeṣaṇa*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and the prompter (*prayoktṛ*). Among these, the qualification of the person to be enjoined is something not to be taken up as a goal (*anupādeya*). And that [qualification] is of two kinds: either a causal condition (*nimitta*) or a fruit (*phala*). Here, one must discern: what is the qualification of the person to be enjoined? And is that a causal condition or a fruit? If the experience of the true nature of the essence of Brahman (*brahma-svarūpa-yāthātmyānubhava*) were the qualification of the person to be enjoined;

In that case, it cannot be the *nimitta* (the causal occasion), because—like the state of being alive—it is unestablished [as a constant]. Furthermore, if it were the *nimitta*, then because it would be eternal, there would follow the consequence of the necessity of performing rituals directed toward it eternally even after liberation (*apavarga*), just as the *agnihotra* and other rites are performed as long as one lives. Nor can it be the fruit (*phala*), because, as a fruit resulting from a ritual injunction (*naiyogika*), it would follow that it is non-eternal, like heaven and other such rewards.

And what here is the object of an injunction (*niyoga*)? If it is argued that it is Brahman itself, we say no; for because it is eternal, it is not of the nature of something to be accomplished (*abhavya*), and because it is not an action (*abhāvārtha*). If it is argued that the non-differentiated (*niṣprapañca*) Brahman is that which is to be accomplished, even if it were to be accomplished, it would still be merely a fruit (*phala*). Because it is not an action, it cannot be the object of an injunction. And to what does this state of being "to be accomplished" belong? To Brahman? Or to the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)? It cannot belong to Brahman, because it is already established and because [if it were to be accomplished] it would follow that it is non-eternal. Suppose, then, it belongs to the cessation of the phenomenal world.

In that case, Brahman cannot be something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). If it is argued that the cessation of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca-nivṛtti*) alone is the object of the injunction, we say no; for that [cessation], being a result (*phala*), cannot be the object of an injunction. Indeed, the cessation of phenomenal manifestation is liberation (*mokṣa*), and that is a result. If this [cessation] were the object of an imperative (*niyoga*), there would be a circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*): the cessation of phenomenal manifestation would follow from the imperative, and the imperative would [follow] from the cessation of phenomenal manifestation.

Furthermore, is the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) to be negated as being false in nature or real? If it is false in nature, then since it is already capable of being negated by knowledge alone, there is no purpose for an injunction (*niyoga*). If it is argued that the injunction serves a purpose by producing the negating knowledge and thereby effecting the negation of the phenomenal world, we reply: that knowledge has already arisen from the very sentence itself; thus, there is no need for an injunction, because by the mere knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, the entire false phenomenal world—which is distinct from Brahman—is sublated.

Furthermore, there is the non-establishment of the injunction (*niyoga*) along with its auxiliaries. If the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is that which is to be removed, is the injunction that removes the world identical to the very nature of Brahman, or is it distinct from it? If it were identical to the nature of Brahman, then because the remover [the injunction] is eternal, the existence of the phenomenal world to be removed would be impossible. Moreover, since the injunction is eternal, its being accomplished through the performance of its object is not tenable. Now, suppose it is distinct from the nature of Brahman.

Since its accomplishment depends upon the performance of an object consisting in the cessation of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and since the agent has perished, [the injunction] is unestablished due to the absence of a substratum. Because by the very performance of the object consisting in the cessation of the phenomenal world, everything distinct from the nature of Brahman has ceased, the fruit called liberation is not something to be produced by a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*).

Furthermore, because there is an absence of an *itikartavyatā* (procedure) for the performance of the injunction (*niyoga*) due to the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and because that which has not been assisted cannot function as an instrument (*karaṇa*), it lacks the status of an instrument. If it is asked how there is an absence of *itikartavyatā*, the answer is as follows: would this *itikartavyatā* be of the nature of an existence (*bhāva*) or of the nature of a non-existence (*abhāva*)? If it were of the nature of an existence, it would be divided into the production of the body of the instrument and the various functions that assist it. However, neither of these two types is possible here.

For no agent capable of abolishing the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) is observed—unlike, for example, the striking of a pestle—and thus a visible purpose is impossible. Nor is it possible for an already accomplished instrument to provide assistance toward the production of an effect, because the very nature of such an instrument, which consists in the abolition of the entire phenomenal world, would remain unestablished as long as there exists even a portion of that which it is meant to assist.

If it is argued that the knowledge of the non-duality of Brahman produces a body of instruments consisting of the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), then by that very fact liberation—consisting of the cessation of the *prapañca*—is accomplished; thus, nothing remains to be produced by instruments and the like, as has already been stated previously. Furthermore, if [liberation] were of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāva*), then because it is a non-entity, it could not produce a body of instruments, nor could it be something to be assisted. Therefore, an injunction whose object is the non-phenomenal Brahman is impossible.

Another also says: although the Vedānta passages do not possess authority by virtue of having as their purport the already-established nature of Brahman, nevertheless, the nature of Brahman is indeed established. Why? By the force of the injunction for meditation (*dhyāna-vidhi*). For they record [the texts] exactly thus: "The Self, verily, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"; "That Self which is free from sin—that is what is to be sought, that is what is to be desired to be known"; "One should worship [it] as the Self alone"; and "One should worship the Self alone as the world."

In this context, the injunction (*niyoga*) has meditation as its object, and since that meditation—which constitutes its own domain—can be defined only by the object of meditation (*dhyeya*), it implies such an object. That object of meditation is the Self (*ātman*) specified by its own scriptural passage. When the question arises as to what its nature is, sentences such as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" and "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" possess authority as supplements to the injunction for meditation, by means of providing the specific details of its essential nature. Thus, there is indeed an intentionality (*tātparya*) even regarding the nature of Brahman, which has entered into the very body of the meditation that is the object of the injunction.

Therefore, through such passages as "One only, without a second," "That is the Truth, That is the Self, That art thou, O Śvetaketu," and "There is no diversity whatsoever here," it is understood that the very nature of Brahman alone is the Reality, and everything other than That is illusory.

Difference is perceived through perception and other means of knowledge, as well as by the ritual scriptures (*karma-śāstra*) which rely upon difference; yet, since difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory, it is determined that non-difference alone is the ultimate reality, for the perception of difference can be accounted for as being rooted in beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*). In this regard, liberation—consisting in the state of Brahman, who is a single essence of knowledge and devoid of the manifold differences created by all ignorance—is attained through the injunction of meditating on Brahman, which has the direct realization of Him as its fruit.

Nor can the state of being Brahman be established merely by the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence from that sentence, because such [realization] is not observed and because the perception of various forms of difference persists. If that were the case, the injunctions for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth would be rendered purposeless.

Now, it may be argued that since we observe the cessation of the fear of a snake through the instruction, "This is a rope, not a snake," and since the complex of the rope and the snake is false in nature and thus sublatable by knowledge, its cessation is properly brought about by the very knowledge produced by the statement; it cannot be brought about by a *niyoga* (an injunction), for if liberation were achievable through an injunction, it would be non-eternal like heaven and other such rewards. Indeed, the eternality of liberation is admitted by all disputants.

Furthermore, since merit and demerit function as cause and effect by way of producing a body conducive to the experience of their own respective fruits, it is unavoidable that they result in saṃsāra, which consists of association with the four types of bodies ranging from Brahmā down to stationary objects.

Therefore, liberation is not to be accomplished by dharma. And thus says the Śruti: "Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant; but for one who exists as bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch him. Since it is heard that in liberation, which consists in the state of being bodiless, there is an absence of the pleasant and unpleasant—which are themselves to be accomplished by dharma and adharma—it is understood that bodilessness is not to be accomplished by dharma.

Furthermore, unlike a specific fruit accomplished by a specific injunction (*niyoga*), bodilessness (*aśarīratva*) is not something to be accomplished by the injunction of meditation (*dhyāna-niyoga*), because bodilessness is one's very nature (*svarūpa*) and thus not something to be produced. As the scriptures state: "The wise man does not grieve, having realized the great, all-pervading Self which is bodiless, abiding within bodies that are themselves transient"; "For He is without breath, without mind, pure"; "For this Person is indeed unattached," and so forth. Therefore, since liberation, consisting of the state of bodilessness, is eternal, it is not to be accomplished through religious duty (*dharma*).
And thus says the Śruti: "That which is other than dharma and other than adharma, other than this cause and effect, other than the past and the future—tell me what you see of that."

Furthermore, liberation cannot possibly have a fourfold nature of being something to be accomplished—namely, by way of origination, attainment, modification, or refinement. First, it is not something to be produced (*utpādya*), because liberation, being the very nature of Brahman, is eternal. Nor is it something to be attained (*prāpya*), because Brahman, being the very nature of the Self, is eternally attained. Nor is it something to be modified (*vikārya*), precisely because that would entail the consequence of impermanence, as in the case of curd and the like. Nor is it something to be refined (*saṃskārya*); for refinement accomplishes its purpose either by removing defects or by imparting qualities.

It cannot be purified by the removal of defects, because Brahman is eternally pure; nor can it be purified by the addition of excellence, because its nature is such that no excellence can be added to it. Since it is eternally changeless, it is not an object of action—whether residing in itself or in another—and thus it cannot be refined by friction, like a mirror and the like. Furthermore, the Self is not refined by acts such as bathing simply because it resides within the body; rather, it is the agent of ego (*ahaṅkartā*) who is grasped by ignorance and associated with the body that is so affected. The experience of the fruits of those actions belongs to that very agent alone.

Nor is the ego-maker (*ahaṅkartṛ*) itself the Self, because it is the witness of that [ego]. Thus says a Vedic mantra: "Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating"; and, "The wise say that the Self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer. Also: "The One God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings, the overseer of actions, the dwelling place of all beings, the witness, the conscious, alone and devoid of qualities."

And [it is said]: "He pervaded that which is bright, bodiless, woundless, without sinews, pure, and unpierced by evil. Thus, the true nature of the Self—which cannot be further enhanced, is eternally pure, changeless, and distinct from the agent of ego (ahaṅkartṛ) grasped through ignorance—is extracted [from its concealment]. Therefore, liberation is not something to be accomplished as a modification of the Self's own nature.

If it is asked, "If this is so, what is accomplished by the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence? we reply: "It is simply the cessation of the obstacles to liberation. And thus say the scriptures: "You indeed are our father, you who carry us across to the further shore of ignorance"; "For it has been heard from those like the venerable one that the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow; such am I, O Venerable One, I am in sorrow; may the Venerable One carry me across to the further shore of sorrow"; and "To him whose impurities have been wiped away, the Venerable One shows the further shore of darkness."

[Such as] "Sanatkumāra," and so forth. Therefore, it is the cessation of the obstruction to liberation itself—an eternal state—that is effected by the knowledge of the meaning of the [Vedic] sentences; and although this cessation is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), being of the nature of a *pradhvaṃsābhāva* (non-existence following destruction), it does not perish.

The scriptural statements such as, "One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and "Having known Him thus, one transcends death," establish that liberation occurs immediately after knowledge and thereby preclude the intervention of a ritual injunction (*niyoga*). Furthermore, there is no entry into the sphere of action either by being the object of the act of knowing or by being the object of the act of meditation, because both types of objective status are denied: "That is indeed different from the known, and likewise from the unknown"; and "By what means could one know Him by whom all this is known?"

And [it is said]: "Know that very Brahman, and not this which they worship here. Nor does the scripture become devoid of an object on this account, because the scripture has as its purpose the cessation of the distinctions imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*). For the scripture does not take Brahman as an object by way of the notion "this"; rather, while establishing the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as being beyond all objects, it removes the division of knowledge, knower, and known imagined through ignorance. And thus says the scripture: "You cannot see the seer of seeing," and so forth.

Nor does the injunction for hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*) and so forth become purposeless on the grounds that the cessation of bondage results from knowledge alone; for those [injunctions] serve as the cause for the comprehension of the meaning of the [great] statement by means of turning one away from all other conceptual constructions that proceed from [ignorance] by their very nature. Nor should it be said that the cessation of bondage is not observed to result from mere knowledge; because bondage is illusory in nature, its continued existence after the arising of knowledge is logically untenable. For this very reason, it is not correct to say that the cessation of bondage occurs only after the fall of the body.

Indeed, the cessation of the fear of a snake that is merely illusory does not require the destruction of the snake beyond the knowledge of the rope’s true nature. If the connection with the body were real, then indeed there would be a requirement for its destruction; however, because it is distinct from Brahman, it is not ultimately real. On the other hand, it is understood that knowledge has simply not arisen for one whose bondage has not ceased, since the effects of knowledge are not observed. Therefore, whether the body persists or not, such a person is liberated immediately upon the knowledge of the meaning of the Great Sentence.

Therefore, since liberation is not to be accomplished through the practice of meditation, Brahman is not established as a subordinate element of an injunction for meditation; rather, it is established by a collection of words dedicated solely to that [Brahman], such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite," "That thou art," and "This Self is Brahman."

That is incorrect; for the cessation of bondage cannot result from the mere knowledge of the meaning of a sentence. Even though bondage, being of a false nature, is sublated by knowledge, nevertheless, because bondage is immediate (aparokṣa), it is not sublated by the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence, which is mediate (parokṣa) in form.

For when the direct perception of a snake regarding a rope or similar object is present, fear is not seen to cease merely through a mediate cognition contrary to that snake-perception—such as the knowledge produced by the instruction of a trustworthy person that "this is not a snake, it is a rope"—but rather, the instruction of the trustworthy person serves as the cause for the cessation of fear only by being the cause for the activity directed toward the immediate realization of the true nature of the thing. To explain further:

A person who has turned away out of fear upon seeing a snake in a rope, when engaged in perceiving the true nature of that object through the instruction of a reliable authority saying, "This is not a snake, this is a rope," turns back from fear upon seeing that very thing with his own eyes. Nor is it reasonable to say that the word itself produces perceptual knowledge, because it is not a sense organ; for among the causal factors of knowledge, the sense organs alone are the means for direct perception.

Furthermore, for a person whose passions (*kaṣāya*) have been attenuated by the performance of actions without regard for their fruits, and who has turned away from hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), the sentence alone does not produce immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*). This is because, even when the obstacles have ceased and the person is intent upon that goal, one observes that the specific causal factors for knowledge—such as the sense organs and so forth—do not transcend their respective limitations regarding their own objects; thus, [the sentence alone] is inadequate. Nor is meditation (*dhyāna*) a means to the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, because that would involve mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*):
meditation would require the knowledge of the sentence's meaning to occur, and the knowledge of the sentence's meaning would occur once meditation has ceased.

Furthermore, there is no difference in the object of meditation (*dhyāna*) and the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārthajñāna*); for if that were the case, meditation would not be a means to the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence. Indeed, meditation upon one thing does not produce an orientation toward another. Since meditation, which consists of a continuous stream of recollection of a known object, necessarily presupposes the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence—given that no other cause for the knowledge of the Brahman that is the object of meditation is possible—it must be preceded by such knowledge.

Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that the knowledge rooted in meditation is produced by a different sentence, while the liberating knowledge is produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). This knowledge rooted in meditation—produced by a different sentence—is either identical in object with the knowledge produced by the sentence "That thou art," or it has a different object. If they have the same object, there is the very same fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). If they have different objects, it is impossible for meditation to bring about an orientation toward that [liberating knowledge].

Furthermore, since meditation depends upon various conceptual elaborations such as the object of meditation and the meditator, it cannot serve as a means—by way of a visible result—for the arising of the knowledge of the meaning of the scriptural sentences whose subject matter is the non-dual identity of Brahman and the Self, which is free from all conceptual elaboration (niṣprapañca). Consequently, for one who asserts that the cessation of ignorance results from the mere knowledge of the meaning of the sentences, the injunctions for hearing, reflecting, and meditating would indeed be rendered useless.

Since ignorance is not removed by the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence because direct (aparokṣa) knowledge cannot arise from a sentence, for that very reason even *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living) is cast far away. What is this *jīvanmukti*? If you say it is liberation for one who still possesses a body, that statement is as inconsistent in meaning as saying "my mother is barren," because you yourself have established through the scriptures that possessing a body is bondage and being bodiless alone is liberation.

Now, if it is argued that when the appearance of having a body persists, for one who has the cognition "this appearance is false," there is the cessation of having a body—no; if having a body is ceased by the cognition "it is false," how can there be liberation for one who possesses a body? For even for one who is not living, liberation is simply the cessation of the false appearance of having a body; so what is this distinction called "liberation while living"?

If it is argued that one for whom the appearance of embodiedness persists—even though it has been sublated, like the cognition of two moons—is a *jīvanmukta* (liberated while living), we say no. This is because the subverting knowledge has as its object all things other than Brahman; since the defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and karma, which serve as the causes [of the appearance], have been sublated by that very same [subverting knowledge] along with the appearance of embodiedness, it is impossible to speak of a "persistence of the sublated."

In the case of the double moon and similar illusions, however, the defect that causes that appearance remains unsublated because it is not the object of the sublatory cognition—the knowledge of the oneness of the moon; therefore, the persistence of the appearance of the double moon is logical.

Furthermore, this scriptural text—"For him there is delay only so long as he is not released, then he shall be united"—stating that for one established in the knowledge of Being (sad-vidyā), liberation requires nothing more than the fall of the body, precludes the possibility of *jīvanmukti*. This very *jīvanmukti* has also been rejected by Āpastamba: "The Vedas... [text truncated]

"One should abandon this world and seek the Self; that attainment of security upon awakening is contradicted by the scriptures. For if there were attainment of security upon awakening, one would not experience suffering even here [in this life]. By this, the [attainment of] the beyond is explained. By this, liberation through mere knowledge is refuted. Therefore, liberation in the form of the cessation of all duality is not possible for one who is still living.

Therefore, through the application of meditation, the cessation of bondage occurs solely as the fruit of the immediate, non-sensory knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Brahman. Nor does it follow that liberation would be impermanent if it were to be accomplished by an injunction (*niyoga*), because what is actually accomplished is merely the removal of an obstruction. Furthermore, the cessation of bondage is not brought about directly by the injunction; rather, it is effected by the immediate knowledge of Brahman, which is of the nature of a single essence devoid of phenomenal plurality (*niṣprapañca*). The injunction, however, generates that immediate knowledge.

If it is asked, "How is it that an injunction (*niyoga*) is the cause for the arising of knowledge?", then how, in your view, do actions whose fruits are not intended (*anabhisaṃhita-phala*) become the cause for the arising of experience (*vedanā*)? If you say, "By means of the purification of the mind (*manonairmalya*)," then it is exactly the same for me as well. For me, knowledge is produced by the scripture once the mind has been purified; but for you, one must state what the causal complex for knowledge (*jñāna-sāmagrī*) is when the mind has been purified by the injunction. To this we reply: the very mind, purified by the injunction of meditation (*dhyāna-niyoga*), is the means.

If it is asked, "By what is this understood?"—is it not understood by you as well that the mind becomes pure through actions; and that when the mind is pure, the scripture produces the knowledge that turns one away from everything else only for one who is already turned away from all other objects through hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption?

If you argue that this is established by such scriptural passages as, "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting," "It is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon," and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," then for me also there are such scriptures as, "It is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"; "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"; "It is not grasped by the eye, nor even by speech"; "But by the purified mind"; and "It is fashioned by the heart, by wisdom, and by the mind. By these and other scriptures, the mind is rendered pure through the discipline of meditation (*dhyāna-niyoga*).
It is understood that the stainless mind produces the direct knowledge of Brahman; thus, this is beyond reproach.
