If it is argued that the capacity of being an object of worship (*upāsyatva*) is prohibited by the statement, "Not this, which they worship," we say no; for here the worshipability of Brahman is not prohibited, but rather the world's dissimilarity to Brahman is established. The meaning of the passage is: "That which living beings worship as this world is not Brahman; know that alone to be Brahman, which is not expressed by speech and by which speech is expressed. Otherwise, the statement "know that alone to be Brahman" would be contradictory.

Furthermore, the injunction for meditation would otherwise be rendered futile; therefore, by the very mandate of meditation—which has the direct realization of Brahman as its fruit—there occurs the cessation of the entire bondage consisting of the phenomenal world of the seer, the seen, and so forth, which is ultimately unreal.

As for what has been said by some—that there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference—that is incorrect; for difference and non-difference cannot coexist in a single entity, just as cold and heat, or darkness and light, cannot.

Now, it might be argued: "Indeed, the entire range of entities must be established through cognition, and everything is cognized as both different and non-different. It is non-different in its causal nature and in its generic nature, and it is different in its effect-nature and in its individual-nature. Furthermore, while in cases such as shadow and light there exists contradiction characterized by non-coexistence and consisting in having different substrata, neither of these two [contradictions] is observed between cause and effect, or between the universal and the individual; on the contrary, a single entity itself is cognized as possessing two forms."

As in the cases: "the clay is the jar," "the spotted cow," or "the hornless cow. Furthermore, not a single entity of a uniform nature has ever been observed in the world; nor is non-difference seen to suppress difference, as is the case with fire and so forth in relation to grass and the like. Thus, there is no contradiction in the nature of things, because that which exists in the form of clay, gold, a cow, a horse, and so on, likewise exists in the form of a jar, a crown, a fragment, a mare, and so forth. Nor is it a decree of the Lord that for an entity that is both non-different and different, non-difference and difference constitute one and the same form.

If it is argued that there is identity because of being perceived as such, then since they are likewise perceived [as distinct], one must also admit a dual nature consisting of both difference and non-difference. For a person with wide-open eyes, while perceiving objects such as a jar, a potsherd, a fragment, or a head, is not able to discern, "This is clay and this is a jar," or "This is cowness and this is an individual"; rather, he perceives simply, "This is a clay jar," or "A fragment, a cow."

If it is argued that "the universal (ākṛti) is the cause, to be understood through a cognition of conformity (anuvṛtti), while the individual (vyakti) is the effect, to be understood through a cognition of exclusion (vyāvṛtti)," this is not so; for no distinct forms are perceived. Indeed, even when examining most minutely, no difference in form is perceived in an object standing before one such that one could say, "this is the conforming [universal] and this is the excluding [individual]."

Just as when an action is undertaken by those who have reached a consensus, a cognition of oneness arises regarding both the effect and its specific quality; in exactly the same way, an undifferentiated cognition of oneness arises regarding that which possesses a cause and that which possesses a universal. In this very manner, even with respect to objects that are absolutely distinct in terms of place, time, and form, there arises the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that very thing. Therefore, since an object is perceived as possessing a dual nature, the attempt to establish an absolute difference between cause and effect, or between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), is contradicted by direct experience.

Now, it might be argued that—just as one says "the clay is the pot" or "the fragment is the cow"—there is a cognition of identity through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expressions "I am a god" or "I am a human," and therefore the self and the body must also be both different and non-different; thus, this attempt to establish difference-and-non-difference is like placing the flames of a fire within one's own house. However, this is merely a display of a failure to understand the meaning of coreferentiality and its nature as a means of proving difference-and-non-difference.

For indeed, it is only a cognition that is itself uncontradicted which establishes an object in all cases. However, the conceit of identity with the self as a god or the like is contradicted by all means of valid knowledge whose objects are the true nature of the self; thus, like the cognition of a snake in a rope, it does not establish non-difference between the self and the body. In the case of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) such as "the spotted cow" or "the hornless cow," no contradiction is observed anywhere by anyone; therefore, there is no over-extension [of the argument].

For this very reason, the individual soul (*jīva*) is not absolutely different from Brahman; rather, by virtue of being a portion (*aṃśa*) of Brahman, it is both different and non-different. In that regard, non-difference alone is its essential nature, while difference is adventitious (*aupādhika*). If one asks how this is known, [it is known] from such scriptural passages as "That thou art," "There is no other seer but He," and "This Self is Brahman," as well as from the passage beginning with "Brahman these two, heaven and earth," which continues: "Brahman are the masters, Brahman are the servants, and Brahman are these gamblers."
Furthermore, because non-difference is heard in the *Brahmasūkta* of the *Saṃhitopaniṣad* of the Atharvaṇikas, which states: "Woman and man were born from Brahman; is woman Brahman, or is it man?"

"He is the eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of the many. "The two unborn ones—the Lord and the non-Lord, the knowing and the unknowing. "Another is seen as the cause of their conjunction, through the qualities of action and the qualities of the self. "The Lord of the primary matter (pradhāna) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), the Master of the guṇas, the cause of bondage, existence, and liberation from saṃsāra. "He is the cause, the Lord of the lords of the senses. "One of them eats the sweet fruit of the fig tree, while the other looks on without eating. "He who dwells within the self... "By means of the conscious self (prājña-ātman)..."

Furthermore, because of scriptural passages that declare their difference, such as "Embraced [by the Supreme], he knows nothing external," "Mounted by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman), he departs casting off [the body]," and "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death," both difference and non-difference must necessarily be accepted for the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para). In this regard, non-difference is understood to be innate, because of the designation of the individual soul’s attainment of the very nature of Brahman at the state of liberation in passages such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and because of the prohibition of perceiving the Lord through difference at that time in the passage, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?"

But surely, by the scriptural mention of "together" in the passage, "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman," a distinction [between the soul and Brahman] is perceived even at that time. Furthermore, the author will state: "Excluding the activity of governing the world, on account of the context and because of non-proximity," and "On account of the indicative mark of equality in enjoyment alone."

This is not so, because hundreds of scriptural passages such as "There is no other seer but He" prohibit any distinction between selves. Furthermore, the statement "He attains all desires together with the wise Brahman" means that he attains Brahman endowed with all its qualities along with all those desires; otherwise, the phrase "together with Brahman" would imply a lack of primacy for Brahman.

Regarding the phrase "excluding the activity of the world," it will be stated that if the liberated one were to remain in a state of distinction [from Brahman], there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of a deficiency in his sovereignty; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "The manifestation [of the self] occurs by its own [nature], because of the word [itself]" (Brahmasūtra 4.4.1).

Therefore, non-difference alone is intrinsic. The difference among individual souls (jīvas) from the supreme Brahman and from one another is caused by the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) of the intellect, the senses, and the body. Although Brahman is partless and all-pervading, nevertheless, just as space appears divided by jars and the like, so too does difference arise in Brahman through the limiting adjuncts such as the intellect. Nor is there a reciprocal dependence (itaretarāśrayatva)—namely, that the connection with the adjuncts of the intellect and so forth occurs in a Brahman already divided, or that division occurs in Brahman due to the connection with the adjuncts of the intellect and so forth.

Because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and its conjunction [with the self] are produced by karma, and because that stream is beginningless; this is what is meant: from the individual soul (*jīva*) connected with prior karma, a limiting adjunct connected to itself arises, and from that [soul] joined with it, karma [arises]. Thus, according to the logic of the seed and the sprout, since the connection between karma and the limiting adjunct is beginningless, there is no fault. Therefore, the non-difference of individual souls from one another and from Brahman is indeed natural; difference, however, is adventitious (*aupādhika*).

Furthermore, just as the non-difference of the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) from one another and from Brahman is natural, so too their mutual difference is natural; for since the adjuncts lack other adjuncts, and because an infinite regress would result if such were admitted, it follows that adjuncts arise with a nature that is both different and non-different from Brahman, in accordance with the karma of the individual soul (jīva).

To this it is replied: since the collection of Vedāntic statements is intended as an injunction regarding the meditation on Brahman—which is non-dual, being, consciousness, and bliss—non-difference (*abheda*) is perceived through the Vedāntic texts. Difference (*bheda*), however, is perceived through the ritual scriptures (*karma-śāstra*), which rely upon difference, as well as by perception and other means of knowledge. Because difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory, and because the perception of difference can be accounted for as being rooted in beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), it has been stated that non-difference alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Regarding that which was stated—that there is no contradiction because both difference and non-difference are established by perception—that is incorrect. For, the distinctness of one thing from another is indeed its difference from it, while its being the opposite of that is non-difference. What sane person would assert the possibility of these two, which consist of being such and not being such, existing in a single locus?

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because of the difference in aspects—namely, non-difference in terms of the nature of the cause and the nature of the genus, and difference in terms of the nature of the effect and the nature of the individual—this is not so, for such an argument cannot withstand scrutiny. For one who asserts non-contradiction on the basis of a difference in aspects, do you mean that there is difference in one aspect and non-difference in another aspect? Or do you mean that both [difference and non-difference] reside in the object itself through its connection with these two aspects? In the first case, since difference would belong to the individual and non-difference to the genus, a single entity could not possess a dual nature.

If it is argued that "universal" (*jāti*) and "individual" (*vyakti*) are one and the same entity, then the absence of contradiction based on a difference in form would have to be abandoned. Furthermore, it has been stated that within a single entity, being distinct and its opposite are contradictory. In the second alternative, however, there would be two mutually distinct forms and a separate entity serving as their substrate that is not perceived. Even upon accepting the third position, only the mutual distinctness of the three would be established; their non-difference would not.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because the two forms possess a state of being both different and non-different from the entity that serves as their substrate, then how could the two forms—which are themselves distinct from the self—that serve as the substrate, function as the means for reconciling the coexistence of two contradictory attributes within that self? How much less so, then, if they were not distinct? Furthermore, if one accepts that both the two forms and their possessor consist of a dual nature, an infinite regress would result due to the necessity of postulating further reconciling factors.

Furthermore, even in the case of an object possessing a universal, a cognition of a single uniform form does not arise in the same way as the cognition of a single individual that is currently being perceived. For every cognition occurs everywhere precisely as a relation between a qualifier (*prakāra*) and a qualificand (*prakārin*), in the form "this is such-and-such. In that context, the aspect of the qualifier is the universal (*jāti*), while the aspect of the qualificand is the individual (*vyakti*); thus, the cognition is not of a single form.

For this very reason, it is not possible for the individual soul (*jīva*) to be both different and non-different from Brahman. Therefore, since non-difference is rooted in the scriptures in a way that cannot be established otherwise, the cognition of difference is rooted solely in beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*). [Objection: If this were so, then ignorance would belong to Brahman itself, and defects such as birth, old age, and death—which are rooted in that [ignorance]—would manifest. Consequently, scriptural passages such as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" and "This Self is free from sin" would be contradicted. [Reply: This is not so, because defects such as ignorance are not ultimately real (*aparamārtha*).

For you, however, who do not admit any other entity distinct from Brahman with its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the contact of the adjuncts with Brahman itself, as well as the defects such as being a living soul (*jīvatva*) and ignorance (*ajñatva*) produced by them, would exist in reality (*paramārthataḥ*). For adjuncts, when they come into contact with Brahman—which is partless and indivisible—do not do so by cutting or breaking it; rather, having joined with the very nature of Brahman, they produce their own effects right there within it.

If one should think: "The individual soul (jīva) is Brahman as conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and it is of atomic dimension (aṇu-parimāṇa) because its limiter—the mind—is atomic; and this limitation is beginningless. Thus, defects that attach to the conditioned part do not attach to the unconditioned, supreme Brahman."

This must be asked: Is the *jīva* a fragment of Brahman cut off by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), resembling an atom? Or is it a specific portion of Brahman that remains uncut but is conjoined with an atomic-sized adjunct? Or is it the very nature of Brahman itself conjoined with the adjunct? Or is it a distinct conscious entity conjoined with the adjunct? Or is it the adjunct alone? The first alternative is not tenable, because Brahman cannot be divided. Furthermore, it would follow that the *jīva* has a beginning in time; for division is indeed the making twofold of that which was previously one.

In the second case, however, all defects would belong to Brahman itself due to its connection with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) at a particular location within Brahman. Since it is impossible for the adjunct, as it moves, to drag along the portion of Brahman with which it is conjoined, there would be a difference in the portions of Brahman conjoined with the adjunct at every moment; consequently, bondage and liberation would occur moment by moment. Furthermore, if dragging were to occur, the entire Brahman would have to be dragged because it is partless. If it is argued that dragging is not possible for that which is partless and all-pervading;

In that case, the very same fault previously mentioned would apply, namely, that it is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) itself that moves. Furthermore, since all limiting adjuncts would be in contact with uninterrupted regions of Brahman, and since all individual souls (*jīvas*) are merely regions of Brahman and thus identical, there would be a recognition [of one's own experiences] by all of them. If, on the other hand, such recognition is denied on the grounds of a difference in spatial regions, then even for a single soul, [recognition would fail] within its own limiting adjunct.

In the first alternative, there would be no rebirth (*pratisandhāna*). In the third alternative, however, because the very nature of Brahman would fall into the state of being a *jīva* through its connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), an unconditioned Brahman distinct from that would be unestablished; furthermore, there would be only one single *jīva* in all bodies. In the fourth alternative, since the *jīva* would be something other than Brahman, the view that the distinction between *jīvas* is merely adventitious (*aupādhikatva*) would be abandoned. And in the final [alternative], the position of the Cārvākas alone would be accepted.

Therefore, by the force of the scriptures teaching non-duality, one must admit that all difference has its root solely in ignorance (*avidyā*). Consequently, even though the authority of the scripture consists in its being directed toward the purposes of engagement and cessation, it is established that the Vedānta passages possess authority regarding the nature of Brahman as being subordinate to the injunctions for meditation. That too is incorrect; for even if the Vedānta passages were subordinate to the injunctions for meditation, their authority would be untenable as long as their subject matter remains [merely] a mental construct.

This is what is meant: Do those sentences whose scope is the nature of Brahman attain authority regarding the nature of Brahman by entering into a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) with an injunction for meditation (*dhyāna-vidhi*), or are they independent? If there is a single syntactical unity, then because the focus is on the injunction for meditation, an intentionality (*tātparya*) toward the nature of Brahman is not possible. If they are separate syntactical units, then due to the absence of any purpose consisting of engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), they would simply be non-informative. Nor should it be argued that meditation consists merely of a continuous flow of memory (*smṛti-santati*).

And since that [object of meditation] is to be defined solely by what is to be remembered (*smartavya*), when the injunction for meditation (*dhyāna-vidhi*) requires a specific object to be remembered, passages such as "All this is what this Self is," "Brahman is the experiencer of all," and "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" provide the nature of Brahman and its specific attributes. Therefore, having attained syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunction, these texts serve as the authority for the actual existence of the object. Even though the injunction for meditation requires a specific object to be remembered, the fulfillment of meditation can occur even through an unreal (untrue) object—just as in the case of injunctions for "seeing" (*dṛṣṭi-vidhi*) such as "The name is Brahman"—because there is no requirement for the reality of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*).

Therefore, since the Vedānta passages are devoid of the purpose of inciting activity or cessation, they terminate merely in providing the essential nature of the object of meditation even when they are subordinate to injunctions for meditation; and even if they were independent, they would—like sentences used to coax children or the sick—accomplish the human goal through mere knowledge alone. Consequently, it follows that Brahman cannot have the scripture as its means of valid cognition, because [the scriptures] lack the capacity to have a perfectly established reality as their object. This is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).

In this regard, it is established by the sūtra: "But that [is established], because of the concordance" (*tattu samanvayāt*). "Concordance" (*samanvaya*) means perfect concordance; the meaning is concordance in the sense of being for the sake of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Since Brahman—which consists of unsurpassed, infinite bliss and constitutes the supreme human goal—is connected as the subject matter, it follows that the scripture is indeed established as the means of valid knowledge regarding It. This is the meaning.

By asserting that the collection of Vedāntic statements—which reveals Brahman as the supreme goal to be attained, whose nature consists of unsurpassed bliss and the total removal of all defects—does not culminate in a purpose because it lacks intent toward engagement or withdrawal, one speaks of a person living in a royal palace as being devoid of purpose for not entering the kennels of the dogs.

This is what is meant: when it is possible for all liberated souls, as well as for oneself, to experience without distinction the true nature of the higher and lower realities—which have been obscured by the shroud of beginningless ignorance in the form of karma—for all those individual knowers (*kṣetrajña*) who are differentiated as male, female, or neuter, and who possess specific, fixed sustainers, nourishers, and objects of enjoyment, including gods, asuras, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, kinnaras, kimpuruṣas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, humans, animals, birds, reptiles, trees, shrubs, creepers, dūrvā grass, and so forth.

A statement that brings about the realization that the Supreme Brahman exists—producing an infinite and unsurpassed bliss through its essential nature, form, qualities, majesty, and activities—is alone effective in fulfilling its purpose. However, a statement focused solely on engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) does not fulfill its purpose until it conveys a connection with the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

In response to the inquiry, "How is such a Brahman attained?", the practice of meditation (*upāsana*) is enjoined as the means for attaining Brahman through terms such as "knowing" (*vedana*), as in the passages: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and "One should meditate upon the Self alone as the world."

Just as one, having learned of the existence of a treasure in one's own house through the statement "there is a treasure in your house," becomes satisfied and subsequently exerts effort toward its acquisition; and just as a certain prince, who was attached to childhood play, departed from the royal palace and became lost, was discovered by the king to have vanished, and while remaining unknown to his father, was raised by a certain eminent brahmin until he reached sixteen years of age—having mastered the Vedas and Shastras and becoming a repository of all arts, skills, and virtues—the [brahmin] would say, "Your father..."

If he hears a statement uttered by some most eminent person, saying, "The Lord of all the world—endowed with the qualities of profundity, magnanimity, affection, benevolence, heroism, valor, prowess, and so forth—is staying in the best of cities, desiring to see you alone, his lost son," then at that very moment, he thinks, "My son lives and my father is enriched with every prosperity," and becomes filled with unsurpassed joy; and the king, having heard that his son is alive, healthy, of most enchanting appearance, and one who has mastered everything to be known, attains all [his desires].
The human goal is achieved; subsequently, one exerts effort toward its acquisition; and finally, both [the knowledge and the object] come together.

Furthermore, as for the claim that a statement whose domain is an already established entity reaches its culmination in the human goal through mere cognition of it—and thus, like a statement used to entice children or the sick, lacks authority regarding the actual existence of the object—that is incorrect. For if the non-existence of the object is certain, then even an object known [through words] does not lead to the human goal.

Even for children, the sick, and others, joy and other such emotions arise from the delusion that an object exists; if, while that very cognition is present, a certainty regarding the non-existence of the object were to arise in them, then at that very moment their joy and other emotions would cease. Likewise, even in the case of Upaniṣadic statements, if there were a certainty that they lack the intent to establish the existence of Brahman, then even when knowledge of Brahman occurs, there would be no culmination in the supreme human goal.

Therefore, it is established that the statement, "From which indeed these beings are born," and so forth, teaches that there exists a Brahman who is the sole cause of the entire universe, who is free from even a trace of all defects, who is the repository of infinite auspicious qualities such as omniscience and the power of true resolve, and who is characterized by unsurpassed and infinite bliss.

It has been stated that Brahman—omniscient, endowed with all powers, the sole repository of auspicious qualities which are the opposite of everything to be discarded, and the one taught by such scriptural passages as "From whence indeed these [beings arise]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1) which declare the cause of the world—is the object of inquiry. Now, it is being shown that those scriptural passages declaring the cause of the world do not intend to propound the Pradhāna or other causes established through inference, by means of the sūtra beginning with "Because of seeing, not that which is non-scriptural" (BS 1.1.5). **Because of seeing, not that which is non-scriptural.** (1.1.5)
This is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second. It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate.

It emitted heat," and so forth. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is that which is denoted by the word "Being" (sat), the cause of the world, the Pradhāna described by others as being inferable through reasoning?

What is Brahman characterized by that which has been stated? What is the prima facie position? That it is *pradhāna*. Why? Because the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," speaks of the causal state of that entity denoted by the word "this"—which is composed of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, is the object of enjoyment for sentient beings, and exists in various modified forms such as ether and so forth. For being an effect consists precisely in a substance that serves as the cause undergoing a change of state; therefore, whatever substance and whatever nature exist in the state of an effect [must likewise exist in the state of the cause].

That very substance existing in the state of a cause has that [same] nature; and the effect consists of the constituents such as *sattva* and so forth. Thus, the Pradhāna alone, in its state of equilibrium of the *guṇas*, is the cause. That same [Pradhāna], when all particularities have been withdrawn and is pure existence (*sanmātra*), is designated by the [scriptural passage]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. For this very reason, there is non-difference between the effect and the cause; and this being so, the promise that through the knowledge of one, all is known, is logically established.

Otherwise, there would be a discrepancy between the illustration and the thing illustrated in the passage beginning with, "As, my dear, by one clod of clay [all that is made of clay is known]," regarding the clod of clay and its products. Therefore, the *pradhāna* alone is taught by the Great Sage Kapila in this statement concerning the cause of the world; and since this statement takes the form of a proposition and an illustration, it is essentially an inference. Thus, that which is denoted by the word "Sat" is merely inferential. To this, it is replied: "Because of seeing (īkṣateḥ), it is not that which is not based on scripture (aśabdam). That for which scripture alone is not the means of knowledge is "not based on scripture," i.e., inferential.

The meaning is "the Pradhāna. It is not that which is propounded by the statements of those who maintain the Pradhāna to be the cause of the world. Why? Because of the hearing of the verbal root *īkṣati* (to see), which denotes a specific activity related to that which is expressed by the word *sat*. [As it says in scripture: "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. And the connection with the act of seeing is not possible in the case of the insentient Pradhāna.

Since this is possible, that particular conscious being capable of such deliberation—the omniscient, omnipotent Supreme Person who is denoted by the word "Sat"—is established. Furthermore, in all accounts of creation, creation preceded by deliberation (*īkṣā*) is clearly perceived in passages such as: "He deliberated, 'Shall I now create the worlds? He created these worlds"; and "He deliberated; He created the vital breath (*prāṇa*)," and so forth. Now, it might be argued that the cause must necessarily correspond to its effect. True; however, [the cause] corresponds precisely to every effect.

The Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is omniscient, omnipotent, and of true resolve; He has as His body the subtle aggregate of conscious and unconscious entities. As it is said: "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are inherent"; "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge"; and "He whose body is the unmanifest, whose body is the imperishable, and whose body is death—He is the inner Self of all beings. This very point will be established in the [sūtras] beginning with "Not so, because of the difference in nature" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.4).

In this regard, it is stated that the passages concerning creation are not capable of establishing the Pradhāna; however, the contradiction regarding the nature of reality will be resolved in that very context. As for the claim that this passage is merely of the nature of an inference due to its connection with a proposition and an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), that is incorrect, because no logical reason (*hetu*) is provided. Indeed, when the intention is to teach the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one—expressed as "by which the unheard becomes heard"—the illustrative example is employed solely to demonstrate the possibility of such knowledge to one who considers it entirely impossible.
For it is precisely from the hearing of terms such as "He saw" (*īkṣati*) that the absence of even a trace of inference is understood.

Now, it might be argued: "The primary act of seeing is not attributed here to the conscious [Self], but rather a secondary (gauṇa) act of seeing is attributed to the Pradhāna, because of its association with secondary seeing in such passages as 'That heat saw' and 'Those waters saw. And the metaphorical attribution of the attributes of a conscious being occurs even in the case of insentient things, as in 'The rice plants await the rain' and 'By the rain, the seed rejoiced. Therefore, the seeing is secondary. Having restated this objection, he refutes it: "If it be claimed that it is secondary, no, because of the word 'Self' (ātman). (Sūtra 6)

As for what was said—that because of its association with the primary act of seeing, the designation "seeing" applied even to the Existent (sat) is figurative, intended to refer to a specific prior state, and thus secondary—that is not so, [given the passage] "This world has that as its essence" (*aitadātmyam*).

Because that which is designated by the word *sat* is referred to by the word *ātman* in the passage, "All this is that; that is the Truth; that is the Self," the following is meant: "All this has that as its self; that is the Self"—this teaching that *sat* is the Self is made with reference to the entire expanse of the sentient and the insentient, and it does not apply to the insentient *pradhāna*. Therefore, since the Supreme Self alone is the Self even of fire, water, and earth, words such as "fire" and so forth are also denotative of the Supreme Self alone.

For instance, [the text] says: "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate names and forms. Thus, it is precisely through the entry of the Supreme Self that fire and the other elements attain their substantiality and receive their respective names. Consequently, even in the passages "That fire thought" and "Those waters thought," the designation of "thinking" (īkṣaṇa) is primary. Therefore, the intention of the Sūtra is that by virtue of this association, any suspicion of the term "it thought" (tad aikṣata) being figurative is cast far away. Furthermore, the Pradhāna is not what is denoted by the word "Being" (sat), because [the scripture speaks of one who is] "intent upon That."

Having instructed the seeker Śvetaketu in the contemplation of his identity with the Existent through the words "That thou art," [the Upanishad states that] for one established therein, "his delay is only so long as..."

"I shall be liberated, and then I shall attain [Brahman]"—thus he teaches that liberation, characterized by the attainment of Brahman, has as its only obstacle the mere falling away of the body. Furthermore, if the insentient *pradhāna* were taught as the cause, then the teaching that meditation on being of the same nature as that [cause] is the means to liberation would be untenable. According to the principle, "As a person's resolve (*kratu*) is in this world, so does he become after departing from here," for one devoted to that [insentient cause], there would only be the attainment of the insentient. Nor is [liberation possible] even through thousands of mothers and fathers...

The scripture is even more compassionate, for it teaches that the accumulation of non-conscious matter (acit) is the cause of the affliction by the three kinds of suffering described above. For even those who maintain the doctrine of Primordial Matter (Pradhāna) as the cause do not admit liberation for one who is established in Pradhāna.
Furthermore, [the Pradhāna is not the cause] because there is no statement regarding its being something to be abandoned. (Sūtra 1.4.8)

If the *pradhāna* alone were the cause denoted by the word "Being," then for the seeker of liberation Śvetaketu, its identity with that [Self] would have to be taught as something to be abandoned, because it is opposed to liberation. But that is not done; on the contrary, it is taught precisely as something to be accepted in such passages as "That thou art" and "For him, there is delay only so long. For this reason also, it is not the *pradhāna*, because it would contradict the initial proposition.

Furthermore, if the Pradhāna were the cause, there would be a contradiction with the initial proposition. For at the beginning of the discourse, the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is proposed. And that must be established by showing that the entire manifold of sentient and insentient things—which are effects—become known precisely through the knowledge of the "Being" (sat), which is their non-different cause.

However, if the Pradhāna were the cause, this would be contradicted because the class of sentient beings could not be the effect of the Pradhāna; thus, the knowledge of the class of sentient beings could not be achieved through the knowledge of the Pradhāna. For this reason as well, the Pradhāna is not [the cause], on account of [the soul's] merging [into it] during deep sleep (svāpyayāt). 10.

He speaks of that very reality denoted by the word *sat* as the primordial nature (*prakṛti*): "Learn from me, my dear, the state of deep sleep (*svapnānta*)—when a person is said to be 'sleeping,' then, my dear, he has become united with *sat*; he has gone to his own self (*svam apītaḥ*). Therefore they say of him 'he sleeps' (*svapiti*), for he has gone to his own self. Thus, [the text describes] the individual soul (*jīva*) in deep sleep as being with *sat*.

Having attained [perfection], one designates oneself as "having merged into one's own self" (*svam apītaḥ svasmin pralīnaḥ*). And "merging" (*pralaya*) means dissolution into one's own cause. Furthermore, the insentient *pradhāna* cannot be the cause of the sentient individual soul (*jīva*). The meaning of "he merges into his own self" is that the individual soul merges into the Self itself. It is stated in the scripture concerning the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa-śruti*) that Brahman alone—whose body is the conscious reality and who constitutes its very Self—is designated by the term "individual soul."

Brahman, which is denoted by the term "that living soul," is at the time of deep sleep—just as at the time of cosmic dissolution—denoted solely by the term "Being" (sat), because of the absence of association with name and form. Thus it is said: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being; he has gone to his own Self. Likewise, in the same context, due to the absence of association with name and form and because of being embraced by the Intelligent One (prājña) alone, it is said: "Embraced by the intelligent Self, he knows nothing that is external, nor anything internal.
This is because the individual soul (jīva) remains associated with name and form until liberation.

For indeed, there is no arising of knowledge whose object is distinct from itself. For it is clearly stated in another scriptural passage that at the time of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), having abandoned name and form (*nāmarūpa*), one is embraced by Being (*sat*); then, upon returning to the waking state, one again embraces name and form and becomes possessed of those names and forms: "Or when one who is asleep sees no dream whatsoever, then he becomes one with this vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone; from that self, the vital breaths emerge according to their respective abodes. Likewise: "They [return] here as a tiger or a lion..."

"Whether they become a wolf, a boar, a gadfly, or a mosquito, they become exactly as they are. Likewise, it speaks of the soul in deep sleep as being "completely embraced by the intelligent Self" (*prājñena ātmanā sampariṣvaktaḥ*). Therefore, that which is denoted by the word *Sat* is the Supreme Brahman, the omniscient Supreme Lord, the Puruṣottama himself. Thus says the author of the Vṛtti: "O dear one, at that time he becomes united with the *Sat*; this is determined by both union and non-union," and it also says, "completely embraced by the intelligent Self. For this reason also, it is not the Pradhāna [that is meant], because of the uniformity of the teaching (*gatisāmānyāt*). (Sūtra 11)

"In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, one only; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. He thought, 'Let me now create the worlds,' and he created these worlds. "From that very Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth. "The Ṛgveda, etc., is the breath of this great Being"—the course or operation of such passages concerning creation is the same as, and possesses the same meaning as, this [present passage].
And in all of those, the Lord of All is understood to be the cause; therefore, it is determined that even here, the Lord of All alone is the cause.
And because it is so stated in scripture. || 12 ||

For indeed, in this very Upanishad, it is heard that this Being denoted by the word *sat* possesses, by virtue of being the Self (*ātman*), the state of having manifested names and forms (*nāmarūpa-vyākṛtatva*), omniscience, omnipotence, the state of being the support of all, freedom from sin and other defects, as well as the possession of true desires and true resolves; as in: "Entering with this living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me manifest names and forms"; "All these creatures, my dear, have their root in the *sat*, their abode in the *sat*, and their rest in the *sat*"; and "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self."

"Whatever he has here and whatever he does not have—all that is gathered within him; all desires are gathered within him. "This Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true. And so too are other scriptural passages.

"He has no master in the world, nor any presiding lord, nor even a mark (liṅga) of his own. He is the cause, the lord of lords of causes; there is no progenitor of him, nor is there any ruler over him. "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and assigned names, remains calling them forth. "He has entered within as the Teacher of men, the Self of all. "The Self of the universe, the ultimate refuge. "The Lord of the universe, the Master of the Self. "Whatever is seen or even heard in this world..."

"Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without"; "This Nārāyaṇa is the inner self of all beings, free from sin, divine, the one God"—and so forth. Therefore, the scriptural texts concerning the cause of the universe are not capable of propounding the Pradhāna or other such principles. Consequently, it is established that the Supreme Person, Nārāyaṇa alone—the omniscient, omnipotent Lord of lords, who is free from even a trace of all defects and is a great ocean of an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities—is the sole cause of the entire universe and the Brahman to be sought through inquiry.

For this very reason, the doctrine of Brahman as pure consciousness devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣacinmātra*) must also be understood as refuted by the author of the Sūtras through these scriptural citations, since he establishes that Brahman—the object of inquiry—is that which possesses the attribute of supreme, primary *īkṣaṇa* (seeing) and other qualities. For in the doctrine of attributelessness, even the status of being a witness (*sākṣitva*) would be non-ultimate; yet Brahman, known through the Vedāntas, is proposed as the object of inquiry, and it is established by such sūtras as "Because of seeing, [Brahman] is not that which is not based on scripture" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*) that it is conscious (*cetana*). Consciousness, indeed, consists in the possession of the quality of sentience (*caitanya*). Therefore, that which lacks the quality of seeing is equivalent to primordial matter (*pradhāna*).

Furthermore, in the doctrine that Brahman is mere light devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa-prakāśamātra*), even its status as "light" is difficult to establish. For "light" is a specific entity that renders both itself and others fit for practical transaction (*vyavahāra-yogyatā*). Since a distinctionless entity lacks the nature of both [self-luminosity and illuminating others], it would be insentient (*acittva*) like a jar or similar objects. If it is argued that even in the absence of those two natures, there exists the capacity for them, that is not so; for "capacity" is nothing other than "efficacy" (*sāmarthya*). Indeed, the claim of a distinctionless entity would be abandoned if it were associated with the quality of efficacy. If it is then argued [that this is accepted] on the authority of scripture (*śruti*):

If it is argued that one specific attribute is admitted [in the case of the individual soul], then, alas, by that very same logic, omniscience, omnipotence, the state of being the Lord of all lords, the source of all auspicious qualities, and the state of being the adversary of everything base—all these must be admitted [of the Lord]. Furthermore, possessing power (*śaktimattva*) consists in being conducive to a particular effect; and that [power] is definable solely through its particular effect. If the particular effect lacks a basis in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the possession of power, which is definable solely through that effect, would likewise lack a basis in valid cognition.

Furthermore, for one who maintains that the ultimate reality is devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣavastuvādin*), even the status of that reality as an actual entity (*vastutva*) lacks any means of valid cognition (*niṣpramāṇa*). It has already been stated previously that perception, inference, scripture, and one's own experience all have as their object only that which possesses distinctions. Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) alone—who is capable of the contemplation "May I become manifold"—is the object of inquiry.

Thus, the distinction of Brahman—which is the object of inquiry—from the non-conscious Pradhāna, which consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas and serves as the object of experience for conscious beings, has been stated. Now, it is established that Brahman is distinct from the pure and impure individual self (pratyagātman), who is subject to karma and submerged in an ocean of manifold and infinite suffering caused by contact with Prakṛti composed of the three guṇas; rather, Brahman is the opposite of all that is to be discarded and is unsurpassed bliss.
"Consisting of Bliss, because of repetition. (1.1.13)

The Taittirīyas study the text: "Now, this person consists of the essence of food," having introduced that subject, they continue, "Different from this which consists of consciousness is another inner self consisting of bliss. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) the Supreme Self, distinct from the individual self (jīva)—which is denoted by the term *pratyagātman* and partakes in bondage and liberation—or is it that very same [individual self]? What is the reasonable conclusion? That it is the individual self. Why? Because of the scriptural statement, "This is indeed its embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*)," which declares that the one consisting of bliss is the embodied self; for the embodied self is the individual self (*jīvātman*) who is connected with a body.

But is it not the case that, for the sake of easy comprehension of Brahman—which has been established as the cause of the world—the text, after enumerating the series beginning with *annamaya*, teaches that very cause of the world as the *ānandamaya*? And since the cause of the world is declared to be omniscient and the Lord of all because of the scriptural mention of "reflection" (*aikṣata*) in the passage "It thought," this has already been stated. True, it has been so stated; however, that [Ānandamaya] is not distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*). By this...

Because of the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the individual soul (*jīva*), who is designated as the cause in the passages, "Having entered by means of the living self (*jīvenātmanā*)," and "That thou art, O Śvetaketu"; for grammatical coordination is intended to establish identity, as in "This is that Devadatta. Furthermore, a creation preceded by deliberation (*īkṣā*) is indeed possible for the conscious individual soul; therefore, [the text] "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" refers to the soul when it is divested from its association with the non-intelligent.

The true nature [of the Self] is taught as that which is to be attained. This is stated to be the definition of the true nature when separated from the non-sentient: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. For liberation is indeed the attainment of that very form. As it is said: "For one who possesses a body, there is no cessation of the pleasant and the unpleasant; but for one who exists bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch him. Therefore, the true nature of the individual soul (jīva), when separated from ignorance, is introduced as that which is to be attained and is taught as the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya). For it is thus:

In order to reveal the true nature of the Self by means of the analogy of the moon reflected in the branches of a tree, [the text] first points to the body as "the person consisting of food" (*annamayaḥ puruṣaḥ*). Then, it points to the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*) which exists within and sustains that body; next, the mind (*manas*) which exists within that; and finally, the intellect (*buddhi*) which exists within that, each designated respectively as "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*), "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), and "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). Having thus indicated them in the sequence of their progressive entry into the intellect, it finally points to the individual self (*jīvātman*), which exists within all, as "another inner self, consisting of bliss" (*anyo 'ntara ātmānandamayaḥ*).

Having thus taught, he concludes the succession of inner selves; therefore, it is determined that the very nature of the individual self (jīvātman) is the Brahman introduced in the statement "He who knows Brahman attains [Brahman]," and that this same [self] is what was taught as consisting of bliss (ānandamaya).

But is it not the case that from the statement, "Brahman is the tail, the support," it is understood that Brahman is something other than the one consisting of bliss? It is not so; Brahman itself, by way of its own specific nature, is designated as having the form of a person, described in terms of head, wings, and tail.

Just as the body composed of food (*annamaya*), which is a whole (*avayavin*), is shown to possess a head, wings, and a tail by means of its own parts—which are not distinct from itself—through such statements as "this is its head," so too is Brahman, which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), shown by means of its own parts, namely pleasure (*priya*) and the rest, which are not distinct from itself. In that context, Brahman, whose nature is undivided, is called "the tail, the support" (*brahma pucchaṃ pratiṣṭhā*) because it serves as the substratum for pleasure, joy, delight, and bliss, which have been figuratively represented as the limbs.

Moreover, if Brahman were other than that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), it would have been pointed out [as such] by saying, "There is another inner Self, Brahman, distinct from this one consisting of bliss"; yet it is not so indicated. This is what is meant: the Brahman introduced at the beginning in the statement, "He who knows Brahman attains the Supreme," is the Truth (*satyam*).

Having established through its definition that Brahman is infinite knowledge (*jñāna*), characterized by a form distinguished from everything else, the text points to that very same reality with the word "Self" (*ātman*) in the passage, "From this very Self," and reveals its nature as the Self by virtue of being the innermost of all. Having transcended the layers beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*)—which were each designated as the Self because they were the interior of the preceding—and having moved through those such as the one consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), the text concludes with the designation of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) as the Self, stating: "There is another interior Self, the one consisting of bliss. Thus, it culminates in the *ānandamaya* by means of the term "Self."

Therefore, it is determined that Brahman, which was introduced by the word "Self," is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Now, an objection may be raised: after stating, "Brahman is the tail, the support," the text says, "He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent; if he knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as existing. This shows that the existence or non-existence of the Self depends on the knowledge or ignorance of Brahman, not on the knowledge or ignorance of the one consisting of bliss.

Furthermore, it is not reasonable to entertain a doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), whose nature as joy, delight, and so forth is well known to all the world; therefore, this verse was not cited with reference to the one consisting of bliss. Consequently, Brahman is something other than the one consisting of bliss. This is not so.

Just as the verses cited here and there—such as "This tail is the support," "The earth is the tail, the support," "The Atharvāṅgirases are the tail, the support," and "Greatness is the tail, the support"—are not intended merely to establish the tail itself, but rather to establish the Person consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth, even so this verse, "Non-existent indeed [was this in the beginning]," pertains to the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), and not to a tail distinct from the one consisting of bliss.

Even though the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is indeed Brahman, it is entirely reasonable to raise the doubt as to whether or not there exists that unlimited bliss which is manifested in the form of joy, delight, and so forth; for even the "tail-Brahman" is itself unknown precisely because of its nature as unlimited bliss. This is because Brahman lacks the status of being a whole possessing parts such as a head and so on.

If it be argued that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not Brahman, then because of the absence of the qualities of being the "tail" and the "foundation," even the tail would not be Brahman. Now, if it is said that this is merely a figurative description—"the tail, the foundation"—because Brahman serves as the substratum for that entity imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), then indeed, there will likewise be a figurative description of that Brahman—which is blissful and non-dual—as having "joy as its head" and so forth.

And thus, by the text "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," that which is distinct from other objects—whether they be subject to modification, insentient, or limited—is shown to be excluded from what is non-bliss; this exclusion is taught as being "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*). Therefore, in Brahman, whose nature is undivided, unitary, and of the form of bliss, the suffix *mayaṭ* in the term *ānandamaya* should be understood as having its own meaning (denoting identity), just as in the case of *prāṇamaya*. Consequently, the innate form of the individual self (*jīvātman*), which is divided by the various and manifold distinctions such as gods and so forth imagined through ignorance, is called "consisting of bliss" because it is undivided, unitary, and entirely composed of bliss; thus, the "consisting of bliss" is the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

This being the case, we reply: "The one consisting of bliss [is the Supreme Self], because of repetition. The one consisting of bliss is the Supreme Self. Why? Because of repetition; for beginning with the words, "Now follows the inquiry into this very bliss," and ending with the passage, "From which words turn back," the text describes [bliss] through a sequence of hundredfold increases, culminating in that which is unsurpassed.

The bliss experienced when practicing the *daśaśiraska* [meditation], being impossible for the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—which partakes only in a minute fragment of limited pleasure mixed with infinite suffering—reveals its own substratum as the Supreme Self alone; for the Supreme Self is the opposite of all that is to be discarded, consists solely of auspiciousness, and is distinct from everything else. As it has been said: "Therefore, indeed..."

"From this [self] consisting of consciousness, there is another inner self consisting of bliss. For the one "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*), not mere intellect; for by means of the suffix *maya*, a distinction [from the constituent parts] is perceived. In the case of the "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*), however, the suffix must be taken in its primary sense (*svārthika*) because there is no other way. But here, since it is possible for the possessor of that [consciousness], namely the individual soul, to exist, it is not right to assume a lack of meaning [for the suffix]. We have already stated that the inner self, whether bound or liberated, is nothing but consciousness. Furthermore, the possibility of the meaning of the suffix *maya* in the cases of "consisting of breath" and so forth will be explained immediately below.

How, then, is the employment of the word *vijñāna* alone in the verse concerning the subject consisting of consciousness—specifically in the phrase "Consciousness performs the sacrifice"—justified? There is no fault here, because the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the Self, who is the knower, is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) due to its self-luminosity; furthermore, the nature of the knower is defined solely by knowledge. For words that express a thing through its defining attributes (*dharmanirūpaṇadharmaśabda*) convey the substratum (*dharmī*), which is its very nature, by means of those attributes, just like the word "cow" and others. This is in accordance with the rule: "The *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes are used diversely."

The Mādhyandinas, who study the section "He who dwells in the self" (*ya ātmani tiṣṭhan*) in place of the corresponding section found in the Kāṇva recension, clarify that the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—referred to by the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) in the Kāṇva text—is indeed meant. Furthermore, the neuter gender of the term *vijñānam* is intended to signify its nature as a reality (*vastutva*). Thus, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), distinct from and inner to the individual soul consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). Although the verse "Consciousness performs the sacrifice" (*vijñānaṃ yajñaṃ tanute*) mentions only knowledge and not the knower;

Nevertheless, in the passage, "There is another inner self consisting of consciousness," that which possesses [consciousness]—namely, the knower—is taught; just as in the verse, "From food indeed creatures are born," although food alone is mentioned, in the subsequent statement, "This very person consists of the essence of food," it is not merely food that is indicated, but rather that which is made of it, its modification. Keeping all this in mind, the author of the Sūtras himself states immediately thereafter, "Because of the designation of difference."

As for what was stated—that because the cause of the world, which was pointed out by the passages "having entered with this living self (jīva)" and "That thou art," is designated in grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the individual soul (jīva), the cause of the world does not transcend the nature of the individual soul; and therefore, having taken the very nature of the individual soul as the subject under discussion in the opening statement "He who knows Brahman attains the Supreme," that nature is taught as "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) by way of its exclusion from suffering and non-duality—[this is now addressed].

That is incorrect; for even though the individual soul (jīva) possesses consciousness, it is impossible for it to possess the capacity for infinite and diverse creation preceded by its own volition—as expressed in [the text]: "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'; it emitted fire. Indeed, even in its pure state, the impossibility of that [soul] engaging in activities such as the creation of the world will be demonstrated in the passages: "excluding the activity of the world" and "because of the indicative mark of equality in mere enjoyment."

If it is asked: "How can the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) expressed in the passages 'by this living self' and 'That thou art' be justified, if one does not accept that Brahman, which is the cause, has the nature of the individual soul (jīva)?"

Or how could Brahman—who is devoid of even a trace of all defects, whose will is true, who is omniscient and omnipotent, who possesses an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities, and who is the cause of all—be of the nature of a *jīva*, whose every activity such as thinking and blinking is dependent on karma that produces various and endless forms of suffering? If you argue that this is possible because one or the other must be false, then tell me, sir: which is it? Is it the one associated with what is to be abandoned (*heya*), or is it the one whose very nature consists solely of auspiciousness, which is the opposite of what is to be abandoned?

If it is argued that the false appearance of a connection with the rejectable (*heya*)—due to Brahman, who is solely devoted to the auspicious (*kalyāṇa*) that is the opposite of the rejectable, being the locus of beginningless ignorance—is itself of a false nature; this which is stated is a contradiction, [since it implies] Brahman possesses the rejectable... [and so forth].

It possesses the state of being a locus (*katānatva*) because it is the substratum of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), and because it is the substratum for the false appearance of infinite objects of suffering. Indeed, the connection with that which is to be abandoned (*heya-sambandha*) consists precisely in being the substratum of ignorance and the substratum for the appearance of suffering, which is its effect. To be connected with that [suffering] and to be its opposite (*tat-pratyanīkatva*) are inherently contradictory. Nevertheless, do not say that there is no contradiction because that [connection] is false (*mithyātva*). For even that which is false is indeed a non-human goal (*apuruṣārtha*); you yourself maintain that all the Vedāntas are commenced for the purpose of removing it.

Furthermore, the association with non-human goals (apuruṣārtha) that must be discarded is contradicted by the fact that [Brahman] is solely intent upon auspicious qualities that are the opposite of what is to be abandoned. What can we do? Having first proposed the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one—"By which the unheard becomes heard"—and having established that Brahman is the sole cause of the entire universe through the passage beginning "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," as well as its possession of true volition through "It thought: May I be many," [the text then teaches] that very same Brahman as "That thou art."

If it is argued that through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*)—the locus of infinite suffering—with [Brahman] is established, and that on the grounds of its otherwise being inexplicable, one must postulate that Brahman alone is the locus of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth; [we reply: even for the sake of explaining what is heard in scripture, one should not postulate what is logically inconsistent or contradictory. Furthermore, if the connection with things to be abandoned (*heya*) were indeed ultimately real, while the nature of being solely auspicious were merely illusory, then alas, the scripture—which was undertaken with the desire to revive the consciousness of those struck by the threefold suffering—would be rendered purposeless.

It correctly revives [the doctrine] by making it understood that for him (Brahman), the affliction by the three-fold suffering is merely apparent, whereas his nature as consisting solely of auspiciousness is imagined through delusion. Now, if—out of a desire to avoid this defect—it is argued that one must conceive that everything other than Brahman’s nature as pure, undifferentiated consciousness, such as the state of being a jīva, suffering, and so forth, as well as its possession of true resolve, its being a mine of auspicious qualities, and its being the cause of the world, is all illusory; then, oh! consider the meaning of your own statement!

Skillfulness: The thesis that all cognitions are [known] by a single cognition will not be established if everything is false, because there would be no object to be known at all. Only if a single cognition has the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) as its object, and everything else is included therein, can it be said that "all cognitions are known" by that knowledge. For the unreal silver resting upon it is certainly not known by the knowledge of the ultimate reality, which is the mother-of-pearl.

Now, if it should be argued that the meaning of the proposition "by the knowledge of one, all is known" is this: only the undifferentiated thing-in-itself is real, while everything else is unreal—then the scripture would not state, "By which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known. For the meaning of this sentence is indeed: "by which, when heard, even the unheard becomes heard."

If it is asserted that only an indeterminate reality, characterized merely as the cause, exists, then even the illustrative example—"Just as, my dear, by one clod of clay everything made of clay is known"—is not tenable. For by the knowledge of the clod of clay, the knowledge of its modification is shown; if you argue that even there the unreality of the modification is intended;

Since the unreality of a modification—such as a rope-snake and the like—is not established for the student, it would be inappropriate to introduce the example "Just so, my dear," as if it were a well-known fact, in order to demonstrate the possibility of the thesis being asserted. Furthermore, prior to the arising of the knowledge produced by sentences such as "That thou art," we do not perceive any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), whether assisted or unassisted by reasoning, that establishes the unreality of the entire class of modifications. This point will be explained under the sūtra: "The non-difference from That [Brahman] [is established] on account of the words concerning 'origin' and so forth."

Likewise, through such passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second"; "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and It created fire"; "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate names and forms"; and "All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, Being as their support; all this has that as its essence"—these [texts] establish that this world has Being as its nature, that prior to creation there was an absence of the distinction between name and form, and [the process] of the world's origination.

"Therefore, there is no fault in [the view that] it is the very nature [of things]. This is without substance; for in all sentences, what is to be conveyed is merely a specific relation between the meanings established through the linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) of the words. In that regard, even for words such as "blue" which function in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*), the meaning established by usage is precisely that which is qualified by blueness and so forth, and this is expressed as related to the meaning of other words.

Just as when it is said, "Bring a blue lotus," that which is qualified by blueness and so forth is indeed brought, and just as in the statement, "In the Vindhya forest there dwells a herd of elephants intoxicated with rut," the object is understood precisely as qualified by the qualifiers cognized from the two words; so too in the Vedāntic sentences involving co-referential designations (*samānādhikaraṇa-nirdeśa*), Brahman is to be realized as qualified by each of those respective qualifiers. Nor, when the qualifiers are intended to be significant, should an entity already qualified by one [attribute] be further qualified by another;
rather, the very essence (*svarūpa*) itself is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) by means of all the qualifiers.

For it is said: "Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the application of words with distinct grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) to a single object. Through either positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or exclusion (*nivṛtti*), the fact that the very same entity is presented by another word—endowed with a different aspect presented by that other word—is the function of co-referentiality. For example: "Devadatta is dark-complexioned, young, red-eyed, not timid, not mean, and blameless. However, where two qualifiers are incompatible with a single entity...

That which is indicated by two words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*)—even there, only one of the two words is taken in its primary sense (*amukhyavṛtta*), not both; as in the case of "The Vāhīka is an ox. However, in cases such as "blue lotus," because there is no contradiction in the connection with two qualifiers, a single entity qualified by both is conveyed.

Now, when a thing is being defined as being related to one particular qualifier, it is distinct from its state of being related to another qualifier; thus, just as in the case of a jar and a cloth, even though they are expressed with the same grammatical case-ending, it is impossible to establish their identity. Therefore, a word in apposition does not aim to express a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), but rather aims to establish the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) by presenting it through the medium of its qualifiers. This might be so; [but...]

If mere relatedness to two qualifiers were to negate oneness, that would not be the case; for it is precisely the state of being qualified by two properties that are incapable of being subsumed within a single substratum (*dharmin*) that negates unity. And this incapacity between the properties of "jar-ness" and "cloth-ness" is established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, in cases such as "the blue lotus," [the properties] are like "staff-bearing-ness" and "ring-wearing-ness," or like "possessing color" and "possessing taste" [which can coexist in one thing].

Furthermore, no contradiction is perceived, as in the case of [the terms] "possessing a bark" (*vattrka*) and "possessing fragrance" (*gandhavat*). Not only is there no contradiction, but through the distinction of their respective grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), they actually establish co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—consisting in their residing in the same object—in the form of being qualified by two distinct attributes. Otherwise, if there were identity merely in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), there would be no ground for the application of multiple words, and thus co-referentiality itself would not exist.

If qualifiers, disregarding their own specific relations, were intended merely as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the essential nature of a thing, then once the thing has been indicated by a single indicator, any further indicator would be entirely useless. If, however, one were to admit a difference in the form of the object indicated by each subsequent indicator, it would follow that the thing possesses distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*) by virtue of those forms. Even in the case of "This is that Devadatta," there is not even a trace of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because there is no contradiction [between the two cognitions]. [The former] relates to a different location...

Because that [past entity], by virtue of its connection with a proximate location, does not contradict its being present; for this very reason, those who maintain the stability of things establish the identity of an object related to two times through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the form "this is that. Otherwise, if there were a contradiction with experience, everything would necessarily be momentary. As for the contradiction regarding the connection with two locations, it is resolved by means of the difference in time.

Since words in grammatical apposition denote a single object qualified by multiple qualifiers, for this very reason, in the injunction "He purchases Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old, yellow-eyed [cow]," the purchase is enjoined as the goal to be accomplished by means of a one-year-old cow qualified by redness and the other attributes.
As it has been said: "When there is a single purpose, there should be a restriction [of the substance and quality] because they perform a single function.

Regarding this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) thinks as follows: although the word *aruṇayā* (with the red one) denotes the quality of redness as extending to the substance—since, like a generic class (*ākṛti*), a quality also possesses the singular nature of being a qualifier of a substance—nevertheless, a restriction of the redness to the *ekahāyanī* (the one-year-old cow) is not possible. This is because of the impossibility of enjoining two distinct meanings simultaneously: namely, that "one buys with the *ekahāyanī*" and "that [cow] is red."

Consequently, the sentence "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*), having set aside the syntactical connection [to the specific animal], expresses the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) without distinction, extending to all substances prescribed by the context. The feminine gender indication in "with the red one" is for the purpose of indicating all substances of every gender prescribed by the context. Therefore, there would be no restriction of the quality of redness to its connection with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*).

To this, it is replied: "When there is unity of purpose, there should be a restriction [of the relation] between a substance and a quality, because they perform a single function. Since the unity of meaning is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words—one denoting the substance qualified by redness (*aruṇā*) and the other denoting the substance *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow)—there is no contradiction in the substance *ekahāyanī* and the quality of redness being expressed as related to one another in the relation of qualifier and qualified by the word *aruṇayā* itself. Consequently, there must be a restriction of the redness to its connection with the *ekahāyanī* which serves as the instrument for the purchase (*kraya*).

If the connection between the redness (*āruṇya*) and the purchase were also to be understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*), as is the case with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), then there would be a prescription of two distinct meanings for a single sentence. But this is not the case; for by the word "red" (*aruṇayā*) alone, a substance qualified by redness is already denoted. Through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "one-year-old cow," only the fact that it is a one-year-old cow is understood, not the connection with the quality [of redness]. Indeed, the meaning of coreferentiality is simply the identity of the qualified substance.

"For words whose grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) are distinct, their occurrence with reference to a single object is co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is indeed the definition of co-referentiality. For this very reason, in expressions such as "the cloth becomes red," there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) due to their having a single referent. For the function of the sentence lies in the connection of the cloth with the action of becoming; however, the connection with the color is already expressed by the word "red" itself. Only this much—that the substance connected with the color is the cloth—is to be understood through co-referentiality.

In this way, having presented a single entity as qualified by one quality, by two, or by many—whether by those terms collectively or individually—and having made it known through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that this single object is characterized by all its qualifiers, there is no contradiction in expressing its connection with an action, as in: "Devadatta, who is dark-complexioned, young, red-eyed, staff-bearing, and wearing earrings, stands"; "one should prepare a curtain with white cloth"; "bring a blue lotus"; or "bring a blue-lotus."

"Bring the white, beautiful-eyed cow"; "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt"; likewise, "One purchases Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old, tawny-eyed [cow]. What is meant by this is as follows: just as in the statement, "One should cook rice in a pot with firewood," a single action qualified by multiple factors is perceived simultaneously; [so too is the case here].

Likewise, there is no contradiction in the fact that each individual *kāraka* (grammatical participant), expressed by a collection of words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), is understood simultaneously—qualified by its respective various qualifiers—at the very moment each specific *kāraka* is apprehended, and thus connects with the action; as in such examples as: "A capable cook should cook milk-rice and boiled rice in a vessel of equal capacity using dry khadira wood."

As for what was stated—that a word denoting a quality occurring in a sentence containing a substance that has already been acquired denotes the quality alone, and thus by the word *aruṇayā* (with the red one), there is the denotation of the quality alone—that is not tenable; for neither in common worldly usage nor in the Veda is a word denoting a quality ever found to denote the quality alone when it stands in grammatical apposition with a word denoting a substance.

Because no expression of a quality [as an independent entity] is observed. A word denoting a quality occurring in a sentence where a substance has already been mentioned is inconsistent even if it were to denote the quality alone; for in cases such as "the cloth is white," even though a substance is mentioned, what is expressed is the substance itself as qualified by the quality. In the case of "the white of the cloth," the failure to perceive the cloth as qualified by whiteness is caused by the use of different case endings, not by the fact that a substance has already been mentioned.
In that very same context, in instances such as "the white part of the cloth," when there is a mention with identical case endings, the substance qualified by whiteness is indeed perceived.
