Furthermore, the claim that the connection of *aruṇimā* (redness) with the purchase (*kraya*) is impossible because the purchase is already restricted by a single [item] is also inconsistent; for there is no contradiction in the connection of a word denoting a quality with a word denoting the substance—provided that substance lacks a conflicting quality—through the expression of the quality residing in that substance, thereby connecting it with the verb. Moreover, the argument that in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), once the verbal connection of *aruṇimā* with the substance is established by the aforementioned logic, their mutual connection follows as a matter of course because it is otherwise impossible for both the substance and the quality to be the means of accomplishing the purchase, is also inconsistent.
Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated.

Therefore, in the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the teaching of identity must be described as occurring precisely without abandoning the specific attributes denoted by the two words. However, this is not possible for one who does not accept a Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—who is distinct from the conscious being that exists in both pure and impure states and partakes in limitless suffering due to beginningless ignorance—and who is exclusively composed of infinite auspicious qualities that are the opposites of everything to be abandoned.

If it is argued that even for one who accepts [the identity], by resorting to the view that words in grammatical apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) are intended to establish the unity of a single entity qualified by its respective attributes as they exist, it would follow that the Supreme Being would incur all the defects perceived in the "thou" (tvam) term—this is not so; for even by the word "thou," it is the Supreme Being Himself who is denoted as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of the individual soul (jīva). This is what is meant:

The Supreme Brahman—denoted by the word *sat* (Being), free from even a trace of all defects, possessing a multitude of infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities combined with the power of true resolve, and being the cause of all—having willed, "May I become many," created the entire universe beginning with fire, water, and earth; and having entered that universe, which is established in various forms such as gods and others, as the conscious class of individual souls (*jīva*) within bodies corresponding to their own karma as their very self, He Himself, by His own will alone...

Having entered as the inner self of living beings, He manifested name and form within such aggregates—ranging from Himself down to the forms of gods and others. The meaning is that He established the reality and the denotability by words of these very aggregates whose nature is thus constituted. By the expression "by this living self" (*anena jīvenātmanā*), which is further specified as "by me" (*mayā*), the text demonstrates that the living being has Brahman as its self. And it is understood that the living being's identity with Brahman results from Brahman’s entry into it as its inner self.

"It created all this, whatever exists here. Having created it, It entered into that very thing. Having entered it, It became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat). Here, the two categories of entities—the conscious and the unconscious—indicated by the phrase "all this," are distinguished and designated by the terms *sat* and *tyat*, as well as by the terms *vijñāna* (consciousness) and *avijñāna* (non-consciousness). This is because the scripture declares the entry of Brahman even into the conscious entity. Therefore, from this differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*), it is understood that all words are denotative of the Supreme Self as qualified by the non-conscious and the individual soul.

Furthermore, having pointed out the entire phenomenal world—including the conscious—as "all this," by the statement "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyamidaṃ sarvam*), it is established that "this is its Self. Thus, since Brahman is the Self of everything—both conscious and unconscious—the entire world, together with the conscious, becomes His body. Accordingly, other scriptural passages state: "He who has entered within, the ruler of people, the Self of all," and "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know."

Beginning with, "He whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal," and continuing with, "He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal," and so forth, [it says]: "He who moves within the earth, whose body is the earth..."

Beginning with the passage, "He who moves within the waters, of whom the waters are the body," and continuing through, "He who moves within the imperishable (akṣara), of whom the imperishable is the body; he whom the imperishable does not know—this is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa," these texts teach the Supreme Self as the Self of that conscious universe by designating the world as His body.

Therefore, even words denoting sentient beings refer only to the Supreme Self, who is the sentient soul's very own self and whose body is that sentience; just as words denoting the insentient bodies of gods and others denote only the individual souls (jīvātman) who possess those respective bodies—as in the passage: "The four [priests] are fifteen... and so forth.

In passages such as "The nights... go to divinity," the meaning is that they become gods (*devā bhavanti*). Since a body is a mode (*prakāra*) with respect to the embodied being (*śarīrin*), and since words expressing a mode terminate in the possessor of the mode, it is logical that words denoting a body terminate in the embodied being. For a "mode" is indeed that aspect perceived as "thus" within an object perceived as "this is thus."

Since the cognition of that [object] depends upon that entity, and because it is dependent on it, its final resolution (paryavasāna) must logically be in that very [entity]; thus, the word that expresses it also finds its final resolution in that very [entity].

For this very reason, words denoting forms (*ākṛti*) such as "cow," "horse," or "human"—which do not terminate in the individual body (*piṇḍa*) that serves as their mode (*prakārin*)—do indeed terminate in the Supreme Self alone. This is because the body is a mode of the conscious being, and the conscious being, whose body is the individual form, is itself a mode of the Supreme Self. Thus, since the Supreme Self alone is the denoted object (*vācya*) of all words, their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting the Supreme Self is primary (*mukhya*).

Now, one might object: "It is observed that only words denoting universals (*jāti*) or qualities (*guṇa*), such as 'the spotted cow' or 'the white [cow],' exhibit grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting substances (*dravya*). However, when substances themselves function as qualifiers of another substance, a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*) is observed, as in 'one who has a staff' (*daṇḍin*) or 'one who has earrings' (*kuṇḍalin*). This is not so. Neither the universal, nor the quality, nor the substance is the sole cause for coreferentiality among these; for each is found to deviate from the others.

For any entity whose very existence consists solely in being a mode (*prakāra*) of something else, its inseparable establishment, subsistence, and cognition justify the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of words denoting it with a word denoting that [substratum] as qualified by its own denotation; for such words denote a substance qualified by their own referent.

However, where a substance established separately and existing in itself is at some time or place intended to be a mode of another substance, there the use of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*) is faultless.

Thus, because the individual soul (jīva), as qualified by the non-sentient (acid-viśiṣṭa), is a mode (prakāra) of the Supreme Self (paramātman) by virtue of being His body, words such as "I" and "you"—which are specific designations for the individual soul—denote the Supreme Self alone. This is concluded through the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the statement, "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).

This being the case, since the individual soul is related to the Supreme Self as His body, the attributes residing in the individual soul do not touch the Supreme Self; just as attributes such as childhood or youth residing in one's own body do not touch the soul itself.

Therefore, in the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the phrase "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the word "That" denotes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—the cause of the universe, whose will is true, the source of all auspicious qualities, and from whom every trace of the rejectable has been dispelled; and the word "thou" denotes that very same [Self] as having the embodied individual soul (*jīva*) as its body. Thus, this coreferentiality is primary in its sense, it is not in conflict with the context, it is not in conflict with any scripture, and there is an absence of even a scent of defects such as ignorance in the blameless Brahman, which consists solely of auspiciousness. Consequently, the coreferentiality with the individual soul is also [established].

Since it brings about the very state of being other than the individual soul (jīva) which serves as its qualifier, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is indeed distinct from the individual soul consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya); he is the Supreme Self (paramātman).

As for the argument that because the statement, "Of him, this very one is the embodied self," describes the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) as being embodied, it cannot be distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*); that is incorrect. For throughout this section, in every instance, the phrase "Of him, this very one is the embodied self, which belongs to the preceding one," designates the Supreme Self alone as the embodied self. How so?

Because of the designation of the Supreme Brahman—which is known to be distinct from the individual soul—as the Self of the entire range of created things beginning with ether, as stated in the passage, "From this very Self, indeed, ether was produced," it is understood that all things from ether down to the food-sheath (*annamaya*) constitute its body. This is shown by such texts as: "He whose body is the earth... he whose body is water... he whose body is fire... he whose body is air... etc.

The *Suvāla-śruti* clearly declares that all principles (tattvas) have the Supreme Self as their body: "He whose body is space... whose body is the Imperishable (akṣara)... whose body is death—this one, the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the sole God, is Nārāyaṇa. Therefore, in the passage "From this very Self," it is understood that the Supreme Self alone is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) of the one consisting of food (*annamaya*).

Having introduced the one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*), the text says: "Of that, this very one is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*), which is the self of the former. The meaning is this: that which is the embodied self of the former—the one consisting of food (*annamaya*)—which is established by another scriptural passage as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who is the ultimate cause, that very same one is the embodied self of this one consisting of breath as well. This should be understood in the same way for the ones consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). However, in the case of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), the specific designation "this very one" is used to show that he is not a different self [from the preceding]. How so?

By the principle already stated, it is understood that even for the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) is none other than the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This being so, when it is said that the embodied self of the one consisting of consciousness is the very same as the embodied self of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), it is understood that the Supreme Self—whose status as the Supreme Self is known through repetition—is itself the self of the one consisting of bliss. And thus, since the entire aggregate of conscious and unconscious entities distinct from himself constitutes his own body, he alone is the unconditioned embodied self.

For this very reason, the learned designate this scripture, which has proceeded with reference to this Supreme Brahman, as the *Śārīraka* (the "pertaining to the embodied one"). Therefore, the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) is indeed other than the individual self (*jīva*) consisting of cognition. || 13 ||

The one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is other than the individual soul (*jīva*), because we hear the suffix *mayat*, which denotes a modification. Regarding the rule "in the sense of both [modification and abundance]," it is recorded in the grammatical tradition that the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs in the sense of a modification after words that are "vṛddha" (containing a long vowel in the first syllable) or beginning with "śara" and so forth, as in the rule: "it is always [used] after vṛddha and śara etc. Now, this word "bliss" (*ānanda*) is indeed a vṛddha word. But is it not the case that *mayaṭ* also occurs in the sense of abundance, according to the traditional rule: "the suffix *mayaṭ* is used to express that which is made up of what is under discussion"? For example, "the sacrifice consists of food" (*annamayo yajñaḥ*). This very same suffix might be used here in that sense. It is not so.

In the phrase "consisting of food" (*annamaya*), the sense of a modification (*vikāra*) has been observed; therefore, by virtue of propriety, it is appropriate that this [term *vijñānamaya*] also signifies a modification. Furthermore, even if it were taken in the sense of "abundance," the distinctness of the Self from the individual soul (*jīva*) would not be established. For instance, when one says "abounding in bliss," the presence of suffering is unavoidable; indeed, the abundance of bliss implies the scarcity of suffering. And it is precisely this mixture with suffering that constitutes the nature of the individual soul. Therefore, it is more appropriate to accept the sense of a modification as established by the context.

In common usage, as in expressions such as "made of clay," "made of gold," or "made of wood," and in the Veda, as in "the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood," "the *sruc* spoons are made of *śamī* wood," and "the girdle is made of *darbha* grass"—because the suffix *mayaṭ* is frequently employed in the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*), that very meaning first presents itself to the mind. Furthermore, the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed a modification of bliss (*ānanda*); for while it is by nature of the form of bliss, its state as a transmigrating being (*saṃsāritva*) is precisely a modification thereof.
Therefore, since the suffix *mayaṭ*, which denotes a modification, is heard [in the text], the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not distinct from the individual soul.
Having restated this, he refutes it:
"If it be said that [the Self is not Brahman] because of the word 'modification,' no, because of abundance. (1.1.14)

This is not correct. Why? Because of abundance—due to the abundance of bliss in the supreme Brahman—and because the suffix *mayaṭ* can be used in the sense of abundance. This is what is meant: since it has been determined that this bliss, which is being repeated in a sequence of hundredfold increase, cannot have the individual soul (*jīva*) as its locus, it must have Brahman as its locus; and since no modification is possible in that Brahman, yet the suffix *mayaṭ* is applicable even in the sense of abundance, the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is the supreme Brahman.

Due to propriety (*aucitya*) and the established usage (*prayogaprauḍhi*), the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*) for the suffix *-maya* is not possible here because it would contradict the meaning. Furthermore, propriety has already been abandoned in the case of the "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*) itself, since the sense of modification is impossible there. Therefore, in that context, the state of "consisting of breath" belongs to the fivefold wind (*pañcavṛttir vāyuḥ*) merely by virtue of possessing the function of breath (*prāṇavṛtti*), or else because of the predominance (*prācurya*) of the breath-function among the five functions—prāṇa, apāna, and so forth. Nor is there a lack of established usage for the suffix *-maya* in the sense of predominance, as seen in such expressions as "a sacrifice consisting mostly of food" (*annamayo yajñaḥ*) and "a journey consisting mostly of carts" (*śakaṭamayī yātrā*).

As for the claim that the abundance of bliss implies the existence of some slight suffering, that is incorrect. For that "abundance" means its preponderance; this does not imply the existence of its opposite, but rather excludes its smallness. The presence or absence of that other element, however, must be determined by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And in this case, its absence is understood through another means of knowledge, such as the passage beginning with "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*).

In this regard, only this much needs to be said: that the abundance of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) is relative to the meagerness of other forms of bliss. And this is indeed stated [in scripture] through such passages as, "That is one human bliss," by which it is shown that, in comparison with the bliss of the individual soul (*jīvānanda*), the bliss of Brahman has attained a state of unsurpassed excellence and is therefore abundant. Furthermore, what was asserted—that the bliss of the individual soul can be a modification (*vikāra*) [of Brahman's bliss]—is also untenable.

The transformation of the individual soul (jīva), whose essential nature is knowledge and bliss, into some form—like that of a jar from clay—is contrary to all Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning. However, it will be demonstrated later that during the state of transmigratory existence, knowledge and bliss are merely contracted by the influence of karma.
Therefore, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is other than the individual soul; it is the Supreme Brahman. 14.
For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is other than the individual soul (jīva), because of the designation of that [soul] as its cause. 1115.

"For who indeed could breathe, who could live, if this bliss were not in the ether? For he alone causes bliss. Thus, because he causes living beings (*jīva*) to experience bliss, he is designated as the cause of the bliss of living beings. Therefore, it is understood that this *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss), who is the causer of bliss, is distinct from the living being who is to be caused to experience bliss; he is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Furthermore, it will be stated immediately hereafter that it is the *ānandamaya* itself that is expressed by the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) in this context. || 15 ||
For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is different from the individual soul (jīva); moreover, he is celebrated exactly as described in the words of the mantra.

The Brahman described in the Vedic mantra, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," is proclaimed as the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). That, however, is the Supreme Brahman, distinct from the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). For instance, in the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," Brahman is indicated as the goal to be attained by the individual soul. Furthermore, regarding the statement, "Concerning that, this verse was spoken": "that" refers to Brahman; having brought it to mind and taken it as the subject to be explained, this *ṛc* was recited by the students.

The meaning is that the clarity of the matter stated by the Brāhmaṇa is established by this mantra. The Brahman to be attained by the living soul (jīva), who is the worshipper, is indeed distinct from it. Furthermore, beginning with "From this very Self, space was produced," and so forth, that same point is elucidated by subsequent Brāhmaṇas and mantras. Therefore, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is other than the living soul. || 16 ||

To this, he replies: Although there must indeed be a distinction between the worshiper and that which is to be attained, nevertheless, the Brahman described in the mantra-text is not a separate entity from the individual soul (*jīva*); rather, it is the very nature of that same worshiper—pure, consisting of the single essence of non-dual consciousness, and free from even a trace of ignorance. That very nature is clarified by the mantra: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite. And that same nature is [described by]: "From whence words turn back..."

By the phrase "not reached by the mind," it is understood that [Brahman] is without distinction because it is beyond the range of speech and mind; therefore, that very [Brahman] is the one described in the mantra-text, and thus the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is not different from it. To this, the author reads the following reply:
"Not the other, because of impossibility" (1.1.17).

The Supreme Self, who is denoted by the term "jīva" even in its state of liberation, is not the one described in the mantra-text. Why? Because it is untenable. For such a self, the quality of being "all-knowing" (*vipaścit*) in an unconditioned sense is not possible. Indeed, this very unconditioned all-knowingness will be explained through the demonstration of His power of true resolve in the passage, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" for all-knowingness (*vipaścit-tvam*) consists in seeing variously.

The word *vipaścit* is derived by eliding the syllable *ya* within the word *paśyat*, according to the rule governing words such as *pṛṣodara*. Although the state of being *vipaścit* (all-seeing) is possible for one who is liberated, nevertheless, that very self was previously not all-seeing during the state of transmigratory existence; thus, an unconditioned state of being *vipaścit* is not tenable. Furthermore, since the liberated one has attained the state of pure consciousness devoid of distinctions, there is an absence of manifold perception, and therefore the state of being *vipaścit* is even more impossible.

Furthermore, it has already been stated that no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can establish a reality devoid of distinctions. Moreover, if the scriptural passage, "from which words turn back," were to express the cessation of speech and mind with respect to Brahman, it would not be able to convey the featureless nature of the reality; rather, it would merely state that speech and mind are not authoritative regarding it. And if that were the case, it would follow that the reality is simply non-existent (*tucchatva*).

Beginning with the words "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]," the text establishes the omniscience (*vipaścittva*) of Brahman, its status as the cause of the universe, its single-minded devotion to knowledge and bliss, its quality of bestowing bliss upon others, its sovereignty over the creation of the entire aggregate of sentient and insentient beings through desire alone, its identity with the created order by entering into it, its being the cause of both fear and fearlessness, its presiding over the wind, the sun, and other elements, its state of unsurpassed bliss increasing in a hundredfold progression, and many other attributes; finally, regarding speech and mind in relation to Brahman—

To claim that Brahman is said to be devoid of any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*) because of the absence of phenomenal activity (*pravṛtti*) is the prattle of a deluded person. For the sentence—"The knower of the bliss of Brahman [does not fear]"—first refers by the word "that" (*yat*) to the object indicated in "from which words turn back," and then, by using the word "bliss" (*ānanda*), refers back to that same object; having established its relation to Brahman through the distinct designation "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*), the sentence then declares the knowledge of that very thing which is beyond the reach of speech and mind by saying "the knower. Thus, this sentence is neither useless like the "old ox" (*jaradgava*) type of utterance, nor is its meaning excluded from the scope of what is expressed.

It may be so. Therefore, having attempted to express the limit of the excellence of the bliss of Brahman by increasing it in a sequence of hundredfold increments, speech and mind turn back from it precisely because that limit does not exist.

It is said, "from which words turn back. Thus, it is stated that one who knows the bliss of Brahman, which is devoid of such limitations, does not fear anything whatsoever. Furthermore, it is perfectly clear that this wise one described in the mantra-text is distinct from the nature of the liberated self—the very nature of whose own volition will be described starting with the words "He desired," and which brings about the creation, sustenance, and the state of being the inner self of the world. || 17 ||
For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is other than the inner self (pratyagātman) in both states, because of the designation of difference. || 1118 ||

Beginning with the words, "From this very Self, indeed, ether [arose]," the passage that reveals the Brahman described in the mantra-text designates its distinction even from the individual soul (jīva), just as it does from food, vital breath, and mind, stating: "Different from this one consisting of consciousness, there is another inner Self consisting of bliss. Therefore, because of the designation of its difference from the individual soul, it is understood that this "consisting of bliss," which is described in the mantra-text, is indeed distinct [from the jīva]. || 18 ||
For this reason as well, [the Self] is other than the living being (jīva) and other than desire; there is no dependence on non-inference. || 1119 ||

For one who is subject to ignorance (*avidyā*), there would necessarily be a dependence on a connection with non-intelligent entities (*acid-vastu*) denoted by terms such as the "Pradhāna" inferred through logic; such indeed is the causality of [beings] like the four-faced Brahmā. However, in this context, the text—"He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—declares that the creation of the diverse intelligent and non-intelligent entities proceeds from His own will alone, without any connection to non-intelligence. Furthermore, it is recited in scripture: "He created all this, whatever exists here.
Therefore, for this Being consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) while creating the world, no dependence on the creation of an inferred non-intelligent entity is perceived. (19)
For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is different from the individual soul (jīva);
for the scripture teaches its connection with that [bliss] in this context.

In this [context], the scripture teaches the connection of this individual soul (*jīva*) with that which consists of bliss—the connection with bliss—stating: "He is indeed essence (*rasa*); for by obtaining essence alone, this one becomes blissful. The meaning is: when it is said that this one, who is designated by the term *jīva*, becomes blissful upon obtaining that which is denoted by the word "essence," what person who is not insane would say that he who becomes blissful by obtaining something is that very thing itself?

Thus, when it is determined that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the supreme Brahman, then in such passages as "That which is this bliss in the ether" and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," it is the one consisting of bliss itself that is referred to by the word "bliss," just as the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is referred to by the word "consciousness. For this very reason, there is the distinct designation in the passage, "Knowing the bliss of Brahman"; and for this same reason, there is the mention of the fruit in the passage, "He approaches the Self consisting of bliss."

Furthermore, since the subsequent section (anuvāka) establishes that those [entities] mentioned in the preceding section—beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*)—are indeed Brahman, through the statements: "He understood: 'Food is Brahman,'" "He understood: 'Breath is Brahman,'" "He understood: 'Mind is Brahman,'" and "He understood: 'Consciousness is Brahman,'" it is recognized that the statement "Bliss is Brahman" likewise establishes the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). For this very reason, the conclusion there also states: "Having reached the Self consisting of bliss."

Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Brahman, which is denoted by the term "Pradhāna," is a distinct entity from the reality denoted by the term "jīva. || 20 || Thus ends the section concerning the "Consisting of Bliss" (Ānandamaya).

Although for beings of meager merit, it is impossible for the creation of the world through desire, the possession of extraordinary bliss, or being the cause of fear and fearlessness to occur, nevertheless, these are indeed possible for those of distinguished merit, such as Āditya, Indra, Prajāpati, and others. To dispel this doubt, [the Sūtra] states:
"On account of the teaching of those attributes within [him]. (1.1.21)

This is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "That golden person who is seen within the sun, with golden beard and golden hair, golden even to his fingernails, entirely of gold; whose eyes are like a lotus blooming on a monkey's haunch; whose name is 'Ut' (the Arising); he is indeed free from all evils."

"He has risen. Indeed, he who knows this rises above all evils. Both the *Ṛg* and the *Sāman* are his two singers"—thus with reference to the deities. "Now with reference to the self (*adhyātma*). Now, that person who is seen within the eye—he is the *Ṛg*, he is the *Sāman*, he is the *Uktha*, he is the *Yajus*, he is the *Brahman*. His form is the same as the form of yonder [sun]. Whatever the singers of yonder are, they are his singers. Whatever the name of yonder is, that is his name."

In this regard, a doubt arises: Is this person situated between the eye and the solar orb—the one denoted by terms such as "Āditya" and possessing sovereignty resulting from the accumulation of merit—the *jīva* itself; or rather, is it the *paramātman* distinct from that? What is the reasonable conclusion? That it is the *jīva* alone who has accumulated merit. Why? Because of the scriptural mention of its having a body. For the connection with a body is possible only for *jīvas*; indeed, the connection with a body is for the sake of experiencing pleasure and pain in accordance with one's karma.

For this very reason, it is stated that liberation—which is devoid of connection with karma—is to be attained through the state of being bodiless: "Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant; but for one who is indeed bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch. Furthermore, an excellence of knowledge and an excellence of power are possible through the preeminence of merit. For this same reason, his lordship over the worlds and desires, and so forth, is logically established. Consequently, he alone is the object of worship and the bestower of fruits.

Furthermore, it serves as a means to liberation by virtue of its power to destroy evil. Even among humans, some who have accumulated merit are seen to be superior through their possession of knowledge, mantras, and so forth; beyond them are the Siddhas and Gandharvas; beyond them the gods; and beyond them Indra and the rest. Therefore, one or another among those beginning with Brahmā, having attained such sovereignty in each respective Kalpa solely through specific merit, performs even the creation of the world and other such acts.

Statements concerning [the Lord's] being the cause of the world, His being the inner self of the world, and so forth, apply only to this very [individual soul] when its specific merits have been fully accumulated, and when it is omniscient and omnipotent. Therefore, there exists no such thing as a Supreme Self distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*). This being the case, scriptural passages such as "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long," which describe "neither coarse nor fine," refer to the essential nature of the individual soul itself. Likewise, the treatises on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) are likewise intent upon teaching that essential nature and the means for attaining it.

This being the case, it is replied: "The one within [is Brahman], because of the teaching of its attributes. The Person who is perceived within the sun and within the eye is none other than the Jīva, but is indeed the Supreme Self (Paramātman). Why? Because of the teaching of His attributes. These attributes—such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth—which are impossible in the case of the individual souls (Jīvas), are taught as belonging exclusively to the Supreme Self who is distinct from them, in such passages as: "He has risen above all evils" (*sa eṣa sarvebhyaḥ pāpmabhya uditaḥ*). For freedom from evil means freedom from karma.

The meaning is that it is the state of being devoid of even the scent of subjection to karma. Indeed, individual souls (*jīvas*) are subject to karma by virtue of their participation in pleasure and pain dependent upon karma; therefore, freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) is an attribute belonging only to the Supreme Self, who is distinct from the individual soul. Preceded by that [freedom from sin], His attributes—such as being the Lord of the worlds and desires, possessing true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), and so forth, as well as being the inner self (*antarātman*) of all beings—belong to Him alone.

As it is said: "This Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true, and whose resolves are true. Likewise: "This is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa."

Such natural attributes as the capacity for the creation of all conscious and unconscious entities preceded by the power of true resolve—as expressed in the passage, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—the state of being the causeless cause of fear and fearlessness, and the possession of infinite, unsurpassed bliss beyond the limitations imposed by speech and mind, are not possible for the individual soul (*jīva*), as they cannot be accomplished through ritual action (*karman*).

As for the claim that [the Self] is not distinct from the individual soul (jīva) because of its connection with a body—that is incorrect. For being embodied does not necessarily prove subjection to karma; for even one whose will is true (satyasaṅkalpa) may have a connection with a body by his own desire. Now, if it be argued that what is called a "body" is an aggregate of elements consisting of transformations of primordial matter (prakṛti) composed of the three guṇas, and that such a connection with it cannot occur through the will of a person who is free from sin and possesses a true will, because it would not be a human goal (apuruṣārtha)—[we reply:]...

However, for one who is subject to karma and ignorant of his true nature, his connection with that [body] is unavoidable—even against his will—for the sake of experiencing fruits corresponding to his karma. This might be so, provided his body were material (*prākṛta*) and composed of the three *guṇas*; but since it is his own desired, self-conforming, and indeed non-material (*aprākṛta*) body, everything is logically consistent.

This is what is meant: the Supreme Brahman alone, who is distinct from everything else by virtue of being the singular essence of infinite knowledge and bliss that is diametrically opposed to all that is to be rejected, possesses a multitude of natural, limitless, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇaguṇa*). Likewise, he possesses a divine form (*divyarūpa*) which is his own natural state—a treasure-house of an infinite multitude of qualities such as uniformity, inconceivability, divinity, wonder, eternity, faultlessness, incomparable brilliance, beauty, fragrance, delicacy, charm, and youth, all of which correspond to his own will.

He alone, by favoring his devotees, assumes various forms according to their respective modes of realization—He who is an ocean of boundless compassion, virtuous conduct, affection, magnanimity, and sovereignty; who is free from even the scent of all that is to be abandoned; who is devoid of sin; the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣottama, Nārāyaṇa.

From such passages as, "That from which these beings are born," "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," and "In the beginning, there was indeed only Nārāyaṇa—neither Brahmā nor Īśāna"—the Supreme Brahman is understood to be the sole cause of the entire universe; and from such passages as, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite," and "Brahman is Consciousness and Bliss," its essential nature is likewise understood.

"Devoid of qualities," "untainted," "free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true"; "of Him there exists neither effect nor instrument; neither his equal nor his superior is seen."

"In Him, His supreme power is heard to be manifold indeed; it is innate, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action"; "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords, Him, the supreme deity among deities"; "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses, and there is neither his progenitor nor is there any lord over him"; "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and created names, abides calling them out"; "I know this Great Person, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness"; "All moments of time were born from the luminous Person"—in such passages, [the attributes] of the Supreme [are described].

Having negated in Brahman the ordinary, rejectable qualities, the connection with an ordinary, rejectable body, and the connection with subjection to karma rooted therein, the scriptures describe His auspicious qualities and auspicious form. This very nature of His, the Supreme Lord who is supremely compassionate, assumes by His own will forms such as those of gods and humans—forms that conform to the perception of His devotees for the sake of favoring them. Regarding this, the Śruti says: "Though unborn, He is born in many ways."

And the *Smṛti* says: "Though I am unborn and my nature is imperishable, though I am the Lord of all beings, yet by presiding over my own *prakṛti*, I manifest myself through my own nature for the protection of the virtuous and for the destruction of the wicked. For the "virtuous" are indeed the worshippers (*upāsakas*). Their protection is the primary purpose; the destruction of the wicked is merely incidental, as that is accomplished even by mere resolve. In the phrase "my own *prakṛti*," *prakṛti* means one's own nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, it means "having resorted to my very own nature."

The meaning is that it is not the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of those subject to *saṃsāra*. Regarding the phrase "by his own *māyā*," the meaning is "by means of knowledge (*jñāna*) in the form of his own volition (*saṅkalpa*). Lexicographers record that the word *māyā* is a synonym for knowledge, as in the statement: "*māyā*, *vayuna*, and *jñāna*. And the venerable Parāśara says: "O King, that other great form of Hari, which is both multiform and yet devoid of form, is that in which all these powers are established. O Lord of Men, he creates forms consisting of all powers."

"The activities designated as those of gods, animals, and humans, which exist through His own sport for the benefit of the worlds, do not arise from the cause of karma. And in the *Mahābhārata*, even the form of the incarnations is said to be non-material: "The body of this Supreme Self is not composed of an aggregate of elements. Therefore, since the Supreme Brahman alone possesses such forms, this [form] is also His very attribute. Consequently, the one who has the solar orb as His locus and is distinct from the individual souls such as Āditya, is indeed the Supreme Self. || 21 ||
And because there is a designation of difference, [the Self] is other [than the body]. || 1122 ||

The distinction of this Supreme Self from the individual souls (jīvas), such as those in the sun and others, is declared [in the scripture]: "He who dwells in the sun, yet is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body the sun is, and who controls the sun from within"; and "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body the self is, and who controls the self from within"; and "He who moves within the imperishable (akṣara), whose body the imperishable is, whom the imperishable does not know."

"He who moves within death, whose body is death, whom death does not know—he is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa. Thus, having designated all individual souls (jīvas) as the body of this supreme Self which is free from evil, the text designates Him as their inner Self. Therefore, it is established that the supreme Self is indeed other than all individual souls, such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others. || 22 ||
Thus concludes the section on the intermediate state.
The Section on Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇa) || 118 ||

From the statement, "That from which these beings are born," it is understood that Brahman is the cause of the world. When there arises the inquiry as to what that cause of the world is, [the answer is given] by means of common terms such as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," "It created fire," "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," "He created these worlds," and "From this very Self, space was produced. This is because [Brahman] possesses the essential nature of specific objects characterized by the specific qualities of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*) and bliss (*ānanda*).

It has been stated that Brahman is distinct from Pradhāna, the Kṣetrajña, and so forth. Now, in the remainder of this chapter, beginning with the sūtra "Ākāśas-talliṅgāt" (1.3.41), it is established that even when the cause of the world and the sovereignty over the world are indicated by specific terms such as "ether" (ākāśa) and others, the Brahman characterized as previously described is indeed something other than the sentient and insentient entities well-known as denoted by those terms like "ether. **Sūtra 1.3.41:** *Ākāśas-talliṅgāt* (Ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark).

This is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "What is the goal of this world? "Space," he replied, "for indeed all these beings arise from space alone; they dissolve back into space. Space is indeed greater than these; space is the ultimate resort. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the word "space" (ākāśa) here denote the well-known physical space, or does it denote Brahman, which possesses the characteristics previously described?

What is established? That it is the well-known ether (*ākāśa*). Why? Because regarding an entity that is accessible through the word alone, whatever meaning is established by convention and understood from the word, that very meaning must be accepted. Therefore, the well-known ether itself is the cause of the entire collection of moving and non-moving beings. Consequently, Brahman is not distinct from that [ether]. But has it not been stated that Brahman is distinct from both the insentient and the individual soul (*jīva*) on account of its prior reflection (*īkṣā*) before creation and other such attributes? True, it was so stated; however, that is untenable.

For instance, when it is stated, "That from which these beings are born... that is Brahman," and there arises an expectation for a specific detail such as "from what are these beings born?", the specific understanding derived from passages like, "All these beings indeed arise from space alone," leads to the certain conclusion that space itself is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world. Consequently, even in passages such as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," the words "Being" and the like—which possess a common form—denote that very same specific entity, namely space. Likewise, [it is said]: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone."

The word *ātman* also occurs in such passages as these, referring to that very same thing [space]. For even in its case, an absolute association with consciousness is not possible, just as in the expression "a jar is made of clay. Furthermore, by the etymological derivation "that which pervades (*āpnoti*) is the self (*ātman*)," the word *ātman* applies to space all the more so. Therefore, when it is thus determined that space alone is the causal Brahman, qualities such as "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) and the like must be described as figurative (*gauṇa*) and consistent with that [nature of space].

For if the cause had been designated by general terms such as "Being" (sat) and so forth, then—by virtue of the requirement of meanings such as "seeing" (īkṣaṇa)—it would have been determined that the cause is specifically a conscious entity. However, since the specific [conscious] entity itself was determined by the word "ether" (ākāśa), there is no need for a determination based on the inherent nature of the meaning.

But is it not the case that the status of space as an effect is also understood from the statement, "From the Self, space was produced"? True. All things, including space, air, and so forth, possess two states: a subtle state and a gross state. Among these, the subtle state of space is the cause, while its gross state is the effect. The statement, "From the Self, space was produced," means that from its own subtle form, it itself emerged in a gross form.

Since it is heard that "all these beings indeed arise from space alone," and because the origin and dissolution of the entire world are stated to proceed from space alone, it is certain that Brahman is that very cause. Precisely because Brahman is not distinct from the well-known space, such scriptural indications as "If this space were not bliss" and "Space, indeed, is the bearer of name and form" are all the more appropriate.
Therefore, Brahman is not distinct from the well-known space.

This being the case, we reply: "The ether (ākāśa), because of its characteristic marks. That which is denoted by the word *ākāśa* is the Supreme Self alone, characterized as previously described, and is an entity distinct from the well-known, insentient ether. Why? Because of its characteristic marks (*talliṅgāt*). Marks of the Supreme Self are observed here, such as being the sole cause of the entire universe, being greater than all, and being the ultimate refuge. For the status of being the cause of the entire universe is not possible for the insentient thing denoted by the term "well-known ether."

Because it is impossible for that which is insentient to be the effect of volition; and because being the "supreme resort" (parāyaṇatva) means being the ultimate goal to be attained by sentient beings, which cannot belong to something insentient, which is to be abandoned, and which is opposed to all human aims. Furthermore, being "superior to all" means possessing an unsurpassed excellence over all things through all auspicious qualities in an absolute sense; this also is not possible for the insentient.

As for the claim that, when there is a desire for a specific cause of the world, the word *ākāśa* provides that specific [cause], and therefore everything else must be described as having the same nature—that is incorrect. For the statement, "All these beings indeed arise from *ākāśa* alone," is an indication made as if it were already well-known, which thus depends on the attainment [of that fact] through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And those other means of knowledge are precisely such passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."

And since those [passages] establish Brahman precisely in the manner already described, the Brahman thus established is indicated by the word "ether" (ākāśa) as if it were something well-known. Furthermore, the Supreme Brahman can appropriately be designated by the word "ether" because it is luminous, in the sense that it "shines forth" (ākāśate) and "causes to shine forth" (ākāśayati).

Furthermore, by using this term "ether" (*ākāśa*), which—though capable of conveying a specific distinction—denotes a particular insentient entity that cannot possibly possess the nature of being a cause with respect to consciousness, you subvert the meaning of the entire sentence; such a subversion of the sentence-meaning—which is capable of establishing a novel object qualified by omniscience, true resolve, and so forth, as determined by specific passages such as "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—does not ascend to the status of valid proof.

Thus, it is not possible for a single statement in the form of a restatement (anuvāda) to otherwise alter the commonality of the progression of multiple sentences, which are capable of conveying a novel meaning distinguished by infinite unprecedented qualifications.

As for the objection that the word *ātman* is not exclusively restricted to the conscious being, because we see such usage as "the jar has clay as its essence" (*mṛdātmako ghaṭaḥ*), to that it is replied: although the word *ātman* is occasionally employed elsewhere than for the conscious being, nevertheless, because of the frequency with which the word *ātman* is used in reference to that which is related to the body, in passages such as "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" (*ātmā vā idameka evāgre āsīt*) and "From the Self, space was produced" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*), it is understood to be precisely the conscious being related to the body.

Just as, although the word "cow" (go) denotes many things, by virtue of its predominant usage, only that which possesses a dewlap and so forth is understood by itself; whereas the cognition of other meanings depends upon specific, unique designations for those respective objects—likewise, the denotation of the conscious being related to the body is obtained by itself, and it is precisely such specific passages as "He thought: 'Shall I create the worlds? and "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" that establish this very point.

Thus, it is established that Brahman alone—the sole cause of the entire universe, characterized by many unprecedented attributes ascertained through specific statements and not shared by anything else, and established by such passages as "Being alone, my dear, was this in the beginning"—is indicated by the word *ākāśa* as if it were well-known, by means of the passage beginning with "All these beings, indeed. || 23 ||
Thus concludes the section on Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇa).
The section concerning Prāṇa:
"For this very reason, [the word 'breath'] refers to Prāṇa. (Sūtra 1.1.24)

This is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: having introduced the topic with, "O Prastotṛ, the deity that is associated with the Prastāva," it continues, "Which is that deity? 'Prāṇa,' he said, 'for indeed all these beings merge into Prāṇa alone, and from Prāṇa they emerge. This is the deity associated with the Prastāva. If you were to chant the Prastāva without knowing this, your head would have fallen off.'"

Here, the word *prāṇa*—like the word *ākāśa*—refers to the Supreme Brahman alone, distinct from the well-known vital breath, because of the characteristic marks such as the entering and exiting of the entire universe, which are unique to that [Brahman] and are indicated as if they were well-known.

A further doubt arises: since it is observed that the maintenance and activity of the entire collection of beings depend upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is well known that *prāṇa* alone deserves to be designated as the cause of the world. The refutation, however, is as follows: because [the functions of] stone, wood, and so forth, as well as those of the conscious self (*cetana*), lack such [dependence], the statement, "All these beings indeed enter into *prāṇa* alone and emerge from *prāṇa*," would not be tenable.

Therefore, because it gives life to all beings, the Supreme Brahman alone is denoted by the word *prāṇa*. Consequently, it is established that the Supreme Brahman alone—which is distinct from the well-known ether, vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth; which is the sole cause of the entire universe; and which possesses an infinite multitude of auspicious qualities such as freedom from sin, omnipresence, and the power of true resolve—is what is designated by the words "ether," "vital breath," and the like. Thus ends the section on the Vital Breath (*Prāṇādhikaraṇa*).
The Section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa):

Hereafter, it is stated that the Supreme Brahman alone is denoted by terms such as "Light" and "Indra," even though these are well-known to have other referents, because it is endowed with some unsurpassed, preeminent quality that pervades the state of being the cause of the world—by means of the sūtra beginning with "Because of the mention of the feet" (jyotiś-caraṇābhidhānāt). 1125.

This is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the highest worlds—this indeed is that light which is within a person here."

In this regard, there arises a doubt: Is the object indicated by the word "light" (jyotis)—which possesses unsurpassed radiance—the well-known light such as the sun and so forth, which serves as the causal Brahman; or is it the Supreme Person (puruṣottama), who is of a different nature from the entire aggregate of sentient and insentient beings, the supreme cause, whose luster is self-effulgent, who is omniscient, and whose will is infallible? What is the reasonable conclusion? That it is the well-known light itself. Why?

Even though the word "light" (jyotis) is well-known [in its ordinary sense], because no specific mark pervaded by the Supreme Self—which is mentioned in its own scriptural context—is observed, as is the case with "ether" (ākāśa), "breath" (prāṇa), and so forth, it is impossible to recognize the Supreme Person [therein]. Furthermore, because of the instruction regarding the identity with the light within the body (kaukṣeyajyotis), the well-known light itself—pervaded by causality and endowed with unsurpassed radiance—is Brahman, the cause of the world.

This being the position reached, we reply: [It is] light, because of the mention of feet. The light designated as connected with heaven, which possesses unsurpassed radiance, is indeed the Supreme Person. Why? Because, in the passage, "All beings are one foot of His; His three feet are the immortal in heaven," all beings are mentioned as the feet of that very [light] which is connected with heaven.

The following is what is meant: although in this sentence, "Now, that light which is beyond heaven," no characteristic mark (liṅga) exclusive to the Supreme Person is perceived, nevertheless, because the Supreme Person was designated in the preceding sentence as being connected with heaven, this light also—which is connected with heaven—is recognized as being that very same one. Furthermore, the instruction on the identity of the gastric light [with the Supreme] is an injunction for the contemplation of its being of that nature for the sake of a specific result; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

Furthermore, that the gastric fire has that very nature was stated by the Blessed One himself: "I, as Vaiśvānara, having become [the digestive fire], have taken refuge in the bodies of living beings."

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [meant here] because of the mention of the Chāndogya [text], we say no; for there is a scriptural teaching regarding the fixing of the mind in that manner, and such is indeed seen [in other passages]. || 1126 ||

If it be argued that in the preceding passage, after designating the metre named Gāyatrī with the words, "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this," and then citing the verse "Such is its greatness" (Tāvān asya mahimā) as something introduced by the phrase "This very thing has been declared by a Ṛk-verse"—since this cited Ṛk also concerns the metre, there is no designation of the Supreme Person here—the answer is: No, because of the scriptural teaching regarding the fixing of the mind [upon Him]. By the word "Gāyatrī," mere metre is not what is denoted here, because it is impossible for mere metre to be the Self of all.

Rather, here the fixing of the mind upon Brahman itself as Gāyatrī is concluded. The meaning is that the contemplation of the similarity between Brahman and Gāyatrī is taught for the sake of a specific result. And such a correspondence is possible, for there is a similarity between the four-footed Brahman—as in the text, "One foot of His is all beings; His three feet are the immortal in heaven"—and the four-footed Gāyatrī. Furthermore, a four-footed Gāyatrī is seen in certain instances, such as: "Indra, the lord of Śacī, oppressed by strength, the unshakable bull."

"Samits are the Sāhas. For likewise, elsewhere as well, a word denoting a meter is seen to be employed in reference to another object because of similarity. As in the Saṃvarga-vidyā, beginning with "These five and those other five become ten," it is said, "This is Virāj, consisting of food. || 26 ||
For this reason as well, Brahman alone is denoted by the word *gāyatrī*, because the designation of the "feet" beginning with "beings" (*bhūta*) is thus appropriate. (Sūtra 1.1.26)
Having pointed out the elements, the earth, the body, and the heart, this designation is appropriate only for Brahman, which is denoted by the word "Gāyatrī. || 27 ||
If it is argued that this is not so because of the difference in instruction, we say no, because there is no contradiction in either case. || 1128 ||

If it be argued that because in the preceding passage Brahman is indicated as the locus by the statement, "Three-quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven," whereas here it is indicated as the limit by the phrase, "beyond heaven," the two teachings differ in form and thus the Brahman mentioned in the former passage is not recognized in the latter—this is not so; for in both teachings, there is no contradiction in recognition due to the identity of the essential nature of the object, just as in the cases: "The hawk is at the top of the tree" and "The hawk is beyond the top of the tree."

Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Person alone possesses unsurpassed splendor, as it is said: "Beyond the heaven shines the light. "Such is His greatness; yet the Person is even greater than this."

It is faultless that the very same Supreme Person—who is described as having four quarters in the passage, "One quarter of Him is all beings; three quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven"—and who is said to possess a non-material form in the verse, "I know this great Puruṣa, refulgent like the sun, beyond darkness," must be the one denoted by the word *jyotis* (light), because His light too is non-material. Thus ends the section on Light (*jyotir-adhikaraṇa*).
The section concerning Indra and Prāṇa (1.1.11–30):

It has been stated that the light denoted by the word "light" (*jyotis*), which is endowed with unsurpassed brilliance and mentioned as being present everywhere, is indeed the Supreme Person. Now, [the Sūtrakāra] declares that even that which is denoted by the words "Indra," "Prāṇa," and so forth—being heard of as the object of meditation because it is the means for attaining immortality and is pervaded by causality—is likewise the Supreme Person alone:
"Prāṇa, because of the concordance [of attributes]. (1.1.29)

In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, within the Pratardana-vidyā, it is heard starting from: "Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra through battle and manliness," and continuing until Indra, who had said, "Choose a boon," was addressed by Pratardana: "You yourself choose for me that boon which you consider most beneficial for a human being. To this, he [Indra] replied: "I am Prāṇa, the conscious self (prajñātman); worship me as life (āyuḥ) and immortality (amṛta)."

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is he who is designated by the words "Indra" and "Prāṇa" as the object of the most beneficial meditation merely the individual soul (jīva), or is he the Supreme Self (paramātman) distinct from that? What is the reasonable position? That it is the individual soul alone. Why? Because the word "Indra" is well-known to refer specifically to a particular individual soul, and the word "Prāṇa," being in grammatical apposition with it, must likewise apply to that same entity.

This very soul (jīva) named Indra, having been addressed by Pratardana with the words, "Choose for me yourself that boon which you consider most beneficial for a human being," instructed him to worship himself, saying, "Worship Me. And the most beneficial thing is precisely the means for attaining immortality. That the meditation upon the cause of the world alone is the cause for attaining immortality is understood from the passage: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [into the Absolute]. Therefore, Indra, who is well-known in his state as a living soul (jīva), is indeed the causal Brahman.

To this objection, it is replied: "The vital breath (prāṇa) [is Brahman], because of the subsequent connection. This being designated by the words Indra and prāṇa is not merely the individual soul (jīva), but rather the Supreme Brahman, which is a distinct entity from the soul. For the subsequent connection—namely, that what was introduced by the words Indra and prāṇa is subsequently associated with the terms "bliss," "undecaying," and "immortal" in grammatical coordination—is only possible if this is so. (Sūtra 29)

"If it be argued that [the Self taught here] is not the Supreme Self because the speaker instructs himself, we say no; for in this [section], there is an abundance of references to the connection with the inner self."

As for the argument that what is designated by the words "Indra" and "Prāṇa" must be the supreme Brahman because of its identity with [the description] "blissful, undecaying, immortal," that is not tenable; for Indra himself is the speaker in such passages as "Know me alone" and "I am Prāṇa, the conscious self; meditate upon me as life and immortality. By means of his own well-known status as a living being—through acts such as the slaying of the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ—he teaches Prātardana that he himself is the object of meditation.

If it is argued that since the opening statement identifies [the subject] as a specific individual soul (*jīva-viśeṣa*), the conclusion—consisting of such statements as "blissful, undecaying, immortal"—must be explained in accordance with that, [the author] refutes this: "For in this [text], there is an abundance of internal connections.

A connection pertaining to the Self (*ātman*) is an "internal connection" (*adhyātma-sambandha*). Its "abundance" (*bhūmā*) means its multiplicity; that is, the state of having many connections due to the great number of things related to the Self as the substrate. And that [abundance] is possible only in the case of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as the speaker. "Just as, for example, a chariot... [and so forth].

"Just as the felloe is fixed on the spokes, and the spokes are fixed on the nave, even so these elements (bhūtamātrās) are fixed on the elements of consciousness (prājñamātrās), and the elements of consciousness are fixed on the vital breath (prāṇa). This very vital breath is the conscious self (prajñātman), blissful, undecaying, and immortal. Having designated the collection of insentient things by the term *bhūtamātrās*, and having designated the class of sentient beings as their support by the term *prājñāmātrās*, and then having pointed out the subject under discussion—the one denoted by the words Indra and Prāṇa—as the support of even those, [the text concludes] that he alone is "blissful, undecaying, and immortal."

Thus he teaches. The meaning is that this state of being the substratum for all things, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, is possible only in this Supreme Self, which is an entity distinct from the individual soul (jīva).

Alternatively, "abundance of internal connection" (*adhyātmasambandhabhūmā*) refers to the abundance—that is, the multiplicity—of connections with attributes unique to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) found in this context. For instance, first we have: "Choose for yourself a boon from me, whatever you consider most beneficial for humanity," and "Worship me."

It is perceived that Indra, who is designated by the word *prāṇa*, possesses the status of being the object of meditation—the means for attaining liberation which is unique to the Supreme Self. Likewise, the quality of being the impeller of all action, as stated in the passage, "He alone makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds; He alone makes him perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead down," is a characteristic of the Supreme Self.

Likewise, [the text states]: "Just as the rim of a chariot wheel is fixed upon the spokes and the spokes are fixed upon the hub, even so these elements of being (bhūtamātrāḥ) are fixed upon the elements of discernment (prajñāmātrāḥ), and the elements of discernment are fixed upon the vital breath (prāṇa). Thus, the quality of being the support of all belongs to that [vital breath] alone. Similarly, [the text says]: "This very vital breath is the conscious self (prajñātman), blissful, undecaying, and immortal. These too are attributes of the Supreme Self alone. Furthermore, [the statements] "He is the lord of the worlds; He is the ruler of all" are possible only in reference to the Supreme Self.
Thus, because there exists here an abundance of internal connections, it is the Supreme Self alone that is indicated here by the words Indra and Prāṇa. 30.
How, then, is the instruction regarding Indra—who was already known to possess the nature of a living being—as the object of worship for his own self consistent? To this, [the author] says:
"But the instruction is by means of the vision of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva. (Sūtra 1.1.31)

By Indra, who had realized his true nature as the living self (jīva), the instruction—"Know me alone," "Worship me"—regarding the Brahman to be worshipped as one's own self, is not based on a perception of one's own self already established by other means of knowledge; rather, it is brought about by the vision of one's own self through the scripture.

This is what is meant: by such scriptural passages as, "Entering with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms"; "All this has that as its self (aitadātmyam)"; "He who has entered within, the ruler of people, the self of all"; "He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who rules the self from within"; and "This is the inner self of all beings, the divine, the one God Nārāyaṇa, free from evil"—by such texts, [it is shown that Brahman] has the individual self (jīvātman) as its body.

Having understood the Supreme Self and having realized that even words such as "I" (*ahaṃ*), which denote the individual self (*jīvātman*), ultimately terminate in the Supreme Self alone, [the Lord] taught that the Supreme Self—whose body is His own self—is indeed the object of worship, saying: "Know Me alone," and "Worship Me."

Likewise, Vāmadeva, perceiving that the supreme Brahman is the inner self of all, that everything has that as its body, and that words denoting bodies ultimately terminate in the embodied self, pointed to the supreme Brahman as having his own self for its body by using the word "I," and then designated Manu, Sūrya, and others through grammatical coordination with it: "Seeing this very [Brahman], the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I became Manu and Sūrya'; 'I am the seer Kakṣīvān, the sage.'"
And so forth. And as Prahlāda says: "Because the Infinite is omnipresent, He alone abides as I; from Me comes all, I am all, and all is in Me, the Eternal," and so on. || 31 ||

In this section, he states the reason for the Supreme Brahman—the object of worship—being denoted by words that primarily signify the individual soul (jīva) or specific insentient entities, by way of a preliminary objection: "If it be argued that [the Supreme] is not [meant here] because of the characteristic marks of the individual soul and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), we say no; because of the threefold nature of meditation, and because that [threefold nature] is applicable here due to its being resorted to. (Sūtra 1.1.31).

If it be argued that the Self connected with the body (*adhyātma*) is not the subject here—on account of marks of the individual soul (*jīva*), such as "One should not seek to know speech, but should know the speaker," and "I slew the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ; I delivered the Arunmukha Yatis to the Sālāvṛkas"; and on account of marks of the chief vital air (*prāṇa*), such as "As long as the prāṇa dwells in this body, so long is there life," and "Now, verily, it is the prāṇa alone, whose self is intelligence, which, having taken hold of this body, makes it rise"—we say: no, because of the threefold nature of meditation.

The meaning is that, in order to teach the threefold nature of meditation (*upāsanā*), [the Lord] designates [Brahman] by various terms; that is, to teach a threefold contemplation: the contemplation of Brahman, who is the cause of all, in His essential nature (*svarūpa*); the contemplation of Him as having the multitude of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ*) as His body; and the contemplation of Him as having the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*) and the instruments of enjoyment (*bhogopakaraṇa*) as His body.

This threefold contemplation of Brahman is also adopted in other sections [of the scriptures], such as in the passages "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and "Bliss is Brahman," which constitute the contemplation of its essential nature (svarūpa); and [in the passage] "Having created that, He entered into that very thing."

The meaning is that in passages such as, "Having entered into that, it became the manifest and the unmanifest, the defined and the undefined, the supported and the unsupported, consciousness and unconsciousness, the true and the untrue; it became the True," there is a consideration [of Brahman] both as the body of the enjoyer and as the body consisting of the objects of enjoyment and the instruments of enjoyment. In this context as well, that threefold consideration is indeed appropriate.

This is what is meant: wherever there is an association with attributes unique to the Supreme Self—whether among the specific sentient beings such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others, or among the specific non-sentient principles such as Prakṛti and others—or wherever the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of words denoting those [entities] with words expressing the Supreme Self is observed; there, the intended teaching is the realization that the Supreme Self is the inner self (*antarātman*) of each of those particular sentient and non-sentient entities.
Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Self alone, who is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), is the one indicated here by the words "Indra" and "Prāṇa. Śrī.
Thus ends the first pāda of the first adhyāya in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja. 111.

In the first chapter (*pāda*), a person who has studied the Vedas and acquired a thorough understanding of the true nature of ritual action through hearing the *Mīmāṃsā* of Action, having realized that mere rituals yield only meager and impermanent fruits, and having developed an expectation for liberation—characterized as the supreme human goal—arising from the contemplation of Brahman as the infinite and eternal fruit as presented by the Vedāntic texts, [proceeds] with the conviction that the power of the words of the Vedāntic texts to denote an already established reality resides in the Supreme Brahman.

It has been stated for the sake of establishing the commencement of the treatise that one who has ascertained the status of [the Vedas] as authoritative means of knowledge should begin the study of the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā*, which consists of its specific methodology (*itikartavyatā*). Furthermore, it was demonstrated that the Supreme Brahman—the sole cause of the great bliss consisting in the arising, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire universe, characterized by endless and diverse moving and non-moving beings, as well as the enjoyer, the enjoyed, the instruments of enjoyment, and the locus of enjoyment—is made known by such scriptural passages as "from which indeed these [beings arise]" (*yato vā imāni*). (2) We have declared that the Supreme Brahman, the sole cause of the world, is known through the scripture alone as its exclusive means of valid cognition, because it is not the object of any other means of knowledge whatsoever. (3)

We have stated that the fact that Brahman has the scripture as its means of valid cognition (*śāstrapramāṇakatva*) is established because the Vedānta sentences are coherently integrated (*samanvaya*) with the Supreme Brahman—which, though devoid of connection to activity or cessation, is itself the supreme human goal by its very nature. (4) Furthermore, we have demonstrated that Brahman, which is the sole cause of the entire universe and is known through the Vedāntas, is indeed a specific conscious being distinct from the Pradhāna inferred [by the Sāṅkhyas], due to the presence of such qualities as "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*). (5)

And we have established in the Smṛtis that He is a reality distinct from the entity denoted by the word "jīva"—whether in its state of bondage or liberation—by virtue of His being naturally possessed of infinite and unsurpassed bliss and wisdom, His being the cause of fear and fearlessness for all conscious beings, His having true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*), and His being the inner self (*antarātman*) of all sentient and insentient things. (6) Furthermore, we have declared that His divine form is non-material (*aprākṛta*) and unique to Him, not caused by karma. (7)

We have already established that he who is designated as the cause of the world by those who describe it through specific non-conscious entities such as the magnitude of space (*ākāśapramāṇa*) and so forth, is indeed distinct from all other conscious and non-conscious things. (8) We maintain that he is the very same one who is denoted by the word "light" (*jyotis*), which possesses unsurpassed radiance unique to the supreme reality (*paratattva*), because he is recognized as being connected with the celestial realm (*dyu*). (10)

We have already stated that, according to the perspective of the scriptures (*śāstra*), the Supreme Person alone—who is the cause for attaining the supreme, uncommon, and immortal state—is denoted by such terms as "Indra" and others. Thus, it has been declared that the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Person, Nārāyaṇa alone, who transcends the scope of all other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is the object of the Vedāntas; He is distinguished from all other things by His ocean-like, immeasurable, and noble qualities, such as omniscience and the power of true resolve.

Beyond this, although Brahman alone—known through the Vedānta—is the subject matter of the second, third, and fourth chapters (*pādas*), there arises the doubt that certain Vedāntic passages are intended solely to establish the nature of specific entities included within *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul). Anticipating this, the text establishes that Brahman is the source of all auspicious qualities by means of refuting those doubts. Among these, in the second chapter (*pāda*), those passages containing indistinct marks (*liṅga*) of the individual soul and so forth are examined; in the third, those with distinct marks; and in the fourth, those that follow the shadow of the respective [non-Brahman] doctrines being presented.
Because the teaching is established everywhere. (Sūtra 1)

This is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Now, truly, a person consists of volition (kratu); as is his volition in this world, so does he become after departing from here. He should form a volition: 'I am composed of mind, my body is breath, and my form is light,'" and so forth.

In this context, it is understood that the object of meditation for the worship (*upāsana*) established by the statement "He should form a resolve" is indicated as "consisting of mind, having breath for its body. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the one possessing qualities such as consisting of mind the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*), or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)? What is reasonable? That it is the individual soul. Why? Because the mind and breath are instruments of the individual soul, whereas for the Supreme Self, there is a prohibition of those very things in the passage, "For He is without breath, without mind."

Furthermore, the Brahman previously designated in the passage "All this, indeed, is Brahman" cannot be connected here as the object of meditation (*upāsya*), because [the present text] has been employed for the purpose of teaching the identity with Brahman—which serves as the means for accomplishing the tranquility that is an instrument of meditation—as expressed in "one should meditate being tranquil. Nor is it reasonable to say that, because the meditation in "He should form a resolve" requires an object of meditation, the Brahman mentioned in another sentence must be connected [here]; for its requirement is satisfied by the [object] mentioned in its own sentence, which possesses qualities such as consisting of mind (*manomaya*).

Because [the individual soul] has already been established [as the subject]; for when it is designated as "consisting of mind, having breath for its body" (*manomayaḥ prāṇaśarīraḥ*) without reference to anything else, the fulfillment of the mutual requirement of both [subject and predicate] is accomplished merely by changing the case-ending.
