Once the status of the individual soul is thus determined, it is concluded that even the word "Brahman" (*brahma*) found in the concluding statement "This is Brahman" (*etad brahma*) is applied to the individual soul itself for the sake of honor.

This being the position reached, we reply: Because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere. The one characterized by the qualities of consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and so forth is the Supreme Self. Why? Because of the teaching of qualities such as consisting of mind, which are well-known in all the Vedāntas as belonging to the Supreme Brahman alone. For qualities such as consisting of mind are indeed well-known of Brahman; as for example: "Consisting of mind, the leader of the body of breath," and "This is the space within the heart; in it is this person consisting of mind."

"He is immortal and golden. "Fashioned by the heart, by insight, and by the mind—those who know him become immortal. "He is not grasped by the eye, nor even by speech; but by the purified mind. Likewise, "the breath of breath," and "Now, indeed, it is breath alone—the conscious self—which, having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise up. "Verily, all these beings [depend] on breath..."

In such passages as, "They enter into breath and emerge from breath," the state of being "consisting of mind" (manomaya) means being perceivable by a pure mind; and the state of having "breath as its body" (prāṇaśarīra) means being the support and the controller of even the vital breath. This being the case, the term "Brahman" in the passage, "This is my Self within the heart, this is Brahman," is indeed used in its primary sense. Furthermore, the text, "For it is without breath, without mind," negates both the knowledge dependent upon the mind and the stability dependent upon the breath in the case of Brahman.

Alternatively, the injunction for meditation is actually given in this very passage: "All this, indeed, is Brahman; as that from which [it comes], into which [it goes], and in which [it breathes]—one should meditate upon it with a calm mind. The statement, "He should form a resolve," is a restatement for the purpose of specifying its qualities. And the qualities to be adopted are those such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya) and so forth; therefore...

The meaning of the sentence is that one should meditate upon Brahman, which consists of all things and possesses qualities such as being composed of mind (*manomaya*). In this regard, there is a doubt: is the individual self (*pratyagātman*) indicated here by the word "Brahman," or is it the supreme self (*paramātman*)? What is reasonable? That it is the individual self. Why? Because it alone is logically consistent with the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) expressed by the word "all. For the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is what is designated by the word "all."

The state of being Brahmā and so forth indeed exists for the inner self (*pratyagātman*), conditioned by specific karmas rooted in beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*); however, for the supreme Brahman—who is omniscient, omnipotent, free from sin, and whose scent of all defects such as ignorance has been utterly dispelled—the assumption of any state consisting of all that is to be rejected is untenable. Furthermore, the word "Brahman" is sometimes applied even to the inner self; for this very reason [the distinction is maintained].

The designation of the Supreme Lord as "the Supreme Self" (paramātmā) and "the Supreme Brahman" (paraṃ brahma) occurs in certain instances as a qualified description. Furthermore, the quality of "vastness" (bṛhattva) exists in the inner self (pratyagātman) when it is free from limiting adjuncts (nirmuktopādhi), according to the Vedic revelation: "And he becomes fit for infinity. Since the birth, subsistence, and dissolution of the world have that very [Self]—when it is ignorant—as their cause due to the influence of karma, the causal designation "born from that, dissolved in that, and originating from that" (tajjalān) is also appropriate. Thus, the meaning is this: this individual soul (jīvātman), being by its own nature Brahman as an unlimited essence, exists in the form of gods, animals, humans, and immobile beings due to beginningless ignorance (avidyā).

To this, the following reply is given: "Because of the teaching of that which is well-known everywhere. In the phrase "all this indeed," with respect to the entire universe thus indicated, it is the Supreme Brahman alone—not the individual self—that is enjoined as its essence by means of the word "Brahman. Why? Because of the teaching of that which is well-known, namely, the statement "all this indeed is Brahman," which is taught as something already established by the reason "it is born from that, dissolves into that, and breathes in that."

Because it is born from Brahman, because it is dissolved into Brahman, and because its very existence is dependent upon Brahman—for these reasons, when it is said that "all this world is indeed of the nature of Brahman," it is understood that Brahman alone is what is meant here, since the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world are well-known in the Vedānta texts.

And that is the Supreme Brahman itself; for thus [the scripture] begins: "That from which indeed these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, that into which they enter at their departure—desire to know that; that is Brahman," and concludes: "He understood that bliss is Brahman."

By the passage beginning with "Verily, these beings are born from bliss alone," the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world are shown to proceed from the Supreme Brahman itself—the "Vipaścit" (the All-seeing) who is endowed with unsurpassed and infinite bliss as established in the preceding section. Likewise, by the statement "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses, and there is no progenitor of Him, nor is there any lord over Him," it is shown that the Supreme Brahman alone is the cause, being the lord of the "lord of the senses," which is the individual soul (jīva).

It is designated [in this way]; thus, in all cases, the causality of the Supreme Brahman alone is established. Therefore, because it is born from the Supreme Brahman, because it is dissolved into it, and because it breathes by means of it, identity is logically justified through that essential nature. Consequently, the Śruti itself—instructing that one should worship the Supreme Brahman, which is of every kind, whose body is everything, and which has become the Self of all, after becoming tranquil—establishes the Supreme Brahman’s state of being the Self of all and teaches its worship.

Indeed, the Supreme Brahman exists in both causal and effected states; as the body of the subtle and gross sentient and insentient entities, It is at all times the Self of all. In establishing such identity, the fact that the Supreme Brahman is the source of all auspicious qualities and is antagonistic to everything that is to be rejected is not contradicted. This is because defects residing in the body, which serves as the mode (*prakāra*), cannot affect the Self, which is the possessor of the mode (*prakārī*); on the contrary, it has already been stated that this results in a quality by bringing about unsurpassed sovereignty.

As for what was stated—that the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with everything is logically consistent—that is incorrect; for since individual souls are distinct in each body, mutual identity between them is impossible. Furthermore, even for the liberated soul, whose nature is unconditioned, identity with the world—on the grounds of being the cause of the world's birth, maintenance, and dissolution—is not possible; thus it is said: "excluding the activity of the world. (*Jagadvyāpāravarjam*)

This will be explained hereafter. Furthermore, the claim that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the cause of the world’s origin, maintenance, and dissolution because these are caused by the soul’s karma is not tenable; for even though the soul’s karma is the instrumental cause, the Lord (*īśvara*) alone is the cause of the world. Therefore, it is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) alone that is denoted here by the word *brahman*. Learned authorities highly esteem this very meaning of the Sūtra. As the author of the Vṛtti said: “In the phrase ‘All this indeed,’ the Brahman who is the Self of all is the Lord.”
And because the intended qualities are applicable [to it]. || 2 ||

Furthermore, the qualities about to be described are appropriate only for the Supreme Self: "Consisting of mind, having the vital breath as its body, luminous, whose resolve is true, whose self is space, performing all actions, desiring all things, possessing all odors, possessing all tastes, pervading all this, without speech, and without regard. "Consisting of mind" means perceivable by the mind alone when it is purified; for it is grasped by a mind made stainless through the worship of the Supreme Self, which is aided by the sevenfold means such as discrimination and detachment.

By this, His nature is described as being distinct from everything else, due to His exclusive devotion to that auspiciousness which is the opposite of what is to be abandoned; for He is perceivable only by those with pure minds, whereas He is perceived as impure by those with impure minds. "Having vital breath as His body" (*prāṇaśarīra*): He is the sustainer of all vital breaths in the world; He whose body is the vital breath—that is, whose body is that which is supported, controlled, and subordinate to Him—is *prāṇaśarīra*.

It will be demonstrated that being the locus of support (*ādheyatva*), being the object of injunction (*vidheyatva*), and being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) are the grounds for the application of the word "body" (*śarīra*). "Consisting of light" (*bhārūpa*) means having a luminous form; the sense is that He is endowed with unsurpassed radiance by virtue of possessing a divine form that is non-material, unique to Himself, and supremely auspicious. "Of true resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpa*) means one whose volition is unimpeded.

"Ākāśātman" means one whose nature is subtle and transparent like space; or, "ākāśātman" means one who is the very self (ātman) even of space, which is the cause of both the manifest universe and that which is other than it; or, "ākāśātman" means one who shines by himself and illuminates others as well. "Sarvakarmā" refers to one for whom the entire world is action (*karma*); or, "sarvakarmā" refers to one for whom all activities (*kriyā*) constitute action.

"Sarvakāmaḥ": "Kāmas" are those things desired; they consist of objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and so forth. The meaning is that all kinds of these are perfectly pure for him. "Sarvagandhaḥ sarvarasaḥ": because of the prior negation of ordinary smell, taste, and so on in the passage beginning with "soundless, touchless," the meaning is that he possesses all kinds of smells and tastes that are non-material (aprākṛta), unique to himself, faultless, unsurpassed, auspicious, and constituting his own objects of enjoyment.

He has taken within himself all this, up to and including taste; he has appropriated this entire collection of auspicious qualities. The word *abhyāttaḥ* is to be understood as having the suffix *kta* in the sense of the agent (kartari), like the expression "the Brahmins have eaten. He is *avākī*: *vāk* means speech, and he is so called because that [speech] does not belong to him.

"He is silent" (*avākī*). Why? He says: "Because he is indifferent" (*anādara*). Since he has attained all desires, there is nothing left to be sought; therefore, he is devoid of concern. For this very reason, he is "silent," meaning he does not speak. Because his sovereignty is complete, he remains in a state of tranquil composure (*joṣam āsīna*), having treated the entire universe—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—as if it were mere straw. These intended qualities are possible only in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
But because of the impossibility [of that], it is not the embodied soul. || 3 ||

The meaning is this: for those who contemplate this ocean of qualities, not even a trace of connection with the meager fragments of the qualities under discussion can possibly belong to the individual soul (jīva)—which is like a firefly, bound by the cause of the body, subject to immeasurable suffering, and existing in states both bound and liberated; therefore, no suspicion arises in this treatise regarding the inclusion of the embodied soul.
And because of the designation of [the Self] as both the agent and the object of action. || 4 ||

In the passage, "Having departed from here, I shall attain this," the Supreme Brahman is designated as that which is to be attained, and the individual soul (jīva) as the attainer; therefore, it is understood that the attainer—the meditating soul—is one thing, and that which is to be attained—the Supreme Brahman, the object of meditation—is indeed another.
Because of the distinction of sound. || 5 ||

"In this my Self within the heart," here the embodied self (śārīra) is indicated by the genitive case, whereas the object of meditation is indicated by the nominative. Likewise, in the Vājasaneyins' section, [it says]: "Within the inner self (antarātman), there is a golden person, like a smokeless light. Here, the embodied self is indicated by the locative case in "within the inner self," while the object of meditation is indicated by the nominative in "the golden person"; therefore, the object of meditation is something other than the embodied self. For this reason also, it is other than the embodied self, and because of Smṛti as well. (Sūtra 6)

"I am seated within the heart of all, and from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss"; "He who, undeluded, thus knows Me as the Supreme Person"; and "The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion as if they were mounted on a machine—seek refuge in Him alone. Thus, the *Smṛti* (the Bhagavad Gītā) shows the embodied soul as the worshipper and the Supreme Self as the object of worship.

If it be argued that [the Self is not the Lord] because of its having a small abode and because of the designation of such [a smallness], we say no; for it is to be perceived as such, and it is like the ether.

"Having a small abode" means having a minute dwelling place; "designation thereof" means the designation of smallness. Because [the Self] resides in the very small abode of the heart—as in "This is my Self within the heart"—and because its smallness is designated by its essential nature in such passages as "smaller than a grain of rice or a grain of barley," this is not the Supreme Self, but rather the individual soul (jīva) alone.

If it be argued that this is not so, because the omnipresence of the Supreme Self is understood from such passages as, "The wise perceive that which is all-pervading, extremely subtle, and imperishable, the source of all beings," whereas the individual soul (jīva) is designated as being the size of the tip of an awl—[we reply: this is not the case; for the Supreme Self alone is designated as being "smaller than the minute" (*aṇīyān*) by way of being something to be perceived (*nicāyyatvena*). That is to say, it is to be perceived in this manner, to be seen in this manner, and to be meditated upon (*upāsyatvena*) in this manner. It does not mean, however, that minuteness itself is its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

And this [Self] is designated as being like space, and its natural greatness is designated right here: "Greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate region, greater than the sky, greater than these worlds. Therefore, the designation of smallness is for the purpose of meditation.

For instance, after enjoining meditation with the words, "All this is indeed Brahman, as it originates from, dissolves into, and breathes within That; one should meditate on it with a calm mind," thereby teaching that one should meditate upon Brahman—which is the Self of all—as the cause of the origin and dissolution of everything and as the sustainer through its entry into all things as their Self; and after stating the attainment of the fruit according to one's meditation in the passage, "Now, man is made of resolve; as is his resolve in this world, so does he become after departing from here"; [the text continues with] "He should form a resolve."

Having restated the meditation for the purpose of enjoining its attributes—establishing as objects of attainment the essential qualities of that which is distinguished by universal sovereignty, namely: "consisting of mind, having breath for its body, of the nature of light, whose resolve is true, whose self is space, the doer of all works, possessing all desires, possessing all odors, possessing all tastes, pervading all this, without speech, and without concern"—it [the text] then describes [the Self] within the heart of the meditator as being subtler than a grain of rice, or a grain of barley, or a mustard seed, or a grain of millet, or the kernel of a grain of millet.

Having stated that the Supreme Person, who is to be meditated upon as the Self, resides [within] for the sake of meditation—saying, "This is my Self within the heart, greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space, greater than the sky, greater than these worlds; possessing all works, all desires, all odors, all tastes, pervading all this, speechless and indifferent"—the text points out the form of that which is to be attained while residing within the heart as the object of meditation, identifying it as such a Supreme Brahman with the words, "This is my Self within the heart; this is Brahman."

Out of supreme compassion and with the desire to elevate us, [the Lord] has established this reflection within our hearts, thinking, "He is present here. Having thus established the reflection on the attainment in accordance with one's meditation—namely, "After departing from here, I shall attain Him"—and having established the reflection on the certainty of attainment as "He who possesses such [knowledge] certainly has no doubt," it is concluded that for the meditator endowed with this certainty regarding the attainment of what is to be reached, there is no uncertainty about reaching Him. Therefore, the qualities of having a small abode and being minute-sized are for the purpose of meditation.
If it be argued that there is the attainment of enjoyment [of the world], we say no, because of the difference in nature. || 8 ||

If it is argued that since the Supreme Brahman is admitted to reside within the body just like the individual soul (jīva), He must likewise experience the enjoyment of pleasure and pain resulting from that connection with the body—this is not so, because of the difference in cause. For residing within the body is not itself the cause for the experience of pleasure and pain; rather, it is being subject to karma in the form of merit and demerit. That [condition] is impossible for the Supreme Self, who is eternally free from sin.
Thus says the Śruti: "Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating."

If the Supreme Self were not the enjoyer, then one might suspect that the individual soul (jīva) alone must be the enjoyer, as it is perceived everywhere as such; anticipating this objection, the author says:
"The Eater [is the Supreme Self], because of the mention of both the moving and the unmoving. (9)

In the Kaṭhavallī it is recited: "He for whom both Brahminhood and Kṣatriyahood are food, and for whom death is the condiment—who indeed knows where He is? Here, a doubt arises as to whether the eater, indicated by the mention of food and condiment, is the individual soul (jīva) alone, or the Supreme Self (paramātman). What is the reasonable conclusion? That it is the individual soul. Why? Because the state of being an enjoyer is caused by karma, and that possibility belongs to the individual soul alone.

To this it is replied: "The Eater [is the Supreme Self], because of the mention of the moving and the unmoving. The Eater is indeed the Supreme Self. Why? Because of the mention of the moving and the unmoving; for the state of being the Eater of the entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is possible only for Him.

Nor is this state of being an enjoyer caused by karma; rather, it is the quality of being the destroyer of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman, who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe. This is evident from the very passage: "He reaches the end of the path, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Likewise, according to the statement, "Death is the condiment for him," the entire world of moving and non-moving beings—both the *brahmin* and the *kṣatriya*—is understood here as the rice to be eaten. For "condiment" (upasecana) indeed means...

Being itself being eaten, it is the cause for the eating by another; therefore, since even Death is being eaten as a condiment (*upasecana*), it is understood that what is intended here is the eating of the entire world—including the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas at its head, consisting of both the moving and the non-moving—by means of that [Death] as the condiment. And such eating is precisely the act of withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*); consequently, this state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), characterized by the withdrawal of such a world, belongs to the Supreme Self alone.
And because of the context. || 10 ||

Moreover, this context concerns the Supreme Brahman alone, for the following has been introduced as the subject: "The wise man, having realized the great, all-pervading Self, does not grieve"; "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing; him alone whom this Self chooses, by him is He attained; to him this Self reveals His own form. Furthermore, the statement "Who indeed knows where He is? is recognized as reiterating the previously introduced theme that He is difficult to comprehend except through His grace.

Now, it might be argued that this person indicated by the "rice-mess of Brahman and Kṣatriyas" is not the Supreme Self free from evil; for immediately following [the description of the rice-mess], there is the statement: "The two who drink the *ṛta* in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest supreme realm—the knowers of Brahman call them shadow and light, as do those who maintain the five fires and the three *Nāciketa* rites. This indicates that the one who enjoys the fruit of action is indeed accompanied by a second entity. And this second entity must be either the vital breath (*prāṇa*) or the intellect (*buddhi*). For drinking the *ṛta* is precisely the enjoyment of the fruits of action, and that is not possible for the Supreme Self.

However, since the intellect (*buddhi*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) are instruments belonging to the enjoyer, the individual soul (*jīva*), it is possible for them to be connected with the act of eating in some way or another; thus, by either of these two, the individual soul alone is presented as being accompanied by a second. And because they belong to the same context, the "eater" previously introduced must also be that very same soul. To this, it is replied:
"The two who have entered the cave are indeed the two selves, for that is seen [in scripture]. (1.2.11)

It is not the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), nor the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul, that are said to have entered the cave and drink the *ṛta*; rather, it is the individual soul and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who are designated in that manner. Why? Because that is seen [in scripture]. In this context, the designation of the entry into the cave is observed for the individual soul and the Supreme Self alone. Regarding the Supreme Self, for instance: "The wise man, having realized through the attainment of the yoga of the self that God is difficult to see, hidden, entered into the cave, seated in the abyss, and ancient, leaves behind both joy and sorrow. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.12)

Regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) as well, [the text says]: "The goddess Aditi, who comes into being with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), who, entering the cave, abides there, and who was born through the elements. Here, the *jīva* is called Aditi because it consumes the fruits of karma. "Comes into being with the vital breath" means it exists together with the vital breath. "Consisting of the deities" means its experiences are dependent upon the sense organs (*indriya*). "Entering the cave and abiding" means it resides within the interior of the heart-lotus. "Was born through the elements" means that, accompanied by the elements such as earth and the rest, it is born in various forms as gods and so forth.
This being the case, the designation "the two who drink the ṛta" is to be understood in the same way as the expression "those with umbrellas are walking.
Alternatively, the status of being the agent of drinking is possible for both the individual soul and the Supreme Self by virtue of their relationship as the instigated and the instigator.
And because of the qualification. || 12 ||

In this section, it is the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) alone that are presented everywhere as characterized by the roles of the worshiper and the object of worship, and the attainer and the goal to be attained. As it is said: "Having known and realized the God who is the source of Brahman and worthy of praise, one attains this ultimate peace. Here, the "source of Brahman" (*brahmaja-jña*) is the individual soul, because it is born from Brahman and possesses the quality of knowing; the meaning is that having known that God who is worthy of praise—that is, having understood the individual self as the worshiper whose essence is Brahman—one attains peace. Likewise: "That which is the bridge for those performing sacrifices, the Imperishable (*akṣara*), the Supreme Brahman..."

In the passage, "May we be able to reach the fearless further shore, the Nāciketa," the Supreme Self (paramātman) is declared as the object of worship. "Nāciketa" means that which is to be attained through the Nāciketa sacrifice. By the passage beginning with, "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself," the individual soul (jīva), who is the worshipper, is described. Likewise, by the passage, "But the man for whom discernment is the charioteer and the mind is the reins, he reaches the end of the journey—that supreme abode of Viṣṇu"—the individual soul and the Supreme Self are designated respectively as the attainer and the goal to be attained.
Here too, "shadow" and "light" are designated as being distinguished by ignorance and omniscience, respectively.

Now, it might be argued: "Since this entire section begins with the question regarding the true nature of the individual soul (jīva)—namely, 'There is doubt concerning this person after death; some say he exists, and others say he does not exist'—it is understood that this whole context concerns the individual soul. This is not so; for this question does not concern a doubt as to whether the soul, as distinct from the body, exists or does not exist. Were that the case, the choosing of the two previous boons would be untenable. To explain:

At the conclusion of his father’s sacrifice, which was to have all the Vedas as its sacrificial fee (*sarvavedasadakṣiṇa*), the youth Naciketas—the foremost among theists—fearing that a deficiency in the ritual would result from the inadequacy of the fee being given, desired to ensure the perfection of the sacrifice even by the gift of his own self. Having asked his father more than once, "To whom will you give me?", and having entered the abode of Death because of his father’s angry words directed at him despite his persistence, he fasted there for three nights after Yama had departed from his own residence and he could not find him.

When three boons were offered by Death, who had been engaged in providing a remedy out of fear of his own fast, Naciketas, through an excess of faith, chose with the first boon the favor of his father toward himself; and this would not be possible for one who does not know the self as distinct from the body. With the second boon, he chose the knowledge of the fire-sacrifice (*agni-vidyā*), which is the means for attaining a fruit to be experienced after the body has passed away; that too is not possible for one who is ignorant of the self as distinct from the body.

Therefore, with this third boon which is chosen—namely, "This doubt regarding a man who has departed: some say 'he exists,' and others say 'he does not exist'; may I be instructed by you in this matter, for this is the third of my boons"—this question is asked here with a desire to know the reality of the Supreme Self, which serves as the means for the true knowledge of liberation characterized by the attainment of Brahman, the supreme goal of man.

And thus, the phrase "that which [is perceived] when one has departed" (yeyaṃ prete) does not intend merely the separation from the body, but rather intends liberation from all bonds. This is as in the statement, "there is no consciousness after departing" (na pretya sañjñāsti).
The meaning is this: regarding a person qualified for liberation who has departed—that is, one liberated from all bonds—there is a disagreement among disputants concerning his true nature.

"I have been instructed by you so that I may know—that is, understand—the true nature of this doubt, which consists of the notions of 'existence' and 'non-existence' regarding the *nimitta* (the objective cause), in order to dispel it. For indeed, people disagree in many ways: some describe liberation as the total destruction of the very nature of the self, which is mere consciousness (*vitti-mātra*); others [describe it] as the cessation of ignorance while the self remains merely as consciousness; and still others [describe it] as the state of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*), characterized by the eradication of all specific qualities such as knowledge, belonging to a self that is like a stone."

Others, however, while accepting the Supreme Self as one whose impurities have been destroyed (*apahatapāpmā*), maintain that liberation consists in the cessation of the state of being a living soul (*jīva*)—which arises from association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—upon the removal of those adjuncts. But those who are experts in the Upanishads [maintain that liberation belongs to] Him who is the sole cause of the entire universe, whose singular nature is infinite knowledge and bliss free from all that is to be discarded, who is a mine of natural, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities, and who is distinct from everything else.

They declare that liberation is precisely the experience of the supreme Self in its natural state, preceded by the destruction of ignorance; this [liberation] belongs to the individual soul (jīva), whose true nature is concealed by beginningless ignorance in the form of karma, whose essence is unconditioned knowledge consistent with the supreme Brahman—which is the Self of all and exists as the body [of that Brahman]—and whose sole flavor is the experience of the supreme Self.

In this regard, having been questioned by Naciketas—"I wish to know, through your grace, the nature of liberation and its means"—Death (Mṛtyu) examined him by demonstrating the difficulty of comprehending that subject and by tempting him with the offer of various enjoyments. Having recognized his fitness, [Death] taught the knowledge of the reality of the higher and lower selves, the meditation upon the Supreme Self, and liberation characterized by the attainment of His state, beginning with the words, "Him, difficult to see, hidden, entered into," and ending with, "He reaches the end of the path; that is Viṣṇu’s supreme abode."

Having taught [the Self] by means of the passage ending with "the state," He also taught the specific qualities required for that; thus everything is consistent. Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Self alone is the Eater. Thus ends the section on the Eater (Atrādhikaraṇa).
[The intermediate state exists] because of the rebirth [into it]. || 13 ||

The Chandogas recite this: "This person who is seen in the eye—this, he said, is the Self; this is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this person, indicated as having the eye as his locus, the reflection-self, or a particular deity presiding over the sense-organ of sight, or the individual soul (jīvātman), or the Supreme Self? What is the reasonable conclusion? That it is the reflection-self. Why? Because of the manner of the description, which is like that of something already well-known.

Furthermore, because of the use of the term "is seen," which denotes direct perception, [it might refer to] the individual soul (*jīvātman*); for its presence in the eye is particularly well-known, as when people open their eyes and observe, they ascertain the staying and moving of the individual soul within the body. Or, based on the Vedic declaration, "By means of his rays, he is established in this [eye]," it might be a particular deity residing in the eye; for among these [possibilities], the designation is appropriate as something well-known. Thus, it must be one of these.

This being the position, we reply: [The one] within [the eye] is the Supreme Self, because of the appropriateness [of the attributes]. The one within the eye is the Supreme Self. Why? Because these qualities are appropriate only for the Supreme Self, as stated: "He said, 'This is the Self; this is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman. They call him Saṃyadvāma, for all blessings (vāmāni) converge upon him; he is indeed the leader of blessings (vāmani), for he leads all blessings. He is indeed the leader of light (bhāmani), for he shines in all worlds. Thus, these qualities are possible only in the Supreme Self.
And because of the designation of place and so forth. || 14 ||

The rules regarding abiding in the eye and so forth are predicated of the Supreme Self alone in such passages as, "He who dwells in the eye. Therefore, by the statement, "This person who is in the eye," it is understood to be that very same [Self]; thus, its description as something well-known is appropriate for the Supreme Self. For that very reason, the designation of direct perception in the phrase "it is seen" is also appropriate, because it is perceived by yogins.
And because [the term] itself denotes a specific excellence of pleasure. || 15 ||

Furthermore, the Supreme Person is the substratum of the eye; for the purpose of prescribing a place of meditation for the Brahman characterized by bliss that was introduced in the passage, "Brahman is Ka, Brahman is Kha," [it is said]: "The eye is Brahman."

Furthermore, because of the statement, "This person who is in the eye," which is intended to enjoin qualities such as being the "conductor" (*saṃyadvādin*), [the Brahman under discussion is indeed present]. The word "only" (*eva*) indicates that the reason is independent [of other factors]. An objection may be raised: "But surely, due to the intervention of the knowledge of the fires (*agnividyā*), the Brahman previously introduced in the passage 'What is bliss (*kaṃ*) is Brahman' is not present here. For instance, after the fires have taught the knowledge of Brahman with the words, "Breath is Brahman; what is bliss is Brahman; space is Brahman," they began by saying, "Then the Gārhapatya fire instructed him," and proceeded to teach the meditation upon the fires.

Nor can it be said that the knowledge of fire (*agnividyā*) is a subordinate limb (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), because we hear of fruits such as the attainment of all life and the non-interruption of its continuity, which are not included within the fruits of the knowledge of Brahman and are even contrary to them. It is replied: because the term "Brahman" is applied to both in the passages, "Prāṇa is Brahman" and "This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman."

Furthermore, from the words of Agni, "But the teacher will tell you the way," it is determined that since the knowledge of Brahman is not yet completed prior to the instruction regarding the way, the knowledge of the fires situated therein is an auxiliary part of the knowledge of Brahman. Moreover, because the instruction on the knowledge of the fires is given to one who is already qualified for the knowledge of Brahman, as seen in the passage, "Then the Gārhapatya fire instructed him. Furthermore, [the seeker says], "I am filled with diseases."

Since it is taught to Upakosala—who was tormented by the fear of worldly existence consisting of various afflictions such as conception, birth, old age, and death, preceded by the frustration of diverse desires distinct from the attainment of Brahman—with the words, "This, my dear, is our knowledge and the knowledge of the Self," taken together, it is understood that the knowledge of the fires (agnividyā) is an auxiliary to the knowledge of the Self, which has liberation as its sole fruit. And when its status as an auxiliary is thus established, it follows that the mention of its specific results is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).

Furthermore, no fruit contrary to liberation is mentioned here; for these fruits—"He destroys evil-doing, he becomes a possessor of the world, he attains a full lifespan, he lives radiantly, his descendants do not perish, and we attend upon him in this world and in the next"—are conducive to one who is qualified for liberation. "He destroys evil-doing" means he destroys sinful karma that obstructs the attainment of Brahman. "He becomes a possessor of the world" means that once the opposing sin has been removed, he attains the world of Brahman.

He attains the full span of life; that is, he reaches the entire lifespan required until the completion of his meditation on Brahman. He lives radiantly (*jyok*), meaning he lives free from affliction by diseases and other such obstacles until the attainment of Brahman. His "other men" do not perish; that is, his disciples, grand-disciples, and so forth, as well as his sons, grandsons, and others, all become knowers of Brahman. Furthermore, it is heard in another Vedic text as a fruit of the knowledge of Brahman: "In his family, no one ignorant of Brahman shall arise."

"We enjoy him here in this world and in the next; we, the fires, enjoy him; we protect him from obstacles until he attains Brahman. Therefore, since the knowledge of the fires (agnividyā) is an ancillary part of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), there is no contradiction in its proximity [to the latter]. Consequently, it is the very same Brahman under discussion that is described—characterized by bliss—for the purpose of prescribing a locus for meditation and for prescribing its attributes.

But surely, since it is said, "The teacher, however, will tell you the goal," and because only the goal remains to be mentioned, it is understood that the teacher will teach the goal alone; so how can it be said that the purpose is to enjoin the place and its qualities? To this, it is replied:

The intention of the statement, "But the teacher will tell you the way," is as follows: when the teacher had departed after failing to instruct Upakosala in the knowledge of Brahman, the fires—the Gārhapatya and others—who were pleased by his service, sought to revive him who was despondent due to that lack of instruction. Having taught him the essential nature of Brahman and the science of the fires which is an auxiliary to it, they considered the meaning of the Vedic text, "Knowledge truly reaches its highest perfection only when learned from the teacher"; thus, for the sake of attaining the state of being most excellent, [they directed him] to the teacher alone.

Thinking, "May [the teacher] instruct me regarding Brahman, which possesses qualities such as being the 'conductor of blessings' (saṃyadvāma), its locus of worship, and the path beginning with light (arcirādi)," they said, "But the teacher shall tell you the way. The mention of the "way" (gati) is intended to indicate the remainder of the knowledge to be taught.

For this very reason, the Teacher [Bādarāyaṇa] also, having begun with the words, "But I shall tell you that as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus," taught that Brahman—distinguished by auspicious qualities such as being the center of blessings (saṃyadvāma)—is to be meditated upon in the location of the eye, and [taught] the path beginning with light (arcirādi). Therefore, since it is the very same Brahman previously introduced as qualified by bliss in the passage "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman" that is denoted here, this Supreme Self is the substratum in the eye.

But how is it understood that the Supreme Brahman is denoted by the words "Kaṃ brahma khaṃ brahma" (Brahman is bliss, Brahman is space), which you claim is mentioned here as having the eye as its locus? For it appears that the instruction "Kaṃ brahma khaṃ brahma" merely enjoins the meditation upon the well-known physical ether and worldly pleasure as being Brahman, due to the similarity with such statements as "Name is Brahman" and "Mind is Brahman. To this, he says:
"And for this very reason, that [eye] is Brahman. (Sūtra 1.1.16)
Because in that context, the statement "That which is Ka is indeed Kha" is a designation of space (ākāśa) as qualified by bliss; for this very reason, that space is denoted by the word *kha*.

"The Supreme Brahman. This is what is meant: When the fires said, "Breath is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman," Upakośala replied, "I understand that breath is Brahman, but I do not understand Ka and Kha. The intention here is this: the fires did not teach the meditation on symbols such as breath, because they were engaged in instructing one who, terrified by the fear of worldly existence—characterized by birth, old age, death, and so forth—sought liberation; therefore, it was Brahman itself that was taught as the object of meditation.

In that context, Brahman is indicated as being in grammatical apposition with the well-known [entities] such as *prāṇa* (vital breath) and so forth. And among these, Brahman’s qualification by *prāṇa* is justified either through its connection with the sustenance of the world, or because *prāṇa* constitutes its body, or because Brahman is the controller of *prāṇa*. Thus he said: "I know that *prāṇa* is Brahman. Likewise, even in the case of *sukha* (bliss) and *ākāśa* (space), they serve as qualifiers of Brahman because they constitute its body and are governed by it; or else, they function as qualifiers by way of mutual exclusion, denoting that which is unsurpassed.

Or is it intended for the purpose of imparting the nature of Brahman as the essence of bliss (*ka*)? In that regard, if the two were distinct and functioned merely as attributes of the body, then Brahman would be the regulator of sensory pleasure and the elemental ether, and thus there would be no realization of its true nature. If, on the other hand, they were mutually exclusive [as defining attributes], Brahman would possess a nature consisting solely of unlimited bliss (*ananta-ānanda*). Therefore, with the desire to determine the internal mode [of its nature], he said: "I do not know *ka* and *kha*."

Knowing Upakosala’s intention, the fires said, "That which is *ka* (bliss) is indeed *kha* (space), and that which is *kha* is indeed *ka*. The meaning is that the very nature of Brahman as bliss is unlimited. Therefore, it is concluded that Brahman—which is qualified by *prāṇa* (the vital breath) because it has *prāṇa* as its body—is itself the unlimited nature of bliss; thus it is said, "And they told him of *prāṇa* and of that space (*ākāśa*)."

Therefore, since in the passage "Kaṃ brahma, khaṃ brahma" Brahman as unlimited bliss is taught, that very Supreme Brahman is the subject under discussion there; and that same Brahman is what is designated here as having the eye as its locus. Thus, the one residing in the eye is the Supreme Self.
This is also because of the mention of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads. (Sūtra 1.3.17)

For one who has heard the Upanishads—that is, for one who has understood the true nature of the Supreme Person—the path beginning with light (*arcis*) and so forth, which is set forth in other scriptural passages as something to be meditated upon, leads to the attainment of the Supreme Person characterized by non-return; this path was described to Upakosala, who had heard about the Person in the eye, starting from the words, "They go to light itself, from light to day, from day to the waxing fortnight," and continuing through "from the moon to lightning; there a person who is not human leads them to Brahman; this is the path of the gods, the path to Brahman, by which..."
He teaches up to the end [of the passage]: "Those who practice this do not return to this whirlpool of human existence"; for this reason as well, this Person in the eye is the Supreme Self.
And because of instability and impossibility, it is not the other. || 18 ||

Because reflections and the like do not necessarily abide in the eye, and because qualities such as immortality cannot possibly exist in them without limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the person in the eye cannot be anyone other than the Supreme Self—neither a reflection nor a shadow. As for a reflection, since it depends upon the proximity of another person, its constant presence in the eye is impossible. Furthermore, even the individual soul (*jīva*) does not reside in the eye; rather, its function resides in a specific location that serves as the root of all the sense organs, so as to be consistent with the operations of all the senses. Thus, [the person in the eye] is not the individual soul.

Regarding the location: because it is stated that the deity abides in this [eye] by means of its rays, in the words, "By its rays, this one is established in this," it is possible for it to preside over the sense organ even while residing in another place; therefore, it does not abide within the eye itself. Furthermore, immortality and other such qualities in their unconditioned form are simply not possible for any of these [individual souls]. Therefore, the person in the eye is the Supreme Self. Thus ends the section on the Intermediate Space (Antarādhikaraṇa).

In the sūtra "And because of the designation of abiding and so forth," it was established—taking for granted that the abiding in the eye, the ruling, and so forth, as set forth in the passage beginning with "He who dwells in the eye"—belong to the Supreme Self alone, thereby proving that the Person in the Eye is the Supreme Self. Now, that very point is further supported:
"The Inner Ruler [is the Supreme Self], because His attributes are designated in relation to the divine, the worlds, and so forth. (1.2.19)

The Kāṇvas, the Mādhyandinas, and the Vājasaneyins recite: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. The same applies to water, fire, and so forth.

Having pointed out that certain Being who dwells within the bear, wind, sun, directions, moon, stars, ether, darkness, and light; within all divine beings and all elemental beings; and within the vital breath, speech, eye, ear, mind, skin, cognition, and semen—as well as within one's own self and what belongs to the self—existing as their inner essence, unknowable by them, having them as His body, and governing them each; He is taught with the words: "This is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal."

In the Mādhyandina recension, however, there are the following variations: instead of the passages "He who dwells in all worlds," "He who dwells in all Vedas," and "He who dwells in all sacrifices," there is the passage "He who dwells in the self" (*ya ātmani tiṣṭhan*) in place of the variation "He who dwells in consciousness" (*yo vijñāne tiṣṭhan*). Furthermore, there is the specific distinction: "That is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is this inner controller the individual self (*pratyagātman*), or is it the supreme self (*paramātman*)? What is the reasonable conclusion? That it is the individual self.

Why? Because in the supplementary portion of the text, it is heard that the knowledge [of the Self] depends on instruments, as stated in the words "the seer, the hearer"; and likewise, because the inner ruler (antaryāmin) is taught to be the seer himself, and there is a negation of any other seer in the words "there is no other seer than this."

This being the position reached, it is replied: "The Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) in the passages concerning the deities, the worlds, and so forth, [is the Supreme Self], because of the designation of His attributes. The Inner Ruler heard in the sentences marked by the terms "with regard to the deities" (adhidaiva), "with regard to the worlds" (adhiloka), and so on, is the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all evil. Both terms, "with regard to the deities" and "with regard to the worlds," are employed to indicate that while there are sentences containing the term "with regard to the deities" and so forth established in the Kāṇva recension, there are additional sentences containing the term "with regard to the worlds" and so forth in the Mādhyandina recension.

Thus, in both these sets of passages, the meaning is that the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) is the Supreme Self (Paramātman). Why? Because of the designation of His attributes (taddharmavyapadeśāt). For this is indeed an attribute of the Supreme Self: that being one alone, He governs all worlds, all beings, and all deities.

Thus, beginning with Uddālaka’s question, "He who controls from within this world and the next world, and all beings—who is that Inner Ruler? Tell me of Him," the answer is stated starting with, "He who dwells in the earth," and so forth.

This—namely, the act of entering within all worlds, all beings, all gods, all Vedas, and all sacrifices, and thereby exercising control in every way and being the Self of all by virtue of being the body of all—is not possible for anyone other than the Supreme Person, who is omniscient and whose will is ever-true. For it is said: "He has entered within as the ruler of people, the Self of all"; and "Having created that, He entered into that very thing; having entered into that..."

Vedic statements from the Upaniṣads, such as "Truth became That which is Truth," declare that the Supreme Self alone is the ruler of all and the Self of all. Likewise, the Subāla Upaniṣad states: "In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here; these creatures are born from that which is rootless and supportless—the one divine God."

"Nārāyaṇa is the eye and that which is to be seen; Nārāyaṇa is the ear and that which is to be heard. Beginning thus, it continues: "The unborn, one, eternal, seated within the body in the secret cave; he whose body is the earth, who moves within the earth, whom the earth does not know; whose body is water," and so forth, until: "he whose body is death, who moves within death, whom death does not know—this is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God."

By the term "Nārāyaṇa," the fact that the supreme Brahman alone is the self of all, the body of all, and the controller of all is established. Furthermore, immortality is an inherent attribute belonging only to the Supreme Self. Nor is the status of being a seer and so forth dependent upon instruments for the Supreme Self; rather, it exists by its very nature through omniscience and the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*). Thus says the Śruti: "He sees without eyes, he hears without ears; handless and footless, yet swift..."

"...the grasper. Furthermore, words such as "seeing" and "hearing" do not denote the cognition produced by instruments such as the eyes; rather, they denote the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of form and so forth. And that direct perception of form and so forth arises from the instruments such as the eyes for the individual soul (*jīva*), whose innate knowledge is obscured by karma, whereas for the Supreme [Self], it exists by its very nature. The statement, "There is no other seer but He," also declares that there is no seer other than the Controller who was mentioned in the preceding passage. "Whom the earth does not..."

Regarding what was previously stated—that by such passages as "He who knows this Self does not know [it]," the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) governs even while remaining unperceived by those governed, such as the earth and the self—that very point is concluded with the words "the unseen seer, the unheard hearer," and then, by the statement "there is no other seer than He," any other controller for that Controller is denied. Furthermore, because the Inner Controller is taught as the Self of the individual soul (jīva)—who is indicated by the genitive case in the phrases "This is your Self" and "That is your Self"—the Inner Controller cannot be the individual self (pratyagātman).
And it is not the one taught in the Smṛtis, because its attributes are not mentioned there; nor is it the embodied soul.

The one taught in the Smṛti is the Pradhāna; the embodied one is the individual soul (jīva); and neither the one taught in the Smṛti nor the embodied one is the Inner Controller (antaryāmī), because there is a description of attributes not belonging to them, which is impossible for those two.

Because of the expression of [specific] attributes: by their very nature, it is impossible for either of those two to possess the capacity for universal seeing, universal controlling, universal selfhood, or inherent immortality. This is what is meant: just as the non-intelligent principle described in the Smṛtis cannot possess omniscience, controlling power, universal selfhood, and so forth, so too the individual soul (jīva) cannot, because these qualities do not belong to its nature. The connection of these qualities with the Supreme Self and their exclusion from the individual self is shown by two Sūtras. Furthermore, he states another independent reason:
For both [schools] indeed study this separately. || 21 ||

Both the Mādhyandinas and the Kāṇvas [read this]; and just as the Antaryāmin is taught as being controlled by non-intelligent entities such as speech and so forth, the embodied self (śārīra) is likewise divided and taught: "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, and who controls the self from within."

"He is that Self, the inner controller, the immortal"—thus the Mādhyandinas [read]; and "He who dwells in consciousness"—thus the Kāṇvas. The meaning is that they study this [Self] as distinct from him [the individual self], by virtue of being controlled by the Supreme Self. Therefore, it is established that the Inner Controller is the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, who is distinct from the individual self and free from all evil. Thus ends the section on the Inner Controller (Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa).
That which possesses the qualities of invisibility and so forth [is Brahman], because of the statement of its attributes. (Sūtra 1.2.22)

The followers of the Atharva Veda study [the following]: "Now, by the higher knowledge, that Imperishable (akṣara) is attained—which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, and without hands or feet; which is eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, extremely subtle, and imperishable; that which the wise behold as the source of all beings. Likewise, later on, it says: "Higher than the high Imperishable. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the Imperishable characterized here by qualities such as invisibility, and is it also that which is "higher than the high Imperishable"?

Are these the *prakṛti* (primordial nature) and the *puruṣa* (individual soul), or rather, in both cases, is it the Supreme Self alone? What, then, is the initial position? That they are *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. Why? Because in this case, unlike in passages such as "the unseen seer," no specific attribute of consciousness such as "being a seer" is heard; furthermore, by the phrase "higher than the high Imperishable," the *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field), the collective *puruṣa*, is presented as being higher than this Imperishable which itself is beyond all modifications.

The following is what is meant: when visibility and other such qualities—which have as their substratum the gross, insentient elements such as earth that possess form and so forth—are negated, they bring to mind only the subtle, insentient form that is of the same genus as earth and the rest; and that is none other than *pradhāna*. Furthermore, supremacy belongs only to the collective *puruṣa*. And it is *pradhāna*, presided over by that [puruṣa], which produces the entire range of transformations from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the specific elements.

Regarding the statement "it has brought forth," illustrative examples are presented there: "As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its thread], as herbs arise from the earth, and as hair and body hair grow from an existing person, so does this universe arise from the Imperishable. Therefore, it is argued that in this context, it is only the Pradhāna (primordial matter) and Puruṣa (the individual soul) that are being expounded.

This being the case, we reply: "The one characterized by the qualities of invisibility and so forth is the mention of His attributes. The one characterized by the qualities of invisibility and so forth, who is higher than the unmanifest (akṣara) and higher than that which is higher, is indeed the Supreme Person. Why? Because of the mention of His attributes; for by such passages as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," His very attributes, such as omniscience and the like, are declared.

For instance, after designating the Imperishable (akṣara) as possessing qualities such as invisibility through the passage beginning, "That by which that Imperishable is attained," and after stating the origin of the universe from it in the words, "From the Imperishable, the universe arises here," [the text continues]: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge—from Him is born this Brahman, name, form, and food."

The omniscience and other attributes of the imperishable source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) are established [in the preceding passages]. Subsequently, in the phrase "higher than the high imperishable" (*akṣarātparataḥ paraḥ*), that very same imperishable source of beings, characterized by invisibility and other qualities under discussion, is designated as "the High" (*para*) precisely because it is omniscient. Therefore, in the expression "higher than the high imperishable," the word *akṣara* ending in the ablative case refers to the aforementioned imperishable source of beings characterized by invisibility and so forth.

The word "Imperishable" (akṣara) does not denote [the Pradhāna], because that Omniscient One, the source of the universe, is superior to everything, and since nothing else can possibly be superior to Him; therefore, in this context, the word "Imperishable" refers to the insentient subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma). For this reason as well, neither the Pradhāna nor the individual soul (puruṣa) [is meant here], on account of the mention of distinct attributes and designations:
"And on account of the mention of distinct attributes and designations, they are not the other two. (Sūtra 1.2.23)

For the context distinguishes [the subject], meaning that it differentiates the Imperishable (akṣara)—the source of beings—from both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, by means of such things as the justification for the promise of knowing all through the knowledge of one. Likewise, the difference of the Imperishable from those two is designated by such passages as, "Higher than the high Imperishable. For instance, in the passage, "He spoke the knowledge of Brahman, the foundation of all knowledge, to Atharvan, his eldest son," the knowledge of Brahman, which is the foundation of all knowledge, is introduced; and this is indeed the higher knowledge.

And this *vidyā*, which is the foundation of all knowledge (*sarvavidyāpratiṣṭhā*)—having been obtained by Aṅgiras through the lineage of gurus beginning with the four-faced Atharvan—was sought by Śaunaka. Desiring to know it, Śaunaka Mahāśāla approached Aṅgiras according to the prescribed rule and asked: "Venerable sir, when what is known does all this become known? Since the knowledge of Brahman is the substratum of all knowledge, and considering that everything becomes known through the realization of Brahman, he has here inquired about the true nature of Brahman.

To him he said: "There are two kinds of knowledge to be known," as those who know Brahman say, "the higher and the lower. The meaning is that one who seeks Brahman must know two kinds of knowledge; regarding the subject of Brahman, two forms of cognition—mediate and immediate—are to be acquired. Among these, mediate knowledge is that produced by the scriptures, while immediate knowledge is that produced by yoga.

For those two, there is immediate knowledge (*aparokṣa-jñāna*) which serves as the means for attaining Brahman, and that [knowledge] has taken the form of devotion (*bhakti*), because it is specifically characterized in the passage: "He is to be attained by him alone whom He chooses. And the means to that [devotion] is the knowledge produced by the scriptures, supported by the sevenfold means such as discrimination (*viveka*), according to the Vedic revelation: "Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting."

And the Blessed Parāśara said: "O Great Sage, both knowledge and action are declared to be the means for attaining That. Knowledge is likewise said to be twofold: that arising from scripture (āgama) and that from discrimination (viveka). By the passage beginning with "Therein, the lower [knowledge consists of] the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda... and ending with "...the Dharmaśāstras," knowledge arising from scripture—which is indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) serving as the cause for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman—is described.

This is because the Veda, along with its auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*), the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, and Mīmāṃsā, is the cause for the production of the knowledge of Brahman. Then, by the words "Now, the higher [knowledge is that] by which That Imperishable is attained," [knowledge] called meditation (*upāsanā*) is described.

Knowledge, which has taken the form of devotion characterized by the direct realization of Brahman, refers to the essential nature of the supreme Brahman—the object of both mediate and immediate knowledge—as described in passages such as, "That which is invisible and ungraspable," and its creative process as described in, "Just as a spider emits and withdraws [its thread]," and so forth.

The origin of the entire universe, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, has been stated to proceed from the Supreme Brahman, the Imperishable (akṣara), whose nature has been described as above. By the use of the word "the universe" (viśvam), it is understood that this does not refer merely to the insentient portion. The manner in which the universe originates from Brahman is stated [in the verse]: "By austerity (tapas) Brahman is built up; from that, food is born; from food, life-breath, mind, truth, the worlds, actions, and immortality. Here, "by austerity" means by knowledge, because it will be stated later: "His austerity consists of knowledge"; "is built up" (cīyate) means it is augmented (upacīyate).

The meaning is that through the knowledge consisting of the volition "May I be many," Brahman becomes intent upon creation. From that, "food" is born; "food" (anna) is so called because it is eaten (*adyate*). The meaning is that the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), which constitute the objects of enjoyment for the entire class of enjoyers and exist in an undifferentiated state (*avyākṛta*), are born from the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, the entire range of modifications—from breath, mind, and so forth, up to the collection of ritual actions (*karman*) that serve as the means for attaining the fruits of heaven and liberation—is born from that very source.

By the passage beginning with "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," omniscience, the power of true resolve, and other such qualities that serve as the instruments for creation are stated. From the Supreme Brahman—the imperishable (akṣara) which is all-knowing and possesses true resolve—this Brahman consisting of cause and effect arises, differentiated by name and form, and existing in the nature of the enjoyer and the enjoyed. By the words "This is the Truth," the unconditioned truthfulness of the Supreme Brahman is declared.

"Those rites which the seers beheld in the mantras, those have been handed down in many ways in the Tretā age; perform them constantly, O you who desire Truth. Thus, desiring the Imperishable Person—who is the repository of auspicious qualities such as omniscience and the realization of true resolves—and being self-evidently truthful, those who are detached from other fruits should perform the rites seen by the seers in the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, which are appropriate for their respective castes and stages of life and have been handed down in many ways in the three sacred fires. This is shown starting from "This is your path" up to "This is your... [end of quote].

By the passage ending with, "The world of Brahmā is for one who has performed meritorious deeds," [the text] describes the manner of performing ritual acts; and having stated that even if there is a deficiency in any one of the rites enjoined by Śruti and Smṛti, the others that have been performed become fruitless, and that what is performed improperly is equal to not being performed at all, [it says]: "For these eighteen forms of sacrifice are but frail rafts, in which the inferior karma is said to reside."

By stating, "Those fools who rejoice in this as the highest good go again and again to old age and death," [the Lord] has declared the return of those who perform inferior action characterized by a desire for rewards and a lack of knowledge; then, by stating, "But those who practice austerity and faith while fasting," etc., He praised action performed by the wise that is free from desire for rewards as leading to the attainment of Brahman, and finally, by stating, "Having examined the worlds," etc., [He spoke of the seeker] who is detached from the fruits of mere action.

Having prescribed the approach to a teacher for one desiring to know that knowledge—which is supported by the aforementioned actions and serves as the means for attaining Brahman—the text, from "This is the truth: as from a well-kindled fire... up to "...he, O gentle one, tears asunder the knot of ignorance here," describes the state of being the universal form (*viśvarūpatva*) of the previously mentioned Supreme Person, the source of beings, the supreme Brahman, through his unmentioned essential nature and qualities, by virtue of his being the inner self of all beings and having the universe as his body.

Therefore, having clearly described the creation of the universe, [the text] teaches—by means of the passage beginning with "It is near at hand"—the method of meditation upon that very Supreme Brahman, who is beyond even the unmanifested (avyākṛta) and the Puruṣa, who is established in the supreme ether (paramavyoman), whose nature is unsurpassed and infinite bliss, and who resides within the cave of the heart; it further teaches that this meditation takes the form of supreme devotion, and that for the meditator, the fruit is the experience of Brahman, which is equal to Brahman itself, preceded by liberation from ignorance.

It has been withdrawn; therefore, because of this qualification and because of the designation of difference, neither the *pradhāna* nor the *puruṣa* are being propounded in this section. For indeed, there is here a designation of difference between the Supreme Brahman and those two: "For that Puruṣa is divine, formless, both external and internal, and unborn."

By such passages as, "For He is without breath, without mind, pure, higher than the high Imperishable," the meaning is that the Supreme Self—designated by the word *akṣara* (Imperishable) and possessing qualities such as invisibility—is higher even than the *akṣara* which is the collective person (*samaṣṭipuruṣa*) beyond the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*). Alternatively, *akṣara* means "He pervades" (*aśnute*) or "He does not perish" (*na kṣarati*). This nature of being imperishable can be established in some way for the undifferentiated as well: either because it pervades its own modifications, or because, unlike the Great Principle (*mahat*) and other categories, it lacks the "perishing" (*kṣaraṇa*) of changing into other designations.
And because of the presentation of form. || 24 ||

"Agni is his head, the sun and moon are his eyes, the quarters are his ears, the Vedas are his uttered speech, the wind is his breath, the universe is his heart, and the earth is indeed his feet; for he is the inner self of all beings"—such a form is possible only for the Supreme Self, who is the inner self of all beings; therefore, he is the Supreme Self.
Vaiśvānara [is the Supreme Self], because of the specific nature of the common term. || 25 ||

The Chandogas declare this, beginning with: "You are indeed studying this very Self as Vaiśvānara; tell us about that," and continuing with: "But he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self, which is measured by a span and is all-pervading. In this regard, there is a doubt: what is this Vaiśvānara?

Is it possible to determine whether [the Vaiśvānara] is the individual self (ātman) or the supreme self (paramātman), or is it not? What is the prima facie position? That it is impossible to determine. Why? Because the word "Vaiśvānara" is seen to be used in four senses. First, with respect to the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni): "This is the Vaiśvānara fire by which this food is cooked—namely, that which is eaten. Its sound is heard as long as one hears it by cupping the ears; when he is about to depart [from the body], he does not hear that sound. [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2]

In the third [section on] the Great Elements (mahābhūta), it says: "The gods made Agni Vaiśvānara the banner of the days for the sake of the entire world"; regarding the deity, it says: "May we be in the good favor of Vaiśvānara, for he is the king and the glory of all beings"; and regarding the Supreme Self, it says: "He was cast into the very self, into the fire Vaiśvānara in the heart," and "This very Vaiśvānara, the universal-formed Prāṇa, rises as Agni.
Even the indicative marks (liṅgas) found in the introductory and other parts of the passages can be interpreted so as to be consistent with all these views.

This being the position reached, it is replied: Vaiśvānara [is] the Supreme Self because of the distinction of words common [to both]. Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Self. Why? Because of the distinction of words common [to both]. "Distinction" (*viśeṣa*) means that which is distinguished; the meaning is that the word *Vaiśvānara*, though common [to both], is distinguished by attributes exclusive to the Supreme Self. For instance:

These five great sages, Aupamanyava and the others, having come together and deliberated, "Who is our Self? What is Brahman?", and having learned of Uddālaka’s knowledge of the Vaiśvānara-Self—thinking, "O venerable ones, this Uddālaka Āruṇi is currently studying this very Vaiśvānara-Self; let us go to him"—they approached him.

And Uddālaka, perceiving that these seekers of knowledge regarding the Vaiśvānara Self were desirous of learning, and considering himself to be one who knew it only partially, said to them: "Sirs, this Aśvapati, the King of Kekaya, is currently studying this very Vaiśvānara Self; come, let us approach him. Then those six, with Uddālaka as the sixth, went to Aśvapati.

Having honored those great sages individually according to their rank, and making known his own fitness for receiving gifts by declaring his state of observance through the words beginning with “I have no thief” and ending with “O venerable ones, I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice,” he informed them that even those learned in the Veda must avoid what is forbidden and perform what is enjoined; then he said, “Venerable sirs, please stay until I give as much wealth to each officiating priest as I shall give to you.”
And those seekers of liberation, desiring to know the Self as Vaiśvānara, said to him, "Tell us that very Self. Thus, "Who is our..."

When those desiring to know Brahman—which is the very Self of the individual souls (jīvātman)—and seeking a knower of That, approach one who knows the Vaiśvānara-Self and inquire, "Is the Self Brahman?", it is understood that the Vaiśvānara-Self is the Supreme Self (paramātman). This is known because, having begun with the two terms "Self" and "Brahman," there is subsequently a consistent usage throughout of the terms "Self" and "Vaiśvānara"; thus, it is understood that the word "Vaiśvānara," being employed in place of the word "Brahman," denotes Brahman itself.

Furthermore, the fact that the fruit of the knowledge of the Vaiśvānara Self—stated as, "He eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all Selves," and "Just as a tuft of cotton-wool thrown into a fire would be consumed, even so are all his evils consumed"—makes it known that the Vaiśvānara Self is the Supreme Brahman. For this reason also, Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Self;
the traditional Smṛti serves as an inference for this. (Sūtra 26)

The form of Vaiśvānara is taught here through the division of its parts, beginning with heaven and ending with the earth. And that [form] is well-known in the Śrutis and Smṛtis as being the form of the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa). Therefore, this very same [form] being recalled here—that is, being recognized—is an inference (*anumāna*), meaning an indicative mark (*liṅga*), for the status of Vaiśvānara as the Supreme Person. The word *iti* expresses a manner; such a form, being recognized, would serve as an inference for Vaiśvānara’s being the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
For the form of the Supreme Person is well-known in this way in the Śruti and Smṛti; as it is said in the Atharvaṇa: "Agni is his head, the moon and sun are his eyes, and the quarters are his ears."

"The Vedas are the manifestation of his speech; Vāyu is his breath, and the universe is his heart. The earth is indeed in his feet—he is the inner self of all beings. Here, "Agni" refers to the heavenly world, according to the Śruti: "That world, indeed, is Agni. And the sages remember it thus: "Know him whose head the wise perceive as heaven, whose navel is the sky, and whose eyes are the moon and sun; know that the directions are his ears and the earth his feet—he is the inconceivable Self, the leader of all beings."

And: "Salutation to that Self of the worlds, whose mouth is fire, whose head is heaven, whose navel is space, whose feet are the earth, whose eye is the sun, and whose ears are the quarters. And here, heaven and the other elements are described as the head and other limbs of Vaiśvānara.

For instance, when the great sages beginning with Aupamanyava asked Kekaya, "You are currently studying this very Self, Vaiśvānara; please explain that to us," he, desiring to instruct them regarding the Vaiśvānara-Self, perceived—on the basis of the impossibility of their specific questions otherwise—that some portion of the Vaiśvānara-Self was known by them while another portion remained unknown. Thus, wishing to ascertain both the known and the unknown portions, he questioned them one by one.

In that context, when [Aupamanyava] was asked, "Aupamanyava, whom do you meditate upon as the Self? and he replied, "The sky alone, O Venerable King," [the Teacher], while subverting his notion that the sky was the complete Vaiśvānara-Self, taught that "the sky is the head of Vaiśvānara," and thus proclaimed "Sutejas" (Excellent Splendor) to be the name of a quality belonging to that sky which is a constituent part of Vaiśvānara. This being so, [the same applies] to those [deities] mentioned by Satyayajña and others as being meditated upon individually—the sun, wind, space, and earth—each one by one.

The names *viśvarūpaḥ* (the universal-formed), *pṛthagvartmā* (having diverse paths), *bahulaḥ* (abundant), *rayiḥ* (wealth), and *patiṣṭhaḥ* (most firm) are taught as the designations for the individual qualities of the Vaiśvānara-Self, and its identity with the eyes, breath, trunk (*sandeha*), bladder, and feet is also taught. The term *sandeha* refers to the middle part of the body; therefore, since the Vaiśvānara possesses such characteristics as having heaven as its head and so forth, it is the form of the Supreme Person alone, and thus Vaiśvānara is indeed the Supreme Person. Again, raising a doubt regarding the lack of a definitive conclusion, he provides a rebuttal:

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the one referred to] because of its being mentioned among sound and so forth, and because of its being established within, we say no; for there is instruction regarding it as being seen in such a way, because [otherwise] it would be impossible, and they also study this as being the Person (Puruṣa). || 27 ||

As for the statement that Vaiśvānara is determined to be the Supreme Self, that is not so; because, on account of the word and other reasons, as well as because of his being established within, the gastric fire is also perceived here. First, regarding the word: in the section on the Vaiśvānara-vidyā of the Vājasaneyins, it is heard in the scripture, "This is that Agni Vaiśvānara," where the word "Agni" is used in grammatical apposition with Vaiśvānara.

In this context, the conceptualization of the three fires within Vaiśvānara—residing in the heart and other parts—is established by the passage: "The heart is the Gārhapatya fire, the mind is the Anvāhāryapacana fire, and the mouth is the Āhavanīya fire. Furthermore, through the statement beginning with, "Whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as a libation; whatever first oblation he may offer, let him offer it with 'Svāhā to Prāṇa'," it is understood that Vaiśvānara is the substratum for the offering to the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti).

If it be argued that Vaiśvānara is the gastric fire—since the Vājasaneyins record his internal abiding within this person thus: "He who knows this Agni Vaiśvānara, who is of the form of man, as abiding within the person"—and because of the grammatical coordination with the word "Agni," the conceptualization of him as the threefold sacrificial fire, his being the locus for the offering of breath-oblations, and his internal abiding, then he is not necessarily the Supreme Self—[we reply:
