no, because there is an instruction for viewing [the Supreme Self] in that manner, as in the case of the previously mentioned one whose body is the three worlds.

Because there is an instruction for the meditation upon the Supreme Brahman as Vaiśvānara, characterized by having the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) as its body; for by means of the word "fire" and other such terms, it is not merely the digestive fire that is taught, but rather the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as qualified by the digestive fire. If it is asked how this is understood, it is because of impossibility: for the digestive fire alone cannot possibly have the three worlds as its body.

The meaning is that the word *agni*, which is perceived as co-referential with Vaiśvānara because [the latter] is understood to have the three worlds as his body, and which is cognized as referring to the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), denotes the Supreme Self alone as qualified by that [digestive fire], since it has the digestive fire as its body. As it was said by the Blessed One: "Becoming Vaiśvānara, I abide within the bodies of living beings; joined with the prāṇa and apāna breaths, I digest the fourfold food. The meaning is: having become the body of the digestive fire.

Therefore, meditation upon Him as qualified by those attributes is taught here. Furthermore, the Vājasaneyins also study this [Self] as the Puruṣa: "This Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the Puruṣa. For the status of being the Puruṣa does not belong to the mere digestive fire; rather, the status of being the Puruṣa belongs exclusively to the Supreme Self in its unconditioned state, as in such passages as "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads" and "The Puruṣa alone is all this."
For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor an elemental being. || 28 ||
For the very reasons already stated, there is no possibility that the deity or even the third great element (mahābhūta) could be Vaiśvānara.
Jaimini [maintains] that there is no contradiction even with direct perception. || 29 ||

It has been stated that the word *agni*, being in grammatical apposition with *vaiśvānara*, denotes the Supreme Self as qualified by the gastric fire (*jāṭharāgni*) which constitutes its body; likewise, it has been stated that the Supreme Self is the object of meditation. However, the teacher Jaimini maintains that just like the word *vaiśvānara*, the word *agni* also directly [denotes] the Supreme Self itself.

It is considered that there is no contradiction whatsoever due to its being a denotative term. This is what is meant: just as the word *vaiśvānara*, although common [to other meanings], is determined to denote the Supreme Self alone—being distinguished by attributes exclusive to the Supreme Self, such as the quality of being the leader (*netṛtva*) of all men (*viśveṣāṃ narāṇām*)—so too [is it here].

The word "great" (mahan) also applies to fire through its connection with a certain quality, such as being the foremost or leading; however, since that very same quality—when free from limiting adjuncts and reached its ultimate limit—is possible only in the Supreme Self, this term, being an unqualified attribute unique to the Supreme Self within this context, denotes the Supreme Self alone.

"But how can it be appropriate for the supreme Brahman, which is unlimited, to be limited by a measure related to the space extending from the sky down to the earth—as in the passage, 'He who thus [knows] this one, a span in size, the all-pervading'? To this, [the Sūtra] says:
"On account of manifestation, so says Āśmarathya. (30)

The teacher Āśmarathya maintains that the Supreme Self possesses the measure of a span (*prādeśamātratva*) for the purpose of manifesting itself as a lay devotee (*upāsaka*). For the Supreme Self—which is free from all measure and completely pervades everything—such limitation by measure is indeed for the sake of manifestation, based on its connection with the regions beginning with heaven, as stated: "Heaven is His head, the sun is His eye, the wind is His breath, space is His middle body, the waters are His bladder, and the earth is His feet. Thus, the possession of a span's measure occurs solely for the purpose of manifestation.

If it is asked for what purpose the Supreme Brahman is described as having the form of a person through specific parts beginning with the head, [the Sūtra] states in response: "On account of remembrance, Bādari [says so]. (31)

The teacher Bādari considers that it is for the purpose of worship (*upāsanā*). For it is said: "But he who worships this Vaiśvānara Self as the one who measures all around (*abhivimāna*)—he eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves. Indeed, worship is taught here for the sake of attaining Brahman. The phrase "this one thus" means in the manner described, namely, in the form of a person (*puruṣākāra*).

That food which exists as an object of enjoyment throughout all worlds, all beings, and all selves—he, being present everywhere, experiences that very Brahman, which is by its own nature an infinite and unsurpassed bliss. However, that food which is enjoyed individually by each self under the sway of karma as something unique and not shared with others is not included here, because it is to be abandoned by those seeking liberation.

If Vaiśvānara is indeed the supreme Self, how then can there be the instruction that the chest and other parts are the altar and so forth? For this [instruction] is appropriate only if the gastric fire is accepted; to this, [the Sūtrakāra] replies:
"On account of the meditative identification (sampatti), Jaimini [holds this view], for thus [scripture] shows. (3.2.32)

The teacher Jaimini maintains that this instruction regarding the chest and other parts being the sacrificial altar and so forth is intended to establish the nature of the *agnihotra* for the oblation of breath (*prāṇāhuti*) performed daily by the practitioners as a means of worshipping this very Vaiśvānara, the Supreme Self, whose body extends from heaven down to the earth. For this Śruti demonstrates that the fruit appropriate to the meditation on the Supreme Self is indeed attained through the oblation of breath, thereby fulfilling the requirements of the *agnihotra*. Thus [the text says]: "He who, not knowing this, performs the *agnihotra*..."

"If one were to offer [the oblation] after removing the embers, it would be as if he offered it in ashes; such would that [offering] be. But for him who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra, his offering is made in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves. Just as a tuft of *iṣīkā* grass consumed in fire is utterly burnt away, even so all his evils are utterly burnt away.
And they record this regarding him in this [text]. (33)

And they declare this Supreme Person, Vaiśvānara, who is characterized by having the sky as his head and so forth, to be within this body of the worshiper for the purpose of being the locus for the oblation of the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*), stating: "Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head indeed is *Sutejas*," and so on.

The meaning is this: Having prescribed the meditation on Vaiśvānara, the Supreme Self whose body is the three worlds, in the passage, "But he who meditates on this very Self as Vaiśvānara, of the size of a span, [as] the all-pervading measure," and having taught the attainment of Brahman as the fruit in the passage beginning with "in all worlds," [the text teaches] the Prāṇāgnihotra, which is an ancillary part of this very meditation, starting with the words, "Of that indeed, of this... and so forth.

He teaches as follows: he establishes, within the body of the worshiper—from the head down to the feet—the constituent parts of Vaiśvānara, who was previously taught as the object of worship, such as fire, the sun, and so forth, which bear the names Sutejas, Viśvarūpa, and the rest. "The head itself is Sutejas" means that the head of the worshiper is the head of the Supreme Self, which is heaven. "The eye is Viśvarūpa" means the sun. "The breath is Pṛthagvartman" means the wind.

The doubt is extensive: the meaning is that for the worshipper (*upāsaka*), the very middle part of his own body becomes the space that constitutes the middle part of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). The bladder itself is *rayi*; the meaning is that his bladder itself becomes the waters which constitute that [Supreme Self’s] constituent part. The earth itself is his feet; the meaning is that the earth, like his feet, becomes his feet.

Thus, having contemplated the Supreme Self—the Vaiśvānara whose body is the three worlds—as being present within his own body, the lay follower (upāsaka) should conceive of his own chest, hair, heart, mind, and mouth as the altar, the sacrificial grass (barhis), the Gārhapatya, Anvāhāryapacana, and Āhavanīya fires, respectively; and having conceived of the oblation of breath (prāṇāhuti) as the Agnihotra sacrifice, he should worship the Supreme Self, Vaiśvānara, by means of such a Prāṇāgnihotra. [The passage continues: "chest..."

Thus it is taught [in the scripture] beginning with, "The altar is indeed this [body], the sacrificial grass is its hairs, and the Gārhapatya fire is its heart. Therefore, it is established that Vaiśvānara is none other than the Supreme Self, the Puruṣottama.
The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word. (Sūtra 1)

The followers of the Atharvaveda study this passage: "In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, as well as the mind together with all the vital breaths—know him alone as the one Self; cast off other words; he is the bridge to immortality. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this [the Self] the... of heaven, earth, and so forth?

Is the one being heard of as the abode (*āyatana*) the individual soul (*jīva*), or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)? What is appropriate? That it is the individual soul. Why? Because in the subsequent verse—"Where the channels converge like the spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel, therein he moves about, being born in many ways"—the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, introduced in the preceding passage, is referred to again by the locative pronoun "wherein" (*yatra*), and its status as the support of the channels is stated; furthermore, it is said, "Therein he moves about, being born in many ways."

Furthermore, its being born in many ways is also stated; indeed, the connection with the channels (*nāḍī*) and the being born in many ways in the form of gods and so forth are attributes of the individual soul (*jīva*) alone. In this verse as well, the statement that the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*) are woven together as a support refers specifically to the attributes of the individual soul. Thus, the nature of the individual soul being certain, the fact of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth must be reconciled in some manner [with that status].

This being the case, we reply: "The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word. The supreme Brahman is the abode of heaven, earth, and the rest. Why? Because of its own word—that is, because of a term that is unique to the supreme Brahman. "He is the bridge of immortality" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5) is a term unique to the supreme Brahman. Furthermore, in all the Upaniṣads, it is heard that He alone is the cause for attaining immortality: "One who knows Him thus becomes immortal here; there is no other path for going" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1). Thus, it is established that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the supreme Brahman.

Since the root *si* has the meaning of "binding," *setu* means that which brings about the attainment of immortality (*amṛta*). Alternatively, it is called a "bridge" (*setu*) because it is like a bridge; for just as a bridge over a river and so forth provides access to the opposite bank, this [Self] provides access to immortality, which lies on the other shore of the ocean of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, the word *ātman*, when devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), is used in its primary sense for the Supreme Brahman; for it is called *ātman* because it pervades (*āpnoti*), and such pervasion is possible only for Him by virtue of His being the controller of everything other than Himself. Therefore, that word also belongs to Him alone. And such passages as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving... [confirm this].

The words [of the mantra] are indeed transformations of the Supreme Brahman itself. Its being the substratum of the channels is also possible, because of the scriptural passage beginning with, "It hangs down, continuous with the veins, resembling a bellows," and concluding with, "In the middle of that crest, the Supreme Self is established. Furthermore, the phrase "being born in many ways" is also consistent with the Supreme Brahman, as in: "Though unborn, He is born in many ways."

"The wise know His origin"—thus it is stated that the Supreme Person, for the sake of being the refuge of the gods and others, is born in many ways by His own will, endowed with the forms, structures, qualities, and actions characteristic of each respective species, yet never abandoning His own essential nature. Smṛti also says: "Though I am unborn and my nature is imperishable, though I am the Lord of all beings, yet presiding over My own material nature (prakṛti), I manifest through My own power of illusion (māyā).
Furthermore, the status of being the substratum for the mind and other instruments of the individual soul belongs only to the Supreme, who is the support of all.
For this reason as well, He is the Supreme Person.
And because there is the designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated. || 2 ||

This Puruṣa, who constitutes the locus of heaven, earth, and so forth, is designated as that which is to be attained even by those liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra: "When the seer beholds the golden-hued one, the agent, the Lord, the Puruṣa who is the source of Brahman; then the knower, having shaken off merit and sin, stainless, attains supreme equality. "Just as flowing rivers disappear into the ocean, casting off name and form..."

"Thus the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high. For it is only those who are liberated from the bonds of *saṃsāra*—having shaken off merit and demerit (*puṇya-pāpa*), being stainless (*nirañjana*), and completely freed from name and form—who [attain this]. Indeed, *saṃsāra* consists precisely in the state of partaking in name and form, which is induced by the contact of consciousness with the intellect (*cit*) and is bound by merit and demerit. Therefore, the Person who is designated as the goal to be attained—the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth—is none other than the Supreme Brahman, [reached] by those who have shaken off merit and demerit, who are stainless, who are devoid of contact with primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and who have attained supreme equality with the highest Brahman.

Having established that it is indeed the Supreme Brahman by means of words and other attributes unique to the Supreme Brahman, [the Sūtrakāra] states that this [Self] is the Supreme itself because of the absence of words unique to the inner Self (pratyagātman), based on inference and because of the word "that" (tat):
"On account of inference and because of the word 'that', and because of the vital breath. (Sūtra 3)

The meaning is that just as in this section the *pradhāna* is not what is to be propounded due to the absence of any word that propounds it, so too is the *prāṇabhṛt* (the individual soul). "Anumāna" refers to the *pradhāna* mentioned by the opponent because it is inferred (*anumīyate*), or alternatively, because it is known through inference (*anumāna-pramita*). "Atacchabdāt" means because there is an absence of any word denoting that [pradhāna]. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule: "When there is an absence of meaning, [the prefix] 'a' is indeclinable."
For this reason as well, this is not the inner self (pratyagātman), because of the designation of difference. (Sūtra 4)

"He who is immersed in the same tree, being deluded, grieves through his lack of lordship (*anīśayā*); but when he perceives the other, the Lord, as beloved, and His majesty consisting in the governance of the entire universe, he becomes free from sorrow. By such passages, He is designated as distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*). The individual soul, being deluded by *prakṛti*—which has become its object of experience through its lack of lordship—grieves. When he perceives the other than himself, the Lord of all, as the Beloved, and the majesty of this Lord in the form of the regulation of the whole world, then he becomes free from sorrow.
Because of the context. || 5 ||

And that this section concerns the supreme Brahman has already been demonstrated in the very sūtra, "On account of the mention of attributes such as invisibility and so forth. Here, we have merely dispelled the suspicion of a break in the context arising from the connection with the channels (nāḍīs), the state of being born many times, and the fact of being the support of the mind and the vital breath (prāṇa).
And on account of abiding and eating. || 6 ||
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree; one of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating."

By the words "one eats the fruit of his actions" and "the other, not eating the fruit of his actions, shines," it is established that one [self] experiences the fruit of its karma, while the other, though not eating the fruit of its karma, exists merely as a shining entity dwelling within the body. In this context, it is the one that does not eat the fruit of its actions, which shines, who can be the omniscient, immortal bridge, the Self of all, and the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth; it cannot be the individual self (pratyagātman), which eats the fruit of its actions and suffers. Therefore, it is proven that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Self. Thus ends the section concerning heaven, earth, and so forth (Dyubhvādy-adhikaraṇa).
The Infinite [is Brahman], because it is taught as being superior to the serene faith (samprasāda).

The Chandogas recite this: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and knows nothing else—that is the Bhūman. But where one sees something else, hears something else, and knows something else—that is the finite (alpa). Here, this word *bhūman* is derived as ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). For instance, the word *bahu* is listed among the *pṛthu*-class [of stems]; then, by applying the suffix *imanic* according to the rule "from *pṛthu* and so on, the suffix *imanic* may be added," [the form *bhūman* is obtained].

By the rule "there is the elision of *bahu* and *bhū* replaces *bahu*," the word *bhūman* arises through a modification of both the base and the suffix. The meaning of *bhūman* is "abundance. Here, this word *bahu* denotes extensiveness (*vaipulya*), not numerical quantity; for it is heard as being contrasted with "the small" (*alpa*) in the passage, "Where one sees something else, that is the small. Precisely because it is intended to present the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the subject (*dharmin*) indicated by the word "other," it is determined to refer to the subject itself, and not merely to a quality (*dharma*). Thus, *bhūman* means "vast" or "extensive."

Furthermore, the Self (*ātman*) is understood here as being distinguished by its vastness (*vaipulya*), because, having begun with the statement "He who knows the Self crosses over sorrow," and having taught the knowledge of the Infinite (*bhūman*), it concludes specifically with that same [Self] by saying "The Self alone is all this. Regarding this, a doubt arises: Is this the inner self (*pratyagātman*) characterized by the quality of vastness, or is it the supreme Self (*paramātman*)? What is the correct position?

"It is the inner Self. Why? Because when Nārada approached [Pippalāda] with the desire to know the Self—after names and so forth had been taught as objects of meditation up to the vital breath (prāṇa)—questions such as "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than name? and "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than speech? were seen, along with answers such as "Speech, indeed, is greater than name" and "Mind, indeed, is greater than speech," all pertaining to those [entities] prior to the vital breath.

However, we do not perceive the vital breath (prāṇa) [itself as the Self]; therefore, it is understood that this instruction regarding the Self extends only up to the vital breath. Consequently, what is designated here by the word "prāṇa" is the inner self (pratyagātman) associated with the vital breath, and not merely a specific form of air.

Furthermore, passages such as "Prāṇa is indeed the father, Prāṇa is indeed the mother" demonstrate that Prāṇa possesses consciousness. This is because, in cases where there is injury to those endowed with Prāṇa—such as parents—the use of condemnatory language based on their being "killers" occurs; whereas, when those very same beings have departed from Prāṇa, even though they may be utterly destroyed, the absence of such condemnatory language shows that the one designated by the word "Prāṇa" is indeed a conscious entity fit for injury. Since the presence or absence of injury is observed only among sentient beings—even among immobile things like plants—and not otherwise, this Prāṇa indicated as being subject to injury must be understood as the individual self (pratyagātman).

It is determined that it is the Self alone; therefore, one should not be deluded into thinking that the Supreme is the one designated by the word "Prāṇa" through the presentation of analogies such as the spokes and the nave. For there is no possibility of injury to the Supreme, and because all insentient matter other than the individual soul—which serves as the object of enjoyment and the instrument of enjoyment for the soul—exists dependent upon the soul, the analogy of the spokes and the nave is appropriate only with respect to the inner Self (the Pratyagātman).

And this very "plurality" (bhūman) is designated by the word "vital breath" (prāṇa), because there is no interruption of the context concerning the vital breath prior to the mention of "plurality," as evidenced by the absence of both a question—"Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than the vital breath?"—and a reply—"That indeed is greater than the vital breath."

Moreover, having stated that one who knows the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is a superior speaker, and having caused him to recognize that very person as such by saying, "But he indeed is a superior speaker," [the text] teaches the speaking of truth as an ancillary part of the meditation on *prāṇa* by saying, "He who speaks the truth is a superior speaker. Then, establishing the knowledge of the true nature of *prāṇa* previously mentioned as the primary goal of the practice of speaking truth—which is itself to be adopted—it teaches: "When one truly understands, then one speaks the truth. Furthermore, for the sake of achieving that [knowledge], it teaches reflection (*manana*), faith (*śraddhā*), steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*), and effort (*prayatna*), and for the commencement thereof—

Having taught the knowledge of the nature of bliss belonging to the inner self (pratyagātman), whose true form is indicated by the words "being" (bhūta) and "life-breath" (prāṇa), the vastness of that bliss is then taught through the instruction: "But the Infinite (bhūman) alone is what one must desire to understand. Thus, it is taught that the very form of the inner self, when freed from ignorance, is abundant bliss; consequently, there is no contradiction with the opening statement, "The knower of the Self overcomes sorrow."

Therefore, because the inner self (pratyagātman) is distinguished by the quality of plenitude (bhūma), and precisely because the inner self is thus distinguished by the quality of plenitude, the text teaches the all-pervasiveness of the inner self within the referent of the "I"—that is, the inner self—beginning with "I am indeed below, I am above," and continuing up to "I alone am all this. Thus, once the nature of the inner self has been ascertained, the remainder of the passage must be interpreted in accordance with that.

This being the case, it is replied: "The Bhūman [is the Supreme Self] because of the teaching that it follows after the state of serene confidence (samprasāda). The one characterized by the quality of plenitude (bhūman) is not the inner self (pratyagātman), but rather the Supreme Self (paramātman). Why? Because of the teaching that it follows after the state of serene confidence. The term "serene confidence" refers to the inner self, as is well known from the Upanishad: "This serene confidence, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own true form."

The meaning is that [the Self] is taught as being superior to the serene inner self (*pratyagātman*), distinguished by its state as the "Full" (*bhūman*) and denoted by the word "Truth" (*satya*). And that which is denoted by the word "Truth" is the Supreme Brahman. This is what is intended: just as among the series beginning with Name and ending with Breath, each subsequent term is designated as superior to each preceding one, and thus each subsequent entity is distinct from those preceding it; so too is this case.

Thus, that which is designated by the word *satya* is indeed a different entity from the inner self (*pratyagātman*) indicated by the word *prāṇa*; for it is taught that the *bhūman* is precisely what is indicated by the word *satya*, meaning that the supreme Brahman, known as *satya*, is the *bhūman*. As the author of the *Vṛtti* says: "But the *bhūman* is indeed [Brahman], because it is taught as being superior to the self through the sequence beginning with Name.
If it is asked how it is understood that the teaching of *satya* is superior to that indicated by the word *prāṇa*, [the answer is: "He, indeed, seeing thus, thinking thus..."

Having stated that one who knows thus becomes an "ativādin" (one who speaks beyond), and then saying, "But he indeed speaks beyond who speaks beyond by means of the Truth," the text uses the word "but" (*tu*) to distinguish this ativādin—who is an ativādin by virtue of knowing the Truth—from the previous ativādin. Therefore, in the passage "But he indeed speaks beyond," there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the one who was previously the ativādin of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Consequently, it is understood that the Truth which is the cause of this [latter] ativāditva is superior to the vital breath, which was the cause of the former ativāditva. But surely, [it might be argued,] it is only for the knower of the vital breath...

It has been stated that speaking the truth is taught as an ancillary part (*aṅga*) [of the practice]; therefore, there is no interruption of the context concerning the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This is not correct; for by the word *tu* ("but"), another person who is a transcendent speaker (*ativādī*) is understood, and not merely the fact that the same transcendent speaker is qualified by the ancillary part of speaking the truth. In passages such as "But he indeed is an Agnihotra-performer who speaks the truth," since no other Agnihotra-performer is perceived, the interpretation that the instruction regarding speaking the truth as an ancillary part applies only to the Agnihotra-performer already perceived is a strained one.

In this context, however, what is understood as the object of the term "Truth" (*satya*) is the Supreme Brahman, which serves as the cause for being an "exceeding speaker" (*ativādin*). Furthermore, the word "Truth" is employed with reference to the Supreme Brahman in such passages as, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. Therefore, since it is possible for one who is devoted to that [Supreme Brahman] to be superior to the former [the individual soul], the distinctness established by the natural sense of the sentence must not be sublated. For "exceeding speech" (*ativāditva*) consists in speaking of one's own object of meditation as surpassing other entities in terms of human purpose.

Because the knower of *prāṇa* speaks of the inner Self (pratyagātman) indicated by the word *prāṇa*—which transcends all objects of worship beginning with Name and extending to Hope—he is called an "exceeding speaker" (*ativādin*). However, since even that [attainment of the inner Self] is a human goal that possesses a higher excellence, only the one who speaks of the Supreme Brahman as the object of worship is truly an "exceeding speaker" in the absolute sense. Thus it is said: "But he indeed is an exceeding speaker who exceeds by means of Truth. In the phrase "by means of Truth" (*satyena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*).

The meaning is that he who speaks beyond [the ordinary] is characterized by the Supreme Brahman, which is Truth (satya). For this very reason, the disciple prays: "O Venerable One, may I speak beyond [the ordinary] through Truth. And the teacher says: "Truth indeed must be sought to be known. Furthermore, regarding the Self designated by the word "prāṇa" in the passage "From the Self, prāṇa... [it follows that the Self is Truth].

[The Self] is said to be the source of origin; therefore, it is understood that the Self introduced in the passage, "He who knows the Self overcomes sorrow," is distinct from that which was designated by the word "prāṇa. As for the argument that—because no question such as, "Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than prāṇa? nor any answer such as, "Yes, there is indeed something greater than prāṇa," are observed—the teaching concerning the Self introduced at the outset must be understood as culminating in the teaching concerning prāṇa—that is incorrect. For it is not solely on the basis of the absence of a question and an answer that a difference in subject matter is established.

Because that [superiority] is possible through another means of knowledge as well; and another means of knowledge has indeed been stated. The intention of the one who asked, "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than breath? is this: although among the insentient objects beginning with Name and ending with Hope—each subsequent one having been taught as being superior in terms of human purpose (puruṣārtha) and each preceding one having been transcended—the teacher did not declare one to be an "over-speaker" (ativādin) merely for knowing those respective things. However, considering that for one who knows the true nature of the inner self (pratyagātman) indicated by the word "breath," there is a further excellence in the abundance of human purpose, [the teacher said]: "He, verily, this..."

"Seeing thus, thinking thus, and knowing thus, one becomes an 'ativādī'"—by this, it is stated that he is a speaker who has transcended all objects. Therefore, the student, believing that the instruction regarding the Self was completed right here, did not ask any further questions. However, the teacher, considering even this to be surpassed and desiring to introduce the Supreme Brahman—which is the unsurpassed human goal and denoted by the word "Truth"—himself added: "But he indeed is an ativādī who speaks beyond by means of Truth. The student also...

When the Supreme Brahman, which is the nature of the supreme human goal, had been introduced, [the disciple], desiring to know its true nature and the reality of its worship, made this request: "O Blessed One, by means of truth, may I speak beyond."

Then, for the sake of establishing the status of being an "exaggerator" (*ativādin*) based on the direct realization of Brahman, [the text] teaches meditation on Brahman—which serves as the means to that realization—by saying, "Truth indeed must be sought to be known. Having taught reflection on Brahman—which is the means to that [meditation]—by saying, "Understanding indeed must be sought to be known," and considering that hearing (*śravaṇa*) is already established by implication since reflection is for the purpose of stabilizing what has been heard, [the text] teaches faith in Brahman—which is the means to hearing—by saying, "Faith indeed must be sought to be known."

Having thus taught that, and having taught its means—which is steadfastness in that—as "But steadfastness itself is what must be sought to be known," and having also taught the activity consisting of exertion and effort toward that, which is the means for that [steadfastness], as "But activity itself is what must be sought to be known," [the text proceeds] for the sake of accomplishing the activity in the form of undertaking hearing and so forth.

Having taught that the nature of bliss must be known for Brahman—which is the object to be attained and is denoted by the word "Truth"—in the passage, "But bliss alone is what one should desire to understand," and having further taught that this very Brahman, whose nature is bliss, consists of unsurpassed and abundant happiness which is the supreme human goal, and that its unsurpassed abundance must be known, in the passage, "But the Infinite (bhūman) alone is what one should desire to understand," this definition is stated regarding Brahman, whose nature is unsurpassed and abundant bliss: "Where..."

"He sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and knows nothing else; that is the Infinite (bhūman). This is the meaning: when Brahman, whose nature is unsurpassed and infinite bliss, is being experienced, the experiencer sees nothing else whatsoever other than that, because the entire aggregate of things is included within the very nature and manifestations of Brahman.

Therefore, he experiences Brahman—which is characterized by the qualities of *vibhūti* (sovereignty, a synonym for *aiśvarya*) and consists of unsurpassed bliss—and because there is no entity other than that, he sees nothing else whatsoever. Furthermore, since everything that can be experienced is of the nature of bliss, he does not see suffering either; for that alone is happiness which, when experienced, is favorable to the person.

Now, one might object: "If this very world is experienced as something other than Brahman—being of the nature of suffering and limited pleasure—how can it become purely of the nature of bliss when experienced as having Brahman as its essence and as a manifestation (*vibhūti*) of Brahman? To this, it is replied:

For the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) who are subject to karma, the entire world—which is experienced as something other than Brahman—becomes characterized by suffering corresponding to their respective karmas and by limited pleasure; therefore, because the experience of the world as something other than Brahman, characterized by limited pleasure and suffering, is caused by karma, for one liberated from the ignorance consisting of karma, that very same world becomes [an object of] its majestic qualities.

The bliss that is contained within the experience of the distinguished Brahman is indeed [supreme] bliss itself. Just as milk being drunk by one afflicted with bile becomes a source of slight pleasure or even the opposite, depending on the degree of the bile, yet that very same milk leads only to bliss for one not afflicted by bile; and just as a royal prince’s playthings do not produce affection when perceived as such, but become most dear when perceived for what they truly are; so too is this case.

Likewise, for one who contemplates the world as the instrument of the divine play (*līlopakaraṇa*) and as identical in nature to Brahman—the Supreme Being whose essence is unsurpassed bliss and who is the source of infinite, unsurpassable, and innumerable auspicious qualities—that world indeed leads to unsurpassed joy. Therefore, experiencing Brahman as characterized by the sovereignty over the world and consisting of infinite, unsurpassable bliss, he perceives nothing else whatsoever, nor does he perceive suffering.

The remainder of the passage establishes this very point: "He who sees thus, who thinks thus, who understands thus, becomes one whose delight is the Self, whose play is the Self, whose companion is the Self, whose bliss is the Self; he becomes self-ruling (svarāṭ), and for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds. But those who know otherwise than this have others as their rulers; their worlds are perishable, and for them there is no freedom of movement in all worlds. Here, "self-ruling" means not subject to karma, while "having others as their rulers" means being subject to karma.

Likewise: "The seer sees neither death, nor disease, nor even suffering; the seer sees everything, he attains everything in every way. Furthermore, the fact that Brahman consists of unsurpassed bliss has been elaborated upon in the sūtra, "It is the one consisting of bliss, because of the repetition" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.12). Therefore, because the term *bhūman* (the Infinite) is taught as referring to Brahman—which is denoted by the word "Truth" (*satya*) and is a distinct entity from the inner self (*pratyagātman*) indicated by the word "vital breath" (*prāṇa*)—the *bhūman* is the Supreme Brahman.
This is also because the attributes [of Brahman] are logically consistent [with this interpretation]. (Brahmasūtra 1.3.8)

Those attributes that are traditionally taught (āmnāyante) regarding this Infinite (bhūman) are also applicable only to the Supreme [Self]. For instance: "This is the immortal" refers to its natural immortality; "in its own glory" refers to its lack of dependence on any other support; "He alone is below," and so forth up to "He alone is all this," refers to its being the self of all; and "From the Self comes the vital breath," and so forth, refers to its being the originator of everything beginning with the vital breath—these and other such attributes belong to the Supreme Self alone. As for the passage beginning with "I alone am below," etc., [it is explained as follows:]...

The state of being the self of all has been taught; now, the meditation upon Brahman—distinguished by those stages—as the "I" (the *ahaṃgraha*) is taught, beginning with the instruction on the "instruction regarding the I" (*atha ato 'haṅkārādeśaḥ*). For even the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), which is the referent of "I," is the Self of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); this is stated in such passages as the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa*.

Therefore, since the referent of the term *pratyak* (the inward-facing) culminates in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the word *aham* (I) also culminates in the Supreme Self. Thus, this instruction on the "apprehension of the I" (*ahaṃgraha*) is for the purpose of meditating upon the Supreme Self as having the inner self as its body. Because the Supreme Self is the Self of all by virtue of being the body of all, the Supreme Self is also the Self of the inner self. This very point is expressed by the passage beginning with "Now, therefore, the pointing out of the Self" (*athāta ātmādeśaḥ*) and ending with "All this is indeed the Self" (*ātmaivedaṃ sarvam*).

To establish this very point, the origin of everything from the Supreme Self—who is the very Self of the inner self (pratyagātman)—is stated in the passage beginning with: "Of that very one who sees thus, who thinks thus, and who knows thus, from the Self comes the vital breath, from the Self comes space," and so forth. The meaning is that the origin of everything proceeds from the Supreme Self abiding as the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin) of the meditator. Therefore, for the sake of establishing the knowledge that the Supreme Self has the inner self as its body, the meditation characterized by "I-grasping" (ahaṃgraha-upāsana) must be performed.
Consequently, it is established that the Supreme Self is distinguished by the attribute of plenitude (bhūman).
The Imperishable [is Brahman], because it supports everything up to the ends of space. || 9 ||

The Vājasaneyins record in the Gārgī-praśna: "He said: 'O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas declare this very Imperishable (akṣara) to be neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, without blood, without fat, without shadow,' and so forth. In this regard, a doubt arises: Is this Imperishable the Pradhāna, or the individual soul (jīva), or rather the Supreme Self? What is the reasonable conclusion? That it is the Pradhāna. Why? Because the word "Imperishable" is seen to be used for the Pradhāna in such passages as "Higher than the Imperishable is the High," and because qualities such as being neither gross nor subtle are consistently associated with it.

If it is argued that the word "syllable" (akṣara) is seen to refer even to the Supreme [Brahman] in passages such as "how that syllable is attained," we say no; for between what is established by another means of knowledge and what is established by the Veda, that which is established by another means of knowledge is apprehended first, and there is no contradiction in accepting what has already been so apprehended.

Furthermore, beginning with the passage, "That which is above the sky, Gārgī, and that which is below the earth," after it has been established that everything existing in the three periods of time rests upon the ether (ākāśa) as its causal substrate, the question is asked: "Upon what, indeed, is this ether woven like warp and woof? When this is asked—seeking to know what the cause of even the ether is, and what serves as its substrate—the syllable (akṣara) mentioned in reply is understood to be the Pradhāna, well-known through other means of knowledge, because it is the substrate of all modifications by virtue of being the cause of all transformations; therefore, the akṣara is the Pradhāna.

This being the position reached, it is said: "The Imperishable [is Brahman], because of its supporting everything up to the ether. The Imperishable is the Supreme Brahman. Why? Because of its supporting everything up to the ether—that is, the ether (ākāśa).

The "end" (*anta*) is the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) that constitutes the limit of space; the meaning is that because this Imperishable (*akṣara*) is taught as its support, by virtue of being the substratum for the maintenance of that [space]. This is the sense: in the passage, "In what, indeed, is space woven across and lengthwise?", the term "space" does not refer to the sky containing air, but rather to the unmanifest that constitutes its limit. Therefore, the Imperishable which is spoken of as the substratum even for that unmanifest cannot itself be the unmanifest.

But how is it understood that what is designated by the word "space" does not consist of mere air? It is said: "That which is above the sky, O Gārgī, that which is below the earth, and that which is between these two, heaven and earth..."

If that is so, let the individual soul (jīva) be the one designated by the word "akṣara," since it is logical for it to be the substratum of the entire non-sentient reality extending down to the subtle elements of matter, and because the attributes stated such as "neither gross" and so forth are applicable to it; furthermore, because the term "akṣara" is seen to be applied to the inner self (pratyagātman) in passages such as, "The unmanifest dissolves into the akṣara," "He whose body is the unmanifest, whose body is the akṣara," and "All beings are called the perishable (kṣara), while the immutable is called the akṣara. To this, the reply is: "And [it is Brahman] because of its presiding over [the world]. (Sūtra 10)

And that support of the sky by this Imperishable occurs solely through its command, as taught in such passages as: "By the command of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and moon stand held apart; by the command of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart; by the command of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, moments, hours, days and nights, fortnights, months, seasons, and years stand held apart. And so forth.

"Supreme governance" means excellent governance. Such governance—consisting of the sustaining of all things dependent upon one's own command—is not possible for the inner self (pratyagātman), whether in its bound, liberated, or both states; therefore, the Imperishable (akṣara) is none other than the Supreme Person (puruṣottama), the Ruler.
And because of the exclusion of other states. || 11 ||

The state of being other (*anyabhāvaḥ*) means difference (*anyatvam*), such as the state of being something other than *pradhāna* and so forth. This difference of this Imperishable (*akṣara*) from the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) is negated in the subsequent portion of the text: "Now, O Gārgī, this Imperishable is unseen yet the seer, unheard yet the hearer, unthought yet the thinker, unknown yet the knower; there is no other seer than this, no other hearer than this, no other thinker than this, no other knower than this. In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the ether (*ākāśa*) is woven like warp and woof. Here, [the attributes of] being a seer, a hearer, and so forth—

By this teaching, the state of this Imperishable (akṣara) as the insentient primary matter (pradhāna) is excluded; and because it is taught to be the seer of everything—even that which is unseen by all—it is excluded from being the individual self (pratyagātman). Thus, this exclusion of other states confirms the supreme-personhood (paramapuruṣatā) of this Imperishable. Or rather, the "exclusion of other states" means the exclusion of the existence of anything else: just as this Imperishable, while unseen by others, is the seer of others, and while existing, [is the seer] of that which is distinct from itself.

It is the substratum of that [unseen]; thus, by saying "there is no other seer than this," he asserts that there exists nothing else which is unseen by it and yet serves as its substratum while being its seer. "There is no other seer than this."

The remainder of the passage beginning with these words, by negating the existence of anything else, excludes the possibility that this Imperishable (akṣara) is either the Pradhāna or the individual self (pratyagātman). Furthermore, from the scriptural statement—"O Gārgī, under the command of this very Imperishable, men praise the giver; the gods depend on the sacrificer; and the ancestors depend on the offering"—it is understood that the Imperishable, by whose authority all ritual actions such as sacrifice, giving, and oblation—whether Vedic or Smārta—are set in motion, is none other than the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is the Supreme Brahman.

Moreover, it is established that this Imperishable (akṣara) is indeed the Supreme Brahman, for the scripture states: "O Gārgī, he who, without knowing this Imperishable, offers oblations, performs sacrifices, and practices austerities in this world for many thousands of years—all that becomes finite for him. He who departs from this world, O Gārgī, without knowing this Imperishable, is pitiable; but he who departs from this world, O Gārgī, having known this Imperishable, is a true Brāhmaṇa. Thus, it is proven that the Imperishable—by the ignorance of which one attains saṃsāra and by the knowledge of which one attains immortality—is the Supreme Brahman itself.
He is that [Brahman], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing. (Sūtra 1.3.12)

The followers of the Atharva Veda study this in the *Satyakāma-praśna*: "But he who meditates upon that supreme Puruṣa by means of this very syllable 'Om' consisting of three measures—he, having reached the sun, becomes one with its radiance. Just as a snake is freed from its skin, even so is he indeed freed from evil. Led upward by the Sāmans, he goes to the world of Brahman; from this mass of living beings, he beholds the Puruṣa dwelling in the city, who is higher than the high."

In this context, the words "meditates" (*dhyāyati*) and "beholds" (*īkṣati*) have a single object, because beholding is the fruit of meditation; for, according to the principle that "as is one's resolve in this world, so shall one become," that which is the object of meditation alone is what is to be attained. Furthermore, there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the same thing as the object of the action in both instances by the phrase "the highest person" (*paraṃ puruṣam*). Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the one designated here as "the highest person" [the individual soul or the Supreme Self]?

Is the one who is the lord of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍādhipati*) and the four-faced Brahmā the collective totality of individual souls (*jīvasamaṣṭi*), or is he the Lord of All, the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*)? What is the correct conclusion? That it is the collective knower of the field (*samaṣṭikṣetrajña*). Why? Because, having commenced with the question, "O Venerable One, if someone among men meditates upon the syllable *oṃ* until the end of his life, what world does he win by that? and having stated that one who meditates on the *praṇava* consisting of a single measure attains the world of men, and having stated that one who meditates on that consisting of two measures attains the world of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), [the text proceeds].

The world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), which is described as the goal to be attained by one who meditates on the "three-measured" [syllables], is understood to be the world of the four-faced [Brahmā]—the collective totality of individual souls (jīvasamaṣṭi)—situated beyond the intermediate space (antarikṣa). And the Lord of that world, who is to be beheld by one who has reached it, is indeed the four-faced [Brahmā] himself.

And regarding the statement, "higher than this mass of life (jīvaghana)," it is appropriate that the Supreme Person is higher than the four-faced Brahmā—the person who is the aggregate (samaṣṭi) residing in the world of Brahman—who himself is a condensed mass of individual lives (jīvavyaṣṭi) together with the bodies, senses, and so forth, which are themselves higher than the body, senses, and other such elements. Therefore, the Supreme Person indicated here is indeed the four-faced one as the aggregate person. Thus, once his identity as the four-faced one is established, qualities such as being ageless and so forth must be interpreted in some way [as applying to him].

This being the position, we reply: "He [is the Supreme Self], because He is designated as the object of the act of seeing. He—the object of the act of seeing—is the Supreme Self. Why? Because of the designation; for He is indeed designated as the object of the act of seeing by way of His being the Supreme Self. For instance, in the verse cited as the subject matter of the act of seeing: "The wise man follows that which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, fearless, and supreme, by means of the syllable Om itself as its abode. Indeed, this form—supreme, peaceful, undecaying, fearless, and immortal—belongs to the Supreme Self alone. This...

This is because of such scriptural passages as, "This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman," and because the designation "higher than the highest from this mass of living beings" (etasmāj jīvaghanāt parātparam) refers specifically to the Supreme Self and not to the four-faced Brahmā, since even he is included within the term "mass of living beings. For one whose embodied state is caused by karma is called a "mass of living beings," and that applies to the four-faced one as well, as seen in such texts as, "He who first creates Brahmā."

Furthermore, as for the argument that the Brahma-world mentioned above the intermediate region (antarikṣa-loka) is understood to be the world of the four-faced [Brahmā], and therefore the one residing there must be the four-faced one—that is incorrect. Since it has been determined through such passages as "That which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, and fearless" that the object of the act of seeing (īkṣatikarma) is the Supreme Self, the Brahma-world designated as the abode of the seer cannot be the perishable world of the four-faced one.

Furthermore, as it is said, "Just as a snake is freed from its skin, even so is he freed from evil"; thus, the place being described as that which is to be reached is not the abode of the Four-faced One (Brahmā). For this very reason, in the illustrative verse, this same [abode] is heard of in reference to the world of Brahman: "That which the seers (kavayaḥ) know. The term "seers" refers to...

The wise (*sūrayaḥ*). And the state of Viṣṇu is indeed visible to the wise, based on such scriptural passages as: "The wise always behold that highest step of Viṣṇu. Nor is the world of the four-faced Brahmā situated beyond the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), because there exist many worlds between them, such as the heavenly world (*svargaloka*) and others. Therefore, in the reply, "O Satyakāma, this *oṃkāra* is indeed the higher and the lower Brahman; therefore, the knower, by this very path, attains one or the other," that which is designated as the lower, effect-Brahman (*kāryabrahma*)—[is what is meant].

Having divided that [meditation] into two types—pertaining to this world and the next—and having declared the fruit for those who meditate on the single-measure *praṇava* as the attainment of the human world in this life, and having declared the fruit for those who meditate on the two-measure *praṇava* as the attainment of the intermediate space (the heavenly world) designated by the term "intermediate space" in the hereafter, [the scripture] teaches that for those who meditate on the Supreme Person by means of the three-measure *praṇava* which denotes the Supreme Brahman, it is the Supreme Brahman itself that is to be attained. Thus, everything is consistent. Therefore, the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣati*) is the Supreme Self. This concludes the section concerning the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa*).
The small one [is Brahman], because of subsequent [scriptural] passages. || 13 ||
The followers of the *Chāndogya* recite this: "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, a small lotus-palace, there is a small space (*ākāśa*) within it;

what is within that is to be sought, and that indeed is what one should desire to understand. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is this small space situated in the middle of the heart-lotus a particular instance of the great elemental ether (*mahābhūta*), or is it the inner self (*pratyagātman*), or is it the supreme self (*paramātman*)? What, then, is the reasonable position? [That it is] the great element...

Regarding the term "distinction": why? Because the word "ether" (ākāśa) has a preeminent conventional usage in reference to the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), and because [in the phrase] "that which is within it is to be sought," it is perceived as the substratum for another object to be sought.

This being the position reached, it is replied: "The small [ether] is [Brahman] because of the subsequent [reasons]. The small ether is the Supreme Brahman. Why? Because of the reasons found in the subsequent statements. For the qualities heard in reference to the small ether—namely, its being the Self without limiting adjuncts, its freedom from sin and so forth, and its having true desires and true resolves, as stated in the passage, "This is the Self, free from sin, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, without hunger, without thirst, whose desires are true, whose resolves are true"—establish that the small ether is [Brahman].

They indicate that it is the Supreme Brahman. By such passages as, "Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds," up to, "Whatever desire he may desire, that arises for him by his mere volition; endowed with that, he exults," the attainment of the state of having true volitions (satya-saṅkalpatva) is stated for the knower of the small ether (daharākāśa), which makes it understood that the small ether is the Supreme Brahman.

Furthermore, the relationship of comparison and object compared in the statement, "As large as this space is, so large is this space within the heart," is only logically consistent if the small space (*daharākāśa*) is the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*). If it is argued that the relationship of comparison and object compared is based on the limitation by the heart, then, in that case, it would not be possible for that which is limited by the heart to be the substratum of everything, including heaven and earth.

But surely, even if the small ether (*daharākāśa*) were the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), its comparison with the external ether would not be possible, because of the scriptural statement in passages such as "greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space," that it is greater than everything. This is not so; for this passage aims at removing the smallness that results from the small ether's location within the lotus of the heart (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*). It is just as the statement "the sun moves like an arrow," although the sun possesses great speed, aims at removing the notion of slowness in its motion.

Now, it might be argued that the small ether (*daharākāśa*) is not being referred to by the passage beginning with "This Self is free from evil," because what is under discussion is something other than the small ether—namely, that which dwells within it, as stated in "In this [ether] there is a small space; that which is within it is to be sought after"—and thus it is more appropriate here to refer to that very thing which is to be sought after by saying "This Self is free from evil."

This might be so, were it not for the fact that the Śruti itself has clearly distinguished the small ether and that which dwells within it; indeed, it did so: "Now, what is here in this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace, and the small ether within it—that which is inside that [ether] is what one must seek. Thus, by using the term "city of Brahman," the body of the worshipper is indicated as the city of the Supreme Brahman—which is proximate as the object of meditation—and that which exists within it is shown to be a constituent part thereof.

Having described the heart—shaped like a lotus and small in size—as the dwelling place of the Supreme Brahman, [the scripture teaches that] the All-Knowing, All-Powerful One, who is the sole ocean of affection for those who take refuge in Him, is present within that dwelling for the sake of favoring His devotees; He is to be meditated upon as subtle in form. This refers to the *dahara* (the small one).

Having indicated [the space] by the word "kāśa," and having [indicated] the collection of natural, unsurpassed, and excellent auspicious qualities—such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and having true desires (*satyakāmatva*), which constitute its nature and from which all defects have been eliminated—as existing within that [space], it is taught that this is what "must be sought" (*tadanveṣṭavyam*). Here, by the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "that must be sought," both the small ether (*daharākāśa*) and the collection of qualities existing within it are referred to, and it is thus taught that both of these together are what must be sought; [as stated in the text]: "That which is here in this..."
Having restated, "In the city of Brahman is a small lotus-palace," [the text speaks of] that small ether within that small lotus-palace, and the collection of qualities existing therein.

The meaning is that both of these are enjoined as things to be sought after (*anveṣṭavya*). If it is asked how it is understood that the one designated by the term "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) is the Supreme Brahman, and that the one designated by the phrase "that which is within it" possesses its qualities, and how it is understood that both are enjoined as objects to be sought after by referring to them with the word "tat" (that), listen with an attentive mind: having declared the extreme greatness of the small ether in the passage, "As large as this external ether is, so large is this ether within the heart," [the text continues], "Both of these... [in this small ether].

"Heaven and earth are contained as it were within it; both fire and wind, both sun and moon, lightning and the stars. Having thus pointed out that very space under discussion by saying "in this," and having stated that it is the substratum of the entire world including the self, [the text continues]: "Whatever exists here of his, and whatever does not exist—all that is contained within this."

By the phrase "it is beneficial," the text again refers back to that very same *daharākāśa* (the small ether), stating that whatever collection of objects of enjoyment belongs to this worshiper here in this world, and whatever exists only within the range of his imagination but is not present here [in the physical world], all that collection of enjoyments is contained within this *daharākāśa*. Having thus described the unsurpassed nature of the *daharākāśa* as an object of enjoyment, it further explains that although this *daharākāśa* resides within the heart—which is a constituent part of the body—[its nature remains unaffected] even when the body undergoes decay, destruction, and so forth.

Having stated that [the inner space] is changeless due to its being the ultimate cause and its extreme subtlety, and having established that this very same subtle space (daharākāśa)—which is the true reality, known as Brahman, and the abode of the entire universe—is the "city" by saying, "Therefore, this is the true city of Brahman," [the text] points to the subtle space with the words, "In this, all desires are contained. By designating the desirable qualities as "desires" (kāmāḥ), it states that they reside within that subtle space; thus, it describes the subtle space itself as the locus of those desirable qualities.

Its excellence in auspicious qualities and its nature as the Self are made clear by the passage beginning with "This Self is free from evil" and ending with "whose resolve is true"; then, starting from "For just as here on earth subjects follow [their king]" and ending with "for them there is no freedom of movement in all worlds," [the text describes] this group of eight qualities and the Self qualified by them—designated by the term "the small ether"—as well as the ritual action for those ignorant of this [Self], in order to accomplish objects of enjoyment distinct from it.

Having stated that those who perform [rites] obtain finite results and possess unrealized intentions, [the text continues]: "Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds," and so forth; thus, by means of this passage, the Self designated by the term "small ether" (daharākāśa) and the desirable objects existing within it, which are free from evil, [are described].

For those who know the qualities beginning with freedom from sin belonging to that Great Ocean, the Supreme Person, it is said that the attainment of all desires and the state of having true resolve arise solely through His grace. Therefore, it is determined that the small ether (daharākāśa) is the Supreme Brahman, and the collection of desirable qualities such as freedom from sin existing within it is what is to be sought after and understood. The author of the Vākyakāra also clarifies this in the passage beginning with, "That which is within it: this is the designation of desires.
For these reasons, the small ether is indeed the Supreme Brahman.
For it is seen thus from both movement and sound, as well as from an inferential mark. || 14 ||

For this reason as well, the small ether is the supreme Brahman: "Just as those who do not know the field might pass repeatedly over a hidden treasure of gold and not find it, even so all these creatures, going day after day to this world of Brahman, do not find it, for they are held back by untruth."

By referring to "this" (etam)—the small ether under discussion—the daily departure of all individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) from it, and the designation of that small ether as the "world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*), lead one to understand that the small ether is the Supreme Brahman. To the question, "How do these two [facts] establish its status as the Supreme Brahman?", he replies: "For it is seen thus. In the Supreme...

It is observed elsewhere that the daily departure of all individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) into Brahman during the state of deep sleep is described thus: "In this very way, my dear, all these creatures, having merged into Being, do not know, 'We are merging into Being,'" and "Having come from Being, they do not know, 'We are coming from Being. Likewise, the term "Brahma-world" (*brahmaloka*) is seen used for the Supreme Brahman: "This, O King, is the Brahma-world," he said.

Let it not be that there is no observation of going elsewhere to Brahman; rather, this very fact—that all individual souls (kṣetrajñas) abide within this small ether (daharākāśa) during deep sleep, with all suffering dispelled as if at the time of cosmic dissolution—is sufficient evidence for its being the Supreme Brahman. Likewise, the term "Brahma-world" (brahmaloka), when used in apposition with this small ether, is sufficient evidence for its being Brahman without depending on any other usage. Thus he says, "And the indicative mark.
And by the principle of the "chief of the Niṣādas" (niṣādasthapati-nyāya), the genitive case is [to be understood as a partitive genitive].

In brief, the logical principle is that of a compound with a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*). Alternatively, the phrase "going day after day" does not refer to movement pertaining to deep sleep; rather, it refers to those who, though going higher and higher day after day—meaning existing at all times—over the *daharākāśa* (the small ether) which dwells eternally as the inner self and constitutes the supreme human goal, do not know him and thus do not find or obtain him.

The meaning is as follows: just as those who do not know the location of a buried treasure of gold do not find it even though they are constantly walking over it, so it is here. Thus, the constant movement of all creatures—who, though governed by it, remain unaware—over this small ether (daharākāśa) which abides as the inner self, leads to the understanding that this small ether is the Supreme Brahman.

For thus, elsewhere, the non-perception by creatures—who abide within [the Lord] and are governed by Him—of the Supreme Brahman existing as their inner self is observed. As in the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa: "He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body the self is, who controls the self from within"; and also, "The unseen seer, the unheard hearer. Let it be that such a perception is not found elsewhere; [yet it is established here].

Moreover, for one who has personally realized through the analogy of the treasure that this [Self] residing in the heart is the supreme human goal, the fact that all creatures—though ignorant—constantly and daily resort to it as their support is sufficient evidence for its being the Supreme Brahman. And for this reason also, the "small ether" (daharākāśa) is the Supreme Brahman:
because of the holding of its greatness within it. (Sūtra 1.3.15)

Now, having pointed out the previously mentioned small ether (daharākāśa) with the words "Now, that which is the Self," the scripture declares its support of the universe in the passage, "It is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded"; this being heard, it leads to the conclusion that the small ether is the Supreme Brahman.

For the sustenance of the world is the majesty of the Supreme Brahman, as stated in such passages as: "He is the Lord of all, He is the Sovereign of all beings, He is the Protector of beings, He is the Bridge, the Sustainer, so that these worlds may not be confounded," and "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and moon stand held apart. This very majesty of the Supreme Brahman, known as "sustenance," is perceived within this small ether (daharākāśa); therefore, the small ether is the Supreme Brahman.
And because of common renown. || 16 ||

Furthermore, the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is well-known in the sense of the Supreme Brahman in such passages as: "For who indeed could breathe, who could inhale, if this ether were not bliss? and "All these beings, verily, arise from the ether alone," and so forth. The intention is that the well-known usage [of the term] for Brahman—endowed with attributes such as being free from sin—is more authoritative than the well-known usage for the elemental ether.
Thus, the view that the small ether is the elemental ether has been refuted. Now, having raised the possibility that the small ether is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), he begins to refute it.
If it be argued that "he" refers to another [deity] because of a subsequent reference, we say no, because of impossibility. || 17 ||

As for what was stated—that on account of the remainder of the passage, the small ether (*daharākāśa*) is the supreme Brahman—that is incorrect; because in the remainder of the passage there is a direct reference to the individual soul (*jīva*), which is other than the supreme, as in: "Now, that serene being (*samprasāda*), having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form; 'This is the Self,' he said; 'This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.'"

Although the elemental ether cannot be intended here—since it is impossible for the ether taught as being situated within the lotus of the heart in the passage, "The small ether within this," to stand in the relationship of simile and thing compared—nevertheless, on account of the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), it is proper to resort to the view that it is the inner Self (*pratyagātman*). If it is argued that the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) may also refer to the individual soul (*jīva*) because of its association with luminosity and other qualities, the answer here is: "No, because of impossibility. This is not the individual soul, for qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth are not possible in the case of the individual soul. And [the Sūtra continues]: "If it be said that [the soul is meant] on account of what follows, [we reply] no, because of the manifestation of its true nature. (1.3.18)

If it is argued that from the subsequent statement of Prajāpati, the connection of the qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) is determined to belong to the individual soul (*jīva*) alone, then this is what is meant: the statement of Prajāpati refers exclusively to the individual soul.

For instance, having heard as a traditional report the words of Prajāpati: "That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand; he who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all desires," Prajāpati [proceeded] to [teach] Maghavan, who had approached him with the desire to know the nature of the Self to be sought, by means of the individual soul (jīvātman) in its embodied state through the successive stages of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

Having instructed Indra—who was desirous of hearing and whose fitness had been tested—by pointing out various objects of enjoyment, [the Teacher] spoke to him, who was now fit for instruction regarding the nature of the pure Self: "O Maghavan, this body is indeed mortal, seized by death; it is the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of that immortal, bodiless Self.

Thus he declared the body to be the substrate and the Self to be the inhabitant (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), and stated that the bodiless Self has immortality as its essential nature. Then he said: "For one who possesses a body, there is no removal of pleasure and pain."

The passage, "Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless," describes how one joined to a body commenced by karma experiences pleasure and pain corresponding to that karma, and states their absence upon liberation from it; then, with the words, "In this very way, this serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own true form," it identifies the very nature of the individual self (*jīvātman*) as bodiless.

He taught [him] as being dissociated [from the body]: "That is the supreme person; he moves about there, laughing, playing, and rejoicing, with women, or with chariots, or with kinsmen, not subject to rebirth."

Having described the supremacy of the supreme light to be attained through the words "remembering this body," and having stated that the inner self—whose veils have been removed upon reaching the supreme light—attains enjoyment as it desires in the world of Brahman, as well as freedom from the pleasant and unpleasant and the non-contemplation of undesirable objects such as the body caused by karma, [the text continues]: "Now, where the eye has entered into this space, that is the person in the eye; the eye is for seeing. And he who knows, 'Let me smell this,' he is the Self."

"He who knows 'let me smell this'—he is the Self; speech is for the purpose of utterance. He who knows 'let me speak this'—he is the Self; hearing is for the purpose of hearing. He who knows 'let me hear this'—he is the Self; the mind is his divine eye. Thus, it is established that the eyes and other organs are instruments (*karaṇa*), while form and other objects are the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).

Having thus demonstrated its nature as a knower and established its distinction from the body and the senses on that very basis, [the text] states: "He, indeed, with this divine eye—the mind—sees these desires and rejoices, which are in the world of Brahman. This declares the experience of all desires by that very self, whose body and senses have been shaken off, through a divine, innate knowledge denoted by the word "mind. Furthermore, it says: "The gods meditate upon this very Self; therefore, all worlds are attained by them, and all..."

Having stated that "the knowers of the Self know the Self as being thus characterized," and having declared the fruit for one who knows such a Self—namely, the experience of Brahman characterized by the attainment of all worlds and all desires, as Prajāpati said: "He who, having found that Self, understands It, obtains all worlds and all desires"—it is understood that in this context, the individual soul (jīva) alone, possessing qualities such as freedom from sin, is the subject introduced as that which is to be known.

Therefore, if it is argued that qualities such as being free from evil (apahatapāpmatva) are impossible for the individual soul (jīva), and that consequently, because these qualities are possible for the jīva mentioned in the supplementary portion of the "small" (dahara) passage, it is determined that the jīva itself is the small ether (daharākāśa).

Regarding this, he says: "But [the Self] whose true nature has become manifest... Previously, his own nature was characterized by qualities such as being free from sin, though these were concealed by unreality; subsequently, having risen out of the body and attained the supreme light, with the bonds of karma liberated, his true nature becomes manifest, and it is this self, distinguished by qualities such as freedom from sin, that is described in the Prajāpati passage. However, in the Dahara passage, the small ether (daharākāśa) is understood precisely as being characterized by an unobscured nature and freedom from sin.

Even for the individual soul (*jīva*) whose true nature has been manifested, qualities such as being a bridge and supporting all the worlds—which are otherwise impossible for it—are established as proving that the inner space (*daharākāśa*) is the Supreme Brahman, since these qualities are understood from the etymological definition of the word "Satya" (Truth) to consist in the governance of both the sentient and the insentient. We shall demonstrate in the section on "The Exclusion of World-Activity" (*jagadyāpāravarjam*) that being a bridge and supporting all the worlds are not possible even for one whose nature has been manifested. If this is so, one might ask: for what purpose is the introduction of the individual soul in the Dahara passage with the words, "Now, he who is this person in the eye," and so forth? To this, [the author] says:
And the reference has another purpose. (Sūtra 19)

The reference here to the individual soul (jīva) mentioned in the Prajāpati discourse is intended to teach a quality unique to the Supreme Person—namely, His being the cause [of liberation]—by describing how the liberated soul, through attaining that [Inner Space], acquires its own natural form characterized by auspicious qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, just as the small space (*daharākāśa*) itself possesses these qualities. Furthermore, in the Prajāpati discourse, the knowledge of the true nature of the liberated self is taught for the purpose of its utility in the Dahara-vidyā.

For the individual soul (jīvātman) who desires Brahman, its own true nature must indeed be known; for even while being possessed of auspicious qualities himself, he will experience the Supreme Brahman, which possesses an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities. Since the knowledge of the true nature of one's own self is included within the fruit of the meditation on Brahman, the results proclaimed in the Prajāpati-vākya—such as "he attains all worlds and all desires" and "there he moves about, laughing and playing"—are likewise the fruits of the Dahara-vidyā alone.
If it be argued that [the knowledge] is of little hearing, that has already been answered. || 20 ||

The scriptural mention of small size in the phrase "small within this" is appropriate only for the individual soul (jīva), which is compared to the point of an awl, and not for Brahman, who is greater than all and whose nature is the opposite of that. || 21 ||

Because of its conformity to that inner space, which is the supreme Brahman, this inner self—characterized by qualities such as being free from evil and released from bondage—is not the small space itself. "Conformity" means similarity to it. For indeed, the conformity of the liberated inner self to the supreme Brahman is heard in scripture: "When the seer sees [the Self]..."

"The wise one, having shaken off merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality with that golden-hued maker, the Lord, the Puruṣa, the source of Brahman. Therefore, the imitator is the one specified in the Prajāpati passage, and the object of imitation is Brahman, the small ether (daharākāśa).
It is also recorded in the Smṛti. || 22 ||

Even for those in the state of transmigratory existence, it is recorded in the Smṛti that in the state of liberation there is an imitation of the Supreme Brahman characterized by the attainment of supreme similarity: "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained My own nature; even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer.
