Some maintain that the two sūtras, "On account of its imitation" (anukṛtes tasya ca) and "And it is also recorded in the Smṛti" (api smaryate), constitute a separate section (adhikaraṇa) intended to determine that the scriptural passage, "Everything shines after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined," refers to the Supreme Brahman.

However, that [interpretation] is improper because the two sections beginning with "The Invisible" (Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa) establish that the context concerns the Supreme Brahman, and because the nature of the Supreme Brahman as consisting of light is understood from such passages as "Light, because of the mention of feet" (Jyotiścaraṇābhidhānāt); thus, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) does not arise, and there is a discordance with the very syllables of the Sūtras.
He is known from scripture alone. || 23 ||

In the *Kaṭhavallī* it is heard: "A person the size of a thumb dwells in the middle of the self, the lord of what has been and what is to be; one does not shrink away from him. This indeed is that. "A person the size of a thumb, like a smokeless light, the lord of what has been and what is to be; he alone is today, he is tomorrow. This indeed is that. "The person the size of a thumb is the inner self, ever seated in the heart of men. One should draw him out from one's own body with fortitude, as one extracts a stalk from a reed."

"One should know that as the bright, immortal. Regarding this, a doubt arises: Is this one measured by the size of a thumb the individual self (pratyagātman), or the supreme self (paramātman)? What is the reasonable conclusion? That it is the individual self. Why? Because elsewhere the individual soul is heard to be of the size of a thumb: "The lord of life moves about according to its own actions."

"One who is the size of a thumb, whose form is like the sun, and who is endowed with volition and egoism. Nor is the Supreme Self heard of as being the size of a thumb anywhere else even for the purpose of meditation. When the individual soul (jīva) is thus determined, its lordship (*īśānatva*) may be understood in relation to the body, the senses, the objects of enjoyment, and the instruments of enjoyment.
This being the position reached, we reply: "He is measured by the word itself. The Supreme Self is measured by the thumb. Why? From the word itself: "The Lord of the past and the future."

Furthermore, it is not possible for the individual soul (jīva), which is subject to its own karma, to be the ruler of all that has been and is to be. How then is the supreme Self (paramātman) described as being the size of a thumb? To this he says:
"But [the measure] is with reference to the heart; [the scripture] has man as its intended audience. (24)

Because the Supreme Self exists within the heart of the worshiper for the purpose of being meditated upon, and because the worshiper's heart is the size of a thumb, its measurement as "thumb-sized" is appropriate in relation to that [heart]. Furthermore, the individual soul (jīva) is also measured by a thumb because it resides within the heart; it is precisely in relation to that [heart] that there is the scriptural statement of its being "the size of the tip of an awn."

Since the scripture concerns the qualification of human beings and the possibility of their becoming lay disciples (*upāsaka*) is under consideration, and because the human heart is measured by that respective thumb, there is no fault even if donkeys, horses, snakes, and so forth are not measured by a thumb; this point will remain settled and be concluded later.
"Above that [the heavens] as well, Bādarāyaṇa [holds it possible], because of the possibility. (Sūtra 1.3.25)

It has been stated that the scripture concerning the meditation on Brahman is intended for human beings, in order to establish that the Supreme Brahman can be measured by the span of a thumb. In connection with that, it is now considered whether gods and others also possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, or not. What, then, is the correct position? That gods and others do not possess the qualification. Why? Because of a lack of capacity; for gods and others who are bodiless lack the capacity to accomplish the meditations on Brahman—which are supported by the seven means such as the liberation from desire—and to bring them to completion.

Furthermore, we do not find any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the corporeality of the gods and others. Although the Vedāntic statements attain the status of valid knowledge regarding the supreme Brahman—even though that reality is already established—because it is possible to derive an understanding of it through linguistic usage, nevertheless, not a single statement is found whose primary purpose is to establish that the gods and others possess a physical form (*vigraha*). As for the Mantras and the Atharva-vidhānas, because they are subordinate to ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*), they have other purposes and are thus incapable of proving the corporeality of the gods and others.

Furthermore, the ritual injunctions do not accomplish anything pertaining to the deities other than making them the objects (uddeśya) required by those rites. For this very reason, it is impossible for them to possess any desire [for the fruits of such rites]. Therefore, due to the absence of both capacity and desire, gods and others lack qualification [for Vedic rituals].

Such being the position reached, we reply: "Beyond that too, Bādarāyaṇa [holds there is qualification], because of the possibility. Beyond that—that is, even among the gods and others—meditation upon Brahman is possible; the venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains this because both their desire and their capacity are possible.

First of all, the desire [to know] arises from being tormented by unbearable internal and other sufferings, and from the knowledge that the Supreme Brahman—whose scent of every defect has been dispelled and who possesses an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities—is the object of unsurpassed enjoyment. Capability also arises from possessing a more refined body, sense organs, and so forth. And the possession of a body, sense organs, and so forth is heard of in all the Upaniṣads within the sections on creation and the sections on meditation concerning Brahmā and the others.

For instance, beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) and "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'; It emitted heat" (ibid. 6.2.3), [the text] describes all insentient matter—starting with fire, water, and earth—in their various specific states; then, having resolved, "Entering by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms," it is stated that [Brahman] created the fourfold collection of beings from Brahmā down to the stationary objects, each possessing a body appropriate to its respective karma and bearing a name suited to it.

Thus, in all passages concerning creation, a fourfold creation consisting of gods, animals, humans, and stationary beings is recorded in the scriptures. Furthermore, the distinction between gods and the other classes depends upon the connection with bodies, sense organs, and so forth, which are suitable for experiencing the fruits residing in the fourteen worlds—beginning with the world of Brahmā—in accordance with their respective karmas; for the selves do not possess the status of gods and so forth by their own nature.

Likewise, in the passage beginning with, "Then both the gods and the asuras understood this; they said, 'Indra indeed departed from among the gods and Virocana from among the asuras; the two of them, without having come to an agreement, approached Prajāpati with fuel in their hands'; and 'The two of them lived the life of students for thirty-two years; Prajāpati said to them,'" the fact that the gods and others possess bodies and sense organs is clearly perceived. Furthermore, even in the mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) which are supplementary to the injunctions for ritual action (*karmavidhi*), such as "Vajrahasta Purandara" and "By him Indra... [the same is evident].

The possession of a physical body and so forth, as understood from such passages as "He who has arisen as a thunderbolt," is indeed an object of knowledge (*prameya*) that is not contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor can it be asserted that the intended meaning of another thing perceived [in the text] is not meant to be expressed, on the grounds that the passage is either for the purpose of revealing a matter to be performed or for the purpose of praise; for it serves the function of praise and the like, and without it, praise and so forth would be untenable. Indeed, the status of being praise (*stuti*) arises through the description of qualities (*guṇa*); if the qualities were non-existent, the very status of being praise would be lost.

Furthermore, no persuasion arises from a quality that does not exist; therefore, explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) persuade toward action precisely by making known the actual existence of such qualities. And the ritual formulas (*mantras*) are likewise employed in rituals.

The injunctions (vidhis), by illuminating the matters to be performed—which serve to effect something in various contexts—do indeed accomplish something there by expressing specific qualities such as the embodied form of deities and so forth; otherwise, the recollection of Indra and others would be untenable. Furthermore, a deity devoid of attributes cannot enter the mind. In that regard, having themselves made known the qualities not obtained through other means of knowledge, they either incite one toward the ritual action through those qualities, or they illuminate the deity as qualified by those attributes.

Having restated those [qualities] already established, they perform the functions of recommendation and illumination; however, when there is a contradiction, they indicate non-contradictory qualities through words expressive of those [contradictory ones]. Furthermore, the injunction of ritual action necessarily requires the sovereignty of the deity; for an action enjoined as something to be performed by one desiring a result, being itself perishable in a moment, requires an agent that can bring about a fruit such as heaven occurring at a later time.

Furthermore, in the case of mantras and arthavādas—such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; he [the sacrificer] approaches Vāyu with his own portion; he (Vāyu) leads him to prosperity," and "Whatever he prays for with this oblation, may he obtain that, may he prosper in that, may the gods grant that to him"—the fact that the deity, when propitiated by the ritual act, bestows the fruit, and the sovereignty corresponding thereto, are perceived and thus required, they are integrated into the meaning of the sentence. Devapū...

From the verbal root *yaj*, which denotes the act of sacrifice (*yāga*), there is understood an action known as sacrifice whose primary focus is the deity to be propitiated. Thus, by a thorough consideration of the entire sentence, everything required by the injunction is understood from the sentence itself; therefore, it is unnecessary to postulate that something like the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*)—which was not understood at the time of linguistic acquisition—is either the denotation or the objective basis in ritual injunctions. Similarly, in the Dharmaśāstras, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, which are rooted in the Brāhmaṇas, Mantras, and Arthavādas, [the status of] Brahmā and the other gods and asuras...

The distinct natures, abodes, enjoyments, functions, and so forth of [the gods] beginning with Prajāpati—such as their bodies, sense organs, and the like—are clearly established; therefore, because they possess embodied forms and other such attributes, gods and others indeed possess the qualification [for ritual action].
If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe multiple ways of attaining [the goal]. || 26 ||

If one accepts that deities and others possess physical bodies and so forth, a contradiction with respect to ritual action (*karman*) would follow; for in the case of many sacrifices performed simultaneously, it would be impossible for a single Indra possessing a body to be present when summoned by such invocations as "O Agni, bring Agni hither" and "O Indra, come hither; O Lord of Bay Steeds, come hither."

Furthermore, the arrival of Agni and others at various places is shown in such passages as: "To whose sacrifice do the gods come, and to whose not? Of many sacrificers, he who first secures the deities sacrifices to them on the following day. If it is argued that there would thus be a contradiction regarding ritual action if [the gods] possessed bodies and so forth, that is not so; for we observe the simultaneous assumption of multiple bodies by those possessing power, such as Saubhari and others.
If it be argued that [the world] is [produced from] sound, we say no; because [the world] originates from this [Brahman], as established by both perception and inference. (27)

The term "contradiction" (*virodha*) carries over from the previous context. Let there be no contradiction regarding action, since the assumption of multiple bodies is possible. However, a contradiction would arise with respect to Vedic speech, because of its connection with non-eternal objects. For if [the gods] possessed physical forms, their impermanence would be unavoidable due to their having constituent parts. Consequently, like the word "Devadatta," the Vedic words for Indra and others would either be devoid of referents or themselves non-eternal—existing before the birth of the object Indra and perishing after its death. If this is argued, it is not so.

"Because it originates from that": because the referent such as Indra arises again and again from the very word "Indra" and so forth. What is meant is this: unlike words such as "Devadatta," Vedic words like "Indra" do not function by means of a convention established for a particular individual; rather, they denote a specific form (*ākṛti*) by their very nature, just like the word "cow" and others. Consequently, when one individual Indra has perished, [the word] still revolves in the mind from that very same Vedic word "Indra."

Through the power of *māyā*, the Creator (Hiranyagarbha), having understood the form of the objects such as Indra that are denoted by those words, creates another Indra possessing that very same form; just as a potter, from the word "pot" revolving in his mind, creates a pot possessing that very form. How is this known? By perception and inference—that is, by *śruti* and *smṛti*.

First, there is the Śruti: "By means of the Veda, Prajāpati differentiated the two forms, the existent and the non-existent"; likewise: "He uttered 'Bhūḥ', he created the earth; he uttered 'Bhuvaḥ', he created the intermediate space," and so forth. [The Lord], recollecting the specific arrangement of each respective object preceded by its expressive word, [creates] that object as characterized by that particular arrangement.

The meaning is that he created each respective object. There is also a Smṛti passage: "This speech, beginningless and endless, consisting of the Veda, was emitted by the Self-existent in the beginning as divine, from which all emanations proceed"; and: "He, moreover, at the beginning fashioned separately the names and the actions of all things, as well as their distinct arrangements, from the words of the Veda alone. "Arrangements" (saṃsthāḥ) means structures, that is to say, forms; likewise: "The name and form of beings, and the detailed expansion of their functions..."

"In the beginning, he created the gods and others from the very words of the Veda. Therefore, even though the gods and others possess physical bodies, there is no futility of the Vedic words, nor does it follow that the Veda has a beginning in time.
And for this very reason, it is eternal. || 28 ||

Precisely because words such as *Indra* and *Vasiṣṭha*, which denote those sages, denote their respective forms, and because the creation of those respective objects is preceded by the recollection of those respective meanings through those respective words, for that very reason [the texts state]: "He chooses the composers of the mantras," "Obeisance to the sages, the composers of the mantras," and "This is that Agni, [belonging] to Viśvāmitra."

Even though Vasiṣṭha and others are perceived as the authors of mantras, the authors of sections (kāṇḍa), and as seers (ṛṣis) through such passages as "the hymn (sūkta) comes into being," the eternity of the Veda remains established. By these very Vedic words, such as "he chooses the makers of mantras," Prajāpati—referring to the generic forms, capacities, and so forth of those seers who are the authors of the respective sections, hymns, and mantras—creates them with those specific forms and endowed with those specific powers, and then appoints them to the composition of those respective mantras and other works.

Empowered by Prajāpati, they too, having performed penance appropriate to each, perceive those very same mantras and other texts—seen previously by Vasiṣṭha and others—which are eternally established, without even studying them, and without error in their accents or phonemes; thus, both the eternity of the Vedas and the status of these individuals as "makers of mantras" (mantrakṛt) are logically established.

Now, it might be argued that in the case of occasional dissolutions (*naimittikapralaya*) and so forth, when Indra and others are produced, the creation of gods and other beings by Prajāpati may indeed be possible through the recollection of previous Indras and others from the words of the Veda. However, in the case of a primordial dissolution (*prākṛtapralaya*), since both the creator Prajāpati and the sound—which is a transformation of the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) consisting of the subtle elements (*bhūta*)—have perished, how can the creation of Prajāpati be established as being preceded by sound?

How can there be eternity for the Veda that has perished in the interval? Therefore, even if one who maintains the eternity of the Veda accepts that gods and others possess embodied forms, one must still resort to the beginninglessness of the stream of worldly usage. To this, he recites the reply:
"And because names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence, as seen from scripture and tradition. (2.1.29)

Even when the entire universe is withdrawn and creation recurs, there is no contradiction whatsoever, precisely because names and forms are the same as previously stated. For instance, that Blessed One...

At the conclusion of the dissolution, Puruṣottama, recollecting the world’s prior configuration and forming the resolve, "May I become many," differentiated the multitude of objects of enjoyment and enjoyers—which had dissolved into him remaining as mere potentiality—and having created the cosmic egg beginning with Mahat and extending up to Hiraṇyagarbha exactly as before, he manifested the Vedas established in their specific former sequences and taught them to Hiraṇyagarbha. Having appointed him to the creation of the world in the forms of gods and others just as previously, he himself also—

He abides as the inner self within that [Veda]; therefore, everything stated above is logically established. This indeed is the non-personal origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) and eternity (*nityatva*) of the Veda: namely, that it is uttered in that very same specific sequence by means of remembering that same particular sequence through the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the sequence of utterances of each preceding generation. This is the same even for me, the Lord of all. The difference, however, is this:

The Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) Himself, without depending on any prior impressions (saṃskāra), connects [the subsequent cognition] by Himself. If it is asked how this aforementioned point is understood, he says: "Because of scripture (darśana) and tradition (smṛti). Scripture, for instance, states: "He who in the beginning fashioned Brahmā and delivered the Vedas to him. Tradition (Smṛti) likewise, that of Manu, says: [He who, having first created the waters... etc.

Beginning with "This was then enveloped in darkness," and continuing up to: "Having meditated, desiring to emit various creatures from his own body, he first created the waters and cast his seed into them. That became a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun. Within that, Brahmā himself was born, the grandfather of all the worlds. Likewise, the Purāṇic account states: "There, O blessed one, a lotus sprang from the navel of the sleeping God; in that lotus was born [Brahmā], the master of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas."

It is said that he spoke thus to the one born from Brahmā: "O high-minded one, create progeny. Likewise: "The supreme deity Nārāyaṇa is the source; from him was born the four-faced one. And likewise: "I shall describe the primordial creation."

Beginning with these words, it is said: "Having created the waters called *nāra*, I remained within them, so that my name might be Nārāyaṇa. In every kalpa, I lie there again; from my navel, while I am thus asleep, let there arise a lotus-born [being]. O Goddess, from the lotus of my navel, the four-faced one was born. He was told by me: 'Create progeny. Jaimini [holds that] because they were not produced in the beginning, there was no authority [for him to create]. (30)

It has been stated that even gods and others possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*); now this is being considered: in those meditations where specific deities themselves are the objects of worship, do they have the qualification for them or not? What is the prima facie view? Jaimini considers that there is no qualification for them in the *Madhu-vidyā* and similar meditations. Why? Because of impossibility. For it is not possible that the Āditya, Vasu, and others who are the objects of worship could be other than the Āditya, Vasu, and others [who are the worshippers]. Nor can the status of being a Vasu and so forth be something to be attained by those who are already Vasus and so forth, because they have already attained it.

In the Madhu-vidyā, it is heard that the portions of the Sun—which, being the substratum of the essence obtained through the rays and accomplished by the rituals taught in the Ṛgveda and other Vedas, receive the designation of "honey"—are to be meditated upon as such, and that the state of being a Vasu and so forth is the goal to be attained. This is stated beginning with, "Yonder sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods," and continuing with, "The Vasus live upon that which is the first nectar," and further, "He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Vasus themselves, becomes satisfied by seeing this very nectar through Agni as his mouth," and so on.
And because of the existence [of the term] in the sense of "light. (31)

"The gods meditate upon that light of lights as life and immortality"—thus, the meditation upon the supreme Brahman as light is heard in scripture regarding the gods. Since it is stated that the gods are the meditators in the meditation on the supreme Brahman, which is common to both gods and humans, this indicates the cessation of their meditation on anything else. Therefore, there is no qualification for the Vasus and others in these [lower meditations]. This being the position reached, it is replied:
"But Bādarāyaṇa [holds] the existence [of qualification], for there is [scriptural evidence]. (1.3.32)

The venerable Bādarāyaṇa considers that even the Ādityas, Vasus, and others possess the qualification for these [meditations]. For it is possible for the Ādityas, Vasus, and others as well to desire to attain Brahman—preceded by their attainment of the state of Vasu and so forth—through the meditation on Brahman in its respective forms. Furthermore, even though they are currently Vasus and so forth, they require the attainment of the state of Vasu and so forth again in another Kalpa.

For here, the meditation upon Brahman in both its causal and effected states is enjoined. Beginning with "That sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods" and continuing until "rising upwards from there," Brahman abiding in specific effected states such as those of Āditya and Vasu is taught as the object of meditation; whereas by the passage beginning "Then, rising upwards from there," Brahman itself in its causal state, abiding as the inner self of the sun, is taught as the object of meditation.

Thus, one who meditates upon Brahman in its state as both cause and effect attains the status of a Vasu or other deity in another kalpa, and at the end of that period, reaches the Supreme Brahman itself, which is the cause. "Indeed, for him, the sun neither rises nor sets."

"For day by day indeed belongs to him who knows this secret doctrine (*brahmopaniṣad*) of the Madhu-vidyā in this way"—since the entire Madhu-vidyā is heard of as a *brahmopaniṣad*, and since its fruit is heard of as consisting in the tasting of the Vasus and others until the attainment of Brahman, it is possible for that portion of the Sun which constitutes the object of enjoyment for the Vasus and others [to be the object of meditation]. And thus, because Brahman alone is the object of worship, such passages as "That the gods know as the light of lights" become appropriate. Regarding this, the author of the Vṛtti says: "For there is indeed the possibility [of Brahman being present] in the Madhu-vidyā and others..."
"Because Brahman alone is to be perceived everywhere. Thus ends the section concerning honey (*madhu-adhikaraṇa*).
For it is indicated by the hearing of that disrespect toward Śuka and by his rushing toward him. || 33 ||

It is now deliberated whether or not a Śūdra also possesses eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). What is the correct view? That he does possess it. Why? Because eligibility is contingent upon desire and capability, and these are possible even for a Śūdra. Although a Śūdra lacks eligibility for those ritual acts accomplished through fire and sacred knowledge (*agnividyā*) because he lacks such fire and knowledge, nevertheless, since the meditation on Brahman consists merely of a mental disposition, he certainly possesses eligibility therein.

Even though meditation requires scriptural action, since only those actions appropriate to one's specific caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama) are required, for a Śūdra as well, the action will simply be service to the higher castes, which is appropriate to his own caste. Furthermore, the statement, "Therefore, a Śūdra is not entitled to the sacrifice," merely reiterates what is established by logic: that he lacks the qualification for rituals such as the sacrifice, which are accomplished through the sacred fires and Vedic knowledge.

Now, one might object: how can the meditation upon Brahman be possible for one who has not studied the Vedas, who has not heard the Vedānta texts, and who is ignorant of the methods of meditating on the nature of Brahman? It is replied: even for one who has not studied the Vedas and has not heard the Vedānta passages, knowledge of the nature of Brahman and its meditation is possible through the hearing of the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*. Furthermore, there is permission for a Śūdra as well to hear the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, as in such passages as: "One should cause the four castes to hear [the Purāṇas], having placed a Brāhmaṇa at their head."

In the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, Vidura and others are seen to be established in Brahman. Likewise, even in the Upaniṣads, the eligibility of a Śūdra for the knowledge of Brahman is perceived in the Saṃvarga-vidyā; for the teacher Raikva, addressing Jānaśruti—who was desirous of service—as "Śūdra," instructs him in the knowledge of Brahman with the words, "Bring these, O Śūdra! By this very mouth you shall cause me to speak," and so forth. Therefore, the eligibility of a Śūdra is indeed possible.

This being the case, it is replied: the eligibility of a Śūdra is not possible, because of a lack of capacity. For one who does not know the nature of Brahman and the method of its meditation, and who is thus ineligible for the recitation of the Vedas, sacrifices, and other rites that are constituent parts thereof, there can be no possibility of the capacity to perform the synthesis of meditation (*upāsanopasaṃhāra*). Furthermore, even if there were a desire in one who lacks capacity, eligibility is not possible. And this incapacity results from the absence of Vedic study.

For just as the injunctions for ritual action do not require other means of knowledge or their prerequisites once the knowledge produced by the study of the Veda—established by the injunction for study directed toward the three higher castes—is obtained, so too it is with the injunctions for the meditation on Brahman. Therefore, since the knowledge acquired through the Veda established by the injunction for study is itself the means for the meditation on Brahman, a Śūdra lacks the capacity for the meditation on Brahman.

Even the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* attain the status of being means [to knowledge] only by augmenting the Vedas, not independently. The permission for a *Śūdra* to hear the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* is for the purpose of attaining fruits such as the destruction of sins, not for the purpose of meditative worship (*upāsanā*). As for Vidura and others, they possessed knowledge because their knowledge acquired in previous births was not lost; however, due to the force of their *prārabdha-karma*, they were joined with such a birth. Thus, their state of being established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭhatva*) is [due to that prior realization].

As for the claim that the address "Śūdra" used in the Saṃvarga-vidyā for the sake of the listener indicates the eligibility of a Śūdra, we say: no. It is indicated rather that grief (śuk) arose in him upon hearing those words of disrespect from the Haṃsa, because he then ran toward Raikva, the knower of Brahman. For it is indicated that grief (śuk) was born in Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa due to his deficiency in the knowledge of Brahman, resulting from hearing the words of disrespect spoken by the Haṃsa; therefore, he is addressed as "Śūdra."

Nor is he [the Śūdra] so by virtue of being the fourth caste. For one who grieves (*śocati*) is a Śūdra; according to the rule "from *śuc*, the suffix *rak* and lengthening of the root," when the suffix *rak* is applied and the vowel of the root is lengthened, with the letter *c* becoming *d*, the form *Śūdra* arises. Therefore, it is precisely the quality of grieving that is indicated by the application of the word "Śūdra," and not a connection with a particular birth-caste (*jāti*).

It is said that Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was one who bestowed much wealth and provided abundant food. While two great souls, who were foremost among the righteous and were pleased with his dharma, were traveling at night not far from him in the form of swans—desiring to instill in him a desire to know Brahman—one of them said to the other: "O Bhallākṣa! O Bhallākṣa! The light of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa is spread out like the sky; do not touch it!"

"May it not burn you! Having heard this statement in the form of praise for Jānaśruti, the other *haṃsa* replied: "Who indeed is this person whom you describe as being like Raikva with the cart? Who is this Jānaśruti whom you speak of as if he were Raikva with the cart—the knower of Brahman, the most excellent in qualities? That knower of Brahman, Raikva alone, is the most virtuous in the world. What quality does this Jānaśruti possess, even though he is endowed with great religious merit, since he is not a knower of Brahman?

The meaning is: "May the splendor produced by his qualities burn me, like the splendor of Raikva. When addressed in this way, being asked by the other, "Who is this Raikva?", he replied: "Whatever good deed is performed anywhere in the world, and whatever knowledge resides in all conscious beings—if both of these are contained within his knowledge and action, he is Raikva."

Having overheard these words of the swan—which, being devoid of knowledge of Brahman, contained self-reproach while simultaneously taking the form of praise for Raikva—Jānaśruti immediately dispatched his steward to search for Raikva. When the steward had found him and returned with that information, Jānaśruti himself approached Raikva, offered six hundred cows, a gold necklace, and a chariot drawn by mules, and entreated him, saying: "O Venerable One, instruct me in that deity upon which you meditate."

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is: "Instruct me regarding that supreme deity whom you worship. And that Raikva, having personally known the three worlds through the power of his yoga, perceived through hearing the words of the swan—which were imbued with disregard caused by Janashruti's lack of knowledge of Brahman—Janashruti's state of being overwhelmed by grief and his status as a Kshatriya. (1.3.34)

Because Jānaśruti is designated as a "giver of much" (*bahudāyī*) by virtue of being a master of charity; because from the passage beginning with "one who has much cooked food" (*bahupākyaḥ*) and ending with "they shall eat my food from all sides," he is understood to be a provider of abundant cooked food; because of his dispatching of a *kṣattṛ* (steward) as expressed in "he, while rising, spoke to the *kṣattṛ*"; and because his status as a ruler of a territory is known from the granting of many villages—therefore, this Jānaśruti is recognized as belonging to the Kṣatriya caste, and not to the fourth caste. || 34 ||

Thus, it has been stated that his status as a Kṣatriya is understood from the introductory narrative; now he says that his status as a Kṣatriya is also understood from the concluding narrative: "And later on, by means of the indicative mark [of the mention] of Caitraratha. (Sūtra 1.3.35)
From the fact that this very Saṃvarga-vidyā is being taught to this Jānaśruti, and from the mention later on of a Kṣatriya named Abhipratārin Caitraratha, his status as a Kṣatriya is understood.

How is it that, by the passage beginning with, "Now, while Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni were being served, a religious student begged of them," and ending with, "O religious student, we worship this [Brahman]," the connection of Kāpeya, Abhipratārin, and the begging religious student with the Saṃvarga-vidyā (the doctrine of the absorber) is understood? Among them, Abhipratārin was a Kṣatriya, while the other two were Brāhmaṇas.

Therefore, in this knowledge, the lineage of a Brāhmaṇa is seen for this [Raikva], while for others it is seen as belonging only to a Kṣatriya, and not to a Śūdra. Consequently, since Jānaśruti is other than Raikva—who is connected to this knowledge—it is proper that he too be a Kṣatriya, and not of the fourth caste. Now, one might object: "In this context, neither the fact that Abhipratārin was a Caitraratha nor his status as a Kṣatriya is heard; so how can this Abhipratārin be a Caitraratha, or how can he be a Kṣatriya? To this, the author says: "On account of an indicative mark (liṅga)."

Now, from the indicative mark of the association with Kāpeya in the passage, "Then [the seers spoke] to Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni," this Abhipratārin's connection with Kāpeya is understood; and elsewhere, in the passage, "The Kāpeyas indeed caused Citraratha to perform sacrifice with this [offering]," the status of being Citraratha is heard for one connected with the Kāpeyas.

Likewise, the Kṣatriya status of Caitraratha is established by the text: "From him was born one named Rathantara, a lord of the Kṣatras among the Caitrarathas. Therefore, it is understood that Abhipratārin was both a descendant of Caitraratha and a Kṣatriya. || 35 ||

Thus, it has been stated that no indicative mark (*liṅga*) is found for the eligibility of a Śūdra in a matter contrary to reason; now, he says that the Śūdra’s lack of eligibility, established by reasoning, is further supported by Śruti and Smṛti: "Because of the reference to sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), and because of the declaration of their absence [in the case of the Śūdra]. (1.3.36)

In the sections concerning the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman, the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*) is referred to in passages such as, "I shall lead you near," and "He initiated him. Furthermore, the absence of the sacraments of initiation and so forth for a Śūdra is declared in such texts as, "There is no sin whatsoever in a Śūdra, nor does he deserve the sacraments," and "The fourth caste is of a single birth and does not deserve the sacraments. || 36 ||
And because activity proceeds when there is a determination of that non-existence. 1.3.37.

"A non-Brāhmaṇa is not entitled to explain this; bring fuel, my dear," [said Śvetaketu]. Since the instruction of knowledge proceeded only after it was determined that Jābāla, who desired to learn, was not a Śūdra, a Śūdra has no entitlement [to Vedic study]. || 37 ||
Because of the prohibition against hearing, studying, and understanding [the Veda]. (1.3.38)

For a Śūdra, hearing the Veda, studying it, and performing its prescribed rites are prohibited by such texts as: "A Śūdra is indeed a walking cemetery; therefore, one should not study in the vicinity of a Śūdra," and "Therefore, a Śūdra, though possessing many cattle, is unfit for sacrifice. The phrase "possessing many cattle" means he is like a beast. Since for one who is [like] a beast, study, knowledge of its meaning, and the performance of its rites are impossible, these too are effectively prohibited. || 38 ||
And because of Smṛti. (1.3.39)

Furthermore, the prohibition of hearing [the Veda] and so forth is recorded in tradition: "Now, if one fills the ears of him who listens to the Veda with molten tin or lac, his tongue is to be cut off for reciting it, and his body is to be torn asunder for retaining it"; and also: "One should not teach him the Dharma, nor should one prescribe a vow for him. Therefore, it is established that the Śūdra has no entitlement [to the study of the Veda]. || 39 ||

However, for those who maintain that Brahman alone—which is consciousness devoid of all distinctions—is the ultimate reality; that everything else is illusory; that bondage is non-ultimate; and that this bondage is removable by the mere knowledge of the true nature of reality arising from the [great] sentence (*mahāvākya*), it cannot be said that Śūdras and others lack qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. This is because even one who is uninitiated, has not studied the Vedas, and has not heard the Vedāntic texts might, from whatever source, learn that "Brahman alone, which is consciousness devoid of all distinctions, is the ultimate reality."
Because of the statement, "Everything else imagined therein is false," there arises the knowledge of the true nature of reality (*vastuyāthātmyajñāna*); and by that alone, bondage ceases.

Furthermore, it cannot be restricted that the arising of knowledge must occur through the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) alone and not through any other sentence, because knowledge is not dependent on a person; for when the causal conditions are present, knowledge arises even against one's will. Nor can it be said that the cessation of bondage occurs only when the true nature of reality is known through a Vedic sentence, because the cessation of delusion occurs whenever the true nature of reality is known by anyone at all—even from human sources—[that Brahman is non-dual pure consciousness devoid of attributes].

Since the cessation of error occurs simply through the arising of knowledge from the statement that "everything else is false," just as the delusion regarding mother-of-pearl as silver is removed for a Brahmin by the words of a trustworthy person—even though those words are of human origin—so too will the cessation of the Lord's delusion occur for a Śūdra as well, through the knowledge of the true nature of reality derived from statements transmitted through the Vedic tradition.

Nor can it be asserted that those who know the Vedas do not speak to Śūdras and others based on such passages as "one should not teach him the Dharma," for those who have realized the identity of Brahman and the Self through sentences such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) abide in the very pinnacle of the Veda; having burnt away all [karmic] entitlements, they are no longer subject to the prohibitions of the scriptural injunctions. Alternatively, knowledge certainly arises in a Śūdra or similar person from a statement uttered by someone who has transgressed the prohibitions.

Nor should it be argued that, just as the delusion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell ceases immediately upon the knowledge of reality produced by a human statement, the world-delusion of a Śūdra does not cease immediately after such knowledge; for even in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, the world-delusion does not cease immediately upon hearing statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). If it is claimed that the statement "That thou art" produces the liberating knowledge only when the latent tendencies toward duality have been eliminated through *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation), then the same applies to human statements for the Śūdra and others as well.

There is no distinction whatsoever. For what is called *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) is the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the meaning of that statement which expresses the identity of Brahman and the Self and is capable of conveying that meaning. It is this very [cultivation] that removes contrary impressions (*viparīta-vāsanā*); thus, you maintain that the injunction for *nididhyāsana* has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*).

Since even the study of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*) and other such practices are useful only for the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), once the desire to know has arisen even in a *śūdra*, and contrary impressions have been removed through *nididhyāsana* and the like based on human-authored statements, knowledge will arise; by that very [knowledge], non-ultimate bondage will cease.

Alternatively, having ascertained—on the basis of perception and inference supported by reasoning—that the entire world, consisting of the manifold and diverse distinctions between knower and known produced by ignorance, is superimposed upon the inner reality which is pure consciousness, devoid of attributes, and the witness of ignorance; and having dispelled contrary latent impressions through constant meditation on such a pure inner reality, even Śūdras and others shall attain liberation by directly realizing that very same inner reality.

Since no purpose whatsoever is seen here for Vedic statements that rely upon infinite extraordinary particulars—such as various false sovereignties and diverse creations—it follows that the eligibility of Śūdras and others alone for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is most excellent. By this very logic, since the realization of Brahman would be established even for Brāhmaṇas and others, the Upaniṣads would be rendered as good as dead.

Nor should it be said that for one who is wandering in the worldly conventions of this non-Vedic world, the desire to understand the operation of perception and inference arises only when someone has presented the claim: "This worldly convention is an error, but the ultimate truth is thus"; for those who are terrified by the fear of worldly existence, it is the Sāṅkhyas and others themselves—who determine the nature of reality through perception and inference—who generate the desire to understand the operation of perception and inference.

And when the desire to know [the truth] has arisen, it is easily discerned through perception and inference—both of which possess distinct natures—that "only eternal, pure, self-luminous, non-dual, and immutable consciousness is real; everything else is superimposed upon it. Furthermore, no further specific attribute is admitted for such a self-luminous reality, even as understood through scripture; for even the scripture, according to your own view, merely serves to negate the superimposed nature that is not that [reality].

Nor should an auxiliary means be sought for the sake of knowing the blissful nature of the existent Self, because its very nature as consciousness—which is distinguished from all other things that do not possess that nature—is itself its blissful nature. However, for one who holds that the knowledge enjoined by the Vedāntic texts as a means to liberation is of the nature of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), and that this worship consists in pleasing the Supreme Person who is the Supreme Brahman, and that this [pleasing] is to be understood solely through scripture—the scripture of worship, moreover, accepts as its own means only that knowledge produced by the study of the Veda after it has been acquired by one refined by initiatory rites (*upanayana*) and the like, when that knowledge is further assisted by the means such as discrimination (*viveka*) and detachment (*vimoka*).

The position is that Puruṣottama, pleased by such worship, liberates the worshiper from bondage by destroying the ignorance born of karma through the granting of knowledge regarding His own essential nature; thus, according to the principle already stated, the eligibility of Śūdras and others for this is established. Thus ends the section on the non-Śūdra (Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa). 9.
Section 6: The Residue (Śeṣa).

Thus, having concluded the discussion on the primary and secondary topics that arose incidentally, [the author] states another reason to support the status of the thumb-sized one as the Supreme Brahman, as understood from his being the lord of what has been and what is to be: "On account of trembling" (1.3.40).

Between these two statements—"The person the size of a thumb stands in the middle of the self"—and "The person the size of a thumb is the inner self"—[we find]: "Whatever there is in this entire world, having issued forth, vibrates with life-breath (*prāṇa*). A great terror, a raised thunderbolt—those who know this become immortal. Out of fear of him, fire burns; out of fear, the sun shines."

"Out of fear of him, Indra, Vāyu, and Death run as the fifth"—this refers to the trembling caused by the great fear arising from that [Puruṣa], wherein the entire world, including fire, the sun, and so forth, abide within this thumb-sized Puruṣa designated by the word "prāṇa," and from which they all emerge.

A trembling is heard [in scripture]. The meaning is that the entire world trembles out of great fear—fear that, upon transgressing his command, what will happen?—as if from a raised thunderbolt or similar weapon. This is because it has the same sense as the statement, "Out of fear of him the fire burns," where the nominative case in the phrase "a great fear, a raised thunderbolt" (*mahadbhayaṃ vajramudyatam*) functions in the sense of the ablative. And this [fear] belongs to the Supreme.

The nature [of this being] is Brahman; for, as it is said: "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable, the sun and the moon stand held apart," and "Out of fear of Him the wind blows, out of fear the sun rises; out of fear of Him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run on. From these [scriptural statements], such sovereign power is understood to belong only to the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣottama. Furthermore, the Puruṣottama is measured by the size of a thumb because of the vision of light (jyotis). 1.3.41.

Between those two very sentences, which have as their subject matter that which is measured by the thumb, there is seen a light of the thumb-measured [being] that is unique to the Supreme Brahman, which obscures all splendors, which is the cause of all splendors, and which is their sustainer: "The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Him alone..."

"Everything shines after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined. This very verse is heard in the Atharva Veda with reference to the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, the quality of being the supreme light is heard everywhere in relation to the Supreme Brahman, as in: "Having attained the supreme light, he appears in his own true form"; "The gods worship Him as the light of lights, as the immortal life"; and "Now, that which is beyond this, the light that shines in the heaven beyond," and so forth.
Therefore, the Supreme Brahman is measured by the size of a thumb. Thus ends the supplementary discussion on the section concerning that which is measured.
Space [is distinct from the Self], because it is designated as being a different entity and so forth. 1.3.42.

In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad it is heard: "That which is called space is indeed the separator of name and form; that which is within them—that is Brahman, that is the Immortal, that is the Self. Regarding this, there arises a doubt: is this entity indicated by the word "space" the liberated self (muktātman), or is it the Supreme Self (paramātman)? What is the reasonable conclusion? That it is the liberated self. Why?

"Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair, and freeing myself like the moon from the mouth of Rāhu, having shaken off the body and being perfected in self, I attain the world of Brahman"—for it is the liberated one who is the subject immediately preceding this; and because by the words "that which is between them," he is designated as being free from name and form. Furthermore, by the words "the ordainer of names and forms," it is he alone who is intended to be characterized by his previous state; for it was he indeed who previously bore the forms and names of the gods and so forth.

Its present state, when completely freed from name and form, is called "that Brahman, that Immortal. And the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is applicable to it as well, because of its association with uncontracted luminosity. But [one might object]: since this is a supplementary portion of the passage concerning the "small" (*dahara*), it is understood to be that very same small ether, and its nature as the supreme Self has already been determined. Not so; for there is the intervention of the Prajāpati discourse. And in the Prajāpati discourse, the nature of the inner Self is described up to its state of liberation.

And immediately following, in the passage beginning "having shaken off evil," that very same one in the state of liberation is introduced. Thus, when it is argued here that "ākāśa" refers to the liberated self, it is replied: "Ākāśa is the Supreme Brahman, because of the designation of being a different entity and so forth. Ākāśa is the Supreme Brahman; why? Because of the designation of being a different entity and so forth. First, as for the designation of being a different entity: "Ākāśa, indeed, is the sustainer of name and form. This quality of being the sustainer of name and form establishes that Ākāśa is a different entity from the inner self (pratyagātman) in its states of both bondage and liberation.

In its bound state, the Self, by its own power of karma, assumes name and form and would not be able to bring them to completion; for one in the state of liberation, the activity of the world is impossible, and thus even less so the capacity to bring name and form to completion. However, it is established by scripture itself that the Lord—who bears the burden of creating the entire universe—is the bringer of name and form: "Entering with this living self, let me manifest name and form," and "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge."

Therefore, in such passages as, "From that, this Brahman is born—name, form, and food," and "The wise one, having fashioned all forms and created names, abides speaking them," it follows that this Ākāśa, which brings forth name and form from the inner self (pratyagātman), is a distinct entity, namely the Supreme Brahman itself. He establishes this very point with the words, "That which is between those two."

Thus [it is said]. Since this space (*ākāśa*) is a distinct entity untouched by name and form (*nāmarūpa*) through its inner essence, it is therefore their "conductor" (*nirvoḍhā*); that is to say, it is the one who brings them forth because it is free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and possesses the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), being Brahman, being the Self (*ātmatva*), and being immortal are included. For qualities such as being the supreme greatness without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika-bṛhattva*) belong only to the Supreme Self; therefore, the "space" here is indeed the Supreme Brahman.

As for the argument that the one recently mentioned as liberated—the one spoken of in the phrase "having shaken off the body"—is the subject [of the subsequent passage], that is not so; for the Supreme Brahman itself is what has been mentioned immediately prior in the words, "I am attaining the world of Brahman. Even though the Supreme Brahman is indicated as the object to be attained by the liberated one who is the attainer, nevertheless, because the liberated attainer cannot possibly possess the capacity to project names and forms and so forth, it must be understood that the Supreme Brahman alone is the object to be attained in that context.

Furthermore, since the "ether" (ākāśa) mentioned here is recognized as the small ether (daharākāśa) under discussion, and since the speech of Prajāpati is intended to describe the nature of the worshipper, it is logical that the very object of worship—the small ether—is concluded here as the goal to be attained. Moreover, the word "ether" has never been seen used for the inner self (pratyagātman). Therefore, the ether here is the supreme Brahman. 42.

Now, it might be argued that there is no other self distinct from the inner self (pratyagātman), because of the teaching of identity and the prohibition of duality. For the inner self in its pure state alone is designated as the Supreme Self (paramātman), the Supreme Brahman, and the Supreme Lord (parameśvara); therefore, the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) to be reached by the liberated soul under discussion cannot be something different from it. Consequently, even the ether (ākāśa) which is the sustainer of name and form must be that very same [Brahman]. To this, the author of the Sūtras replies:
"On account of the difference [of the soul] in deep sleep and at departure" (1.3.43).

The phrase "because of designation" (vyapadeśāt) continues [from the previous sūtra]. Because the Supreme Self (paramātman) is designated as distinct from the inner self (pratyagātman) during deep sleep and departure from the body, the Supreme Self indeed exists as something other than the inner self. For instance, in the Vājasaneyaka: "Which is the Self? [and so forth].

Regarding this very self consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), which is the subject under discussion—the inner self that is ignorant of everything during the state of deep sleep—it is recorded in scripture that it is embraced by the omniscient Supreme Self: "Embraced by the conscious Self (*prājña ātmā*), it knows nothing external, nor anything internal. Likewise, even at the time of departure, it is said: "Mounted by the conscious Self, it goes forth, emitting [the breath]."

Furthermore, for one who is either sleeping or departing [from the body] and is at that time devoid of knowledge, neither embracing nor ascending is possible through union with the Omniscient One Himself. Nor is it possible through another Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), because it is impossible for that other Knower of the Field to be omniscient as well. || 43 ||

For this reason as well, he states that the Supreme Self is an entity distinct from the inner self (pratyagātman), based on such terms as "Lord" (pati) and so forth: "On account of the words 'Lord' and so forth" (1.3.44).

This Embracing Supreme Self is designated by such terms as "Lord" and so forth in subsequent passages: "The Lord of all," "The Ruler of all, the Sovereign of all," "He does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action; He is the Lord of all, He is the Overlord of beings, He is the Protector of beings, He is the Bridge, the Sustainer, so that these worlds may not be confounded. The Brāhmaṇas seek to know Him through the study and recitation of the Vedas... Only by knowing Him does one become a sage."
"Seeking this very world, mendicants go forth into the homeless life"; "He indeed is the great unborn Self, the eater of food, the giver of wealth";

and "The unborn, immortal, fearless Brahman. Furthermore, these attributes—such as being the Lord of all, the sustainer of the universe, and the Lord of all—are in no way possible in the individual self (pratyagātman), even in its state of liberation. Therefore, the ether which is the negation of name and form must be an entity distinct from the liberated self.

However, the teaching of identity—that everything consisting of the conscious and the unconscious has Brahman as its self because it is the effect of Brahman—is established by such scriptural passages as "All this is indeed Brahman, from which it is born, into which it dissolves, and in which it breathes," as has already been demonstrated. Furthermore, the negation of duality follows from that very same source; thus, there is no fault. 43. Thus ends the section concerning the designation of being something else and so forth.
If it be argued that [the Self] is also inferable as being one among many, we say no; for [the scripture] shows that it is grasped as presented through the metaphor of the body. || 1 ||

It has been stated that Brahman—the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe—is the object of inquiry because it is the means for attaining liberation, which is characterized as the supreme human goal; that it is distinct from insentient matter such as *pradhāna* and from both bound and liberated sentient beings; and that it is free from even a trace of anything to be discarded, omniscient, omnipotent, of true resolve, composed of all auspicious qualities, the inner self of all, and possessed of unimpeded sovereignty.

Now, there are certain passages in some [Upaniṣads] that follow the shadow of the doctrine establishing Primordial Matter (pradhāna) as the cause, by means of propounding such things as Primordial Matter and the Spirit (puruṣa), which are non-Brahman in nature according to the established tenets of the Sāṅkhya system.

Fearing that [the elements] might be thought to exist within the branches [of the tree], this [theory] is refuted in order to establish the fact that Brahman alone is the single cause. In the Kaṭha Upaniṣad it is taught: "Higher than the senses are the objects; higher than the objects is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; higher than the intellect is the Great Self; higher than the Great is the Unmanifest; higher than the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa; there is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), established in the Sāṅkhya system as non-Brahman in nature, denoted here by the word "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*), or not? What is the reasonable conclusion? That it is the *pradhāna*. Why? Because it is recognized through the identification of the system of principles established in that [Sāṅkhya] treatise, namely: "The Unmanifest is beyond the Great One (*mahat*); the Person (*puruṣa*) is beyond the Unmanifest"; and because of the negation of any principle beyond the twenty-fifth principle, the Person, as stated in: "There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal."

Therefore, it follows that the unmanifest (avyakta) is the cause. This is what was stated [by the opponent]: "If it be argued that for some, it is inferential" (sūtra 1.4.1). If it be argued that in the recensions of certain branches (śākhins), even the Pradhāna—which is inferential—is taught as the cause, the answer here is "no. It is not the unmanifest.

The *pradhāna*, consisting of truth and non-Brahman, is what is denoted here. Why? Because it is grasped as that which was set forth in the metaphor of the body; that is to say, because the body—which was set forth through the metaphor of a chariot among the self, body, intellect, mind, senses, and objects, all of which were represented in the form of a charioteer, a chariot, and so on—is here grasped by the term "the Unmanifest. This is what is meant: for in the preceding passage it was said, "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself... [and so forth].

By the passage beginning with, "Know the intellect to be the charioteer and the mind indeed as the reins; they call the senses the horses, and the objects their range," and ending with, "He reaches the end of the journey, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu," [the text] describes the seeker who desires to reach the Vaiṣṇava abode—the end of the path of saṃsāra—by metaphorically representing his body and so forth as the chariot and its parts. It shows that he alone whose chariot and other components remain under control reaches the end of the journey, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

Having stated that [the Self] attains [objects], those among the body and so forth—which are represented as the chariot and its parts—that are primary in terms of being subject to control are described by the passage beginning with, "Higher than the senses."

In this context, among those things metaphorically represented as horses—the sense organs—that which is metaphorically represented as the object-field is "higher" insofar as it is that which must be brought under control; for even in one who has mastered the senses, the senses are difficult to restrain when objects are present. Higher than even those is the mind, metaphorically represented as the reins, because when the mind is inclined toward objects, the mere absence of objects is of no avail. Higher than that, too, is the intellect, metaphorically represented as the charioteer, because in the absence of the intellect’s determinative function (*adhyavasāya*), the mind itself is ineffective.

Because it is something to be employed (*ñcitkaratvāt*). Its self, described as the charioteer, is intended primarily as the agent; and because everything here is dependent upon the will of the Self, the Self alone is specified as "the Great One. For this reason also, the body described as the chariot is superior, since all activities of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) directed toward accomplishing any human goal are dependent upon it.

Therefore, for this reason as well, the Supreme Person is the inner self of all others, the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), and the further shore of the path; for everything up to the individual self, as previously described, has its activity dependent upon His will. Indeed, He is also the one who brings about the completion of the meditation performed through the state of being the inner controller. For it will be stated [in the Sūtra] that "the agency of the individual soul depends on Him, because of the scriptural statement to that effect" (*parāttu tacchruteḥ*). He alone is the ultimate limit of the means for accomplishing the meditation on those to be brought under control, and He is the supreme goal to be attained. This is what is now expressed:

"There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal. Likewise, in the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa, [it is said] through passages such as, "He who dwells within the self," and so forth, that everything—

It is stated that "realizing everything, He controls all," and thus, by the text "there is no other seer besides Him," any other controller is negated. Furthermore, in the *Bhagavadgītā*: "The locus, as well as the agent, the various instruments, the diverse and distinct activities, and destiny (daiva) as the fifth. Here, "destiny" refers to Puruṣottama himself, according to the statement: "And I am seated in the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss."

And the means of bringing him under control is precisely taking refuge in him. As it is said: "The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all beings to revolve by his illusory power, as if they were mounted on a machine; seek refuge in Him alone."

Thus, since the senses and so forth—introduced through the metaphorical designations of the charioteer and the rest in the passage beginning with "Know the Self as the rider"—are recognized by their own specific terms in the verse "The objects are indeed higher than the senses," and not the body which was metaphorically represented as the chariot, it is determined by the method of elimination that the body is what is denoted by the term "the Unmanifest" (avyakta). Therefore, there is no possibility whatsoever of the Pradhāna established in the Sāṃkhya system being referred to here.

Nor is there here a recognition of the process of *siddhi* according to that [Sāṃkhya] system, because of the mention of the superiority of objects—sound and the rest—over the senses in the statement, "The objects are indeed superior to the senses. For in their view, sound and the other objects are not the causes of the senses. Furthermore, the statement, "And the mind is superior to the objects," is also not consistent with that system, precisely because [the mind] is not its cause; likewise, "of the intellect... [and so on].

The statement, "the Self is the great, the supreme," is also inconsistent, because it is accepted that the word *buddhi* denotes the principle of *mahat* (the Great). Indeed, it is not possible for the Great to be greater than itself. Furthermore, the qualification of the Great by the word "Self" does not cohere; therefore, only those [elements] presented as metaphors are to be understood. And the text itself shows this: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth."

"But it is seen by subtle seers through a sharp and subtle intellect. And: "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the self of knowledge; he should restrain the knowledge in the Great Self; and he should restrain that in the Peaceful Self."

Having described the difficulty of perceiving this Supreme Person by means of the internal and external organs which are difficult to conquer, the following method for bringing the senses and so forth—which have been compared to horses and other animals—under control is stated: "One should restrain speech in the mind. This means that one should restrain speech within the mind; the sense of the statement is that one should restrain the organs of action and the organs of knowledge, all of which are preceded by speech, within the mind.

In the word *vāk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the second case ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. In *manasī*, the lengthening of the vowel is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) feature of the locative case. Regarding the phrase "he should restrain that in the self of knowledge" (*tadyacchet jñāna ātmani*), one should restrain that mind in the intellect (*buddhi*). Here, by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), the previously mentioned intellect is designated. The expression "in the self of knowledge" (*jñāna ātmani*) is used with different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

The two locative endings [indicate] that one should restrain [the mind] while abiding in the Self; this is the meaning. "One should restrain knowledge in the Great Self" means that one should restrain the intellect within the Great Self, which is the agent. "One should restrain that in the peaceful Self" means that one should restrain that agent in the Supreme Brahman, the inner controller of all. By this transposition, the word *tat* takes a neuter gender. The meaning is that the state of Viṣṇu is to be reached by such a charioteer. [An objection is raised: How can the word *avyakta* (unmanifest) denote the manifest body? To this, he says:
But it is subtle because it is worthy of that.

For the body is that which has reached a particular state of the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) in their undifferentiated (avyākṛta) condition; that undifferentiated state, existing here in the form of the body, is denoted by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta). This is because it is fit for that—namely, because that non-intelligent substance (acidvastu), having undergone modification, is fit for activity as a means to achieve the goals of the person (puruṣārtha), much like a chariot. If the subtle elements in their undifferentiated state are accepted, what is the prejudice against the material cause (upādāna) established in the Sāṅkhya system? For there too, the cause of the elements is indeed called the "Unmanifest. To this he replies:
"On account of its being dependent on That [the Self], it is purposeful" (Sūtra 1.4.3).

The subtle [cause] is purposeful because it is dependent upon the Supreme Person, who is the ultimate cause. This is what is meant: we do not accept the unevolved [Prakṛti] and its specific transformations as having an independent nature; rather, we accept them as the body of the Supreme Person, for they lack existence apart from being of His essence. Indeed, it is by virtue of being of His essence that Prakṛti and the others accomplish their own purposes; otherwise, there would be no distinction between their essential nature, their persistence, and their activity. It is precisely because of this non-acceptance [of independence] that the process established in our system is valid.

Regarding the term “refutation”: for in the Śruti and Smṛti texts concerning the doctrines of the origin and dissolution of the universe, as well as the doctrines regarding the majesty of the Supreme Person, the primary material cause (prakṛti), its transformations (vikṛti), and the individual soul (puruṣa) are mentioned as being of that [Supreme] nature. For example, beginning with “Earth dissolves into water,” it continues: “The subtle elements (tanmātra) dissolve into the principle of egoity (bhūtādi); the principle of egoity dissolves into the Great Principle (mahat); the Great Principle dissolves into the Unmanifest (avyakta); the Unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable (akṣara); and the Imperishable dissolves into Darkness (tamas).”

"In the supreme deity, darkness becomes one. Likewise: "He whose body is the earth, whose body is water, whose body is fire, whose body is air, whose body is space, whose body is the ego, whose body is the intellect, whose body is the unmanifest, whose body is the imperishable, whose body is death—this inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one god Nārāyaṇa. And likewise: "Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, and intellect as well."

This nature of Mine, called egoism, is divided eightfold. But know that this is the lower one; other than this, know My higher nature, which is the life-force, O mighty-armed one, by which this world is sustained. All beings have this as their source.

"Understand that all things are so. I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world. There is nothing whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya. All this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread. And: "The manifest, as well as the unmanifest, the Puruṣa, and Time itself—this very nature which has been described by Me as having the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and these two, the Puruṣa and Prakṛti, both dissolve into the Supreme Self."
"And the Supreme Self, the support of all, the Supreme Lord, is celebrated in the Vedas and in the Upanishads by the name Viṣṇu. Also:
"And because there is no statement [in the scripture] that he is an object of knowledge. (Sūtra 1.1.4)

If that which is established in the Tantras were intended here as the Unmanifest (avyakta), then its status as an object of knowledge (jñeyatva) would have been intended; for those Tāntrikas who assert that liberation comes from the knowledge of the Manifest, the Unmanifest, and the Knower admit that all of these are objects of knowledge. Yet, this [Unmanifest] is not stated here to be an object of knowledge. Therefore, what is established in the Tantras is not what is being grasped here. || 4 ||
If it be argued that [the Self] speaks, we say no; for it is the intellect (prajñā) that speaks, as is evident from the context.

If it is argued that the Śruti passage—"Having perceived that which is soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying, likewise tasteless, eternal, and odorless; which is without beginning or end, beyond the Great (Mahat), and fixed—one is liberated from the jaws of death"—speaks of the Unmanifest (Avyakta) as the object of knowledge, this is not so; for in this verse, the Prājña, the Supreme Person alone, is presented as the object to be perceived: "But the man who has discernment as his charioteer and holds the mind with the reins... [Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.3–4].

"He reaches the end of the journey, that highest step of Viṣṇu. [And as for the verse: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; but it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect"—because it is the *prājña* (the conscious one) who is the subject under discussion here; for this very reason, the statement "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa" is not a denial of anything other than the twenty-fifth principle (*pañcaviṃśaka-puruṣa*). Furthermore, the attributes of that Supreme Puruṣa, such as being "inexpressible by sound" (*aśabda*) and so on, are well-known from such scriptural passages as "That which is invisible, ungraspable," etc. And even the phrase "higher than the Great" refers to the "Great Self" (*mahān ātmā*) of the intellect (*buddhi*).
The word "paraḥ" (the Supreme) expresses precisely the transcendence of the individual self (jīvātman) previously under discussion. || 5 ||
And thus, the presentation and the question refer only to these three.

For in this section, there is indeed an introduction of only three things—the means (upāya), the goal (upeya), and the attainer (upetṛ)—as objects to be known; and a question regarding them is seen, but not concerning anything else, such as the Unmanifest (avyakta) and so forth. To explain:

Naciketas, desiring liberation, having obtained through the first of the three boons granted by Death his father’s goodwill—which provides for the soul’s fitness for the goals of human life—chose as the second boon the knowledge of the Nāciketa fire, which serves as a means to liberation, saying: "O Death, you who know the fire that leads to heaven, teach it to me who have faith; those who reach the heavenly worlds attain immortality; this I choose as my second boon."

In this context, by the word "heaven" (svarga), liberation (mokṣa), characterized as the supreme human goal, is denoted; for it is said that "they partake of immortality," and for one situated therein, there is no birth or death.

Because of the subsequent mention of the state of being (*bhāva*), and because of the observation of a censure of actions that yield perishable fruits; and because of the reply: "The one who has kindled the *Nāciketa* fire thrice, having attained the union by means of the three, the performer of the three-fold action, transcends birth and death. By means of the third boon, through the inquiry into the nature of liberation, the nature of the goal, the nature of the attainer, and the nature of the meditation supported by action were asked: "This doubt which exists among men—some say it exists, and others say it does not exist."

"Having been instructed by you in this knowledge, this is the third of my boons. When liberation had thus been requested, [the Teacher], having examined his fitness for that instruction, taught him: "Him who is difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret cave, situated in the depths, the Ancient One..."

"Having known the God through the attainment of internal yoga, the wise man leaves behind both joy and sorrow. Since this has been taught in general terms, Naciketas, being pleased, asks again in order to resolve any contradiction regarding the essential nature of the following: the God who was indicated as the object of meditation in the phrase "having known the God," who is described as the goal to be attained; the individual self (pratyagātman) who was indicated as the attainer in the phrase "through the attainment of internal yoga"; and the meditation on Brahman which was indicated in the phrase "the wise man leaves behind both joy and sorrow."
He asked: "Apart from dharma and apart from adharma, apart from this that has been done and what has not yet been done, apart from the past and the future—that which you perceive, tell me."

"Tell me that. Thus, when the triad—distinct from all else, whether past, future, or present, and distinct from the goal, the means, and the agent—had been questioned, [the Teacher], having first praised the *praṇava*, explained it as follows, while again describing in general terms the nature of the object to be attained which is denoted by it, the nature of the attainer contained within it, and the means which is its expressive form: "That state which all the Vedas proclaim, which all austerities declare, and desiring which they lead a life of celibacy—that..."

"I shall state the word in brief: it is 'Om'. Having taught thus, and having further praised the *praṇava*, he first describes the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), the attainer, with the words beginning, "The wise one is neither born nor does he die," and so forth.

While teaching the nature of the supreme Brahman Viṣṇu, who is to be attained, through the passage beginning with "smaller than the small" and ending with "who indeed knows where He is," [the Upaniṣad] states in the middle—through the verse beginning "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing"—that the worship which serves as the means is of the nature of devotion (*bhakti*).

And by the passage, "The two drinking the Truth (ṛta)," the Teacher has stated that the object of meditation exists together with the meditator, thus making it easy to meditate upon; then, from the words "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot" up to "the poets call that a difficult path," He has described the method of meditation and the attainment of the supreme station of Viṣṇu for the meditator. Finally, He concludes with the passage beginning, "Soundless, touchless. Therefore, only these three are presented here as objects of knowledge and are the subject of the questions; hence, there is no reference here to the "Unmanifest" (avyakta) of the Sāṅkhya system. || 6 ||
And like the Great [Self]. || 7 ||

Just as in the passage, "The Great Self is superior to the intellect," the term *mahat* (the Great) is not understood as the principle established in the Sāṅkhya system because of its grammatical coordination with the word *ātman* (Self); so too, since the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is designated as being superior to the Self, it is established that it is not the Unmanifest as established in the Sāṅkhya system that is intended here.
It is like the cup, because there is no distinction.
