Here too, it is the system established by the Tantras that is being refuted, not the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the great principle (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth, which are essentially Brahman; for their Brahman-nature is established by both Śruti and Smṛti. As the followers of the Atharva Veda recite: "She who produces transformations, who is ignorance, who has eight forms, who is unborn and eternal—she is meditated upon as presided over by Him; she is stretched out and impelled again by Him; and presided over by Him alone, she brings forth the world for the sake of the Puruṣa."

She is white, without beginning or end, the mother, the source of all beings; she is white, black, and red, the cow of plenty for the Lord. The ignorant children drink her indiscriminately, following their own whims.
But the one God drinks her at his own will, following his own power. By means of meditation and action, that omnipresent Lord forcibly enjoys her, who is common to all.

"The milch-cow being milked by the sacrificers"—thus the unmanifest, which consists of twenty-four principles, is called the manifest. Herein, the essential nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the other categories has been stated. That Supreme Person, of whose nature these [categories] beginning with primordial matter consist, is also described as such: "They call Him the twenty-sixth; others, however, the twenty-seventh."

It is established that "the Atharvaśiras knows the Person (puruṣa) as devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) according to Sāṅkhya"; furthermore, other followers of the Atharva Veda study [the text]: "Eight are the primary natures (prakṛtis), sixteen are the transformations (vikāras)"; and the Śvetāśvataras likewise declare the nature of Prakṛti, Puruṣa, and Īśvara: "The Lord sustains this entire universe—the perishable and the imperishable, the manifest and the unmanifest—while another, who is not the Lord, is bound due to the state of being an enjoyer."

"Having known the God, one is released from all bonds. "The two unborn ones—the Knower and the Unknower—are the Lord and the Unlord; for the Unborn is indeed one, joined with the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment. And the infinite Self, whose form is the universe, is the non-agent. When one perceives this triad as Brahman... "The perishable is the primary matter (pradhāna), the immortal and imperishable is Hara; the one God rules over both the perishable and the Self. Through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and by His power, there occurs at the end the cessation of the entire illusion (māyā). Likewise: "The meters, sacrifices, seasons, and vows..."

"The past, the future, and that which the gods speak of—the Magician (Māyī) creates all this from Him, and another, bound by His Māyā, resides within it. Furthermore: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the wielder of Māyā as Maheśvara; by His constituent parts, this entire world is pervaded. Likewise, later on:

"The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas, is the cause of bondage, stability, and liberation in saṃsāra. Smṛti also says: "One should know both Prakṛti and Puruṣa to be indeed beginningless."

Know that both the modifications and the qualities arise from Nature (prakṛti). Nature is said to be the cause in the agency of action and its instruments; the Person (puruṣa) is said to be the cause in the experience of pleasure and pain. Although the Person resides in Nature, it experiences the qualities born of Nature. Attachment to these qualities is the cause of its births in good and evil wombs. Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are the qualities born of Nature; they bind the immutable embodied soul within the body, O mighty-armed one.

Likewise: "O son of Kuntī, at the end of a kalpa all beings go to my own nature; again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth. Taking hold of my own nature, I repeatedly send forth this entire multitude of beings, which is powerless under the sway of nature. Under my supervision, nature produces the world of the moving and the unmoving. It is by this means, O son of Kuntī, that the world undergoes its cycles."

Therefore, those principles such as *prakṛti* established in the Sāṅkhya system are refuted on the grounds that they are not identical with Brahman. In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad it is heard: "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form; the one unborn male, enjoying her, lies by her, while another unborn male leaves her after he has experienced his enjoyment. Regarding this, there is a doubt: does this mantra refer to *prakṛti* as established solely in the [Sāṅkhya] system, or is she of the nature of Brahman?

What is correct? That it is "alone. Why? Because this primordial matter (*prakṛti*), described as "the one unborn," is heard to be non-productive; and because it is heard that she is the independent creator of many similar offspring, as stated in the passage, "creating many diverse offspring of her own form. This being the position reached, it is replied: "Like the cups, because there is no distinction."

Because the term *ajā* (the unborn) merely establishes the state of being unborn by stating "it is not born," no specific distinction is perceived when referring to the *ajā* established in the *Tantra* (the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*) as being non-Brahman in nature. This is like the case of the *camasa* (sacrificial cup); just as in the mantra, "The *camasa* is hollow below and broad above," the word *camasa* conveys only that the object is an implement for drinking, and one does not perceive a specific type of *camasa* from that alone, because derivative (*yaugika*) words cannot determine a specific meaning without the context of the subject matter and other factors.

In that case, just as the determination that the head is the *camasa* (cup) is made by the remainder of the passage beginning with, "As this head is a cup with its mouth below and its bottom above," so too here the *ajā* (goat/she-goat) must be determined by means of the sense, context, and other such factors; and there are no reasons such as sense or context present here for taking the *ajā* as established in the [Tantric] system.

[The Jā] is seen [in the mantra], yet its status as a creator independently is not accepted; for from the phrase "creating many offspring," there is only the perception of the quality of being a creator. Therefore, by this mantra, the Jā that is non-Brahmanic in nature is not denoted. (8) He states that there is a specific reason for accepting the Jā as being of the nature of Brahman: "But [the Jā] begins with light, for thus it is studied by some. (9)

The word *tu* (but) is for the purpose of emphasis; this *ajā* (the unborn) has light as its beginning (*jyotirupakramā*), for light is Brahman, as is well known from such scriptural passages as, "That indeed is the light of lights," and "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven."

The meaning is that [the creation] begins with light and has Brahman as its cause; for this reason is stated by the phrase "so indeed some recite. Because some branches of the Veda—the Taittirīyas—recite that this Unborn (ajā) has Brahman as its cause: "Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, the Self is hidden in the cave of this creature. Having thus declared that Brahman is present within the cave of the heart as the object of meditation, and having then described the origin of all the worlds and of Brahmā and the others from that [Self] in the passage beginning, "From Him the seven vital breaths arise," and so forth.

"The Unborn (Ajā), who has become the cause of all, is said to have been produced from that [Supreme Self]: 'The one Unborn, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form; indeed, the one Unborn [Self] lies by her, enjoying her.'"

"He leaves her behind, having enjoyed his enjoyment, while another [takes her up]"—this means that since it is being taught in the context of explaining how the entire multitude of things other than that [Brahman] originates from it and is therefore of its nature, this "Unborn One" (ajā) must be understood as being born from Brahman and consisting of Brahman; she is the creator of many similar offspring, who is enjoyed by one self under the influence of karma, while being abandoned by another self who possesses knowledge, just like the vital breaths, the ocean, the mountains, and so forth.

Therefore, by virtue of this supplementary statement from another Vedic branch—which is similar in form and whose meaning is recognized as identical—it is determined that the goat is restricted to being of the nature of Brahman.

In this context as well, at the beginning of the section, starting with "What is the cause? Brahman," and continuing with "Those who have attained the yoga of meditation beheld the power of the divine Self, concealed by its own qualities," there is the realization of the Unborn (ajā) as the power (śakti) of the Supreme Brahman; and from what follows: "The Illusionist (māyī) creates this entire universe, and within it, another is bound by illusion (māyayā)," "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the wielder of Māyā (māyin) as the Great Lord (maheśvara)," and "He who, being one, presides over the womb [of] the womb."

And thus, because of this very understanding [of the passage], there is not even a trace of the conception of an independent *prakṛti* established by the Tantras in this mantra. How then is there the "unborn-ness" (*ajatva*) of this *prakṛti*—which begins with light and has the forms of red, white, and black—or how can that which is "unborn" (*ajā*) begin with light? To this he says:
"And because of the teaching of a figurative conception, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth. (Sūtra 1.4.10)

The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of removing a possible doubt; it means that the fact that this *prakṛti* is unborn (*ajātva*) and the fact that it begins with light (*jyotirupakramātva*) are not contradictory. Why? Because of the teaching of "kalpanā. *Kalpanā* means *klṛpti*, which is creation; thus, the meaning is "because of the teaching of the creation of the world. Just as in the passage, "The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon as before," where *kalpanā* means creation, so too here, in the phrase, "The Illusionist creates this entire universe," the creation of the world is taught.

The meaning is that the Lord of All, possessing *māyā*, creates the entire universe from this cause which exists in an undifferentiated and subtle state. By this teaching of conceptualization, it is understood that this primordial nature (*prakṛti*) possesses two states of existence in the form of effect and cause; for at the time of dissolution, having attained the state of Brahman, she remains in a subtle form with name and form undifferentiated. At the time of creation...

That which possesses qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, which is denoted by terms like "the Undifferentiated" (*avyakta*) when name and form are not yet divided, and which, having transformed into the forms of fire, water, and food, exists in the appearance of red, white, and black—that is the "Unborn" (*ajā*) in its causal state; and in its effected state, it begins with light (*jyotis*). Thus, there is no contradiction.

Just as in the case of honey and so forth, it is not contradictory for the Lord to conceive of the sun—which exists as a single entity in its causal state—as having the nature of honey in its effected state; this is for the purpose of making it an object of enjoyment for deities such as the Vasus by serving as the substratum for the essences produced through the rituals expounded in the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, and thus to conceive of its rising and setting.

This has been stated in the Madhuvidyā, beginning with "That sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods" and ending with "Then, rising upwards, he neither rises nor sets; he remains alone in the center. Here, "alone" (ekala) means having a single nature. Therefore, it is established by this mantra that the non-born (aja) is denoted as being of the nature of Brahman, and not as established in the Kāpila system.

Others, however, maintain that in this mantra a single "Unborn" (*aja*) characterized by fire, water, and food is denoted; they should be asked: Is this single Unborn merely fire, water, and food themselves? Or is it Brahman itself, whose form consists of fire, water, and food? Or is it some other entity that serves as the cause of fire, water, and food? In the first case, because fire, water, and food are many, the description "the single Unborn" (*ajām ekām*) would be contradicted. Nor can it be argued that although fire, water, and food are many, they attain oneness through the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*).

Even in the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), plurality does not disappear, because of the instruction for the triplication of each individually in the passage: "These are the three deities; let me make each of them threefold. The second alternative must be considered: Is *aja* (the Unborn) Brahman itself, modified into the forms of fire, water, and food? Or does it abide in its own nature, unmodified? The first alternative is rejected precisely because plurality would not be relinquished. In the second case as well, the description as "red, white, and black" would be contradicted.

It cannot even be said that Brahman, abiding in its own nature, is characterized by fire, water, and food; for even in the third interpretation, one must accept that the word "unborn" (*ajā*) refers to fire, water, and food, and thereby brings about the presentation of their causal state. Therefore, it is better to take the word "unborn" as denoting the very state of the cause of fire, water, and food, which is well-known from the Śruti. As for the further claim that this Prakṛti is taught through the word "unborn" by imagining her to be a she-goat, that too is inconsistent, being devoid of purpose.

Just as in passages such as "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot," the body and other elements are metaphorically described as a chariot and so forth in order to demonstrate that they are the means for attaining Brahman; and just as the sun is imagined as honey in order to show that it is the object of enjoyment for the Vasus and others—what possible use is there in imagining this primordial matter (prakṛti) to be a goat? Not only is there a lack of utility, but there is even contradiction.

It is indeed contradictory to conceive of her—who is the cause of the entire world, who is eternally connected to all conscious beings since beginningless time, and who serves as the means for the experience of all pleasure and pain as well as liberation for every sentient being—as having the nature of a goat; for such a conception would imply that she, who is insentient, lacks the capacity to abandon her own self for the sake of a single, extremely minor purpose involving the union with a transient, insignificant being, and instead possesses the character of a goat, which is a specific type of sentient being capable of abandoning its own kin.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to assume various inconsistent meanings for the word *ajā* (the unborn) in the passages "the one unborn," "for the one unborn," and "another unborn. If you argue that goat-nature is attributed to it everywhere, then this assumption of goat-nature—whether by this [verse] or another—is utterly contradictory to the fact that the wise man, who effects the absolute abandonment of *prakṛti*, is described in the words, "The other unborn leaves her once her enjoyment has been experienced," as being incapable of ever again entering into a connection with her. The section concerning the *camasa* cups is concluded.
Nor [is the number five established] even by the inclusion of a specific enumeration, because of the diversity [of the items mentioned] and because of the excess [over that number]. || 11 ||

The Vājasaneyins recite: "In whom the five groups of five and space are established—him alone I consider the Self; knowing him as the immortal Brahman, one becomes immortal. A doubt arises: does this mantra aim to propound the categories established in the Sāṅkhya system, or not? What is the reasonable conclusion? That it aims to propound the categories established in that system. Why? Because of the word *pañcajana*, which is qualified by the word *pañca* ("five").

This is because of the comprehension of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*). What is meant is this: the compound *pañcajanāḥ* refers to a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). "The five people" (*pañcajanāḥ*) means a collection of five persons, just like the term *pañcapūlyaḥ*. The change of gender in the word *pañcajanāḥ* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). And when there is an expectation as to how many such aggregates they are—

By the first word "five," which qualifies the term *pañcajana*, groups are understood to be five, just as in the expression "five bunches of five [flowers]. Therefore, when the twenty-five principles are understood from the phrase "five five-people" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*), and there arises the expectation of knowing which ones they are, it is understood that they are precisely primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the others, which are well-known in the Smṛtis as objects to be known by seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) due to the context of liberation: "Root-nature is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (Intellect), are both nature and evolutes."

"For the sixteenfold group is a modification; the Puruṣa is neither a primal nature nor a modification"—such is the well-known tenet of the followers of Kapila; therefore, [the Sūtra] is intended to establish the principles as they are established in that system. To this we reply: "Not even because of the inclusion of the number."

Even from the inclusion of the number twenty-five in the phrase "five five-people" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*), there is no comprehension of the categories (*tattva*) established in the Tantras. Why? Because of their distinctness: these "five-people," specified by the number five, are separate from the categories established in the Tantras. For in the passage, "In whom the five five-people and space are established," it is understood that these [five-people] have Brahman as their sole essence, since they are supported by Brahman, which is indicated by the word "in whom" (*yasmin*). "Him thus... [and so on].

In the passage, "I consider myself a wise one, Brahman, immortal, [and] immortal," it is understood that Brahman—indicated by the word *yat* (which) in the correlative reference *tam*—is the subject. Therefore, these "five groups of five" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*) are not established as independent categories (*tantra-siddha*). Furthermore, because of the excess: there is an excess of principles here over those established in the systems of the Tantras, for both the Self (*ātman*) indicated by the word *yat* and the ether (*ākāśa*) are additional.

Therefore, the Supreme Person, the Lord of all lords, who is the substratum of all principles (tattvas) as established in the scripture, "They call him the twenty-sixth, and another the twenty-seventh," is what is denoted here. Regarding the phrase "even because of the inclusion of the number," the intention of the word "even" (*api*) is that the apprehension of twenty-five principles is not even possible in the passage "five five-people" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*). Why? Because a group composed of five [sets] of five is impossible.

In the case of the five principles established in the Tantras, there is no genus (*jāti*) or the like that serves as the basis for assigning those respective numbers. Nor can it be argued that there exists a basis for assigning intermediate numbers—such as "five organs of action," "five organs of knowledge," "five gross elements" (*mahābhūta*), "five subtle elements" (*tanmātra*), and "the remaining five"—because the collection of gross elements formed by the five [subtle elements] is not established, since *ākāśa* is mentioned separately. Therefore, this compound *pañcajāḥ* is not [a *taddhita* formation].

The former [the compound *pañcapūlya*] has as its object a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), whereas this [the compound *pañcajana*] has as its object a specific technical designation (*saṃjñā*) according to the rule "in the case of a name following a direction or a number. Otherwise, there would be a change of gender in the form *pañcajanāḥ*. There exist certain beings called *pañcajanāḥ*, and they are qualified by the number five, as in "five *pañcajanas*," just like the expression "seven *saptarṣayaḥ*. || 11 ||
The sense is that [the five] would not exist; as for the question "Who then are these five pentads?", he says: "The vital breaths and so forth, because of the remainder of the passage" (Sūtra 12).

From the supplementary passage, "Those who know the breath of breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food, and the mind of mind," it is understood that the five *pañcajanas* are indeed the five [senses] beginning with breath, which have Brahman as their support. Now, an objection might be raised: the mantra "in whom the five *pañcajanas* [dwell]" is common to both the Kāṇvas and the Mādhyandinas; however, in the supplementary passage "the breath of breath," etc., the reading of "food" (*anna*) does not exist for the Kāṇvas. Therefore, it cannot be said that for them the five *pañcajanas* are the [five senses] beginning with breath. To this, the following reply is given:
According to some, [the sacrifice] is by means of the *jyotiṣṭoma* when food is not available.
In the reading of certain Kaṇvas, where it says "when food does not exist, the five people are known by means of light," the remainder of that passage is presented for the sake of illustration.

This is what is meant: in the mantra preceding "In whom the five groups of five," namely, "The gods worship Him as the light of lights, as life, as immortality," Brahman is designated by way of being the "light of lights. Certain lights, which have their own effects dependent upon Brahman, are thus understood; and since these are the senses that illuminate objects, they are recognized through the unspecified reference "in whom the five groups of five."

By the word "of breath" (*prāṇasya*), the sense-organ of touch is understood, because the sense-organ of touch is connected with air (*vāyu*), whereas it is impossible for the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) to be indicated by the word "light" (*jyotis*). By "of the eye" (*cakṣuṣaḥ*) is meant the visual sense-organ; by "of the ear" (*śrotrasya*) is meant the auditory sense-organ; and by "of food" (*annasya*) there is a simultaneous mention (*tantra*) of both the olfactory and gustatory organs.

Because it is connected with the earth, which is denoted by the word *anna* (food), the sense of smell (*ghrāṇendriya*) is included here. Since "food" (*anna*) is that by which one eats, the sense of taste (*rasanendriya*) is also included; thus, the mention of "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*) refers to the mind itself. The simultaneous inclusion (*tantra*) of both smell and taste ensures that the number five is not contradicted. These five illuminating senses, ending with the mind, are designated by the term *pañcajana*; for the sake of avoiding contradiction with that, smell and taste are included simultaneously.

Thus, in the passage, "In whom the five groups of five and space are established," it is demonstrated that the sense organs designated by the term *pañcajana* and the great elements indicated by the word "space" are both established in Brahman.

Since this establishes that all principles (*tattvas*) have Brahman as their substratum, there is no occasion for the twenty-five principles established in the Sāṃkhya system. Therefore, it is settled that whether a specific number is mentioned or not, there is no cognition of the principles established in the Sāṃkhya system anywhere in the Vedānta texts. The section concerning the inclusion of numbers is concluded.
And because, in the case of ether and so forth, there is a statement as previously designated regarding their being causes. 14.

Again, the proponent of the doctrine of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause objects: "It is not tenable that Brahman alone is the single cause of the world, because the Upanishads do not record creation from a single source. For instance, in the passage 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone' (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), creation is recorded as preceded by Being (*sat*). In another place, 'In the beginning, this was non-being alone' (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.7.1), it is recorded as preceded by non-being (*asat*). And elsewhere: 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-being; that became Being; that evolved.'"*

Therefore, it cannot be determined from the Vedānta texts that Brahman alone is the cause of the world’s origin and subsistence; on the contrary, it can be determined that Pradhāna is the cause. For, after stating the dissolution of the world into the unmanifest Pradhāna in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest," the subsequent statement, "It was manifested through name and form," declares the creation of the world from that very unmanifest source.

For the "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*) is the unmanifest (*avyakta*); the meaning is that it is not differentiated, nor manifested, by name and form. This unmanifest is indeed the *pradhāna*. Since its nature is fixed and it serves as the substratum for transformation, the terms "being" (*sat*) and "non-being" (*asat*) found in the statements of those who maintain the world has a cause will not be contradictory when applied to this [unmanifest], just as they are not contradictory when applied to Brahman. Thus, once the unmanifest is determined to be the cause, qualities such as "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*), which reside in the cause, are to be understood as intending its orientation toward creation.

The words "Brahman" and "Ātman" also refer to the Pradhāna alone by virtue of its greatness and pervasiveness; therefore, it is the Pradhāna, as established by Smṛti and reasoning, that is the cause of the world.

When it is argued that [Brahman] is established by the Vedānta texts [merely as the material cause], we reply: "[Brahman is the cause] also as the efficient cause, because He is described exactly as He has been defined in the case of ether and the rest. The word "ca" (also) has the sense of "but" (tu). It can be determined that the world arises from the Supreme Brahman alone—He who is omniscient, the Lord of all, whose will is infallible, and from whom every trace of defect has been dispelled. Why? Because He is declared to be the cause as the efficient cause in the case of ether and the rest, being characterized by omniscience and other attributes, in such passages as "From which the birth, etc., of this [world proceed]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1).

It is said that Brahman has been established exactly as it was designated, because that single [Brahman] alone is declared to be the cause of ether and the rest. In such passages as, "From this very Self, indeed, ether was produced," and "It created fire," it is Brahman alone, the omniscient, that is stated to be the cause.

For instance, in the passages, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and "He attains all desires together with the wise Brahman," it is the very same "wise" (vipaścit) Brahman under discussion that is referred to by the words "from this very one. Likewise, the omniscient Brahman designated in the passage, "It thought: May I be many," is the very same that is referred to in the passage, "It emitted heat. This should be understood in the same way throughout all passages concerning creation; therefore, it is determined that Brahman alone is the single cause of the universe. But [it may be argued] that in the passage, "Non-being indeed was this in the beginning," it is non-being itself [that is the cause].
Since [the world] is designated as having a cause, how then is it determined that Brahman alone—the omniscient one whose resolve is true—is the cause? To this he says:
"Because of the drawing together" (samākarṣāt). || 15 ||

In the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," the very same Brahman—consisting of bliss, whose will is true—is likewise drawn forth by the wise one; for how [could it be otherwise]? "From this self consisting of consciousness, there is another inner self consisting of bliss"; "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"

By means of the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with, "He created all this, whatever exists here; having created it, He entered into it; having entered it, He became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat)," the Brahman consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), whose resolve is true, the creator of all, who has become the Self of all through His entry into everything, is described. Then, the verse "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*) is cited as a witness to the entire meaning stated in that [Brāhmaṇa] by the words, "And concerning this, there is this verse."

Likewise, later on, by the passage beginning with "From fear of Him the wind blows," that very same Brahman is referred back, and its qualities such as being the ruler of all and possessing unsurpassed bliss are declared; therefore, this mantra has that [Brahman] alone as its subject. At that time, because there is no differentiation of name and form, there is an absence of existence in relation to them; thus, Brahman itself is expressed by the word "non-existent" in the statement, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent. In that case as well—

This is the resolution. As for what was said—that in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest" (*taddhedaṃ tarhyavyākṛtamāsīt*), the Pradhāna alone is designated as the cause of the world—that is not so; for even there, by the word "unmanifest," Brahman itself is designated as having an unmanifest body. This is because in the passage, "He has entered here unto the tips of the fingernails; seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, thinking with the mind—one should meditate on Him as the Self," the pronoun "He" (*sa eṣa*) refers back to that which was indicated by the word "unmanifest" as having entered within.

Because [the Self] is drawn forth as the ruler, and because it is well known that the supreme Brahman—the omniscient creator—enters into the effect and differentiates names and forms, as stated in the passages: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing," and "Entering by means of this living self (jīva), let me differentiate names and forms"; and because this entering is for the purpose of governing, as expressed in "He has entered within as the ruler of people, the Self of all"—such an entering is not possible for the non-intelligent Pradhāna alone.

Therefore, Brahman—which is unmanifest and has an unmanifest body—is said to have been "differentiated by name and form" (*tannāmarūpābhyāṃ vyākriyata*). That very Brahman, which was previously undifferentiated in name and form, being omniscient and of true resolve, differentiates name and form by itself and is thus said to have differentiated itself. This being the case, [the attributes] such as "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) and so forth become primary; and the words "Brahman" and "Self" (*ātman*) likewise [attain their primary sense].

Since the quality of pervading all objects for the purpose of regulating their unsurpassed magnitude is not possible in any way in Pradhāna, it is established that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. The section concerning the causality [of Brahman] is concluded.
Because it denotes the world. || 16 ||

The Sāṅkhya again objects: although the Vedānta texts establish a conscious principle as the cause of the world, nevertheless, no entity other than the *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* established in their own system is perceived from them as the cause of the world to be known. For instance, in the dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, the Kauṣītakins record that the *puruṣa*, who is the enjoyer, is taught as the cause to be known; for, having begun with "I shall tell you of Brahman," [it continues]: "He who..."

He who is the cause, and whose karma—characterized by merit and demerit—is the cause for the existence of this [body], he indeed should be known; his essential nature should be understood as distinct from *prakṛti*. Likewise, later on, such things as the two [deities] approaching the sleeping person, the striking with a staff, and the awakening, are indicative marks (*liṅga*) for the demonstration of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).

Likewise, even further on, it is the enjoyer alone who is established: "Just as a master enjoys with his own people, or as his own people enjoy with the master, even so this self consisting of intelligence enjoys with these selves, and even so these selves enjoy him."

When Bālāki did not understand the meaning of what was asked—"Where, O Bālāki, did this person lie? Where was he then? Whence did he come?"—Ajātaśatru himself said to him: "There are the channels called *hitā*; therein he is when, being asleep, he does not see any dream at all. Then he becomes one with this vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone; then speech merges into it along with all names, and the mind merges into it along with all thoughts. When he awakens, it is like [the sparks] from a blazing fire."

"Just as sparks fly out in all directions, even so from this Self the vital breaths (prāṇas) go forth each to its own place; from the vital breaths the gods [proceed], and from the gods the worlds. Thus, by virtue of being the substratum of deep sleep, he has described this very individual self (jīvātman)—which exists during the states of dreaming, deep sleep, and waking, and which is the locus for the dissolution and emergence of the instruments such as speech—as that wherein "then the vital breath becomes one alone. This word "prāṇa" is used here with reference to this individual self because it is the bearer of the vital breaths. "When he awakes... [and so on].

Because awakening is heard [to occur] for that which is designated by the word *prāṇa*, and because both deep sleep and awakening are impossible for the Supreme Lord (*īśvara*), who is the primary authority (*mukhya-pramāṇa*); or else, the two locative cases in "in this *prāṇa*" (*asmin prāṇe*) are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*): while this Self (*ātman*) exists, the collection of instruments such as speech becomes one in *prāṇa* alone. Thus, even if the word *prāṇa* refers to the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), it is the individual soul (*jīva*) alone that is being propounded in this context, since the vital breath is inherently an instrument of the soul.

Therefore, since Brahman was introduced as that which is to be explained, and [it is stated] that "Brahman is indeed the Person," there is no proof for an Īśvara distinct from Him. Furthermore, qualities such as *īkṣaṇa* (seeing) residing in the cause—which are attributes of a conscious being—are appropriate only in this [Person]; thus, it follows that the *pradhāna* presided over by Him alone is the cause of the world. To this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: "[He is Brahman] because of the mention of the world. Here, [the person] is subject to merit and demerit...

The term *kṣetrajña* does not denote the individual soul (*puruṣa*), which is limited and becomes the cause of the transformations of *prakṛti* through the superimposition of the attributes of *prakṛti* upon itself; rather, it denotes the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), who is free from even a trace of defects such as ignorance, who is a treasury of countless, unsurpassed, and infinite auspicious qualities, and who is the sole cause of the entire universe. Why? Because in the passage "of whom this is the work," the word *karman* (work), being conjoined with the word "this" (*etat*), refers to the universe which constitutes the body of the Supreme Person.

For this word "this" (etad), by virtue of its unrestricted function through the context of the meaning and other factors, has as its object the entire world consisting of a mixture of sentient and insentient beings presented by means of valid cognition such as perception; nor is action characterized by merit and demerit the referent of the word "action" here, since [the objects] were pointed out by Bālāki as being Brahman after the introduction, "I shall tell you of Brahman."

Since the persons whose substrata are the solar orb and so forth were shown not to be Brahman by the statement, "Indeed, you have been speaking falsely to me," Ajātaśatru set aside that speaker of non-Brahman and introduced this passage beginning with "O Bālāki, he who... in order to make known the Brahman unknown to him.

Since the Sun and others who serve as the substrates, as well as the persons belonging to their same class, are connected with actions characterized as meritorious and non-meritorious and are already known by him through that very [knowledge], this word "karma" (action) is intended to make known a specific person not yet known to him; it does not denote merely merit and demerit, nor does it denote action in general. Rather, it denotes the fact that the entire world is an effect. In this way alone is an unknown matter truly taught.

Furthermore, there would be a resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the instruction that the innate nature of the person—which is characterized by its connection to action—is something to be known when it is actually unknown; for the mere connection with action alone constitutes the definition of that whose nature is to be known, since that is established by the statement "He to whom this action belongs is to be known. Moreover, the word "this" (*etad*) in the phrase "or he to whom this is the action" would be redundant. And the purpose of the separate mention in "He who is the agent of these, or he to whom this is the action" would be nearly meaningless, as for those [actions] which have been mentioned by you...

Those persons who are designated as being of the nature of Brahman—He who is their maker, of whom they are the effects—what more need be said? The entire universe is His effect; He, of whom all things—whether superior or inferior, sentient or insentient—are equal in being His effects, is to be known as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the ultimate cause.

Even though the origin of the world is dependent upon the karma of individual souls (*jīva*), the soul is not itself the creator of the objects of its experience and the instruments thereof; rather, it experiences everything created by the Lord (*Īśvara*) in accordance with its own karma. Therefore, agency toward persons does not logically belong to it. Consequently, it is the Supreme Brahman alone—well-known in all the Vedāntas as the ultimate cause—that is taught here as that which is to be known. || 16 ||
If it be argued that [the Self spoken of here] is not the Supreme Self because of the marks of the individual soul and the chief vital breath, that has already been explained.

Now, as for what was said—that because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the mention of the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), it is the enjoyer alone who is taught in this section, and not the Supreme Self—that has been explained. Its resolution was stated in the context of the Pratardana-vidyā. This is what is meant: where, by considering the beginning and the conclusion, it is certain that a passage refers to Brahman, there any other marks must be interpreted in conformity with that [Brahman]; this was established in that case. Here too, at the beginning, Brahman is introduced in the words, "I shall tell you about Brahman."

And in the middle, it is stated in the passage, "He whose work this is," that it is not merely a person, but rather Brahman alone, the sole cause of the entire universe. Furthermore, in the conclusion, the fruit of the meditation on Brahman is heard in the text: "Having shaken off all evils, he who knows thus attains the preeminence, sovereignty, and overlordship over all beings"; thus, by the certainty that this passage has Brahman as its subject, [the conclusion follows].

The marks (liṅgas) pertaining to the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) must also be interpreted as being directed toward that [Brahman]. For in the Prātardana section, it was stated that the marks of the individual soul and the chief vital breath have Brahman as their ultimate purport. Here too, since the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) expressed in the phrase "Now he becomes one with this very breath" is possible, it is improper to resort to a non-coreferential construction (vaiyadhikaraṇya). Furthermore, because the use of the word "breath" (prāṇa) is determined to refer to Brahman itself, the mention of the breath is appropriately a mark for the purpose of meditating upon Brahman whose body is the breath. As for how the marks of the individual soul can have Brahman as their purport, he says:
But Jaimini [holds that it] has another purpose, on account of both the question and the explanation; and some [teachers] also [hold this] in the same way. (18)

The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude the possibility that the sentence is concerned with the individual soul (*jīva*) by virtue of the soul being mentioned therein. The teacher Jaimini maintains that the mention of the soul is for another purpose, namely, to bring about an understanding of the nature of Brahman as distinct from the soul.

Why? Because of the question and the explanation. First, the question—beginning with "The two [Balaki and Ajatasatru] went to a sleeping man" (Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.1)—is seen to be intent on awakening the individual soul (*jīva*), who is distinct from the vital breath (*prāṇa*), by means of addressing him with the names of the vital breaths while his breath is active upon waking and by rousing him with a blow from a staff; and then it proceeds to awaken [him to] Brahman, which is distinct from the individual soul, as follows: "O Balaki, where was this person lying when he slept thus? (Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.1).

"Where was this [person] then? Whence did he come? Regarding this, the explanation—"When, sleeping, one does not see any dream at all, then he becomes one with this very breath (prāṇa); from this self (ātman) the vital breaths (prāṇas) proceed according to their respective stations; from the vital breaths the gods, and from the gods the worlds"—refers exclusively to the Supreme Self, which is a distinct entity from the individual soul (jīva).

For when the individual soul (*jīva*) is in deep sleep—having reached a state of composure free from the turbidity caused by the experience of various pleasures and pains associated with the states of waking and dreaming—the one from whom it emerges again for the sake of enjoyment is this Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Thus, it is said regarding the locus of deep sleep: "My dear, at that time he becomes united with Being (*sat*), embraced by the conscious Self (*prājña ātman*); he knows nothing external, nor anything internal. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.2)

By that [statement], it is established that the *prājña* (the conscious one), the supreme self (*paramātman*), is an entity distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, it is determined that the mention of the *jīva* through the question and the answer is for the purpose of establishing the supreme self as an entity distinct from the *jīva*. As for what was stated regarding the explanation of the question—that the place of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and the collection of organs are the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) alone, and that the group of instruments becomes unified within the *jīva* himself who is indicated by the term "prāṇa"—that is incorrect;
for the channels are the locus of dreaming, whereas according to the reasoning already stated, deep sleep belongs to Brahman alone.

And because it is the locus; for it is stated that the individual soul and the aggregate of its instruments, such as speech, which serve as its adjuncts, attain unity with Brahman alone, who is indicated by the word "prāṇa," and then undergo separation from it. Moreover, some, namely the Vājasaneyins, in this very dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, teach the Supreme Self as the substratum of the conscious self, distinguishing it from the latter in the state of deep sleep: "Where was this person consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya) then? Whence did he come? Where was he when he lay thus asleep? [and so on].

"The person consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya), having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths (prāṇas) by means of his own consciousness, lies in that space which is within the heart. And the word "space" (ākāśa) is well-known to refer to the Supreme Self, as in the passage, "The space within this [heart] is the small one. Therefore, it is understood that the mention of the individual soul (jīva) here is for the purpose of awakening the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman, the Prājña, who is a distinct entity from it.

Therefore, since in this passage it is the Supreme Brahman alone—which is distinct from the Puruṣa and is the cause of the entire universe—that is declared as that which is to be known, it is established that the causality of the Puruṣa as established by the Sāṅkhya system, or of the Pradhāna presided over by him, is not perceived anywhere in the Vedānta.
Because of the connection with the sentence. || 19 ||

Anticipating the objection that even here a statement is seen intended to reveal the principle of the Puruṣa as established in the Sāṃkhya system—and thus that no one called Īśvara exists apart from that—he refutes it. In the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, it is heard: "Verily, O Maitreyī, a husband is not dear for the sake of the husband; rather, a husband is dear for the sake of the Self," beginning thus and continuing until, "Verily, O Maitreyī, all is not dear for the sake of all; rather, all is dear for the sake of the Self."

"But it is for the sake of the Self that everything becomes dear; indeed, O Maitreyī, the Self must be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. Verily, when the Self is seen, heard, reflected upon, and known, all this is known. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the one being taught here as the object to be seen merely the *puruṣa* established in the Tantras? Or is it the omniscient Lord of all, whose resolve is true? What is the correct conclusion? That it is the *puruṣa*.

Why? Because the Person alone is perceived in the beginning, middle, and end. To begin with, at the outset, it is the individual self (jīvātman) alone that is perceived as being associated with the state of being dear through [the mention of] husband, wife, son, wealth, cattle, and so forth. In the middle as well, by virtue of its connection with origination and dissolution in the passage, "Being a mass of consciousness alone, having arisen from these elements, it perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death," it is understood to be that very same self.

Likewise, at the end [of the passage], with the words, "By what, O Maitreyi, would one know the knower? it is that very knower, the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), who is understood, not the Lord (*īśvara*). Therefore, it is determined that this statement is intended to propound the *puruṣa* as established in the Sāṃkhya system. Now, an objection may be raised: since the opening states, "But there is no hope for immortality through wealth," it is understood that this statement is intended to teach the means for attaining immortality; how then can this statement have the purpose of propounding the *puruṣa*?

This is explained as follows: for this very reason, there is here a presentation of the *puruṣa*. In this system (*tantra*), it is precisely the knowledge of the true nature of the *puruṣa*—which is free from the superimposition of insentient attributes—that is declared to be the cause of immortality. Therefore, the true nature of the individual self (*jīvātman*) when separated from *prakṛti* is taught here for the sake of immortality in such passages as, "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen.

Since the true nature of all selves, when separated from *prakṛti*, is of one and the same form, by means of the knowledge of the true nature of one's own self as separated from *prakṛti*, all selves become known; thus, the knowledge of all through the knowledge of the Self is logically established.

Since the nature of the Self (*ātman*) is uniform as pure consciousness (*jñānaikaprakāratva*) across all beings from the gods down to stationary objects, there is the teaching of non-dual identity (*aikātmya*) in the statement, "All this is what this Self is. Furthermore, because the forms of gods and others are themselves the form of the Self, there is the negation of their difference through such passages as, "All that is other than Him [is cast aside]. Moreover, by the negation of multiplicity in the passage, "For where there is duality as it were," it is stated that multiplicity—arising from the distinctions in the transformations of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) into gods and so forth—is false within the Self, which is indeed of a single nature.

Even such passages as, "Verily, this Rigveda is the breath of this great Being," are consistent with the view that the origin of the world has the Person as its cause, because [the world] proceeds from Prakṛti under His superintendence. Thus, since it is certain that this sentence refers to the Puruṣa, all Vedānta texts, by virtue of having the same purport, denote the Puruṣa established by the Tantras; therefore, it is Prakṛti alone, presided over by Him, that is the material cause of the world, and not the Lord (Īśvara).

This being the case, we reply: "On account of the syntactical connection. In this passage, the Lord of All alone is understood. Why? Because only in this way does the mutual connection of the various parts of the sentence become coherent.

When Yājñavalkya stated, "There is no hope for immortality through wealth," Maitreyī replied, "What should I do with that by which I would not become immortal? Tell me only that which the Blessed One knows as the means for attaining immortality. To her, who thus requested the very means for attaining immortality while disregarding wealth and other such things as being non-means for it, this Self was taught as the object to be seen as the means; and this [Self] is indeed the Supreme Self (Paramātman), for it is said: "Knowing Him alone, one goes beyond death," and "Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here."

Because passages such as "There is no other path" establish that immortality has the knowledge of the Supreme Person alone as its means, the true nature of the individual self—the attainer—who is a manifestation of the Supreme Person, must be understood as being useful for the knowledge of the Supreme Person which is the means to liberation, and not as a means in its own right; therefore, it is taught here that "the Supreme Self alone is to be seen as the means to immortality," and so forth.

Likewise, the causality of the entire universe, as stated in such passages as, "Verily, this Rigveda is the breath of this great Being," cannot belong to any person other than the Supreme Person—whether that be one who is subject to karma, one who is liberated, or a mere person devoid of activity. Similarly, the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one thing, as expressed in such passages as, "By the seeing of the Self, indeed, O Maitreyi," is possible only in the case of the Supreme Self, who is the Self of all.

As for the claim that because the selves are of a single nature, the knowledge of all selves arises through the knowledge of one self—that is incorrect; for there would be no knowledge of all things due to the absence of knowledge regarding the insentient phenomenal world (*acetana-prapañca*). Furthermore, in order to substantiate the initial proposition, [the text] begins with "This is Brahminhood, this is Kshatriyahood," and concludes with "All this is what this Self is."

Thus, having pointed out this phenomenal world (prapañca) as a mixture of consciousness and unconsciousness established through perception and other means by the words "this," the teaching of non-dual identity in the form "this Self is That" is only logically possible in reference to the Supreme Self. For this world, denoted by the word "this" as a mixture of conscious and unconscious entities, does not attain oneness with the Person—whether in His state as conjoined with the unconscious, separated from it, or in His own essential nature. Precisely for this reason, there is the censure of one who perceives everything as distinct from the Self: "Everything abandons him who knows everything as other than the Self."

Likewise, in the first Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, qualities such as greatness and so forth—heard in the text, "The great being, infinite, boundless"—are possible only for the Supreme Self; therefore, it is the Supreme Self alone that is being propounded here. As for the argument that because the passage begins with the individual self (jīvātman) as connected with the dear things such as husband, wife, son, wealth, and cattle, and is presented as the object to be sought, this statement must refer only to that [individual self]; [we reply:]...

That is incorrect, because [if one were to interpret it thus], there would result a lack of syntactic connection between the word *ātman* in the phrase "But for the love of the self" (*ātmanas tu kāmāya*)—which refers to the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—and the subsequent statement "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ*). It is understood that "But for the love of the self" is taught as being for the purpose of making the Self the object of vision. "For the love of the self" means for the fulfillment of the desires of the self; "desires" (*kāmāḥ*) are so called because they are desired—that is to say, for the attainment of what is dear to the self.

Furthermore, when it is stated that husbands and others become dear for the sake of the attainment of what is desired by the individual soul (jīvātman), it follows that the true nature of that soul must be sought. For it is only the "dear" object itself that ought to be sought, not the nature of the master (śeṣin) with respect to that which is dear, devoid of its dear objects. Since husbands and others become dear for the sake of the soul's attainment of what is desired, it would be inconsistent to say that one should abandon the dearness of husbands and others and instead seek the nature of the self as something separate from them.

On the contrary, it is not because they are subordinate to the husband and others that the husband and others are dear; rather, it is because they are subordinate to the Self that the husband and others are dear. If this were stated, those very [husbands and others] would become objects to be sought after for their own sake as being subordinate to themselves. Furthermore, if the subsequent part of the passage "But for the love of the Self, everything becomes dear" were not connected with what precedes it, a syntactical split (vākya-bheda) would result. Even if such a syntactical split were admitted, no purpose for the preceding sentence would be observed.

Therefore, having abandoned everything dear such as husband and the rest, the meaning of the sentence must be described in such a way that it is understood that the Self alone is to be sought; this is stated as follows: "But there is no hope for immortality through wealth. By this, he declares that wealth and the like are not means for attaining immortality—which is by nature eternal, faultless, and unsurpassed bliss. Furthermore, the fact that wealth, sons, husband, wife, and so forth are experienced as occasionally dear, mixed with surpassable suffering, is not caused by their essential nature as husband and so on, but rather—

It is impelled by the Supreme Self, whose very nature is unsurpassed bliss; therefore, it is taught that He alone—the Supreme Self—who, being Himself unsurpassed bliss, causes others also to become the locus of even a slight degree of dearness, is the one who must be seen.

This is the meaning: "Indeed, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear; nor indeed do wife, children, wealth, and so forth become dear through their own volition, thinking, 'May I be dear to him for my own purpose. Rather, they are dear for the sake of the Self—that is to say, for the fulfillment of the desired end consisting in the attainment of the state of being dear to the Supreme Self, who is one's own true nature."

For the Supreme Self, when propitiated by various actions, brings about for the worshippers—according to those respective actions—a specific degree of affection toward those particular objects, characterized by a definite place, time, nature, and magnitude; as the scripture states: "For He alone causes bliss. However, because the word *ātman* is used [in both cases], and because of the previously mentioned method in the passages "But for the sake of the desires of the Self" and "The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen," the two uses of the word *ātman* refer to one and the same subject. Furthermore, even according to another view, he says [the following] to demonstrate that the Supreme Self can be designated by the word *jīva*:
"Āśmarathya holds that it is a sign [of identity] because the initial proposition is thereby established" (Sūtra 1.4.20).

The teacher Āśmarathya held the view that this is the indicative mark for establishing the proposition that "by means of one cognition, all cognitions are known": namely, that the Supreme Self is denoted by words expressive of the individual soul (*jīvātman*). For if this individual soul were not indeed the Supreme Self by virtue of being His effect, then the knowledge of it would not be established through the knowledge of the Supreme Self, as it would be distinct from Him.

Because of the determination of oneness prior to creation in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," and because of the scriptural statements regarding the origination of individual souls from Brahman—such as, "Just as sparks of the same nature fly forth by the thousands from a well-kindled fire, so, my dear, various beings are born from the Imperishable, and into It they also merge"—and because of the statement regarding their dissolution into That very same source, it is understood that the identity of the individual souls with Brahman exists insofar as they are effects of Brahman; therefore, the term "individual soul" (jīva) denotes the Supreme Self.
Auḍulomi [holds that the soul departs] because it is about to pass away from such a state. || 21 ||

As for the claim that Brahman is presented by means of the term "jīva" for the purpose of establishing the proposition that through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all—on the grounds of the jīva’s oneness with Brahman as its effect—that is incorrect.

Because of scriptural texts such as "The wise one is neither born nor dies," which declare the unborn nature of the individual selves (*jīvātman*), and because the creation of the world is accepted for the sake of the enjoyment of the fruits of past karma, and because otherwise an unequal creation would be inexplicable; furthermore, since liberation—characterized by the individual self, which is an effect of Brahman, attaining its own nature as Brahman—is inevitable like that of space and other elements, the injunctions and performance of the means to that liberation would be purposeless; and finally, because liberation would lack the status of a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) if it were of the nature of destruction, like the dissolution of a jar upon reaching its cause.

The logical justification for the doctrine of the origination and dissolution of the individual self (*jīvātman*) will be elaborated upon later. Therefore, the teacher Auḍulomi maintains that the Supreme Self is designated by the term "individual self" with reference to its state as the departing soul, based on such passages as: "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form"; and "Just as rivers flowing along disappear into the ocean, casting off name and form, so the knower, freed from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high. Thus, the Supreme Self is spoken of by the word "individual self" in relation to its condition at the time of departure.
On account of the abiding [of the Self in all beings], so says Kāśakṛtsna. (22)

As for the claim that the term "Brahman" refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) because it attains the state of Brahman upon departing [from the body], that too is untenable, as it cannot withstand critical analysis. Is this non-Brahman state of the individual soul prior to its departure innate (*svābhāvika*), or adventitious (*aupādhika*)? Even if it were adventitious, would it be ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) or not? If it were innate, the attainment of the state of Brahman would be impossible; for since difference is inherent to one's own nature (*svarūpa*), as long as that nature persists, that difference cannot be removed.

If it is argued that the essential nature (svarūpa) also departs along with the difference, then, because it would have perished, it could not be Brahman—this is the sense; furthermore, defects such as its not being a human goal (apuruṣārtha) would follow. If [the difference] were ultimately real or merely adventitious (aupādhika), then Brahman would remain exactly as it was even prior [to liberation], and thus it would be improper to state the distinction [found in scripture]: "Because of the state of being thus at the time of departing."

For in this view, since there is no other entity apart from the limiting adjunct (upādhi) and Brahman, and since it is impossible for a partless Brahman to be divided by a limiting adjunct, the distinction resides solely within the adjunct; thus, even prior to departure, it is Brahman itself. If the distinction based on the adjunct were not ultimately real, it must be stated whose state of being Brahman occurs upon departure.

If it is argued that [the soul] is Brahman itself whose true nature is concealed by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), this is not so; for it is impossible for the nature of eternally liberated, self-luminous consciousness to be concealed by the adjunct of ignorance. Concealment (*tirodhāna*) means the cessation of the manifestation of a thing while its essential nature remains present. If one were to admit that the essential nature of a thing is its manifestation itself, then there would be either an absence of concealment or the destruction of the essential nature. Therefore, since its true nature is eternally manifest, there is no difference whatsoever between the state of liberation and the state of departure (*utkrānti*), as Brahman would be non-existent [only] upon departure.

Thus, the qualification "about to depart" (utkramiṣyataḥ) is indeed redundant. The statement "having risen up from this body" does not, at that time, describe the attainment of Brahmanhood for one who was not already of such a nature; rather, it refers to the manifestation of a pre-established essential nature. For it will be stated later in such passages as: "The manifestation [of the self] occurs upon reaching [Brahman], because of its own word," and so forth.

Therefore, [the texts state]: "Entering with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms"; "He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller (antaryāmin), the immortal"; "He who moves within the Imperishable (akṣara), whose body is the Imperishable, whom the Imperishable does not know—this is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa"; and "He has entered within as the ruler of people, the self of all."

The teacher Kāśakṛtsna held the view that Brahman is denoted by the word *jīva* because it abides as the self within the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which is its own body; furthermore, it was stated previously that the word *jīva* denotes the individual soul only insofar as it culminates in the Supreme Self, and not merely the individual soul alone, as in the passage: "He evolved names and forms."

In the passage beginning with "vāṇi," by thus establishing identity through the relationship of self and body, the Sūtrakāra has accepted the view of Kāśakṛtsna alone; for in this way, all the Śrutis—which describe the unassailable sinlessness, omniscience, and other attributes of the supreme Brahman; which speak of liberation for the ignorant, grieving individual soul (jīva) through the meditation on Brahman; which declare the creation and dissolution of the world; and which are intent upon teaching the identity of the world with Brahman—become properly explained. This is the meaning of the sentence here.

When Maitreyī asked about the means to immortality, Yājñavalkya stated that the meditation upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the means to immortality through the passage beginning with "The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen. Then, through the passage beginning with "But when the Self has been seen, my dear," he described the characteristics of the object of meditation and, by means of analogies such as the drum, explained the restraint of the instruments of perception—such as the mind—which serve as the tools for meditation.

Having stated this in general, [the text] elaborates—in passages such as "Just as the moisture of wet wood... and "Just as the ocean is the single goal of all waters..."—that the Supreme Brahman, which is the object of meditation, is the sole cause of the entire universe and the controller of the aggregate of the organs that serve as the root of activity toward all objects.

Having taught this with the passage beginning, "Just as a lump of salt," and so forth, [the text] establishes that the Supreme Self, abiding in the form of the individual soul (jīvātman), possesses the nature of undivided knowledge alone, in order to encourage engagement in the means for attaining immortality. Then, having stated that this very same entity—possessing the nature of undivided knowledge—undergoes transformation following the elements during the state of transmigratory existence, by saying, "Being a mass of consciousness alone, it emerges from these elements and perishes after them," it further declares regarding the state of liberation: "After death, there is no consciousness."

Having stated that, due to the absence of any contraction of his own innate, unlimited knowledge, there is an absence of knowledge regarding forms such as gods within himself because he does not identify with the aggregate of elements, [the text continues] again: "Where..."

By such passages as, "For where there is duality, as it were," it is established that the perception of manifold objects as having a nature other than Brahman is produced by ignorance (*ajñāna*). Having thus refuted the perception of difference for one who has discarded all ignorance and experiences the entire world as consisting of Brahman—since no object exists apart from Brahman—and having further stated, "By what should one know Him by whom one knows all this?", [it is shown that] the individual soul (*jīvātman*), possessing knowledge imparted by that Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who abides as its own self, knows all this; [the text asks] by what means one should know that [Self].

By what means could one know [Him]? By nothing at all—thus, having established the difficulty of perceiving the Supreme Self, [the text continues] with "This is 'not this, not this,'" and so forth. This...

Having declared that the Lord of All, whose nature is distinct from all other conscious and unconscious entities, exists as the body of all and as the Self of all—therefore not touched by the defects inherent in those conscious and unconscious entities that constitute His own body—it is stated: "By what means, O Maitreyī, would one know the Knower? You have been instructed; this much indeed, O Maitreyī, is immortality. Thus, [the text points to] the Knower of all, who is of a different class from all things, who is the sole cause of the entire universe, and who has cast off all [limitations].

Since it has been stated that "By what means other than the mode of worship described by Puruṣottama could one know [Him]?"—and thus this very worship is the means to immortality, and because attaining Brahman alone is designated as immortality—it follows that in this passage the Supreme Brahman alone is the subject.

Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Brahman alone is the cause of the world, and not the Puruṣa nor the Prakṛti presided over by him. The section on the "Connection of the Sentence" (Vākyānvaya-adhikaraṇa) is concluded.
And [Brahman] is the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. 23.

When the Sāṅkhya system without a Lord has thus been refuted, the Sāṅkhya with a Lord (Seśvara-sāṅkhya) objects as follows: "Even though the Vedāntas establish an omniscient Lord as the cause of the world because He possesses qualities such as the power of vision (*īkṣaṇa*), nevertheless it is understood from the Vedāntas themselves that primordial matter (*pradhāna*) alone is established as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world. For the Vedāntas do not convey that the world has a cause other than primordial matter—an insentient, transforming entity that is to be presided over by a Lord who is omniscient, unchanging, and the presiding controller."

For thus they study this very [Self] as changeless, while its presiding material nature (prakṛti) is studied as changing: "Partless, actionless, tranquil, faultless, and stainless"; "He indeed is that great unborn Self, undecaying and immortal"; "The unborn, eternal, eightfold form, the source of transformations, the ignorant [nature], presided over by Him, is meditated upon; it is expanded, impelled again, and, presided over by Him alone, it gives birth to the world for the sake of the Puruṣa"; and "The cow is without beginning or end, the mother, the bringer-forth of beings."

Thus, it is heard in scripture that the Lord creates the entire universe only by presiding over primordial nature (*prakṛti*) as its material cause: "From Him, the Illusionist (*māyī*), He creates this universe," and "One should know Māyā as primordial nature and the Great Lord as the Illusionist. Smṛti also states: "Under my supervision, primordial nature produces the world of the moving and the unmoving. Even though the fact that primordial nature is the material cause is not explicitly stated [in the Upanishads], the very fact that the scriptural teaching of Brahman as the cause of the universe would otherwise be inexplicable establishes both the essential nature of primordial nature and its status as the material cause of the universe under the supervision of the Lord.

In this very way, an absolute distinction between the efficient cause (nimitta) and the material cause (upādāna) is observed in the world: for instance, non-conscious substances such as clay or gold serve as the material causes for objects like jars or bracelets, whereas conscious agents such as potters or goldsmiths serve as their efficient causes.

It is observed as a certainty that the accomplishment of an effect invariably depends upon multiple causal factors. Thus, the Vedāntic texts are not capable of establishing that Brahman alone is both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*), by overstepping the rule of the distinction between these two causes and the rule that the production of an effect requires dependence on multiple causal factors. Therefore, Brahman is only the efficient cause, not the material cause; the material cause, however, is only the *pradhāna* presided over by it.

This being the case, it is replied: "And [Brahman] is the material cause, because that does not contradict the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. That is to say, Brahman is both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause; the meaning is that Brahman alone is the material cause as well. Why? Because that does not contradict the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. For only in this way are the initial proposition and the illustrative examples not contradicted.

First, the proposition (*pratijñā*) is: "You have been obstinate; did you not ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? This has as its object the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one thing. Furthermore, the illustrations—"As, my dear, [by one nugget of gold... and "As, my dear, by one pair of nail-clippers..."—have as their object the knowledge of the effects through the knowledge of the cause. If Brahman were merely the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) of the world, then the entire world would not be known through the knowledge of it.

It might be argued: "Indeed, a jar or the like is not known through the cognition of a potter and so forth; therefore, there is indeed a contradiction between the proposition and the example. [We reply: If Brahman alone is the material cause, then—just as by knowing the material lump of clay one knows the jar, or by knowing a piece of gold one knows the necklace, or by knowing a nail-cutter one knows the ring, crown, axe, or hatchet—when Brahman, who is the material cause of the entire universe, is known, His entire effect, the whole world, would be known.

The effect is merely the cause itself having entered into another state, and not a different substance; thus, by supporting the proposition through examples such as clay and its modifications, it is determined that Brahman alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world. As for the claim that a distinction between the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause is perceived by the Scripture itself, that is incorrect; for the identity of the efficient cause and the material cause is perceived in such passages as: "Or have you asked for that instruction, by which the unheard becomes heard? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3).

That by which one is commanded or instructed is called the *ādeśa*, according to the scriptural passage, "O Gārgī, under the command (*praśāsana*) of this very Imperishable," and so forth. Here, the agent is intended in the sense of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*).

You should have questioned that commander (*ādeṣṭṛ*), by whom—by that commander, the presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*)—when heard, even the unheard becomes heard; thus, the identity of the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*) is perceived. This is because, prior to creation, the unity is determined in the text, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only," and because the term "without a second" (*advitīya*) excludes any other presiding controller.

But if this were so, how do we account for the eternity and the status as the material cause of the world that are heard of in such passages as "the producer of transformations," "the cow is without beginning or end," and so forth? [The Sūtra answers:
"And because of the teaching of the desire-to-create. (2.3.14)

For this reason as well, both [the individual soul and the material world] are Brahman alone; because of the teaching that the Creator-Brahman Himself formed the resolve to become manifold, namely: "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and "It thought, 'May I be many, may I procreate. Indeed, creation is taught as being preceded by the resolve: "May I myself become manifold in the form of various conscious and unconscious entities, and likewise may I procreate."
And because both are explicitly mentioned in the sacred tradition.

This matter is not determined merely by means of propositions, illustrations, intentions, or instructions; rather, that Brahman alone is both the efficient cause and the material cause is directly declared in scripture: "What was the wood, what was that tree, from which they carved out heaven and earth? O wise ones, ask with your mind as to what it was upon which he stood while supporting the worlds. Brahman was the wood, Brahman was that tree, from which they carved out heaven and earth.
O wise ones, I declare to you with my mind: [it was] Brahman, standing over the self-creation. (RV 10.31.7)

"He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—thus, regarding Brahman who is the subject under discussion as desiring to create, the text "He made Himself by Himself" indicates that He is both the object and the agent of creation. Therefore, because He alone brings about His own multiplicity, He is perceived as both the efficient cause (*nimittatva*) and the material cause (*upādānatva*). The Self, whose name and form were undifferentiated, is the agent; that same Self, when name and form are differentiated, is the effect. Thus, there is no contradiction between His being the agent and the object.
Since He made Himself in that manner by Himself, He is both the efficient cause and the material cause. (26)

"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"; "Brahman is bliss"; "He is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst"; "Partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless"; "This indeed is the great unborn Self, undecaying and immortal. Thus, because of the transformation of the Supreme Brahman—who by His very nature is devoid of even a trace of the defects characteristic of all sentient and insentient beings, who is solely intent upon unsurpassed knowledge and bliss—there arises the locus of various and infinite non-human goals (purusharthas). || 27 ||

Because transformation is its inherent nature; the intention here is that it is not the inherent nature of the transformation being taught to bring about any defect in the supreme Brahman, but rather, on the contrary, it brings about unimpeded sovereignty. For it is precisely in this manner that transformation is taught.

The Supreme Brahman—who is the sole focus of all auspicious qualities that are the antithesis of everything to be abandoned; who is distinct from all other entities; who is omniscient; whose will is ever true; who has attained all desires; who is of unsurpassed and infinite bliss; who is the Self of the entire aggregate of sentient and insentient things that constitute His own play and instruments, since they exist as His body; and who, when the phenomenal world—which is His own body—has been reduced through the successive sequence of causes beginning with *tanmātra* and *ahaṅkāra* until only the extremely subtle insentient substance denoted by the word "darkness" (*tamas*) remains—even while that darkness [remains] as His body...
