When [Brahman], having become one with itself through the attainment of an extremely subtle state that is no longer fit for separate designation, forms the volition (saṅkalpa), "May I become Brahman whose body is such darkness," and then transforms itself into the body of the world through the process of dissolution, this is the teaching of transformation (pariṇāma) found in all the Vedāntas.

Likewise, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, the fact that the entire world is the body of Brahman and that Brahman is its Self is recorded in scripture: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth... [and so forth].

"He whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. Beginning thus, [the text continues]: "He whose body is water," "He whose body is fire," "He whose body is the intermediate space," "He whose body is air," "He whose body is heaven," "He whose body is the sun," "He whose body is the quarters," "He whose body is the moon and stars," "He whose body is the ether," "He whose body is darkness," "He whose body is light."

"The body"—referring to the passage in the Kāṇva recension ending with: "of whom all beings are the body," "of whom breath is the body," "of whom speech is the body," "of whom sight is the body," "of whom hearing is the body," "of whom mind is the body," "of whom skin is the body," "of whom discernment is the body," and "of whom semen is the body"; whereas in the Mādhyandina recension, the distinction is that in place of "discernment" (vijñāna), it says, "of whom the self (ātman) is the body."

The status of the worldly sacrifices and the Vedas as the body of the Supreme Self is further established. In the *Subāla Upaniṣad*, after declaring that the principles beginning with earth are the body of the Supreme Self, it is heard in the *Vājasaneyaka* that even those principles not mentioned there are His body and that Brahman is their Self: "He whose intellect is the body," "He whose ego is the body," "He whose mind is the body," "He whose unmanifest is the body," "He whose imperishable is the body," and "He who moves within death, of whom death is [the body]."

"That body which death does not know—this is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa. Here, by the word *mṛtyu* (death), the extremely subtle insentient entity denoted by the word *tamas* is intended; for in that very Upaniṣad, there is a sequential recognition: "The unmanifest dissolves into the imperishable (*akṣara*); the imperishable dissolves into darkness (*tamas*). Indeed, because it is the root of the affliction that veils the knowledge of all selves, that very *tamas* is designated by the term *mṛtyu*.

In the Subālopaniṣad itself, the dissolution of the principles—which are of the nature of Brahman as its body—into Brahman alone is recorded: "Earth dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire; fire dissolves into air; air dissolves into space; space dissolves into the senses; the senses dissolve into the subtle elements (*tanmātras*); the subtle elements [dissolve into the ego]."

"The elements dissolve into the *bhūtādi*; the *bhūtādi* dissolves into the *mahat*; the *mahat* dissolves into the unmanifest (*avyakta*); the unmanifest dissolves into the imperishable (*akṣara*); the imperishable dissolves into darkness (*tamas*); and darkness becomes one with the Supreme Deity. Even in the state of attaining non-distinction, it will be stated later that the conscious and unconscious entities remain in an extremely subtle state along with their residual impressions (*saṃskāra*): "If it is argued that there is no [dissolution] because of the non-distinction of action, we say no; because of beginninglessness, it is logical and is also observed."

Thus, from Brahman—which is non-dual, unsurpassed bliss, omniscient, and of true resolve; which is one alone, being the body of extremely subtle sentient and insentient entities that have become unified with the Supreme Self such that they cannot be designated as distinct from It—there is heard a transformation into the form of the world, preceded by the volition to become manifold by assuming the body of gross sentient and insentient entities capable of differentiation into name and form. As it is said: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," and "From this very Self consisting of consciousness..."

"There is another inner self consisting of bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5); "For he alone causes bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7); "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he created all this, whatever exists here. Having created it, he entered into it. Having entered it, he became the manifest and the unmanifest, the defined and the undefined, the supported and the unsupported, consciousness and non-consciousness, truth and falsehood; he became truth" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).

Here, by the word *tapas*, knowledge consisting of the contemplation of the form of the ancient world is denoted, according to such scriptural passages as, "His austerity consists of knowledge. The meaning is that, having contemplated the configuration of the world created previously, He created this world with that same configuration. For in this very way, Brahman [acts] toward all.

The Creator creates the world in exactly the same form throughout the kalpas, according to the Śruti and Smṛti: "The Ordainer fashioned the sun and the moon as before, and the heaven, the earth, the intermediate space, and also the celestial realm"; and "Just as the characteristic signs of the seasons, though diverse in form, are seen to be the very same in their recurrence, so too are the entities at the beginnings of the yugas."

The meaning of this is as follows: The Supreme Self (Paramātman), whose essential nature is self-luminous knowledge and bliss, who is identical with that [nature] by virtue of having as His body the sentient and insentient entities that serve as the instruments for His own play—entities which, due to their extreme subtlety, are like non-existent things—desiring to obtain various and infinite toys, transformed Himself into everything down to the gross elements through a succession of collective bodies consisting of Prakṛti and Puruṣa; thus becoming identical with them, He further became the world in the form of diverse beings mixed with sentient and insentient matter, ranging from gods to immobile objects, which is denoted by the terms "Sat" and "Tyat."

Thus [it is said]: "He entered into that very [being]; having entered it... This means that the Supreme Self alone, who existed as the Self in the causal state, remains as the Self even of the substance undergoing modification into the form of the body, and is therefore said to have "become that. In this way, within the Supreme Self—which has undergone transformation into the form of the world consisting of a conglomeration of the Supreme Self, consciousness, and matter—all defects (apuruṣārtha) residing in the conscious portion that constitutes the body of the Supreme Self, as well as all modifications residing in the insentient portion, reside in the Supreme Self.

The state of being an effect; yet, as the controller and essential self of those two states, He is not touched by the modifications consisting of the non-attainment of human goals inherent in them. Consisting of unlimited knowledge and bliss, and remaining eternally uniform, He abides in the sport of the world's transformation. This very point is stated [in the Śruti]: "Both the true and the untrue became the True."

The meaning is that although Brahman undergoes transformation in the form of the diverse sentient and insentient, it remains truly real; it remains of one uniform nature, entirely free from even a trace of defect, and possessed of unimpaired knowledge and bliss. All sentient and insentient entities, both in their subtle and gross states, are the instruments for the divine play (*līlā*) of the Supreme Brahman, and creation and so forth constitute that play—thus it has been stated by the venerable Vāyana (Vyāsa), Parāśara, and others: "Endowed with the power of transformation from the unmanifest up to the specific [material objects]..."

"Understand that all this is the perishable play of Hari; behold His activity like that of a playing child," as stated in passages such as "The Child has Hari as His toy. And He will further declare: "But [His] sport is unique, as in the world."

"The Illusive One (māyī) projects this entire universe, and another, bound by that very illusion, is confined within it. Thus, even while Brahman undergoes modification into the form of the world, all modifications residing in the insentient portion (*acid-aṃśa*) which serves as its mode, as well as those residing in the sentient individual (*kṣetrajña*) who is likewise a mode of it—namely, those things that do not constitute the human goal—are distinguished for the sake of discernment. Furthermore, although Nature (*prakṛti*) and the Person (*puruṣa*), being the body of Brahman, have at that time become one with Brahman by attaining an extremely subtle state that precludes such designation, they are nevertheless designated separately [in the verse], as in: "Then he [Brahman] made himself... [and so forth].

This is because [the scripture] has the same purport as passages such as "He Himself performed [it]. Likewise, there is the statement of Manu: "Desiring to emit various kinds of creatures from His own body, He meditated and first created the waters; into them He cast His seed. For this very reason, the scriptural texts concerning Brahman's faultlessness and changelessness are also justified. Therefore, Brahman alone is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the world. || 27 ||
For it is indeed proclaimed as the source. || 28 ||

For this reason as well, Brahman is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the world, since it is designated as the "source" (*yoni*): "the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3), and "that which the wise behold as the source of beings" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.6). Furthermore, that the word *yoni* denotes the material cause is understood from the complementary passage: "as a spider emits and reabsorbs [its thread]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.7). || 28 ||

By this collection of logical principles stated in the four quarters [of the verse], all specific passages in every Vedānta text that are intent upon propounding the cause of the universe have been explained as being devoted to propounding the Brahman who is omniscient, omnipotent, and distinct from both the sentient and the insentient. Furthermore, it has been argued that the Brāhmaṇa caste is understood to have a connection with fire through the designation, "You are a Brāhmaṇa among men. However, these three points are untenable, because it is impossible to subvert the conformity of such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and because the causality of the universe has been established as a unique attribute belonging exclusively to the Supreme Self.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the primary meaning of the word *brahman* as it occurs at the beginning [of the passage]; moreover, it is impossible for a mere phoneme (*varṇa*), or for the deity named Agni, or for the phoneme presided over by him, to be the creator of all the deities such as Indra, Varuṇa, and Soma. This is because, based on scriptural statements such as "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth... from his feet the Śūdra," and "From his mouth Indra and Agni," it is heard that the Brāhmaṇa, Indra, and Agni were created by the Supreme Person; thus, it is impossible for Indra and the others to have been created by Agni.

It is untenable to assume that this scriptural passage—given the possibility of alternative interpretations—intends to describe a difference in creation due to a difference in cosmic cycles (kalpa), for the following reasons: The statement, "Through fire alone he became Brahman among the gods, and a Brāhmaṇa among men," indicates that the Brahman under discussion, referred to by the pronoun "that" (tat), is distinct from both fire and the Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, the statement, "Therefore, desiring the world among the gods, one should seek it in fire alone; and desiring it among men, in a Brāhmaṇa; for through these two forms Brahman became manifest," establishes a grammatical distinction (vaiyadhikaraṇya) between fire and the Brāhmaṇa.

By the designation of the nature of Brahman, it is also understood that [the subject] is distinct from the embodied Brahman. Likewise, because of its being the creator of Indra and others, and because of its separate designation, the possibility that the word "Brahman" refers to the Supreme Self abiding in the form of fire is also excluded. For the origin of Indra and others cannot proceed from the Brahman that has the form of fire; therefore, the assumption of a qualification by fire is futile. Furthermore, this is not supported by the words of the text, for the word "Brahman" alone does not denote the Supreme Self abiding in the state of fire.

If the first occurrence of the word *brahman* refers to Brahman in the state of fire, then the use of the pronoun *tat*—which refers back to the subject under discussion in the phrase "by that [Brahman] indeed through fire"—would result in a lack of grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇyam*), which is untenable. Furthermore, it is improper for Brahman in the state of fire to be qualified by fire itself, because it is illogical for the same fire to function as its own qualifier; nor, if another fire were postulated, would that [first fire] be able to serve as the form (*rūpa*) of that other fire.

[Objection: Surely the creation of Indra and the others is not intended [to be primary]; for if that were intended, it would be impossible for the passage to have the Brahmin as its primary subject. Rather, it is only the creation of the *kṣatra* and so forth, presided over by those deities, that is intended. Furthermore, the two sentences—"By means of Agni alone he became the *brahman* among the gods, and the Brāhmaṇa among men; for by these two forms he became the *brahman*"—are aimed at showing the twofold nature of the Brāhmaṇa caste itself through the division into gods and humans. [Reply: It is said in response:

First of all, one cannot claim that there was no intention to speak of the creation of Indra and the others at the conclusion of the fourfold caste system in the passage, "This is Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra. For when the inquiry arises as to how the fourfold caste system [comes about]—since the creation of the three castes beginning with the Kshatriya has already been stated—it is explained that the number four is completed by Agni among the gods. And Agni, as previously mentioned, is created by the Supreme Self who has as His subtle body the non-conscious principle (acit) known as Death; for it is said: "From Him, being weary and heated, His essence of heat emerged as Agni."

The word *śrānta* (exerted) refers to effort through a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of its cause; the meaning is "of one who has formed a resolution. Regarding *taptasya*, [the root] *tap* means "to contemplate"; thus, the meaning is "of one who possesses contemplation regarding the class of things to be created. In this way, it is Agni alone who is heard there as the creator, and not the Brāhmaṇa caste presided over by him.

Here too, because the number four is completed by him, it is understood—according to the principle of preeminence—that the creation of Indra and others who possess the conceit (*abhimāna*) of those [castes] is intended, in the same manner as the division into *kṣatra* and so forth, and not merely the creation of the social classes (*varṇa*) presided over by them. The statement, "By means of Agni alone he became the Brahman among the gods, the Brāhmaṇa among humans," makes known that the Brāhmaṇa caste was not previously designated by the word "Brahman"; for the previously mentioned Indra, the Kṣatriya, and others are not mentioned again by this particular mode of expression.

For no such statement is heard in scripture that "the Kṣatra-varṇa among the gods became the Kṣatra through Indra, [whereas] among humans it became so through the Kṣatriya. For this very reason, it is established that Agni also is not designated by the word "Brahman. Indeed, there is no such scriptural statement as "Indra among the gods became the Kṣatra in his form as Indra, [whereas] among humans it became so through the Kṣatriya. If it is argued that the text "through a Kṣatriya [one becomes] a Kṣatriya, through a Vaiśya a Vaiśya, and through a Śūdra a Śūdra" is indeed heard, what follows from that? If you say that a twofold distinction is perceived even among the other castes, we say no, because that would contradict the structure of the passage beginning with "by Agni alone... and so forth.

For it is not heard in scripture that the Kṣatra-varṇa existed among the gods in the form of Indra and others, while it existed among humans as a Kṣatriya; nevertheless, if the passage were intended to establish a twofold division of other classes (varṇas), there would be the undesirable consequence of requiring numerous elliptical additions (*adhyāhāra*). What, then, is the meaning of this scriptural statement? It is said: since the creation of Agni—who possesses the conceit (*abhimāna*) of being a Brāhmaṇa—was previously mentioned, the creation of Indra and others—who possess the conceit of being Kṣatra and so forth—is stated here, thereby recalling the creation of Agni by means of the sentence "by that very Agni" (*tenāgninaiva*); in the phrase "by Agni," the instrumental case is used in the sense of "in such a manner" (*itthambhāve*).

That Supreme Brahman, distinguished by means of Agni, became Brahmā among the gods; the meaning is that through Agni, it came to possess the presiding consciousness (*abhimāna*) of the Brāhmaṇa class. By this, it is established as a matter of implication that the Supreme Brahman alone possesses the presiding consciousness of the Kṣatriya and other classes through Indra and the others. Furthermore, there is either a division into Brāhmaṇahood and so forth among the deities presiding over the social classes (*varṇa*) due to their specific ascetic practices (*tapas*), or the conventional usage of terms such as "Brahma-Kṣatra" and so on is based on scriptural authority such as: "Brahmā is Bṛhaspati, the Kṣatra is Indra, and the Maruts are indeed the Viś (the commoners) among the gods."

In that case, the division into Brahminhood and so forth would have been stated as belonging to the Supreme Brahman alone through the medium of Agni and others; for the manifoldness of all kinds, expressed in the words "May I become many," resides in Brahman through those respective media. Thus, the creation of the presiding deities of the castes has been described.

Now, relying upon the creation of the Brāhmaṇas and others who are the objects of [the Lord’s] conceit—well-known from such Vedic texts as, "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms"—the Supreme Self’s assumption of the division of human castes, which results from that [creation], is stated [in the verse]: "Among humans, the Brāhmaṇa... That Supreme Brahman assumes the form of a Brāhmaṇa among humans.

Through that [fire], Brahman became [associated with] the Kṣatriya; the meaning is that that Brahman, being distinguished by the Kṣatriya, became as if it possessed the nature of a Kṣatriya through that medium, just as earth becomes as if it possesses hardness through the medium of stone. Since the construction is possible by supplying the words heard in the text, it is improper to resort to a construction by supplying words not present in the sentence; for there is praise of fire and the Brāhmaṇa in between: "Therefore, among the gods, the Brāhmaṇa, desiring a world, seeks it in fire alone; [and] among men... (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.4.1.10).

He states the reason for their praise: "For by these two forms, Brahman came into being. The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman became distinguished by means of the two forms of Agni and the Brāhmaṇa. Although Indra, the Kṣatriya, and others are not different from the Supreme Self in their essential nature, the specific mention of Agni and the Brāhmaṇa as having that nature is intended for the purpose of praising them. It is improper to claim that the sentence beginning with "for by these two" (etābhyāṃ hi) is merely concerned with the duality of castes, as there would be no purpose in doing so.

Indeed, the mere statement that there are two kinds of *varṇa* does not constitute an exaltation; rather, it is understood from the word *hi* that this sentence serves to establish such an exaltation. As for the discrepancy in the meaning of the word *brahman*, it is consistent with the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, as in the passages "Brahman is built up by austerity" (*tapasā cīyate brahma*) and "Therefore, this is Brahman" (*tasmādetadbrahma*). For while one may accept a figurative meaning when the primary meaning is impossible, there is no reason to accept a non-primary meaning even when the primary meaning is possible; indeed, it will be stated later: "And it may belong to one [word] like the word *brahman*."

Regarding the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), it has been stated that the mention of the creation of the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras is established otherwise; furthermore, because of the scriptural hearing of the creation of the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriyas, it is improper to abandon the status of the Supreme Self for the sentence "Brahman indeed this [was]"—which is based on its similarity to a causal statement—and instead resort to the view that the word *brahman* refers to the first caste and its presiding deity. This is because, even in the sentence "Being alone, my dear," the creation of fire, water, and food is about to be described, and thus the word *sat* (Being) as well...

Because there would otherwise be the contingency of [the passage] referring to air and its presiding deity; as for the masculine designation in the phrase "He created the Viśas," it is intended to refer to the word *ātman*.

For this [passage] begins with the Brāhmaṇa section, where it is heard in scripture: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" (*ātmaivedamagra āsīt*). Therefore, the reference "he" (*saḥ*) is not intended as praise for the Kṣatriya, but refers to the word "Brāhmaṇa" under discussion. Indeed, it is observed in the Śrutis that a pronoun may take on the gender of a remote word, as in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose glory extends over this earth—in the divine city of Brahman, in the ether, this Self is established."

"The mind-made [self], the leader of the body of vital breaths, is established within, having taken its seat in the heart. By the knowledge of that, the wise behold the immortal form of bliss which shines forth. Here, although the word *ātman* is present, it refers to Brahman whose characteristics are being described; thus, with the intention of referring to the distant term *brahman*, it is indicated as "that which is immortal," rather than in the masculine gender as in the passage, "That is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal."

Indeed, in this very Brāhmaṇa, after asking: "Regarding that which men think they shall become everything through the knowledge of Brahman—what was it that Brahman knew, by virtue of which it became everything?", it says: "It knew only itself, thinking 'I am Brahman'; therefore it became everything. Among the gods, whoever realized that, he alone became that; likewise among the ṛṣis, and likewise among human beings. Thus, [it refers to] the one denoted by the word "Brahman," which was concealed by ignorance, as "I..."

It is not so; for even at the beginning [of the passage], the word *brahman* refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and in that context, concealment by ignorance (*avidyā-tirodhāna*) is not heard of, as there is no word expressive of such a thing. This is because scripture declares that through the knowledge "I am Brahman" (*brahmāsmi*), one attains the state of being the self of all, and because concealment by ignorance is impossible in the case of the Supreme Brahman, whereas it is possible in the case of those belonging to the Brāhmaṇa caste and others. Thus, while it might be argued that the word *brahman* in the opening passage refers to the Brāhmaṇa caste in accordance with its occurrence elsewhere where that sense is possible, this interpretation is untenable here. The word *brahman* in the opening passage refers to the Supreme Self, and in that context, concealment by ignorance is not mentioned, precisely because of the absence of any term denoting it.

For instance, humans—desiring the manifestation of everything up to the Supreme Self denoted by the word "all," and thinking that they shall become all through the knowledge of Brahman—wonder: "Did that Brahman know something else, because of knowing which it became all? Thus arises the desire to know whether there exists even beyond Brahman some other object to be known or worshipped, such that by knowing it, Brahman itself became all.

He provides the answer that there is no other object of worship: "Then he knew only himself: 'I am Brahman. Therefore, he became all this. The meaning is that he knew only the Self, and not some other object of worship; therefore, he became all this. The intent is to negate the status of knowing anything else as a means, rather than to enjoin the knowledge of one's own self as a means.

Just as in the passage, "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses; there is no progenitor of Him, nor is there any lord over Him," the status of being the supreme cause is established by the negation of any other cause, so too here it is intended that Brahman is the supreme object of worship by the negation of any other object of worship. The absence of any other object of worship is the result of the absence of any other cause, for it is the Cause alone that is to be meditated upon. Thus, he states the fruit for one who knows Brahman as devoid of any other object of worship in the words, "That which... (tad yo yaḥ).

Therefore, the consistency of the introductory statement also establishes that the subject refers to the Supreme Self; consequently, the supremacy of the Supreme Person is established by such passages as, "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman, one alone."

Likewise, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka itself, it is heard: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, in the form of a person; looking around, he saw nothing other than himself," and so forth. Although a conscious being is established here by the word "Self" and by the act of seeing, he is not the Supreme Self. For that [Supreme Self] is unsurpassed bliss, whereas here, the connection with fear is understood from the passage: "He was afraid; therefore, being alone, he was afraid; he looked for a companion. Indeed, the Supreme Self is not the locus of fear, as the scripture states: "From fear of Him the wind blows," and so on.

It is said: this is the Supreme Self (paramātman), because this sentence shares the same character as sentences concerning the cause [of the universe]. For its status as a sentence concerning the cause is understood from the phrase, "In the beginning, he existed. Furthermore, the fact that this Self has the form of a person (puruṣavidhatva) makes known its nature as consisting of bliss (ānandamayatva); for, having begun with "From the Self, space was produced," and having stated, "Therein is another inner Self, consisting of bliss," the text subsequently establishes its form as a person by saying, "Because he burned away (auṣat) all evils prior to all this, therefore he is called 'Puruṣa'."

Furthermore, because it is understood that [the Puruṣa] is denoted by the word *puruṣa* due to its quality of burning away all evils, the connection with fear pertains only to the Supreme; however, this connection with fear does not belong to the Paramātman, but rather to the *puruṣa* who is His effect. For it is stated in that very same passage: "He first uttered, 'I am he'; therefore, He became known by the name 'Aham' (I)."

The name *Hiraṇyagarbha* refers to the "I" (*aham*). Because he was the first among the individual persons (*vyaṣṭipuruṣa*) who serve as the locus for the conceit of "I," he is called Hiraṇyagarbha. Likewise, in the *Mokṣadharma*, it is understood that the four-faced one (Brahmā) has the designation of "I-consciousness" (*ahaṅkāra*): "In the past, Brahmā was created by me; when he himself performed sacrifices, I, being pleased, granted him unsurpassed boons: 'At the beginning of the kalpa, you shall have the status of my son and the lordship over the worlds; furthermore, [the term] 'I-consciousness' (*ahaṅkāra*) is indeed a synonym for you. Thus it is said.

In that very same dialogue between Bhṛgu and Bharadvāja, it is stated: "From that lotus arose Brahmā, consisting of the Vedas, the Ordainer, known as Ahaṅkāra, the creator of the self-nature of all beings—the Brahmā of great splendor who is these five elements. Therefore, the meaning is this: he uttered the words of volition, "I am," "May I be," "May I become four-faced"; consequently, he became the four-faced one named Ahaṃ. This is the sense.

Therefore, since the Supreme Self in the form of the four-faced one (Brahmā) is the subject under discussion, His quality of being the burner of all sins is stated as a direct qualification; and that four-faced one, who is of His nature, is called the "refuge from fear" because He is non-different [from Him]. Thus, it is established that the *ātman* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Likewise, it is heard in this very *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*:

"In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here; this was covered by Death alone, for Death is hunger. He created the mind," and so forth. Here, that which is designated as "Death" is not the Supreme Self, because its specific attributes are not heard [in this context] and because it is characterized by hunger. For the Supreme is heard in scripture as "without hunger and without thirst"; moreover, the status of being an agent of actions such as worship is heard in the passage, "He moved about worshipping," whereas the Supreme is not subject to karma, as it is heard: "He has risen above all evils; He is one whose evil has been destroyed."

For this very reason, one should not suspect that Nārāyaṇa is meant by the creation from the element of water, because he is "the divine, unique god Nārāyaṇa, free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*), as stated in scripture. Therefore, is it the well-known Death (*mṛtyu*) or the Sun (*sūrya*) that is intended here? [The latter], because it has been said that the Sun's nature is that of the *arka* (fire/sun). It is replied: Because he is in the causal state, this one designated as "Death" is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) whose body is non-sentient matter (*acit*). This is according to the scriptural text: "He whose body is death—that is the divine, unique god Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore, "hunger" (*aśanāyā*) is the desire to withdraw the world.

The word *aśanāyā* (hunger) is applied to Him by virtue of possessing that quality; the phrase "He made that mind" (*tan mano 'kuruta*) establishes His transcendence. The meaning of the word *arcann* is as follows: *arcana* means pleasing, and the object of the action is Himself alone, because it is more appropriate for the subject of the context itself to be the object than to supply an unstated word. Since the suffix *-śatṛ* is used here in the sense of "characteristic" or "cause" according to the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*, the meaning is that He moved about in order to please Himself through the sport of the world's activity.

Furthermore, the creation of the waters is a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the creator being Nārāyaṇa, because of the Śruti passage beginning, "In the beginning, indeed, there was only Nārāyaṇa," and continuing, "These were the waters. Moreover, the word *arka* applies to the Supreme Being due to His connection with the quality of delighting (*prīṇana*); for this very reason, He is recited in the *Sahasranāma* as "Arka, Vājasana, Ṛṅgī. The essence of the waters is their solidified portion; the creation of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is described [in the text]: "That condensed, and it became the earth. And the *Mahopaniṣad* states: "Those waters became that golden egg."

Because they share this same single purpose, it is Nārāyaṇa, whose body is the subtle death (mṛtyu), who is the subject to be established here. In the Subāla Upaniṣad it is heard: "Regarding this they say: 'What was there then? To him he said: 'Neither being, nor non-being, nor being-and-non-being. From that, darkness was born."

In this [passage], the act of seeing and so forth is not understood, nor are words denoting the substratum (*dharmin*) such as "Being" (*sat*), "Brahman," and so on, employed; therefore, a cause that is both existent and non-existent, and thus indefinable (*anirvacanīya*), is perceived. Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa, who is set forth later, is not the ultimate cause; for after describing the creation beginning with *Tamas* and stating the production of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) in the words "that became an egg," it is stated, "In its midst is the divine Person, the thousand-headed Person," thereby establishing that he exists within the effects. [And it is said: "Death, indeed, is the supreme deity..."

"Beyond that, it becomes one; it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent"—from this, the transcendence of the Divine (deva) over that which is characterized as being distinct from both existence and non-existence is understood. This is not so; for it is stated that the supremacy of Nārāyaṇa is established precisely because He is the cause.

The repeated exposition of Nārāyaṇa alone in this Upaniṣad is an indicator of its primary purport (*tātparyaliṅga*). Beginning with, "This mass of consciousness, when departing, by what means and which place does it leave behind as it departs? To him he said," and continuing from, "He pierces the sheath for the sake of non-rebirth," up to, "Having pierced the Imperishable, he pierces death; death indeed becomes one with the supreme deity beyond; neither being, nor non-being, nor being-and-non-being"—the merging into the supreme deity beyond death is thus heard in scripture.

Death is darkness (*tamas*), for it is heard in scripture that this [darkness] is beyond the Immutable (*akṣara*) by way of its locus and measure; therefore, the Reality described as being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent—which is the cause of death designated as darkness—is understood to be the Supreme Deity (*paro devaḥ*), because that which is the site of non-differentiation is precisely the source of differentiation. And the Supreme Deity is Nārāyaṇa, since it is stated: "The divine, unique Deity is Nārāyaṇa. Nor is there anything beyond the Deity that is distinct from the existent, the non-existent, or both.

But it is indeed the Lord (deva), because there is oneness between the locus of non-distinction and the material cause designated as *tamas*; therefore, since the nature of the Lord is understood through His being both the material cause of *tamas* and the locus of non-distinction, and because He is Nārāyaṇa and the goal attained by the liberated, Nārāyaṇa alone is distinct from both existence, non-existence, and their combination.

Because Nārāyaṇa is distinct from pure consciousness, from insentient matter, and from individual entities that are a mixture of both, he is described as "neither being nor non-being, nor being-and-non-being. The statement "the divine Person in the midst" shows his abiding within the cosmic egg in the form of the four-faced Brahmā whom he himself created; the word "Person" (puruṣa) alone refers to the four-faced one, while the Supreme Self, having him as His body, is called "the thousand-headed Person."

The creation of the three-headed Death, as stated in the passage, "He first created Death, the ender of beings," was performed by the Supreme Self (Paramātman) assuming the form of the four-faced Brahmā; for this very reason, it is subsequently stated that "Brahmā was terrified of him. Therefore, it is established that Nārāyaṇa is the cause of the world, described as "neither being nor non-being, nor both being and non-being. Furthermore, [the text] states, "That Āditya is Brahman," meaning that he is indeed Brahman.

The repetition of the word "explained" (*vyākhyāta*) is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter. Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja. And the chapter is completed.
If it is argued that this leads to the fault of leaving no room for memory, we say no; because that would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other forms of memory. || 1 ||

In the first chapter, it was stated that Brahman—the sole cause of the entire universe, the inner Self of all, and the object of knowledge of the Vedāntas—is an entity distinct from the non-conscious objects within the scope of means of valid cognition such as perception, as well as from consciousness when conjoined with or separated from them; and that this Brahman is entirely free from even a trace of the undesirable qualities of ignorance and the like, consisting solely of infinite knowledge and bliss, and is an ocean of immeasurable and sublime attributes.
Immediately following this, the second chapter is commenced in order to demonstrate that this subject cannot be assailed by any possible form of objection. First...

First, having raised the objection that the Vedāntas do not have that [Brahman] as their primary purport because they contradict the Smṛti of Kapila, that objection is now refuted. How can the Śruti be considered to have another purport on account of a contradiction with Smṛti? For it has been stated: "In case of contradiction, however, [the Smṛti] should be disregarded," which establishes that a Smṛti opposed to Śruti is not to be respected. True; in cases such as "Having touched the Audumbarī post, one should sing the Udgītha," since the determination of the meaning is possible through the Śruti itself, a Smṛti opposed to it is indeed to be disregarded.

In this context, however, because the reality known through the Vedānta is difficult to comprehend, it is not contradictory to establish that the Śruti does not intend [the literal meaning] by means of the Yoga-smṛti, which provides certainty regarding the true sense when there is a conflict with the Smṛtis composed by the Great Sage (Vyāsa).

This is what is meant: by one who properly accepts the Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, Jyotiṣṭoma, and other rituals—which are the means for attaining all worldly prosperity arising in the eastern portion [of the path]—it is impossible for those of little learning and dull intellect to understand the supreme beatitude and its means without the support of the Smṛti composed by the Great Sage Kapila, who is proclaimed as authoritative in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas through such statements as "the seer Kapila, the well-born," and who has set forth that knowledge.

Because it is impossible to determine the meaning of the Vedānta [texts] through reasoning alone, and because if one were to accept the literal meaning [of the Upaniṣads], there would be the undesirable consequence that the entire Smṛti of Sāṅkhya—composed by an authoritative person (*āpta*)—would find no scope [for application], one must necessarily admit as a matter of force that the very meaning established by Smṛti is what is to be known from the Vedānta. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, there would be the defect of leaving no scope for the Smṛtis of Manu and others which likewise maintain that Brahman is the sole cause; for they do find scope in providing an expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the earlier portions of the Veda which are intent upon teaching Dharma.

However, since this [Smṛti] is entirely devoted to establishing that [Brahman] as the reality, if it were not accepted as such, it would be rendered completely without scope. He raises this objection: "If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis.

To that, the reply is: "No, because that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis. For other Smṛtis, such as those of Manu and others, declare that Brahman alone is the cause. As Manu says, beginning with "This was then enveloped in darkness," and continuing: "Then the self-existent Lord, the unmanifest, making this manifest, whose power operates through the great elements..."
"The dispeller of darkness appeared. "Desiring to emit various kinds of creatures, he, having meditated upon his own body, first emitted water; into that [water] he cast his seed."

[He] created [it]. And in the Bhagavadgītā: "I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe," and "I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds. In the Mahābhārata, when asked: "From where was this entire world, both moving and unmoving, created? And unto whom does it go at the time of dissolution? Tell me that, O Grandfather," he replied: "Nārāyaṇa is the embodiment of the world, the infinite self, the eternal."

Likewise: "Therefore, O best of the twice-born, the unmanifest, which consists of the three qualities, was produced [from Him]" and "The unmanifest, O Brahmin, is dissolved into the inactive Puruṣa. And the Blessed Parāśara said: "The world has arisen from Viṣṇu and is situated in Him alone; He is the author of the maintenance and withdrawal of this world, and the world is He. And Āpastamba said: "All living beings are indeed cities..."

Beginning with the words, "Of him who dwells in the cave, who is not slain, and who is free from stain," and ending with, "From that body all bodies originate; he is the root, eternal and permanent," [it is established]. If the meaning of the Vedānta passages were determined by the Smṛti of Kapila, then a great defect would result—namely, the lack of scope for all these other Smṛtis.

This is the meaning: although the Vedānta texts are devoted to establishing a subject matter that transcends the scope of all other means of knowledge such as perception, it might be argued that there is no room for the numerous Smṛtis—which were composed by the most authoritative sages, follow the sense of those Vedānta texts, and are intended to supplement them—to provide clarity on their respective meanings for those of limited learning. This [is not the case].

The Smṛti of Kapila, which contains meanings contrary to the Śruti, must be disregarded on the grounds that it would lead to undesirable consequences (prasajyeta). Furthermore, "expansion" (upabṛṃhaṇa) consists in the clarification of the meanings established by the Śruti; and this cannot be accomplished by a Smṛti whose meaning is contradictory [to the Śruti]. Nor can these Smṛtis find scope through the clarification of those portions of Dharma mentioned in the ancient parts [of the Veda].

For these [scriptures], which enjoin duties as a means of propitiating the Supreme Person who is the Supreme Brahman, it would be impossible to enjoin duties that constitute such propitiation if they did not establish that Supreme Person who is to be propitiated. Indeed, it is recorded in the Smṛti that all ritual actions consist in the propitiation of the Supreme Person: "From whom proceeds the activity of beings, by whom all this is pervaded..."

"By worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains success. "One should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa during rites such as ritual bathing; one attains the world of Brahmā and does not return to this world again. O Lord, by those who are devoted to their own duties...

"You have been propitiated by men; they cross over this entire *māyā* for the sake of self-liberation. Nor can it be argued that these [scriptures] possess scope merely through the exposition of rituals that achieve worldly and otherworldly results within *saṃsāra*; for even the nature of those rituals is solely the propitiation of the Supreme Person. As it has been said: "Even those who, endowed with faith, worship other deities, they too, O son of Kuntī, worship Me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule."

"For I alone am the enjoyer and the Lord of all sacrifices; yet they do not know Me in truth, and therefore they fall"—and likewise, "O Acyuta, You who consist of all the gods are eternally worshipped by sacrifices; You alone are the consumer of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings, assuming the forms of both the ancestors and the gods. As for the argument that because Kapila is proclaimed as an authoritative seer (*āpta*) in the passage, "the seer Kapila, who was born of [the power] of the Creator," it is therefore proper to establish the meaning of the Vedānta according to his Smṛti—[this is refuted as follows].

That is incorrect, because Bṛhaspati is proclaimed in the Śrutis and Smṛtis as the exemplar of those possessing superior knowledge among all, and thus there is the possibility that the meaning of the Śruti might be established by means of the Lokāyata system composed by him.

Now, it might be argued: "Since Kapila, through the power of his own yoga, has perceived the true nature of reality, the meaning of the Vedānta should be established in accordance with his Smṛti. To this, the author reads the following sūtra:
"And because others are not found [to possess such knowledge]. (2)

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of the word *tu* (but), intended to remove the doubt that has been raised. Since other authorities such as Manu and others—many who have directly perceived the true nature of the higher and lower principles through the power of their own yoga, whose words are like medicine for the entire world, and who are renowned in the Śruti according to the text, "Whatever Manu said is indeed medicine"—have not perceived the reality in the manner seen by Kapila, it is established that Kapila’s perception, which contradicts the Śruti, is rooted in error; therefore, the meaning of the Vedānta as stated above cannot be shaken by it. Thus ends the section on Smṛti (Smṛtyadhikaraṇa).
By this, Yoga is refuted. || 3 ||

By this refutation of the *Sāṃkhya-smṛti*, the *Yoga-smṛti* is also answered. What, then, is the specific doubt here that necessitates the extension of the same reasoning (*nyāyātideśa*) for its refutation? It might be argued that since the *Yoga-smṛti* accepts the existence of God (*īśvara*), mentions yoga as enjoined in the Vedānta as a means to liberation, and since its author, Hiraṇyagarbha, was authorized to promulgate all the Vedāntas, it is logical that the Vedānta should be supplemented by that *smṛti*.

The rebuttal, however, is as follows: because [the Yoga system] maintains a doctrine of the Pradhāna—which is not of the nature of Brahman—as the material cause, and accepts only the Lord as the efficient cause; and because Yoga, which consists of meditation, can only be defined by its object of meditation, and since the two objects of meditation—the Self and the Lord—lack the nature of being of the essence of Brahman and the possession of all auspicious qualities such as being the material cause of the world, it is non-Vedic; furthermore, even for the speaker, Hiraṇyagarbha, who is himself a *kṣetrajña*, there is the possibility of occasional subjugation by *rajas* and *tamas*. Thus, the *Yoga-smṛti* is also [invalidated].

Since that [Smṛti] possesses a basis in delusion—just like the Purāṇas whose root is passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas)—it is not proper for it to serve as a supplement to the Vedānta. Thus ends the section on the refutation of Yoga.
Not so, because this [world] has different characteristics; and its being thus [as the scripture says] is due to the word. Sūtra 4.1.4.

Again, the proponent of the contradiction with Smṛti, relying on reasoning, objects: "That which was stated—namely, that the world is an effect of Brahman by means of the refutation of the Sāṅkhya Smṛti—is not tenable; for this world, which consists of both conscious and unconscious elements and is perceived through perception and other means as being insentient, impure, non-superintending, and of the nature of suffering, is distinct from the Brahman you accept, who is omniscient, the Lord of all, opposed to everything to be abandoned, and whose sole essence is bliss."

The world's distinctness is perceived not only through perception and other means of knowledge, but its state of being distinct is also perceived from scripture (*śabda*), such as: "Consciousness and non-consciousness"; "In this very way, these elements of being (*bhūtamātrā*) are deposited in the elements of intelligence (*prajñāmātrā*); the elements of intelligence are deposited in the vital breath (*prāṇa*"); "A person is submerged in the same tree; lying in the fire, he grieves, deluded"; and "The self, lacking mastery, is bound by its state of being an enjoyer," and so forth.

For in the case of the world, which is an effect, qualities such as insentience and suffering are pointed out. Whatever is an effect is non-different from its cause, just as a jar or a golden ornament is non-different from clay or gold respectively. Therefore, since this world is different in nature from Brahman, it cannot possibly be its effect; thus, in accordance with the Smṛti of the Sāṅkhyas, the cause must be Pradhāna itself, which is of the same nature as its effects.

Furthermore, although the scripture is independent and has as its domain objects that transcend the senses, reasoning (*tarka*) must nevertheless be followed; for in every case, all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) serve as causes for the ascertainment of an object only when they are assisted by reasoning. Indeed, reasoning is an inquiry concerning the essential nature of an object.

First of all, there is no similarity in all respects [between the world and Brahman], because the relationship of cause and effect would be untenable. Indeed, in the effects of a lump of clay, such as jars and bowls, the persistence of the state of being a "lump" (piṇḍatva) and so forth is not observed. Now, if similarity is intended in respect of some attribute or other, then that is possible even for the world and Brahman, characterized by existence (*sattā*) and so forth. To this it is replied:

The persistence of that very nature by which a causal entity is distinguished from other entities within its effect is the similarity between cause and effect; for the specific form in which gold is distinguished from clay and the like is seen to persist in its effects, such as earrings and the like. And since Brahman has the nature of knowledge, bliss, and sovereignty—which are the opposites of all that is to be discarded—while the world has a nature opposed to those, Brahman cannot be its material cause.

But surely, even in the case of dissimilarity, a causal relationship is observed: for instance, insentient hair, nails, teeth, and body hair are produced from a sentient person, and a sentient scorpion is produced from insentient cow dung; likewise, insentient thread is produced from a sentient spider. This is not so, because even in those cases, the causal relationship exists only between the insentient portions.

Now, it might be argued that even for those things considered insentient, a connection with consciousness is heard of in the Śrutis: "The Earth spoke to him," "The Waters indeed desired," and "These vital breaths, disputing among themselves as to who was superior, went to Brahmā. Furthermore, the authors of the Purāṇas maintain that even rivers, oceans, mountains, and so forth possess sentience; therefore, there is no difference [between them and the conscious Self]. To this, he reads the following reply:
"But [the reference is] to the presiding deities, on account of distinction and association. (Sūtra 2.1.5)

The word *tu* (but) is for the purpose of removing the doubt that has been raised. The deities presiding over earth and the other elements are designated by the words "earth" and so forth in such passages as, "The earth said to him. Why? Because of both distinction (*viśeṣa*) and accompaniment (*anugati*). "Distinction" means qualification; earth and the others are denoted as being qualified by the word "deity," as in, "Come, let me enter these three deities"—where fire, water, and food are qualified by the word "deity"—and [in the passage], "All the deities indeed... [are so qualified].
"...quarreling for the sake of their own superiority," and "those gods, having understood the supreme good in Prāṇa"; "following after" means entering into. "Agni, becoming speech..."

"The Sun entered through the mouth, becoming the eye; he entered the eyes; Vāyu, becoming the breath, entered the nostrils"—through such passages, the entry of Agni and the others as the presiding deities (abhimānin) of speech and the other organs is heard in scripture. Therefore, because the world is of a different nature from Brahman due to its insentience, the production of the world from Brahman is untenable; thus, in accordance with Smṛti supported by reasoning, the Vedāntas establish that the world has Pradhāna as its material cause. || 5 ||
This being the case, it is replied:
"But it is seen. (Sūtra 6)

By the word "tu" (but), the position is reversed. As for what was stated—that because the world is of a different character from Brahman, it is impossible for Brahman to be its material cause—that is incorrect, because the relationship of cause and effect is observed even between things of different characters. For indeed, the production of worms and other such beings, which are of a different character, is seen to arise from honey and other such substances. Now, it might be argued that there is homogeneity only in the insentient portion, since it is only in that aspect that the relationship of cause and effect exists.

It is true that this has been said; however, by that much alone, the similarity (*sālakṣaṇya*) between the cause and the effect as intended by you is not established. For if similarity were established in any way whatsoever, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everything could arise from everything due to the universal similarity of all things. Therefore, you have accepted that similarity consists in the persistence (*anuvṛtti*) of a form (*ākāra*) which serves as the cause for the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of one thing from another. Yet, such a rule is not observed in the case of the production of insects and the like from honey and so forth. Thus, even though the world is dissimilar to Brahman, it is [still] the effect of Brahman.

This is not untenable; for a persistence of a unique form—which serves as the cause for the exclusion of other things—is not observed in cases such as bees, cow-dung beetles, and scorpions, in the same way that it is observed in clay jars, golden crowns, and the like. 6.
If it be argued that [the world] is non-existent, we say no, because [the scripture] consists merely of a negation. (Sūtra 7)

If it is argued that if Brahman, which is the cause, is distinct from the world, which is its effect, then—because cause and effect would be different substances—the effect, the world, does not exist within the supreme Brahman as its cause, and thus the production of a non-existent world would follow; this is not so.

For in the preceding sūtra, the intention was merely to negate the rule that cause and effect must possess identical characteristics; it was not intended to assert that the effect is a different substance from the cause. That Brahman, which is the cause, transforms itself into the form of the world—which is dissimilar to itself—has not been abandoned. Indeed, even in the case of a worm and honey, despite their difference in quality, there is still identity of substance, just as there is between a bracelet and gold. Here, an objection is raised: "If [the world] merges [into Brahman], then [Brahman] would become like that [world]; therefore, [the doctrine] is untenable. (2.1.8)

The phrase "in dissolution" (*apītau*) is intended to indicate that creation and the rest are preceded by dissolution; for in such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1) and "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 1.1.1), we observe that the teaching of creation and so forth is preceded by the instruction on the state of dissolution.

If the identity of substance between cause and effect is accepted, then, given that the effect—the world—is dissolved into and created from Brahman, Brahman itself would undergo those respective states. Consequently, all the imperfections residing in the effect would necessarily attach themselves to Brahman, just as the particularities belonging to a bracelet attach to gold.

Consequently, the entire corpus of Vedāntic statements would become inconsistent, such as: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving"; "Free from evil, ageless, deathless"; "For him there exists neither effect nor instrument; neither one equal nor superior to him is seen"; "One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other Self is powerless, bound by the state of being an enjoyer"; and "Bewildered, he grieves through his lack of sovereignty"—all of these referring to a single entity.

This is because it would follow that these mutually contradictory attributes would apply to the same entity. Now, if it were argued that since the Supreme Brahman alone has the conscious and unconscious entities as its body, and since the causal and effected states belong to that very Brahman, the defects residing in the conscious and unconscious entities—which constitute its body—do not apply to the embodied Brahman in either its state as cause or its state as effect—that is incorrect, because the relationship of body and embodied between the world and Brahman is itself impossible.

Furthermore, even if such a Brahman were possible, defects rooted in connection with a body would be unavoidable; for it is not possible for the conscious and unconscious entities to constitute the body of Brahman, since a "body" is defined as that which consists of pleasure and pain resulting from the fruits of karma.

The body is a specific aggregate of the elements such as earth and so forth, which serves as the substratum for the sense organs that are the means of enjoyment and whose maintenance depends upon the fivefold functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); for it is precisely such a thing that is well-known as "body" (*śarīra*) in both worldly usage and the Veda. Furthermore, the Supreme Self is described by such passages as: "Free from evil, ageless," "Another looks on without eating," "He moves swiftly, yet has no hands or feet; He grasps, yet has no eyes; He hears, yet has no ears," and "For He is without vital breath and without mind."

Because of the absence of karma and the experience of its fruits, because there is no experience dependent upon the senses, and because there is no possession of vital breath (*prāṇa*), neither the conscious nor the unconscious constitutes a body in relation to it. Furthermore, it is not possible for insentient individual forms such as grass and wood, nor for the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) in their collective form, to serve as the substratum of the senses and so forth. Moreover, the subtle elements do not possess the nature of being an aggregate of earth and the other gross elements.

However, for consciousness (*cetanā*), which consists solely of the form of knowledge, none of this is possible; thus, the possibility of its being a body is even further removed. Nor can the state of being a body be defined as "the locus of experience" (*bhogāyatana*), because that would result in the absurdity of houses and the like—being loci of experience—not being recognized as bodies. For [the definition would apply] only to that wherein one currently resides...

If it is argued that the experience of pleasure and pain is itself the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*), we say no; for it is not established that another's body—which serves as the locus for experiencing the pleasure and pain arising from entering another's body—becomes the "entered body" [of the self]. Furthermore, in the case of Īśvara, who possesses by his own nature eternal and unsurpassed bliss, it is impossible for there to be a fixed rule regarding consciousness and matter serving as the locus for experience. By this, the claim that the body is merely the instrument of experience is refuted.

Now, as for the view that "whatever has its nature, existence, and activity dependent upon the will of another is the body of that [other]," and that because everything has its nature, existence, and activity dependent upon the will of the Lord, it is possible for everything to be the Lord's body—that too is not sound, because among those things commonly known as bodies, there is an absence of having their nature dependent upon the will of that particular conscious being [the owner].

Because a diseased body lacks activity dependent upon that [will], and because a dead body lacks existence dependent upon it, and because in the case of statues and the like—which possess their own form, existence, and activity dependent on the will of a conscious being—the status of being "that body" is not established, and because a permanent conscious being lacks a nature dependent on the will of the Lord, the possibility of being "His body" does not exist. Nor can it be said that whatever is governed by one, supported by one, and subservient to one as its sole remnant is the body of that [being].

Because there is deviation [from the rule] regarding action and so forth; and because the absence of a body in the Lord is established by such passages as "bodiless among bodies" and "handless and footless, yet swift and a grasper," the doctrine that Brahman is the cause is inconsistent with the Vedānta texts. This is because the relationship of body and embodied being between the world and Brahman is impossible, and if such a relationship were possible, it would entail the consequence of defects in Brahman.
To this, the following reply is given:
"But it is not so, because of the existence of examples. (9)

There is no such inconsistency, because even when a single entity undergoes two states, the distinction between virtue and defect is established, as evidenced by existing examples. Here, the word "tu" (but/however) indicates the impossibility of even a trace of connection with anything to be abandoned (*heya*). This is what is meant: there is no contradiction whatsoever in the Supreme Brahman—which has the conscious and unconscious entities as its body and is their very self—undergoing the two states of cause and effect characterized by contraction and expansion; for contraction and expansion [are properties of the body].

Regarding the conscious and unconscious entities that constitute the body of the Supreme Brahman: defects residing in the body do not attach to the Self, nor do qualities residing in the Self attach to the body. Just as in the case of embodied individual souls (kṣetrajñas) such as gods and humans, states residing in the body—such as childhood, youth, and old age—are not connected to the Self; and qualities residing in the Self—such as knowledge and happiness—are not found in the body.

Moreover, designations such as "a god is born," "a human is born," and likewise "he himself is a child, a youth, and an old man" are primary (mukhya); for it will be stated in the sūtra "Upon entering into that other [body]" (*tadantarapratipattau*) that the state of being a god, a human, and so forth belongs to the *kṣetrajña* alone, who possesses a subtle body composed of the elements. As for what was further argued—that the status of the gross and subtle world, consisting of both consciousness and non-consciousness, as a body with respect to the Supreme Self is not logically tenable; [this is not so].

That is the mere display of a clever logician, fabricated by his own imagination, for he has not perceived the excellence of the Vedānta texts as supported by the correct method of reasoning; for indeed, every Vedānta text proclaims that everything—whether gross or subtle, conscious or unconscious—is the body of the Supreme Self.

In the *Vājasaneyaka*, specifically in the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa* of both the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions, beginning with the passage, "He who dwells in the earth, whose body is the earth," all insentient objects such as the earth and so forth are individually designated; likewise, sentient beings are designated individually in the passages, "He who dwells in the intellect (*vijñāna*), whose body is the intellect," and "He who dwells in the self (*ātman*), whose body is the self. Thus, each of these is declared to have the Supreme Self as its body.

And in the *Suvālopaniṣad*, beginning with "He who moves within the earth, whose body is the earth," and likewise declaring that the Supreme Self is the body of both the conscious and the unconscious in all their states, it concludes: "This is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, the divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa"—thus establishing His nature as the inner self (*ātman*) in relation to all beings.

And they record [this] in such passages as: "The entire world is Your body," "That which is water is the body of Viṣṇu," "All that is indeed the body of Hari," "All those are His form," and "Having meditated, from His own body... and so forth. The meaning is: "from His own body consisting of the subtle elements."

In the world, the word *śarīra* (body) is observed to be used non-figuratively with respect to substances that possess extremely diverse forms—such as worms, insects, moths, serpents, humans, and animals—even though, like words such as *ghaṭa* (pot), it is established as having a fixed application to substances of a single form. Therefore, the determination of its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) must be made in a way that is consistent with all its usages. Furthermore, the definition of the basis for application stated by you—that it is "the cause for the experience of the fruits of karma," and so forth—is not consistent with all usages.

Because [the definition] does not extend to the earth and other elements mentioned as being the body of the Lord; furthermore, because that definition is non-pervasive with respect to the bodies of the Lord’s will—as understood from such scriptural passages as "He becomes singlefold"—and with respect to the bodies of the liberated, since these lack the cause of connection with the fruits of karma; and because the bodies of the Supreme Person’s will are not specific aggregates of the elements such as earth and so forth, according to the Smṛti: "The body of this Supreme Self is not a configuration of an aggregate of elements."

Therefore, the body’s being composed of a collection of the elements (*bhūtasaṅghātarūpatva*) is non-pervasive, as it does not apply to all bodies; and its being maintained by the fivefold-functioning vital breath (*pañcavṛttiprāṇādhīnadhāraṇatva*) is also non-pervasive with respect to immobile bodies (*sthāvaraśarīra*), for although vital breath exists in immobile beings, it does not exist there as the sustainer of the body by abiding in a fivefold manner. Furthermore, the body’s being the locus of the senses (*indriyāśrayatva*) and its being the cause of pleasure and pain (*sukhaduḥkhahetutva*) are non-pervasive in the case of Ahalyā and others, whose bodies were made of stone, wood, and so forth due to their karma.

Therefore, the definition of a body (*śarīra*) must be accepted as follows: that substance which can be entirely controlled and maintained by a conscious being for its own purposes, and whose sole essential nature is to exist as a subordinate to that being, is its body. The non-perception of control and other functions in cases such as a diseased body is caused by an obstruction to the existing power of control itself, just as heat and other qualities are not perceived in fire and the like when their power is obstructed. Furthermore, a dead body begins to disintegrate at the very moment of separation from the conscious being and is completely dissolved in the subsequent moment.

Previously, the designation "body" was applied because [the individual soul] was conceived as a part of the aggregate that constitutes the body; therefore, since everything—whether sentient or insentient—is governed by the Supreme Person for His own purpose, supported by Him as His very self, and has its sole essential nature as being subservient to Him, all of it is His body. Furthermore, passages such as "He who is bodiless among bodies" are intended to deny a body caused by karma, because of the scriptural hearing of His aforementioned status as the body of all things; this will be further established in the subsequent sections.

By the two sūtras, "In dissolution, there would be the same contingency; therefore it is inconsistent" and "But not so, because of the existence of examples," the point established in the section beginning with "Because of the designation of the other" is recalled.
And because of the defect in one's own position. || 10 ||

This resort to [the doctrine of Brahman as the cause] is not based solely on the faultlessness of the theory of Brahman as the cause; rather, because the theory of Pradhāna as the cause is defective, one must abandon that and resort to this alone. For in the theory of Pradhāna as the cause, the activity of the world is not logically possible. In that view, the activity of the world is supposedly based on the superimposition of the attributes of Prakṛti upon the Puruṣa—who is changeless and consists of the single essence of pure consciousness—due to its proximity to Prakṛti.

It must be investigated what the nature of the proximity of *prakṛti* is, which serves as the cause for the superimposition of the attributes of *prakṛti* upon the immutable one whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Is it the mere existence of *prakṛti*, or some modification belonging to it, or perhaps some modification residing in the *puruṣa* itself? First, it cannot reside in the *puruṣa*, because that is not admitted [by you]. Nor can it be a modification of *prakṛti*, because that which is accepted as the effect of superimposition cannot possibly be the cause of that very superimposition. Furthermore, if mere existence were the proximity, then the consequence would follow that even a liberated soul (*mukta*) would undergo superimposition; thus, the world [would persist] according to your position.

Therefore, its activity is not tenable. This point will be elaborated upon at the time of refuting the Sāṃkhya position, starting with the statement: "Even if [the self] were admitted, there would be no purpose," and so forth.
Also because reasoning is not firmly established. || 11 ||

Furthermore, because reasoning (*tarka*) is unstable, one must rely exclusively on the doctrine that Brahman is the cause, which is rooted in the Śruti, and not on the doctrine that the Pradhāna is the cause. The instability of reasoning is understood from the mutual contradictions among the reasonings of the Śākyas, Ulūkyas, Akṣapādas, Kṣapaṇakas, Kapilas, and Patañjalis.
If it is argued that the object of inference is otherwise, even so, there follows the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation.

If you argue that we shall now refute the reasoning of the Śākyas and others currently existing, and by demonstrating flaws other than those already shown, we shall infer [the truth] regarding the doctrine of Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause; even so, since this [reasoning] relies solely on logic rooted in human intellect, it remains impossible to escape the fault of the "instability of logic" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhāna*). For there is the possibility that in other places and at other times, the reasoning might be subverted by the conjectures of persons more skilled in fallacious logic (*kutarka*) than yourself. Therefore, with regard to objects beyond the senses, scripture alone is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Logical reasoning (*tarka*) is to be accepted solely for the purpose of supplementing that [scriptural knowledge]; thus it has been said: "He who investigates the traditional teaching of Dharma and the instruction on Dharma by means of reasonings that do not contradict the Vedic scriptures—he, and no other, knows Dharma. The meaning is "by means of those that do not contradict the scripture known as the Veda. Therefore, because it contradicts the Veda, the *Sāṅkhya-smṛti* is not to be respected for the purpose of employing the kind of reasoning that supplements the Veda by clarifying its meaning. The section concerning the difference in nature (*vilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained. || 13 ||

"Remnants" (*śiṣṭāḥ*) means those who remain; "without acceptance" (*aparigrahāḥ*) refers to those for whom there is no acceptance of the Vedas; thus, "remnants without acceptance" (*śiṣṭāparigrahāḥ*). By this refutation of the Sāṅkhya position—which is not accepted by the Vedas—it should be understood that the remaining positions not accepted by the Vedas—namely, those of Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣika), Akṣapāda (the Naiyāyika), Kṣapaṇaka (the Jaina), and Bhikṣu (the Buddhist)—are also refuted. Since all of these agree in their doctrine of atoms as the cause, it follows that reasoning concerning the nature of causal entities is unstable.

The objection that "it cannot be said [that there is no contradiction]" represents an excessive doubt. The rebuttal is as follows: even if there were agreement on those points alone, since the basis remains equally rooted in mere reasoning (*tarka*), and because we observe contradictions regarding the very nature of atoms—such as whether they are void or non-void, whether they consist of cognition or an object, whether they are momentary or eternal, whether they are exclusively unitary or manifold, and whether they are real or unreal—it follows that [the system] is indeed unstable.
If it be argued that there is no distinction because of the identity of the enjoyer, [we reply] that it may be so, as in the case of the world. 14.

Furthermore, the Sāṅkhya objects: as for what was stated—that because the Supreme Brahman, whose body consists of gross and subtle sentient and insentient entities, exists in the form of both cause and effect, the distinction between the intrinsic natures of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is logically established—that distinction is not possible if Brahman possesses a body.

For that [Brahman] would incur the status of being an enjoyer; since, if it possessed a body, it would be unavoidable for the Lord—as well as for the individual soul—to be an enjoyer of pleasure and pain resulting from having a body. Now, one might argue that the contingency of the Lord’s enjoyment was already refuted in the Sūtra, "If it be argued that there is the attainment of enjoyment, no, because of the difference" (BS 1.2.8). This is not so; for in that context, it was stated that the contingency of enjoyment does not exist merely by virtue of the Lord's presence within the body—residing in the heart as the object of meditation—whereas here, the case is that of Brahman being like the individual soul.

It is argued that if [the self] were possessed of a body, then, just as in that case, the undesirable consequence of being an experiencer (*bhoktṛ*) of pleasure and pain would be unavoidable. For it is observed that embodied living beings, even when free from bodily modifications such as childhood or old age, are joined with pleasure and pain caused by the equilibrium or imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). And scripture states: "Indeed, for one who is embodied, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant; but for one who is indeed bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch."

If it is argued that, because the distinction between the essential natures of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is impossible under the theory of a corporeal Brahman as the cause, and because under the theory of Brahman alone as the cause there follows the undesirable consequence that Brahman—like clay or gold—would be the substratum of all worldly distinctions such as lack of human purpose (*apuruṣārtha*), the theory of Pradhāna as the cause is indeed superior;

to this the reply is: "It may be so, as in the world. Indeed, the distinction between the essential natures of the individual soul and the Lord is possible. For the individual soul's state of being an enjoyer of pleasure and pain, caused by the equilibrium or imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), is not produced by its possession of a body, but rather by karma in the form of merit and demerit (*puṇya-pāpa*).

The statement, "Indeed, for one who possesses a body," also refers to the body initiated by karma; for there is not even a trace of anything contrary to the supreme human goal for one who, though possessing a body, has manifested his true nature and is liberated from the bondage of karma—as seen in such passages as, "He becomes singlefold, he becomes threefold," "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers," and "There he moves about, eating, playing, and rejoicing."

However, since the Supreme Self is free from evil (apahatapāpman), even though it has the entire universe—both in its gross and subtle forms—as its body, there is not even a trace of connection with karma; thus, there is all the less any possibility of the consequence of being connected to that which is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha). Just as in the world, although those who obey a king’s commands and those who disobey them experience pleasure and pain resulting from the king’s favor or punishment, the mere fact of having a body does not entail that the ruler, the king himself, becomes an enjoyer of the pleasure and pain caused by obedience to or transgression of his commands.

As the author of the Dramiḍa-bhāṣya has said: "Just as in the world a king, though residing in a region full of venomous snakes and terrible calamities, is not touched by defects because his body is brushed away by fans and the like; and just as he protects the desired worlds and maintains enjoyments such as perfumes that are to be experienced by all people, so too does this Lord of the World, whose own power is ever-active..."

"The yak-tail whisk (*cāmara*) is not touched by defects, and it protects the worlds beginning with the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), while maintaining enjoyments that are to be experienced by all people. However, a transformation of the nature of Brahman—like clay or gold—is certainly not accepted, because of scriptural texts such as those concerning its changelessness and freedom from defects.
