As for the interpretation offered by others regarding the Sūtra which, having raised the objection that there would be no distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed in the doctrine of Brahman as the cause, explains this distinction through the analogy of the ocean, foam, and waves—that is incorrect.

For those who accept that creation proceeds from Brahman as conditioned by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), whose power is internalized, such objections and their refutations are inconsistent. This is because the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*) is that which is qualified by the limiting adjunct of ignorance residing within the cause, while the object of experience (*bhogya*) is the adjunct itself.

Indeed, it is impossible for these two distinct entities to undergo a mutual transformation into one another; furthermore, even they do not admit a modification of the essential nature (*svarūpa-pariṇāma*), since [the Sūtra] "If it be said that there is no [creation] because of the non-distinction of action, we say no, because of beginninglessness" establishes the beginninglessness of both the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) and the karma residing within them.

Even if one accepts that [the Self] undergoes modification of its own nature (*svarūpapariṇāma*), no one at all need fear the confusion of the enjoyer and the enjoyed; for the distinction between enjoyer and enjoyed is logically established, just as there is a distinction between a jar, a bowl, an earring, or a crown—all of which are modifications of clay or gold. Furthermore, if there were a modification of the very nature of Brahman, it would follow that Brahman itself becomes both the enjoyer and the enjoyed, and thus there would again be a lack of consistency. Thus ends the section on the "Enjoined Enjoyer" (*Bhoktrāpatti-adhikaraṇa*).
The non-difference of that [effect] from that [cause] follows from the words concerning "origination" (ārambhaṇa) and so forth. (2.1.15)

In passages such as, "If it be said that [the effect] is non-existent, no, because [the scripture] is a mere negation," the fact that Brahman is the cause of the world was established by accepting the non-difference of the world, which is the effect, from Brahman, which is the cause; now, that very non-difference is challenged and resolved. In this regard:

The followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) say: "It is not possible for the effect to be non-different from its cause, because they are apprehended by distinct cognitions; indeed, the cognition regarding the threads and the cloth, or the lump of clay and the jar, and so forth, is not of a single form. Furthermore, because of the difference in words: for threads are not called 'cloth,' nor is cloth called 'threads.'"

And because of the difference in function: for water is not carried by a lump of clay, nor is a wall constructed by a jar. And because of the difference in time: the cause exists at an earlier time, and the effect at a later time. And because of the difference in form: the cause has the form of a lump, while the effect has the form of a broad base and belly; thus, even while the clay remains, one speaks conventionally of "the jar having been destroyed. Furthermore, a difference in number is observed: there are many threads, yet the cloth is one.

Furthermore, there would be the futility of the activity of causal factors (*kāraka-vyāpāra*): if the effect were identical to the cause, what would be accomplished by the activity of the causal factors? If it is argued that even when the effect exists, the activity of the causal factors must still occur for the sake of its utility, then the activity of the causal factors could never cease. Since everything would exist at all times, the distinction between the eternal (*nitya*) and the non-eternal (*anitya*) would not exist.

Now, if it is argued that the effect exists even previously but was merely unmanifest, and is manifested through the operation of causal factors (kāraka), and therefore the utility of the operation of causal factors and the distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal are maintained—this is incorrect. For if manifestation requires another manifestation, there would be an infinite regress; if it does not require another, the effect would necessarily be perceived eternally; and if one accepts its production [rather than manifestation], it follows that one is a proponent of the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*).

Furthermore, if the operation of the causal factors (*kāraka*) were merely manifesting [what already exists], it would follow that by the operation of the causal factors intended for a jar, even a water-pot (*karaka*) and other such things would be manifested; for among lamps and other well-known manifestors, no restriction regarding specific objects to be manifested is observed. Indeed, a lamp brought forth for the sake of a jar does not fail to manifest a water-pot and the like. Therefore, the utility of the operation of causal factors lies solely in being the cause of the production of an effect that was previously non-existent; consequently, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is not established.

Furthermore, the employment of specific causes does not prove that the effect exists [prior to its production], because that is established simply by the restriction of the causal capacity. Now, it may be argued: "Even for one who maintains that the effect is non-existent, the operation of the causal factors is untenable, because the effect is non-existent prior to its production; the operation of the causal factors must pertain to something other than the effect. Since there is no distinction regarding 'being other,' it would follow as an absurd consequence that the operation of the causal factors residing in the threads could produce a jar. This is not so.

That which is capable of producing an effect is the cause, because the production of that effect is established through the operation of the causal factors inherent in it. Regarding this, they say: the effect is not other than the cause; for in ultimate reality, there exists no entity called an "effect" distinct from the cause. Since all effects and their conventional usage are based upon ignorance (*avidyā*), just as the effects such as jars and bowls—which are perceived in modifications of the causal substance of clay—are false and have mere conventionality as their basis, being non-distinct from the causal substance of clay.

This alone is the truth: just as [the world appears], so too, the entire phenomenal expansion (prapañca)—which is the substratum for empirical usage such as the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra) and is distinct from Brahman, which is the cause consisting of pure Being (sanmātra)—is false; only Brahman, the cause consisting of pure Being, is real. Therefore, since there is no effect apart from its cause, the effect is non-different from the cause. Nor should it be argued that the illustration is untenable because the unreality of effects such as jars is not well-established in the same way as [the unreality of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; [for such unreality is indeed established].

Since even there, by means of reasoning, only the substance of clay is established as real, while that which exceeds it is sublated by reasoning—what then is the reasoning here? It is the persistence of the mere substance of clay and the exclusion of that which exceeds it.

For in the case of the rope-snake and similar illusions, it is observed that the rope and so forth, which persist as the underlying substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), are real, whereas the snake, the patch of earth, the leaf, or the streak of water, which recede from view, are unreal; likewise, the material substance of clay, which persists as the substratum, is alone real, while the jar, the bowl, and other such forms, which recede, are unreal.

Furthermore, since there is no destruction of an existing self (*ātman*) and since non-existent things such as a hare’s horn are not perceived, it is understood that an effect—which possesses both perception and destruction—is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) in terms of being either existent or non-existent. And this indefinability is merely illusory, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; its indefinability is established by both its appearance and its subsequent sublation.

Furthermore, in producing an effect, does the causal substance, such as clay, produce that effect while remaining entirely unmodified? Or does it do so having undergone some modification? It cannot produce it while remaining unmodified, because that would entail the consequence that it must produce the effect at all times. Nor can it produce it by undergoing another modification, because that further modification must itself be preceded by yet another modification, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) as the same logic would apply to each subsequent one. [If you argue] that it produces the effect while remaining unmodified... [regarding] location...

If it is argued that [the cause] produces an effect through its connection with specific temporal conditions (*kāla-nimitta-viśeṣa*), we say no; for even a connection with specific spatial conditions (*deśa-ādi-viśeṣa*) is impossible for that which remains unmodified, as well as for that which has attained another modification, just as before. Nor should it be said: "The production of jars, earrings, curd, and so forth from clay, gold, milk, and the like is observed; furthermore, unlike the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, no sublation (*bādha*) is seen regarding the conditions perceived in space, time, and so on; therefore, those who rely on empirical cognition must necessarily accept the production of an effect from a cause. [This is because] such things as jars, earrings, and curd are indeed not produced from clay, gold, and milk respectively, but rather from the *mṛdvikalpa* (clay-potentiality), the *suvarṇavikalpa* (gold-potentiality), and the *kṣīravikalpa* (milk-potentiality). Furthermore, since the very nature of these [causes] is established by perception, they cannot be sublated by inference. Moreover, the production of an effect from a cause is not observed in the case of the ether (*ākāśa*), etc., nor is there any proof for it. Therefore, the doctrine of the non-difference between cause and effect is established. Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is that the cause and the effect are non-different. This is what is intended. Furthermore, this is stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "The non-difference of the cause and the effect is established by the fact that the effect is perceived as having the same nature as the cause. This is the meaning. This is the meaning. And this is stated in the *Vedānta-siddhānta-sudhā-nidhi*: "

Since it cannot withstand critical analysis, is it the gold alone that is the originator (*ārambhaka*) of the svastika and so forth, or is it the necklace (*rucaka*) and so forth, or is it the gold as the substratum (*āśraya*) of the necklace and so forth? First of all, the gold alone is not the originator; for there is no effect distinct from the gold, and because it is impossible for a thing to be its own originator with respect to itself. If it is argued that a svastika is seen distinct from the gold, we say no; it is not distinct from the gold, because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the gold and because no other object over and above it is perceived.

If it is argued that the existence of a distinct entity is established by means of different cognitions, words, and so forth, we say no; for cognitions, words, and the like, which have as their basis an entity not yet determined, are rooted in error—just like the cognition and word of "silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl—and thus they cannot prove the existence of a distinct entity. Nor does the *rucaka* (necklace) originate from the *svastika* (cross-shaped ornament), for you yourself do not perceive the *rucaka* within the *svastika*, just as one does not perceive threads in a cloth.

Nor is gold the substratum of the necklace (*rucaka*), because gold is not perceived in the form of the necklace when it exists as a *svastika* [another ornament]. Therefore, since an effect is seen to be unreal when distinct from its cause such as clay, the entire world, being an effect distinct from Brahman, is false. This unreality of the effect has been established by resorting to the imagined reality of clay and so forth, merely for the sake of easily understanding the falsity of everything other than Brahman.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, even causes such as clay or gold are false (*mithyā*), just like their effects such as pots or golden ornaments, because there is no difference in their being effects of Brahman. This is confirmed by such scriptural passages as: "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth"; "There is not the slightest diversity here"; "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity"; "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another"; "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?"; and "Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion" (*māyā*). Thus, by these and other such scriptures, [the falsity of the world] is established in relation to Brahman.

The falsity of that which is other [than Brahman] is understood. Nor should a contradiction with perception be suspected regarding an object known through scripture; for, according to the manner already stated, all effects are understood to be false, and perception has "pure Being" (sanmātra) as its sole object. Even if there were a contradiction, since the final [means of knowledge], being free from the possibility of defect, depends upon perception and the like for its own existence and so forth, yet in the production of valid cognition, the scripture is more powerful because it is independent and finds no other scope [for its application].

Therefore, everything other than Brahman, which is the cause, is false. Nor should the falsity of the individual soul (*jīva*) be suspected on account of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because Brahman itself exists in the state of the individual soul. Indeed, Brahman alone experiences the state of the individual soul within all bodies, as evidenced by such scriptural passages as: "Having entered [the worlds] with this living self (*jīva-ātman*)," "The one God is hidden in all beings," "The one God has entered in many ways," "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth," and "There is no other seer but He."

If it is argued that there is indeed only one Brahman experiencing the state of an individual soul (jīva) within all bodies, then there would be a recollection of pleasure and pain across all bodies—just as one says, "I have a pain in my foot" or "I have pleasure in my head"—and the established distinctions between the individual soul and the Lord, the bound and the liberated, the disciple and the teacher, and knowledge and ignorance would not exist.

In this regard, some who indeed accept the non-duality of Brahman offer this resolution: the states of happiness, suffering, and so forth, belonging to the individual souls (jīvas) which are reflections of the one Brahman alone, are established according to their respective limiting adjuncts (upādhis), just as smallness, largeness, dirtiness, and clarity are perceived in the various reflections of a single face in jewels, swords, mirrors, and the like.

Now, it has been stated that on the basis of such scriptural passages as, "Having entered with this living self (jīva-ātman)," the individual souls (jīvas) do not differ from Brahman; this is true from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha). However, this systematic arrangement is stated by relying upon a conceptual distinction (kalpanika-bheda). But whose is this conceptualization? It cannot belong to Brahman, for He, whose nature is pure knowledge, is devoid of conceptualization. Nor can it belong to the individual souls, because that would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya): the state of being a soul is dependent upon conceptualization, yet conceptualization is dependent upon the soul.

This is not so, because the states of ignorance and the individual soul (jīva) are beginningless, according to the analogy of the seed and the sprout. Furthermore, it is logically consistent, like the swallowing of a palace and so forth.

Since ignorance (*avidyā*) is of the nature of a mere appearance and lacks substantial reality, defects pertaining to real entities—such as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) and the like—do not apply to it. Although the individual souls (*jīvas*), being in reality non-different from Brahman, are inherently pure, the possibility of impurity arising through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is established, just as a reflection of a face appears dark in a sword or similar object. Thus, the status of ignorance as a conceptual construction is justified; for the impurity residing in the soul, like the darkness in a reflection, is merely an illusion, otherwise the consequence would be the impossibility of liberation.

[The opponent argues: "Since the stream of the delusion of living beings (*jīva*) is beginningless, its cause need not be sought. This is merely a manifestation of the desire for the gaze of respect from people who are devoted to the doctrine of duality (*bhedavāda*) because they do not know the true nature of non-duality (*advaita*). To explain: if the individual soul (*jīva*) were the locus of ignorance (*avidyā*) by virtue of its own unimagined, natural form, it would amount to saying that Brahman itself is the locus of ignorance. On the other hand, if it were the locus of ignorance by means of an imagined form distinct from that [natural one], it would amount to saying that an insentient (*jaḍa*) entity is the locus of ignorance.

Indeed, the proponents of non-duality (advaitavādins) do not accept any form distinct from those two [the pure consciousness and the ignorance]. If it is argued that the status of being the locus of ignorance belongs to the essential nature itself as qualified by an imagined form, that is not so; for the essential nature, which is partless and of a single flavor, cannot be established as having a qualified form without ignorance, since it is precisely the form of the locus of ignorance that must be defined. Furthermore, the adoption of the theory of individual souls' ignorance (*jīvājñānavāda*) is indeed for the sake of establishing the systematic distinction between bondage, liberation, and so forth.

But that systematic arrangement is not established even under the view that ignorance belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*). For liberation is indeed the destruction of ignorance; in that case, when one [soul] is liberated, others too would be liberated due to the destruction of ignorance. If it is argued that ignorance persists because it has not been destroyed for another [soul], then there would be no liberation even for that one, since ignorance has not been destroyed. If it is argued that a distinction between ignorances is postulated for each individual soul—such that he whose ignorance is destroyed will be liberated, while he whose is not destroyed will remain bound—that is not so.

When you say "for every living being," you do so by relying on a plurality of souls (*jīvabheda*). Is this plurality of souls innate (*svābhāvika*) or imagined through ignorance (*avidyākalpita*)? It cannot be innate, because it is not admitted [by you], and because the postulation of ignorance for the sake of establishing that plurality would be redundant. If, on the other hand, it is imagined through ignorance, then is this ignorance that imagines the plurality of souls located in Brahman or in the souls themselves? If you say it is in Brahman, then you have come to my own path.

Now, do you forget that this [variety of ignorance] is intended for the purpose of establishing the distinction between individual souls? Or, if you think that the very ignorances postulated for the sake of establishing the distinction between the bound and the liberated for each soul also constitute the distinction between souls—then there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): those [ignorances] are established once the distinction between souls is established, and the distinction between souls is established once they are established.

Furthermore, the logic of the seed and the sprout does not hold here. For in the case of seeds and sprouts, one distinct seed is the producer of another distinct sprout; but in this case, since those very same ignorance-s (avidyās) by which living beings (jīvas) are conceptualized must depend upon those very beings for their own establishment, it is impossible [to maintain the analogy]. If you think that, according to the logic of the seed and the sprout, successive conceptualizations of living beings arise based on preceding ignorance-s that depend upon preceding living beings, then it would follow that living beings are transitory, and there would be the undesirable consequences of "attaining what was not done" (akṛtābhyāgama) and "the loss of what was done" (kṛtavipraṇāśa).

For this very reason, the view that the successive states of being a jīva are imagined for Brahman by means of the respective ignorance (avidyā) residing in each preceding jīva is also refuted. If a stream of ignorance is admitted, then the state of being a jīva imagined at each stage would likewise have to be beginningless as a stream; it could not possess a permanent nature, [as that would contradict the nature of] illusion (āmo).

Furthermore, the permanence of the individual soul (*jīva*) would not be established. As for the argument that because ignorance (*avidyā*) consists of a non-entity, it is characterized solely by its impossibility, and thus defects pertaining to real entities—such as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*)—do not apply to it: if that were so, ignorance would have to reside in liberated souls and in the Supreme Brahman. If you argue that because its nature is pure knowledge (*vidyā*), impurity does not attach to it, then is ignorance something that conforms to logical justification? If so, then by those same arguments, it should not reside in individual souls either.

Furthermore, when ignorance (*avidyā*), which has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its substrate, is destroyed by the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), does the soul perish or not? If it perishes, liberation (*mokṣa*) would consist in the annihilation of one's own nature (*svarūpa-ucchitti*). If it does not perish, there is no liberation even upon the destruction of ignorance, because the state of being an individual soul remains distinct from the nature of Brahman.

As for what was said—that the establishment of distinctions such as purity and impurity is possible, just as the impurity or clarity of a face perceived in a jewel, a sword, a mirror, and so forth [is relative]—this must be examined: when would the defects such as smallness and impurity, which are caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), cease? If it is argued that they cease upon the removal of the adjuncts such as the sword, then does the reflection, which is the locus of that smallness and so forth, persist or not? If it persists, then since the *jīva* occupying that position would also persist, there follows the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣa*).

If it were to perish in that same way, then liberation—characterized by the destruction of one's own nature through the destruction of the living soul—would result. Furthermore, for one who perceives a defect in the form of something that is not a human goal, the eradication of that [defect] constitutes a human goal.

In this regard, does the appearance of defects caused by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-doṣa*) belong to Brahman, which stands in the position of the original object (*bimba*), or to the individual soul (*jīva*), which stands in the position of the reflection (*pratibimba*), or to some other entity? In the first two alternatives, this illustration is not applicable, because neither the face nor its reflection is subject to the appearance of defects such as smallness; for neither the face nor its reflection perceives itself. Furthermore, if the appearance of defects belonged to Brahman, it would entail the consequence of Brahman being possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*).

The third alternative also is not tenable, because there exists no seer apart from the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman. Furthermore, it must be determined who the creator of the individual soul—which is itself a product of ignorance—is. It cannot be ignorance, because ignorance is insentient. Nor can it be the individual soul, because that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), and because the state of being an individual soul is itself a product of ignorance, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. If it is argued that Brahman alone is the creator, then that results in nothing other than the admission of Brahman’s own ignorance.

Furthermore, if the ignorance of Brahman is not admitted, does Brahman perceive the individual souls (jīvas) or not? If it does not perceive them, then Brahman’s creation of the manifold world preceded by reflection, as well as its differentiation of names and forms, and so forth, would be impossible. If, on the other hand, it does perceive them, then since Brahman—which is partless and of a single homogeneous essence—cannot perceive the individual souls without the existence of ignorance (avidyā), the consequence follows that Brahman itself possesses ignorance. For this very reason, even the doctrine that distinguishes between Māyā and Avidyā is refuted; for without ignorance, even for Brahman as the possessor of Māyā (māyin), [such perception would be impossible].

The Lord would not possess the quality of seeing individual souls (*jīva-darśitva*). Furthermore, a magician is not capable of deluding others without first seeing them; nor is *māyā* a means for the magician’s own perception, since its function is solely to delude others once they have been seen. If you then think that the *māyā* of Brahman, by effecting His vision of individual souls, is the cause of their delusion, then *māyā*—which is synonymous with *avidyā*—would be that which effects the perception of "others" (i.e., the individual souls) by Brahman, who is otherwise pure, partless, of one essence, and self-luminous. Thus, it would be nothing other than ignorance (*avidyā*).

Now, it might be argued that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of perceiving things erroneously, whereas *māyā*—by showing that which is unreal and distinct from Brahman as being indeed unreal—is not the cause of erroneous perception regarding Brahman; therefore, it is not ignorance. This is not so, because even the cause of seeing two moons when the oneness of the moon is known is ignorance. Furthermore, if Brahman were to know that which is distinct from itself as being unreal, then it would not delude [itself].

For one who is not insane does not seek to delude those who already know a thing to be false. Now, if it is held that *avidyā* (ignorance) is the cause of perceiving what is not the supreme goal of man (*apuruṣārtha*) and what is not the ultimate reality (*aparamārtha*), whereas *māyā* is not the cause of Brahma’s perception of what is not the supreme goal of man—and therefore *māyā* is not *avidyā*—that is not correct. For even though the cognition of two moons is not itself a non-goal of man (*apuruṣārtha*) because it lacks the quality of being a cause of suffering, its cause is indeed *avidyā*; and people exert effort toward its removal.

And if *māyā* does not consist in the perception of that which is not the supreme human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), then, being incapable of cessation, it would be eternal and inseparable from the nature of Brahman. If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", the fault is precisely the perception of duality. For non-dual scriptures such as, "Where there is, as it were, duality... but where for him everything has become the Self alone, by what and whom should he see? would be contradicted.

If it is argued that the scriptural texts concerning non-duality (*advaita*) have the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) as their object, and thus there is no contradiction because *māyā* is not ultimately real, [we reply: the perception of *māyā*, which is not ultimately real, and the possession of it by Brahman—whose sole nature is unlimited bliss—would not be possible without ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, what purpose does Brahman have for an eternal *māyā* that is not ultimately real? If it is said to be "the deluding of the individual soul" (*jīva-mohana*), [we reply:]...

What purpose is served by this delusion, which is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*)? If you say it is for the sake of play (*krīḍā*), then what need has one whose bliss is unlimited for play? If you argue that in the world play is seen as a human goal only for those who possess complete enjoyment (*bhoga*), we reply: this is not tenable here. For the savor of play cannot be produced in those who are not insane by means of toys for play that are unreal, which appear as unreal, and by means of a play that is accomplished as something unreal, nor by that appearance of it as something unreal.

Furthermore, as before, one must recognize that it is impossible to postulate a jīva as the locus of ignorance distinct from Brahman, which is accepted as the locus of illusion; therefore, those who maintain that Brahman is non-dual must accept that Brahman itself, variegated by beginningless ignorance, perceives its own internal manifoldness.

As for the objection that the distinction between bondage and liberation is untenable, that is not a valid criticism against the proponent of Brahman-ignorance (*brahmājñānavādin*). For it is the one and same Brahman who, being ignorant, is to be liberated through the cessation of his own ignorance; thus, there is no actual distinction such as "bound" or "liberated. Furthermore, the conventionally employed distinction between the bound, the liberated, the disciple, and the teacher is merely conceptual (*kālpinika*), since all such conceptualizations are possible through the ignorance of a single individual, just as in the case of a dreamer. Indeed, disciples, teachers, and so forth are seen by a single dreamer.

These [distinctions] are merely imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*); for this very reason, even the postulation of manifold ignorances is not logical. Even by the proponent of the ignorance of the individual soul (*jīvājñānavādin*), an ultimate distinction between bondage and liberation, as well as the distinction between self and other, is not admitted. However, a non-ultimate distinction is possible for a single [Self] alone due to its ignorance. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the distinctions of bondage and liberation, as well as the distinctions of self and other, are imagined through one's own ignorance, because they are non-ultimate, like the distinctions seen in a dream.

Other bodies as well possess a self only through me, because they are bodies, just like this body. Other bodies as well are fashioned by my ignorance, because they are bodies, or because they are effects, or because they are insentient, or because they are imagined, just like this body. The entire collection of sentient beings under dispute is indeed myself, because they are sentient; for whatever is not "I" is seen to be insentient, such as a jar. Therefore, the distinction between self and other, and the established order of the bound and the liberated, of disciples and teachers, and so forth, are all imagined through the ignorance of the One.

Even for the proponent of dualism (*dvaitavādin*), the distinction between the bound and the liberated is difficult to establish. Since past *kalpas* are infinite, even if one soul were liberated in each *kalpa*, liberation would eventually be possible for all, making the existence of the unliberated untenable. If it is argued that there are unliberated souls because the selves (*ātman*) are infinite, what does this "infinity" mean? If you say it means "innumerability," no; for although they may be innumerable to those of limited knowledge due to their great number, to the omniscient Lord (*īśvara*), they must be numerable. If even He could not count them, His omniscience would be compromised.

If it is argued that because the Self is devoid of number (*niḥsaṅkhyatva*), the absence of the cognition of number in the Lord does not entail ignorance, [we reply: if there were difference (*bhinnatva*), the state of being devoid of number would not be tenable. Those who possess number are distinct from the Self, because they are different, like beans, mustard seeds, jars, cloths, and so forth. Furthermore, if there were difference, it would follow that the Self is insentient (*jaḍatva*), non-self (*anātmatva*), and perishable (*kṣayitva*), just like a jar or similar objects. Moreover, Brahman would lack infinity (*anantatva*). Infinity consists precisely in the absence of limitation (*aparicchedarahitatva*).

Furthermore, in the doctrine of difference (bhedavāda), it is impossible to assert that Brahman is in reality devoid of limitation by virtue of being distinct from other entities; for the very existence of other entities constitutes limitation in reality.

In reality, it is not logical for that which is limited by substance to be unlimited by space and time; for objects such as jars, being distinct from other entities, are indeed seen to be limited by substance and likewise limited by space and time. Thus, all conscious beings and Brahman, being limited by substance, are also limited by space and time.

And thus, there would be a contradiction with such passages as "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," which declare that [Brahman] is devoid of all forms of limitation. Furthermore, birth, destruction, and so forth would necessarily follow for both the individual souls and Brahman; for being subject to birth and destruction is indeed nothing other than limitation by time. Therefore, the entire universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is a manifestation of ignorance projected upon the one, undivided Brahman.

The establishment of the transition between pleasure and pain, and so forth, is also possible due to the inherent nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), just like the arrangements seen in a dream. Therefore, the one reality alone—which is eternal, liberated, and self-luminous by nature—manifests as the world through the power of beginningless ignorance. Thus, since in ultimate reality there is nothing apart from Brahman, the world is non-different from it.

To this it is replied: that Brahman, which is without distinction and is mere self-luminosity, perceives its own internal multiplicity because its true nature has been concealed by beginningless ignorance—this is contrary to all means of valid cognition and contradicts its own words, as has already been stated; for since Brahman is of the nature of light and partless, concealment in the form of the cessation of that light would entail the destruction of its very nature, and thus concealment is impossible.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the effect is distinct from its cause and is therefore an illusion—like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—due to being sublated by reasoning, that is incorrect, because such reasoning does not exist. As for the argument that the persisting cause alone is real while the receding effects, such as jars and bowls, are unreal, that too has already been refuted previously by the point that the fact of something perceived elsewhere receding elsewhere does not constitute a sublation. And as for the claim that the unreality of the effect is established by its being indescribable as either existent or non-existent due to its being both perceived and subject to destruction, that is also false.

Indeed, the connection with the destruction of perception does not establish falsity (*mithyātva*), but rather impermanence (*anityatva*). For the cause of falsity is precisely the sublation (*bādhitatva*) of that which was perceived as connected to a particular place and time by its being connected to that same place and time. On the other hand, the sublation of what was perceived as connected to one place and time by its being connected to another place and time merely establishes its extension across different places and times; it does not, however, establish falsity.

Furthermore, effects such as jars and the like are real, because they are unsublated within their perceived conditions of space, time, and so forth, just like the Self (Ātman). As for the claim that the production of an effect is impossible from a cause that is either unmodified or modified, that is incorrect; for the production of an effect is possible from a cause when it is accompanied by auxiliary factors such as space and time. And as for the statement that such accompaniment is impossible for both the modified and the unmodified [cause], that is untenable; because the accompaniment by time and other factors is possible precisely for that which has not yet performed its prior function.

If it is argued that because there is no difference in its unmodified state, the conjunction of place, time, and other factors would have necessarily occurred even previously, we say no; for the conjunction of place, time, and so forth depends upon other causes and is not dependent upon this [unmodified state]. Therefore, it is not the case that anything is lost by the principle that a cause produces an effect only when it has attained a specific state consisting of the conjunction of place, time, and other factors. Furthermore, the causality of a cause toward an effect—which is observed and remains uncontradicted—cannot be denied in any manner whatsoever.

As for the claim that it is impossible for mere gold (*hemamātra*) to be the originator (*ārambhakatva*) of an effect such as a necklace (*rucaka*), or for gold itself—which serves as the substratum (*āśraya*)—to be so, that is incorrect; for it is possible for mere gold, when endowed with the aforementioned auxiliary conditions (*parikara*), to function as the originator. Nor can it be asserted that no effect is ever observed apart from the originating gold.

This is because a svastika distinct from gold is observed, and because the existence of a separate entity has been established through arguments such as the difference in cognition and the difference in verbal designation. Furthermore, this is not an illusion like that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, since no sublation is perceived for that which is apprehended during the interval between its production and destruction, given its connection with that specific place and time.

Nor is any reasoning seen to contradict this perception; for even at the time of perceiving a swastika that was previously unperceived, the recognition of gold as the substrate of the swastika is not contradictory, since the gold persists. Furthermore, the proof of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) by means of scripture has already been refuted. Whatever else remains here to be addressed regarding the lack of contradiction with perception and so forth, all of that has also already been well-stated.

As for the claim that all bodies possess a self by virtue of there being only one self, that is incorrect; for it would entail the undesirable consequence that a single individual would experience the pleasure and pain associated with every body. Indeed, in cases such as Saubhari and others, we observe a single person experiencing the pleasure and other sensations associated with multiple bodies precisely because of the unity of the self. Nor can it be argued that the absence of such cross-experience is due to a difference in the "I-sense" (the knower) rather than a difference in the self.

The Self is indeed known, and that is precisely the referent of the "I" (ahamartha); for it has been established that the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), being of the nature of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is not the knower due to its insentience and its status as an instrument, just like the body, the senses, and so forth. Furthermore, as for the claim that all bodies are equally products of ignorance (*avidyā*) because they share the qualities of being bodies, being insentient, being effects, and being imagined—that too [is untenable].

It is untenable [to claim that all bodies are unreal], because there is an absence of the very fact that all bodies are constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, their non-existence is refuted by the demonstration of the reality of that which is unsublated. As for the argument that all conscious beings are non-different because one observes insentience in whatever is other than consciousness, that too is refuted precisely by the demonstration of difference through the established distinction between pleasure and pain.

As for that which I myself established—the identity of the referent "I" by demonstrating that all conscious beings are endowed with selfhood and are merely imagined through my own ignorance—that is the prattle of a delusion belonging to one who has not understood his own doctrine; for in your view, the Self is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), distinct from the various forms of "I," "you," and so forth. Furthermore, for one who asserts that everything other than non-dual, attributeless pure consciousness is false, the effort toward hearing [the scriptures] and so on for the sake of liberation is fruitless, because it would be the product of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Just as the effort toward the acquisition of silver and the like in the case of mother-of-pearl and similar objects is futile, so too the effort for the sake of liberation is futile; for its effect, which is knowledge, depends upon an imagined teacher, just like the efforts of Śuka, Prahlāda, Vāmadeva, and others.

Knowledge produced by sentences such as "That thou art" does not remove bondage, because it is produced by a sentence imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is itself of the nature of ignorance, because it has as its locus a knower imagined through ignorance, or because it is produced by hearing that depends upon an imagined teacher—just like the knowledge produced by a sentence that removes bondage in a dream.

Furthermore, Brahman as pure consciousness devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣacinmātra*) is false, because it is cognizable by a cognition that is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*), or because it is cognizable by a cognition whose locus is a knower imagined through ignorance, or because it is cognizable by a cognition whose nature is ignorance; for whatever is thus is so, just like a dream or a city of Gandharvas. Nor does Brahman as pure consciousness devoid of distinctions manifest itself (*svayaṃ-prakāśate*), such that it would not depend on any other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

As for that self-luminous knowledge which is seen as being witnessed by itself, it has already been stated previously that this is seen only as residing in the knower, consisting in the establishment of a particular object of knowledge. Furthermore, those logical arguments presented to prove its featureless nature have been refuted by the immediately preceding inferences beginning with "because it is an effect of ignorance. Nor can pure consciousness, devoid of all distinctions, be the witness of ignorance, the ego-sense, and so forth.

The delusion of the world is thus established, for even such things as the delusion regarding the nature of a witness are observed to reside in a specific knower, not in pure consciousness (*jñapti*) alone. Furthermore, its status as illumination—or self-dependent luminosity—is not proven; for illumination is seen to belong to some person with respect to some particular object in the form of a cognition, and it is precisely because of this that its self-luminosity is established even by you. Moreover, luminosity is not possible for that which is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*) and lacks such characteristics.

Furthermore, as for the proclamation within one's own circles that even from the non-ultimate (aparamārtha) a supreme effect (paramārtha-kārya) is seen to arise—that too is refuted by their own admission, since all such effects are uncontradicted appearances (abādhitakalpa), which are conventionally real (vyāvahārikasatya) but in reality consist of nothing but ignorance (avidyātmaka). We have already refuted this previously, while establishing that the production of all effects everywhere arises solely from the ultimate cause (paramārtha-kāraṇa).

Furthermore, you cannot assert that these inferences contradict the Śruti, because the Śruti itself—being an effect of ignorance and consisting of ignorance—is no different from the examples already cited. As for the claim that Brahman is indeed real because no subsequent sublation is observed even though it is known through non-ultimate cognition, that is incorrect; for once it is certain that something is known through a cognition produced by a defective cause, the absence of subsequent sublation is irrelevant.

Just as, even when no subsequent sublation is observed for the knowledge produced by the statement "emptiness alone is reality," the unreality of its object is established solely through the ascertainment that it is rooted in a defect.

Furthermore, in the passages "There is no diversity whatsoever here" and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," it is stated that because [the Upanishads] negate the entire range of entities beyond mere consciousness, they are superior to all else, and thus no subsequent sublation is observed. However, for one who asserts that even that [consciousness] is non-existent—claiming that the reality is merely emptiness—a subsequent sublation is indeed observed due to its being surpassed by something higher. Since it is impossible to negate anything other than the negation of the emptiness of all things, there is no observation of subsequent sublation for that [emptiness] alone. Moreover, the fact that perception and the other means of knowledge are rooted in defects is no different for the cognition of universal emptiness born from the Vedanta as it is for them.

Therefore, the entire collection of cognitions resides in the ultimately real knower; and while it is itself of the nature of ultimate reality, it takes the form of the establishment of specific objects. In this regard, unless one accepts that some cognition is rooted in defects—wherein even the defect is ultimately real—and that some is faultless, being produced by an ultimately real causal complex, then the distinction between true and false objects, as well as worldly convention, will not be established.

For worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*), whether it be ultimate or of the nature of error, is preceded by a manifestation consisting in the establishment of a specific object residing within an ultimate knower; however, since it is impossible for that which is mere Being (*sanmātra*)—whether ultimate or non-ultimate—to serve as the cause for such manifestations and so forth, worldly transaction is not possible [in its absence].

Furthermore, their assertion that the pure Being (*sanmātra*) which serves as the substrate for all superimpositions must be ultimately real—on the grounds that an error cannot occur without a substrate—is also refuted; for just as an error is possible even if the defect, the locus of the defect, the knower, and the cognition itself are not ultimately real, so too an error is possible even if the substrate is not ultimately real.

Now, if you think that since no error is ever observed in the absence of a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the ultimate reality of pure existence (*sanmātra*) must necessarily be accepted—well then, since no error is ever observed even when defects, the locus of defects, the knower, and knowledge are not ultimately real, their ultimate reality must also necessarily be accepted in accordance with observation; thus, there is no distinction whatsoever except for your zeal in this matter.

As for the objection that, even on the view of difference, since past kalpas are infinite and all selves would have been liberated, no bound self could exist and thus the distinction between the bound and the liberated is impossible—that is refuted by the infinity of selves.

As for the argument that if the selves were distinct, they would necessarily possess numerical plurality—like beans, mustard seeds, jars, or cloths—that example is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because jars and the like are also infinite in number. If it is argued that numerical plurality is observed in cases such as "ten jars" or "a thousand beans," that is true; however, that numerical plurality does not belong to the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the jars and so forth, but rather to the jars and so forth as conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as space and time. We likewise accept such numerical plurality for the selves.
Yet, this does not entail the consequence of universal liberation (*sarvamukti*), because the selves are infinite in their essential nature (*svarūpa*).

As for the objection that if selves were distinct, they would necessarily follow as being insentient, non-self, and perishable—just like jars and other such objects—that is incorrect; for the distinction among things belonging to a single class does not entail that those things belong to a different class. Indeed, the distinction among jars and the like does not cause them to become cloth.

As for the objection that, if Brahman were distinct in reality, it would follow that it is also delimited by space and time, and thus its infinity would not be established—that is incorrect. For we observe that even among things delimited in reality, there is no fixed rule regarding their delimitation by space and time due to variations in degree. Furthermore, since the extent of a thing’s connection with space and time must be determined by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no contradiction even if Brahman’s connection with all space and time is established through another means of knowledge.

If it is argued that, in reality, even from mere delimitation (*pariccheda*), infinity is not established because there is an absence of being devoid of all forms of delimitation, then this is equally true for you as well, who accept that Brahman is distinct from ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, by accepting that the existent Brahman is distinct from ignorance, all defects resulting from duality would likewise attach to you on account of Brahman’s distinctness. If, on the other hand, its distinction from ignorance is not accepted, then Brahman would simply be of the nature of ignorance itself.

Even the defining statement, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," would consequently become meaningless. For if the reality of difference is not admitted, everything would be inconsistent due to the absence of any distinction between the establishment of one's own position and the refutation of the opponent's position. Furthermore, the well-known status of infinity consists merely in being devoid of spatial and temporal limitations; it does not consist in being devoid of limitations in terms of substance as well, for nothing of that latter kind is ever perceived, being as non-existent as a hare's horn.

For the proponents of difference (*bhedavādins*), however, because Brahman possesses all modes of being by virtue of having all conscious and unconscious entities as its body, no limitation exists either intrinsically or extrinsically. Thus, since the effect is distinct from the cause and real, the entire world, which is the effect of Brahman, is indeed other than Brahman.

This being the position reached, we reply: "Its non-difference [from Brahman] is established on account of the words concerning 'originating material' (ārambhaṇa) and so forth. From that Supreme Cause, Brahman, the non-difference of the world is understood from the words concerning "originating material" and other passages that establish it. Those sentences of which the word "originating material" is the first are "the words concerning originating material," such as: "The modification is a mere name arising from speech; the clay alone is real" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4), and "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second; it thought... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).

"I shall become many, I shall procreate"—thus [the Self] emitted heat; "having entered by means of this living self"; "All these creatures, my dear, have their root in Being (sat), they have Being as their abode, Being as their support; all this has that as its essence; That is the Truth, That is the Self; That art thou, Śvetaketu. These, and other passages of a similar kind situated in different contexts, are intended here. For these passages establish the non-difference of the world, consisting of the conscious and the unconscious, from the Supreme Brahman.

For instance: "But you, being obstinate, did not ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known. Having kept in mind that the entire world has Brahman as its sole cause and that the effect is non-different from its cause, and having thus proposed that by the knowledge of Brahman—the cause—all that is an effect would be known, the disciple, who did not understand how the entire world has Brahman as its sole cause, asked: "How indeed, O Venerable One, is that instruction?"

Having been urged by the objection that the cognition of one thing cannot result in the cognition of another, and intending to teach that Brahman is the sole cause of the world, [the author] first demonstrates—on the basis of what is established by common worldly experience—that the effect is non-different from its cause, saying: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known. The meaning is this: since jars, bowls, and other such objects produced from a single lump of clay do not possess any substance distinct from it, they are known through the knowledge of that [lump].

Here, having raised the objection—based on the doctrine of the followers of Kaṇāda—that the effect is a distinct substance from its cause, [the text] establishes the non-difference of the effect from the cause by means of common worldly experience: "The modification is a verbal handle, a mere name; 'clay' alone is the reality. *Ārambhaṇam* means that which is undertaken, grasped, or touched. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (karma), according to the rule "the *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes are used diversely. The meaning is: "by means of speech," that is, by reason of conventional usage preceded by words.
For conventional usage, such as "fetch water with a jar," is indeed preceded by words; of that [usage]...

For the sake of establishing conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), by means of that very same clay substance, there arises a modification characterized by a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*)—such as having a broad base and a bulbous belly—and the name "jar" and so forth, which is applied on account of that [configuration]. For the sake of accomplishing specific conventional activities such as fetching water, the clay substance itself comes to possess a different configuration and a different name.

Therefore, even a jar and the like are real only as clay; they are real only as the substance clay, meaning they are perceived by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as such, and not as distinct substances. Consequently, for that very substance—such as clay or gold—the occurrence of different cognitions and terms is logically accounted for simply through its assumption of different configurations (*saṃsthāna*). This is just as for a single person, Devadatta, different cognitions and terms such as "child," "youth," and "old man," as well as specific functional differences, are observed according to his various states.

As for what was stated—that because of the conventional usage "the jar is destroyed while the clay itself remains," the effect is something other than the cause—that is refuted precisely by the admission that production, destruction, and so forth are merely particular states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the very substance (*dravya*) which constitutes the cause. It is logical that the various words and the various effects belong to that single substance as it exists in those respective states. Since the substance’s possession of those respective states depends upon the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*), that [operation] is purposeful.

The objections concerning the persistence of manifestation are already answered by the very fact that we do not accept [manifestation as a distinct entity]. Even if origination is accepted, the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) is not contradicted, because it is precisely that which already exists that originates. To say that "it already exists previously" and yet "it originates" is a contradiction; this objection arises from one who does not understand the true nature of origination and destruction.

The conjunction of subsequent configurations with a substance that was previously established in prior configurations constitutes its destruction; however, there is the arising of the substance in its own state. Therefore, because the substance exists in all its states, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is not contradicted. If it is argued that this leads to the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) because a non-existent configuration arises, [we reply: no.

Even for those who maintain the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*), if production were itself unproduced, it would follow that the effect is pre-existent (*satkāryavāda*). If, however, production is produced, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For us, however, because the state (*avasthā*) is incapable of being perceived or functioning independently of the possessor of the state, all processes such as production and so forth belong to the possessor of the state alone; thus our position is faultless. Just as there is the state of being a jar through the relinquishing of the states of being potsherds, powder, or a lump, there is the state of multiplicity through the relinquishing of the state of unity, and the state of unity through the relinquishing of that [multiplicity]; hence, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Likewise, in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second," it is established that this very Being—though now appearing as the manifold world with diverse names and forms—is in the beginning one alone due to the absence of the differentiation of names and forms; and because it possesses all powers and cannot admit another presiding agent, it is without a second, thus demonstrating its non-difference from itself.

Likewise, because the creation of the world is described in the passage, "Then it thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" wherein the Self, having resolved upon its own manifold becoming as the world consisting of various stable and moving forms such as fire and the rest about to be created, the non-difference of the world—which is an effect—from the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause, is established.

Regarding the phrase "the state of being the essence" (*tattvamattva*): as for our position, "but for us" means that while distinct entities—which are incapable of being perceived separately because they are attributes inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*)—require a separate origination and so forth, those attributes which are incapable of being perceived separately do not depend on a separate origination. For this very reason, origination itself is independent of an originator and the like. Therefore, the meaning is that attributes inseparably established are themselves the states of origination and so forth belonging to the substratum.

The word "but" (tu) is intended to highlight the inconsistency in one's own position: that the arising of a thing is indeed the arising of its state, whereas there is no such thing as the arising of a state itself. He resolves the objection regarding the difference in number with the words "the state of being shards" (kapālatva), meaning that there is no contradiction because [the two] are mediated by an intermediate factor, whereas there is a contradiction due to the difference in time.

Thus, the meaning of the passage beginning with "merely a modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*) has been explained. Now, regarding the passages included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the Sūtra, he explains the illustrative passage beginning with "Being alone" (*sadeva*), using the word "likewise" (*tathā*). The syntactical connection is: "In the same way, non-difference itself has been established. The word *sat* (Being) denotes either fitness for connection with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or it denotes Brahman. Even if it has one of these two meanings, the sense of the word "non-different" (*ananya*) is established; for by the restriction "Being alone," any possibility of its being unreal is excluded.

The phrase "one only" indicates the absence of any differentiation between name and form. By the word "without a second," the meaning is the negation of any other presiding agent. He explains the word "this" found in the passage beginning with "Being only," as referring to that which possesses differentiated names and forms. To the question, "If this world is indeed Being alone, how is the process of creation and so forth possible? he replies with the word "in the beginning. He explains the word "without a second" by means of the phrase "possessing all powers."

The fact that these words have the aforementioned meaning as their sole purpose is understood precisely because they serve to establish the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, all is known"; for the establishment of the proposition does not require the exclusion of similar or dissimilar things. He further establishes that these words have this single intended meaning through the subsequent sentences, beginning with "It thought, 'May I be many'."

It is explained as follows: An objection is raised: "How is it possible that the Supreme Brahman—denoted by the word *sat* (Being), omniscient, whose will is true, and faultless—is designated as this world in the statement 'this was indeed Being' (*sadeva idam*); how is it possible that the world itself, denoted by the word *sat*, is a unity devoid of the differentiation of name and form and independent of any other presiding agent; and furthermore, how is it possible for that very same [Brahman] to have the intention of becoming many through this world of diverse, unstable, and mobile forms, and to bring about creation according to that very intention? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"That deity thought: 'Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate name and form,' and [she made] each of them threefold, threefold," and so forth. By the phrase "the three deities," the entire non-conscious entity (acid-vastu) is indicated; it is stated that, by entering into them as her own self in the form of the individual soul (jīva), she shall cause this [universe] to possess diverse names and forms. The meaning is: "By this living self—by the individual soul whose essence is myself—having entered as the Self, I shall cause this [universe] to possess diverse names and forms."

It has thus been stated that the assumption of name and form is brought about by the entry [of Brahman] into the individual soul (jīva) as its very self. This is made clear by another scriptural passage: "Having created that, it entered into that very thing; having entered into it, it became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat). Thus, the world, together with the individual soul, is entered by the supreme Brahman as its own self.

Thus, this fact—that the entire reality consisting of both sentient and insentient entities, whether in their causal or effected states, and whether gross or subtle, constitutes the body of the Supreme Brahman, while the Supreme Brahman constitutes their Self—is established in such texts as the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa and is here recalled. By this, the previously raised doubt is dispelled.

Since the acid substance (acid-vastu) is alive and exists as the Self (ātman) within Brahman, and because of the scriptural statement regarding the differentiation of name and form (nāmarūpa-vyākaraṇa), it is established that Brahman alone—having the sentient and insentient entities as its body—is what is denoted by the word "world. Consequently, such passages as "In the beginning, this was Being alone, one only," become most appropriately explained. Furthermore, since all modifications and all things that are not conducive to human welfare reside in the sentient and insentient entities that constitute His body, Brahman’s state of being free from blemish and His nature as a mine of auspicious qualities are firmly established.

This very point he will state immediately after [the sūtra] "But [Brahman is] greater, because of the designation of difference. Likewise, in the passage "All this has that as its self," he teaches the identity of the entire universe—both sentient and insentient—with Brahman; and he concludes that very same point with "That thou art."

Likewise, even in sentences situated in other contexts—such as "All this, indeed, is Brahman," "Verily, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this is known," "All this is that which is this Self," and "Brahman alone is all this"—non-difference is perceived; and likewise, difference is denied: "Everything abandons him who perceives everything as other than the Self," and "There is no diversity whatsoever here."

"He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity. Likewise, "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another; but where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? By thus establishing that the ignorant person perceives duality while the wise person perceives non-duality, [the scripture] demonstrates that non-difference alone is the ultimate reality.

Thus, by means of the arguments concerning "origin" (*ārambhaṇa*), "word" (*śabda*), and so forth, the non-difference of the world from the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause, is established. Herein lies the essential truth: Brahman alone—of which the conscious and unconscious entities constitute the body and which thus stands as their mode—is always denoted by all words. At times, when the conscious and unconscious entities have entered into a subtle state such that they are incapable of being designated as separate even from the perspective of being its own body, [Brahman remains the sole referent].

The body is Brahman in its causal state; and at other times, it is the body consisting of sentient and insentient entities that have reached a gross state suitable for the empirical usage of distinct names and forms, which is the state of effect. Thus, the world in the form of an effect is not different from the supreme Brahman, the cause; and between the body—the sentient and insentient entities—and the embodied Brahman, there exists a fixed distinction of nature and a fixed distinction of qualities and defects in both the causal and effected states, as established by hundreds of scriptural texts, according to the principle: "But [the objection is] not [valid], because of the existence of illustrations."

This has been stated here. As for those who describe the non-difference between cause and effect by resorting to the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the effect—for them, the non-difference between cause and effect is not established, because the identity of a real and a false object is untenable; if that were the case, either Brahman would be false or the world would be real.

Furthermore, as for those who maintain that even the effect is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), asserting that the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) while their non-difference is natural (*svābhāvika*), whereas both [difference and non-difference] are natural in the case of the insentient (*acid*) and Brahman;

Since there is no other entity distinct from Brahman apart from its limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and because the connection with an adjunct belongs to Brahman itself—which is partless and indivisible—there would be a transformation of the very nature of Brahman into a form subject to rejection if one were to admit a transformation of its power (śakti). Furthermore, since power and Brahman are non-different, the Śrutis which declare the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman regarding their subjection to karma and freedom from sin, as well as those which speak of the transformation of the non-intelligent (acid) and Brahman's lack of transformation, would become confused and contradicted.

Furthermore, those who maintain that Brahman is the cause which is the substance of pure existence (*sanmātra-dravya*) endowed with all powers, wherein the disturbances of conceptual constructions such as "the enjoyer" and so forth have been entirely cast out; and that at the time of dissolution, it remains distinct from consciousness—like the self in deep sleep—even though it is self-luminous and free from all particular experiences of pleasure and pain; and that at the time of creation, it assumes forms such as jars and bowls like the substance of clay, or forms such as foam, waves, and bubbles like the ocean.

It exists in a threefold state consisting of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller; therefore, the states of being the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller, as well as the virtues and defects resulting therefrom, are established as distinct functions belonging to it—just as the potness, jar-ness, and bowl-ness belong to a single lump of clay, or as different effects reside within that same material. Furthermore, the oneness of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller in their essence as Being (*sat*) is logically consistent, just as jars, bowls, and pots are one in their essence as clay. Consequently, they maintain that the world is non-different from Brahman, for it is the substance of pure Being alone that persists through all states of existence.

For them, there is a contradiction with the entirety of the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, and Nyāya; for all the Śrutis, together with the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, establish Brahman as the supreme cause—the Lord of all lords, eternally omniscient, omnipotent, whose will is true, who is faultless, and whose bliss is unlimited, unsurpassed, and unconditioned by space or time—but they do not establish a mere existence (sanmātra) that is an Ishvara higher than even the Ishvara.

For instance: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman alone; being one, it did not flourish. It emitted the nobility (kṣatra) as its superior form—those who are the divine nobilities: Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna. And: "In the beginning, this was the Self alone, one only; nothing else whatsoever stirred. It looked around: 'Shall I now create the worlds? And: "Nārāyaṇa alone indeed..."

"There was neither Brahmā nor Īśāna, nor heaven and earth, nor the stars, nor water, nor fire, nor Soma, nor the Sun; he, being alone, did not rejoice while abiding in the midst of his meditation"—from such passages as these, it is understood that Nārāyaṇa alone is the supreme cause and the Lord of all lords.

For the words *sat*, *brahman*, and *ātman*, occurring in the same context, are qualified by the word *Nārāyaṇa* which stands in that same context, and thus they refer to Him alone: "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords, and the supreme divinity among deities; He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the organs, and there is no progenitor of Him, nor is there any lord over Him. Thus, the causality belongs to the Lord (Īśvara) alone. The Smṛti of Manu also states this, beginning with "Then the Blessed Self-existent One," and continuing: "He, desiring to emit various creatures, meditated upon His own body."

"In the beginning, he created the waters alone; into them he infused his seed. Even the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* declare that Puruṣottama alone is the supreme cause, as in such passages as: "Nārāyaṇa, whose form is the universe, the infinite self, the eternal; desiring to create, he emitted from a thousandth part of himself two kinds of persons"; and "The world has arisen from Viṣṇu, and in him alone it remains," and so forth. Nor can it be said that the Lord is merely pure Being (*sanmātra*), because he is admitted to be a part of that [Being] and because he possesses specific attributes.

Nor can it be said that His possession of infinite auspicious qualities, such as knowledge and bliss, is occasional, because they are natural and therefore eternal. This is established by such scriptural passages as: "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold; knowledge, strength, and action are natural to Him," and "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving. Do not say that only the possession of the powers of knowledge, bliss, and so forth is His natural state, for since the text makes a separate mention—"His power is natural" and "knowledge, strength, and action are natural"—it would entail the fault of resorting to figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*).

Nor can it be maintained that, as in the case of "cook" (*pācaka*) and similar terms, the *kṛt* suffix in words such as "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) denotes mere capacity; for there is no traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) that the *kṛt* suffix in general has capacity as its meaning. Indeed, in rules such as "the *kṛt* suffixes [denote] capacity in the case of *hastin* and *kavāṭa*," it is recorded that only certain specific *kṛt* suffixes have capacity as their domain. In the case of "cook" and the like, however, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is resorted to because there is no other way.

Furthermore, since [the individual soul] is a specific part (aṃśa) of Īśvara, and because the whole (aṃśin) is greater than its part—just as the ocean is greater than a wave—the hundreds of scriptural passages concerning Īśvara, such as "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords," and "No one equal to Him or superior to Him is seen," would be contradicted. Moreover, if pure Being (sanmātra) were the self of all and Īśvara were a part thereof, then the teachings regarding His being the self of all and His being the whole would be undermined, as He would merely be a specific part.

For neither the nature of being a gem nor the state of being a part thereof belongs to the jar, the bowl, and so forth. If it is argued that because Pure Being (*sanmātra*) is complete within all its own parts, it is likewise complete even in the part that is the Lord (*īśvara*), and therefore other objects are of His nature and are His parts—this is not so; for since Pure Being is equally complete in the jar as well, the jar would also possess the nature of the Lord.

Because it would follow that [the pot] is a part (*aṃśa*) of that [Being]. Furthermore, for pure Being (*sanmātra*), which is understood as a property of objects through such cognitions as "the pot exists" or "the cloth exists," neither substantiality (*dravyatva*) nor causality (*kāraṇatva*) is tenable; for existence (*sattva*) is indeed the fitness for worldly transaction (*vyavahārayogyatā*). Non-existence (*asattva*) is the fitness for a contradictory transaction regarding that which is fit for its own transaction. If one were to accept that only substance is existent, it would follow that action (*kriyā*) and so forth are non-existent, since they would be like grasping at *kāśa* grass and *kuśa* grass [in desperation].

Nor is a single, uniform existence (*sattā*) applicable everywhere; for if everything were non-different by virtue of having the nature of "being," it would follow—as has already been stated—that because one would be omniscient and thus cognizant of the nature of all things, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a confusion between all virtues and defects. Therefore, non-difference must be understood precisely in the manner previously described.

Now, it might be argued: "Even when there is only a single entity undergoing a change of state, different cognitions and words are observed, as in the cases of childhood, youth, and so forth; they are also observed when there is a difference in substance, as in the case of clay, wood, gold, and the like. Therefore, how can it be determined that in instances such as clay and a jar—which stand in the relation of cause and effect—the different cognitions and words are based solely on a change of state? To this, the reply is:
"And because [the effect] is perceived in the existence [of the cause]. (Sūtra 16)

Furthermore, because the gold, which serves as the cause, is perceived even when effects such as earrings exist—meaning that there is recognition [of it] as gold in the form "this earring is gold"—and because earth and other causes are not perceived in this way within other substances such as gold, it is therefore declared that the effect is merely the causal substance itself having reached another state, just like a child or a youth.

Furthermore, since the application of different cognitions and terms is already accounted for by the admission of a change of state even by one who maintains the existence of a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*), it is improper to postulate an unperceived distinct substance. Moreover, this recognition is not based on a genus (*jāti*), because no distinct substance serving as the substratum of that genus is perceived.

A single substance of the nature of gold is seen to exist in both causal and effected states. Nor can it be maintained that, despite a difference in substances, there is a recognition of the effect as being the same due to the persistence of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); for if there were a difference in substances, it would be impossible for there to be such recognition in another substance residing therein merely through the persistence of its substratum. If it is argued that no such recognition of the cow-dung occurs in the case of a scorpion produced from cow-dung, we say no; [for such recognition exists in other cases].

In that case as well, there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the substance earth, which serves as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).
