If it is argued that the recognition of fire is not observed in smoke, which is an effect of fire—let it be so, and let there be no such recognition there; nevertheless, there is no fault, because fire is merely the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). For smoke is produced from moist fuel conjoined with fire.

Furthermore, because of the identity of its odor, smoke is indeed the effect of moist fuel; therefore, since that very same thing is perceived as "this" when the effect exists, it is understood that differences in cognition, terminology, and so forth are based solely on differences in state. For this reason, the effect is non-different from the cause.
And from this existence, there is another existence. (17)

Furthermore, because the effect exists within the cause, the effect is non-different from the cause. For in both common worldly usage and the Veda, the effect itself is designated as the cause; as in the world, for example: "All this—the jar, the bowl, and so forth—was previously nothing but clay"; and in the Veda: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone.

If it is argued that this is not so because of the designation of the effect as "non-existent," we say no; for [the existence of the effect] is established by means of another attribute, through the remainder of the sentence and logical reasoning, and by the use of different words. (Sūtra 2.1.18)

As for the statement that the existence of the effect in the cause is understood from both common experience and the Veda—that is incorrect; because there is a designation of non-existence, such as: "In the beginning this was indeed non-existent," "In the beginning this was verily non-existent," and "In the beginning this was nothing at all"; and in common experience, it is said: "All this, such as the jar and the bowl, did not exist in the forenoon. Therefore, if it is argued that what has been stated is untenable, we say no; for such a designation is made by means of a different attribute (dharma).

Indeed, that which is designated as "non-existent" (asat) refers to that very same effect-substance at a prior time by way of another property—that is, another configuration—and not by way of the "insubstantiality" (tucchatva) intended by you. For it has been stated that existence and non-existence are properties of a substance. In this context, non-existence is a property distinct from the property of existence. For the world, as indicated by the word "this" (idam), the property of existence consists of name and form (nāmarūpa), while the property of non-existence is its opposite: the subtle state.

Therefore, the non-existence of the world—which is characterized by name and form—is its attainment of a subtle state that is opposed to those [name and form]. How is this understood? From the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), from reasoning (*yukti*), and from another scriptural word (*śabdāntara*). First, as for the remainder of the passage: regarding the statement, "In the beginning, indeed, this was nothing at all," it continues, "That, being non-existent, resolved: 'May I be.'"

By means of this indicative mark of mental attention (*manaskāra*) found in the supplementary passage, once it is determined that the referent of the word "non-existent" (*asat*) is something distinct from a mere void (*tuccha*), it is then established—on account of its having the same meaning—that in passages such as "this was indeed non-existent," the word "non-existent" has this very same sense. Furthermore, through reasoning (*yukti*), the non-existence [of the effect] is understood to be a distinct attribute (*dharma*); for reasoning indeed makes known that existence and non-existence are attributes of an entity.

The connection of the clay substance with the form of a broad base and belly is the cause for the conventional usage "the jar exists"; the connection of that very same substance with another state opposed to it is the cause for the conventional usage "the jar does not exist. In this regard, since the state of being shards and so forth is what opposes it, that very state is the cause for the usage "the jar does not exist" while it is in its jar-state. Furthermore, no such thing as a "jar-absence" distinct from that is perceived; nor is it postulated, for by that much alone [the phenomenon of] absence is accounted for.

Because [the meaning] is established through common usage (*vyavahāra*). Likewise, from another scriptural passage, it is understood that at the prior time there was indeed a connection with other attributes (*dharmāntara*). This other passage is the one previously cited: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*), and so forth. For in that context, having rejected the view of non-existence (*tucchatva*) with the words, "How indeed, my dear, could it be thus?", it is established that "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. Furthermore, it is stated very clearly: "This world was then undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name and form" (*taddhedaṃ tarhyavyākṛtamāsīt tannāmarūpābhyāṃ vyākriyata*).
Now, he demonstrates with two aphorisms the non-difference of the effect from its cause by means of two illustrations, beginning with: "And like a cloth" (paṭavat ca). || 19 ||
Just as threads themselves, when undergoing a particular kind of interconnection, assume another name, form, and function such as "cloth," so too does Brahman.
And as in the case of the vital breath and so forth. || 20 ||

And just as the single air, assuming various functions within the body, takes on different names, forms, and effects such as prāṇa (out-breath), apāna (in-breath), and so forth; in the same way, Brahman alone becomes the world in its diverse forms of moving and non-moving beings. Thus, it is established that the world is non-different from the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause.
Because of the designation of [the Self] as something else, there would follow the defect of not performing what is beneficial and so forth. (Sūtra 21)

It has been stated that by means of such passages as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and "This self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*), which establish the non-difference of the world from Brahman, the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) from Brahman is also designated. To this, the following objection is raised: if the state of being Brahman for the other—the individual soul—is designated by these sentences, then defects such as the failure to create a world consisting of beneficial things and the creation of a world consisting of harmful things would follow for the Self, which is endowed with omniscience, the power of true resolve, and so forth.

Moreover, this world is a mine of infinite sufferings—internal, celestial, and elemental; and no wise person, being independent, would engage in such self-destructive activity. Furthermore, the scriptural passages declaring a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman have been abandoned by you yourself, who maintain the non-difference (*ananyatva*) of the world and Brahman, for as long as there is difference, non-difference cannot be established. If it is argued that the texts concerning difference refer to a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), while the texts concerning non-difference refer to natural non-difference, then this must be addressed:

Does Brahman, the cause of the universe, know the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is non-different from itself by its very nature—as being unconditioned, or not? If it does not know it, there is a loss of its omniscience. If it does know it, then for Brahman—which knows that the suffering of the soul, which is non-different from itself, is its own suffering—an unavoidable consequence of faults such as failing to act for its own benefit or acting to its detriment arises. If it is argued that the difference between the *jīva* and Brahman is caused by ignorance (*avidyā*), and that the scriptural texts concerning their non-difference refer to that [ignorance], [the response follows...]

Even in that regard, under the view that the individual soul (*jīva*) is ignorant, the aforementioned dilemma and its consequences remain as they were. Under the view that Brahman is ignorant, it is impossible for Brahman—which is self-luminous by nature—to be the witness of ignorance or to perform the creation of the world caused by it. If it is argued that light is concealed by ignorance, then since concealment consists in the cessation of light, and since light is the very essence of Brahman, this would result in the cessation of its own essence; thus, thousands of defects such as the destruction of its own nature have already been pointed out.
Therefore, this [doctrine of] Brahman being the cause of the world is untenable. To this, it is replied:
But it is more [than one], because of the mention of a distinction. || 22 ||

The word *tu* (but) sets aside the previous position: Brahman is something other than, and superior to, the inner self (*pratyagātman*) which is subject to internal and other forms of suffering. Why? Because of the designation of difference. For the supreme Brahman is designated as distinct from the inner self in such passages as: "He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body the self is, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal"; and "Having understood Him as distinct from the individual selves and as their impeller. [Objection: This is untenable, as it would be like [the distinction between] stones and the like. 23.

Just as it is impossible for non-sentient objects—such as stones, wood, clods of earth, grass, and the like, which are utterly fit for rejection, constant seats of transformation, and specific instances of insentience—to be identical in nature with Brahman (whose essence consists of infinite knowledge and bliss, who is faultless, changeless, the opposite of all that is to be rejected, solely composed of auspiciousness, distinct from all other things, and possessed of various infinite great manifestations), so too it is impossible for a sentient being—who is subject to the experience of infinite suffering—to be identical with Him.

For one who is like a firefly, the state of being Brahman—as understood from scriptural passages such as "He who has removed all evil," which describes a source of infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities that are the opposite of every cause of impurity—is impossible.

Furthermore, the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) found in such Vedic texts as "He whose self is the body" is not contradictory; rather, it supports this very point. This is because the individual soul (*jīva*) is the body of Brahman, and since Brahman exists as the self of the soul by virtue of having the soul as its body, these texts are intended to teach Brahman as characterized by the soul. This has been demonstrated more than once in passages such as "On account of the abiding [of the soul], [Brahman is the Self], so says Kāśakṛtsna."

Therefore, since Brahman in every state has the sentient and insentient entities as its body, Brahman with the subtle sentient and insentient entities as its body is the cause; that same Brahman, having the gross sentient and insentient entities as its body, is the effect known as the world. Thus, the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the world and Brahman is established. Furthermore, the world is the effect of Brahman, and the world is non-different from Brahman; yet, while the insentient entity and the individual soul (*jīva*) are subject to transformation and suffering respectively, Brahman is the mine of auspicious qualities.

There is no confusion of natures and no contradiction with any scriptural statement. Even in the state of non-differentiation, as expressed in the text, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only," the existence of the individual soul (jīva) conjoined with ignorance must necessarily be admitted as persisting in a subtle form by virtue of being the body of Brahman. This is because the persistence of the soul in a subtle form even at that time is declared by two sūtras: "The charge of partiality and cruelty [does not apply] to God, because He has regard for [the karma of souls]" (VS 2.1.34), and "If it be argued that [karma] cannot exist due to the absence of division [of bodies], we say no, because of beginninglessness; and this is both logical and observed" (VS 2.1.35). Thus, even then, the soul exists in a subtle form.

Non-differentiation, however, is established because of the absence of differentiation between name and form; therefore, Brahman’s status as the cause is indeed possible. On the other hand, for those who describe this distinction with reference to the state of this very individual soul when it is free from ignorance, all of this would be inconsistent; for in that state, omniscience, universal lordship, being the cause of everything, being the self of all, and being the controller of all, and so forth, do not exist.

Indeed, by these very forms and scriptural passages, the difference of the inner self (pratyagātman) [from others] is established; for all of that is imagined through ignorance (avidyā), since in your own view, all of that is indeed imagined through ignorance. Furthermore, the mutual difference among things imagined through ignorance—such as the difference between mother-of-pearl and silver during the state of ignorance—is not what is being propounded here by the author of the Sūtras in passages such as "But [the soul is] greater, because of the mention of difference," etc.;

rather, [it concerns] Brahman, who is the cause of the birth and so forth of the world, and who has been introduced as the object of inquiry in the statement, "The inquiry into Brahman ought to be undertaken."

The fact that [Brahman] is to be known through Vedānta is established, as well as the removal of contradictions with Smṛti and reasoning. The two sūtras, "If [the world were merged into Brahman], there would be the consequence of it becoming like that [Brahman]; therefore it is inconsistent," and "But this is not so, because of the existence of illustrative examples," restate what is established in this section; for in that case, the very possibility of a causal relationship between two dissimilar things is the subject matter of the section. Furthermore, the sūtra "If it be said that [the effect is] non-existent, no, because it is a mere negation" restates what was contained in the preceding section.
If it be argued that [the Lord cannot be the material cause] because we observe the withdrawal [of the world], we say no; for it is like milk. 24.

It has been established that it is not contradictory for the supreme Brahman—who is omniscient and whose volitions are true—to be the Self of all and to be distinct from everything else, by virtue of having as His body all sentient and insentient things in their gross and subtle states, thus existing in every possible mode. Now, it is established that it is not contradictory for the supreme Brahman, whose volitions are true, to possess the capacity to create the diverse universe through mere volition.

But surely, since it is observed that those possessing limited powers depend upon the collection of causal factors (*kāraka-kalāpa*), how can the objection be raised that there is a contradiction regarding Brahman—the possessor of all powers—being the cause of the world if He does not depend on a collection of causal factors? It is said in reply:

In the world, it is observed that even those endowed with the power to produce various specific effects still require various corresponding instruments. Consequently, a doubt may arise in some of dull intellect that the supreme Brahman, though possessed of all powers, cannot logically be the creator if he is devoid of such instruments; this doubt is now refuted. It is seen that potters, weavers, and others who are the causes of jars, cloths, and so forth, possess the capacity to produce them, yet they exercise their agency only by assembling certain specific instruments.

Those things which lack the power to produce [an effect] are unable to produce it even when the collection of causal factors (*kārakakalāpa*) is present; conversely, those that possess such power do produce it when the collection of causal factors is present—this is the distinction. Furthermore, although Brahman is omnipotent, its capacity to produce everything is not possible unless its instruments (*upakaraṇa*) are withdrawn; moreover, its state of being without assistance prior to creation is understood from such passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), and "Nārāyaṇa alone existed" (*Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad* 1.1).

Therefore, the conclusion reached is that the status of being a creator is not tenable; this is what is raised as an objection in the words: "If it be said that [it is] not so, because a withdrawal [of powers] is observed."

[The opponent] objects: "It does not [transform] like milk. [The reply is: It is not the case that all things possessing the power to produce an effect depend upon an auxiliary cause for that production—just as milk, water, and so forth, though possessing the power to produce curds or ice, do not require such an auxiliary for that production. Likewise, since Brahman itself possesses the power to produce everything, its status as the creator of all is logically established. The particle *hi* ("indeed") is used here as a reference to what is well-known in order to demonstrate the weakness of the objection. In the case of milk and the like, the requirement for coagulation (*ātañcana*) and so forth is not for the sake of bringing about the state of being curds and so on, but rather for the sake of speediness and for the sake of a particular flavor.
And [the soul's existence] in this world is like that of the gods and others. || 25 ||

Just as gods and others create in their respective worlds whatever they require by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*), so too this Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) creates the entire universe by mere volition. It should be understood that the mention of gods and others—who possess powers known through the Vedas—is taken as an illustration for the purpose of easily grasping the power of Brahman, whose power is not known through the Vedas.
Either there would be the consequence of [the whole] being affected simultaneously, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning its partlessness. (Sūtra 2.1.26)

In such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," "In the beginning, indeed, this was nothing at all," and "In the beginning, this was the Self alone, one only," it is stated that in the causal state, Brahman alone existed, being partless; thus, it is established that in the causal state, Brahman alone existed, being partless because the distinction between consciousness and non-consciousness had been eliminated.

It has been stated that Brahman—which is one and partless, being without division—having formed the resolve, "May I become many," became divided into the elements such as ether and air, and into the divisions of individual knowers (kṣetrajña) from Brahmā down to a blade of grass; this being so, it must be admitted that that very same Supreme Brahman is entirely employed as the effect.

If it is then said that the conscious portion (cid-aṃśa) is divided by the distinction of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and the unconscious portion (acid-aṃśa) is divided by the distinction of space and so forth, then scriptural passages such as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," and "Brahman is one alone, the Self is one alone," which declare that the causal Brahman is partless, would be contradicted and subverted.

Even though it is accepted that Brahman, whose body consists of the subtle sentient and insentient entities, is the cause, while Brahman, whose body consists of the gross sentient and insentient entities, is the effect; nevertheless, because it is also accepted that the substratum (the embodied one) is an effect, the aforementioned defect is unavoidable, and its becoming manifold—as something partless—is not logically tenable. Furthermore, the persistence of a portion of it that is not utilized for being an effect is also not logically tenable. Therefore, it appears as if inconsistent. To this objection, he provides the reply:
"But on account of Scripture, for [Brahman] has the Word as its source" (ŚB 2.1.27).

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the aforementioned objection. There is no such inconsistency; why? Because of scripture (*śruti*). Scripture indeed declares that Brahman is partless and yet [describes] a manifold creation from it; the meaning is that one must accept the scriptural matter exactly as it is stated in scripture. But is it not the case that even scripture is incapable of establishing a meaning that is mutually incompatible—like saying "one should sprinkle with fire"? To this he says: "Because it has the Word as its source."

Since this object is of a nature entirely distinct from all other things because it has scripture alone as its means of valid cognition, its possession of diverse powers is not contradictory; thus, neither an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) nor a refutation thereof is applicable to Brahman.
And likewise in the case of the Self, for [the Upaniṣads state]: "And indeed, [powers] are manifold in the Self. (2.1.28)

Furthermore, if a property belonging to one entity were thus superimposed upon another entity, then properties [belonging] to insentient things like jars would also follow as applying to the sentient, eternal self, which is of a different nature from them. And that such a consequence does not occur is due to the diversity of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of entities; thus he says, "And they are indeed diverse. Just as the powers such as heat and so forth, which belong to fire, water, and other such things that are mutually dissimilar, are seen to be themselves dissimilar;

Therefore, it is not at all untenable that there exist thousands of powers in the Supreme Brahman—which is of a nature entirely different from what is seen in the world—that have never been observed in various other instances. As the venerable Parāśara stated, having raised an objection based on general observation: "How can the agency of creation and so forth be attributed to Brahman, who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), immeasurable, pure, and of stainless nature? He then replied: "The powers of all entities fall within the scope of inconceivable knowledge."

"Therefore, O best of those who practice austerity, those powers of manifestation such as creation and the rest belong to Brahman, just as heat belongs to fire. And the Śruti says: "What was the wood, what was that tree, from which they carved out heaven and earth? O wise ones, ask with your mind concerning that upon which he stood while supporting the worlds. Brahman was the wood, Brahman was that tree, from which they carved out heaven and earth."

"I declare to you with my mind, O wise ones: Brahman stood firm, upholding all worlds. The meaning is that an objection based on general observation does not apply to the Supreme Brahman, who is distinct from all things.
And for this reason as well, because of the defects in our own position. || 29 ||

In our own position, since the doctrine of a cause such as *pradhāna* lacks the quality of being dissimilar from worldly objects, the defects observed in the world would necessarily apply there as well. Therefore, Brahman alone—distinct from everything else—must be accepted as the cause. Furthermore, *pradhāna* is partless (*niravayava*); how, then, can the commencement of the diverse world, beginning with the *mahat*, be logically accounted for by that which is partless? If it is argued that its parts exist in the form of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, then this must be examined: is *pradhāna* a mere aggregate of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*?

Or is *pradhāna* commenced by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*? In that case, there would be a contradiction with your own accepted doctrine that *pradhāna* is the cause in the immediately preceding kalpa, as well as a contradiction with the number [of constituents] you yourself have accepted. Furthermore, on the view that they are a collection (*samūha*), since they are partless, it cannot be established that they initiate a gross substance when conjoined without depending on a distinction of spatial parts (*pradeśabheda*).

Even in the theory of atoms as the cause, the same applies; for atoms are indeed partless and devoid of spatial divisions, and thus, even if they were to conjoin with one another without depending on a distinction of spatial parts, they would not be capable of initiating a gross effect.
And she is endowed with all [qualities] through the sight of him. || 30 ||

The supreme deity is distinct from all other things and is endowed with every power. Indeed, the Śrutis reveal the supreme deity in this very way: "His supreme power is heard to be manifold indeed; it is inherent, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action. Likewise, having established that the supreme deity is of a nature entirely different from everything else—stating, "He is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst"—they further establish His possession of all powers by declaring, "He whose desires are true, whose resolves are true."

Likewise: "Consisting of mind, having the vital breath for its body, whose form is light, whose desires are true, whose resolves are true, whose self is space, possessing all works, possessing all desires, possessing all odors, possessing all tastes, pervading all this, without speech and without regard.
If it be argued that [the Lord] does not [possess these qualities] because He is devoid of instruments (vikaraṇatvāt), that has already been answered. || 31 ||

If it is argued that although Brahman alone is unique from everything else and possesses all powers, nevertheless—given the scriptural statement, "In Him there is neither effect nor instrument"—the commencement of an effect is not possible for Him who is devoid of instruments, the answer has been stated as: "Because He has the Word as His source" and "For [His powers] are diverse. The meaning is that Brahman, whose sole authority is the Word (*śabda*), is capable of producing various effects even in the absence of specific instruments, being unique from everything else. Thus says the Śruti: "He sees without eyes, He hears without ears; He is swift and a grasper, though without hands or feet," and so forth.
Not so, because it possesses a purpose. || 32 ||

Even if the Lord, being one alone prior to creation, endowed with the power for all purposes due to His nature as distinct from everything else, is capable of creating the manifold world by Himself; nevertheless, the doctrine of the Lord as the cause is not tenable, because a manifold creation must have a purpose, and the Lord lacks any such purpose. For among those who act with deliberation, the motive for an undertaking is of two kinds: either for their own sake or for the sake of others.

For the Supreme Brahman, who by its very nature has all desires already fulfilled, there is no purpose whatsoever to be achieved through the creation of the world that was not already attained. Nor is it for the sake of another, since one whose desires are fulfilled acts for the sake of others only through the grace of favoring them; yet a compassionate being would not create a world so full of manifold and infinite sufferings such as conception, birth, old age, death, and hell, but rather would produce a world consisting solely of happiness if he were creating out of compassion.
Therefore, due to the absence of any motive, Brahman’s status as the cause is untenable.
This being the case, we reply:
"But as in the world, His activity is mere sport. (2.1.33)

For one who has attained all desires and is perfectly fulfilled, the sole purpose in the creation of this manifold and diverse world—composed of a mixture of consciousness and unconsciousness and brought about by the modification of His own volition—is mere sport (*līlā*).

Just as in the world, even for a great king who rules over the earth with its seven continents and possesses complete valor, heroism, and prowess, activities such as playing with balls and the like are seen to have sport as their sole purpose; in the same way, it is beyond reproach that for the Supreme Brahman as well, the sole purpose in the origination, maintenance, and dissolution of the world—all of which are accomplished by His mere volition—is sport alone.
[The objection that] there would be partiality and cruelty [on the part of the Lord] is not valid, because He has regard for [other factors]; for thus [the scripture] shows. (2.1.34)

Although it might be possible for the Supreme Person—who is distinct from all other sentient and insentient entities and possesses inconceivable power—to create this diverse world of mixed sentient and insentient beings even while being single and partless prior to creation, nevertheless, partiality would result from creating gods, animals, humans, and stationary beings as superior, middling, and inferior; and cruelty would be unavoidable due to the infliction of most terrible suffering. To this, the reply is: "Not so, because [the Lord] has regard for [other factors]. (na sāpekṣatvāt).

Inequality and cruelty would not follow [for the Lord]. Why? Because [the creation] is dependent; for the diverse creation is dependent upon the karma of the individual selves (kṣetrajña), such as the gods and others, who are being created. Indeed, the Śrutis and Smṛtis show that the connection of the individual selves—the gods and others—with their respective bodies as gods and so forth is dependent on their particular karma: "One who performs good deeds becomes good; one who performs evil deeds becomes evil; by a meritorious deed one becomes meritorious, and by an evil deed one becomes evil. Likewise, the venerable Parāśara also [states] the cause of the diversity among gods and others:

It has been stated that for the *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls) being created, it is solely the power of their past karma: "He [the Lord] is merely the instrumental cause (*nimittamātra*) for the acts of creation of those things to be created, since the powers of the things to be created have the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) as their material cause. Having abandoned even the status of being a mere instrumental cause, He does not depend on anything else; O best of ascetics, a thing is led to its state of being a real entity by its own power, that is, by its own karma. Thus, the manifestation of entities such as gods and others occurs through their own power, which is their own karma. If it is argued that this is not so because there was no prior division of karma, we say: no, because of beginninglessness; and it is both logically consistent and observed. (Sūtra 2.1.35)

If it is asked: "How can there be those called *kṣetrajñas* prior to creation? For [the scripture] declares non-differentiation: 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone' (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1). Therefore, since they do not exist at that time, their karma does not exist; how then can the inequality of creation be said to depend upon it?"—we reply: No, because the *kṣetrajñas* are beginningless.

And regarding the streams of those [individual] karmas: even though they are beginningless, their non-distinction is logically consistent; for that [stream], having abandoned name and form in relation to the reality of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), is extremely subtle and incapable of being designated as separate even in its state of being the body of Brahman. Otherwise, if this were not admitted, there would follow the fallacies of the acquisition of what was not done and the loss of what was done. Moreover, their beginninglessness is perceived in the scripture: "The wise one is neither born nor does he die."

The beginninglessness of the stream of creation is established from such passages as, "The Creator fashioned the sun and moon as they were before," and from the scriptural hearing that there was merely the manifestation of names and forms: "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest; it became manifest through names and forms. Thus, the beginninglessness of the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) in its essential nature is proven. Furthermore, in the *Smṛti* it is said: "Know both Prakṛti and Puruṣa to be indeed beginningless.

Therefore, because it is distinct from everything else, because it possesses all powers, because its sole motive is divine play (*līlā*), and because it brings about a manifold creation in accordance with the karma of the individual souls, Brahman alone is the cause of the world.
And because all phenomena arise. || 36 ||

Since all those characteristics—both those already mentioned and those yet to be stated—that were cited as deficiencies in the causality of *pradhāna*, atoms, and so forth, are found to be applicable to Brahman as the established cause, it is settled that Brahman alone is the cause of the world.
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, inference [is not valid]; and because of [the nature of] activity.

It has been stated that the Supreme Brahman is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world; therein, the objections raised by others have been refuted. Now, for the sake of protecting our own position, the positions of others are being rejected. Otherwise, some person of dull intellect—who does not recognize that those other positions are rooted in fallacious reasoning—might, due to the suspicion that they possess authority, experience even a slight deficiency in faith toward the Vedic position.

Therefore, the subsequent section proceeds for the purpose of refuting the opposing view. Among these, the doctrine of the followers of Kapila (Sāṃkhya) is first set aside, because this system possesses an excessive capacity to cause the delusion that the true position might be subsumed within a summary of doctrines such as the *satkāryavāda* accepted by the Vedists. While in passages such as "Because of [the soul's] being a knower of the field, [Pradhāna] is not based on scripture" (*Brahma Sūtra* 1.1.5), it was merely stated that Vedic statements do not have that [Sāṃkhya] as their purport; here, however, the actual nature of that position is refuted, so there is no suspicion of redundancy.

For this is the established position of the Sāṃkhyas: "The root-primal nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; the seven beginning with the Great One (mahat) are both primal natures and modifications; the group of sixteen is only a modification; and the Spirit (puruṣa) is neither a primal nature nor a modification. Such is the compendium of principles (tattvasaṃgraha). What is called the root-primal nature consists of effects that are entirely beyond the senses—namely, pleasure, pain, and delusion—which have as their functions lightness, illumination, mobility, obstruction, heaviness, and covering. These effects [constitute] the primal nature.

The substances *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are incapable of being defined as distinct from one another, neither deficient nor excessive, and they exist in a state of equilibrium. This equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is *prakṛti*; it is one, itself unconscious, yet exists for the sake of the experience and liberation of many conscious beings. It is eternal, all-pervading, and in a state of constant transformation, but it is not a modification of anything else; rather, it is the ultimate cause itself. The seven principles beginning with the Great One (*mahat*) are its modifications, and they are also the material causes (*prakṛtis*) of other things.

The great ego (mahān-ahaṅkāra) consists of the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell. In this regard, the ego is threefold: the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *bhūtādi*; these correspond respectively to the *sāttvika*, the *rājasa*, and the *tāmasa* types. Among them, the *vaikārika* is the *sāttvika* ego, which gives rise to the sense organs and so forth; the *bhūtādi* is the *tāmasa* ego, which is the cause of the subtle elements that serve as the causes for the gross elements; and the *taijasa* is the *rājasa* ego, which assists both. The five gross elements are space and the others.

The five organs of cognition, beginning with the ear; the five organs of action, beginning with speech; and the mind—these constitute the sixteen purely evolutes. The Puruṣa, however, because it is devoid of transformation, is neither the material cause (prakṛti) of anything nor the product (vikṛti) of anything. For that very reason, it is devoid of attributes, its essence being pure consciousness alone; it is eternal, inactive, all-pervading, and distinct in each individual body. Due to its changelessness and inactivity, agency and enjoyership are not possible for it.

Even though reality is thus constituted, the deluded, through the mere proximity of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, superimpose consciousness upon *prakṛti* and agency upon *prakṛti*—just as the redness of a hibiscus flower is superimposed upon a crystal—and they superimpose this [agency] upon the *puruṣa*, thinking, "I am the agent, I am the enjoyer. Thus, from ignorance comes bondage (*bhoga*), and from knowledge of reality comes liberation (*apavarga*). They establish this very point through perception, inference, and scripture; among these, there is no significant ground for dispute regarding those categories established by perception.

Scripture (*āgama*) as well is rooted in the knowledge of omniscient beings such as Kapila; that too has been thoroughly refuted in the first chapter (*kāṇḍa*), "The Definition of the Means of Valid Cognition" (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*). As for this inference that *pradhāna* alone is the cause of the world—by refuting that, their entire doctrine is refuted—and thus it is that very [inference] which is being refuted here. They describe it as follows: the fact that the entire world has a single root must necessarily be accepted; for if one were to accept the production of effects from multiple causes, there would be an infinite regress of causes (*kāraṇānavasthā*).

For parts such as threads, being joined with one another by their six sides—which are themselves composed of their own constituent parts—produce the composite whole; and those threads and so forth are likewise produced by their own parts of that same nature; and those [parts] in turn by their own parts of that same nature. Thus, it must be admitted that even atoms produce their own effects only when joined by their own six sides; otherwise, the production of magnitude (prathimā) would be impossible.

Even atoms, by virtue of being divisible, are produced from their own parts in that very same manner, and those [parts] likewise from their own parts; thus, there would be no established limit to causes anywhere. Therefore, for the sake of establishing a causal order, one must accept as the cause a single substance endowed with the power for various and manifold transformations, which, while its own nature remains entirely unchanging, serves as the substratum for infinite states such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest.

And they set forth the reasons for postulating that single cause, which is *pradhāna* consisting of the equilibrium of the three *guṇas*, as follows: "Because of the finite measure of diverse objects, because of their homogeneity, because of the activity [of the world] proceeding from a power, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-distinction of the manifest form—there exists an unmanifest cause."

Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning: *vaiśvarūpya* (the state of being multiform) is indeed the possession of all forms (*viśvarūpya*). It refers to the entire world, consisting of bodies, worlds, and so forth, which has a variegated arrangement. And since that world, by virtue of its variegated arrangement, is an effect, it must have as its cause an unmanifest (*avyakta*) entity of the same nature as itself. Why? Because it is an effect. For in the case of every effect, a separation from a specific cause of the same nature is observed, and likewise, a reintegration into that very same cause is observed.

Just as there is a separation of an effect such as a jar or a crown from its cause such as clay or gold—which possesses the same form as them—and their reintegration into that very cause, so too the world, which has a manifold form, arises from the Pradhāna which possesses the same form as it, and is dissolved back into that very same source.

The world has *pradhāna* alone as its cause. *Prajdhāna*, which consists of the equilibrium of the three *guṇas*, is indeed the material cause (*sarūpakāraṇa*) of the world; for the world is composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion, which are themselves made up of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Just as clay is the sole cause of a jar whose nature is clay—since it is observed that only that [clay] possesses the power of activity known as the production of the jar—so it is here.

The causality of the Unmanifest—which consists of the equilibrium of the *guṇas* and is itself unlimited by space and time—is understood from the fact that the various effects, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), are limited. Since the Great Principle and the others are limited like jars and other objects, they lack the power to produce the entire universe; therefore, it is concluded that the three-fold world has as its sole cause the *Pradhāna*, which is the state of equilibrium of the three *guṇas*. To this, it is replied: "And because of the impossibility of the arrangement [of the world], there is no inference [of a single cause]; and because of activity. That which is inferred is called an "inference" (*anumāna*).

The *pradhāna* asserted by you is not capable of creating the diverse world, because it is insentient and lacks the knowledge and supervision of its own nature; for whatever is thus [insentient and lacking such knowledge] is so, just as mere wood and the like are in the construction of chariots, palaces, and so forth.

Since it is observed that insentient things like wood do not initiate an effect unless supervised by the knowledge of that [agent], and since it is observed that they do proceed to initiate an effect when supervised by the knowledge of that [agent], it is stated that the *pradhāna*—not being supervised by intelligence—is not the cause. By the word "and" (*ca*), the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding the partless [cause] is further combined.

For properties such as whiteness and cowness, though they are concomitant [with their substrates], are not pervaded by causality. Nor should it be argued: "Let it be that properties such as whiteness, even if concomitant, lack causality; however, substances such as gold, which are concomitant with their effects, certainly possess the pervasion of causality; and thus existence (sattva) and the other gunas, being substances concomitant with their effects, are likewise pervaded by causality."

Since existence (*sattva*) and the other qualities are substantial properties (*dravyadharma*), they are not the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the substance itself. For existence and the others are merely specific characteristics (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) of substances such as earth that serve as the causes for lightness, luminosity, and so forth; they do not exist as substances in their own right, like clay or gold.

Qualities are perceived as being conjoined with their effects; moreover, the established usage of the terms *sattva* and so forth is precisely as "qualities" (*guṇas*). Furthermore, that which was stated—that the world has a single root in order to establish a fixed causal order—is also untenable because *sattva* and the others are multiple. For this very reason, the fixed causal order is not established. According to your own doctrine, the *pradhāna* is nothing other than *sattva* and the others in their state of equilibrium (*sāmyāvasthā*). Therefore, due to the multiplicity of causes, the problem of infinite regress remains exactly as it was. Nor can a fixed order be established on the grounds that they are unlimited in number.

For if all three were indeed infinite, then because they would be omnipresent, there could be no state of deficiency or excess; consequently, since inequality would be unestablished, the initiation of an effect would be impossible. Therefore, for the very purpose of initiating an effect, their finitude must necessarily be admitted.

He states that everything other than those things—such as chariots—in which the state of being presided over by a conscious agent is clearly observed, is made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣīkṛta*):
"If [it is argued] that it is like milk and water, even there..."

As for what was stated—that the creation of the manifold world is impossible for *pradhāna* if it is not presided over by an intelligent being—that is not so; because its activity is possible, like that of milk and water. For instance, when milk transforms into the state of curd, a succession of transformations beginning with the initial movement [of coagulation] occurs spontaneously, without depending on anything else. And just as water released from a rain cloud, though having a single uniform taste, undergoes transformation into various tastes through contact with the *nālikera*, coconut, *tāla*, mango, wood-apple, *nimba*, tamarind, and so forth.

Activity is observed to occur spontaneously; likewise, for the Pradhāna—which is by nature subject to transformation and remains unguided by anything else—though it persists during the state of re-absorption through a homogeneous transformation, a manifold transformation caused by the inequality of the *guṇas* becomes possible during the state of emanation. As it has been said: "From transformation, like water, due to the specific differences in the substrates of each individual *guṇa*. If it is argued that the Unmanifest thus proceeds independently of anything else, the answer to that is: "In that case also... (tatrāpi).

Regarding that which was demonstrated by way of the examples of milk, water, and so forth, even there, activity is not possible without the superintendence of an intelligent being (prājña). The intention is that this too has already been made the subject of the previous argument. In the sūtra, "If it be said [that the case is] not so because of the observation of the withdrawal [of the organs], we say no, for it is like milk," it was merely stated that a specific transformation is possible even for that which lacks other observed auxiliary factors; it was not stated that superintendence by an intelligent being is unnecessary, because of such scriptural texts as, "He who dwells in the waters... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.4). ||2||

Furthermore, since its transformation depends upon the superintendence of a Lord whose will is true, it cannot be uncontrolled by the Intelligent One (Prājña), for otherwise there would be the consequence of its remaining unsettled in the state of dissolution apart from the period of creation.

Pradhāna is the material cause; when it is presided over by the Intelligent One (prājña), the orderly arrangement of creation, dissolution, and various diverse emanations is established through His power of true resolve. Nor should it be argued that even if it were presided over by the Intelligent One, the same defect would apply—namely, that because He has attained all desires, is perfectly complete, possesses unsurpassed and infinite bliss, is faultless, and is stainless, there would be no cause for the distinction between creation and dissolution, and furthermore, that He would be subject to the charge of cruelty due to creating an unequal world; for [this objection does not hold].

Even for one who is already perfect, activity may occur for the sake of sport (*līlā*); for that omniscient being, there exists the possibility of a specific transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) which serves as the cause for the particularities of creation and re-absorption (sarga and pratisarga) in the form of a vision [of that nature]; and because it is precisely the actions of the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*)—whether meritorious or non-meritorious—that establish the order of unequal creation. Now, if all these arrangements are established by the very actions of the individual souls in the form of merit and demerit, what is the use of a presiding Lord (*īśvara*)?

Primordial nature (prakṛti) itself, conditioned by actions performed in the form of merit and demerit, will transform in various ways according to the requirements of the Spirit (puruṣārtha), through a fixed order; just as a specific transformation of food, drink, and so forth—which have been rendered poisonous by [certain] plants or strengthened by particular medicinal herbs—is seen to become the cause of pleasure or pain according to the constraints of place and time.

The arrangement of creation and re-absorption, the unequal creation of gods and others, and the arrangement regarding liberation are all possible only for the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), which possesses the power of transformation in every way. You, however, are ignorant of the true nature of meritorious and non-meritorious karma; for the nature of merit and demerit can be understood solely through the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*).

The Scripture (*śāstra*) is the mass of syllables known as the Veda, which is without beginning or end and possesses an uninterrupted tradition of recitation, untainted by even the slightest scent of defects such as negligence; it declares that merit and demerit consist in actions that are the worship of the Supreme [Lord] and their opposite, and that the fruits thereof—happiness and suffering—are dependent upon His grace and His restraint. Thus says the Teacher Dramiḍa: "For, desiring a share in the fruit, they please the Self with rituals; when He is pleased, He is sufficient for the fruit"—this is the standard of the Scripture.

And thus says the Śruti: "The navel of the universe sustains the world—the manifold, born, and purified through sacrifice. Likewise, it was said by the Blessed One himself: "By worshipping Him, from whom proceeds the activity of beings and by whom all this is pervaded, through one's own action, a human being attains perfection. And: "Those hateful and cruel ones, the lowest of men among transmigrating beings..."

"I cast [them] incessantly into inauspicious, demonic wombs alone. Thus the Blessed One, Puruṣottama—having attained all desires, omniscient, the Lord of all, whose resolve is truth, and who engages in pastimes consistent with His own majesty—having established the duality of karma by determining "these actions are righteous" and "these are unrighteous," and having generally bestowed upon all individual souls (kṣetrajñas) the appropriate bodies, senses, and so forth for the undertaking of those actions, as well as the power to govern them;

Having revealed the scripture for the realization of His own teaching, He remains present by entering within as the inner self (*antarātman*), guiding through His sanctioning power (*anumantṛtā*). However, the individual souls (*kṣetrajñas*), empowered by Him and provided with instruments such as bodies as ordained by Him, and supported by Him, themselves undertake actions consisting of merit and demerit according to their own desires. Then, recognizing one who performs meritorious deeds as a follower of His teaching, He causes them to prosper through virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.

And since he joins [beings] with the opposites of those [faults] by means of transgressing the teaching, objections regarding a lack of independence and so forth find no opportunity; for that which is called compassion—

Indifference to one's own interest and an inability to endure the suffering of others—though this [compassion] may exist even in one intent on transgressing their own command, it does not conduce to virtue; on the contrary, it brings about impotence. Therefore, the restraint of such [transgression] is itself the virtue in that case, for otherwise, it would follow that the restraint of enemies and the like would not be considered virtues. By merely ceasing the intent to transgress one's own command and by refusing to accept the infinite, unbearable offenses accumulated over beginningless and endless kalpas, one exerts oneself spontaneously for the increase of unsurpassed happiness.

As it has been said: "To those who are constantly devoted and worship Me with love, I give that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me. Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge. Therefore, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), when not presided over by the Wise One (the Lord), is not the cause. || 3 ||

Now, it might be argued: "Even though it has been stated that the activity of motion in *prakṛti* is not possible if it is not presided over by an intelligent being (*prājña*), nevertheless, the activity of transformation is possible for that which is independent, because such is observed. For grass, water, and so forth, when consumed by a cow or other animals, are seen to transform of their own accord into the form of milk and the like. Therefore, *prakṛti* too will transform itself into the form of the world. To this, he says:

This is not tenable, because the example is unestablished: grass and the like do not undergo transformation unless presided over by an intelligent being. How is it unestablished? Because such a thing does not occur elsewhere. For if grass, water, and so forth—once consumed or discarded by a bull or other animal—were to transform into the form of milk, then one could claim that they transform even without being presided over by an intelligent being. But this is not the case. Therefore, it is the Intelligent Being alone who turns what has been consumed by a cow or similar animal into milk. This very point, which was stated in the verse "If [you say] 'like milk and water,' then there too... (2.1.4), has been elaborated here to demonstrate the fallacy [of the opponent's argument] in that very context. || 4 ||

Now, it might be argued: although the Puruṣa consists solely of consciousness and is devoid of the power of action, and the Pradhāna is likewise devoid of the power of vision, nevertheless the insentient Pradhāna proceeds due to the proximity of the Puruṣa, because such is observed. Just as an eyeless man who possesses the power of vision but lacks the power of locomotion proceeds when in proximity to a lame man who possesses the power of consciousness and is aided by that consciousness, and just as iron moves due to the proximity of a magnet.

Thus, the creation of the world proceeds from the conjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. As it has been said: "For the sake of the *puruṣa*'s perception and for the sake of the isolation (*kaivalya*) of *pradhāna*, there is a conjunction of both, like that of a lame man and a blind man; from that conjunction, creation is produced. The meaning is that, for the sake of the *puruṣa*'s experience of *pradhāna* and for the sake of its isolation, *pradhāna* begins to operate at the start of creation due to the proximity of the *puruṣa*. To this, the reply is: "Even so... (tathāpi).

Even so, the impossibility of the activity of Pradhāna remains exactly as it was. For a lame man, though devoid of the power of locomotion, there exist thousands of occasional specific conditions such as the sight of a path or instructions regarding it; likewise, a blind man, being conscious, proceeds by understanding those instructions and the like. Similarly, even for a magnet, there is the drawing near of iron and other such phenomena; however, for the Puruṣa, who is actionless, no such modifications are possible.

Because mere proximity is eternal, there would follow the consequence of an eternal creation; and because [the soul] is eternally liberated, there would be an absence of bondage and consequently an absence of liberation. || 5 ||

For it is accepted by you that the evolution of the world proceeds from the relationship of primary and subordinate among the qualities (guṇas), based on their respective increase and decrease, due to the specificities of each substratum of the qualities. However, in the state of dissolution (pratisarga), because the qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—exist in a state of equilibrium, there is an absence of mutual excess or deficiency; thus, since the relationship of primary and subordinate cannot be established, the creation of the world is not possible. Furthermore, if you were to admit an imbalance even then, it would follow that creation is eternal.
Therefore, the Pradhāna, when unguided by an intelligent being (prājña), is not the cause.

Furthermore, if the Pradhāna were inferred through a mode of inference other than those already refuted, then because the Pradhāna lacks the capacity for cognition, those same defects would arise. Therefore, the Pradhāna is not established by inference in any way whatsoever. || 7 ||

If one accepts the establishment of *pradhāna* through inference, then since there is no purpose for *pradhāna*, it should not be inferred. For the purpose of *pradhāna*—as stated in the principle "for the sake of the Puruṣa’s perception and for the sake of isolation (*kaivalya*) of the *pradhāna*"—is held to be the experience and liberation of the Puruṣa; yet these two are not possible [if *pradhāna* is not real].

For the Puruṣa, whose nature consists solely of consciousness, who is inactive, changeless, and stainless—and for that very reason eternally liberated by nature—neither experience, which consists in the perception of Prakṛti, nor liberation, which consists in separation from it, would be possible. If experience, consisting in the perception of pleasure and pain as specific transformations of Prakṛti, were possible for such a being merely through proximity to Prakṛti, then because that proximity is eternal, liberation would never be achieved at any time. (8)

Furthermore, this Sāṃkhya doctrine is internally contradictory. For, while they admit that the Puruṣa—the enjoyer, the controller, the seer, and the witness—is distinct from Prakṛti because Prakṛti exists for another's sake, is an object of perception, and is an object of enjoyment, they nevertheless maintain that his liberation (kaivalya) is to be attained through Prakṛti alone acting as an instrument or servant; yet they also assert that his nature is eternally changeless pure consciousness, and thus declare that his non-agency and liberation are his very own essential nature.

They say that due to the proximity of the Puruṣa—who is thus characterized as changeless and indifferent—there occurs the activity of creation and so forth through the mutual superimposition of Prakṛti upon the other, for the sake of the Puruṣa’s experience and liberation: "Because the composite is for the sake of another; because of the reversal [of the qualities] such as the three *guṇas*; because of being presided over; because there must be an experiencer; and because of the activity for the sake of isolation (*kaivalya*). And from this very reversal, his status as a witness is established."

[The Sāṃkhya-kārikā says: "Of the *puruṣa* [there are] isolation, neutrality, the state of being a witness, and the absence of agency. Having stated, "The activity of *pradhāna* is likewise for the sake of the liberation of the *puruṣa*," they say this: "Therefore, no one is bound, nor is anyone liberated, nor does anyone transmigrate; it is *prakṛti*, which has various supports, that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated. Likewise: "Therefore, through union with that [the *puruṣa*], the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were sentient."

"And likewise, while the qualities (guṇas) are the agents of action, the indifferent one appears as if he were the agent; for the sake of the Puruṣa’s perception and for the sake of the Pradhāna’s isolation (kaivalya), there is a conjunction of both, like that of the lame and the blind, and from that comes creation. Witnessing, seeing, and being an enjoyer, and so forth, are not possible for one who is eternally changeless, a non-agent, indifferent, and whose sole nature is isolation.

For such a being (the Puruṣa), even an error rooted in superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is impossible, because both superimposition and error are modifications (*vikāra*), and these two cannot belong to primordial nature (*prakṛti*). This is because they are attributes of consciousness (*cetana*). Indeed, what is called superimposition is the attribution by a conscious being of the qualities of another to something else; and since that is an attribute of consciousness and a modification, it cannot apply to the Puruṣa. Furthermore, superimposition and the like do not occur in the Puruṣa merely through proximity to *prakṛti*; for if they did occur simply due to that, they would follow as being eternal, precisely because the Puruṣa is changeless.

Furthermore, the fact that proximity (*sannidhi*) is ineffective has been established in the section beginning with "not because of the difference in characteristics" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*). [Objection: If it is the *prakṛti* alone that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated, how can it be said to be beneficial to the eternally liberated *puruṣa*? For they say: "By various means, the benefactor [Prakṛti] acts for the sake of the *puruṣa*, who is a non-benefactor; though she herself possesses qualities, she acts fruitlessly for him who is devoid of qualities."

They say that *prakṛti* withdraws from that very person at that very moment, according to her own nature and the manner in which she was perceived by him. "Just as a dancer, having displayed herself on the stage, ceases from her dance; so does *prakṛti*, having manifested herself to the *puruṣa*, withdraw. It is my conviction that there is nothing more subtle than *prakṛti*."

The claim that "once seen, she does not come again within the sight of the Puruṣa" is also inconsistent; for since the Puruṣa is eternally liberated and changeless, he never sees her, nor does he superimpose her upon himself. Furthermore, he does not see his own self, because he is insentient. The Puruṣa does not superimpose the seeing of his own self as "seeing itself," because he is himself insentient and because any modification in the form of seeing is impossible for the Puruṣa.

Now, if it is argued that "seeing" is merely proximity (*sannidhi*), it has already been stated that this leads to the consequence of seeing being eternal because proximity is eternal; furthermore, even a temporary proximity distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is not possible for that which is eternal and changeless.

Furthermore, if the very presence (*sannidhāna*) of the Self in its own nature is the cause of liberation, then that same presence would also be the cause of bondage; thus, both bondage and liberation would exist eternally. If it is argued that the cause of bondage is the perception of the Self as it is not (in its true form), while the cause of liberation is the perception of its true nature as it is, [we reply: since both types of perception do not exceed the nature of mere presence, both would necessarily result at all times. If presence were non-eternal, its cause would have to be sought, and for that [cause] as well, another would be required—leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, if it is argued that proximity (*sannidhi*) is simply the existence of the essential nature (*svarūpa-sadbhāva*) itself in order to avoid this fault, then because the essential nature is eternal, bondage and liberation would likewise be eternal. Therefore, due to such contradictions, the doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas is untenable. As for those who...

Those who assert that Brahman—which is immutably eternal, devoid of distinctions, and pure self-luminous consciousness—is the witness of ignorance and thus participates in the bondage and liberation of the finite self, for them too there is indeed an inconsistency, because the aforementioned [arguments] regarding the impossibility of the superimposition of the status of being the witness of ignorance and so forth apply. However, this is the distinction: the Sāṃkhyas maintain a plurality of puruṣas in order to establish the fixed order of birth, death, and so on; they, however, do not even accept that, and thus their position is all the more inconsistent.

As for the argument that—whether the *prakṛti* be ultimately real or not ultimately real—it is untenable for the eternally changeless, self-luminous, and uniform pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) to be a witness (*sākṣin*) distinct from itself; and if it were not ultimately real, it would be even more inconsistent, since its status as an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*) and sublation (*bādhyatva*) must be admitted. Furthermore, even in the theory of difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bhedavāda*), the inconsistency has already been stated previously: namely, that this very nature belongs to Brahman as the possessor of the adjuncts, and thus the connection with the adjuncts and so forth remains logically untenable.
The section concerning the impossibility of creation is concluded.
Or [the production of] the large and the long is like [the production of] the short and the circular. 10.

It was stated that the doctrine of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause is inconsistent because it is based on fallacious reasoning and is contradictory; now, the inconsistency of the doctrine of atoms (*paramāṇu*) as the cause is also demonstrated by the sūtra: "Or like the large and the long from the short and the spherical," where the word "inconsistent" (*asamañjasam*) carries over, and the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "and" (*ca*).

From two *paramāṇus* of short and spherical dimensions, [a dyad] arises, just as [a dyad arises from two atoms], like the doctrine of the production of a triad (*tryaṇuka*), and everything else accepted by them is inconsistent. The meaning is that, like the doctrine of the world’s production from *paramāṇus* through the sequence of dyads and so forth, other things are also inconsistent. For instance, parts such as threads, when conjoined with their own six sides, produce a whole (*avayavin*); yet the same applies to *paramāṇus*.

Only by being conjoined with their own six sides could [atoms] be the producers of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth; otherwise, since there would be no distinction of spatial parts (*pradeśabheda*) among atoms, even when a thousand atoms were conjoined, the size would not exceed that of a single atom, and thus qualities such as minuteness, grossness, shortness, and length would remain unestablished. If one admits a distinction of spatial parts, then atoms themselves would possess parts (*sāṃśa*) by means of their own parts, and those [parts] would likewise [require] their own parts, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Nor should it be argued that the difference between a mustard seed and a mountain is due to the smallness or greatness of their parts; for if even an atom possessed infinite parts, then because of the equality of having infinite parts, the difference between a mustard seed and a mountain would remain unestablished. Thus, one must necessarily admit a limit to the reduction of parts. Otherwise, since atoms would lack distinct spatial divisions, no dimension greater than that of a single atom could arise, and consequently, the very existence of a mustard seed and a mountain would be impossible.

If you ask, "What should we do?", let the Vedic position be accepted. As for the fact that others have explained this Sūtra as being intended to refute the objections raised against the doctrine of Brahman as the cause; that is inconsistent and redundant, because the objections stated by opponents regarding the doctrine of Brahman as the cause were already refuted in the previous Pāda, while it is in this Pāda that the rejection of the opposing views is carried out. Furthermore, the possibility of the world's origination from the conscious Brahman has already been elaborated upon in the very Sūtra, "Not on account of the difference of nature" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*).

Therefore, just as from the short and the circular [atoms] there arises the large, the long, the short, and so forth, everything else accepted by them is likewise inconsistent; such is the meaning of the Sūtra. || 10 ||
"What else here is inconsistent? To this he says:
"In either case, there is no action; therefore, there is an absence of that [result]. (11)

For in the theory that atoms are the cause [of the world], the production of the universe is held to occur through the sequence beginning with dyads, preceded by their conjunctions produced by motion residing in the atoms; in that regard, it is accepted that the initial motion residing in the atoms—which serves as the cause for the production of the entire universe—is brought about by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

"The upward flaming of fire, the horizontal movement of air, and the initial action of atoms and the mind are caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Now, is this action residing in the atom caused by an *adṛṣṭa* inherent in itself, or caused by an *adṹṛṣṭa* inherent in the self? It is not possible in either case; for an *adṛṣṭa* produced by the performance of merit or demerit by the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) cannot possibly reside in the atom. And even if it were possible, there would follow the consequence that [the action] would be produced at all times.

Furthermore, it is not possible for the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the self to be the cause for the production of motion residing in atoms. If, on the other hand, motion arises in atoms due to contact with a self possessing the unseen force, then—since that stream of the unseen force is eternal—there would follow the consequence of an eternal creation. [Objection: But the unseen force is capable of producing its fruit only in dependence upon its ripening (*vipāka*). Some unseen forces ripen at that very time, some in another birth, and some in another eon (*kalpa*). Therefore, because it depends upon ripening, there is no consequence of [motion] being produced at all times.

This is not so; for it is unproven that there is a simultaneous ripening of various unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*)—produced by numerous diverse actions performed sequentially by infinite selves based on convention—at a single time in a uniform manner. For this very reason, neither the simultaneous dissolution of all things nor their remaining without ripening for two *parārdha* periods is tenable. Nor can action arise in atoms due to a conjunction with unseen forces qualified by the will of God, because the existence of an inferential God has been refuted in the section beginning with the sūtra "Because He is the Source of Scripture" (*Śāstrayonitvāt*). Therefore, the production of the world does not have action inherent in atoms as its antecedent. || 11 ||
And because of the admission of inherence, there would be an infinite regress due to its being equal [to the categories it relates]. || 12 ||

Furthermore, it is inconsistent due to the acceptance of *samavāya* (inherence); why? Because of the lack of finality resulting from parity. Since *samavāya*—like the whole (*avayavin*), the genus (*jāti*), and the quality (*guṇa*)—stands in need of another establishing factor, that other establishing factor likewise requires one, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*). Thus, it is indeed inconsistent. This is what is meant: *samavāya* is accepted as that relation which, being the cause of the notion "it is here," pertains to things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relation of container and contained.

If *samavāya* (inherence) is postulated as that which accounts for the existence of universals (*jāti*) and so forth—which are perceived as not existing separately [from their substrates]—then since *samavāya* itself stands on the same footing, a further cause for its such existence must be sought; and if that too requires another, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*). If it is instead imagined that the non-separate establishment of *samavāya* from its substrate is its very nature (*svabhāva*), then this same nature should be attributed to universals and qualities themselves.
It is not reasonable to first postulate an *samavāya* never before observed and then imagine that this is its specific nature. || 12 ||
This same fault applies whether inherence is eternal or non-eternal; and he states another fault regarding its eternality: "And because it exists eternally" (sūtra 13).
Since inherence is a relation, if the relation were eternal, then because its relatum—the world—would also necessarily be eternal, it would be illogical.
And because they possess form and so forth, there is a reversal [of the nature of atoms], as is seen from observation. || 14 ||

Since it is admitted that the four kinds of atoms—earthy, watery, fiery, and airy—possess color, taste, smell, and touch, there follows as a consequence their impermanence, grossness, and possession of parts, which are the opposites of the intended permanence, subtlety, and partlessness; for we observe that jars and other objects possessing color and the like are impermanent because they are produced from other such causes.

For an unperceived object being postulated in accordance with what is observed cannot be established in the specific manner one desires; for you postulate that atoms possess color and other qualities precisely because it conforms to observation. For this reason as well, [the theory] is inconsistent. (14) Now, if—wishing to avoid this fault—one does not admit that atoms possess color and other qualities, then he says:
"And because there is a fault in either case" (15).

Not only is there a fault in the admission that atoms possess color and other qualities (*rūpa*), etc., but even if they were devoid of color and so forth, since the qualities of an effect are preceded by the qualities of its cause, earth and the other elements would be devoid of color and the rest. If one admits that they possess color and so forth in order to avoid that [consequence], then the previously mentioned fault occurs. Thus, because of faults in both cases, the theory is inconsistent.
And because of non-possessiveness, there is absolute lack of concern. || 16 ||

Although the position of Kapila has been abandoned because it contradicts scripture and logic, it is nonetheless accepted in some respects by the followers of the Veda due to its doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) and other points; however, since this position of Kaṇāda is not accepted in any respect whatsoever and is logically untenable, those seeking the supreme good must treat it with absolute disregard. || 16 ||
Even if both causes were present for the collection [of atoms], that [perception] would not be attained. || 17 ||

The Vaiśeṣikas, who maintain the doctrine of atoms as the cause [of the world], have been refuted; however, since the Buddhists (Saugatas) likewise accept that atoms are the cause of the world, it is now stated that even according to their view, the origin of the world and its subsequent conventional usage are untenable. They hold two positions: some accept external objects—composed of aggregates of four kinds of atoms, namely earth, water, fire, and air—as well as internal entities consisting of mind and mental factors, all established through perception and inference. Others, however, assert that all external objects such as earth and the rest are merely inferable from consciousness.

Others, however, maintain that consciousness alone is ultimately real and devoid of external objects, while external objects are like those in a dream. All three of these [schools] declare that the entity they accept as real is momentary; they do not admit, even in its own right, the existence of a self, space, and so forth, distinct from the aforementioned mind and mental factors, or from the primary elements and their derivatives.

Others, however, maintain that everything is empty; among them, those who assert the existence of external objects are first refuted. They think as follows: atoms of earth have the nature of form, taste, touch, and smell; those of water have the nature of form, taste, and touch; those of fire have the nature of form, taste, and touch; and those of air have the nature of touch. These [atoms] aggregate in the form of earth, water, fire, and air, and from these elements—earth and the others—there arise the aggregates consisting of bodies, sense organs, and objects. And therein...

It is the very continuum of consciousness (*vijñānasantāna*), mounted upon the conceit of being a grasper residing within the body, that persists as the self; from that alone does all worldly transaction proceed.

To this it is replied: Even in the case of a composite whole (*samudāya*) that has both [types of] causes, the attainment of that [result] is not possible. This refers to the fact that the production of a composite whole consisting of the world is not tenable—meaning that it is impossible—in either kind of aggregate: namely, that aggregate which consists of the primary elements (*bhūta*) such as earth and so forth and is itself causeless, and that aggregate which consists of bodies, sense organs, and objects and has earth and so forth as its cause. This is because atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the primary elements such as earth are admitted to be momentary; thus, atoms and the elements perish in a single moment.

Furthermore, when do they function in combination? When are they combined? When do they become objects of consciousness? And when do they serve as the basis for worldly transactions such as rejection and acquisition? Who is the cognizing self (*vijñānātman*), and what object does it touch? Which cognizing self perceives which object at what time? Or, who acquires which known object at what time? For the toucher has perished when the touched is present, and likewise the knower has perished when the known is present; how then can one perceive what was touched by another, or acquire an object known by another?

Even if there were unity among the continua (*santāna*), since it is not admitted that they are in reality distinct entities from the members of the continuum (*santānin*), linguistic usage and the like based upon them are not tenable. Furthermore, it has already been established previously that the self is precisely the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*), and that this [self] is indeed a knower. ||17||
