If it is argued that [the world] is established because of mutual conditionality, we say no, because that is not the cause for the existence of composite entities. || 18 ||

If it is argued that the state of being an aggregate and so forth is established through the mutual causality of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors, this is what is meant: although all things are momentary, nevertheless all of this is rendered possible by ignorance. For ignorance is, by definition, a perverted cognition. Through it—having as its object such things as permanence in what is actually momentary—there arise the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), namely attachment, aversion, and so on. From those arises consciousness (*vijñāna*), which consists of the illumination of the mind; from that arise the mental states and mental factors (*nāma*) known as "name," as well as material substances (*rūpidravya*) such as earth and the rest.

From that arises the group of six sense-bases called the *ṣaḍāyatana*; from that arises the body called contact (*sparśa*); from that arise sensation (*vedanā*) and the rest; and from those, once again, ignorance (*avidyā*) and the others as previously described. Thus, this beginningless cycle of the twelve links, rooted in one another, revolves like a wheel. Furthermore, all of this is not possible without the collection of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), such as earth and the rest; therefore, the existence of such a collection is established. To this, the reply is: "No, because there is no cause for the existence of a collection."

This is not tenable, because these factors, beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), cannot serve as the cause for the state of being an aggregate of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), such as earth and so forth; for indeed, one does not [perceive] stability and so on in things that are unstable and so on through the cognition of stability and so on.

Neither fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*) nor its effects, such as passion and hatred, can serve as the cause for the aggregation of a distinct, momentary entity. For the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl does not become the cause for the aggregation of the object that is mother-of-pearl. Furthermore, for one who perceives stability in what is momentary, that very person has perished at that same moment; for whom, then, would passion and the like arise? Moreover, for those who do not accept a single, stable substance as the substratum of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), it is impossible to explain the persistence of those impressions. || 18 ||
And because the preceding ceases when the succeeding arises. (19)

Furthermore, on the view of momentariness, the production of the world is not tenable; because at the time of the arising of the subsequent moment, the preceding moment has already perished, it cannot function as a cause for that subsequent moment. If non-existence were to serve as a cause, everything would arise from everything at all times.

Now, if it is argued that "causality" consists simply in existing in the immediately preceding moment, then in that case, any single moment of a jar would become the cause of all things—cows, buffaloes, horses, walls, stones, and so forth—that exist throughout the three worlds and arise at subsequent moments. Alternatively, if it is maintained that causality belongs only to what is of the same kind and exists in the preceding moment, even then, a single jar existing in the preceding moment would be the cause of all jars existing in subsequent moments across every location.

Now, if you think that there is only one cause for a single [effect], even so, it is not known which specific cause belongs to which specific effect. Furthermore, if you argue that the momentary jar existing in a particular location is the cause of the subsequent jar-moment associated with that same location, do you maintain that the location itself is permanent? Moreover, because an object conjoined with the eye and other sense organs does not persist at the time of the arising of cognition, it is impossible for any object whatsoever to be the objective referent of that cognition. || 19 ||
If it were non-existent [at that time], there would be a contradiction of the thesis; otherwise, there would be simultaneity. (20)

It has already been stated that if an effect were to arise even in the absence of a cause, then everything would arise at all times; moreover, this not only contradicts the principle of origination, but also [contradicts] one's own thesis.

Your own position would be contradicted. For it is your thesis that the four conditions—the dominant, the co-operative, the object, and the immediately preceding—act as causes for the arising of consciousness, and the dominant condition is the sense-faculty (*indriya*). Now, if, in order to avoid contradicting this thesis, you maintain that the production of a subsequent moment of the jar occurs while the very same moment of the jar still persists, then it would follow that two moments of the jar—one as cause and one as effect—would be perceived simultaneously.

And it is not perceived in that way; otherwise, the thesis of momentariness would be lost. If it is argued that momentariness remains established [even so], then it would follow that there is simultaneity between the contact with the sense organ and the cognition. || 20 ||
There is no non-attainment of analytical cessation and non-analytical cessation because there is no interruption. || 21 ||

Thus, the arising of what is non-existent has first been refuted. Now it is stated that the destruction of what is existent without leaving a trace (*niranvaya-vināśa*) is also untenable. According to the proponents of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatvavādin*), two kinds of traceless destruction are designated by the terms "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): one is gross, consisting in the finality of a similar continuum and perceivable as occurring immediately after the impact of a hammer or the like; the other is subtle, occurring at every moment within a similar continuum and imperceptible. Neither of these is possible.

This is the meaning. Why? Because there is no interruption; for that which exists, an interruption without a trace (niranvaya-viccheda) is impossible. This impossibility arises because what we call the production and destruction of an existing thing is merely its transition into another state; and since the substance (*dravya*), which possesses these states, is one and the same and stable, non-difference of the effect from the cause has been established by us in the section titled "Non-difference from That" (*Tadananyatvam*).

If it is argued that because the lamp of nirvāṇa is seen to perish without leaving a trace (niranvaya), destruction elsewhere is also inferred to be without a trace, we say no; for since it is certain—in the case of jars, bowls, and the like—that destruction is merely the attainment of another state by an existing substance, as evidenced by the persistence of the substance such as clay, it is logical to assume even in the case of a lamp that destruction is simply the attainment of another state, since its non-perception can be explained by its transition into a subtle condition. || 21 ||
And because there would be faults in either case. || 22 ||

It has been stated that it is impossible for an arisen thing to arise from a void (*tuccha*) as accepted by the proponents of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatvavādin*), nor is it possible for an arisen thing to fall into the state of being void; furthermore, there is a fault in accepting either of these two modes. If there were arising from a void, the effect would have to be of the nature of a void itself. For whatever arises from something is seen to be of the nature of that [cause], just as necklaces, crowns, and the like produced from clay or gold are seen to be of the nature of clay or gold. Yet, you do not accept that the world is of the nature of a void, nor is it so perceived.

If there were destruction without any continuity for an existent thing, then immediately after a single moment, the entire world would necessarily lapse into nothingness. Furthermore, if the world were to arise from that subsequent nothingness, it would possess the very nature of nothingness as just described. Therefore, because of these faults in both cases, the modes of arising and ceasing as stated by you are untenable. (22)
And because there is no distinction in space. || 23 ||

In order to establish the stability of external and internal entities, the insubstantiality (*tuccharūpatā*) of both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) has been refuted. By extension, the insubstantiality of space (*ākāśa*), which the Buddhists enumerate as insubstantial along with those two, is also rejected. Furthermore, it is not tenable for space to be indefinable (*nirupākhya*), because—just like earth and the other elements accepted as positive entities (*bhāvarūpa*)—space is likewise established by uncontradicted cognition.

For indeed, in space, one perceives: "The hawk is flying here, the vulture is flying there," [identifying it] as the locus of the flight of hawks and other birds. Nor can it be said that space is merely the absence of earth and so forth, because such a claim cannot withstand logical analysis (*vikalpa*): Is space the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of earth and the rest, its non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), their mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), or their absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*)? In no case, however, would the perception of space be possible. Thus it must be.

If prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) were space, then while earth and other elements exist, there could be no cognition of space, and thus the world would be devoid of space. Even if mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) were space, since mutual non-existence resides within each respective object, there would be no cognition of space in the intervals between them. Furthermore, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is not possible for earth and the other elements. Moreover, because it has been established that non-existence is a particular state of an existing entity, even if space were of the nature of non-existence, it would not be a mere indefinable nothingness (*nirupākhya*).

Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the visibility of this space existing within the cosmic egg, because it possesses color through the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa) as demonstrated by the instruction on triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa). || 23 ||
And because of continuous existence. || 24 ||

The very stability of the object previously introduced is now established: recollection is a cognition having as its object an entity previously experienced, which is to say recognition; thus, the entire range of objects experienced in past time is recognized as "this is that very same thing."

Nor can it be argued that this delusion of oneness is based on similarity—like the case of sparks from a fire—because a single cognizer who undergoes such delusion is not admitted [by you]. For one person does not connect the oneness or the similarity of what was experienced by another with what was experienced by oneself. Therefore, those who claim that the delusion of oneness is based on the experience of similarity residing in objects existing at different times must necessarily admit the oneness of the cognizer.

Nor do we perceive any means of valid cognition that establishes a difference even in objects of knowledge such as jars, as we do in the case of flames and the like, by which we might postulate that recognition is based on similarity; and as for what is said—that the momentariness of jars and other things is established through both perception and inference—[that too is not the case].

To begin with, perception—which has the present object as its domain—makes known that which is excluded from non-present entities and excludes them from its own domain, just as [it perceives] blue [and excludes other colors]. In this way, the distinctness of the present entity from the past and future is understood. Inference also [establishes this]: because it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and because it exists, a jar and the like are momentary; whereas that which is non-momentary, such as a hare’s horn, does not perform causal efficiency and does not exist. Likewise, the existence of the preceding jar-moment [is established] by virtue of the existence of the subsequent jar-moment.

[The argument that things are] perishable because they exist at the moment of the pot, like the existence at the final moment of the pot—this has already been refuted previously by [arguments such as] the impossibility of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Furthermore, the exclusion of the present from the non-present as apprehended by perception does not lead to the understanding of the present as a distinct entity; rather, it indicates merely its connection with the present time. And by that much alone, its status as a distinct entity is not established, since it is possible for that very same thing to be connected with another time. As for the claim that [momentariness follows] from existence and from the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*): [The text continues: ...[the argument for] momentariness... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the preceding arguments regarding the refutation of momentariness based on the nature of temporal connection and causal efficiency.)

Two reasons have been stated; they are contradictory because they prove the opposite of what is intended. For it can also be said: "Because of existence, or because of performing a purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*), a jar and the like are stable; whereas that which is unstable is non-existent and does not perform a purposeful action, just like a rabbit’s horn. Furthermore, the very fact of performing a purposeful action would actually prove non-momentariness itself.

For it has been stated that because momentary entities lack causal activity (*vyāpāra*), their capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*) is impossible; likewise, since the destruction of the final moment of a jar is observed to be caused by an external factor, other moments of the jar must also have destruction dependent upon causes. Thus, [the jar] would remain stable until the occurrence of causes such as a hammer.

Nor should it be argued that hammers and the like are not causes of destruction, but rather causes for the production of a dissimilar continuum such as potsherds; for it has already been established that the very attainment of the state of being potsherds constitutes the destruction of jars and the like. Even if one accepts that destruction is distinct from the production of potsherds, it is logical that hammers and the like are indeed the causes of destruction because of their immediate succession. Therefore, the stability perceived through recognition cannot be denied by any means whatsoever.

One who asserts that recognition—which has as its object the identity of an entity connected with prior and subsequent times—has a different object [than what it appears to have], would likewise have to assert that cognitions of blue and so forth also have objects other than the blue and so forth themselves. Furthermore, for those who maintain the momentariness of both the knower and the known, even the acceptance of inference—preceded by the determination of pervasion and the recollection thereof—is difficult to sustain. Likewise, this [entity] is momentary...

Even the presentation of reasons preceded by a thesis, such as "it is eternal" and so forth, is not tenable for you; because the speaker has perished at the very moment the thesis is commenced, it is impossible for others—who do not know what was commenced by another—to bring it to completion. || 24 ||
Not from the non-existent, because it is not observed. || 25 ||

Thus, the common objections against both the Vaibhāṣikas and the Sautrāntikas, who maintain the existence of external objects, have been stated. Regarding the point that was raised—that because an object associated [with cognition] does not persist at the time the cognition arises, it is impossible for any object to be the objective domain of cognition—the Sautrāntika counters: the non-persistence of the object at the time of cognition is not the reason for its not being the objective domain of cognition; rather, being the cause of the arising of cognition is precisely what constitutes being the objective domain of cognition, and it is not by this much alone [that it ceases to be so].

It would follow that the eye and other sense organs would be objects of cognition, because it is accepted that only that which causes cognition by imparting its own form is the object of cognition; for even if an object has perished after imparting its own form to the cognition, it is inferred through the blue or other forms residing in the cognition. Furthermore, the form of a subsequent cognition cannot be established by a preceding cognition, because it would follow that in a stream of cognitions of blue, a cognition of yellow could never arise. Therefore, the diversity of cognitions is produced solely by the object. To this, it is replied: "Not [from what is] non-existent, because it is not observed."

This form (*ākāra*), such as blue and so forth, which is perceived in cognition, cannot be the form of an object that has perished and is non-existent. Why? Because it has not been observed. Indeed, when a substratum (*dharmin*) has perished, the transfer of its property (*dharma*) to another object is never observed. Even in the case of a reflection and the like, it occurs only for that which is stable; moreover, even there, it is not the mere property that is transferred.
Therefore, the variety of cognition caused by the variety of objects arises only from the continued existence of the object at the time of the cognition. (25)
Furthermore, he states a common refutation: "And in this way, there would be the accomplishment [of the goal] even for those who are indifferent. (26)

Thus, if one were to accept such positions as momentariness, non-existent origination, causeless destruction, and so forth, then even for those who are indifferent and not exerting effort, there would be the accomplishment of all goals. For it is through effort and other such means that the attainment of the desired or the cessation of the undesired is achieved.

For if all entities were to perish in every moment, then no preceding object, nor any quality residing therein—such as mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the like, or ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth—would persist into the subsequent moment. Consequently, nothing could be accomplished through effort and other such means. This being the case, since all accomplishments would be established without a cause, even those who are indifferent would achieve results both in this world and the next, as well as liberation (*mokṣa*). || 26 ||
Not non-existence, because it is perceived. (27)

The Yogācāras, who maintain that only consciousness exists, offer this rebuttal: what was stated—that the diversity of cognitions is produced by the diversity of objects—is untenable. This is because, just like objects, cognitions themselves possess forms and are inherently diverse. Furthermore, that diversity of intrinsic nature is established solely through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). And a latent impression is simply a continuous stream of distinct cognitions.

The cognition having the form of a jar is the producer of the cognition having the form of potsherds; the producer of such [a cognition] as that is the preceding cognition of the jar; and the producer of such [a cognition] as that is the cognition of the jar preceding that—this very stream is what constitutes the latent impression (*vāsanā*).

It is said: How can it be asserted that the form of external things such as mustard seeds and mountains belongs to internal cognition alone? Because even the object's fitness for practical activity (*vyavahāra-yogyatva*) depends upon the illumination of cognition; otherwise, there would be no distinction between what is known by oneself and what is known by another. Furthermore, since cognition is manifesting, its possession of a form (*sākāratva*) must necessarily be accepted, because that which is formless cannot be manifest. And this single form that is perceived belongs to cognition alone.

And although that [object] appears as if external, it is produced by delusion; furthermore, because of the rule of the simultaneous perception of cognition and its object, the object is not distinct from the cognition. Moreover, even for those who accept an external object, in cognitions such as "pot" or "cloth," the cognition's specific relation to each respective object is not possible without a similarity to that respective object; therefore, one must necessarily admit a form within the cognition that is similar to the object.

Since all worldly transactions are established by that alone, the postulation of an object distinct from that [cognition] lacks any basis in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, when it has been reached that consciousness alone is reality and no external object exists, we reply: "Non-existence [of the object] is not [possible], because of its apprehension. It is impossible to assert the non-existence of an object distinct from cognition. Why? Because of its apprehension—that is, because cognition is apprehended in the form of producing in the knowing self a state of fitness for the practical transaction (*vyavahāra*) with specific objects.

In this very way, all worldly people understand, "I know the jar. Thus, by means of the meaning of the verbal root *jñā* (to know), which is accompanied by an object and an agent and which appears as something immediate and witnessed by the whole world, those who attempt to prove that consciousness alone is the ultimate reality become objects of derision for the entire world. This has been explained in greater detail in the *Nipūṇataraprapañca*, which refutes the Buddhists disguised under the cloak of Vedic speech.

As for the claim that “because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*), there is no difference between blue and the cognition thereof,” this is contradicted by its own statement, because coexistence (*sāhitya*) is caused by a difference in objects. Since cognition has as its sole nature the fitness for the practical usage of those objects, its rule of simultaneous apprehension with them [is established]; therefore, it is not [the case that they are non-different].

And the claim that there is a means of establishing [the existence of] specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇya*) is laughable; for since cognitions perish without leaving a trace (*niranvaya-vināśin*), they lack a persisting form, and thus it is difficult to establish the existence of mental impressions (*vāsanā*). How can a subsequent cognition, which has not yet arisen, be impressed by a preceding cognition that has already perished? Therefore, the diversity of cognitions is caused solely by the diversity of objects. The uniqueness of a cognition—which is directly perceived as consisting in the production of a capacity for the practical engagement (*vyavahāra*) with this or that object—is dependent upon its connection with that respective object.

And the relation [between them] is characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*). For even cognition is indeed a substance (*dravya*). It has been stated that, just as the substance of light—which is a quality (*guṇa*) of the lamp—is not incompatible with being a substance, so too it is not incompatible for cognition, which is a quality of the self (*ātman*), to be a substance. Therefore, there is no absence of external objects. || 27 ||
As for the claim made by others—that even the cognitions of the waking state are without an objective basis (nirālambana) by means of the analogy of dream-cognitions—the Sūtra replies:
"And because of the difference in nature, [the waking state] is not like a dream, etc. (2.2.28).

It is not tenable to assert that waking cognitions are devoid of objects on the grounds of their dissimilarity to dream cognitions; for dream cognitions are produced by sense organs impaired by defects such as sleep and are sublated, whereas waking cognitions are the opposite of those, and thus they cannot be equated. Furthermore, if all cognitions were devoid of objects, even the object of your own proof would not be established, because the inference [of universal objectlessness] itself would lack an objective basis (*nirālambana*). Moreover, if that inference possessed an objective basis, then the reason (*hetu*) "being a cognition" (*jñānatva*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and thus the absence of objects could never be proven. || 28 ||
There is no existence, because it is not perceived. || 29 ||

The existence of a cognition devoid of an object is not possible; why? Because it is never perceived anywhere. Indeed, no cognition that is without an agent or without an object is ever perceived. It has been established in the *Khyātinirūpaṇa* (Examination of Manifestation) that even in cases such as dreams and mental cognitions, there is no absence of an object. || 29 ||
Thus concludes the section on perception.
And because it is impossible in every way. || 30 ||

Here the Mādhyamika, the proponent of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyavāda*), objects: indeed, the pinnacle of the Sugata’s doctrine lies precisely in the doctrine of emptiness. Moments of existence such as momentariness were taught through the acceptance of objects and so forth, in accordance with the fitness of the disciples' intellects; yet, neither consciousness nor external objects exist—all are empty, for emptiness alone is the reality. Furthermore, this alone is the Buddha's intention: that liberation is simply the attainment of non-existence. For that alone is logical, since emptiness, being neither caused nor producible, is established by itself.

For a cause must be sought only for that which already exists; and that which exists does not arise from either existence or non-existence. First of all, the arising of anything from existence is never observed, for a jar or the like is not produced unless the lump of clay and so forth have been destroyed. Nor is arising from non-existence possible, for if a jar or the like were produced from non-existence once the lump of clay has perished, it would itself be of the nature of non-existence. Likewise, arising neither from itself nor from another is possible.

If [existence] arises from itself, there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) and a lack of purpose; if it arises from another, then because "otherness" is indistinguishable, there would be the consequence that everything could arise from everything. Since there is no birth, there is likewise no destruction; therefore, emptiness alone is the reality. Consequently, birth, destruction, existence, non-existence, and so forth, are mere illusion. Nor can one maintain that some ultimate reality must be accepted as the substratum of illusion, on the grounds that an illusion cannot exist without a substratum.

Just as the occurrence of an error is possible even when the defects, the locus of those defects, and the knower are not ultimately real, so too the occurrence of an error is possible even when the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) is not ultimately real. Thus, when it is argued that "emptiness alone is the reality," it is replied: "And because it is untenable in every way. Total emptiness, as intended by you, is not possible. Do you assert that everything is existent? Or that it is non-existent? Or otherwise?
In every respect, the emptiness intended by you is not possible, because in the world the words "existence" and "non-existence," as well as the cognitions corresponding to them, are indeed present.

Since it has been demonstrated that pride (*māna*) itself actually has as its object a particular state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*), therefore, by one who asserts that "everything is empty" (*sarvaṃ śūnyam*), just like one who asserts that "everything exists" (*sarvaṃ sat*), the very capacity for everything that exists to assume a particular state is what is asserted; thus, the non-existence (*tucchatā*) you intend is not established from any source whatsoever. Furthermore, by one who desires to prove emptiness after having accepted the unreality of something based on some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the reality (*satyatva*) of that very means of valid cognition must be admitted.

If that [emptiness] were unreal, then everything would be real; thus, the universal emptiness of all things is in every way untenable. || 30 || Thus concludes the section on the untenability of [emptiness] in every respect.
Not so, because it is impossible in a single [locus]. (31)

The followers of the Buddha have been refuted. Since the Jains also maintain that the world has atoms as its cause and so forth, the Jain position will be rejected immediately hereafter. They indeed believe that this world consists of souls and matter and is devoid of a Lord (nirīśvara); furthermore, it is composed of six substances (ṣaḍ-dravya). These [are...]

And the substances (*dravya*) are those known as soul (*jīva*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), matter (*pudgala*), time (*kāla*), and space (*ākāśa*). Among these, souls are of three kinds: bound (*baddha*), perfected through yoga (*yogasiddha*), and liberated (*mukta*). That which is called merit (*dharma*) is a specific substance pervading the universe that serves as the cause of motion for things possessing movement. Demerit (*adharma*) is likewise all-pervasive, serving as the cause of rest. That which is called matter (*pudgala*) is a substance possessing color, odor, taste, and touch; it is of two kinds: in the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and in the form of their aggregates. [This includes] wind, fire, water, earth, bodies, the world, and so forth.

Time (*kāla*) is that subtle substance which exists as the cause of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), such as "it is" or "it was. Space (*ākāśa*) is also one and possesses infinite points (*anantapradeśa*). These substances, excluding the atom (*aṇu*), are collectively subsumed under the category of the five "existential bodies" (*pañcāstikāya*): the existential body of living beings (*jīvāstikāya*), the existential body of merit (*dharmāstikāya*), the existential body of demerit (*adharmāstikāya*), the existential body of matter (*pudgalāstikāya*), and the existential body of space (*ākāśāstikāya*). The term "existential body" (*astikāya*) is applied to a substance that occupies multiple spatial locations.

They also provide another summary conducive to the liberation of living beings: "Living beings (jīva), non-living beings (ajīva), influx (āsrava), bondage (bandha), shedding (nirjarā), restraint (saṃvara), and liberation (mokṣa). By this summary of liberation, the means to liberation is also included, and that consists of right knowledge (samyag-jñāna), right perception (samyag-darśana), and right conduct (samyak-cāritra). Among these, the living being possesses the qualities of knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy. Non-living beings comprise the entire collection of objects to be enjoyed by the living being; influx refers to the sensory organs and so forth, which constitute the instruments for their enjoyment.

Bondage (*bandha*) is of eight kinds: the four destructive karmas (*ghāti-karma*) and the four non-destructive karmas (*aghāti-karma*). Among these, the former obstructs the innate qualities of the soul—namely, knowledge, perception, power, and bliss; the latter serves as the cause for the body, its configuration, the ego-identification with it, its duration, and the resulting pleasure, pain, and equanimity. Nirjarā (dissociation) is the means to liberation; it consists of austerity (*tapas*) as understood through the teachings of the Arhat.

Restraint (*saṃvara*) is a form of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) consisting in the cessation of the sense faculties. Liberation (*mokṣa*), however, is the manifestation of the innate nature of the self for one whose afflictions such as passion have ceased. Furthermore, the atoms that serve as the causes of earth and the other elements are not of four kinds, as held by the Vaiśeṣikas and others; rather, they possess a single nature.

The differentiation of earth and the other elements, however, is produced by transformation (*pariṇāma*). Furthermore, they maintain that the entire range of existing things is indeterminate with respect to existence, non-existence, permanence, impermanence, difference, non-difference, and so forth; for everywhere the method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) is applied: "in some sense it exists," "in some sense it does not exist," "in some sense it both exists and does not exist," "in some sense it is inexpressible," "in some sense it exists and is inexpressible," "in some sense it does not exist and is inexpressible," and "in some sense it exists, does not exist, and is inexpressible."

They establish that every class of entity consists of substance (*dravya*) and modification (*paryāya*); thus, by way of its substantial nature, it possesses existence, unity, permanence, and so forth, while by way of its modificational nature, it possesses the opposite qualities. Furthermore, modifications are specific states of the substance. Since these possess the nature of both being and non-being, everything—including existence and non-existence—is logically consistent. To this, it is replied: "Because [these] are impossible in one [entity]."

This is not tenable; why? Because of the impossibility [of opposites] in one [entity]. For in a single entity, contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence cannot occur simultaneously, like shadow and light. What is meant by this is that since the substance (*dravya*) and its specific states (*avasthā*), which are denoted by words expressing particular modifications (*paryāya*) serving as its qualifiers, are distinct categories of reality (*padārtha*), the coexistence of contradictory attributes in one [entity] is impossible. Thus, by means of a single state such as existence...

At that very moment, it is impossible for that which is qualified by one attribute to be simultaneously qualified by its opposite, such as non-existence and so forth. Furthermore, impermanence consists in a substance being the locus of specific modifications known as arising and destruction; how then could its opposite, permanence, inhere in it? Likewise, distinctness consists in being the substratum of contradictory attributes; how then could its opposite, non-distinctness, inhere in it? Just as horsehood and buffalo-hood cannot coexist in a single thing at once.

This point was already elaborated upon previously, at the time of refuting the proponents of difference and non-difference, in the commentary on the sūtra "But that [Brahman], because of its underlying unity" (*tattu samanvayāt*). Since time is perceived only as a qualifier of other entities, its separate existence or non-existence need not be asserted, nor does it require a defense. The conventional usage among speakers of "time exists" or "time does not exist" is equivalent to the usage regarding the existence or non-existence of genus (*jāti*) and so forth; for it has already been stated that genus and the like are perceived only as qualifiers of substances.

But how is it that the Vedic scholars (śrotriya) declare that Brahman alone is the self of all? It has been stated that this is because the Supreme Person (puruṣottama)—who is omniscient, omnipotent, and whose resolve is ever-true—has all conscious and unconscious beings as His body. Furthermore, the absolute difference between the body and the embodied one, as well as between their respective attributes, has also been explained.

Furthermore, regarding the six substances such as the soul (*jīva*) and so forth, since they are distinct substances and do not possess the nature of being a single substance’s mode (*paryāya*), it is difficult to establish unity and plurality within them through the oneness of substance and the manifoldness of modes. If it is argued that these six substances exist in such a way by means of their own respective modes and their own respective selves, even so, this contradicts the accepted doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*), because there is an absence of mutual identity. Therefore, this Jaina doctrine is not tenable.
In the theory that atoms are the cause [of the world] without being presided over by a Lord, the previously mentioned defects remain exactly as they were. || 31 ||
And thus, the self would be non-omnipresent. (32)

If your position is accepted in this way, it follows that the self would be non-omnipresent (akārtsnya). For your established doctrine is that the living soul (*jīva*) consists of innumerable spatial units (*pradeśa*) and is equal in size to the body it occupies. In that case, when the self residing in a body such as that of an elephant enters the body of an ant, which is of a smaller dimension, it would follow that it does not pervade the entire space; that is to say, it would follow that it is incomplete (*aparipūrṇatā*). || 32 ||

Now, if it is argued that the contradiction is avoided by the fact that the Self undergoes different states denoted by synonymous terms through the nature of contraction and expansion, to that he says: "Nor is there non-contradiction even on account of synonymy, because of [the scriptural mention of] modification and so forth. (2.3.33)

Nor can the contradiction be resolved even by the occurrence of different states consisting of contraction and expansion, because that would entail the defects of being a modification and the impermanence resulting therefrom, leading to the undesirable consequence [of the Self] being equivalent to a jar or similar objects. || 33 ||
And because of the persistence of the final state, and because both [the cause and the effect] are eternal, there is no distinction.

The final dimension of the soul, which occurs in the state of liberation, remains fixed because there is no subsequent assumption of another body; since both that dimension and the self in the state of liberation are eternal, that very dimension must be the soul's natural one. Consequently, there would be no difference from that [final state] even previously, and thus the Jaina doctrine—that the soul has the dimension of the body—is indeed inconsistent. || 34 ||
On account of the inconsistency of the Lord [being the cause]. 35.

It has been stated that the systems of Kapila, Kaṇāda, Sugata, and the Arhats are to be disregarded by those seeking the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) because they are inconsistent and fall outside the Vedic fold; now, the system of Paśupati is declared to be disregarded because it contradicts the Vedas and is inconsistent. And its followers—

They are of four kinds: the Kāpālas, the Kālāmukhas, the Pāśupatas, and the Śaivas. All of these postulate a system of principles (*tattva-prakriyā*) that contradicts the Vedas, as well as various conceptualizations for the means to achieve worldly and transcendental welfare. They maintain a distinction between the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*), and they declare Paśupati to be the efficient cause. Likewise, they prescribe the wearing of the six seals (*mudrikā-ṣaṭka*) and so forth as the means to attain the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). As the Kāpālas say: "One who knows the reality of the six seals and is proficient in the supreme seal [attains liberation]."

"Meditating upon oneself as seated on the *bhaga*-throne, one attains *nirvāṇa*. A necklace, a breast-ornament (*rucaka*), earrings, a crest-jewel, sacred ash, and the sacrificial thread—this is proclaimed as the sixfold *mudrā*. One whose body is sealed with these is not born here again," and so forth.

Likewise, the Kālāmukhas also proclaim that eating from skull-bowls, bathing with the ashes of corpses, consuming those ashes, carrying a staff, placing jars of liquor, and worshipping deities installed upon them are the means for achieving all fruits pertaining to both this world and the next. Furthermore, it is well known in the Śaiva Āgamas: "A bracelet of rudrākṣa on the hand, a single lock of matted hair on the head, and bathing with ashes [are the marks of a true ascetic]."

Likewise, some claim that through a particular ritual act, even those of a different caste may attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa and enter the highest stage of life (āśrama), stating: "By the mere entry into initiation, one becomes a Brāhmaṇa in an instant; by undertaking the practice of the skull, a human being becomes an ascetic (yati). To this, it is said: "On account of the inconsistency of the Lord [Paśupati]. From the previous sūtra, "because of the impossibility in one," the word "not" (na) is carried over. The doctrine of the Lord Paśupati is not to be respected; why? Because of its inconsistency.

The inconsistency of their doctrines arises from mutual contradiction and from opposition to the Vedas. Wearing the six seals (*mudrā*), sitting upon the female organ (*bhaga-āsana*), meditating on the Self, placing a jar of wine, worshipping the deity residing therein, secret practices, bathing in ashes from the cremation ground, and meditating preceded by the *praṇava*—these are mutually contradictory. Furthermore, this conceptualization of reality, as well as their forms of worship and conduct, are in opposition to the Vedas.

Indeed, the Vedas declare that Nārāyaṇa alone, the Supreme Brahman, is both the efficient and the material cause of the universe: "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme reality; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light, the Self; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme. Furthermore, they state that meditation upon the Supreme Person, who is the Supreme Brahman—as expressed in such passages as "He thought, 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and "He made Himself by Himself"—is the very means for attaining liberation.

"I know this great Puruṣa, sun-colored, beyond darkness; knowing Him, one becomes immortal here in this world; no other path for going [to liberation] exists"—by such passages as these, all the Vedāntas arrive at unity [with Brahman]. And they declare that the ritual action (*karman*) which serves as the means to that [knowledge] consists precisely of the sacrifices and so forth, connected to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*) ordained by the Veda: "Brahmins desire to know this very [Self] through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, and through austerity... [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.2.1].

"By means of the Śaka [tree], those who desire this very world go forth as renunciants," and so on. Furthermore, words such as Prajāpati, Śiva, Indra, Ākāśa, and Prāṇa—which are heard in certain passages intended for injunctions regarding meditation and the like—are shown to refer to the reality established by the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka, which is solely devoted to expounding the supreme reality; this was established in the sūtra: "But the instruction is by way of the vision of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva. (Brahmasūtra 1.1.30)

Likewise, beginning with the passage, "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed; neither Brahmā nor Īśāna," and continuing with "He, being alone, did not rejoice," the common terms *sat*, *brahman*, and so forth—found in passages such as "In the beginning, this was Being alone"—denote Nārāyaṇa himself, who is the creator mentioned in that section on creation. This was established in the Sūtra, "From which [arise] the birth and so forth of this [world]. Therefore, because it prescribes the practice of meditating upon a reality that contradicts the Vedas, the system of Paśupati is certainly to be disregarded. || 35 ||
And because the existence of a substratum is untenable. || 36 ||

For those outside the Veda, the conception of a Lord who is merely an instrumental cause arises from inference; if that were so, then, following observed experience, He would have to be an operative agent like a potter and others. However, the presiding over *pradhāna* by Paśupati, who is himself insentient, is not tenable—unlike the presiding over clay and other materials by a potter—because he lacks a body. Indeed, the power of presiding is observed only in potters and others who possess bodies. Nor should the Lord be admitted to possess a body, for if His body were composed of parts, its eternity [could not be maintained].
And because the fault has already been stated regarding impermanence in the [sūtra] "Because it has the scripture as its source" (Śāstrayonitva). || 36 ||
If it be argued that [the soul] is like an instrument, we say no, because of enjoyment and so forth. || 37 ||

If it is argued that just as the embodied soul (*jīva*), though itself bodiless, is seen to preside over the instruments and the body, so too the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*), though bodiless, can appropriately preside over *pradhāna*, we say no; because of [the necessity of] experience and so forth. For that presiding is caused by unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) for the sake of experiencing the fruits of actions consisting of merit and demerit. Similarly, if the Lord of Creatures (*Paśupati*) were likewise possessed of unseen merit and demerit, it would follow that he must experience all their fruits, such as pleasure and pain; therefore, such presiding is impossible.
Either it would have an end, or it would lack omniscience. || 38 ||

The word *vā* has the sense of "and. Even though it has been established that the doctrine of Paśupati is to be disregarded—because if Paśupati possessed unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), he would, like the individual soul (*jīva*), be subject to finitude, be the locus of creation, dissolution, and so forth, and be non-omniscient—the present section is commenced again with the words "Because of the lack of consistency in [the nature of] the Lord" (*patyurasāmañjasyāt*) in order to demonstrate its contradiction with the Vedas. This is so even though [the system] is called Pāśupata-Śaiva.

Although certain doctrines appear to be non-contradictory to the Vedas, nevertheless, because they are rooted in the postulation of distinctions regarding causes and materials, and the inversion of the principles of the higher and lower [realities], everything is entirely inconsistent; thus it was said: "Because of inconsistency" (sūtra 2.2.1).
Because of the impossibility of origination. || 39 ||

Because it shares commonalities with the *Kapila* and other tantras, the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) is suspected even for the *Pañcarātra-tantra*, which explains the means to the supreme liberation taught by the Blessed One; therein, the following suspicion is raised: "From Vāsudeva, who is the supreme cause and the supreme Brahman, there arises a living being named Saṅkarṣaṇa..."

"From Saṅkarṣaṇa, that which is named Pradyumna—the mind—is born; from that, that which is named Aniruddha—the ego (ahaṅkāra)—is born"; such indeed is the process according to the Bhāgavata. Herein, the birth of the individual soul (jīva) appears to be contrary to the Śruti; for the Śrutis declare the beginninglessness of the soul, as in: "The wise one is neither born nor does he die," and so forth. (39)
And there is no instrument for the agent. || 40 ||

[Objection: Since it is stated that "from Saṅkarṣaṇa, the mind known as Pradyumna is born," the production of the instrument, the mind, from the agent, the individual soul (jīva), is impossible; for there is a scriptural revelation that the mind, like the vital breath and all the senses, is produced from the Supreme Brahman itself: "From Him are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses. Therefore, because this system propounds a meaning contrary to scripture, its authority is also refuted. [Reply: This being the position, we reply:
"Or rather, since [the mind] exists as a form of consciousness and so forth, there is no refutation of that. (Sūtra 2.3.41)

By the word "or" (*vā*), the position is reversed: "and consciousness, etc. Since Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are also of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, the authority of the scripture which aims to explain them is not negated. What is meant is this: this objection—that the production of the individual soul (*jīva*) has been stated in contradiction [to scripture]—is raised by those who do not understand the system of the Bhāgavatas.

The established doctrine is that the Supreme Brahman itself, known as Vāsudeva, who is affectionate toward those who take refuge in Him, abides in fourfold forms by His own will for the sake of being the object of refuge for those who have sought Him; as stated in the *Pauṣkarasaṃhitā*: "That scripture in which the fourfold nature (*cāturātmya*) is to be meditated upon according to its sequence, by means of its own names, is indeed [the one] for the Brāhmaṇas," and so forth. Furthermore, this meditation on the fourfold nature is the meditation on the Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva.

Regarding the word *sanam*, it is stated in the *Sātvata-saṃhitā*: "For the Brāhmaṇas who sacrifice to the Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva, this great scripture, the *Brahmopaniṣad*, is the supreme bestower of discernment. Indeed, that Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva—whose form consists of the complete sixfold attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*) and who is divided into the subtle (*sūkṣma*), the manifested (*vyūha*), and the incarnated (*vibhava*) forms—is fully attained by devotees through ritual action preceded by knowledge, according to their respective capacities.

They say that by worshipping the *vibhava* [manifestations], one attains the *vyūha* [emanations]; and by worshipping the *vyūha*, the supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva is attained in its subtle form. For the *vibhava* refers to the group of manifestations such as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others. The *vyūha* consists of the fourfold emanation in the forms of Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. The subtle [form], however, is the supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva, whose body consists solely of the six divine attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*). As it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*: "Because from that [emanates] the supreme, imperishable Brahman known as Vāsudeva..."

"From this scripture, [the goal] is attained through action preceded by knowledge," and so forth. Therefore, since even Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others are forms of the body assumed by the Supreme Brahman according to His own will, there is no negation of the authority of the scripture that speaks of them; for it describes a birth in the form of a voluntary assumption of a body caused by His affection for His devotees, as established by the Śruti: "Though being unborn, He is born in many ways. Thus, the validity of the scripture teaching that is not denied.

In this regard, it is not contradictory that Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—the presiding deities over the principles of the individual soul (jīva), egoism (ahaṅkāra), and the intellect (tattva)—are designated by such terms as "the living being" (jīva) and so forth; just as Brahman is designated by terms such as "ether" (ākāśa) and "breath" (prāṇa). || 41 ||
And because of contradiction. || 42 ||

For even in that system (the Pañcarātra), the production of the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed contradicted; as it is stated in the *Paramasaṃhitā*: "The insentient, for the sake of another, eternal, and constantly changing, consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), the field of those who act—this is said to be the nature of *prakṛti*. And the connection between this [prakṛti] and the *puruṣa* by way of pervasion is indeed beginningless and endless, determined as the ultimate reality. Thus, because the eternality of the soul is declared in all the *saṃhitās*, the production of the essential nature of the soul is strictly prohibited in the Pañcarātra system.

How the worldly and Vedic conventions regarding birth, death, and so forth apply to the individual soul (jīva) will be explained in the sūtra "The Self [is not produced], because of the absence of scriptural statement" (BrSū 2.3.18). Therefore, since the production of the soul is refuted there as well, any suspicion regarding the lack of authority in the doctrine of the soul's production is cast far away.

As for the claim made by some—"Śāṇḍilya, failing to find finality in the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (sāṅga-veda), studied the Pañcarātra scripture"—and the consequent assertion that the Tantra is contrary to the Veda because of the statement that he did not find finality regarding the goals of man (puruṣārtha) in the Vedas with their limbs, this too is merely a manifestation of the faith of those who have neither smelled the words of the Veda nor grasped the collection of logical principles that supplement them. It is just as it has been said: "Those who offer the Agnihotra in the city before sunrise speak falsehood every morning"; this was stated for the purpose of censuring the un-sunrise sacrifice and praising the sunrise sacrifice.

And just as in the section on the Knowledge of the Infinite (Bhūmavidyā), after Nārada has stated, beginning with "O Venerable One, I study the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaṇa as the fourth, and the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth," and having thus enumerated all the branches of knowledge, he says, "O Venerable One, I am merely a knower of mantras, not a knower of the Self"; this statement regarding the lack of attainment of self-knowledge in all sciences other than the Knowledge of the Infinite is made for the purpose of praising the Knowledge of the Infinite that is about to be taught.

Alternatively, this dispute by Nārada is caused by his failure to attain that supreme reality which is expounded in the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs; the same applies to Śāṇḍilya. This is understood from the subsequent mention of the supreme Brahman-reality known as Vāsudeva, who is to be known through the Vedānta; likewise, it shows that the meaning of the Vedas is difficult to comprehend.

The purpose of the composition of this treatise for the sake of easy understanding is stated in the *Paramasaṃhitā*: "O Blessed One, the Vedas have been studied by me in their entirety, along with the *Aṅgas* and *Upāṅgas*, as well as the various branches of learning (*aṅgas*) together with the *Vākovākya*. Yet, amidst all these, I do not perceive anywhere a path to the highest good (*śreyas*) free from doubt, by which perfection might be attained. "The learned Lord Hari, out of compassion for his devotees, having extracted the essence from the Vedāntas..."

"And he [the Lord] withdrew [the world] at his pleasure. Therefore, that Blessed One—Vāsudeva, who is known solely through the Veda, designated as the Supreme Brahman, an ocean of infinite and noble qualities such as knowledge and bliss, the sole repository of all auspicious attributes, the absolute opposite of everything to be abandoned, whose will is ever-true, and who is a vast ocean of boundless compassion, gentleness, affection, and magnanimity—beheld his devotees established within the system of the four castes and four stages of life, and oriented toward the human goals (puruṣārtha) known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.

It is beyond reproach that [the Lord], having composed the Vedas—divided into the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, *Sāman*, and *Atharvan* with their innumerable branches, consisting of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras—which reveal His own nature, His manifestations, the means of worshipping Him, and the true nature of their fruits, and which are difficult for all other gods and men to fathom; and having understood them, He Himself composed the scripture of the *Pañcarātra* to reveal the true nature of their meaning. As for the interpretation offered by others, who claim that the four aphorisms are intended to negate the authority of certain contradictory portions, that is inconsistent with the literal words of the aphorisms and contrary to the intention of the author of the aphorisms.

For instance, after the author of the Sūtras had composed the aphorisms that set forth the principles of Vedānta, and was composing the *Bhārata-saṃhitā* consisting of one hundred thousand verses for the purpose of augmenting the Vedas, he stated in the *Mokṣadharma*, within the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*): "The householder, the student (*brahmacārī*), the forest-dweller, and the mendicant..."

"Whichever deity one who desires to attain perfection should worship"—beginning thus, and having established the system of the *Pañcārtha-śāstra* through an extensive treatise, [it continues]: "This [work] has been extracted from the vast narrative of the *Bhārata*, which consists of a hundred thousand verses, by churning it with the churning-stick of the intellect, like clarified butter from curd; just as butter is from curd, as the Brāhmaṇa is among bipeds, as the *Āraṇyaka* is from the Vedas, and as nectar is from medicinal herbs. This is the Great Upaniṣad, endowed with the four Vedas."

"This which is proclaimed by the *Sāṅkhya-yoga-kṛtānta* and elucidated by the *Pañcarātra*—this is the highest good, this is Brahman, this is the unsurpassed benefit; it is honored by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the Atharva-Āṅgirasa [Veda]. This alone shall be the authority, this very instruction. Here, by the absence of the words *Sāṅkhya* and *Yoga*, the *Jñāna-yoga* (path of knowledge) and *Karma-yoga* (path of action) are intended; as it has been said: "By the *Jñāna-yoga* for the *Sāṅkhyas*, and by the *Karma-yoga* for the *Yogins*."

Also in the Bhīṣmaparvan: "Mādhava—who was sung of by Saṅkarṣaṇa after he had adopted the Sātvata rule—is to be honored, served, and worshipped by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have performed the initiatory rites. How could Vādarāyaṇa, the foremost among the knowers of the Vedas, speak thus while asserting the invalidity of the Sātvata scripture, which is devoted to propounding the worship and adoration of Vāsudeva, the Supreme Brahman known through the Vedānta?

But is it not the case that the venerability of Sāṅkhya and the other systems is also stated in passages such as, "O Sage, are Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata—do these have a single foundation? and so forth, even in the Śārīraka [Brahma-sūtras] regarding Sāṅkhya and the rest?

[The opponent argues: "These [other systems] are established as valid; therefore, this Tantra (*tantra*) is also equal to them. To this it is replied: "No," because even in those [systems], he introduces this very same logic stated in the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtras) by posing the question: "Are these [systems] based on a single foundation or on separate foundations? The meaning of this is: Do Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pāśupata, Veda, and Pañcarātra aim to propound a single reality (*tattva*), or do they aim to propound separate realities? If they aim to propound a single reality, what is that one reality?

When these [scriptures] are intent on establishing separate principles, then—because they are intent on establishing mutually contradictory meanings and because conceptual alternatives regarding a single reality are impossible—one must accept only a single authority (*pramāṇa*). To provide the answer to the question "What is that one?", he says: "O Royal Sage, know that these are various cognitions belonging to different philosophical systems."

Beginning with the statement, "Kapila is the proponent of Sāṅkhya," [the text] establishes the human (pauruṣeya) origin of the Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and Pāśupata systems by identifying them as being composed by Kapila, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Paśupati, respectively. Having declared the non-human (apauruṣeya) origin of the Vedas with the words, "He who is called Avāntaratamas is said to be the teacher of the Vedas," it then states regarding the Pañcarātra system: "Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the Pañcarātra. Thus, it asserts that Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the Pañcarātra Tantra.

The intention of one who speaks thus is as follows: because human-authored tantras speak of mutually contradictory matters, their validity regarding the true nature of reality is difficult to establish—both because they are rejected as being non-human (apauruṣeya) [in the sense of being unreliable], and because they express things contrary to the reality known through the Vedas, which are free from even a trace of defects such as negligence; and that which is known through the Vedas is Nārāyaṇa, who is the Supreme Brahman.

Therefore, the reality of the principles (tattvas) such as Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Paśupati, which are taught in those respective systems, must be accepted as having Nārāyaṇa—the Supreme Brahman who is the object of knowledge in Vedānta—as their very essence. This is stated [in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa]: "O best of kings! In all these systems of knowledge, the Lord Nārāyaṇa is seen as the ultimate foundation, according to scripture and according to reason. By the phrase "according to scripture and according to reason," it is shown that for one who reflects upon the reality taught in each respective scripture as supported by reasoning, Nārāyaṇa alone is seen to be the final ground of all things.

The meaning is that for one who contemplates the nature of Brahman in all principles (tattvas) taught in their respective Tantras—by means of such [scriptural] passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman" and "The universe is Nārāyaṇa"—it is understood that Nārāyaṇa alone is the ultimate goal (niṣṭhā).

Therefore, since Nārāyaṇa, who is the Supreme Brahman known through the Vedāntas, is himself the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra, and since that system (tantra) expounds His essential nature and His worship, it is impossible for anyone to attribute to it any commonality with other systems (itara-tantra). Thus, it is said therein: "In this way, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, the Vedas, the Āraṇyakas, and [the Pañcarātra]—these are mutually limbs of one another, yet they are called the Pañcarātra."

Sāṅkhya and Yoga constitute "Sāṅkhyayoga"; the Vedas and the Āraṇyakas constitute "Vedāraṇyaka. These, being mutually complementary and unified in their intent to establish a single reality, are called the "One Pañcatantra."

The following is what is meant: having accepted the twenty-five principles (tattvas) taught by the Sāṅkhya, the yoga consisting of restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth as taught by the Yoga school, and the essential nature of the rituals prescribed by the Veda, the Āraṇyakas declare that the principles have Brahman as their essence, that yoga is a mode of meditating upon Brahman, and that ritual acts are a form of worshiping Him; thus they establish the true nature of Brahman. This very point has been clarified by the Supreme Brahman Nārāyaṇa himself in the Pañcarātra Tantra.

In the *Śārīraka*, only the non-Brahman nature of the principles (tattvas) taught by the Sāṅkhya was refuted, not their essential form (*svarūpa*). Likewise, in the systems of Yoga and Pāśupata, the Lord’s status as a mere efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), the erroneous conception of the higher and lower principles, and the exclusion of those outside the Vedic fold from proper conduct were refuted, but not the essential form of Yoga itself, nor the essential form of Paśupati.

Therefore, it is said that Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata—these are authoritative regarding the Self and should not be refuted by mere reasoning; only the specific nature of each as propounded therein should be accepted. Nothing should be rejected en bloc, like the principles taught by the Jina or Sugata, for this is in agreement with the scriptural statement: "The Lord Nārāyaṇa is the final goal according to the respective systems. (42)
Space does not exist [as a substance], because it is not mentioned [in the relevant scriptural passages]. || 1 ||

It has been stated that systems outside the Veda, such as Sāṃkhya and others, are inconsistent because they are rooted in fallacious reasoning and involve contradictions; now, in order to demonstrate that our own position is free from defects such as contradiction, the manner in which the world—consisting of conscious entities—which is accepted as an effect of Brahman, comes into being is clarified. In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether the ether (*viyat*) is produced or not. What is the correct view? That the ether is not produced. Why? Because it is not so heard [in scripture].

For that which is possible can indeed be heard [in scripture], whereas for that which is impossible—such as the production of a sky-flower or space—the status of being denotable by words is not possible. Indeed, just like the Self, the production of space, which is partless and all-pervading, cannot be established; and for this very reason, because production is impossible, [it is stated] in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:

In the section on creation, the origin of fire and the other elements alone is recorded in the scripture: "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'; it emitted fire. However, in the Taittirīya, the Atharvaṇa, and other texts—such as "From this very Self, space was produced," and "From this [Self] are born breath, mind, and all the senses, as well as space, air, light, water," and so forth—the production of space (viyat) that is heard is set aside due to a contradiction in meaning. This being the position reached, it is replied:
"But it exists" (Sūtra 2).

However, there is indeed the origination of space. For the Śruti, which has as its object supersensuous matters, is indeed capable of establishing the origination of the ether (*viyat*), even though it transcends other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor can an inference of non-origination—based on reasons such as partlessness that contradict the Śruti—arise regarding a matter established by the Śruti; for it will be stated later that the non-origination of the Self (*ātman*) is not necessitated by its partlessness. || 2 ||
Again, he objects: "Because a figurative sense is impossible and because of the word [itself]. (Sūtra 3)

Therefore, it is proper to consider that the scriptural passage concerning the origin of ether, beginning with "From this very Self, ether was produced," is figurative; for it is impossible to establish the production of ether by means of the priority of the production of fire—as in the statement "It created fire"—which describes how fire first arises from Brahman desiring to create; furthermore, because of the term "unborn" applied to ether in the passage, "Air and the intermediate space were born from this. (Sūtra 3)
If it is asked how the single word "originated" can be secondary in relation to space and primary in relation to fire and so forth, he says in response:
"And it may be so for a single [word], as in the case of the word 'Brahman'. (2.3.4)

In this very case, since the primary sense of the word "originated" (*saṃbhūta*) is impossible with respect to space—as in the passage, "From that very Self, space originated"—the word "originated," though used figuratively here, must indeed have its primary sense in the cases of air, fire, and so forth, just like the word "Brahman"; as for example, the word "Brahman" in the passage, "From that, this Brahman—name, form, and food—is born."

Just as in the passage, "When used in a subordinate sense for the primary [subject], it does not arise in that very [context]," the word is used in a subordinate sense for the *pradhāna*, yet within that same context, in the passage, "Brahman is built up by austerity; from that food is born," it is used in its primary sense for *brahman*; so it is here. And in the case of an *anupaṅga* (supplying a word from a previous context), there is indeed a repetition of the designation, just as there is a repetition of hearing [the word]; this is the meaning. || 4 ||
He avoids [this objection], for there is a loss of the thesis because there is no distinction. || 5 ||

It is not appropriate to assume that other scriptural passages asserting the origination of ether are figurative in accordance with the *Chāndogya* Śruti; for the origination of ether is actually accepted by the *Chāndogya* Śruti itself. This is because, through the declaration "by which the unheard becomes heard," etc., there is a promise of the knowledge of all things through the knowledge of Brahman; and the non-abandonment of that promise occurs precisely because ether, being an effect of Brahman, is non-different from it.
From words. || 6 ||

Furthermore, the origination of ether (*viyat*) is understood from the *Chāndogya* Upaniṣad. This is because, prior to creation, there is the statement defining oneness—"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second"—and because of such words as "All this has that as its self," through which the non-difference of the effect from Brahman is perceived. Nor does the scriptural text regarding the origination of fire—"It created fire"—preclude the origination of ether;

for the primacy of fire, which appears merely from the fact that the origination of ether is not mentioned there, is not sufficient to negate the origination of ether established by another scriptural passage. 6.
But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the case of the world. (Sūtra 7)

The word *tu* has the sense of *ca* (and). By such statements as "All this has that as its self," which declare that space (*ākāśa*) is an effect (*vikāra*), the division—that is, the origination—of that space from Brahman is indeed already stated. It is like the worldly case: just as in the world, after stating "All these are the sons of Devadatta," by mentioning the birth of some among them from him, the birth of all of them is effectively stated; so it is here. And this being the case, the statement "Air and the intermediate space, this is immortal" intends their long duration, similar to [the term] used for the gods (*surāḥ*).
By this, Mātariśvan is explained. || 8 ||

By this very same reasoning, the origin of air (mātariśvan) from ether is also explained; the separate mention of ether and air [in the sūtra] is for the purpose of referring back to air in the subsequent statement, "Fire from that, for so it says. || 8 ||
But the non-existence of that which exists is impossible, because it is not logically tenable. || 9 ||
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of restriction; "impossibility" means non-origination. It is impossible for anything other than the existent Brahman itself to originate.

Because [origination] is not possible for that which exists. This is what is meant: the demonstration of the origination of ether (*viyat*) and air (*mātariśvan*) is for the sake of illustration. However, the impossibility of origination for that which exists—the supreme cause, the highest Brahman itself—is established; for it is understood through such means as the promise of the knowledge of all by the knowledge of one, that there is no origination of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—which is distinct from Him and consists of the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the great principle (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the senses, ether, air, and so forth—since its nature as an effect has already been determined. Thus, [origination] is not tenable. || 9 ||
The section concerning ether is completed.
Fire [arises] from that, for thus it says. || 10 ||

It has been stated that everything other than Brahman is an effect of Brahman. Now, it is considered whether those effects which are separated [in the sequence] arise solely from their respective immediate causes, or rather from Brahman in its specific form as those causes. What is the correct view? That they arise solely from their respective entities. Why? Because fire arises specifically from air, for the scripture says, "From air, fire. (10)
The waters. || 11 ||
Water also arises from fire alone; for [the scripture] says, "From fire, water," and "He created water. || 11 ||
The earth. || 12 ||
"The earth arises from water"; thus he says, "From water, the earth," and "They created food. || 12 ||
But how can the earth be denoted by the word "food" (anna)? To this, he says:
"On account of the context, the form, and other words. (Sūtra 13)

From the context of the creation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is understood that earth alone is denoted by the word "food" (*anna*). Since everything edible is a modification of earth, the term for the effect is applied here to the cause. Likewise, in the subsequent passage describing the forms of the elements—"That which is the red form of fire is the form of heat; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food"—it is understood that the word "food" refers specifically to that which is of the same nature as water and heat.

Furthermore, in the same context, another word is heard in scripture: "From fire, water; from water, earth. Therefore, since the word *anna* (food) denotes earth itself, it follows that earth is produced from water. The examples beginning with fire (*tejas*) cited above are for the sake of illustration; even the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the others arise only from the entity immediately preceding them, so as not to contradict the acceptance of what is stated in scripture: "From this [Self] are born breath, mind, and all the senses; ether, air, light, water, and earth, the supporter of the universe. Therefore, this Brahman is both name and form.

Therefore, such scriptural passages as "From this very Self, space was produced," and "It created fire," are also consistent with Brahman being the cause through a series of successive stages. || 13 ||
This being the case, we reply:
"But he [proceeds] from that very meditation on Him, because of His characteristic mark. (1.3.14)

By the word "but" (tu), the previous position is set aside: even for effects such as Mahat and the rest, that same Supreme Person alone, having those respective subsequent entities as His body, is the cause. Why? Because of the inferential mark consisting of His volitional thought (abhidhyāna).

The term *abhidhyāna* refers to the volition (*saṅkalpa*) "May I become many. From the scriptural hearing that "That heat [tejas] reflected: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and "Those waters reflected: 'May we be many, may we procreate,'" it is understood that even for the causes such as the Great Principle (*mahat*), the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), and space (*ākāśa*), their creation of their own effects is preceded by such reflection. And such reflection is possible only for the Supreme Brahman, who possesses those respective bodies.

Moreover, the fact that the Supreme Brahman is the Self of all by virtue of being the body of all is heard in the Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa: "He who dwells in the earth, who dwells in the waters, who dwells in fire, who dwells in the air, who dwells in space," and so forth. And in the Suṇḍalopaniṣad, beginning with "He whose body is the earth," it continues: "He whose body is the ego, whose body is the intellect, whose body is the unmanifest," and so on. (14)

In such passages as, "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind, and all the sense organs," and regarding what was said—that the creation of the vital breaths and so forth from Brahman, though heard in scripture, is possible through a traditional succession—it is replied here: "But the sequence is the reverse of that, and it is thus justified. (Sūtra 15)

The word *tu* (but) is for the purpose of emphasis. Regarding the sequence of all effects—which is understood from such passages as "From this, the vital breath is born" (*etasmāj jāyate prāṇaḥ*)—to be the immediate succession [of Brahman] in reverse order from the unmanifest (*avyakta*), mahat, ahaṅkāra, ākāśa, and so forth: that sequence is only logically possible if each respective effect arises directly from Brahman in its respective form. For if the causality were merely indirect (*paramparayā*), the scriptural teaching of immediate succession would be contradicted. Therefore, even passages such as "From this, [it] is born" serve to support the direct origination of everything from Brahman. || 15 ||

If it is argued that consciousness and the mind arise in succession because their respective marks appear in sequence, we say no, because there is no distinction [in the nature of the process]. || 16 ||

The sense organs are called "consciousness" because they are the means for consciousness; as for what was stated by the passage beginning with "from this [Brahman] is born," it is taught that everything is the immediate effect of Brahman; therefore, it might be argued that by this sentence the direct origination of everything from Brahman is supported, as understood through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the creative meditation (*abhidhyāna*). That, however, is not tenable, because this sentence is intent upon a specific order, since a sequence is perceived here among all things as well.

If it is argued that, in the case of the *svādhiṣṭhāna* and others, a sequence established by another scriptural passage (*śruti*) is perceived here as well; and that by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of their being mentioned together with those [elements], it is understood that *vijñāna* and *manas* also arise in sequence between the elements (*bhūta*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*); and therefore, this sentence does not serve to support the view that everything arises directly from Brahman alone—[we reply: that is not so, because there is no distinction. For there is no distinction [made] by the statement, "From this, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is born."

Since the relationship of direct origination expressed by the phrase "from this [the Self] is born" applies equally—without distinction—to all things from the vital breaths down to the earth, as well as to consciousness, the mind, and the sense organs such as hearing, that very relationship is what is intended to be enjoined, not the sequence. Furthermore, because it would contradict the sequence established in other scriptural passages, this text does not aim to prescribe a sequence; for instance, [another text states], "The earth is dissolved into water."

Since an alternative sequence is perceived by the passage beginning with "Thus it begins" and ending with "Darkness becomes one," therefore the origin of all effects proceeds from the Supreme Brahman alone, whose body consists of the unmanifest (avyakta) and so forth; and words such as "fire" (tejas) and the like denote that very Brahman which constitutes their essence. || 16 ||

[Objection: But if all words thus denote Brahman, then the conventional designation of various objects by their respective words—established through linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*)—would be obstructed. To this, he replies:
