"But the designation of moving and non-moving things would be figurative, because it occurs when that [Brahman] exists. (1.1.17)

The word *tu* (but) serves to remove the doubt that has been raised. The designation by various words based on all moving and stationary beings is figurative (*bhākta*); the meaning is that it applies to a single part of the denotable object.

This is because Brahman, who is the substratum (*prakārī*) of all things, is not an object of perception or other means of knowledge that grasp only the modes (*prakāra*)—since prior to hearing the Vedāntas, there is no cognition of the substratum—and because the final determination of its nature is contingent upon the cognition of that substratum. Therefore, in common worldly usage, those various words are designated as being "broken" (*bhaṅga*) or "unbroken" (*abhaṅga*) with respect to their own respective parts of the denotable object, which consist merely of those particular things.

Alternatively, one might suspect that the designation of Brahman by words such as "fire" (*tejas*) and so forth—being understood as denoting merely those respective objects—would be figurative (*bhākta*) or non-primary; anticipating this doubt, the Sūtra states: "But [the designation] has its basis in the moving and the unmoving. The "basis in the moving and the unmoving" refers to the designation of that [Brahman], that is, the word denoting it. Words denoting the moving and the unmoving are not figurative with respect to Brahman, but are indeed primary. Why? Because the denotative capacity of all words is permeated by the nature of Brahman; for this is understood from the Śruti concerning the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*). The section on Fire (*tejodhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
The Self is not [the body], because it is eternal according to scripture and because of those [scriptural] passages. (18)

The origin of the entire world, beginning with space, has been stated to proceed from the supreme Brahman. Now, a doubt arises as to whether the individual soul (jīva) also has an origin or not. What is the correct view? That it does have an origin. Why? Because the proposition that through the knowledge of one, all is known, is thereby rendered consistent, and because the state of oneness is determined prior to creation.

There are indeed scriptural passages stating the origination of the individual soul (*jīva*) just like that of space and other elements, such as: "From whom the progenitor of the world was born, he emitted living beings upon the earth by means of water"; "Prajāpati created the creatures"; "All these creatures, O Somya, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support"; and "From which indeed these beings are born."

Thus, from the statement regarding the origin of the conscious world, the origin of the individual soul (jīva) is also perceived. Nor should it be argued that the soul is eternal because Brahman is eternal and because the identity of the soul with Brahman is understood through such texts as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*); for since the identity of everything including space and so forth with Brahman is understood through such passages as "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*) and "All this is indeed Brahman" (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma*), it would follow that space and the rest are also eternal.

Therefore, when it is argued that the individual soul (jīva) also arises just like ether and the other elements, the following is stated in reply: "The Self [does not arise], on account of scriptural statement. The Self does not arise. Why? Because of scriptural statement; for the non-arising of the individual soul is indeed heard in such passages as, "The wise one is neither born nor dies," and "The two—the Knower and the ignorant—are both unborn. Thus, the prohibition of the soul's origination is established by scripture.

The eternity of the self is understood from those very scriptural texts, such as: "He is the eternal among the non-eternal, the conscious among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of many," and "Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient, he is not slain when the body is slain," and so forth. Therefore, the self is not produced. How then is the promise that through the knowledge of one, all is known, to be justified? It is justified in this way: because the individual soul (jīva) is also an effect, and because there is no difference between the effect and its cause.

If that were so, then it would follow that [the soul] possesses origination (*utpattimat*), just like space and the other elements. To this we reply: "No. For what is called "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is simply the attainment of a different state by a single substance, and that certainly applies to the soul as well. However, there is this distinction: the kind of transformation (*anyathābhāva*) found in non-conscious things like space is not the same for the soul. The soul's transformation consists in the contraction and expansion of knowledge (*jñāna*), whereas the transformation of space and the rest consists in a change of essential nature (*svarūpa*).
It is this kind of origination, characterized by a change in essential nature, that is denied of the soul.

This is what is being said: having established that the objects of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the controller possess distinct natures; having denied arising and other such qualities pertaining to the object of enjoyment in the case of the enjoyer and established his eternity; having denied arising and other such qualities pertaining to the object of enjoyment as well as the state of being a locus for what is not the goal of man (apuruṣārtha) in the case of the controller, and having established his eternity, faultlessness, omniscience at all times, the possession of true resolve, lordship over the lords of the instruments (the senses), and lordship over the entire universe.

In both states, it has been established that the sentient and insentient constitute His body and that He is their Self; therefore, Brahman always has the sentient and insentient entities as His body and is thus qualified by them (*tatprakāra*). At times, He exists with the sentient and insentient entities in a subtle state, from which they are not yet fit to be designated as distinct from Himself; this is Brahman in His causal state (*kāraṇāvastha*).

And at times, when name and form have become differentiated, there is the gross object, which is the body; and that is in a state of effect. In that context, when the causal state attains the state of effect, a modification occurs in the non-conscious (acid) portion—which was devoid of sound and other qualities in its causal state—consisting of a change in its own nature by becoming possessed of sound and other qualities for the sake of being an object of enjoyment. Furthermore, a modification occurs in the conscious (cid) portion, consisting of an expansion of knowledge corresponding to that [body], for the sake of being the enjoyer of specific fruits of karma. This applies to the aspect of the controller (niyantṛ-aṃśa), which is characterized by both these modes.

There occurs a modification in the form of being qualified by both [cause and effect] in their respective states; this modification, consisting in the attainment of a different state from the causal state, is common to both the two modes and to the possessor of those modes. For this very reason, with reference to the modification consisting in the attainment of a different state for a single entity, the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is promised in the passage, "By which the unheard becomes heard," and illustrated by the examples of clay and so forth in the passage beginning, "Just as, my dear, by one [clay]," and so on.

The scriptural passages such as "Prajāpati created the creatures," which speak of the birth and death of the individual soul (*jīva*), intend to refer to the connection with and separation from various bodies that cause the contraction and expansion of such knowledge. On the other hand, the scriptural passages such as "It is not born, it does not die," and "Of the eternal ones, the eternal one," which speak of the prohibition of birth and of eternity, intend to show that—unlike the insentient portion—the soul undergoes no change in its essential nature.

The intention [of these texts] is to convey the absence of both types of undesirable modifications—namely, those consisting of a change in essential nature (*svarūpānyathātva*) and those consisting of the contraction or expansion of knowledge (*jñāna*). To this effect are the scriptural passages concerning the Supreme Reality, such as: "That indeed is the great, unborn Self—undecaying, undying, immortal, Brahman," and "The eternal among the eternals. Likewise, the determination of the oneness of Brahman, who is always qualified by the sentient and insentient entities prior to creation, is due to the absence of the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-vibhāga*).

It is stated: "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest; it expressed itself through name and form as manifoldness and unity. As for those who maintain that the state of being a *jīva* (individual soul) is conditioned by the adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), those who say it is produced by a real adjunct, and those who claim that Brahman—which is pure Being (*sanmātra*)—itself exists in a threefold manner as the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller, all [of them] agree that even though the powers of ignorance, the powers of the adjuncts, and the powers of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller persist at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*).

At that time, they establish the determination of oneness precisely because there is no differentiation of name and form; furthermore, this is because the difference between individual souls (*jīva*) and the stream of their karma are accepted as being beginningless, as stated in the two sūtras: "Inequality and cruelty [on the part of the Lord] do not follow, because He is dependent [on karma]; if it be objected that [karma] cannot exist due to the non-differentiation [of souls], we say no, because [the cycle] is beginningless; and this is both logical and observed."

This is the distinction: in one case, beginningless ignorance causes Brahman itself to become deluded; in the other, Brahman is bound by itself through a real, beginningless limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because there exists no other entity apart from the limiting adjunct and Brahman. For another [view], Brahman itself transforms into diverse forms and experiences undesirable fruits of karma; although the Controller lacks the status of an enjoyer, because He is omniscient, He perceives the enjoyer as non-different from Himself and thus experiences [the results] Himself.

For us, however, Brahman—whose body consists of the sentient and insentient entities in both gross and subtle states—remains at all times free from even a scent of any external defect, and is an ocean of boundless, noble qualities such as the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpa*), even while abiding in both the states of cause and effect. Therefore, the sentient and insentient [entities] are merely its modes (*prakāra*). 19.

It has been stated that the individual soul (*jīva*) is not produced, like space and other such entities; following from that, the nature of the soul is now being determined. Is the true nature of the self merely consciousness (*cinmātra*), as maintained by the Sugata and Kapila? Or is its nature insentient (*acit*), like a stone, as maintained by Kaṇabhuj, being merely adventitious?

Does it have consciousness as its attribute? Therefore, is its essential nature (*svarūpa*) indeed that of being a knower? What is correct? That it is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Why? Because of such scriptural testimony (*śruti*). For in the *Antaryāmin-brāhmaṇa*, in place of the Mādhyandina recension’s passage, "He who dwells in the self," the Kāṇvas read, "He who dwells in consciousness (*vijñāna*). Likewise, [the text] says, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice, and it also performs ritual acts. Thus, it is heard in scripture that consciousness alone is the essential nature of the self, which is the agent.

Furthermore, in the *Smṛtis*—in passages such as "and [the Self] is, in the ultimate sense, of the nature of knowledge and absolutely pure"—the fact that the Self has the nature of knowledge is perceived. However, another [objection] is raised: if the individual soul (*jīvātman*) were admitted to have knowledge and the status of a knower as its inherent nature, then, because it is all-pervading, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its cognition being perceived everywhere at all times; moreover, the sense organs would become useless. This is because consciousness is not perceived even though the Self exists during states such as deep sleep or fainting, whereas the production of knowledge is observed when one is awake and the necessary causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present. Therefore, this [nature of knowledge does not belong to the Self].

Its nature is knowledge; nor is it the state of being a knower, for consciousness is merely adventitious. Furthermore, the all-pervasiveness of the self must necessarily be accepted, because effects are perceived everywhere and because the presence of the self is admitted to exist everywhere. Moreover, since the accomplishment of an effect is possible simply by the self’s movement to the body, there is no evidence for postulating its actual motion. Even scripture shows the absence of knowledge at the time of deep sleep: "Indeed, in this state, he does not know himself as 'I am this'; no, indeed..."

"These beings [perish]. Likewise, it shows the absence of knowledge at the time of liberation with the words, "After death, there is no consciousness. As for the usage of phrases such as "the very nature of knowledge," this is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), since knowledge is a quality unique to that [Self]. This being the position reached, we reply: "The Self is a knower, for this very reason. This Self is indeed a knower, having the nature of being a cognizer; it is not mere knowledge, nor is it insentient by nature. Why? "For this very reason"—that is, on account of the scriptural teaching itself.

The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) refers back to the scripture under discussion, namely the scriptural passage [beginning with] "The Self is not [known] through scripture. Likewise, in the Chāndogya, within the Prajāpati discourse describing the nature of the liberated and unliberated selves, it says: "Now, he who knows 'let me smell this,' he is the Self"; "He rejoices, seeing with the mind alone these desires that are in the world of Brahman"; "His desires are true, his resolves are true"; "Not remembering this body into which he was born"; and elsewhere, "The seer does not see death. Similarly, in the Vājasaneyaka, one asks: "Which is the Self? [and so forth].

"This person consisting of consciousness, who is among the vital breaths, the light within the heart"; likewise, "O Maitreyī, by what means could one know the knower?"; "This person indeed knows"; similarly, "For he is the seer, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the perceiver, the agent—the person whose self is consciousness"; and "In this very way, these sixteen parts belong to this all-seeing witness. || 19 ||

As for what was said—that if the nature of being a knower were inherent, it would follow that an all-pervading self would be perceived everywhere at all times—it is replied to this: "Because of its departure, movement, and return" (20).

This Self is not all-pervading, but rather this Self is indeed atomic (aṇu). Why? Because of the scriptural statements regarding its departure, going, and returning. First, its departure is heard [in scripture]: "By that light, this Self departs, either from the eye, or from the head, or from other parts of the body. Its going is also [stated]: "Whoever departs from this world, they all go to the moon. Its returning is also [stated]: "From that world, it returns again to this world for the sake of karma. For if it were omnipresent (vibhu), these [processes] such as departure and so forth would not be possible. (Sūtra 2.3.20)
And by its own nature, it is the cause of the two subsequent [moments]. (21)

The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis. Although departure (*utkrānti*), in the form of separation from the body, can somehow be possible for a permanent self; however, going and returning (*gatyāgatī*) cannot be possible in any way [for such a self]. Therefore, these two must be accomplished by the self itself. || 21 ||
If it be argued that [the soul] is not atomic because of the mention of "one whose head is cut off," we say no, because of the reference to another [state]. || 22 ||

If it be argued that the individual soul (jīva) is not atomic because of the scriptural declaration of its greatness—having introduced the jīva with the words, "This one which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths," and then stating, "That indeed is the great, unborn Self"—we say no, because of the context of something other than the jīva; for in that passage, the Supreme Lord (prājña), who is other than the jīva, is the subject under discussion. Although the jīva is introduced at the beginning, nevertheless, since the Supreme is taught in the middle with the words, "He whose Self is known and perceived," this greatness belongs to Him and not to the jīva. || 22 ||
And [the conclusion follows] from its own word and from measurement. || 23 ||

The word *aṇu* (minute) itself is heard directly [in scripture]: "This minute Self is to be known by the mind, into which the fivefold vital breath has entered. Having set aside the measure (*māna*) as a standard of measurement (*unmāna*), the scripture declares that the soul possesses the measure of something similar to a minute thing: "The soul is to be known as a part of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided again a hundredfold. And also: "For even the lower [Self] is seen to be the size of the point of an awl. Therefore, this Self is indeed minute. || 23 ||
Now, it might be argued that if the self were atomic in size, a sensation pervading the entire body would be impossible; regarding this, he states the resolution according to another view:
"There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood. (24)

Just as a drop of yellow sandalwood paste, though residing in only one part of the body, produces a refreshing sensation that pervades the entire body, so too the self, though residing in only one part of the body, experiences a feeling that extends throughout the whole body. || 24 ||
If it be argued that this is due to a difference in state, we say no, because [the soul] is admitted [to exist] in the heart. || 25 ||

If it is argued that such a state [of pleasure or pain] occurs in the case of a drop of yellow sandalwood and the like because of its specific location on a particular part of the body, whereas that does not exist for the Self, we say no; for even the Self is admitted to abide in a specific part of the body, since the abiding of the Self in the region of the heart is heard in scripture: "For this Self is in the heart; there are one hundred and one channels."

Likewise, having introduced the subject with "What is the Self?", [the text states]: "That which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart. To demonstrate the Self's abiding in a specific location, the analogy of sandalwood is presented; however, this does not imply that sandalwood itself has a requirement for a specific location. || 25 ||
He states, according to his own view, the manner in which that which exists in one part performs an effect pervading the entire body:
"Or [it is] due to its quality, like light. (26)

The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to exclude other opinions. The self (*ātman*) exists pervading the entire body by means of its own quality, knowledge (*jñāna*), like light. Just as the light of gems, the sun, and so forth, though residing in one place, is seen to pervade many places, so too the knowledge of the self situated in the heart exists pervading the entire body. It was established in the first sūtra that the occurrence of knowledge—which stands in the place of radiance for the knower—outside of its own substrate is possible, just like the radiance of a gem. || 26 ||
But has it not been stated that the Self is merely knowledge? How then can it be said that knowledge possesses qualities distinct from its own nature? To this he replies:
"The distinction [of knowledge from the Self] is like that of fragrance; and so the scripture shows. (27)

Just as there is a distinction between the earth and its fragrance—which is perceived as a quality of the former—likewise, the distinction between the Self and cognition—which is perceived as a quality of the knower—is established by the fact that it is cognized as "I know. Furthermore, scripture confirms this in the passage: "This person certainly knows. || 27 ||
Because of the separate instruction. || 28 ||
By its own specific term, consciousness is taught as distinct from the knower in the passage: "For there is no loss of the consciousness of the knower. (28)

As for what was stated—namely, that in passages such as "He who, dwelling in consciousness, performs the sacrifice through consciousness," and "He whose nature is knowledge, absolutely stainless," knowledge itself is designated as the Self—to that he replies:
"But because its essence consists of those qualities, it is so designated, as in the case of the Prājña. (2.3.29)

The word "but" (tu) sets aside the objection. Because its essence consists of that quality—that is, because its essence consists of the quality of consciousness—there is this designation of the Self as "consisting of intelligence" (vijñānamaya). Consciousness alone is its essential quality; just as for the Prājña [the Self], bliss is an essential quality, and thus the Prājña is designated by the word "bliss," as in: "If this bliss did not exist in the ether... [he] understood that bliss is Brahman. For bliss is indeed the essential quality of the Prājña, as in: "That is one [measure] of the bliss of Brahman; he who knows the bliss of Brahman..."

"...he fears nothing from anywhere. Or, as in the case of the designation of the wise one (*vipaścit*), the Prājña, by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) in such passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite" and "Together with the wise Brahman, he who is all-knowing," it is understood that knowledge is the essential quality of the Prājña. || 29 ||
And because [the self] has been cultivated as long as one's own being, there is no fault, since one perceives it as such. || 30 ||

Since consciousness (*vijñāna*) is a property that persists as long as the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) lasts, there is no fault in designating it by that term. Likewise, for example, individual cows (*khaṇḍādayaḥ*) are seen to be designated as "cow" by means of the word for the property of "cowness" (*gotva*), which persists as long as their own nature; the meaning is that this is because [the property] is a characteristic that defines their very nature. By the word "and" (*ca*), he combines the point that, just like cognition, since the self is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), there is no fault in designating it as "consciousness."

Regarding the argument that because there is an absence of cognition during deep sleep and other such states, cognition does not possess a property that is intrinsically connected to its own nature, he says:
"But it is like manhood and so forth; for this [cognition], which exists, there is a connection with manifestation. (3.2.31)

The word "tu" (but/however) is intended to remove the raised doubt. Since this knowledge exists even during states such as deep sleep and is manifested during states such as waking, its status as an attribute inherent to one's essential nature (*svarūpānubandhidharma*) is established—just like masculinity (*puṃstva*) and so forth. For example, although the specific faculty of masculinity exists in the state of childhood, it remains unmanifest; yet when it becomes manifest in youth, the man's possession of that quality does not become merely occasional. Indeed, the fact that the body is composed of the seven constituents (*saptadhātumayatva*) is an attribute inherent to its essential nature.

This body consists of seven constituents, possesses three impurities, has two origins, and is composed of four kinds of food; such is the description of the body's true nature. It has already been stated previously that the referent of "I" (the *ahamartha*) is manifest even during states such as deep sleep. That existing consciousness is observed to have objects within its range during waking and other states. Furthermore, these attributes of the Self, such as being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), have already been established. Therefore, the very nature of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is that of being a knower. And this Self is of atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*).

The statement "there is no consciousness after death" does not mean that there is an absence of knowledge for the liberated one; rather, it means that what was perceived during the state of transmigratory existence—namely, the perception of birth, death, and so forth, which is conditioned by conformity to these elements—is no longer present for the liberated one. This is because it is consistent with such scriptural passages as: "He who sees does not see death, nor disease, nor even suffering; the seer sees everything and attains everything in every way," and "Not remembering this body into which he was born, he rejoices, beholding with the mind these desires," and others.
Now, regarding the doctrine that the self consists of cognition (*jñānātmavāda*), he states the refutation of its being omnipresent:
"Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception, or else the restriction of one or the other.

(3.2) Otherwise—that is, under the position that it is omnipresent and under the position that it is mere cognition—both perception and non-perception would necessarily occur simultaneously; or else, there would be a restriction to one or the other.

Either *yama* or perception itself would have to be eternal, or else non-perception itself; what is meant by this is that, in the world, regarding the perception and non-perception of the self as they exist in the present, this soul consisting of knowledge would have to be the cause of everything, being either the cause of perception alone or of non-perception alone.

If both were the cause, it would follow that both [perception and non-perception] would occur at all times and in all places: if perception alone were the cause, there would never be non-perception of anything, anywhere, or at any time; whereas if non-perception alone were the cause, there would never be perception of anything, anywhere, or at any time. For us, however, because the self resides only within the body, the restriction is established that perception occurs only there and not elsewhere.

Even regarding the perception [of objects] as dependent upon the instruments (karaṇa), since all selves are omnipresent and thus always in contact with all instruments, and since there is no restrictive rule for the unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa) and so forth, the aforementioned defect remains the same. The section concerning the knower (jña-adhikaraṇa) is concluded.
The Lord is the creator, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless. || 33 ||

It has been stated that this self is the knower and that it is of atomic dimension; now, it is considered whether it is itself the agent, or whether, being itself a non-agent, it merely superimposes upon itself the agency of the insentient *guṇas*. What is the correct position here? That the self is indeed a non-agent. Why? Because the non-agency of the self and the agency of the *guṇas* alone are heard in the scriptures on the supreme self (*adhyātma-śāstra*).

For instance, in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, after denying all such things as birth, old age, and death—which are attributes of *prakṛti*—to the individual soul (*jīva*) through the passage beginning with "It is not born, nor does it die," its agency even in actions such as killing is denied: "If the slayer thinks he slays, or if the slain thinks he is slain, both of them do not understand; this one neither slays nor is slain. The meaning is that one who perceives the Self as the slayer does not know the Self. And thus, the Blessed Lord himself has stated that the non-agency of the individual soul is its true nature (*svarūpa*), whereas agency is [an attribute of the intellect].

Regarding the pride of being an agent, it is said: "All actions performed in every way by the qualities of *prakṛti*, one whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the doer. When the seer perceives no agent other than the qualities, *prakṛti* is said to be the cause in the state of being the agent of both the effect and the instrument. And also: "The *puruṣa* is said to be the cause in the state of being the experiencer of pleasures and pains. Therefore, the *puruṣa* possesses only the quality of being an experiencer (*bhoktṛtva*), whereas agency (*kartṛtva*) belongs solely to *prakṛti*.

This being the case, we reply: "The Self alone is the agent, because otherwise the scriptures would be purposeless. It is the Self alone that is the agent, not the qualities (guṇas). Why? Because otherwise the scriptures would be purposeless. For the scriptures—such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" and "One desiring liberation should meditate upon Brahman"—enjoin the very enjoyer of fruits such as heaven and liberation to be the agent; for if an insentient entity were the agent, no one else could be enjoined. Furthermore, it is called a "scripture" (*śāstra*) because it instructs (*śāsana*), and instruction consists of instigation to action.

Furthermore, the scripture functions as an initiator by means of generating knowledge, and the insentient *pradhāna* cannot be made to know. Therefore, the fruit of the scripture accrues to the agent. As for what was stated in the passage beginning with "If the slayer thinks... (*hantā cenmanyate*), whereby the non-agency of the self in the act of killing is heard in the Śruti—that is said because the self, being eternal, cannot be slain. And as for what is recorded in the Smṛti in the passage beginning with "Actions are performed by the qualities of nature" (*prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni*), which attributes agency to the *guṇas* alone—[that too is consistent].

The agency attributed to this [Self] regarding worldly activities is produced by its association with the qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; it is not inherent to its own nature. Through the discrimination between what is attained and what is not attained, it is stated that agency belongs to the *guṇas* alone. And so it is said in that very same place: "Attachment to the *guṇas* is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs. Likewise, having accepted the agency of the Self, it is further stated there: "In that case, he who perceives the isolated Self as the agent..."

"Because his intellect is unrefined, that dull-witted person does not see. [And as it is said: "The locus, likewise the agent, the various instruments, the diverse and distinct activities, and destiny as the fifth—since the self's agency is dependent upon these factors beginning with the locus and ending with destiny, he who considers the self alone to be the agent does not see; this is the meaning. (33)
Because of the teaching on abiding through grasping. || 34 ||

Having introduced the subject with the words, "Just as, O Great King," it is taught that the Self is the agent in both the grasping and the abandoning of the vital breaths (prāṇas), in the passage: "In this very way, having taken hold of these vital breaths, he moves about at will within his own body. || 34 ||
And because of the designation [of the agent] in the action; for if it were not so, there would be a reversal of the grammatical indication. || 35 ||

And because of the designation of agency in both worldly and Vedic activities in the passage, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice and also performs the ritual acts," it is the agent. If it is argued that the word "consciousness" (vijñāna) does not designate the Self, but rather the internal organ—the intellect (buddhi)—then, if that were the case, there would be a reversal of the grammatical indication; since the intellect is an instrument, the instrumental case would have been used as "by consciousness" (vijñānena). || 35 ||
There is no fixed rule, just as in the case of perception. || 36 ||

The defect in the soul being a non-agent is stated as follows: Just as the lack of restriction regarding perception was explained by the argument that if the soul were all-pervading, there would be the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception, so too, if the soul were a non-agent and Prakṛti were the agent, then because Prakṛti is common to all souls, all actions would result in experience for everyone, or else they would not result in experience for anyone at all. Furthermore, since the all-pervasiveness of the souls is admitted, their proximity [to Prakṛti] is likewise undifferentiated for all; for this very reason, no restriction of the internal organs and so forth is possible, upon which the established order of things depends. || 36 ||
Because of the reversal of capacity. || 37 ||

If the intellect (*buddhi*) were the agent, then since it is impossible for one who is the agent to be something other than the experiencer, the power of experiencing would also belong to that very [intellect] alone; thus, the Self’s power of experiencing would be lost. Furthermore, since experiencing would then result from the intellect alone, there would be a lack of evidence for the existence of the Self. For their own accepted position is that "the Person exists because there must be an experiencer. (37)
And because of the absence of meditative concentration (samādhi). || 38 ||

If the intellect were the agent, then it would also be the agent in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that serves as the means to liberation. Yet, that absorption consists in the realization "I am other than nature" (*prakṛti*); and nature is not capable of concentrating itself on the thought "I am other than nature. For this reason as well, the Self alone is the agent. (38)
Now, if the agency of the Self were admitted, one might object that its state of being an agent would never cease; to this he says:
"And as a carpenter [acts] in both ways" (3.2.40).

Even though the Self is endowed with instruments such as speech and the rest, it acts only when it desires and does not act when it does not desire; just as a carpenter, although possessing tools such as an axe, acts or refrains from acting according to his own will. However, if the insentient intellect were the agent, then because there would be no cause for regulating its desire for experience and so forth, it would be an agent at all times. || 39 || The section on the Agent (Kartṛ-adhikaraṇa) is concluded.
But [the self] is from another, because of the act of cutting. || 40 ||

Is this agency of the individual soul (jīva) independent, or is it dependent upon the Supreme Self? What is the prima facie view? It is independent. For if it were dependent upon the Supreme Self, the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would result in being purposeless. Indeed, only one who is capable of initiating activity or cessation by means of his own intellect becomes a fit subject for injunction (niyojya). Therefore, since its agency is independent, [the opponent] having thus argued, it is replied: "But from the Supreme, because of scripture" (Brahma Sūtra 2.3.41). The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.

This agency of the individual soul (jīva) arises solely from the Supreme Self (paramātman); why? Because of the scriptural text: "He who has entered within, the ruler of people, the Self of all; He who, dwelling in the self, controls the self from within, whom the self does not know, whose body the self is, who controls the self from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal."

Smṛti also states: "I am seated within the heart of all; from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss"; and "The Lord, O Arjuna, dwells in the heart-region of all beings, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion (māyā), as if they were mounted on a machine. || 40 ||
But was it not said that, in this case, the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would result in futility? To that, he says:
"But [the Lord], having regard for the effort performed, [takes into account] what is enjoined and what is prohibited, because of their non-futility and so forth. (4.1.41)

In all actions, the Inner Controller, the Supreme Self, impels a person’s effort or exertion by granting His permission; the meaning is that without the permission of the Supreme Self, this person's activity would not be possible. Why is this so? Because of the non-futility of prescribed and prohibited injunctions, and so forth—the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes favor (anugraha), restraint (nigraha), and the like. Just as, when wealth is common to two people, the transfer of ownership to another cannot occur without the consent of one party, yet even though the other's consent is required, the fruit belongs to the one who actually performed the act because it was done by him alone.

It has been established in the *Sāṅkhyasamavāyanirūpaṇa* that even for one who has the power to turn others away from evil deeds, the state of being a mere consenter does not entail cruelty. Now, an objection is raised: if this were so, then the following scriptural passage would be untenable: "For he alone makes him perform good deeds whom He intends to lead upward from these worlds; he alone makes him perform evil deeds whom He intends to lead downward. This suggests that by His own will—through the desire to lead upward or the desire to lead downward—He Himself causes both good and evil actions to be performed.

It is said: this is not common to all. However, the Blessed One, favoring one who acts while established in extreme conformity with the Supreme Person, personally generates an inclination toward those most auspicious actions which are the means for attaining Him. And toward one who acts while established in extreme opposition, He, restraining him, generates an inclination toward those actions that are contrary to attaining Him and lead to downward rebirths.

As the Blessed One himself has said, beginning with: "I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds. Thinking thus, the wise, endowed with devotion, worship me," and continuing: "To those who are ever-devoted and worship me with full conviction, I grant the yoga of discernment by which they come to me."

"Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge" (Gītā 10.11); likewise, after stating, "To them, this world is unreal, without foundation, and without a Lord," and so forth, ending with, "Hating Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, these envious ones," it is said: "Those cruel haters, the lowest of men, I incessantly hurl into the cycles of worldly existence, into the wombs of the asuras alone, which are inauspicious" (Gītā 16.19). Thus ends the section on dependence on another (*parāyattādhikaraṇa*).
The Self is not [the individual soul], because of the designation of difference, and also because some record that it possesses the nature of a servant, a fisherman, and so forth. (Sūtra 1.1.42)

It has been stated that the agency of the individual soul (jīva) is dependent upon the Supreme Person. Now, a doubt arises: is this jīva absolutely different from the Supreme? Or is it the Supreme Brahman itself under delusion? Or is it Brahman itself as delimited by limiting adjuncts (upādhi)? Or is it a part of Brahman? This doubt arises because of conflicting scriptural statements. But is it not the case that this matter has already been settled in the sūtras "Non-difference from That [is established] on account of such terms as 'origin' and so forth" and "But there is more [to the soul], on account of the declaration of difference"?

True. That very point, having been raised through the contradiction of scriptural texts concerning multiplicity and unity, is now determined in its specific nature by establishing that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman. For as long as the fact that the individual soul is a part of Brahman is not established, the non-difference of the soul from Brahman and the superiority of Brahman over it cannot be firmly established. What, then, is the prima facie view? That they are absolutely distinct; why? Because of the declaration of difference in such passages as, "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord," and so forth.

The scriptural texts asserting the non-difference between the Knower and the ignorant are figurative, as they convey contradictory meanings—like the statement "one should sprinkle with fire. If the individual soul (*jīva*) were a part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman, being a single portion of it, then the defects residing in that [soul] would accrue to Brahman. Nor can the soul be established as a part by being a fragment of Brahman, because Brahman is incapable of being fragmented, and because it would entail the defects previously mentioned. Therefore, it is difficult to establish that something entirely distinct could be a part of it. Alternatively, one might claim that the soul is simply Brahman itself under delusion; but why? Because of such texts as "That thou art" and "This Self is Brahman."

This is because of such teachings regarding the identity of Brahman and the Self. As for those [scriptural passages] that speak of plurality, since they merely restate matters established by perception and other means of knowledge, they are shown—just like perception and the rest—to be contained within ignorance (*avidyā*), being sublated by those scriptural texts whose primary intent is the teaching of non-duality, which cannot be explained otherwise. Alternatively, the individual soul (*jīva*) is Brahman itself as delimited by beginningless adjuncts (*upādhi*). Why? Precisely because of that same teaching regarding the identity of Brahman and the Self. Nor can it be said that this adjunct is imagined through delusion, because of the systematic distinction between bondage, liberation, and so forth.

"Because it is not logically possible"—this being the position reached, it is replied: [The individual soul] is a part of Brahman. Why? Because of the designation of manifoldness, and because of the designation of oneness; for both kinds of designation are observed. To begin with, the designation of manifoldness is seen through such attributes as creator and created, ruler and ruled, omniscient and ignorant, independent and dependent, pure and impure, the mine of auspicious qualities and the opposite thereof, the master and the subordinate, and so forth.

Furthermore, non-difference is designated by such statements as "That thou art" and "This Self is Brahman. Moreover, some recite that Brahman possesses the nature of fishermen, slaves, and so forth: "Brahman is the fishermen, Brahman is the slaves, Brahman these gamblers"—thus the followers of the Atharva Veda recite that Brahman even has the nature of fishermen, slaves, and the like. Therefore, the meaning is that non-difference is designated because [Brahman] pervades all living beings. Thus, in order to establish the primacy of both designations, one must accept that this individual soul (jīva) is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman.

Nor can the designations of difference be established otherwise (anyathāsiddha) by virtue of their objects being well-known through perception and other means; for [the distinctions consist in] the individual soul’s being created by Brahman, being governed by Him, having Him as its body, being subordinate to Him, having Him as its support, being protected by Him, being withdrawn by Him, being His worshiper, and being the recipient of the human goals (puruṣārtha)—namely dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—which are obtainable through His grace. Furthermore, the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman caused by these factors is not established otherwise because it is not within the scope of perception and other such means. Therefore, [there is no contradiction] with the scriptures declaring the creation of the world and so forth.

[The Upanishads] are intent upon teaching that [the Self] is false by way of restating distinctions already established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor is it the case that [the Upanishads] fail to reveal the non-difference of the Self from Brahman—which is of the nature of pure consciousness, partless and of a single essence—nor do they fail to teach the creation of ether and the rest preceded by the volition "to become many," the entry [of Brahman] into that [creation] in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), the differentiation of diverse names and forms, the experience of infinite objects resulting from that [differentiation], the sharing in pleasure and pain caused by such experience, and the state of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) by remaining there as the enjoyer and governing it. [This applies to the Upanishads] regarding that which has become the individual soul...

It is taught that one should not wander [in error] while performing the contemplation of one's own identity with the causal Brahman, seeking liberation from saṃsāra, and composing the scriptures that teach this; for if that were the case, it would result in nothing but the ravings of a madman. Furthermore, the view that the individual soul (jīva) is Brahman delimited by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is not tenable, precisely because it contradicts the previously mentioned designations such as being "governed" (niyāmyatva) and so forth. Indeed, one cannot establish a relationship of ruler and ruled between a single person like Devadatta merely through the difference of limiting adjuncts such as his house and so on. Therefore, to justify both sets of scriptural designations, it must be accepted that this individual soul is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman. 42.
On account of the wording of the mantra. || 43 ||

And from the wording of the mantra, "A foot of him are all beings; three feet of him are the immortal in heaven," the individual soul (jīva) is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman. For the word "foot" (pāda) denotes a part. In the mantra, the plural form "all beings" (viśvābhūtāni) is used because of the multiplicity of individual souls, whereas in the Sūtra, the singular form "part" (aṃśaḥ) refers to the genus.

In the passage "The Self is not [one] because of scripture," the singular number is intended to denote a genus (*jāti*), for scripture—such as "Of the eternal, He is the conscious one among the conscious; He is the One who ordains the desires of many"—declares the plurality and eternality of the selves in their distinction from the Lord. Thus, while the plurality of eternal selves is established by authoritative means, and all are of a single form insofar as they consist of the nature of consciousness, the aspect that differentiates them would be perceived by those capable of knowing the true nature of the self. Furthermore, immediately following this, in the sūtra "And because there is no continuity, there is no confusion," he will state the plurality of the selves. (43)
It is also recorded in the Smṛti.

"In the world of living beings, My very own eternal portion has become the individual soul (jīva)"—thus the individual soul's state of being a portion of the Supreme Person (puruṣottama) is recorded in the Smṛti; therefore, this [soul] is a portion. 44.

Even if the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part [of Brahman], one might suspect that because it is a single portion of Brahman, the defects residing in the soul belong to Brahman itself; anticipating this objection, he says:
"But the Supreme is not so, like light and other [examples]. (45)

The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the objection. The individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), just like light and so forth. For example, just as the luminous form of fire, the sun, and other radiant bodies is a part, or just as the specific qualities such as "cowness" are parts of entities qualified by those qualities—such as cows, horses, white things, or black things—or just as the body is a part of embodied beings such as gods or humans, so it is here. Indeed, being a part consists in being a single portion of one entity; for the qualifier of a single qualified entity is itself a part.

And so, discerning people designate a qualified entity by saying, "this is the qualifying part" and "this is the qualified part. Even though the qualifier and the qualified are related as part and whole, a difference in their intrinsic natures (svabhāva) is observed. In this way, it is logically consistent that the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified, part and whole, while possessing a distinction in their essential natures. This is expressed as: "The Supreme is not thus," meaning that the Supreme is not of the same nature as the individual soul.

For just as light is not something other than its radiance, so too the Supreme, who is the possessor of parts, is a distinct entity from the individual soul (jīva), which stands in the place of that radiance; this is the meaning. Thus, designations of difference proceed by relying on the distinction in essential nature produced by the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the individual soul and the Supreme. However, designations of non-difference refer to qualifiers that cannot exist independently [of the qualified].

They do not hold as primary [meanings] by relying on their being coextensive with everything. In passages such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) and "This self is Brahman" (ayam ātmā brahma), the words *tvam*, *ayam*, and *ātmā*—just like the words *tat* and *brahma*—denote Brahman as having the individual soul as its body; thus, they express a single referent. This point has already been explained in detail previously. || 45 ||
And they remember it. || 46 ||

In this way, Parāśara and others record the relationship of part and whole between the world and Brahman through the forms of light and its radiance, power and its possessor, and body and soul, as follows: "Just as the moonlight of a fire situated in one place spreads far and wide, so too is this entire world the power of the Supreme Brahman. O twice-born one, whatever being is created by which [cause], in the production of that which is created, all of that is indeed the body of Hari. And so forth.

Because of the word "also," it is said that the Śrutis as well—such as "He whose self is the body"—declare the relationship of part and whole through the state of being the body and the self. || 46 ||

Thus, since being a portion of Brahman, being impelled by Brahman, and being a knower are common to all, one might raise the objection: how is it that in the scriptures there is the permission for some to study the Vedas and perform their prescribed duties while others are prohibited from doing so; and how is it that there is the permission for some to see or touch [the scriptures] while others are prohibited? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Permission and prohibition [apply] due to the non-connection with a body, as in the case of light and so forth. (2.3.47) This means that just as light, air, and the like are not inherently pure or impure, but become so only through contact with specific objects, so too the soul is neither inherently subject to injunctions nor prohibitions. These apply only when the soul is associated with a body. Therefore, the distinctions of permission and prohibition in the scriptures are established based on the particular bodies with which the souls are connected. Thus, there is no contradiction.

Even though all beings are of a uniform nature by virtue of being portions of Brahman (*brahmāṃśa*) and possessing knowledge (*jñatva*), the rules of what is permitted and what is to be avoided are justified based on their connection with bodies that are pure or impure—such as those of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and so forth. This is just as, although fire is of a uniform nature as fire, it is fetched from the house of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) but avoided when coming from a cremation ground; and just as food and the like are permitted for a learned scholar but avoided when coming from one accused of a crime. || 47 ||
And there is no confusion because of the non-continuity [of the mental stream]. || 48 ||

Even though there is oneness [of the self] due to being a portion (*aṃśa*) of Brahman and so forth, because individual souls (*jīva*) are mutually distinct and, by virtue of their atomic nature (*aṇutva*), are separate in each body, a confusion of experiences (*bhogavyatikara*) is impossible. With the intention that in the theory of the soul as an illusory Brahman (*bhrāntabrahmajīvavāda*) and in the theory of the soul as the conditioned Brahman (*upahitabrahmajīvavāda*), all defects such as the confusion of experiences between the Supreme Self and the individual souls, or among the individual souls themselves, would exist, the absence of confusion of experiences in his own position has been stated. || 48 ||

[Objection: But even in the doctrine of the illusory individual soul (*bhrāntajīva*), the determination of experiences and so forth is possible due to the distinctions among limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) created by ignorance (*avidyā*); therefore, [the Sūtrakāra] says: "And it is merely a reflection" (Sūtra 2.3.50).

The *ābhāsa* (appearance) alone is the cause for establishing the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) preceded by the concealment of one's own nature, for that which consists solely of the light of non-dual, uniform essence. It has already been established that for that whose sole nature is light, the concealment of light is indeed the destruction of light. Alternatively, there is the reading *ābhāsā eva*; in that case, the appearances (*ābhāsāḥ*) are the causes. Furthermore, by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), there is no contradiction with such scriptural passages as: "Thinking itself and the Impeller to be separate... the two, the Knower and the Unknower; of these, the other eats the sweet fruit."

For, since it is admitted that the essential nature of the Self as conditioned by all its adjuncts is one, the confusion of experiences remains exactly as it was when there are distinctions among adjuncts imagined through ignorance. (49)

Anticipating the objection that, in the doctrine of the individual soul (*jīva*) as Brahman conditioned by ultimate adjuncts (*upādhi*), the systematic distinction [between souls] will be established by the power of beginningless unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) which serves as the cause for the diversity of those adjuncts, he says:
"Because there is no restriction regarding the unseen. (Sūtra 50)

Even for the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), which serves as the cause for the succession of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there would be a total lack of regulation because it lacks a restrictive cause by virtue of its having the very nature of Brahman as its substratum; for it is impossible for the nature of Brahman to be partitioned by limiting adjuncts or unseen forces through their mere connection with it. (50)
And the same applies to intentional meanings (*abhisandhi*) and so forth. (51)
Even in the case of intentions and so forth that have become unperceived causes, there is indeed no certainty for the very reason already stated. 51.

He raises a doubt regarding the immediately preceding sūtra with the words "pāramārthika" (ultimate). The meaning of the word "api" (also) is that he states this [objection] as well, having raised it as a doubt: "If it is argued that [the universal] is not perceived because of the difference in location, we say no, because it is included within [the individual]. (52)

If it is argued that although the nature of Brahman is one and indivisible, and thus incapable of being cut, yet the regulation of experience (bhoga-vyavasthā) is indeed possible because of the distinction between different spatial locations of Brahman associated with various limiting adjuncts (upādhi), this is not so; for since the adjuncts move here and there, all spatial locations would be included within all adjuncts, and the confusion (vyatikara) remains exactly as it was.

Even if a relationship [between the soul and Brahman] were established through a distinction of parts (*pradeśabheda*), since every [soul] would be a part of Brahman, the suffering associated with each respective part would belong to Brahman alone. Previously, in the two sūtras "Otherwise, there would result either constant perception or non-perception, or else the restriction of one or the other" and "As in the case of perception, there would be no restriction," the fault was stated for those outside the Veda who maintain that the individual soul (*jīva*) is omnipresent.

Here, however, by means of the sūtras beginning with "And it is merely a reflection" (*ābhāsa eva ca*), the fault is stated for those who rely on the Veda and maintain the unity of the Self (*ātmaikatva*). || 52 || Thus ends the section on Parts (*aṃśādhikaraṇa*). || 7 ||
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
Likewise, the vital breaths. || 1 ||

Having stated that the entire universe beginning with ether (*viyat*)—being distinct from Brahman—is an effect produced [from Him], it was refuted that the individual soul (*jīva*), though an effect, undergoes production characterized by a change in its essential nature (*svarūpa*); and in connection with that, the true nature of the soul was clarified. Now, the manner of the origin and so forth of the senses, which are the instruments of the soul, as well as of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is being clarified. In this regard, it is considered whether the senses are effects like the soul, or like ether and the other elements.

What is logical? The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are likewise. Here, "vital breaths" refers to the sense organs (*indriyāṇi*). Just as the living self (*jīva*) is not produced, so too the sense organs are not produced. Why? Because of scripture (*śruti*). Just as the non-origination of the living self is understood from scripture, so too the non-origination of the vital breaths is understood from scripture alone. Thus, by the phrase "the vital breaths are likewise," the same means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is extended [to this case].

What, then, is the scriptural authority for this? [The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa states: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent. Regarding that, they ask: 'What existed then? The sages (ṛṣis), they say, existed then. Regarding that, they ask: 'Who were those sages? The vital breaths (prāṇas), they say, were the sages. Thus, the existence of the sense organs prior to the origin of the world is heard in scripture. By the use of the plural in the word *prāṇa*, it is determined that these are indeed the sense organs.

Nor can this scriptural passage be interpreted as referring to long-term persistence—like the statements, "Vāyu and the intermediate space, these are immortal," or "This deity that is Vāyu never sets"—because of the hearing [in scripture] of its existence even at the time of the dissolution of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), in the text, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent. As for those passages speaking of origination, they are to be understood in the same way as those speaking of the origination of the individual soul (jīva). This being the position reached, it is replied: The vital breaths (prāṇas) originate just like ether and the other elements. Why? Because [of the text]: "Being alone, my dear, this was in the beginning... [and so on].

Because of the determination of oneness prior to creation in such passages as, "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," and because of the scriptural hearing of the origin of the senses in, "From this [Self] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses," it is impossible for them to exist in a prior state.

Furthermore, theories regarding the origination of the sense organs cannot be assimilated [into the doctrine of non-origination] in the same way as the theory of the origination of the Self, because we do not find scriptural texts that negate the origination of the senses, nor do we find texts asserting their eternity as we do for the Self. Even in such passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," it is the Supreme Self alone that is indicated by the word *prāṇa*, since the word *prāṇa* is well-known to refer to the Supreme Self as well, in accordance with the text: "All these beings indeed enter into *prāṇa* alone, and from *prāṇa* they emerge."
And the word "ṛṣi," as in the phrase "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the ṛṣis," is applicable only to that omniscient one, and not to the insentient sense organs. || 1 ||

If it be asked how the scriptural statement in the plural, "The vital breaths (prāṇās) are the seers (ṛṣayas)," is to be understood, he says in response: "Because a secondary sense is impossible, and because of the prior mention of that [the one]. (Sūtra 1.1.6)

The scriptural mention of the plural number is figurative, because multiple entities cannot exist [prior to creation], precisely because scripture declares that the Supreme Self alone existed prior to creation. || 2 ||
Because speech is preceded by that [mind]. (3)

For this reason as well, the word *prāṇa* denotes the Supreme Self: because speech—the naming function whose object is distinct from the Supreme Self—is preceded by the creation of ether and the other elements, which are the objects of speech. [This is known from the text: "In the beginning, this was indeed unevolved; it was then evolved through name and form. At that time, since there was an absence of those things that partake of name and form, and because of the absence of the effects of the senses such as speech, the meaning is that they did not exist. || 3 || Thus ends the section on the origin of the vital breaths (*prāṇotpattyadhikaraṇa*).
And because it is specified as being characterized by seven courses.

It is now considered whether these sense organs are only seven or whether they are eleven. A doubt arises due to conflicting scriptural statements. What is the prima facie view? That there are seven. Why?

And because their movement is specified. Movement, in the form of wandering through the worlds together with the living self that is being born and being sustained, is heard of as belonging to only seven: "These seven worlds exist, in which move the breaths (*prāṇa*s) dwelling in the cave, deposited seven by seven. This plurality is intended with reference to the distinction between individual persons. Furthermore, those moving breaths are specified by their own nature: "When the five [sensory] cognitions, along with the mind, come to rest..."

"And when the intellect does not stir, they call that the supreme goal. Departing from the body to go toward liberation is the supreme goal. Thus, because it is heard that only seven [organs] move along with the individual soul (jīva) during birth and death, and because they are specifically qualified as "the organs of knowledge" in the state of yoga, it is understood that the individual soul has exactly seven instruments: hearing, touch, sight, taste, smell, intellect, and mind.

However, as for those other senses which, by virtue of being the perceivers of objects, are understood in scriptural passages teaching the vital breaths—such as "the eight graspers," "there are seven vital breaths in the head and two downward ones," and so forth—as numbering up to fourteen, namely the senses called speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, ego, and mind; since there is no mention of their departure along with the individual soul (jīva), they are designated as "vital breaths" only figuratively, based solely on their providing a small degree of assistance to the soul. || 4 ||
This being the position reached, we reply: "But because hands and so forth exist when that [body] is present, it is not thus. (1.1.20)

There are not only seven faculties, but rather eleven, because even the hands and so forth serve as instruments for the soul while it resides in the body and because they perform distinct functions. For a difference in function is observed in the case of the hands and so forth, just as in the case of the ears and other [faculties], such as grasping and the like; therefore, these too certainly exist. Thus, the meaning is that one should not think that the hands and so forth do not exist.

The mind itself is designated by the terms *buddhi*, *ahaṅkāra*, and *citta* according to its different functions of determination (*adhyavasāya*), self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and reflection (*cintā*); thus, there are eleven organs. Therefore, in the passage, "These ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, with the self (*ātman*) as the eleventh," the word *ātman* refers to the mind. Furthermore, the number of organs established by such scriptural and traditional authorities as, "The organs are ten and one, and five are the objects of the organs," and "They say the organs are taijasa; the ten gods are vaikārika, and the mind is the eleventh here," remains constant.

The assertions of a higher number refer to the distinctions among the various modes of mental activity; whereas the designations of a lower number are employed in specific instances to indicate particular bodily functions, such as movement, which are intended to be expressed. || 5 || The section concerning the seven courses of rebirth is concluded.
And they are atomic.

Since there is a scriptural statement regarding their infinity—“All these are indeed equal, all are infinite”—it might be concluded that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) possess omnipresence (*vibhutva*). To this, it is replied: because of the scriptural statements concerning departure and so forth, such as “When the [chief] breath departs, all the breaths depart after it,” their limited size is established; and since they are not perceived by bystanders during such departures and other states, the breaths are atomic (*aṇu*). As for the scriptural mention of infinity, such as “Now, he who meditates upon these as infinite,” that is intended to refer to the great abundance of their functions (*kārya*), being an attribute of the specific breaths to be meditated upon. (Sūtra 6)
And he is the most excellent. || 7 ||

Regarding the doubt that the *mukhya-prāṇa*—which was determined to be the most excellent as the cause of the body's maintenance in the dialogue with the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*)—is not produced, because the statement "That breathed without wind by its own power, being one" (*ānīd avātaṃ svadhayā tadekam*) indicates the existence of the act of breathing (its effect) at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), and because the mention of its birth in the passage "From this [Self] is born... (*etasmāj jāyate...*) can be explained as referring to the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) rather than the *prāṇa* itself; [the Sūtra replies: this is not so, because it would contradict the determination of oneness prior to creation and other such statements, as seen in the text: "From this, the *prāṇa* is born" (*etasmāj jāyate prāṇaḥ*).
Nor [are] air and its function [distinct from the self], because they are taught separately. 8.

Regarding this preeminent *prāṇa*, there arises a doubt: is it merely the air (*vāyu*) as the second of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), or its activity in the form of vibration, or rather, is it air itself having attained a certain specific state? On this point, the initial position is that it is simply air, because of the designation, "That which is *prāṇa* is air. Alternatively, since the status of being *prāṇa* is not well-known in relation to mere air, and since the word *prāṇa* is well-known in relation to the activity of air such as inhalation and exhalation, the initial position is that it is merely that activity. To this, it is replied: it is neither mere air nor its activity.

Why? Because of its separate instruction: "From this [Self] are born breath (*prāṇa*), mind, and all the senses, as well as fire, wind... Since it is thus taught separately from those very elements, *prāṇa* is not the activity of wind either. For the activity of fire and the other elements is never taught as a separate substance alongside them. However, the statement "that which is the wind of *prāṇa*" is intended to make known that *prāṇa* is simply wind that has attained a different state, and not a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*) like fire and the others.
Since the vital breath (prāṇa) vibrates even during inhalation and exhalation, the conventional usage of the word "prāṇa" applies to a substance that possesses action, not to action alone.
Is this vital breath (prāṇa), being a modification of air, a separate element like fire? No; [the Sūtra] says:
"But it is like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them and for other reasons. (2.4.9)

This [prāṇa] is not a specific element (bhūtaviśeṣa), but rather a specific instrument of the living being (jīvopakaraṇaviśeṣa), like the eye and other senses. That it is an instrument is understood from its being taught alongside the specific sense organs, as in the passages concerning the colloquy of the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃvāda) and so forth. For in those instances, this prāṇa is taught together with the eyes and other senses; indeed, it is logical that it should be taught alongside them only if it belongs to the same class as they do.

Among the organs comprised by the term "prāṇa," this specific designation is understood through the word "ādi" (and so forth), because of the specific mention in such passages as, "Now, indeed, that which is this chief prāṇa," and "That which is this middle prāṇa," and so on. || 9 ||

If it is argued that, since this [prāṇa] is also an instrument like the eye and other organs, it must likewise possess a specific action consisting of a service rendered to the individual soul (jīva), yet such [action] is not perceived; therefore, this [prāṇa] cannot be an instrument like the eye and so forth—regarding that, he says: "And because it is not an instrument, there is no fault; for thus scripture shows. (10)

The objection raised—that because it is not an instrument (*akaraṇatvāt*), it cannot be an instrument (*karaṇam*), and because it is not an action (*akriyatvāt*), it lacks the specific activity that constitutes a service to the individual soul (*jīva*)—is invalid. For the Śruti demonstrates that it does indeed perform specific services in the form of actions such as sustaining the body and the senses. Having stated, "That one upon whose departure this body appears most wretched is the preeminent one," the text shows that even when speech and the other organs depart, the body and the senses remain intact; yet, it describes the loosening of the body and the senses upon the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Thus, the objection does not hold.

Therefore, this vital breath (prāṇa), existing in five forms as prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna, assists the individual soul (jīva) by sustaining the body and the senses; thus, it possesses the status of an instrument (karaṇa), like the eye and other organs. || 10 ||
[Objection: "In that case, due to the difference in names and the difference in functions, prāṇa, apāna, and so forth would be distinct principles (tattvāntara). To this he replies:
'The fivefold function is designated like the mind. (Sūtra 11)

Just as, despite the difference in the functions such as desire and the resulting difference in their effects, desire and the rest are not separate principles from the mind—because of the scriptural statement: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all this is indeed the mind"—so too, because of the statement: "Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—all this is indeed prāṇa," it is understood that apāna and the others are merely specific functions of prāṇa itself, and not separate principles. || 11 ||
The section concerning the functions of air is completed. 4.
And it is atomic.

And this [self] is atomic, as before, because of scriptural statements regarding its departure and so forth, such as: "When it departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after it. However, there is a further doubt based on such passages as: "It is equal to these three worlds, equal to this entire universe"; "Everything is established in the vital breath"; and "All this is indeed enveloped by the vital breath."

Is the soul minute (*aṇu*) or all-pervading (*sarvagata*)? Or is it minute? Regarding the statement "equal to these worlds," does this designation of infinity imply omnipresence (*vibhutva*), or not? When the scriptural mention of its departure (*utkrānti*) does not lead one to understand that the designation of infinity is figurative (*gauṇa*), then, because that designation of infinity implies omnipresence, the soul is all-pervading. When, however, it leads one to understand its figurative nature, then, because the statement of infinity is figurative, the soul is minute. Passages such as "equal to these three" are not recited in a fixed sequence in a single place.

Regarding the phrase "and [the vital breath] is the best," although the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument arises from the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) in the Sūtra, the refutation is similar to that of the preceding section, because of the hearing of such statements as "due to its singleness, its being undivided," and so forth; thus it is said to be of "great dimension. However, the refutation is this: since its unboundedness is established by the hearing of passages such as "it departs," and since the existence of the entire class of living beings depends upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the doctrine of its omnipresence (*vaibhava*) is logically consistent. Thus ends the section on the minuteness of the best (the vital breath). 5.12.12.
But the presiding over fire and the other elements belongs to Him, because of the scriptural teaching; [He acts] through the possessor of breath, according to the sacred word. 13.

The origin, extent, and measure of the principal vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and the Brahmins have been stated; furthermore, their presiding by deities such as Agni and others was previously established in connection with the sūtra: "But there is designation according to the presiding deities, because of distinction and following" (*abhimānivyapadeśastu viśeṣānugatibhyām*). Moreover, it is well-known in the world that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the presiding controller over these means of its own experience, as it is said: "In this very way, having taken hold of these vital breaths, he moves about in his own body according to his desire."

This is also established by such praises as these. Now, regarding the doubt as to whether this presiding over the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by the individual soul (*jīva*) and the deities such as Fire is dependent on itself or dependent on the Supreme Self—since there appears to be independence, it is initially concluded that it is self-dependent. To this, it is replied: "The presiding of Light and the others. The presiding over the vital breath by the deities such as Fire, along with the individual soul who possesses the vital breath, occurs through the meditation upon them; that is, it comes about through the meditation upon that Supreme Self.

"Āmanana" means thinking with direct orientation; the meaning is that it occurs solely from the volition of the Supreme Self. Why is this so? Because of the scriptural authority [śabda] stating that the sense organs, along with their presiding deities, and the individual self (jīvātman) are dependent upon the contemplation of the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa) for their respective functions.

As in the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa and other texts: "He who, dwelling in fire, is within fire, whom fire does not know, whose body is fire, who controls fire from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal"; and "He who dwells in wind," "He who dwells in the sun," "He who dwells in the self," "He who dwells in the eye," and so forth; and as it is said: "From fear of Him the wind blows, from fear the sun rises; from fear of Him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run on."
Likewise: "By the command of this Imperishable, indeed, heaven and earth, as well as the sun and the moon, remain held apart," and so forth. || 13 ||
And because that [ether] is eternal. || 14 ||

Since the state of being presided over by the Supreme Self is eternal for all [beings], and since it is necessarily bound to their very nature (*svarūpa*), their being presided over by Him must inevitably follow from His will alone. By such passages as, "Having created that, He entered into it; having entered it, He became the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*)," the entry of the Supreme Person into all conscious and unconscious entities as their ruler is heard to be inseparable from His own nature; and it is likewise remembered in the Smṛti: "Pervading this entire world, I stand with but one part."
14. The section concerning the presiding deities of light and so forth is completed. 6.
These are the faculties (indriya), because they are designated as such in relation to that [the mind], except for the preeminent one. || 15 ||

Are all those designated by the word *prāṇa* sense-organs (*indriya*), or only those distinct from the chief *prāṇa*? Since they are denoted by the word *prāṇa* and possess the nature of instruments (*karaṇa*), the prima facie view is that all of them are indeed sense-organs. To this, it is replied: only those *prāṇas* distinct from the chief one are sense-organs. Why? Because the designation of "sense-organ" is applied specifically to those *prāṇas* other than the chief one. In such passages as, "The sense-organs are eleven, and the objects of the sense-organs are five," the term "sense-organ" is applied exclusively to the eyes and the rest. || 15 ||
On account of the scriptural statement of difference and because of their distinct characteristics. || 16 ||

From such passages as, "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind, and all the sense organs," because the vital breath is heard of separately from the sense organs, it is understood that the sense organs are indeed distinct from the vital breath.
