Although the mind is also heard of separately, its inclusion among the other sense organs is stated elsewhere in such passages as, "The sense organs, with the mind as the sixth.

Furthermore, a distinction between the preeminent vital breath and the eyes and other organs is perceived: for during deep sleep, the activity of the vital breath is observed, whereas the activity of the eyes and other organs is not observed.

The function of the eyes, speech, and so forth, together with the mind, is to serve as the instruments for knowledge and action; whereas the function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the sustenance of the body and the senses. Indeed, because their sustenance is dependent upon the *prāṇa*, the term *prāṇa* is applied to the senses themselves. Thus says the Śruti: "They all assumed his very form; therefore they are designated by that name. "Assumed his form" means they assumed the body, or rather, they became subject to its activity, being dependent upon it. Thus ends the section on the Senses (*indriyādhikaraṇa*).
But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the tripartition, because of the scriptural teaching. (Sūtra 17)

It has been stated previously that the collective creation of the elements, the sense organs, and so forth, as well as the agency of individual souls, proceeds from the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, it was recently recalled for the sake of confirmation that the souls' presiding over their own respective sense organs is dependent upon that Supreme Being.

Now, this individual creation of the manifold world (*prapañca-vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*), which consists in the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-vyākaraṇa*), is considered here: Is it the work of Hiraṇyagarbha alone, who is the collective soul (*samaṣṭi-jīva*)? Or is it the work of the Supreme Brahman, who has Hiraṇyagarbha as His body—just as He is the agent of the prior creation of fire and so forth, having fire and the rest as His body? What is the correct view? That it belongs to the collective soul. Why? Because of the scriptural statement regarding the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*): "Entering with this living self (*jīva*), let me differentiate names and forms. For the Supreme Deity does not [act] by Himself...

He reflected, "By means of *rūpa*, I shall unfold name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)," yet this was not by means of his own part, the individual soul (*jīva*), as indicated by the statement, "by this living self. Now, one might object that in such a case, the use of the first person in "I shall unfold" would be figurative, and the verb "to enter" would be secondary (metaphorical), just as in the expression, "Having entered the enemy's army by means of a spy, he surveyed it," where the agent is distinct from the action.

It is not so; for in that case [the example of the king and the spy], there is a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇikatva*) due to the difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) between the two. Here, however, since the individual soul (*jīva*) is also an integral part (*svāṃśa*) [of Brahman] and thus identical in essential nature, its entry and manifestation (*vyākaraṇa*) are in fact those of the Self alone; therefore, there is no occasion for a figurative sense. Nor is this instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) to be understood as denoting association (*sahayoga-lakṣaṇā*), because when a case-ending expressing a grammatical relation (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is possible, it is improper to resort to a case-ending based on a mere accompanying word (*upapada-vibhakti*). Furthermore, the instrumental case cannot denote the instrument (*karaṇa*), because the soul lacks the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) in the entry and manifestation whose agent is Brahman.

Furthermore, the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) does not terminate merely in its entry [into the egg]; nor can it be said that the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) belongs to Brahman alone, because the use of the suffix denoting agency (*kartṛtva-pratyaya*) indicates a common agent for both actions. Although the *jīva* is identical in essence to Brahman as its own part (*svāṃśa*), the reference "by this *jīva*" treats it as distinct in order to differentiate it from the supreme nature. Therefore, this differentiation of names and forms has Hiraṇyagarbha as its agent.

For this very reason, in the Smṛtis, within the context of the creation performed by the Four-faced One (Brahmā), the differentiation of names and forms is proclaimed: "In the beginning, he [Brahmā] fashioned the names and forms of beings and the expansion of their activities for the gods and others, solely from the words of the Veda," and so forth. This being the position reached, it is replied: "But the fashioning of names and forms... The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous view.

The "fashioning of names and forms" (*saṃjñāmūrtiklṛpti*), which is the differentiation of name and form, belongs to the Supreme Brahman alone who performs the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), because the instruction regarding that very [Brahman] is given as the differentiator of name and form. For it is precisely while performing the tripartition that the differentiation of name and form is taught: "This divinity thought: 'Come, let me enter these three divinities with this living self and differentiate name and form; let me make each one of them threefold. This is because the identity of the agent is perceived [in both acts].

The tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) cannot belong to the four-faced Brahmā who exists within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), for the egg is produced by the elements of fire, water, and food after they have been triplicated; moreover, the birth of the four-faced one within the egg is recorded in Smṛti: "In that egg was born Brahmā, the grandfather of all worlds. Furthermore, it is understood that the tripartition belongs to the Supreme Brahman alone, and the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*), which has the same agent as that tripartition, also belongs to Him alone. How, then, is the phrase "by this living self" (*anena jīvena*) to be reconciled?

Because of the grammatical coordination in the phrase "by the self, by the living soul" (*ātmanā jīvena*), the Supreme Brahman itself, having the living soul as its body, is denoted by the word "living soul" (*jīva*). Just as in the passages, "That heat [tejas] thought," "It emitted the waters," "Those waters thought," and "They emitted food," it is the Supreme Brahman alone that is denoted as having heat and so forth as its body. Therefore, the differentiation of names and forms is the work of the Supreme Brahman itself, which has Hiraṇyagarbha—the collective totality of living souls—as its body.

And thus, in the passage "having entered, let me evolve name and form," both the verb "entering" and the first-person pronoun are unstrained and maintain their primary meanings. Furthermore, the identity of agent for both "entering" and "evolving" is logically consistent. Since the diverse creation of gods and so forth is the work of the Supreme Brahman alone, who has the four-faced Brahmā as His body, it is also logical that the instruction on the evolution of name and form occurs within a context where the creation is attributed to the agent who is the four-faced one.

Therefore, the meaning of the passage beginning with "This deity" is as follows: "Having entered these three deities—fire, water, and food—by means of this living self (the Self characterized by the aggregate of individual souls), let me unfold names and forms; that is, let me create the diverse creation of gods and so forth, along with their respective designations. For that purpose, let me make each of these fire, water, and food—which have not yet reached mutual conjunction and are incapable of specific creation—triple-combined (trivṛt) in order to acquire that capacity. Thus, this unfolding of names and forms is the work of the Supreme Brahman alone. || 17 ||

Now, it might be argued that because the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) shares the same agent as the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), it must have the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as its agent; however, this cannot be maintained, for the tripartition—

For even the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) can possibly have the individual soul (*jīva*) as its agent; indeed, after the creation of the cosmic egg, the method of triplication is taught with respect to the souls created by the four-faced Brahmā, beginning with: "But truly, my dear, when these three deities reach the person, each becomes threefold—know that from me. And: "Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts: its coarsest portion becomes feces, its middle portion becomes flesh, and its finest portion becomes the mind," and so forth.

Likewise, in the preceding passage as well, the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is heard in the text beginning with: "That which is the red form of fire is the form of heat; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food," and so on, regarding the fire, sun, moon, and lightning created by the Four-faced One (Brahmā): "This very divinity, having entered these three divinities by means of this living self (*jīva-ātman*), differentiated name and form; she made each one of them threefold."
Regarding this, he says:
"The [elements] such as flesh belong to the earth; for the other two, it is according to their names. (18)

As for the claim that this instruction on triplication—“He made each of those threefold”—refers to the deities and others created by the four-faced Brahmā after the creation of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), that is not tenable. For in the passage, “Food, when eaten, becomes divided into three parts,” since the flesh and mind are designated as being coarser and subtler than feces and breath respectively, it would follow that they too are composed of earth and fire (rather than water). Similarly, in the passage, “Water, when drunk...,” the same would apply to urine and breath, which are coarser and subtler [than the other products].

Furthermore, it would follow that [the mind] is composed of earth (*pārthiva*) and composed of fire (*taijasa*), yet this is not accepted. For flesh and so forth are accepted as being of the earth; indeed, both flesh and the mind are accepted as being of the earth, belonging to the earth-element, because of the introductory statement, "Food, when eaten, becomes threefold," and because of the corresponding statements for the other two [elements]: "Water, when drunk... and "...fire."

Regarding the two terms *aśita* (eaten) and its synonym (*pīta*, drunk), transformations are held to follow the literal meaning of the words. From the statement, "Water that has been drunk is transformed threefold," a threefold transformation of water alone is understood from the word itself; likewise, from the statement, "Fire that has been eaten is transformed threefold," a threefold transformation of fire alone is understood from the word itself. Therefore, it must be understood that feces, flesh, and mind are modifications of earth; urine, blood, and breath are modifications of water; and bones, marrow, and speech are modifications of fire.

Furthermore, this is because it would contradict the remainder of the passage: "For, my dear, the mind consists of food, breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire. Therefore, the manner of triplication described in the statement, "He made each of those threefold," is not demonstrated by the section beginning with "Food, when eaten," and so forth; for if that were the case, since all three—mind, breath, and speech—would be minute and thus fiery (taijasa), the statement "For, my dear, the mind consists of food," and so on, would be contradicted.

Even before the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) of earth and the other elements that have reached the person, the threefold transformation of each one is described by the passage beginning with "Food, when eaten," and so forth. Furthermore, the tripartition of fire, water, and food must have occurred even prior to the creation of the cosmic egg, because those elements, if not yet tripartite, would lack the capacity to initiate an effect. For it is only when they are mutually conjoined that they possess the capacity to initiate an effect; and that very conjunction is what constitutes tripartition.

And thus it is recorded in Smṛti: "Having diverse potencies and being separate, they were unable to create progeny without union, having failed to come together entirely. Having come together in mutual conjunction and being dependent upon one another, those principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the Egg.
For this very reason, [the Śruti says]: "Entering by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), he unfolded names and forms; he made each of these threefold."

The order of the text is set aside by the order of the sense. The demonstration of the triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa) regarding fire, the sun, and so forth—which exist within the cosmic egg—is made for the sake of Śvetaketu, who is situated inside the egg; for it is impossible to demonstrate the triplication to him with respect to things existing outside the egg. Therefore, the demonstration is performed with respect to the effects of the triplicated elements, namely fire, the sun, and so forth. || 18 ||

It might be argued: "Since food that is eaten, water that is drunk, and fire that is consumed are each composed of the triad [of elements], and thus each possesses a threefold nature consisting of fire, water, and food, how is it justified to designate them by a single form as 'food,' 'water,' or 'fire'? To this, he says:
"But on account of preponderance, there is that designation; there is that designation. (2.4.19)

"Specificity" (vaiśeṣyam) means the state of being specific. Even though [the three elements] have become threefold in form through the process of tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa), because of the predominance of food and so forth in each respective one, there is a designation as "food" and so on in those respective cases. The repetition [of the word] indicates the completion of the chapter. || 19 ||
The section concerning the designation, manifestation, and conceptualization [of the world]. || 8 ||
In the transition between [two states of existence], he departs enveloped [by subtle elements], on account of both the questions and the detailed explanations. (1)

By means of the two preceding chapters, this matter has been established—along with the reasons for its being unassailable—through the purification of the nature and form of the subject matter, consisting of the removal of contradictions with Smṛti and reasoning, the refutation of opposing views, and the resolution of mutual contradictions among Vedāntic texts; namely, that the Vedāntas teach the Supreme Brahman as the object of meditation for those seeking liberation, who is the sole cause of the entire universe, from whom even a scent of all defects has been removed, who is an ocean of immeasurable and sublime qualities, and who is distinct from everything else.

Thus, the nature of Brahman has been established by means of the first two chapters. Now, by means of the subsequent [chapters], it is intended to investigate the manner of attaining that [Brahman] along with the means for its attainment. In this regard, the third chapter contains an investigation concerning the meditations (*upāsanā*) which serve as the means. And the means most conducive to the commencement of meditation are dispassion toward things other than the object to be attained, as well as longing for that object to be attained.

For the purpose of establishing that [liberation], the defects of the individual soul (*jīva*) as it wanders through other worlds—whether waking, dreaming, deep asleep, or in a state of swoon—and the absence of such defects in the Supreme Brahman, along with His being a mine of auspicious qualities, are treated in the first and second quarters [of the first chapter].

It is being established: In this regard, there arises the inquiry whether this *jīva*, when moving from one body to another, goes enveloped by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) which are the cause for the commencement of the new body, or not. On the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is argued that since subtle elements are easily available wherever the *jīva* goes, it goes unenveloped. [The author] will later refute this by presenting the seeds of the prima facie argument. Therein, he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Upon reaching the next state, it moves enveloped."

In the passage "the fashioning of names and forms" (*saṃjñāmūrtikalpti*), the word "form" (*mūrti*) refers to the body; that [body] is referred to by the pronoun "that" (*tat*). The meaning is that upon entering into another state—that is, when moving to another body—the individual soul (*jīva*) proceeds, going forth enveloped by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*).

This is known from the nature of the questions and answers; for in this very Pañcāgnividyā (the knowledge of the five fires), such questions and answers are recorded: Pravāhaṇa Jaibali, the son of Aruṇa, having questioned Śvetaketu as to whether he knew the destination of those who perform ritual acts, the manner of their return, the divergence of the paths of the gods and the fathers, and the non-attainment of that world, asked this further question: "Do you know how, at the fifth libation, the waters come to be called 'man'? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3).

Then, answering this final question and figuratively representing the heavenly world as fire, [the text states]: "Into this very fire, the gods offer faith; from that oblation, King Soma arises," and so forth; thus, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the living being, called "gods," are represented as fire.

In the world of heaven, which is conceived as fire, they cast in the substance called faith (*śraddhā*); and that faith transforms into the form of an immortal body known as King Soma. Those very vital breaths (*prāṇa*) cast that immortal body into the rain-cloud, which is conceived as fire; and that body, once cast therein, becomes rain. Those same vital breaths cast that rain into the earth, which is conceived as fire, and it, being cast there, becomes food. And those same [breaths] cast that food into the person, who is conceived as fire.

In that context, it becomes semen; they deposit that very semen into the woman who has been represented as fire; and that which is deposited there becomes the embryo. Having stated this, [the text] says: "Thus, at the fifth oblation, water comes to be called 'man'"; thus, when the fifth oblation has been offered, water comes to be designated by the word "man."

The meaning is that they become expressible by words. When this has been said, it is stated that even in the previous oblations, it is precisely the waters in their subtle form that continue on and now assume the shape of a person. Therefore, through these questions and answers, it is understood that [the soul] goes from place to place together with the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) which constitute the cause of the body. || 1 ||

[Objection: But since it has been stated that "the waters have the form of man," there arises the perception of the transformation of the waters into the shape of a man; therefore, it is understood that they alone are embraced by the departing soul. How then can it be said that all the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) are embraced? To this, he says:
"But because [the soul] consists of three [elements], on account of the predominance [of water]. (2)

The word "but" (tu) sets aside the objection. It is not possible for water alone, which initiates the body, to bring about the formation of a body; for their initiation as the body and so forth requires the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), whereby each single element is made threefold. As for the mention of water alone, it is because of its preponderance; and since blood and other such substances abound in the body, the preponderance of water among the constituent elements is understood. || 2 ||
And because of the movement of the vital breath. || 3 ||

For this reason as well, it is understood that there is a departure of that which is enveloped by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*); for when the individual soul (*jīva*) departs, the following of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is heard in scripture: "As he departs..."

"The vital breath (prāṇa) departs; as the vital breath departs, all the other vital breaths depart. And it is also stated in Smṛti: "The Lord draws away the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in their source; when the body obtains [another] and when He departs, He goes taking these along, just as the wind carries fragrances from their receptacles. Since movement is not possible for those that are without a substratum, one must also admit the movement of the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) which serve as their substratum. || 3 ||
If it be argued that [the soul does not go to Brahman] because of the scriptural mention of its going to Agni and others, we say no, because that is figurative.

If it be argued that because of the scriptural statement, "When this person has died, speech merges into fire, breath into wind, and sight into the sun," etc., there is no departure of the vital breaths along with the individual soul (jīva) at the time of death—since they are heard to merge into fire and other elements—the scriptural texts concerning their departure must be interpreted otherwise; we say no, because the statement regarding their merging into fire and so forth is figurative (*bhākta*). How is it figurative? Because it is heard in conjunction with hair and the like which do not merge, as in the passage, "The hairs [merge] into herbs, the hair of the head into trees.
Therefore, the scriptural statement regarding the merging of sight and the other organs refers to the departure of the presiding deities. || 4 ||
If it be argued that [the intermediate state] does not exist because it is not mentioned in the first [chapter], we say no; for it is indeed those very [beings] that are logical.

As for the claim that it is understood from the question and answer that the individual soul (jīva) departs enveloped by subtle waters mixed with other elements—that is not tenable, because in the first oblation concerning the fire of the heavenly world, water is not heard of as the substance to be offered. In the text, "In this very fire, the gods offer faith (śraddhā)," it is *śraddhā* alone that is heard of as the object of the oblation. And *śraddhā* is well known as a particular modification of the mind belonging to the individual soul.

If it is argued that, for this reason, water is not to be offered as an oblation there, we say no; because those very waters are designated by the word *śraddhā* (faith) in that context. Why? Because of the consistency between the question and the answer. For at the beginning of the answer to the question, "Do you know how, in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'?", *śraddhā* is heard as the substance to be offered into the fire of the heavenly world (*dyuloka*). In that case, if the waters were not denoted by the word *śraddhā*, then the question would be one thing and the answer another, which would be inconsistent.
[The text continues: "Thus, in the fifth oblation, the waters..."

Regarding how the nature of water (*aptva*) is indicated, he says: "Do you know? The conclusion of the response, "Thus [is] the personification of the man," indicates that the very nature of water is being pointed out. For the manner presented in the question, "Do you know how?", is concluded in the answer by the word "thus" (*iti*) in the phrase, "But at the fifth oblation. Having described the transformation of water into the forms of faith (*śraddhā*), King Soma, rain, food, semen, and the embryo, it is concluded that "thus indeed is water the personification of the man."

Furthermore, the word *śraddhā* (faith) is seen used for water in Vedic usage: "He leads forward the waters; the waters, indeed, are faith. And [in the passage], "They offer faith as an oblation; from that oblation King Soma arises," it is logical that the transformation into the form of Soma belongs to the waters themselves. Therefore, it is established that the individual soul (*jīva*) departs enveloped by waters mixed with the other elements. || 5 ||
If it be argued that [the ancestors do not ascend] because they are not mentioned [in the relevant texts], we say no, because those who perform sacrifices such as the iṣṭi are known [to do so].

As for the claim that the meaning—that the individual soul (jīva) departs enveloped by water—is understood from this statement, that is not tenable, because the soul is not explicitly mentioned in this sentence. For here, it is only the specific states of water, such as faith (śraddhā) and so forth, that are heard as being offered in sacrifice, and not the soul enveloped by them. To this we say: no, because those who perform sacrifices and other works are recognized [in this very context]. For later in this same passage, it is stated that those who perform sacrifices, meritorious works, alms-giving, and so forth—provided they are devoid of knowledge of Brahman—reach the heavenly world and become King Soma.

And it is said that at the conclusion of their meritorious karma, they return and enter a womb: beginning with, "Now, those who in this world worship with the thought, 'Sacrifices have been offered, oblations have been poured, gifts have been given,' they pass into smoke," and continuing, "From the world of the fathers they go to space, from space to the moon; that is King Soma, the food of the gods, which the gods eat. "Having dwelt there until the [karma] is exhausted, they then return again by this very same path. For whosoever eats the food and whosoever sheds the semen, he becomes that very thing again.

[The text] says: "...it comes to be. Here too, in the context of the heavenly fire, it is said: "They offer faith as an oblation; from that oblation, King Soma arises. Because this has the same meaning [as the previous passage], it is understood that what was stated—namely, that [the soul] becomes characterized by a body in the state of faith, and subsequently characterized by a body in the form of Soma—is intended. Since a word denoting a body—which has its essential nature solely as a qualification of the living being (jīva)—ultimately refers to the qualified entity, the living being itself, it is therefore logical that the living being, enveloped by [subtle] matter, departs. || 6 ||

But is it not the case that Soma is called "King," because of the statement, "The gods consume him," which implies he is consumed by the gods; and since the individual soul (jīva) cannot be eaten, [it follows] that it is not the jīva being spoken of? To this, the Sūtra replies:
"Or [the term 'king'] is figurative, because [the gods] do not know the Self; for thus Scripture shows. (7)

The word *vā* (or) sets aside the objection. Because those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* lack self-knowledge (*anātmavit*), they exist here and in the hereafter as instruments for the enjoyment of the gods. Here, by performing worship through sacrifices like the *iṣṭi*, they serve [the gods]; having reached that world granted by the gods who have been propitiated, they become instruments for them, sharing the same enjoyments there. The Śruti shows the state of being an instrument for the gods for those lacking self-knowledge in the passage: "As is a beast, so is he to the gods."

The *Smṛti* also demonstrates that for those who know the Self, there is the attainment of Brahman, whereas for those who do not know the Self, there is the state of being an object of enjoyment for the gods, as it says: "Those who worship the gods go to the gods; my devotees come to me as well. Therefore, the statement regarding the living self (*jīva*) being eaten as food is intended to show its status as an instrument of enjoyment for the gods; thus, it is figurative. Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that for the gods, satisfaction itself constitutes eating: "Truly, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by beholding this nectar."

Therefore, it is established that the individual soul (jīva) departs enveloped by the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma). Thus ends the section concerning the attainment of another [body] within that interval. 1.1.7. || End of Section 1 ||
"At the end of what has been performed, [the soul] returns with a remainder, on account of scriptural statement and Smṛti; as it went, and also not so.

Now, it is traditionally taught that those who perform only sacrifices (iṣṭa), works of public utility (pūrta), and acts of charity (datta) travel by the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) via smoke and so forth, and that they return again at the conclusion of the fruit of their karma, according to the text: "Having dwelt there as long as their [merit] lasts, they then return again by that very same path. In that regard, does the soul descending [from heaven] possess a remainder (anuśaya)?

A doubt arises as to whether or not one descends with a remainder of karma (*anuśaya*). What is the correct position? It is argued that since the entirety of the karma has been experienced, there is no remainder of karma; this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). For a remainder of karma is that portion of karma which remains after being experienced. And when the fruit of the whole has been enjoyed, nothing remains. Furthermore, from the scriptural statement "having dwelt as far as the point of exhaustion" (*yāvat-sampātam uṣitvā*), it is understood that the enjoyment is complete. "Sampāta" refers to karma, so called because by means of it one "falls" (*sampatanti*) into the heavenly world.

And another scriptural passage states: "Having reached the end of that karma, whatever this person does here [in this world], from that world he returns again to this world for the sake of karma. This being the position reached, it is replied: "He descends accompanied by a remainder (anuśaya). Why? Because of perception and tradition—that is, because of Śruti and Smṛti.

First, the Śruti declares regarding those who have descended [from the world of the fathers]: "Now, those here whose conduct has been pleasant, it is likely that they will attain a pleasant womb—either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya; but those here whose conduct has been foul, it is likely that they will attain a foul womb—either the womb of a dog, the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla. Thus, for those who have descended from that world, those whose actions were pleasant attain a pleasant womb, such as that of a Brāhmaṇa or others.

The phrase "those of foul conduct" (*kapūyacaraṇāḥ*)—meaning those whose actions are contemptible—shows that those who have descended [to the earth] attain a contemptible womb, such as that of a dog, a pig, or a *caṇḍāla*, thereby demonstrating their connection with both meritorious and sinful karma. Smṛti also states: "The castes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*), being devoted to their own duties, after dying and experiencing the fruit of their actions, then by the remainder [of their karma], obtain birth characterized by excellence of place, caste, family, form, lifespan, sacred learning, wealth, conduct, happiness, and intelligence; whereas those who act otherwise fall away in all directions and perish."

Likewise: "Then, upon returning [to earth], by means of the remainder of the fruits of their karma, they obtain birth, form, complexion, strength, intelligence, wisdom, wealth, and the performance of dharma; this proceeds like a wheel, resulting in happiness in both worlds. The phrase "until the exhaustion of the residue" (*yāvat-sampātam*) refers specifically to those particular karmas that have begun to yield their fruit. If it is argued that the statement "whatever he does here" (*yat kiñca iha karoti*) also refers to conduct (*caraṇa*), Kārṣṇājini says no, for that [mention of conduct] is intended as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*). (Sūtra 9)

Regarding the terms "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*) and "those of foul conduct" (*kapūyacaraṇāḥ*), it is not by the word *caraṇa* that action in the form of merit and demerit is denoted; for the word *caraṇa* is well-known in both common usage and the Veda as referring to conduct (*ācāra*). Indeed, worldly people consider *caraṇa*, *ācāra*, *śīla*, and *vṛtta* to be synonyms. Furthermore, in the Veda, conduct and action are designated as distinct, as in: "Those actions which are blameless should be practiced," and "Those good deeds of ours are to be emulated by you. Thus, conduct and action are mentioned separately.

If it is argued that the attainment of a particular womb results from conduct (*caraṇa*) and not from residual karma (*anuśaya*), that is not so; for the teacher Kārṣṇājini considers the scriptural mention of "conduct" to be intended as an indicator of all action (*karman*), since the attainment of pleasure and pain cannot result from mere behavior alone. For pleasure and pain are indeed the fruits of actions consisting of merit and demerit. || 9 ||
If it is argued that [the Veda] would be purposeless, we say no, because it depends upon that.

If it is argued that, in that case, because conduct prescribed by the Smṛti would have no fruit, it is indeed useless—this is not so, because merit depends upon it. Only one possessed of good conduct has the qualification for meritorious actions, according to such scriptural statements as: "One who neglects the Sandhyā prayers is eternally impure and unfit for all rites," and "The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of good conduct. Therefore, Kārṣṇājini’s intention is that the Vedic mention of "conduct" (caraṇa) is intended as an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) for [the performance of] ritual action (karman). || 10 ||
"But it is only good and evil deeds," says Bādari. (11)

Because of the usage of the verb *carati* with the object (accusative) in expressions such as "he performs meritorious action" (*puṇyaṃ karma carati*) and "he performs sinful action" (*pāpaṃ karma carati*), and because the separate mention [of *caraṇa*] is justified by the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*govālīvardanyāya*)—since it refers respectively to what is established by direct Vedic revelation and what is established by a Vedic text inferred from observed conduct—the teacher Bādari maintains that when a primary meaning is possible, a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate; thus, the words *sukṛta* and *duṣkṛta* alone are denoted by the term *caraṇa*. In this matter, the view of Bādari alone is his own position, as it is based on the Vedic injunctions inferred from observed conduct.

However, it is accepted that the fruit of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and other such rites is the attainment of eligibility for other ritual acts; therefore, they indeed descend with their residual karma (*sānuśaya*). || 11 || The section concerning the passing away of what has been performed (*kṛtātyayādhikaraṇa*) is concluded. || 2 ||
And it is also heard in scripture regarding those who perform undesirable acts and so forth. || 12 ||

It has been stated that those who perform only sacrifices (*iṣṭa*), public works (*pūrta*), and acts of charity (*datta*) go to the moon and return with a remainder of their karma (*sānuśaya*). Now, it is considered whether even those who perform undesirable acts and the like go to the moon or not. Those who do not perform what is enjoined and those who perform what is prohibited—both these types of evildoers are "performers of undesirable acts and the like. What is logical? That they also go to the moon?
Why? Because their going there is also heard in scripture; for, without distinction, the movement of all alike is heard in the text: "All who depart from this world go to the moon. (12)
If that were so, then the destination for both those who perform good deeds and those who perform evil deeds would be indistinguishable. To this he says:
"But having experienced [the results] in Saṃyamana, there is ascent and descent for them, because of the observation of their respective courses. (1.2.13)

The word *tu* (but) removes a doubt: for others—those who perform undesirable acts and so forth—the ascent to and descent from the moon occurs only after experiencing the punishments ordained by Yama under his command, and not otherwise. Why? Because their course is seen [in scripture]. Indeed, the going of evildoers to him under the subjection of Yama is seen in such passages as: "Thinking 'this world does not exist, nor the next,' he falls again and again into my power," and "Yama, the King, the son of Vivasvat, the assembler of people," and so forth. || 13 ||
And they remember it. || 14 ||
And Parāśara and others remember the subjection of all to Yama, as in such passages as: "O Blessed One, indeed all these come under the power of Yama," and so forth. (14)
Even seven. || 15 ||
They also remember the seven hells, beginning with Raurava, as the destinations for those who have committed evil deeds. || 15 ||
[Objection: But how can those traveling through the seven worlds reach the abode of Yama? To this he says:
"Even there, because of his activity, there is no contradiction" (16).

Since they too proceed to those seven [worlds] solely by the command of Yama, there is no contradiction. Therefore, even for those who perform undesirable acts and the like, after reaching the world of Yama and experiencing torments corresponding to their own karma, there subsequently follow the ascent to and descent from the moon.
This being the position reached, it is said: "But [the path belongs] to knowledge and action, because they are the subjects under discussion. (17)

The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude the [previous] position. It is not tenable that even those who perform undesirable acts reach the moon; why? Because the paths of the gods and the fathers have as their purpose the enjoyment of the fruits of knowledge and ritual action (*vidyā-karma*). This is what is meant: just as for those who perform undesirable acts there is an absence of knowledge...

Just as going by the path of the gods (*devayāna*) is not possible for you, likewise, because of being devoid of sacrifices, works of public utility, and gifts, going to the moon by the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*) is also not possible. If it is asked how it is understood that the path of the gods has knowledge (*vidyā*) as its subject matter and the path of the fathers has meritorious deeds (*puṇyakarman*) as its subject matter, [the answer is] because those two are the subjects under discussion.

For knowledge is indeed the subject under discussion in relation to the path of the gods (*devayāna*), and ritual action in relation to the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*). This is because, after stating, "Those who know thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity," the text speaks of the path of the gods with the words, "They pass into the light, from the light into day," and so forth; and because, after stating, "Now, those who in the village worship with sacrifices, gifts, and charity," the text speaks of the path of the fathers with the words, "They pass into smoke," and so forth.
Even this statement, "Whoever depart from this world, they all go to the moon," is to be understood as referring to "those who perform sacrifices and other such rites. || 17 ||

[Objection: But surely, if those who have performed evil deeds do not go to the moon, then because the fifth libation would be impossible, the very commencement of a body would not be possible; for the commencement of a body is heard of in scripture in the passage, "In the fifth libation, the waters come to be called 'man,'" and it has been shown that this libation is preceded by the reaching of the moon. Therefore, for the sake of the commencement of a body, their ascent to and descent from the moon must necessarily be admitted.
To this, [the author] says: "Not so in the third case, for it is perceived thus. (2.1.18)
There is no requirement for a fifth libation for the commencement of a body in the case of the third place; why? Because it is so perceived: by the term "third place," only evil [is meant].

Actions are spoken of; it is observed that in the commencement of their bodies, they do not depend upon a fifth oblation. This is evident from the answer to the question, "Do you know how that world is not filled? which states: "Now, those beings who do not travel by either of these two paths become these small creatures that return repeatedly, being born and dying; this is the third place. Because of this, that world is not filled. Thus, the third place is characterized by the absence of ascending to and descending from the heavenly world.

Because it is stated that the heavenly world is not fully completed [by this], there is no requirement for a fifth libation for the commencement of a body in this third place. Furthermore, the statement "in the fifth libation" merely establishes that the connection of the waters with the fifth fire is the cause for attaining the state of being called a "person" (puruṣavacastva), and it does not exclude anything else, as no restrictive particle (avadhāraṇa) is heard [in the text]. || 18 ||
And it is also recorded in common worldly usage.

In this world, it is recorded in tradition that for some even among those of meritorious deeds, the commencement of a body occurs without dependence on the fifth oblation, as in the case of Draupadī, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and others. || 19 ||
And because it is seen [in scripture]. || 20 ||

Even in the Śruti, the commencement of a body is seen for some without dependence on the fifth oblation: "Of these beings, there are indeed only three seeds: the egg-born, the viviparous, and the soil-born. Thus, the production of soil-born and sweat-born beings is seen to occur without the fifth oblation. (20)

But is it not the case that there is no mention here of those born from sweat, because of the statement, "There are only three seeds"? To this he replies: "The third term includes those born from moisture. (Sūtra 21)

The meaning is that even those born from moisture and born from sweat are included—that is, subsumed—under the third category, the term *udbhijja*, in the phrase "born from an egg, born from a living being, and born from a sprout"; therefore, the attainment of the moon is not possible for those whose karma consists solely of evil deeds. || 21 ||
The section concerning those who perform undesirable acts and so forth is completed. || 3 ||
The attainment of that very nature [of Brahman] occurs because it is logical. 22.

It has been stated that those who perform sacrifices and other rites, enveloped by the subtle elements of the body and accompanied by their residual karma (*sānuśaya*), descend from the moon; and the manner of this descent is described by the scriptural passage: "Then they return again by the same path as they came: to the ether, from the ether to the air; having become air, he becomes smoke; having become smoke, he becomes mist; having become mist, he becomes a cloud; having become a cloud, he rains down."

It has been stated that "in this way" and "not in this way. Regarding that, there arises the doubt: when one attains the state of ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth, does one become ether and so forth in the same manner as one becomes a god or a human? Or is it merely the attainment of similarity to them? Since there is no distinction [in the text]—just as there is the state of being Soma for one established in faith—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that one becomes ether and so forth. To this, it is replied: it is indeed the attainment of their own nature (*tatsvābhāvyāpatti*). "Attainment of their own nature" means the attainment of similarity to them. Why is this so? Because of logical consistency (*upapatti*); for in the case of becoming Soma, a human, and so forth, that state exists for the purpose of experiencing pleasure and pain. However, in the case of ether and so forth, there is no such experience. Therefore, it is the attainment of similarity to them. Furthermore, because there is no mention of a departure from the body (*vigama*) in the case of ether and so forth, whereas there is such mention in the case of rain and so forth, it is understood that the soul remains within the body even while in the state of ether and so forth. Thus, it is established that the soul attains a state of similarity to ether and the rest. As for the statement, "Having dwelt there until the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), he is born again with a new body," this refers to the fact that at the time of the great dissolution, the souls of those who have attained the state of ether and so forth remain in that very state, and upon the subsequent creation, they are born again with a new body. This is like the case of those who have attained the state of smoke and so forth. Therefore, it is concluded that the soul attains a state of similarity to ether and the rest. Thus ends the section on the attainment of the state of ether and so forth. Now begins the section on the attainment of the state of food (*anna*). In the passage, "From the earth, to food; from food, to semen; from semen, to beings," the doubt arises: does the soul become food itself, or does it merely attain similarity to food? Here too, since there is no mention of a departure from the body, the prima facie view is that it becomes food itself. To this, it is said: it is the attainment of similarity to food. Why? Because of logical consistency. For if the soul were to become food itself, it would follow that it would be consumed by those who eat it, and thus its transmigratory journey would be interrupted. Therefore, it is the attainment of similarity to food. Furthermore, because the text says, "From food, to semen," and because semen is a product of food, it is understood that the soul becomes similar to food through its transformation into semen. Thus, it is established that the soul attains a state of similarity to food. Thus ends the section on the attainment of the state of food. Now begins the section on the attainment of the state of semen. In the passage, "From semen, to beings," the doubt arises: does the soul become the individual beings themselves, or does it merely attain similarity to them? Here too, since there is no mention of a departure from the body, the prima facie view is that it becomes the beings themselves. To this, it is said: it is the attainment of similarity to beings. Why? Because of logical consistency. For if the soul were to become the beings themselves, it would follow that it would be subject to birth, death, and other such states, and thus its transmigratory journey would be interrupted. Therefore, it is the attainment of similarity to beings. Furthermore, because the text says, "From semen, to beings," and because the soul enters the womb through the medium of semen, it is understood that the soul becomes similar to beings through its connection with semen. Thus, it is established that the soul attains a state of similarity to beings. Thus ends the section on the attainment of the state of semen. Now begins the section on the attainment of the state of the person (*puruṣa*). In the passage, "From the person, to women," the doubt arises: does the soul become the woman herself, or does it merely attain similarity to her? Here too, since there is no mention of a departure from the body, the prima facie view is that it becomes the woman herself. To this, it is said: it is the attainment of similarity to the woman. Why? Because of logical consistency. For if the soul were to become the woman herself, it would follow that it would be subject to the woman's various states, and thus its transmigratory journey would be interrupted. Therefore, it is the attainment of similarity to the woman. Furthermore, because the text says, "From the person, to women," and because the soul enters the womb through the medium of the woman, it is understood that the soul becomes similar to the woman through its connection with her. Thus, it is established that the soul attains a state of similarity to the woman. Thus ends the section on the attainment of the state of the person. Now begins the section on the attainment of the state of the embryo (*kalala*). In the passage, "From the woman, to the embryo," the doubt arises: does the soul become the embryo itself, or does it merely attain similarity to it? Here too, since there is no mention of a departure from the body, the prima facie view is that it becomes the embryo itself. To this, it is said: it is the attainment of similarity to the embryo. Why? Because of logical consistency. For if the soul were to become the embryo itself, it would follow that it would be subject to the embryo's various stages of development, and thus its transmigratory journey would be interrupted. Therefore, it is the attainment of similarity to the embryo. Furthermore, because the text says, "From the woman, to the embryo," and because the soul enters the womb through the medium of the embryo, it is understood that the soul becomes similar to the embryo through its connection with it. Thus, it is established that the soul attains a state of similarity to the embryo. Thus ends the section on the attainment of the state of the embryo. Now begins the section on the attainment of the state of the fetus (*ghana*). In the passage, "From the embryo, to the fetus," the doubt arises: does the soul become the fetus itself, or does it merely attain similarity to it? Here too, since there is no mention of a departure from the body, the prima facie view is that it becomes the fetus itself. To this, it is said: it is the attainment of similarity to the fetus. Why? Because of logical consistency. For if the soul were to become the fetus itself, it would follow that it would be subject to the fetus's various stages of development, and thus its transmigratory journey would be interrupted. Therefore, it is the attainment of similarity to the fetus. Furthermore, because the text says, "From the embryo, to the fetus," and because the soul enters the womb through the medium of the fetus, it is understood that the soul becomes similar to the fetus through its connection with it. Thus, it is established that the soul attains a state of similarity to the fetus. Thus ends the section on the attainment of the state of the fetus. Now begins the section on the attainment of the state of the limbs (*praśākhā*). In the passage, "From the fetus, to the limbs," the doubt arises: does the soul become the limbs themselves, or does it merely attain similarity to them? Here too, since there is no mention of a departure from the body, the prima facie view is that it becomes the limbs themselves. To this, it is said: it is the attainment of similarity to the limbs. Why? Because of logical consistency. For if the soul were to become the limbs themselves, it would follow that it would be subject to the limbs' various states, and thus its transmigratory journey would be interrupted. Therefore, it is the attainment of similarity to the limbs. Furthermore, because the text says, "From the fetus, to the limbs," and because the soul enters the womb through the medium of the limbs, it is understood that the soul becomes similar to the limbs through its connection with them. Thus, it is established that the soul attains a state of similarity to the limbs. Thus ends the section on the attainment of the state of the limbs. Now begins the section on the attainment of the state of the body (*śarīra*). In the passage, "From the limbs, to the body," the doubt arises: does the soul become the body itself, or does it merely attain similarity to it? Here too, since there is no mention of a departure from the body, the prima facie view is that it becomes the body itself. To this, it is said: it is the attainment of similarity to the body. Why? Because of logical consistency. For if the soul were to become the body itself, it would follow that it would be subject to the body's various states, and thus its transmigratory journey would be interrupted. Therefore, it is the attainment of similarity to the body. Furthermore, because the text says, "From the limbs, to the body," and because the soul enters the womb through the medium of the body, it is understood that the soul becomes similar to the body through its connection with it. Thus, it is established that the soul attains a state of

In this context, however, since there is an absence of the experience of pleasure and pain in [elements] such as space (*ākāśa*), the attainment of that [state] is impossible; therefore, the statement regarding such attainment is intended to mean the attainment of similarity [to it] through association with it. || 22 || The section concerning the attainment of the nature of that [state] is concluded. || 4 ||
Not after a long time, because of the distinction. || 23 ||

Regarding the question whether one remains for no very long time at each stage—from the attainment of space up to the attainment of rice and so forth—or whether there is no fixed rule, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since there is no reason for a restriction, there is no fixed rule. To this, it is replied: "Not for a very long time. Why? Because of the specific distinction made later regarding the attainment of rice and so forth, where, in the phrase "from there indeed it is more difficult to escape" (*ato vai khalu durniṣprapataram*), a specifically arduous departure is mentioned; therefore, [the duration] must be short in the preceding stages as well.

Here, it is understood that there is not a long delay in departing after reaching space and the other stages; the form *durniṣprapataram* is a Vedic usage resulting from the elision of the suffix *-tas*, meaning "more difficult to depart" or "departing with greater difficulty. || 23 || The section [concerning] "Not too long" is completed. || 5 ||
[The soul is] presided over by another, because of the designation [of the body] as before. || 24 ||
It is heard in scripture that descending souls are born in the form of rice and so forth: "Having become rain, it rains down; these are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans."

Regarding the doubt as to whether they cling to rice and other grains presided over by other enjoyers who possess bodies made of rice and so forth, or whether those enjoyers themselves are born with bodies made of rice and so forth—the prima facie view being that, because of the statement "they are born," they enter into bodies of rice and so forth just as one says "a god is born" or "a human is born"—it is replied: "presided over by another. Their connection is merely an attachment to a body of rice and so forth already presided over by another living soul.

Why? Because, as before, there is a mention of that alone, just as in the passage beginning with "ether" and ending with "clouds. For wherever the state of being an enjoyer is intended, the action that serves as its means is mentioned, namely: "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct."

Furthermore, in this context, no further action is denoted, as is the case with ether and so forth. This is because the action—such as an *iṣṭi* sacrifice—which has begun to yield its fruit, is brought to completion precisely through the enjoyment of heaven; and because no other action remains to be commenced, as will be stated later: "Those of pleasant conduct, those of foul conduct. Moreover, there is no intervening action. Therefore, just like the statement regarding becoming ether and so forth, the statement regarding birth in the form of rice and so forth is figurative. || 24 ||
If it be argued that [the world] is impure, we say no, because of the Word (Śruti). || 25 ||

This is not so; for when rice and other plants are presided over by another [being], there is merely a state of conjunction, and because the cause for being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is absent, there is no birth in the form of rice and the like. However, because the cause for being an enjoyer does exist, the karma consisting of sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi*—which has heaven as its enjoyable fruit—is indeed impure and mixed with evil, since it involves violence such as that toward the animal for Agni-Soma. And violence is certainly evil, as it is prohibited by the injunction: "One must not harm any living beings."

Furthermore, in this case, the relationship of general rule and exception (utsarga-apavāda) is not possible—as it is, for example, between the rules regarding the *pada* and the *āhavanīya* fires—because their spheres of application (*viṣaya*) are distinct. For the injunction regarding the Agniṣomīya sacrifice teaches that violence serves as an auxiliary to the ritual (*kratūpakārakatva*), whereas the [injunction] "One should not kill" [teaches] that killing is a source of evil. Moreover, those who understand the matter call even a physician a protector, despite his causing momentary, slight pain, and they honor him. || 25 ||
Now, the connection with the emitter of semen. || 26 ||

For this reason as well, the statement regarding birth as rice and so forth is figurative. Just as the subsequent mention of the state of being rice and so forth is followed by the scriptural statement, "Whoever eats the food and whoever sheds the semen, he becomes that very thing again," which indicates for those with residual karma (*anuśayin*) merely their connection with the shedder of semen; in the same way, the state of being rice and so forth [is merely figurative]. This is the meaning. || 26 ||
From the womb comes the body. || 27 ||

The acquisition of a body by those possessing latent dispositions (*anuśayin*) occurs only after reaching the place of birth (*yoni*), because it is precisely there that the experience of pleasure and pain exists; prior to that, from the time of reaching space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, there is merely the connection with them—this is the meaning. [End of] the Section on Being Presided Over by Another (Anyādhiṣṭhitādhikaraṇa). 6.
The creation occurs in the intermediate state (the dream state), for so the scripture declares. || 1 ||

Thus, the state of suffering for the living being while awake—due to its connection with coming and going and birth in accordance with its karma—has been explained. Now, its state of dream is examined; concerning the dream state, it is heard in scripture: "There are no chariots there, no yoke-animals for chariots, and no roads, yet he creates chariots, yoke-animals, and roads; there are no joys, delights, or pleasures there, yet he creates joys, delights, and pleasures; there are no pools, lotus ponds, or flowing streams there."

"He creates lotus-pools; for he is the creator. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is this creation of chariots and so forth performed by the individual soul (*jīva*) alone, or rather by the Lord (*īśvara*)? What is the correct view? That the creation in the intermediate state (*saṃdhye*) is performed by the individual soul. Why? Because the intermediate state is said to be the state of dream, according to the scriptural statement: "The third is the intermediate state, the state of dream. And that [creation] is performed by the individual soul alone, for the text says: "He creates; for he is the creator. Indeed, it is the individual soul who is perceived as the dreamer there. (Sūtra 1)
And some [hold that the Lord is] the creator, as well as sons and so forth. (2)

Furthermore, certain followers of a particular Vedic branch study this individual soul (*jīva*) as the creator of desires in the dream state, according to the text: "The Person who wakes among these sleeping ones, creating desire after desire. And here, sons and so forth are designated by the word "desire" (*kāma*) because they are objects of desire, not mere longing; for in the preceding passage, "Ask for all desires according to your wish," and "Choose sons and grandsons with a lifespan of a hundred years," it is sons and the like that are introduced as the "desires. Therefore, the individual soul creates chariots and other such things in the dream state.

Furthermore, the quality of having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) is heard in the Prajāpati discourse regarding the individual soul (*jīva*); therefore, even in the absence of external instruments and the like, creation is possible. || 2 ||
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"But it is mere illusion (māyāmātra), because its true nature is not manifested in its entirety. (Sūtra 3)

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position; the meaning is that the collection of objects such as chariots and lotus ponds in a dream is merely *māyā* (illusion), created by the Supreme Person. For the word *māyā* indeed denotes something wonderful.

This is because such is seen in Vedic passages such as, "Born in the lineage of Janaka, she was fashioned like divine illusion. Here too, the statement "There are no chariots, no draft-animals for chariots, and no roads" means that these do not exist insofar as they are not experienced by any person other than [the dreamer]. Then, the statement "He creates chariots, draft-animals for chariots, and paths" indicates its very nature as a marvel, meaning that he creates them as things to be experienced only by the dreamer, which cease to exist at that very moment.

A creation of such a wondrous nature is possible only for the Supreme Person whose will is ever-true, and not for the individual soul (jīva); for even though the soul possesses true will and other qualities, its essential nature remains entirely unmanifest during the state of worldly existence, and thus such a marvelous creation is not possible for the individual soul.

And by the statement, "Desiring his own desire, the Person creates," [the text] speaks of the Supreme Person alone as the creator. Furthermore, because the unique nature of the Supreme Person is perceived in both the opening and the conclusion—namely, "That which wakes while these sleep, that indeed is the Bright, that is Brahman, that is called the Immortal; on it all worlds rest, and no one transcends it"—and because of its agreement with the other scriptural passage, "He creates ponds, lotus-pools, and flowing rivers; for He is the agent," [this text] declares the Supreme Person alone to be the creator. || 3 ||
If the qualities such as being free from sin are inherent to the individual soul (jīva), why are they not manifested? To this he says:
"But [these qualities] are concealed by the contemplation of the Supreme; for from that [concealment] come its bondage and its opposite. (1.3.4)

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of removing doubt. From the meditation upon the Supreme—that is, from the volition of the Supreme Person—the natural form of this individual soul becomes concealed. For the Supreme Person causes the concealment of the soul's naturally auspicious form, since this soul has committed offenses through a beginningless succession of karma.

Therefore, the bondage and liberation of this individual soul (jīva) are indeed heard [in scripture] to arise from that very volition (saṅkalpa): "For when he finds fearlessness as his foundation in that which is invisible, incorporeal, indefinable, and supportless, then he becomes free from fear; but when he perceives even the slightest difference in it, then fear comes to him"; "For he alone causes bliss"; "From fear of Him the wind blows," and so forth. || 4 ||
Or that [knowledge] also [arises] from the conjunction with a body. || 5 ||

That concealment (*tirobhāva*) occurs either through connection with a body or through connection with the subtle power of consciousness (*acicchakti*); it occurs at the time of creation due to conjunction with a non-sentient entity (*acidvastu*) existing in the form of a body, and at the time of dissolution due to conjunction with an extremely subtle non-sentient entity that is incapable of being distinguished by name and form.

Therefore, because its own nature is unmanifest, the individual soul (*jīva*) is not capable of creating chariots and other objects by mere volition in a dream. For attributes such as being awake while all others sleep, and being the support of all worlds—as in the text, "In Him all worlds are supported; no one transcends Him"—belong to the Supreme Person alone. Consequently, for the sake of the individual souls experiencing fruits corresponding to their respective small actions, He produces those objects which are perceivable by them alone and which last only for that specific duration. || 5 ||
For it is indicated by scripture, and those who know that declare it so.

For this reason as well, the objects of dreams are not preceded by the volitions of the individual soul (*jīva*); because it is understood from scripture that dream is an indicator of prosperity and adversity: "When, during rites performed for desired ends, one sees a woman in dreams, one should know that prosperity will attend him in accordance with that vision in the dream"; and also from such passages as, "Now, if one sees a man with black teeth in a dream, he kills him," and so forth. Furthermore, those learned in the science of dreams declare that a dream is an indicator of good and evil fortune. This quality of being an indicator...

Furthermore, it is not possible for [the dream] to depend upon one's own volition; likewise, since the inauspicious is undesirable, [the dreamer] would see only that which indicates the auspicious after having created it. Therefore, the creation in a dream is performed by the Lord alone. // 6 //
The section concerning the twilight [prayers] is completed. || 1 ||
Its absence [is found] in the channels and in that which consists of a hundredfold self.

Now the locus of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is examined. This is recorded in scripture: "When, being thus asleep, composed and serene, one does not perceive any dream, then he has entered into these channels (*nāḍī*). Likewise: "And when one is in deep sleep, when one knows nothing at all..."

"For the channels called *hitā*—seventy-two thousand in number—extend from the heart to the pericardium; having descended through them, he sleeps in the pericardium. Likewise: "When, my dear, a person is said to be 'sleeping,' then he has become united with Being (*sat*). Thus, the channels, the pericardium, and Brahman are heard in scripture as the locations for deep sleep.

In the doubt as to whether there is an option (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*) among these, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is an option, because they are perceived as independent of one another and because it is impossible for [the soul] to reside simultaneously in multiple places. To this, it is replied: "The absence of that" (*tadabhāva*). The absence of that dream is deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which occurs in the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*), in the pericardium (*purītat*), and in the Self (*ātman*); the meaning is that there is a combination of these places. Why? Because of the scriptural statement of them as such—because of the hearing of all three being stated as places.

Furthermore, when a combination [of options] is possible through a difference in function, it is not logical to resort to an alternative (vikalpa) that involves the possibility of partial sublation. And a difference in function among the channels (nāḍīs) and so forth is indeed possible, as in the case of a palace, a bedstead, and a couch. In this context, the channels and the *purītat* correspond to the palace and the bedstead, while Brahman corresponds to the couch. Therefore, Brahman alone is the direct locus of deep sleep. || 7 ||
Therefore, awakening arises from this.

Since Brahman alone is the direct locus of deep sleep, therefore the awakening of these individual souls from this Brahman—as heard in such passages as, "Having come from Being, they do not know; we have come from Being"—is logically consistent. Thus ends the section concerning the absence of that [dream].
But he [the individual soul] is indeed that very same [self], on account of the scriptural declarations concerning action, remembrance, and words. (Sūtra 9)

Is it the very same one who was in deep sleep who rises at the time of awakening, or is it another? When this doubt arises, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it must be another, because for one who has been merged into Brahman and is thus freed from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is no connection with the previous body, senses, and so forth—being indistinguishable from one who is liberated. To this, it is replied: "But he indeed [rises]. The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the opposing position. He alone rises. Why? Because of action (*karman*), recollection (*anusmṛti*), scriptural words (*śabda*), and injunctions (*vidhi*).

First, the karma—consisting of merit and demerit—performed previously while in deep sleep must be experienced by that very same person prior to the dawn of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). There is also recollection (*anusmṛti*), as in: "I who was asleep am now awake. Furthermore, scripture shows that he who has awakened from deep sleep is indeed that same person, stating: "Whatever they were here—a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a mosquito, or a gadfly, or a gnat—becoming this or that, so do they become. And there are injunctions regarding liberation.

If the objects of the waking state were useless for one who is liberated in deep sleep, then that person—freed from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and manifest in his true nature—would not exist; for with reference to deep sleep, in the passage beginning, "Now, when he is thus in deep sleep," it is said: "Indeed, at this time he does not know himself as 'I am this,' nor indeed these beings; he has gone to utter destruction; I see no enjoyment here. Thus, [the objects] are not useless.

Furthermore, regarding the liberated one, it is heard in scripture that he possesses omniscience and other such qualities: "Having attained the highest light, he appears in his own true form"; "There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing"; "He becomes self-luminous; for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds"; and "The seer sees everything; he attains everything in every way. Therefore, while transmigrating in the state of deep sleep—having exerted all his organs and being incapable of cognition or enjoyment—he attains the Supreme Self as a place of rest, and having become refreshed, he rises again for the sake of experience. || 9 ||
The section concerning the non-removal of karma and the injunctions regarding words is completed. || 3 ||
O charming one, the attainment of the half [of the body] follows by way of elimination. || 10 ||

With reference to one who has fainted (*mugdha*), it is considered: Is this state of fainting (*mūrchā*) one of the states such as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and so forth, or is it a distinct state? Regarding this doubt, since the common designation of "fainting" is established within one of the states such as deep sleep, and there is no evidence for postulating a separate state, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is one of those [known] states. To this, it is replied: "In the case of the fainted person, there is a half-attainment. In a person who has fainted, that state is a half-attainment leading toward death. Why? By the method of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*).

It is not [the state of] dream or waking, because of the absence of cognition; nor is it deep sleep or death, due to the dissimilarity of the cause and the dissimilarity of the form. For the cause of fainting (mūrchā) is such things as a blow; by process of elimination, fainting is a half-attainment of death. Death is indeed the cessation of the connection between all the vital breaths and the body, whereas fainting is the persistence of the connection with the subtle vital breath and body. The Section on the Fainting Person (Mugdha-adhikaraṇa) is completed. 4.
The Supreme possesses neither dual characteristics nor even a single characteristic, for everywhere it is so.

The specific states of the individual soul (*jīva*) have been described in order to give rise to detachment through the perception of defects. Now, in order to generate a longing for the attainment of Brahman, the author begins the demonstration that the attainable Brahman is free from defects and consists of auspicious qualities. In this regard, it is investigated whether the defects belonging to the soul—which arise from its respective locations during the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, swoon, and departure—also belong to the Supreme Brahman, who is its inner controller (*antaryāmī*), as He likewise resides in those various places; or rather, that He does not.

What is correct? That [the Lord] exists. Why? Because He abides within bodies in their respective states. But has it not been stated in such passages as, "If it be said that there is attainment of the state of enjoyment, no, because of difference," and "And because of staying and eating," that the Supreme Being is not subject to karma and thus free from defects? How then can a defect be attributed to the Supreme Brahman—who is not subject to karma—due to His connection with various locations? It is replied as follows: even karmas depend upon the body.

It has been stated in the verse "or from connection with a body" (*dehayogād vā*) that [the Lord] brings about the production of human goals (*puruṣārtha*). And that occurs because connection with a body is not itself a human goal. Otherwise, the *karmans* alone would produce suffering; what need would there be for a connection with a body?

Therefore, even though He is not subject to *karman*, connection with a body of various kinds of impurities is indeed not a human goal. Consequently, even if He enters such a body by His own will for the sake of restraining it, the connection with that which is not a human goal is unavoidable; for immersion in pus, blood, and so forth is indeed not a human goal, even if performed by one's own will.

Therefore, although Brahman is the sole cause of the universe and a mine of auspicious qualities such as omniscience, nevertheless—on account of scriptural statements such as, "He who dwells in the earth," "He who dwells in the self," "He who dwells in the eye," and "He who dwells in the semen"—it might be argued that because He abides in various places, there exist for Him the undesirable states (apuruṣārtha) consisting of connection with those respective locations. To this we reply: "Not even on account of His station is there any [impurity] for the Supreme. That is to say, even on account of His stationing in the earth, the self, and so forth, there is not even a trace of any undesirable state for the Supreme Brahman.

It is possible. Why? Because it possesses both characteristics everywhere; for in all the Śrutis and Smṛtis, the Supreme Brahman is described as having both characteristics—that is, as being endowed with the characteristics of being free from all defects and being a mine of auspicious qualities—as in: "He is free from sin, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true, and whose resolves are true"; and "He consists of all auspicious qualities, and by a mere fraction of His power He brings forth the creation of beings."

"Brahman is the sole mass of qualities such as splendor, strength, sovereignty, great awakening, excellent heroism, and power; He is the highest of the high, the Lord of the high and the low, in whom no afflictions or other defects exist. From such scriptural and traditional texts as, "The supreme state called Viṣṇu is devoid of all that is to be rejected," Brahman is indeed understood to possess both characteristics. || 11 ||
If it is argued that [the whole] exists because of its difference [from the parts], we say no, because each part is stated not to be that [whole]. || 12 ||

Just as the individual soul (jīva), despite possessing both sets of characteristics—such as being free from sin as understood from the Prajāpati statements—yet comes into contact with that which is not the supreme human goal due to the difference in its states consisting of connection with the bodies of gods and others; so too, for the Supreme Inner Controller (antaryāmī), who is by nature possessed of both sets of characteristics such as being free from sin, contact with that which is not the supreme human goal is unavoidable due to the difference in its states consisting of connection with the respective bodies of gods and others.

If this is argued, it is not so; for in each instance, that [nature] is not denied. In passages such as, "He who dwells in the earth," "He who dwells in the self," and so forth, in every successive turn it is stated, "That is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. By thus declaring the immortality of the inner controller—who exercises his own willful governance in each respective locus—any undesirable consequence resulting from those various associations is precluded. As for the individual soul (*jīva*), however, that [immortal] nature is concealed, as stated in the passage: "But through meditation on the Supreme, it is concealed."

Now, it was argued that even for one who acts according to his own will, the connection with the human goal (puruṣārtha) is unavoidable, being dependent on the specific nature of each respective object; this is not correct. For even an insentient object is not, by its very nature, of the form of a non-human goal. Rather, through the volition of the Supreme Person, in accordance with the nature of the karma of those bound by karma, a single and the same object becomes a source of pleasure or pain at different times and for different persons.

If, however, the nature of things were determined solely by the intrinsic essence of the object itself, then everything would always result in pleasure for everyone or else in pain for everyone; yet this is not observed to be the case. Thus it has been said: "O best of the twice-born, sin and merit are indeed designated as 'hell' and 'heaven. Yet a single entity leads to suffering and to happiness, to envy and to gain, and to anger. Therefore, how can an object possess a fixed, inherent nature? That very same thing, having become a source of joy, later becomes a source of pain; that very same thing leads to anger and yet also arises as a cause for serenity."

"Therefore, nothing exists that is essentially suffering, nor does anything exist that is essentially happiness. Consequently, because the individual soul (*jīva*) is subject to karma, its connection with various objects in accordance with those respective karmas would constitute a state contrary to the supreme human goal (*apuruṣārtha*); however, for the Supreme Brahman, who is self-dependent, that very same connection serves solely as the aesthetic delight of His play (*līlā*), consisting in the governance of those various diverse manifestations. || 12 ||
Moreover, some [hold] thus. || 13 ||
