Moreover, certain followers of a Vedic school (śākhins) record in their own words that within a single conjunction with a body, the individual soul (jīva) experiences what is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha), whereas the Supreme Soul (para) lacks that [suffering] and possesses a connection to splendor dependent on His sovereignty in the form of control: "Two birds, closely joined and friends, cling to the same tree; of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. (Rigveda 1.164.20).

Now, it might be argued: "Having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms"—thus, since the evolution of names and forms is preceded by the entry of the living self whose essence is Brahman, Brahman itself, being identical with that [self], possesses the form of gods, humans, and so forth, and shares in their names. Consequently, as it falls within the scope of scriptural injunctions and prohibitions such as "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice," its subjection to karma is unavoidable. To this, he replies:
"For that [Brahman] is indeed without form, because it is the principal [subject]. (Sūtra 1.2.14)

Even when Brahman enters the bodies of gods and others, being endowed with their respective forms, it remains "as if formless," meaning it is exactly like that which is devoid of form. The sense is that this [Brahman] lacks the state of being subject to karma, which is based on having a body like that of a *jīva*. Why? Because of its primacy as the sustaining agent (*nirvāhakatva*). The passage, "Space, indeed, is the sustainer of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman," demonstrates that Brahman's nature is precisely that of a sustainer of name and form, by virtue of not being touched by the effects of name and form even while entering all things.

Now, an objection may be raised: if [the Supreme] is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) by virtue of having that [individual soul] as its body, how can it be said to be "formless" (*arūpavat*), which implies a state of being devoid of any connection to form? The answer is as follows: just as the individual soul (*jīva*) has a connection to various forms by virtue of experiencing the pleasure and pain produced by those [actions], the Supreme lacks such [a connection] and is therefore formless. Furthermore, the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions (*vidhi-niṣedha-śāstra*) apply only to one who is subject to karma; therefore, the Supreme Brahman is indeed equal to the formless. Consequently, even while abiding in the form of the inner controller...

But surely, through such passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite," Brahman is understood to have a nature consisting solely of non-distinctive light. Furthermore, other qualities—such as omniscience, the power of true resolve, being the cause of the world, being the inner self of all, and having true desires—are to be understood as unreal because they are negated by such statements as "not this, not this. Therefore, how can Brahman possess both characteristics (ubhayaliṅgatva), namely, being a mine of auspicious qualities and being free from all defects? To this, he says:
"And [its qualities are real] like light, because [otherwise] there would be no purpose [for the scriptures]. (15)

And just as the nature of Brahman is accepted as being of the essence of light so that statements such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" may not be rendered meaningless, likewise, because statements declaring its possession of true volition, omniscience, being the cause of the entire universe, being the self of all, and being free from all defects such as ignorance are not to be rendered meaningless, Brahman possesses both characteristics (ubhayaliṅga). 15.
And it says: "It is merely that. (16)

Furthermore, the statement "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" and so forth establishes only that Brahman has the nature of light, but it does not negate other qualities such as the possession of true volition (satyasaṅkalpatva) understood from other scriptural passages; moreover, the object of the negation "not this, not this" will be explained immediately hereafter. || 16 ||
Furthermore, it is shown [in scripture] and is also recorded in traditional memory (smṛti). || 17 ||

Furthermore, the collection of Vedānta texts demonstrates that [the Lord] is a mine of auspicious qualities and is entirely free from all defects: "Him, the supreme Great Lord of lords, the supreme Divinity of divinities; He is the cause of the causes, the Lord of the lords of organs; there is no progenitor of Him, nor is there any ruler over Him. No effect or instrument of His is known; neither one equal to Him nor one superior to Him is seen. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.7–9)

"His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action"; "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge"; "From fear of Him the wind blows, from fear the sun rises"; "That is one Brahman’s bliss"; "From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it"; "The knower of the bliss of Brahman fears nothing whatsoever"; and "Partless, actionless, peaceful, irreproachable, and stainless," and so forth.

And it is remembered [in the Śruti]: "He who knows me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds... having pervaded this entire universe, I remain with but one part of myself. "Under my supervision, O son of Kuntī, nature brings forth the moving and the unmoving; by this cause, indeed, the world revolves. "But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self, the Imperishable Lord who, entering the three worlds, sustains them. "He is all-knowing, the doer of all, possessed of all power, and endowed with knowledge, strength, and prosperity."

"He is neither diminished nor increased; he is self-dependent, beginningless, and sovereign; he is untouched by fatigue, sloth, fear, anger, desire, and the like; he is irreproachable, supreme beyond attainment, without a substrate, and the sequence of the imperishable"—and so forth. Therefore, because Brahman, though abiding everywhere, possesses both sets of characteristics (ubhayaliṅgatva), the defects occasioned by those various locations do not touch the Supreme Brahman. || 17 ||
And for this very reason, there is a comparison with the reflection of the sun and so forth. (18)

Since the Supreme Brahman, even when situated in various locations, does not partake in the defects caused by those locations, for this very reason the scriptures employ analogies such as the sun reflected in water or a mirror to show that the Supreme Self remains faultless despite being present here and there: "Just as the one ether appears distinct within jars and other vessels, so the one Self, though dwelling in many places, is like the sun reflected in various receptacles of water. Indeed, the single Self of all beings is established in every being;
it is seen as one and also as many, like the moon in the water," and so forth. (18)
On this point, an objection is raised:
"But because it is not apprehended like water, it is not so. (Sūtra 1.1.19)

The word *tu* (but) indicates an objection. The suffix *-vat* is applied to the locative form *ambuvat* (as in water). Just as the sun and other objects are perceived in water, leaves, and so forth, the Supreme Self is not perceived in such locations as the earth and so on. For the sun and others are perceived in water and the like through delusion as if they were situated there, but in reality they are not situated there.

In this context, however, by such passages as "He who dwells in the earth," "He who dwells in the waters," and "He who dwells in the self," it is understood that the Supreme Self alone exists in the earth and other elements in the ultimate sense. Therefore, there is no attachment to the defects caused by clouds, mirrors, and so forth, because He does not actually abide in those things. Thus, the subject of the illustration (the dārṣṭāntika) does not possess that same nature; the meaning is that it is not identical to the illustration (dṛṣṭānta). || 19 ||

[The Sūtra] refutes [the objection] that [the soul] would be subject to increase and decrease because of its inclusion [within the body], since both [states] are consistent and because it is observed to be so. || 20 ||

Because the Supreme Brahman, who is the substratum, is included within the locations such as earth and so forth, the mere possibility of His being subject to defects such as increase and decrease—which belong to those locations—is refuted by the examples of the sun and others. How is this understood? It is determined that it is so because of the consistency of both [examples]; for only in this way is there consistency between the two sets of examples: "Just as the one ether appears distinct within jars and other vessels..."

In the phrase "like the sun in reservoirs of water," both the example of space—which, though actually situated [within them], is not so in reality—and the example of the sun—which is not actually situated [therein]—are employed for the purpose of establishing that the Supreme Self does not partake of the defects residing in earth and other elements. For instance, just as space, even when separately joined with various objects such as jars and water-pots that undergo increase and decrease, is not touched by the defects of increase, decrease, and the like; so too is the case here.

Just as the sun, though seen in various reservoirs of water, is not affected by the increase, decrease, or other changes occurring therein, so too this Supreme Self, though situated within the diverse forms of insentient matter such as the earth, and within sentient beings, remains untouched by the defects of their respective increases, decreases, and so forth; existing everywhere yet remaining one, He is untainted by even the scent of defect and is solely a mine of auspicious qualities.

This is what is meant: just as the sun, which in reality does not abide in water and the like, has no connection with the defects of the water and so forth due to the absence of a cause for such a connection, so too the Supreme Self, although abiding in earth and other elements, has no connection with defects because of the absence of any cause for defects, owing to His nature being the very opposite of defects. Furthermore, this is observed: even when there is no complete similarity in every respect, an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is employed based on similarity in the intended aspect, as in "the boy is like a lion" and similar expressions.

Therefore, for Him whose scent of all defects such as ignorance has been naturally dispelled and who is a mine of all auspicious qualities, no possibility of defect arises even from abiding in earth and other elements. || 20 ||

Now, it might be argued as follows: Having introduced the two forms of Brahman with the words, "Verily, there are two forms of Brahman—the formed and the formless," and having referred to the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) in its gross and subtle aspects as the form of Brahman; and having further described specific features of its appearance with the words, "The form of this very Puruṣa is like a cloth dyed with saffron," and so forth; [the text] then, by means of the word "neti" (not this), refers back to all that has been previously mentioned as the mode of Brahman, saying, "Now, therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this'; for there is nothing higher than this 'not this'."

Having negated all that, [the scripture] shows that Brahman is indeed Being-only (*sanmātra*), the substratum of all particularities (*viśeṣa*); for particularities are merely imagined by Brahman when it does not know its own nature in such a way. Therefore, how can Brahman possess both characteristics? To this, [the Sūtrakāra] says:
"For it negates the extent of what has been presented, and then declares more than that" (Sūtra 3.2.22).

This is not tenable—that the Brahman’s possession of specific attributes, which was previously mentioned, is negated by the words “not this, not this” (neti neti); for if that were so, it would be like the prattle of a deluded person. For no sane person, having first taught everything unknown through other means of knowledge as an attribute of Brahman, would then subsequently negate that very same thing.

[The opponent] objects: "Even though some of the categories being specified are established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless their mode of being as aspects (*prakāratva*) of Brahman remains unknown; and as for the others, both their essential nature and their status as aspects of Brahman are unknown. Therefore, since it is impossible to refer back to them (as something already known), they are taught right here. Consequently, their negation is not tenable. Because this is so, this sentence negates the "extent of what has been previously introduced" regarding Brahman.

The specific qualities of Brahman that have been introduced are negated by the phrase "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) because Brahman is perceived as being characterized by them. "Not this, not this" means "it is not thus, it is not thus"; Brahman does not consist merely of the aforementioned modes. The meaning is that the limitation of Brahman which was introduced as being characterized by those aforementioned modes is what is referred to here by the word "this" (*iti*). Furthermore, since after the negation the text declares a multitude of further qualities of Brahman, it follows that the negation only denies Brahman's association with the previously mentioned qualifications.

Indeed, it speaks further of the multitude of qualities: "For there is nothing else higher than this, namely 'not this, not this'; then comes the name, the Truth of truth; the vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth, and he is their truth. This is the meaning: that Brahman which has been established as "not this, not this"—there is no other reality higher than this; the meaning is that there is nothing else superior to Brahman, either by way of essential nature or by way of attributes.

And that Brahman, who is the Truth of truths, has the name "the Truth of truth. Its etymological explanation is: "The vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) are indeed truth; He is the truth of them. By the word "vital breaths," the individual souls (jīvas) are referred to by virtue of their association with the vital breaths. They are "truth" because, unlike ether and the other elements, they lack any modification consisting of a change in their essential nature. Of them, this Supreme Person is the "truth"; for while the individual souls possess contraction and expansion of knowledge according to their karma, He does not.

But for the Supreme Person, who is free from evil, those two do not exist; therefore, He is more real than even they. And thus, because of His connection with the collection of qualities mentioned in the supplementary portion of the text, the statement "not this, not this" does not negate the fact that Brahman possesses specific attributes, but rather negates only the limited extent previously attributed to it. Therefore, the supreme Brahman indeed possesses both characteristics. || 21 ||

Since Brahman is not within the scope of other means of knowledge, it is impossible to negate its forms—such as the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta)—by way of restating them as being related to it; therefore, what is stated here is a negation of its specific measure (iyattā). That very fact—that it is not within the scope of other means of knowledge—is confirmed by the Sūtra:
"For it says that it is unmanifest" (tad-avyaktam āha hi). || 22 ||

That Brahman is not manifested by any other means of valid cognition; for the Scripture says: "Its form does not stand within the range of vision; no one sees it with the eye," and "It is not grasped by the eye, nor even by speech," and so forth. || 22 ||
Moreover, [the Lord] is perceived through direct perception and inference even during the act of propitiation. || 23 ||

Moreover, it is understood from both Śruti and Smṛti that the direct realization of this [Self] occurs only through *nididhyāsana*—which consists of perfect propitiation and devotion—and not by any other means. The Śruti states: "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing; but he whom this [Self] chooses, by him is it attained. To him, this Self reveals its own form. And: "With the clarity of knowledge, one whose being is purified then sees Him, the partless, while meditating."

The Smṛti as well states: "Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in this way, O Arjuna! But by unswerving devotion alone am I, who am such, capable of being known in truth, seen in truth, and entered into, the Supreme. Since worship that has taken the form of devotion is *saṃrādhana*, its "propitiation" is said to be nothing other than pleasing [the Lord].

Therefore, when the scripture beginning with "Two indeed are the forms of Brahman" teaches the nature of Brahman for the sake of *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation), it is not capable of restating the fact that Brahman possesses two forms—the embodied and the unembodied—which were previously unestablished. || 23 ||
And there is no difference [between the knower and the known], as in the case of light and so forth; and there is illumination regarding the object through practice. 24.

For this reason as well, [the scripture] negates only the "extent of the manifest" (*prakṛtaitāvatva*) and not the fact that [Brahman] is qualified by the formal and the formless (*mūrtāmūrta*); because in the case of Vāmadeva and others who have directly realized the nature of the Supreme Brahman, it is perceived—just as in the case of light—that the qualification by the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), such as the formal, is no different from qualities like knowledge and bliss belonging to Brahman, as seen in passages such as: "Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I was Manu and I was the Sun. etc.

The light, bliss, and other qualities that constitute the very nature of Brahman are perceived by Vāmadeva and others through the practice of the rite consisting of *saṃrādhana*; likewise, for those who have practiced *saṃrādhana*, their state as qualified by both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) is also perceived without distinction—this is the meaning. || 24 ||
He concludes the statement regarding Brahman’s possession of both characteristics with the sūtra:
"Therefore, [Brahman is] with the infinite; for thus is the indicative mark. (2.1.25)

Therefore, by the reasons stated, it is established that Brahman is distinguished by an infinite multitude of auspicious qualities; for this being so, Brahman is shown to possess both characteristics. || 25 || The section concerning the possession of both characteristics is concluded.

In this section, because there is an abundance of intermediate doubts and their refutations, the comprehension of the final thesis might become confused. Anticipating this, he explains the Sūtra with the word "ataḥ" (therefore) in order to remove that confusion by concluding the ultimate thesis. For it is thus: the phrase "tathā hi sati" (when this is so), meaning when the purpose is the negation of [any] finite measure, implies that not only is the non-contradiction of the two-fold nature maintained, but rather, the two-fold nature is actually established—this is the sense.
As for those who hold that the two-fold nature exists because of the twofold designation, like a serpent and its coils: || 26 ||

The fact that the insentient phenomenal world, consisting of both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), is a form (*rūpa*) of Brahman is taught in such passages as, "There are indeed two forms of Brahman. Then, by the statement, "Now, therefore, the instruction is: 'Not this, not this'," the limitation of Brahman as being of the nature of the formed and formless insentient entities is negated. Furthermore, by the statement, "For there is nothing else higher than this 'Not this,'" it is established that there exists nothing superior to Brahman.

To establish this, it is stated: "Now, the name of the Truth is 'the Truth of truths'; the vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth, and He is their truth. This is said because, even compared to the sentient beings designated by the term *prāṇa*, He is the Truth, owing to His never having any contraction of knowledge and other attributes. Likewise, this meaning is understood from such scriptural passages as: "The Lord of the primary matter (pradhāna) and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Master of the qualities (guṇas)"; "The Lord of the universe, the Sovereign of the Self"; and "The Eternal among the eternals, the Conscious among the conscious."

Now, the manner in which that insentient entity (acidvastu) possesses the nature of Brahman is considered for the purpose of establishing the faultlessness of Brahman: does this non-sentient entity have the nature of Brahman according to the analogy of the serpent and its coils; or rather, like light and its source, through the connection with a single genus; or else, like the individual soul, through the relation of part and whole by way of being the qualifier and the qualified?

Here, having accepted the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) as that which is established, it was stated in the [Sūtras] "And the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples" (*prakṛtiśca pratijñādṛṣṭāntānuparodhāt*) and "Its non-difference [from the cause], on account of such terms as 'originating' (*ārambhaṇa*)," that the origination of Brahman—qualified by subtle sentient and insentient entities—is from Brahman itself qualified by gross sentient and insentient entities, and that there is non-difference [between them]. Which of these two views is correct? [The view] that it is like a serpent and its coils. Why? Because both descriptions are given.

Because of the designation of identity in such passages as "Brahman alone is all this" and "The Self alone is all this," and because of the designation of difference in such passages as "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self," non-sentient entities are merely particular modes of that very Brahman, just as the states of being a coil or being straight belong to a serpent. || 26 ||
Or rather, it is like light and its substratum, because of its nature as luminosity. || 27 ||

The word "vā" (or) is for the purpose of setting aside the previous position. If the very nature of Brahman were to exist in the form of the non-intelligent (acid), then the scriptural texts concerning difference, as well as those declaring that Brahman is unchanging ( apariṇāmin ), would be contradicted. Therefore, the meaning is that—just as there is identity between light and its substratum even though they are distinct by virtue of being light and [its locus] respectively—so too the non-intelligent phenomenal world (acid-prapañca) is the form of Brahman. || 27 ||
Or as before. || 28 ||

The word "vā" (or) is intended to exclude both positions. [In the first case,] because the very substance that is Brahman itself possesses particular states and thus takes on the form of non-intelligent matter (*acid-dravya*), there would be no liberation due to the aforementioned defect. Alternatively, [in the second case,] it might be argued that there is merely a connection with the genus "Brahmanhood" between non-intelligent matter and Brahman, like that between dawn and its substratum.

If that were so, then Brahman would also be a commonality (sāmānya) persisting through both the conscious and unconscious entities, just as "horseness" and "cowness" do; this would contradict all the scriptures, traditional codes, and common usage, exactly as before. Furthermore, according to the [Brahma-sūtras] "A part [of the Lord], because of the designation of diversity" and "But the Supreme is not like that, being like light," the unconscious entity is a part of Brahman by virtue of being an attribute incapable of independent existence, just as the individual soul (jīva) is.

The conventional usage of non-difference is primary insofar as [the attributes] are parts of a single distinguished entity; the conventional usage of difference is primary due to the distinction between the essential nature and intrinsic character of the qualifier and the qualified. Furthermore, the faultlessness of Brahman is thus preserved. This is because there is a negation of the definition of "non-separate existence" (aprthaksiddhi) regarding light, genus, and qualities in relation to the gem, the individual, and the substratum of the quality, respectively. || 29 ||

Furthermore, because of the negation of non-conscious attributes in Brahman through such passages as, "This indeed is that great unborn Self, undecaying and immortal; it does not decay with this [body's] decay," the relationship of part and whole exists precisely as a qualifier-qualified relationship. Therefore, it is logical that Brahman qualified by the subtle conscious and unconscious entities is the cause, while Brahman qualified by the gross conscious and unconscious entities is the effect; thus, the non-difference of the effect from the cause, the knowledge of the effect through the knowledge of the causal Brahman, and so forth, are all established.
The faultlessness of Brahman is thus preserved; and by virtue of His being faultless and a mine of auspicious qualities, His possession of both genders (ubhayaliṅgatva) is also established. || 29 ||
The section concerning the serpent and its coils is completed.
It is superior [to Brahman], because of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and distinction. (Sūtra 30)

Now, having raised the doubt through certain fallacious arguments that there exists some reality even beyond this Supreme Brahman—the ultimate cause of the world in the form of both its efficient and material cause—this [Brahman] is refuted; for this object of worship is faultless and possesses infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities.

For the sake of establishing the stability of [Brahman] as the source of all qualities, there arises this doubt: Is there some other reality even beyond this Supreme Brahman, which is characterized by both [transcendent and immanent] attributes, and from which this entire world originates? Why? Because of the designation of that Supreme as a "bridge" in the passage, "Now, that Self is a bridge, a support. And since the word "bridge" is well-known in common usage as the means for reaching the opposite bank, it is understood that there is something else to be reached beyond this.

Likewise, it is stated that this [Brahman] is something to be crossed over: "Having crossed this bridge, he who was blind becomes non-blind. Therefore, there is something else to be attained. Furthermore, because of the designation of measurement, this Supreme Brahman is measured and limited, as seen in the designation of measurement: "Brahman has four quarters and sixteen parts. And this very designation of measurement indicates the existence of that which is not measured, which is to be attained by means of that bridge.

Likewise, a designation of relationship is observed between the bridge and that which possesses the bridge, characterized by the status of being the means of attainment and the object of attainment, as in: "The supreme bridge of immortality, like fire whose fuel has been consumed," and "This is the bridge of immortality. Therefore, there exists something higher than the highest. Furthermore, that which is higher than the highest is designated as distinct [from it], in such passages as: "He reaches the Person who is higher than the highest," and "That which is higher than the highest, greater than the great."

Likewise: "All this is filled by that Person," and "That which is higher than that is formless and free from suffering. For these reasons, it is understood that there is something even beyond the supreme Brahman. || 30 ||
This being the case, it is replied: "But on account of the generality. (Sūtra 31)

The word *tu* (but) sets aside the previous position. As for what was stated—that there exists something higher than the highest because of the designation of a "bridge" (*setu*)—that is not tenable. For here, it is not said that this [Brahman] is a bridge in relation to anything to be reached; rather, it is called a bridge because of its commonality with a bridge, as the scripture states that it prevents the confusion of all worlds: "for the non-confusion of these worlds. It is called a bridge because, like the root *si* (to bind), it binds within itself the entire aggregate of sentient and insentient things without intermixture. Furthermore, in the phrase "having crossed this bridge," the verb *tarati* (crosses) signifies reaching, just as in the expression "he crosses to the end of the Veda. || 31 ||
The purpose is for the sake of cognition, as in the case of the feet. || 32 ||

This designation of measurement, namely, "the four-footed Brahman consisting of sixteen parts" and "all beings are one foot of Him," is for the purpose of the intellect—that is, for the purpose of meditation—because it is understood from such passages as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" that Brahman, the cause of the world, is unlimited, and therefore measurement is impossible by its very nature. Indeed, its status as the cause of the world is heard in scripture: "From this very Self, space was produced" and "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"

Therefore, just as the designation of speech and so forth as the "feet" of Brahman—in the passage beginning, "Speech is a foot, breath is a foot, the eye is a foot, the mind is a foot"—is for the purpose of meditation, so too is this [designation]. || 32 ||
To the question, "How can there be a measurement for that which is not itself measured, even for the purpose of worship? he says:
"On account of a particular location, as in the case of light and so forth. (Sūtra 33)

The meaning is that, due to the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of specific locations such as speech and so forth, the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of [the Self] as being measured by virtue of its connection with them is possible; just as, for example, it is possible to contemplate an extended light as being delimited by the distinctions of locations such as windows or jars. || 33 ||
And because of logical consistency. || 34 ||

As for the argument that because of the designation of a relationship between the goal and the means in the statement, "This is the bridge to the Immortal," there exists another goal distinct from the means; that is not so. For it is logical that the Supreme Person, who is the goal to be attained, is Himself the means for His own attainment, since scripture declares that He is the exclusive means: "This Self is not to be obtained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much learning. Only by whomsoever this One chooses is He obtained; to him He reveals His own form. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.3) || 34 ||
Likewise, because of the negation of others. || 35 ||

As for what was further stated—that because of designations of difference such as "that which is higher than that," "the Person higher than the high," and "higher than the Imperishable," there exists something higher than the High—that is not tenable, because in that very context anything other than That is denied: "There is nothing else higher than whom; there is no one smaller or greater than whom. This means that there is nothing else higher than Him in any manner whatsoever. Likewise elsewhere: "For there is nothing else besides this... [and so on].
The meaning is that there is nothing else superior to this Brahman which has been indicated by "not this, not this" (*neti neti*). Likewise: "No one rules over him;

his name is Great Glory. For this very Puruṣa, who was just mentioned as the material cause of the universe in such passages as, "All moments of time were born from the luminous Puruṣa," and "He milked forth these two worlds and the waters," and so on, as well as in the verse, "From the waters arose Hiraṇyagarbha—the eight [verses]," serves to identify Him as the cause of the world.

If it is asked, "Then what is meant by the phrase 'that which is higher than that'?", [the answer is: In the preceding passage, after teaching that the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman, the Great Person—stated as, "I know this great Puruṣa, the first-born, beyond darkness; knowing Him alone, one transcends death; there is no other path for the journey"—and declaring that there is no other path to immortality, [the text] provides the following justification: "Than whom there is nothing higher, than whom there is nothing lower, than whom there is none smaller and none greater."

Having established the supremacy of the Puruṣa through the verse, "Like a tree, he stands alone, steadfast in heaven; by that Puruṣa all this is filled," and having shown the impossibility of anything else being supreme, the text concludes the previously stated point with a logical reason: "That which is higher than that is formless and free from suffering; those who know this become immortal, while others enter only into suffering."

That which is the furthermost reality of the Person (puruṣatattva) is itself formless and free from affliction; therefore, those who know this reality of the Person become immortal, whereas others surely enter only into suffering.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the introductory context and a contradiction with what was stated immediately prior. In the preceding passage, "He attains the divine Person who is higher than the high," and in the phrase "higher than the Imperishable," that Supreme Person—who is omniscient and possesses qualities such as invisibility and so forth, and who is higher than the Imperishable (the unmanifest), namely the Collective Person (samaṣṭipuruṣa)—is here also referred to as "higher than the high," being described as higher than the Collective Person. || 35 ||
By this [sūtra], its omnipresence [is established] on account of the words "extent" (āyāma) and so forth. 36.

By this Brahman, the all-pervasiveness—that is, the state of pervading the entire universe—is understood from words such as *āyāma* and others that denote universal pervasion; it makes one understand that there is nothing higher than this. To begin with, the word *āyāma* [is seen in the passage]: "All this is filled by that Puruṣa," and "Whatever is seen or even heard in this world."

"Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without"; "The wise behold Him as eternal, omnipresent, extremely subtle, and imperishable, who is the source of all beings. By the word "etcetera," such passages as "All this is indeed Brahman" and "All this is indeed the Self" are included. Therefore, this Supreme Brahman alone is higher than everything. 36.
Thus ends the section concerning the Supreme (Parādhikaraṇa).
The fruit [proceeds] from Him, because that is logical. || 37 ||

It has been stated that the individual soul (jīva) is always defective in all its states, for the purpose of generating a desire to worship [the Lord], and because the object to be attained is heard of as supreme in the scriptures. || 38 ||

"He indeed is that great, unborn Self, the eater of food, the giver of wealth; for he alone causes bliss"—thus it is heard in scripture that he alone bestows the fruit consisting of enjoyment and liberation. || 38 ||
Now he states the prima facie view:
"Jaimini [holds that] dharma [is known through the Veda], for that very reason. (40.39)

For this very reason, and on account of scripture as well, the teacher Jaimini considers that only dharma—consisting of sacrifice, gift, oblation, and meditation—is the bestower of results. For in the world, actions such as agriculture or giving are seen to be the means of attaining results either directly or through a succession of steps; likewise, in the Veda too, although sacrifices, gifts, and oblations lack direct efficacy as means to results, their status as means to results is established through a succession of steps by way of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency).

Likewise, scriptural injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" also, by teaching that sacrifices and the like are duties for one who desires to attain heaven, lead to the understanding—through the necessity of another explanation being impossible—that they are the means to the fruit by way of the *apūrva*. || 39 ||
But Vādarāyaṇa holds the former view, because of the mention of a reason.

The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude the alternative view. The venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the previously stated fact—that the Supreme Person alone is the bestower of results—is indeed so. Why? Because of the designation of a cause (*hetuvyapadeśāt*). In such passages as "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," even in those very texts, the deities—such as Agni, Vāyu, and others—who constitute the objects of worship in sacrifices and other rites, are designated as the causes of their respective fruits by means of the formula "Vāyu is the swiftest deity; [one should sacrifice] to Vāyu with his own... and so forth. Thus, it is established that the Supreme Person alone is the bestower of results.

In passages such as, "He approaches with his own portion; he alone leads him to prosperity," there is an instruction regarding the manner in which one who desires [a result] may achieve the means for attaining the fruit they wish to accomplish.

Since even this [aspect] is precisely what is required by the injunction (*vidhi*), it is not reasonable to suspect that the scripture is not intent upon it. Furthermore, when the manner in which [the act] is a means to the fruit is understood from the word itself—even though such a manner was previously required—authoritative persons do not tolerate its abandonment, nor the postulation of an unscriptural *apūrva* and so forth. Moreover, it has already been stated that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others express the fact that the root-meaning—the sacrifice and so on, which consists in the propitiation of a deity—is to be accomplished by the agent's activity (*kartṛvyāpāra*), a fact established by linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) and sanctioned by the grammatical treatises (*śabdānuśāsana*); they do not denote anything else that is non-worldly (*alaukika*).

Thus, from such scriptural statements as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity," it is understood that Vāyu and others are the bestowers of results. Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that the Supreme Person alone exists as the object of worship and the giver of results in the form of Vāyu and the rest: "The center of the universe sustains the world—the sacrifices and works of public utility, the many things born and being born; He is indeed Agni, He is Vāyu, He is Sūrya, and He is Candramas."

And in the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa it is heard: "He who dwells in the wind, whose body is the wind; he who dwells in fire; he who dwells in the sun," and so forth. And it is also stated in the Smṛti: "Whatever form a devotee desires to worship with faith, I make that very faith of his unshakable. Endowed with that faith, he seeks the propitiation of that [deity] and thereby obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by Me alone."

"For I am indeed the enjoyer and the Lord of all sacrifices"—here, "Lord" (prabhu) means the bestower of the fruit. And: "The worshippers of the gods go to the gods; My devotees come to Me; even those who sacrifice to Me come to Me. In the world as well, people acquire various kinds of material goods through agriculture and other means, and then honor the king either through his servants or directly; and it is observed that the king, being thus honored, bestows a reward corresponding to that specific worship.

The Vedānta texts, however, establish the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)—who transcends the sphere of all other possible means of valid cognition, who is free from even the slightest scent of defects such as ignorance, and who is an ocean of natural, infinite, unsurpassed, and immeasurable noble qualities—and they describe His modes of worship consisting of sacrifice, charity, and burnt offerings, as well as praise, prostration, chanting, worship, and pilgrimage; and they declare that from the Supreme Person thus propitiated, there arises the fruit in the form of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Thus, everything is entirely consistent. || 40 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the fruit (phalādhikaraṇa). 8.
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
There is the same cognition regarding all Vedānta texts, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth. || 1 ||

It has been stated everything that needed to be said regarding Brahman, up to its status as the bestower of fruits, for the purpose of generating the desire to meditate upon it. Now, the investigation into the distinction between various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*) is commenced in order to determine whether there is a combination or an optionality of attributes in the meditations on Brahman. First, it is considered whether a single meditation, such as the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, which is heard of in multiple Vedic branches (*śākhā*), constitutes one and the same knowledge or constitutes distinct knowledges.

For this very reason, the restriction that the teaching of this knowledge of Brahman is to be imparted only to those Ātharvaṇikas who have duly performed the *śirovrata*—as stated in the text, "One should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to those by whom the *śirovrata* has been performed according to rule"—is appropriate. For if the knowledge were one and the same, then since the *śirovrata*, as an auxiliary to that knowledge, would apply to followers of other branches as well, such a restriction would be untenable. This being the position, it is replied: the meditation is one and the same, recognized across all Vedānta texts. Why? Because there is no difference in the injunctions (*codanā*) and so forth. First, the injunction is of the nature: "One should meditate," "One should know," and so on.

This refers to the injunction regarding the specific meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the conjunctions, forms, and names mentioned in the *Sūtra* of the section on different recensions (*śākhāntara*) of the Karma-kāṇḍa—namely, "Or [it is] one, because there is no difference in conjunction, form, injunction, and name"—are included. Because these injunctions and so forth are not different, it is recognized as the same knowledge (*vidyā*) in another recension; for instance, in both the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka, the injunction "one meditates upon Vaiśvānara" is of a single uniform nature, since the essential nature [of the object] is defined solely by what is to be known.

Because the Vaiśvānara who is the object of knowledge is one and the same, the form [of the meditation] is also not different. The name, "Vaiśvānara-vidyā," is likewise identical. Furthermore, the connection with the fruit—attaining Brahman—is also identical in both cases. Therefore, due to this recognition through these [factors], there is unity of the vidyā even across different recensional branches (śākhā). || 1 ||

Having restated the objection that the unity of the knowledge (vidyā) is not established because a difference in the things to be enjoined is perceived due to the repetition of the same words without distinction and because of a change of context, he refutes it with the sūtra: "If it be said [there is no unity] on account of the difference [of details], we say no, even in the case of a single [knowledge]. (2)

If it be argued that because of the repetition of the text without distinction and because of the difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*), there is a difference in what is enjoined (*vidheya*) and thus no unity of knowledge (*vidyaikyam*), we reply: even within a single knowledge, the repetition of the text and the difference in context are justified by the difference in the persons who receive the instruction (*pratipattṛ*). For where, in the case of a single person receiving instruction, both repetition and a different context exist, then—due to the impossibility of any other explanation—a difference in knowledge arises from the difference in what is enjoined; but when there is a difference in the persons receiving instruction, since the repetition and so forth are justified as being for the sake of their respective understanding, there is no possibility of a further thing to be enjoined (*vidheyāntara*) therein. || 2 ||

As for what was said—that a difference in knowledge (vidyā) is perceived because a restrictive rule regarding the instruction of that knowledge is seen only among the Ātharvaṇikas who observe the "head-vow" (śirovrata)—to this he replies: "For [the rule] applies to the study of one's own Veda; since it is authorized in the *Samācāra* [Smṛti], its restriction is like that of the *Sava* sacrifice. (Sūtra 3).

It is not the case that the observation of the rule for the instruction of the "head-vow" (śirovrata) indicates a difference in the knowledge (vidyā), because the head-vow is not an integral part of the knowledge. For if it were so [an integral part], then the rule regarding it would be for the sake of establishing the status of the Vedic study (svādhyāya) as such; indeed, the rule for the instruction of the head-vow is for the sake of establishing that the Vedic study possesses the refinement (saṃskāra) produced by it, and not for the sake of the knowledge itself.

Why is this so? Because of the connection with study in the statement, "One who has not observed the vow should not study this"; because of the qualification in the *Samācāra* [text]; because of the extended application (*atideśa*) in the work called *Samācāra*, which says, "This too is explained by means of the Vedic vow"; and because the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is shown [to belong] to them alone in the passage, "To them alone one should declare this knowledge of Brahman. || 4 ||

Furthermore, scripture demonstrates that meditative worship (upāsana) is characterized by the same content across all Vedānta texts. For instance, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, after stating, "That which is within it is what must be sought," the text poses the question, "What is there that is to be sought? and subsequently declares that the Supreme Self, distinguished by the eight qualities such as freedom from sin, is the object of worship therein.

In the Taittirīyaka, however, by referring back to the instruction found in the Chāndogya, it is stated: "Therein is the small ether free from sorrow; that which is within it is to be meditated upon. Thus, the meditation on the Supreme Self as characterized by the eight qualities is taught; this is possible only through the combination of qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra) based on the identity of the knowledge (vidyaikatva) in both places. || 4 ||

Thus, having established the identity of the knowledge (vidyaikya) as proven in the section concerning different recensions (śākhāntarādhikaraṇa), he states its purpose: "There is a combination [of details] because there is no difference in the object, as in the case of supplementary injunctions, when [the knowledge] is the same. (Sūtra 5)
Thus, since meditation is the same in all Vedāntas, the qualities mentioned in one Vedānta must be combined with those mentioned in another Vedānta; why is that?

Because there is no difference in the object, as in the case of supplementary ritual details (*vidhiśeṣa*). Just as a quality heard in one Vedāntic text—such as those belonging to the Vaiśvānara or Dahara meditations—is practiced for the sake of accomplishing its purpose, which consists in assisting that meditation through its connection with it, so too a quality mentioned in another Vedāntic text must be combined (*upasaṃhartavya*), since it is likewise connected to that same meditation and thus assists it without distinction. The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis. The section on the uniformity of all Vedāntas (*sarvavedāntapratyayādhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
If it is argued that there is a change [in the cognition] because of the word, we say no, because there is no distinction.

Thus, it has been stated that because there is no difference in the injunctions and other such factors, the unity of the knowledge (vidyā) follows, and that when there is unity, the combination of qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra) must be performed. Hereafter, with reference to certain specific knowledges, it is determined by investigating whether or not there is a non-difference in the injunctions and other factors that serve as grounds for recognition. There exists [the meditation on] the Udgītha...

The *Vidyā* belongs to both the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas. Regarding the Vājasaneyins first: beginning with "Two classes indeed were the offspring of Prajāpati, the gods and the Asuras," and continuing with "Those gods said, 'Come, let us overcome the Asuras in the sacrifice by means of the Udgītha,'" they propose the destruction of the Asuras through the Udgītha. Having stated that the Udgītha is subject to defeat by the Asuras when viewed as speech (*vāk*) and the other organs up to the mind (*manas*), they then describe the defeat of the Asuras through the vision of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the Udgītha, starting from "Then they spoke to this Prāṇa within the mouth," and so on, concluding with "He prospers in himself, while his enemy perishes."

"He who knows thus becomes one whose enemy is defeated"—thus, the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the *udgītha* is enjoined for the fruit of conquering enemies. Similarly, among the Chandogas, beginning with "The gods and the Asuras, indeed, once contended," and continuing with "Then the gods took up the *udgītha*, [thinking] 'By this we shall strike them down,'" they first propose the defeat of the Asuras through the *udgītha*. Then, having pointed out the defects in meditating upon speech and the other organs as the *udgītha*, they state: "Now, they meditated upon that which is this principal breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) as the *udgītha*."

Having stated that the defeat of the Asuras occurred through the meditation on the *udgītha* as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), beginning with truth, it is said: "Just as a clod of earth striking a solid stone is shattered, even so is he shattered who desires evil against one who knows this. Thus, for the purpose of defeating enemies, the meditation on the *udgītha* as the vital breath is enjoined; for even though no verbal suffix expressing an injunction (*vidhi-pratyaya*) regarding the object of knowledge is heard here, there is a result [which implies an injunction].

Because it is heard that [the meditation] is a means (*sādhana*), an injunction (*vidhi*) having knowledge as its object is inferred. Although meditations such as that on the *udgītha* have the excellence of the sacrifice (*kratusādguṇya*) as their fruit by virtue of being for the sake of the sacrifice, it has been established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* that even a fruit mentioned in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) must be accepted provided it is not contradictory to that. In this regard, a doubt arises: is there identity of the meditations here, or not? What is the correct view? That there is identity of the meditations. Why? Because in both cases, the *udgītha* itself—upon which the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is superimposed—is heard to be the object of meditation, and because there is no difference in the injunction (*codanā*) and other factors.

To begin with, the connection with the fruit—consisting in the overcoming of enemies—is not distinct; the form (*rūpa*) is also not distinct because of the identity of the object of meditation known as the *udgītha*, upon which the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been superimposed; the injunction (*codanā*), consisting in the meaning of the verbal root *vid* (to know), is likewise not distinct; and the name, "the *udgītha*-knowledge," is also not distinct. Here, having raised an objection from the perspective of the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he refutes it: "If it be argued that there is a difference on account of the word, we say no, because there is no distinction. As for what was stated—that there is identity of knowledge—that is not tenable, because of the difference in form.

Indeed, a difference in form is understood from the word itself; for in the Vājasaneyaka, after describing the defeat of the Asuras by viewing the breath (*prāṇa*) as the agent of the *udgītha* chant—stating, "Then they said to this breath in the mouth, 'Chant the *udgītha* for us,' and he, the breath, chanted for them"—the text concludes with "He who knows thus," whereby, by virtue of the word "thus" (*evam*), it is understood that the view of the breath as the agent alone is intended. In the Chāndogya, however, it says, "Then they meditated upon that very chief breath as the *udgītha*," [referring] to the *udgītha* chant.

Having described the defeat of the Asuras by means of the vision of the vital breath (prāṇa) upon the ritual *udgītha*, the text states, "He who desires evil against one who knows thus"; because of the word "thus," the vision of the vital breath is prescribed specifically upon the ritual *udgītha*.

Therefore, because there is a clear difference in form—due to the term "meditation on the vital breath" (*prāṇadṛṣṭi*) being applied to the agent in one instance and to the object in another—and because a difference in the forms implies a difference in the injunctions to be performed, the mere absence of distinction in the *codanā* (the scriptural impetus) and other factors is irrelevant; thus, the meditations must be distinct. To this we say: no, for in both cases, without distinction, the overcoming of others by means of the *udgītha* is perceived in the opening statement. In the Vājasaneyaka, it is heard in the opening: "Those gods said, 'Come, let us overcome the Asuras in the sacrifice by means of the *udgītha*.'"

In the Chāndogya as well, we find: "The gods, indeed, took hold of the Udgītha, thinking, 'By this we shall strike them down. Therefore, in order not to contradict the introductory statement, the Udgītha—in which the nature of Prāṇa has been superimposed—is referred to as the agent of the act of singing (udgāna), just as rice and other materials are referred to as agents in the acts of cooking and so forth, with the intent of expressing an excellence of facility. Otherwise, the word "Udgītha" occurring in the introduction would have to be taken figuratively in the sense of the agent. Thus, the oneness of the meditation (vidyaikyam) [is established]. To this, we reply:
"Not so, because of the difference in context, as in the case of the 'Higher than the High' (parovarīyastva) and other meditations. (Sūtra 7)

He refutes the position that there are nine [meditations]; for this is not the case, namely, that there is identity of knowledge. Why? Because of the difference in context. Having introduced the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) as a constituent part of the *udgītha* in the passage, "One should meditate on this syllable, the *udgītha*," and then beginning with, "Now follows the further explanation of this syllable," and "The gods and the Asuras, indeed, once contended," it continues, "Then they meditated upon that which is this chief vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the *udgītha*."

Thus, the Chandogas study a meditation concerning the *praṇava*, which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*; however, the Vājasaneyins, because they lack such a preceding context, study the entire *udgītha*—beginning with "Come, let us overcome the Asuras at the sacrifice by means of the *udgītha*" and continuing with "Then they said to this breath in the mouth, 'Sing for us as the *udgātṛ*'" and so forth. Therefore, due to the difference in context (*prakaraṇa*), there is a difference in what is enjoined (*vidheya*), and due to the difference in what is enjoined, there is a difference in form (*rūpa*); thus, there is no identity of knowledge (*vidyaikyam*). Furthermore, [the Vājasaneyins] state: "Now, this indeed is the principal breath (*mukhya prāṇa*); that [is the *udgītha*]... and so on.

Thus, it is the very *praṇava*, which was previously introduced as a constituent part of the *udgītha* and upon which the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been superimposed, that is to be meditated upon by the Chandogas; whereas for the Vājasaneyins, the Udgātṛ priest, who is the performer of the entire *udgītha*, is to be meditated upon through the vision of the vital breath.

Then they said to the breath in the mouth, "Sing the Udgītha for us"; "So be it," and this breath sang the Udgītha for them. Having thus pointed out the superimposition of the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa) upon the Udgātṛ priest, the text prescribes that the Udgātṛ himself, in whom the state of being the vital breath has been superimposed, is the object of meditation, as in the passage, "He who knows thus. Consequently, there is a difference in form (rūpabheda). Nor should one suspect a contradiction with the introductory narrative of the story—"By means of the Udgītha, let us overcome [the demons]"—once the Udgātṛ is prescribed as the object of meditation.

In the meditation on the Udgātṛ priest, because the Udgītha—which is the object of the act of singing—is necessarily required, that [meditation] also serves as a cause for the fruit known as "the humiliation of others. Therefore, due to the difference in form, there is a difference in the meditations; thus, even though the injunctions and other factors are not different, there is no identity of the meditations. Just as in the case of the "higher than the high" (parovarīyastva) and so forth, although there is a similarity in the prescription of the vision of the Supreme Self upon the syllable *praṇava*—which is a constituent part of the Udgītha—even within a single Śākhā, the prescription of the vision of the golden person (*hiraṇmayapuruṣa*) constitutes a distinct matter from the prescription of the vision characterized by qualities such as being "higher than the high. || 7 ||
If it is argued that this is due to conventional designation, then it has already been stated that even such a thing exists.

If it is argued that the identity of the knowledge is established because of the identity of the name "Udgītha-vidyā," such identity of name exists even when there is a difference in the injunctions; for example, the name "Agnihotra" applies both to the obligatory Agnihotra and to the Agnihotra within the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana sacrifice, and likewise the name "Udgītha-vidyā" applies to the many different meditations taught in the first chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. || 8 ||
And because of pervasion, [the word] is properly applicable. || 9 ||

In the first chapter (*prapāṭhaka*) of the *Chāndogya*, even in the various meditations (*vidyā*), there is a pervasive treatment of the *praṇava*—which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*—as the object of meditation from its very first introduction. Consequently, the occurrence of the word *udgītha* in the passage, "The gods indeed took up the *udgītha*" (*taddha devā udgīthamājahruḥ*), is most appropriately understood as referring to the *praṇava*. Furthermore, the use of a term for a whole to denote a part is observed in common usage, such as in "the cloth is burnt. Therefore, it is the *praṇava* itself, as a constituent part of the *udgītha*, that is indicated by the word *udgītha*; thus, it is that very [syllable] which is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

In the *Chāndogya*, he is to be meditated upon as the syllable *oṃ*; however, in the *Vājasaneyaka*, since the word "udgītha" refers to the entire *udgītha* chant, the *udgātṛ* priest who performs the entire *udgītha* is to be meditated upon as the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Thus, the difference between the two meditations is established. || 9 || The section concerning "Otherwise-ness" is concluded.
These others [are included] because there is no difference from all [of them]. 10.

The Prāṇa-vidyā is taught in both the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka: "He who knows the oldest and the best indeed becomes the oldest and the best; the Prāṇa, verily, is the oldest and the best," and so forth. Having established the Prāṇa as the object of meditation characterized by the qualities of being the oldest and the best, and having then attributed to speech, sight, hearing, and mind the qualities known as pre-eminence (*vasiṣṭhatva*), stability (*pratiṣṭhātva*), prosperity (*sampad*), and abode (*āyatanatva*), [the text proceeds] regarding speech and the others, and the body...

Having established the preeminence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by demonstrating that its own existence depends upon it and that various functions depend upon it, [the text] further establishes that qualities such as "being the most excellent" (*vasiṣṭha*), which were heard in connection with speech and the other senses, actually belong to the vital breath. Thus, in both the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka Upaniṣads, the vital breath—characterized by the qualities of being the oldest (*jyeṣṭha*) and the most excellent (*śreṣṭha*), as well as the qualities of being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*) and so forth—is presented as the object of meditation.

In the Kauṣītakins' teaching on the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*), the vital breath is established as the object of meditation precisely with the qualities of being the oldest and the best; however, qualities related to speech and the other organs—such as being the "belonging to Vasiṣṭha" (*vāsiṣṭhatva*) and so forth—are not established here as belonging to the vital breath. In this regard, a doubt arises: is there a difference in the meditative knowledge (*vidyā*) here, or not? What is the correct view? That it differs. Why? Because of the difference in form (*rūpa*).

Although in both cases the vital breath (prāṇa) alone, characterized by the qualities of being the oldest and the best, is the object of meditation, nevertheless, in one instance the vital breath is understood to be meditated upon as endowed with further qualities such as being the most excellent (vasiṣṭhatva) and so forth.

But since in the other [text] he is devoid of those qualities, there is a difference in the form of the object of meditation, and thus a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*)—this being the position reached—we reply: "Because of the non-difference of all [elements], these [qualities] exist elsewhere; here there is no difference in the knowledge. Elsewhere, even in the *Prāṇavidyā* of the Kauṣītakins, these qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhatva*) and so forth are also objects of meditation. Why? Because of the non-difference of everything; for even there, the entire method of establishing the pre-eminence and superiority of the *prāṇa*, as promised at the outset, remains non-different.

For instance, in the Prāṇavidyā of the Chāndogyas and Vājasaneyins, having commenced with the passages, "These deities indeed disputed for pre-eminence" and "quarreling for pre-eminence," and having demonstrated that upon the departure of each one beginning with Speech, the other sense organs along with the Prāṇa and the body remained intact in their respective functions, and having stated that upon the departure of the Prāṇa all of them fell apart and became incapable of performing their functions, [the text establishes] the superiority of the Prāṇa over all others, such as the senses, by virtue of its being the substratum of their existence and their dependence on it for their functioning.

The preeminence [of Prāṇa] has been established. Thus, the dependence of the functions of speech and the other organs upon Prāṇa has been demonstrated. This is further confirmed by the speech and the other organs themselves, as stated in passages such as: "Then Speech said to him: 'Insofar as I am the most excellent (vasiṣṭha), you are that most excellent one. Even in the Prāṇa-vidyā of the Kauṣītakins, qualities such as being the most excellent are attributed to Speech and the others for the purpose of establishing the preeminence and superiority of Prāṇa.

It has been established [in the preceding section] by the passage beginning, "Then those deities approached their father Prajāpati and said, 'Who among us is the best? that the qualities residing in speech and the other organs, as well as speech and the others themselves, and even the body, are dependent upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*); thus, the preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*) of the *prāṇa* was demonstrated. However, this was not merely a restatement of the fact that the qualities of speech and the others—such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhatva*), and so forth—are dependent on the *prāṇa*; for there is no difference in form here, since it is precisely by demonstrating that the functions of speech and the others, though endowed with qualities such as excellence, are dependent on the *prāṇa*, that [the point is made].

Since it is established that the Prāṇa is the cause of the qualities such as being the most excellent (vasiṣṭhatva) in speech and the other organs, that very causality of speech’s excellence and so forth constitutes the Prāṇa’s possession of the qualities of excellence and the rest. Therefore, because of the possession of these qualities like excellence here as well, the Prāṇa is recognized as the eldest; thus, there is no difference between the two meditations. || 10 || The section on the non-difference of all [meditations] is concluded.

Another investigation concerning the scope of the limbs (*aṅga*) of the science of breath (*prāṇavidyā*) will be undertaken immediately hereafter. Just as in the Kauṣītaki Prāṇavidyā, qualities such as being the best (*vasiṣṭhatva*)—though not explicitly mentioned—are understood because the meditation on pre-eminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*) and excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*) is impossible without the meditation on those qualities, so too this point is established in the sūtra *Ānandādayaḥ pradhānasya* (1.3.11): those attributes without which the meditation on the nature of Brahman is untenable must be meditated upon in all meditations on Brahman.

In this regard, it is deliberated whether there is a synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) of the qualities of the nature of Brahman in all higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), or not. Since there is no authority for the synthesis of qualities studied outside of a specific context, the conclusion reached is that synthesis applies only to those qualities heard within a specific context. To this we reply: "Bliss and so forth [belong] to the Principal," because of non-difference; this [phrase] continues from the previous sūtra. Because the Principal—the possessor of qualities, namely Brahman—is non-different in all meditations, and because the qualities do not exist apart from the possessor of qualities, bliss and the other qualities belonging to Him must be synthesized everywhere. || 11 ||

If that were so, then because they are not distinct from the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), just like bliss (*ānanda*) and the rest, the attributes such as having joy as the head (*priya-śirastva*)—which are heard in passages such as "Joy indeed is its head"—would also necessarily apply everywhere as qualities of Brahman. To this he says:
"There is no application of having joy as the head and so forth, for increase and decrease exist only where there is difference. (Sūtra 1.1.12)

When the attainment of the qualities of the nature of Brahman is being discussed, qualities such as having pleasure as the head (*priyaśirastva*) and so forth are not attained, because they are not qualities of Brahman; for qualities such as having pleasure as the head are included merely within the figurative representation (*rūpaṇa*) of Brahman as having a human form. Otherwise, if there were a distinction of limbs such as head, wings, and tail, it would follow that Brahman also undergoes increase and decrease (*upacayāpacaya*). And if that were the case, it would contradict such scriptural passages as, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite."

12 || [Objection: "But surely, in this very way, since the infinite qualities related to Brahman—such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), profundity (*gāmbhīrya*), magnanimity (*audārya*), and compassion (*kāruṇya*)—exist merely as non-different from the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), the doubt for the next sūtra is raised with the word 'but surely' (*nanu*). The particle *eva* in "in this very way" (*evameva*) connects to the subsequent statement: "In this very way, they would follow here. Since such an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is unavoidable, if there were a collection (*upasaṃhāra*) even of those qualities not explicitly mentioned in a given context, then everything would apply everywhere; furthermore, there would be an inability to collect them all due to their infinity. To this, he says: "But the others, on account of the sameness of purpose" (Sūtra 3.3.13). || 13 ||

The word "but" (tu) sets aside the objection; however, the other qualities such as bliss (ānanda) and so forth follow everywhere because of the identity of the object. Those qualities which are identical with the object—insofar as they are attributes that define the very nature of the object and are inseparable from the cognition of the object—follow everywhere like the nature of the object itself. And these qualities are truth (satya), knowledge (jñāna), bliss (ānanda), purity (amala), and infinity (anantatva). Brahman, characterized as the cause of the universe by the passage beginning with "from which indeed these [beings arise]," is described as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinity" and "Bliss indeed is Brahman."

Thus, bliss (*ānanda*) and other qualities are defined by their very nature. Therefore, for the sake of comprehending the essential nature of Brahman as the object of meditation, bliss and the rest recur in all meditations (*vidyās*). As for those qualities such as compassion which are recognized as belonging to Brahman whose nature has been thus defined—although these qualities do not exist apart from the possessor of the qualities (*guṇin*), they need not be combined [in every meditation] because they lack a necessary connection to the cognition [of the essence]. Hence, only those qualities that are heard in a particular context should be combined there; this is faultless. || 13 ||

If, due to the consequence of [the Brahman's] increase and decrease, the qualities such as having a head that is dear and so forth are intended merely for the sake of figuratively representing the Brahman as being human-shaped, and are not actual attributes of the Brahman, then for what purpose is this figurative representation of the Brahman—which is not of such a form—as being of such a form performed? For when something that is not of a certain nature is represented as being of that nature, there must be some specific purpose; just as [in the case of the statement], "He who knows himself... [as the Brahman].

It has been stated that in passages such as "Know the charioteer," the description of the meditator and his instruments as a charioteer, a chariot, and so forth, is intended for the purpose of bringing under control the body, senses, and other means belonging to the meditation. However, no such purpose is seen here [in the case of the qualities like having joy as the head]. Therefore, one must necessarily accept that qualities such as having joy as the head are attributes of Brahman. To this, he says:
"For the sake of meditation, because there is no other purpose. (1.2.14)

Because there is no other purpose, the instruction regarding the representation [of Brahman] as a form is given for the sake of meditation (*ādhyāna*). Meditation means constant reflection; it is called worship (*upāsana*). Indeed, for the sake of establishing the realization in the form of meditation—as taught in the passage "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"—the Brahman consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is presented by dividing it into the forms of joy, delight, and so forth, and representing it as having a head, wings, and other limbs, in order to facilitate the comprehension of Brahman as the one consisting of bliss.

Just as this body, consisting of food (*annamaya*), is superimposed upon the intellect by means of its head, wings, and so forth—as in the passage, "Of that, this indeed is the head"—and just as those consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*), mind (*manomaya*), and consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) are [superimposed] by means of their heads and so forth, as in the passage, "Of that, breath itself is the head."

The parts, such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), are superimposed upon the intellect (*buddhi*); in the same way, the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), which is a distinct entity from these [parts], is also superimposed upon the intellect for the sake of meditation by means of its constituent parts—namely, joy (*priya*), delight (*moda*), and so forth—which are figuratively represented as the head and other limbs. Thus, because the possession of a head made of joy and the rest serve merely as indicators for the Self consisting of bliss, they do not necessarily persist whenever there is a cognition of the Self consisting of bliss. || 14 ||
And because of the word "self. (Sūtra 15)

Because of the designation by the word "Self" in the phrase "another inner Self consisting of bliss," and because a head, wings, and a tail are impossible for the [actual] Self, it is understood that its having joy as a head and so forth is merely a figurative representation intended for easy comprehension. || 15 ||

[Objection: But since the word "self" (ātman) was previously used even for non-selves in the passages, "Another inner self consisting of breath" (prāṇamaya) and "Another inner self consisting of mind" (manomaya), how can it be determined that the word "self" in the passage, "Another inner self consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), refers to the [true] Self? To this, he says:
"The grasping as 'Self' [occurs] because of what follows, as in other cases. (Sūtra 1.1.16)

In the passage, "Another inner self consists of bliss," the word *ātman* refers exclusively to the Supreme Self; this is just as in other instances, where in passages such as, "Verily, in the beginning this was the Self alone, one only; He thought: 'Let me now create the worlds,'" the word *ātman* refers exclusively to the Supreme Self—so it is here. Why is this so? Because of the subsequent statement concerning the one consisting of bliss: "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate. (Sūtra 1.1.16)
If it is argued that [the self exists] because of positive concomitance (anvaya), [we reply] that this would be so only due to a restrictive determination (avadhāraṇa). || 17 ||

If it be argued that because the word "Self" (ātman) is seen applied to non-self entities such as the "consisting of breath" (prāṇamaya) in the preceding sections, the meaning cannot be determined from what follows, [we reply]: it can indeed be determined because of the definitive statement. Why? Because of the definitive statement; for even in the preceding section, in the passage "From this very Self, space was produced," there is nothing new, since it describes the effects of the Supreme Self alone. || 18 ||

Now that which is supplementary to the previously introduced knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) is considered. In both the *Chāndogya* and the *Vājasaneyaka*, having stated that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the object of meditation as being the oldest and best, water is designated as the clothing of the vital breath. In the *Chāndogya*, it says: "She said, 'What shall be my clothing? They replied, 'Water. Therefore, those who are about to eat surround [the food] with water both before and after; he indeed becomes a possessor of clothing and does not remain naked."

In the Vājasaneyaka, when asked by Prāṇa, "What is my garment?", Vāk and the others replied, "Water is the garment. Regarding this, the learned Śrotriyas, before eating, sip water, and after eating, they sip water; thinking thereby that they are making this very [Prāṇa] non-naked. Therefore, it is said: "One who knows this should sip water before eating and should sip water after eating; thereby he makes this very one non-naked. In this regard, a doubt arises: is the sipping of water (ācamana) enjoined here, or is it the contemplation of water as the garment of Prāṇa?

Because the injunctive suffix is heard in the rule regarding sipping water—"One should sip water before eating, and one should sip water after eating"—whereas there is no injunctive suffix in the passage concerning knowledge, "By this very [act], he makes that food non-naked," the mention of being "non-naked" is merely a eulogy.

And because the syntactical connection is established by that very purpose, it follows that since rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) as an ancillary to eating is already obtained through Smṛti and custom, another rinsing of the mouth is enjoined as an ancillary to the Prāṇa-vidyā by the force of the injunctive suffix. To this we reply: here, what is enjoined as something new and not previously obtained is the contemplation of these waters for rinsing as being the "clothing" of the Prāṇa; the meaning is that because of the "description of what is already known" (i.e., the act of rinsing), which is obtained from other sources, and because the word has its purpose in describing what was not previously established.

The meaning is as follows: since the beginning and conclusion of the passage—namely, "What is my garment?", "Water is my garment," and "They clothe him with water"—are understood to have the purpose of enjoining the contemplation of water as the garment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and since the act of sipping water is already established by Smṛti and custom, the text merely restates the sipping of water and enjoins the mental reflection upon those waters as being the garment of the vital breath.

For this very reason, in the Chāndogya [Upaniṣad], it is stated: "Therefore, those who are about to eat wrap this [the mouth] around with water both before and after," thus mentioning only the wrapping around with water, not the sipping (ācamana). The section concerning the description of the action (kāryākhyānādhikaraṇa) is concluded.
And it is the same because there is no difference. || 19 ||

In the *Vājasaneyaka*, within the *Agnirahasya*, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā is taught, beginning with: "One should meditate on Brahman as Truth; for this person indeed consists of resolve," and continuing: "He should meditate on the Self as consisting of mind, having the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) as its body, whose form is light, whose resolve is true, [and which is] space..."
