Thus, in that very same Bṛhadāraṇyaka, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā is again taught: "This person consists of mind, is composed of light, and is true; within his heart, like a grain of rice or a grain of barley, he is the ruler of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of all; he governs this entire universe, whatever exists. In this regard, there arises a doubt: is there a difference here [between these two passages], or not?

It might be argued that, although there is no difference regarding the designation of the connection [with Brahman], there is a distinction between the meditations (*vidyā*) due to a difference in form caused by the different qualities to be meditated upon, such as "lordliness" (*vaśitva*) and so on. To this, it is replied: "In the same way, they are identical. Just as in the *Agnirahasya* it is heard that [Brahman] consists of mind (*manomaya*), has vital breath for its body (*prāṇaśarīra*), has light for its form (*bhārūpa*), and possesses a multitude of qualities such as "truthful resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), so too in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, when the qualities beginning with "consisting of mind" are common, there is no difference in form because the additional qualities like lordliness do not differ from the quality of truthful resolve. Therefore, the meditation is one and the same. (Sūtra 19)
The section on coreferentiality is completed.
In the same way, it is due to the connection [of the word] even in other cases as well. || 20 ||

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, beginning with "Truth is Brahman," and then starting with "That which is Truth is yonder sun—the person who is in this orb, and also the one in the right eye"—it is stated that the Brahman of Truth is to be meditated upon as having the *vyāhṛtis* as its body within both the solar orb and the eye. Then two secret names (*upaniṣads*) are given: "Its secret name is 'Ahar' with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*)," and "Its secret name is 'Aham' with respect to the self (*adhyātma*)."

In the *Nidāna-sūtra*, two secret names (*rahasyanāmanī*) are recorded as being supplementary to the meditation (*upāsana*). A doubt arises: are these restricted to their specific locations as heard in the text, or are both to be applied in both places without restriction? Since the Brahman to be meditated upon—whose body consists of the *vyāhṛtis*—is connected to both locations, and since there is no difference in form due to the identity of the quality and no difference in conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it follows that the meditations (*vidyā*) are one and the same, and thus there is no restriction. This is stated [in the sūtra]: "Because of the connection, it is so even elsewhere."

Just as there is a combination of qualities because of the unity of the meditation—due to the non-difference of form resulting from the oneness of that which is distinguished by qualities such as "consisting of mind"—so too, elsewhere, because of the oneness of the True (Satya) Brahman related to the eye and the sun, there is a combination of both [qualities] in both places due to the unity of the meditation. || 20 ||
This being the case, we reply:
"Not so, because of a distinction. (Sūtra 21)

Nor is it the case that there is a combination [of details] because of the identity of the knowledge (*vidya*). Why? Because of a distinction—namely, a distinction in the form of the object of meditation (*upāsya*). Even though Brahman is one, in one instance it is to be meditated upon as residing in the solar orb, while in the other it is to be meditated upon as having the eye as its locus; thus, due to the difference in form caused by the difference in connection with the location, there is a difference in the knowledge. This is not so in the case of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, for the objects of meditation do not differ there, since in both cases it is to be meditated upon as having the heart as its locus. Therefore, the rule stands. || 21 ||
And it is also shown. || 22 ||

Furthermore, [the scripture] demonstrates the non-combination of the qualities of the two supports—the eye and the sun—by means of the extension (*atideśa*) of form and other attributes in such passages as, "The form of this [sun] is indeed the same as the form of that [eye]," and so forth. For when [qualities] are not obtained by themselves, there is a requirement for their attainment through extension. The section concerning the connection (*sambandhādhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
And for this reason, there is also the accumulation, the rising, and the pervasion. || 23 ||
In the *Taittirīyaka*, in the *Nārāyaṇīya* section and in the *Khilas*, it is said: "The powers have Brahma as their eldest; they were gathered together; Brahma was the first-born in the beginning."

"He stretched out the sky; he was born as the first among beings, having become Brahman. Who, then, is able to rival that Brahman? Thus, a collection of qualities such as the accumulation of pre-eminent powers and the pervasion of heaven is recorded regarding Brahman. Since these qualities—studied here outside of any specific context—are to be combined with all meditations (*vidyās*), it is said: "The accumulation and the pervasion of heaven. The term *sambhṛtidyuvyāptī* is a singular compound formed from a collective dvandva.

Although the *sambhṛti* (the gathering of powers) and so forth are studied as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*) passages, they are nevertheless to be established [as belonging] to specific places for that very reason; they are not to be combined with all meditations. How is it that those studied as unattached are restricted to specific locations? We reply: by their own inherent capacity. First of all, pervasion cannot be combined with meditations whose scope consists of small locations such as the heart; since the *sambhṛti* and the rest are its companions and occupy the same location, they too are not to be combined with meditations that have small locations as their object.

In the case of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the Dahara-vidyā, and other such meditations whose scope is limited, attributes such as "greater than the earth" and "as large as this external space, so large is this space within the heart" cannot be combined in each instance; rather, they are intended solely to establish the majesty of the object of meditation as characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind (manomaya) and being free from sin (apahatapāpman). || 23 || || The section on the Sambhṛti [is concluded].
And because in the Puruṣavidyā as well, the others are not mentioned. (Sūtra 24)

In the *Taittirīyaka*, the Puruṣavidyā is handed down: "Of this sacrifice of one who knows thus, the self is the sacrificer, faith is the wife, the body is the fuel, the chest is the altar, and the hair is the sacrificial grass," and so forth. In the *Chāndogya* as well, the Puruṣavidyā is handed down: "Man indeed is the sacrifice; those which are his twenty-four years," and so forth. In this regard, there arises a doubt: is the knowledge here different, or not?

It might be argued that there is identity of knowledge because of the identity of name (*puruṣavidyā*), because of the identity of form through the commonality of conceiving the limbs of the sacrifice within the limbs of the person, because no connection with a fruit is heard in the *Taittirīyaka*, and because the very fruit of the *Puruṣavidyā* mentioned in the *Chāndogya*—"he lives for one hundred and sixteen years"—is indeed the fruit here as well; thus, due to the lack of distinction in the connection with the fruit, the knowledge is identical. To this, it is replied:

Even though both meditations recorded in the two [texts] are indeed "Puruṣavidyās," there is nonetheless a difference between the two meditations. Why? Because the other [details] are not recorded [in one]. For instance, those [details] recorded in the Taittirīyaka—such as "That which is in the evening, in the morning, and at midday, these are the *savana*s"—are not recorded as *savana*s in the Chāndogya; rather, in the Chāndogya, the human lifespan divided into three parts is conceived as the *savana*s.

In the *Chāndogya*, the assumption that the [rites] such as *aśiśiṣā* (the desire not to eat) constitute the *dīkṣā* (initiation) and so forth was not made; furthermore, the postulation of the sacrificer, his wife, and others is different [from the *Taittirīyaka*]. Therefore, the form (*rūpa*) differs in both places, and likewise the connection with the fruit (*phala-saṃyoga*) also differs. For in the *Taittirīyaka*, having taught the knowledge of Brahman in the preceding section with the words, "One should yoke oneself with the thought 'Om, for the sake of greatness, for Brahman,'" and having stated as its fruit, "He attains the greatness of Brahman," it continues: "For one who knows thus... [and so on].

From such passages as these, it is understood that the *puruṣavidyā* (the knowledge of the person) taught here is the conceptualization of this very knower of Brahman as a sacrifice. Therefore, because it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the knowledge of Brahman, the attainment of Brahman itself is the fruit; and according to the maxim, "that which is without a fruit [is an auxiliary] when in proximity to that which possesses a fruit," it is understood that the *puruṣavidyā* mentioned in the Taittirīyaka is an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman. In the Chāndogya, however, it is stated that the *puruṣavidyā* has the attainment of long life as its fruit. Thus, because of the difference in form and connection, there is a difference between the two knowledges, and consequently, there is no inclusion (*anupasaṃhāra*) of the qualities mentioned in one place into the other. || 24 ||
The section concerning the Knowledge of the Person (Puruṣavidyā) is completed.
Because there is a difference in purpose, such as piercing and so forth. || 25 ||

The Ātharvaṇikas recite at the beginning of their Upaniṣad such mantras as "Having pierced the bright [sun], having pierced the heart"; the Sāma-gāmins recite at the beginning of the *Rahasyabrāhmaṇa* "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice, impel [it]"; the Kāṭhakas and Taittirīyakas [recite] "May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious [to us]"; and the Śāṭyāyanins [recite] "The horse is white, you are greenish-blue," and so forth.

The followers of the Aitareya recension study the *Mahāvrata-brāhmaṇa*, beginning with: "Indra, having slain Vṛtra, indeed became great," and so forth; the Kauṣītakins likewise study the *Mahāvrata-brāhmaṇa*: "Prajāpati is indeed the year; this Great Vow (*mahāvrata*) is his very self," and so on; while the Vājasaneyins study the *Pravargya-brāhmaṇa*: "The gods, indeed, sat down for a sacrificial session (*satra*)," and so forth. In this regard, a doubt arises: are the mantras studied at the commencement of the Upaniṣads, such as "Piercing the bright [soma]" (*śukraṃ pravidhya*) and "May Mitra be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no mitra*), [to be applied here] or not?

Thus, it is understood that these [mantras] are subordinate to rites such as *abhicāra* (malevolent magic). In exactly the same way, by the very power of mantras such as "I shall speak the truth" (*ṛtaṃ vadiṣyāmi*) and "May our study be brilliant" (*tejasvināvadhītamastu*), it is understood that mantras like "May there be peace, O Mitra" (*śanno mitra*) are subordinate to the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*). Therefore, they do not have knowledge (*vidyā*) as their constituent part (*aṅga*). As for the recitation here of mantras such as "Piercing the bright [light]" (*śukraṃ pravidhya*) and the Brāhmaṇas concerning the *pravargya* rite and so forth, this is due to their being designated as *divākīrtya* (to be recited during the day) and *āraṇyaka-anuvāka* (forest-recitations). || 25 ||
The section concerning piercing and so forth is completed.

But in the case of falling away [from a higher state], it is not so, because of the subordinate nature of the word "attaining" (upāyana); it is like the case of the kuśa grass, the meters, the praise, and the singing; this has been stated [in the Sūtra]. || 26 ||

The Chandogas say: "Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair, and shaking off the body as a wind sheds clouds from the sky, being perfected in soul, may I attain the uncreated world of Brahman. And the Atharvaṇikas say: "Then the knower, having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, attains the supreme equality. But the Śāṭyāyanins say: "His sons inherit his property, his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds," and so forth.

The Kauṣītakins, however, state: "He shakes off his good and evil deeds; his dear relatives obtain his good deeds, and those not dear obtain his evil deeds. Thus, in some places the casting off of merit and demerit is heard of, in some places their acquisition by dear and non-dear ones, and in some places both are mentioned. Although both are mentioned in individual meditations (*vidyā*), they must be understood as auxiliary to all meditations, because for one established in any meditation on Brahman who attains Brahman, the abandonment of merit and demerit is necessarily required. [Therefore, even when not explicitly mentioned, they are] abandoned...

And because the act of bringing [the fruits] is itself the object [of meditation], that meditation being enjoined ought to be an auxiliary to all meditations (*vidyā*). In this regard, it is considered whether the meditation on the taking away (*hāni*), the meditation on the bringing (*upāyana*), and the meditation on both should be treated as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*) or as things to be combined (*upasaṃhāra*). What is appropriate? That they should be alternatives. Why? Because of the force of their separate scriptural mention.

For if there were a cumulative connection (*sasuccaya*), there would have to be a coordination of both [the abandoning and the taking] everywhere; and since that is already established by the Kauṣītaki passage itself, the recitation elsewhere would be entirely purposeless. Therefore, the purpose of the recitation in multiple places is precisely to allow for an option (*vikalpa*). Nor can the recitation in multiple places be resolved by appealing to a difference among students; for it is a repetition without distinction that is resolved by a difference among students, whereas here, in one Śākhā, there is only abandoning (*hāni*), while in the other, there is only taking (*upāyana*).

Nor can it be established on the basis of a difference in the specific knowledge (*vidyā*), because it has been stated that this "connecting" (*anusandhāna*) is subsidiary to all [meditations]. To this, it is said: "But in the case of abandonment (*hāni*), [the attainment of the fruit follows] because of the word 'attainment' (*upāyana*) being the remainder. The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous position. The term "in the case of abandonment" is for the sake of illustration; when abandonment alone or attainment alone is heard in scripture, there must necessarily be a mutual conjunction of the two. Why? Because of the word "attainment" being the remainder—[that is,] because of the mention of attainment.

Because the statement regarding "taking away" (upāyana) is a supplement to the statement regarding "casting off" (hāni). For it is indeed appropriate that the statement on taking away is a supplement to the statement on casting off, since the statement on taking away refers to the place of entry for the merit and demerit cast off by the knower. Examples are adduced to show that a statement recited in one location can be a supplement to a statement recited in another location: "as in the case of the *kuśā* grass, the meters, the hymns of praise, and the singing. The Kauṣītakins record: "The *kuśā* grasses are of the nature of trees," and so forth.

In the case of the Śāṭyāyanins, however, the sentence "The *kuśa* grasses are made of *udumbara*" functions as a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) of that [general injunction], because it specifies that the *kuśa* grasses—already understood in general as being derived from trees (*vānaspatya*)—are specifically made of *udumbara*. Similarly, when there is a general context regarding the meters (*chandas*) of the gods and the asuras through such statements as "with the meters of the gods and asuras," the statement "the meters of the gods come first" proceeds as a further supplementary part by establishing a specific order of sequence.

Likewise, when it is established without qualification that "one begins the *ṣoḍaśin* stotra with gold," there arises the specific rule: "When the sun has reached the midpoint, one begins the *ṣoḍaśin* stotra. In this case, [the former] being general...

A statement concerning a specific subject becomes a supplement to that [general] statement; likewise, the sentence "The *adhvaryu* should not join in the singing," which applies when no distinction has been made by the rule "The priests join in the singing," attains the status of a supplement by making known that the prohibition concerns those other than the *adhvaryu*. Thus, for those who do not accept the status of a supplement for a statement capable of restricting a meaning understood in a general sense to a particular case, an option (*vikalpa*) between the two meanings must be admitted.

And that [option] is not permissible when a way [of reconciling the texts] exists; as it was stated in the previous section: "But rather, because it is a supplementary part of the sentence, and because an option is improper, it should be a partial application of the injunctions.

Thus, since the two sentences concerning mere abandonment and mere acquisition form a single syntactical unit, and because there is no such thing as abandonment alone or acquisition alone, an option is not tenable. As for the mention of both by the Kauṣītakins, it is not contradictory because it is a repetition without distinction for the sake of different types of practitioners. 26.
The section concerning decrease is completed.
Because there is nothing further to be crossed in the next world; for thus say others. (27)

It has been stated that the casting off and the taking up of good and evil deeds must be considered in all meditations (vidyās). Regarding the doubt as to whether this casting off occurs at the time of separation from the body, on the path after the soul has departed from the body, or only at the time of separation from the body—the reasonable conclusion is that it occurs in both cases, because it is so taught in both ways in the scriptures.

For thus the Kauṣītakins record, beginning with: "Having entered upon this path of the gods, he goes to the world of Agni," and continuing: "He comes to the river Virajā; he crosses it with his mind, and thereby shakes off his good and evil deeds. In this passage, the casting off of good and evil deeds is understood to occur on the way. However, the Tāṇḍins [state]: "Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair, and freeing oneself as the moon frees itself from the mouth of Rāhu..."

"Having shaken off the uncreated body, with self perfected, may I attain the world of Brahman. Here, however, it is understood that this occurs at the very moment of separation from the body. In the Śāṭyāyanaka as well, it is heard: "His sons inherit his property, his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds. Since the transfer of good and evil deeds is mentioned as occurring simultaneously with the transfer of the inheritance to the sons, it is understood to take place at the time of separation from the body. Therefore, a portion of the good and evil deeds is cast off at the time of separation from the body; the remainder, however, [is cast off] on the path.

This being the position, it is said: "At the time of the transition" (*sāmparāye*). At the very moment of transition, at the time of departing from the body, the good and evil deeds of the knower are discarded without remainder. Why? Because there is nothing further to be crossed; for after the knower's separation from the body, there is no longer any enjoyment of the results to be traversed by means of good and evil deeds, as that [enjoyment] is the fruit of knowledge itself.

For indeed, apart from the attainment of Brahman, there exist no pleasures or pains to be experienced through good and evil deeds. Thus, other [scriptural passages] teach that after the separation from the body, there is an absence of the experience of pleasure and pain distinct from the attainment of Brahman: "Verily, neither pleasure nor pain touches one who is bodiless"; "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form"; and "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be united. || 27 ||
Because there is no contradiction with one's own desire. || 28 ||

Thus, since the nature of the matter establishes that the destruction of good and evil deeds occurs at this time, the syntactical connection of the words should be described according to one's preference—that is, as desired—without contradicting either the scriptural statement or the nature of the matter. The meaning is that in the Kauṣītaki passage, the latter part of the sentence, "he shakes off his good and evil deeds," must be construed before the first part of the sentence, "having entered upon this path of the gods. || 28 ||

On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) objects: "The purposefulness of the movement [of the soul] is established in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction. (Sūtra 29)

At the time of separation from the body, there is the destruction of a portion of good and evil deeds, and the remainder is destroyed afterwards. Thus, it is only when the exhaustion of karma occurs in both these ways that the journey has purpose—that is, the scriptural teaching regarding the path of the gods (devayāna) possesses meaning. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction; for if all karma were exhausted at the very moment of separation from the body, the subtle body would also perish. That being the case, the movement of the self alone would not be possible. Therefore, it is not tenable that the wise person's karma is entirely exhausted at the time of departure. || 29 ||
To this, the following answer is appropriate:
because the object characterized by that [form] is perceived, as is the case in the world. (30)

The destruction of all karma occurs precisely at the time of departure [from the body] upon rebirth; for how else could there be the perception of objects characterized by that [rebirth], given that even one whose karma is exhausted perceives objects characterized by a connection to a body once his true nature has manifested?

In such passages as "Having attained the highest light, he manifests in his own form," "There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing," "He becomes self-ruling; in all worlds, he has freedom of movement according to his desire," and "He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold," and so forth, the state of being connected with a body is indeed understood. Therefore, even for one whose karma is exhausted, travel by the path of the gods is logical provided he is still joined with the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*).

If it is asked how the subtle body persists even when the karma that initiated it has been destroyed, we reply: it is by the power of knowledge (*vidyā*). For although knowledge itself does not originate the subtle body, it maintains the subtle body so that it may travel by the path of the gods (*devayāna*) to lead the soul to the attainment of Brahman—which is its own fruit—even when all the gross bodies and all karmas, which are the means for experiencing worldly pleasure and pain, have been exhausted without remainder. This is like the case in the world: [The example follows: Just as a king, though he has no further need for his royal chariot once his reign has ended, keeps the chariot for the sake of visiting his ancestral kingdom; or as a man who has attained wealth through his efforts preserves that wealth for the sake of his son or grandson; or as a man who has crossed a river on a raft keeps the raft for fear of wild beasts or robbers; or as a man who has reached the top of a mountain keeps his climbing rope for fear of falling—so too, although the subtle body is not required for the attainment of Brahman, it is maintained for the sake of traveling by the path of the gods. Thus, the persistence of the subtle body is established.

Just as when a tank or similar work is begun for the sake of prosperity such as that of the world, even though the causes of it—such as the desire for it and so forth—have perished, people still maintain that very tank and perform bathing, drinking, and other activities therein; so it is here. 30.

Now, it might be argued: "It has been stated that for the knowers who have directly realized the supreme reality, because their karma is destroyed without remainder at the time of the body's fall, only the subtle body persists after the fall of the body for the purpose of movement, and no experience of pleasure or pain exists. This [assertion] is not tenable;

for in the cases of Vasiṣṭha, Avāntaratapas, and others who have directly realized the supreme reality, we observe the assumption of another body after the fall of the previous body, as well as the experience of pleasure and pain caused by events such as the birth of a son. To this, the author reads the following reply:
The abiding of those who hold office lasts as long as their term of office. || 31 ||

We have not stated that for all knowers (jñānins), there is a destruction of good and evil deeds at the time of the fall of the body; rather, it has been stated that for those knowers who attain the path beginning with light (arcirādi-gati) immediately after the fall of the body, there is the abandonment of good and evil deeds at the time of that fall. However, in the case of Vasiṣṭha and others who hold office (adhikārika), there is no attainment of the path beginning with light after the fall of the body, because their commenced office has not yet reached its completion.

For those who have attained a specific office by virtue of a specific karma, that karma which initiated their office does not perish until the completion of that office. For indeed, only through experience can karma already begun (prārabdha) be exhausted. Therefore, the karma that initiated the office of those holding authority persists as long as the office lasts. Consequently, for them, there is no attainment of the state of Akṣara and so forth immediately after the fall of the body. || 31 ||
The section concerning the state after death is completed.
There is no restriction for all; there is no contradiction, because of both scripture and inference. 32.

Regarding those meditations on Upakośala and others in which the departure via the path of light (*arcir-ādi-gati*) is heard, there arises a doubt: is the attainment of Brahman through that path for those devoted to those specific meditations alone, or for all those devoted to the meditation on Brahman? Since the departure is not mentioned in the case of other [meditations], and because there is no evidence that the passages such as "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" and "They worship faith as truth" apply to all other forms of knowledge of Brahman, the prima facie view is that it is only for those devoted to those specific ones. To this, it is replied: "There is no restriction. *Note: The term *aniyamaḥ* here signifies that the rule of the path of light applies universally to all who are devoted to the realization of Brahman, regardless of the specific meditation.*

Since all those devoted to every form of worship must proceed by that very path, there is no restrictive rule that it belongs exclusively to them. For if all were to proceed by that path alone, there would be no contradiction with verbal testimony and inference—that is, with Śruti and Smṛti; otherwise, there would indeed be a contradiction. As for Śruti, the passages on the Pañcāgni-vidyā in the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka Upaniṣads state that all those established in the meditation on Brahman proceed by the path beginning with light (arcirādi).

"In the Vājasaneyaka: 'Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship faith and truth—they pass into the light. And in the Chāndogya: 'Now, those who know it thus, and those who in the forest worship faith and austerity—they pass into the light.'"

By the passage beginning with "And those who in the forest," etc., the path consisting of light and so forth is taught for those who meditate upon Brahman preceded by faith; for the word *satya* (truth) is well-known to denote Brahman, as seen in such texts as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite" and "Truth indeed is what one should seek to understand. Since the word *tapas* (penance) has the same meaning as that [word *satya*], Brahman alone is denoted by the two words *satya* and *tapas*.

Furthermore, the worship of Brahman preceded by faith is heard elsewhere in the Śruti, beginning with "Truth indeed is to be sought after," and continuing with "Faith indeed is to be sought after. Smṛti also states, "Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice—departing there, the people who know Brahman go to Brahman," thus declaring that all knowers of Brahman travel by this very path. There are many such Śrutis and Smṛtis of this kind.
Thus, this path, which is common to all forms of knowledge, is indeed attained and subsequently restated in the Upakosala-vidyā and other such teachings.
The section on non-restriction is concluded.

But there is an inclusion of those meditations on the syllables [Om] because of the commonality and the presence of that [syllable], as in the case of the Aupasadā [offerings]; this has been stated. (Sūtra 33)

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka it is heard: "O Gārgī, this indeed is that Imperishable (akṣara) which the Brāhmaṇas revere as neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red nor oily, without shadow, without darkness, without air, without ether, unattached, tasteless, odorless, without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind, without radiance, without breath, without mouth, without measure, having nothing inside and nothing outside; nothing whatsoever eats it. By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart."

Likewise, in the *Ātharvaṇa* [Upaniṣad]: "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained—that which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without caste, without eyes or ears, and without hands or feet. Regarding this, a doubt arises: Are these qualities, such as being non-material (*asthūla*) and so forth, which are heard as connected with the Brahman designated by the word "Imperishable," to be meditated upon in all meditations on Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) as constituting its nature as the opposite of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)? Or are they to be applied only where they are actually heard? What is the reasonable conclusion? That they apply only where they are heard.

Why? Because there is no evidence that the qualities which constitute the form of one knowledge can constitute the form of another knowledge; and because these [qualities], being of the nature of negations, cannot serve as means for the comprehension of the essential nature [of Brahman] in the same way as bliss (*ānanda*) and other such qualities do. For it is only when the essential nature of Brahman has been comprehended through bliss and other such qualities that the worldly attributes such as grossness (*sthūlatva*) are negated, since a negation without a substratum is impossible.

This being the case, we reply: "But there is an inclusion of the meditations on the Imperishable. This means that the meditations on the attributes such as "not gross" and so forth, which relate to the Imperishable Brahman, are included—that is, subsumed—within all meditations on Brahman. Why? Because of their commonality and because of the existence [of those attributes] therein; for the Imperishable Brahman, the object of meditation, is the same in all meditations, and attributes such as "not gross" exist for the purpose of realizing its true nature. What is meant by this is that the apprehension of a thing occurs indeed through its unique characteristics.

Nor does bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth alone bring to mind the unique form of Brahman, because bliss and the like also exist in the inner self (*pratyagātman*). For bliss and the rest, being the opposite of all that is to be discarded (*heya*), constitute the unique nature of Brahman. However, although the inner self is by its own nature devoid of anything to be discarded, it still possesses the capacity for connection with what is to be discarded. Furthermore, the state of being the opposite of all that is to be discarded consists in having a form contrary to attributes such as grossness, which belong to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) composed of consciousness and matter (*cid-acit*).

Therefore, for one who meditates upon Brahman through its uncommon form, Brahman must be meditated upon in the form of knowledge, bliss, and so forth, as qualified by "not gross" and other attributes; thus, the qualities such as "not gross" are [to be understood] like bliss and the rest.

Since the realization of the nature of Brahman is included within all Brahma-vidyās, Brahman must be meditated upon in that very same way in each case. To provide an illustration for the principle that subordinate elements (guṇas) follow the principal element (pradhāna), he says, "like the Aupasada. Just as the mantra beginning with "Agnir vai hotraṃ vetu," which is read in the Sāmaveda and serves as a subordinate quality of the *puroḍāśī* Upasad in the four-night Jāmadagnya sacrifice, is employed inaudibly according to the Yajurvedic rule because it follows the principal rite; this was stated in the first section (*Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtra*): "In the case of a conflict between the subordinate and the principal, the connection with the Veda belongs to the principal, because [the subordinate] exists for its sake. || 33 ||

[Objection: But if this were so, since Brahman alone is the possessor of attributes (guṇin) in all Brahma-vidyās, and since attributes must follow the principal, there would be a lack of restriction even for the collection of attributes—such as "possessing all works, all smells, all tastes"—which are established separately in each vidyā. To this, he says:
"On account of the mention of this much [only]. (Sūtra 34)

"Āmanana" means mental orientation, that is, contemplation. For this reason of *āmanana*, this entire collection of qualities—namely, bliss and so forth, as qualified by "not gross" and the rest—is obtained as something to be connected with everywhere. The meaning is: only that collection of qualities, without which the contemplation of the nature of Brahman as distinguished from all else would not be possible, must be followed through everywhere; and that is precisely this much.
However, other qualities such as "having all works" and so forth, although following the primary subject, are restricted to each specific meditation (*vidyā*) as objects of contemplation. || 34 ||
The section concerning the Imperishable is completed. 14.
If it be argued that, like the various classes of living beings, the distinction of the Self from itself would otherwise be untenable, we say no; for it is as in the case of instruction. (Sūtra 35)

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, within the Uṣasta-praśna, it is thus recorded: "Explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all. The reply to this is: "That which breathes by means of the prāṇa is your Self, which is within all; that which breathes out by means of the apāna is your Self," and so forth.

Being unsatisfied with that, he asked again, and [Yājñavalkya] said: "You should not see the seer of seeing; you should not hear the hearer of hearing; you should not think the thinker of thinking; you should not cognize the cognizer of cognition. This is your Self, the innermost of all; everything other than this is afflicted. Likewise, immediately following that, in the question of Kahola, it is similarly handed down in scripture: "Explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, the Self that is within all."
And the reply is: "He who transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow and delusion, old age and death—having known this Self thus, a Brahmin [renounces] the desire for sons and the desire for wealth."

From the passage beginning with "And of the quest for wealth" up to the end of "Therefore, everything else is afflicted. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is there a difference between these two meditations (vidyās), or not? What is the reasonable position? That there is a difference. Why? Because of the difference in form (rūpa). The form differs due to the difference in the answers. For even though the question is uniform, the manner of the answer is perceived as distinct. In the former case, the agent of breathing and so forth is described as the innermost Self of all; in the latter, [the Self] is described as being devoid of hunger, thirst, and the like.

Therefore, in the former [passage], that which is distinct from the body, senses, intellect, mind, and vital breath is declared to be the individual self (*pratyagātman*); but in the latter, it is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), distinct from that and free from hunger, thirst, and so forth. Thus, the form [of the subject] differs. Furthermore, since the inner self of that collection of elements is the individual self, its status as the "innermost of all" (*sarvāntaratva*) is also logically established.

Although the innermost nature of the individual self (*pratyagātman*) is relative—being so only in relation to the aggregate of elements—nevertheless, that alone must be accepted as the referent. Otherwise, if one were to adopt the Supreme Self out of a desire to grasp the primary "inner self," the distinction between the two answers would not be tenable. For the first answer concerns the individual self, since the functions of breathing in and breathing out are impossible for the Supreme Self; whereas the latter answer concerns the Supreme Self, because it transcends hunger, thirst, and the like.

One might raise this objection: "If [it is argued that] there is no possibility of a different distinction for one's own self, as in the case of the group of elements (*bhūtagrāma*) within. This means: "In the first reply, because [the Self] is the innermost Self of all, it is said to be 'like the group of elements,' i.e., the inner Self, the inward-facing Self (*pratyagātman*), which is the innermost of all. If it were otherwise, there would be no justification for the difference between the two replies—namely, "He who breathes by means of breath" and "He who is beyond hunger, thirst, and so forth. To this, the answer is: "No."

The meaning is that there is no difference in the knowledge [taught]. This is because both the question and the answer have the Supreme Self as their object. To explain: the question, "That Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all," refers exclusively to the Supreme Self. Although the word *brahman* is unique to the Supreme Self, since its usage is sometimes seen metaphorically applied to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), the qualification "that which is immediate Brahman" is employed to exclude the latter and establish the Supreme Self.

Immediacy (*aparokṣatva*)—that is, the state of being connected to all places and all times—is possible only for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is understood as infinite in the passage, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. Furthermore, being the innermost of all (*sarvāntaratva*) is possible only for the Supreme Self, the inner ruler of all (*sarvāntaryāmin*), as established by the sequence beginning with, "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth," and ending with, "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self."

The reply as well refers likewise to the Supreme Self; for in the statement, "He who breathes by means of the vital breath," the agency of breathing without any limiting adjunct belongs to the Supreme Self alone, since the individual self lacks agency with respect to breathing during deep sleep.

Not being satisfied because Uṣasta had merely stated that the act of breathing belongs to the individual self (prāṇana), thinking that this reply was common to all selves, and having asked again, the Teacher spoke to him of the Supreme Self as the agent of breathing who is distinct from the individual self due to its being free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), by means of the passage beginning with, "You cannot see the seer of seeing."

You should not think that the inner self (pratyagātman), which is the agent of seeing, hearing, thinking, and cognizing—functions dependent upon the senses—is referred to here as the agent of breathing; for it is not the agent of breathing and so forth during deep sleep, fainting, and similar states. Indeed, the fact that the cause of the breathing of all living beings belongs solely to the Supreme Self is heard elsewhere in scripture: "For who indeed could inhale and who could exhale, if this bliss were not in the ether (ākāśa)?"

Therefore, since the previous question and its answer refer to the Supreme Self, so too do the subsequent ones; for the state of being beyond hunger and other such needs is unique to the Supreme Self. Furthermore, the concluding statement in both cases, "Other than this is perishable," is of one and the same form. The repetition of the questions and answers, however, is intended to establish that the Supreme Brahman—the cause of the vitalization of all living beings—is beyond hunger and the rest. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "as in the case of instruction."

Just as in the *Sadvidyā* [the teaching of Being], after the instruction on Being has begun with the words, "Have you asked him for that instruction? there occurs a repeated recurrence of the question—"Venerable sir, do tell me that truly"—and the answer—"This subtle essence (aṇimā), all this has that as its self; that is the Truth"—for the purpose of demonstrating the various specific greatnesses of the Being that is Brahman. It is just like that.

Therefore, because the single Brahman, who is the innermost being of all, is established as having a uniform nature through the teaching that He is the cause of the life-breath of all living beings and is beyond hunger and other such needs, there is identity of the meditation (vidyaikya). || 35 ||

Now, it might be argued that although both the question and the answer refer to the supreme Brahman, nevertheless, a difference in the meditations (*vidyā-bheda*) is unavoidable. This is because there is a difference in form due to the difference in the qualities of the object of meditation: in one case, it is to be meditated upon as the cause of the vitalization of all living beings, while in the other, it is as that which transcends hunger and so forth; furthermore, there is a difference in the questioners. For in the former instance Uṣasta is the questioner, whereas in the latter it is Kahola. To this, the Sūtra replies:
"There is an interchange [of attributes], for they distinguish [the two] as in the other cases" (3.3.36).

There is no difference in the knowledge [taught] here, because the two questions and their two answers are perceived to form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) through their common subject matter and through the presence of a single injunctive term. First, both questions concern Brahman as qualified by the attribute of being the innermost self of all. In the second question, the phrase "that which is Brahman, immediate and direct, that which is the Self within all," and specifically the use of the restrictive particle *eva*, confirms—by virtue of its connection with what was previously mentioned—that Kahola’s question concerns Brahman as qualified by the attributes already inquired after.

Furthermore, the reply in both places—"That is your Self, which is within all"—is of one and the same form, concerning Brahman as characterized by being the Self within all; moreover, an injunctive suffix is seen only in the latter passage: "Therefore, having discarded learning, a Brāhmaṇa should remain in a state of childlike simplicity."

Thus, when it is determined that both [questions] have as their single object Brahman characterized as the inner Self of all, then, since the Brahman characterized as the inner Self of all is the sole object of meditation for both Upastaka and Kahola, an exchange of their respective cognitions regarding one another must be performed. That cognition which Upastaka possesses concerning the fact that the Brahman who is the inner Self of all is the cause of the vitalization of all living beings must likewise be produced by Kahola, the questioner.

And that cognition of Kahola regarding that very Brahman as being beyond hunger and other such needs must also be formed by him [Uṣasta]. Thus, when the exchange has been made, the exclusion of the individual soul from the Brahman that is within all is understood through both [questions]. Indeed, Yājñavalkya’s answers qualify this innermost Self—which is distinguished from the individual self—by establishing its nature as the cause of the vitalization of all living beings and its transcendence of hunger and other such needs, thereby making it known as distinct from the individual self.

Therefore, the quality to be meditated upon (*upāsya-guṇa*) is precisely Brahman’s nature as the inner self of all; whereas its being the cause of the vital functions (*prāṇana-hetutva*) and so forth are merely its supporting attributes (*upapādaka*), not themselves the objects of meditation. Now, if the quality to be meditated upon is indeed only its nature as the inner self of all, for what purpose is there this exchange of inquiry by the questioner regarding both its being the cause of the vital functions and its transcendence of hunger and so forth? To this it is replied: when Brahman, as the inner self of all, is distinguished from the individual soul (*jīva*) and determined by the worshipper through its being the cause of the vital functions of all living beings, then by Kahola—

Thinking that the Inner Self of all must be investigated as distinguished by a specific nature that is impossible for the individual soul (jīva) to possess in its entirety, the question was asked again. Yājñavalkya, recognizing that intention, stated that the inner self possesses a state contrary to hunger and other such needs, which is impossible for the individual soul.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the cognition of the distinction of the object of meditation, an exchange of ideas between the two must take place; just as in the *Sadvidyā*, through repeated questions and answers, that very Brahman, which is Being (*sat*), is distinguished [from what it is not]. It is not, however, the case that the object of meditation is presented as being qualified by a different attribute than the one previously apprehended, as might otherwise be thought. Thus ends the section. (36)

If it be asked how unity can be understood when there is such a difference between the questions and the answers, he says in response: "For that same [meditation] is indeed [described by] 'Truth' and so forth. (37)

For that very Supreme Deity, who is the ultimate cause and is denoted by the word *sat* (Being), is what is introduced in all the subsequent sections, such as "That Deity thought," "The fire [was produced] in the Supreme Deity," and "Just as, my dear, the honey-makers prepare honey. Since this is so, everything in this world has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self—and thus, the terms "Truth" (*satya*) and the others mentioned in the first section are established and concluded throughout all the sections.

However, some describe the two sūtras—"vyatihāro viśiṃṣanti hītaravat" and "saiva hi satyādayaḥ"—as two distinct sections (*adhikaraṇa*). Regarding this, they say that by the former [sūtra], it is taught that in the passage, "O venerable deity, I am indeed you; O venerable deity, you are indeed me; that which I am, that are you; that which you are, that am I," there is the instruction for the mutual exchange (*vyatihāra*) of meditation between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*). As for that [passage], "All this is indeed Brahman" and "This [Self]... [etc.].

Since this sentence—“All this is indeed the Self; thou art That”—has as its object the realization of the state of being the Self of all, there is nothing new to be established here; thus, [the objection] is to be disregarded. This, however, will be explained in the sūtra: “But they approach [the teacher] as the Self, and they cause [the disciple] to grasp it as such. Furthermore, apart from the contemplation of the universal Self, neither the contemplation of the individual soul (jīva) as the supreme Brahman nor the contemplation of the supreme Brahman as the individual soul is possible in reality.

And by the subsequent scripture, the identity is established between the meditation on Truth (*satyopāsana*) taught in the passage beginning with "He who knows that great, first-born being, the Truth, Brahman," and the meditation taught in the passage beginning with "That which is Truth is yonder sun, the person who is in this orb, and he who is in the right eye."

That too has been stated: in the subsequent passage, the difference between the two meditations (*vidyā*) based on the distinction between the locations of the eye and the sun was already established by the sūtra "Or rather, not so, because of the difference [of location]" (*na vā viśeṣāt*). Furthermore, since these two meditations possess form—having the *vyāhṛtis* and so forth as their bodies—and since they are enjoined separately with distinct results, such as "He who knows thus slays sin and leaves it behind," and "He who knows that great, first-born being as the True Brahman conquers these worlds," [the meditations are distinct].

Because they possess conjunction, form, and other such qualities, identity with the preceding meditation cannot exist independently; nor can there be a status as a subordinate section concerning the fruit of a quality (guṇaphala-adhikāra) based on the statements "he destroys evil" and "he abandons [it]," for there is a lack of evidence. If it is argued that the evidence is the fact of being a single knowledge (ekavidyātva) with the preceding one, we say no, because that would involve mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva).

When it is certain that there is only one single knowledge (*vidyā*), the former fruit alone is the primary fruit, while the two subsequent fruits are secondary fruits; and when it is certain that those two are secondary fruits, because there is no difference in their connection (*saṃyoga-bheda*), there is identity of knowledge with the former—thus, by such arguments as "mutual dependence" (*itaretarāśrayatva*) and so forth, the two sūtras are to be understood exactly in the manner already described. || 37 ||
The section concerning the inner self is concluded.
Desire and so forth [are absent] elsewhere than in those respective bases and so on. || 38 ||

In the *Chāndogya* it is heard: "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, a small lotus-palace, within that is a small ether; what is within that is to be sought," and so forth. And in the *Vājasaneyaka*: "This indeed is the great unborn Self, who consists of cognition among the vital breaths; he lies in that ether which is within the heart; he is the ruler of all, the lord of all," and so forth. In this regard, a doubt arises: is there a difference between these two meditations (*vidyā*), or not? What is the reasonable conclusion? That there is a difference.

Why? Because of the difference in form (*rūpabheda*). In the Chāndogya, the object of meditation is perceived as the ether (*ākāśa*) characterized by the eight qualities beginning with freedom from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*); however, in the Vājasaneyaka, that which lies within the ether is perceived as the object of meditation characterized by qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*). Therefore, due to this difference in form, there is a difference between the two meditations (*vidyābhedah*).

This being the case, we reply: there is no difference. Why? Because of the non-difference of form; for in both places, the very same form consisting of "desires" and so forth [is present]. The meaning is that in both the Vājasaneyaka and the Chāndogya, Brahman qualified by "true desires" (*satyakāma*) and other attributes is the object of meditation. How is this understood? From the abode and other characteristics; for by such features as having the heart as the abode, being a bridge, and being a support, that same meditation (*vidyā*) is recognized as identical in both cases.

Furthermore, the powers such as mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth, which are heard of in the *Vājasaneyaka*, are merely specific instances of "truthfulness of resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), which is one of the eight qualities heard of in the *Chāndogya*. Thus, they lead us to understand the existence of all the qualities beginning with "having true desires" (*satyakāmatva*) and ending with "freedom from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*), which accompany truthfulness of resolve. Therefore, the form [of Brahman] does not differ.

Even the union [with Brahman], being of the nature of attaining Brahman—as expressed in such passages as "Having attained the highest light, he appears in his own form" and "He indeed becomes the fearless Brahman"—is not different [from liberation]. That the word *ākāśa* in the Chāndogya refers to the Supreme Self has been determined in the section beginning with "The small [ether] because of the subsequent [texts]. However, in the Vājasaneyaka, there is the mention of mastery (*vaśitva*) and other qualities belonging to one who lies within the *ākāśa*.

Since that [space] which is heard of while lying down is the Supreme Self, it is understood that the word *ākāśa*, which denotes its substratum, refers to the space within the heart denoted by the word *suṣira* (the subtle cavity), according to the passage: "In its center is a subtle cavity. Therefore, there is identity of the vidyās. || 38 ||

Now, it might be argued that what was stated in the *Vājasaneyaka*—namely, that the existence of qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) is understood along with qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*)—is not tenable; for in that context, qualities such as mastery do not exist in an ultimate sense. And their non-existence [there] is established by the text: "It is to be perceived by the mind alone; here there is no diversity whatsoever."

"He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity," and "This immeasurable, eternal [reality] is to be perceived as one alone"—from this contextually relevant statement, as well as from the subsequent passage yet to be quoted, "This Self is 'not this, not this,'" it is understood that the Brahman which is the object of meditation is devoid of all distinctions. Therefore, qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth are also to be negated, just like grossness (*sthūlatva*) and other attributes.

For this very reason, even in the Chāndogya, qualities such as "having true desires" (satyakāmatva) and so forth are not stated to be the ultimate attributes of Brahman. Therefore, because these kinds of qualities are not ultimate, they are omitted in meditations intended for liberation; to this, the Sūtra replies: "There is no omission on account of reverence" (ādarālopaḥ). || 39 ||

By virtue of being qualities of Brahman, these qualities—such as having true desires and so forth—which are not established by any other means of knowledge, are [established] through these two scriptural passages and others: "In Him, what is within that must be sought... this Self is free from sin, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true"; and "The ruler of all, the lord of all"; and "This is the Lord of all, this is the sovereign of beings, this is the protector of beings, this is the bridge and the support so that these worlds may not be confounded," and so forth.

Because these [qualities] are taught with reverence as attributes of the Brahman that is to be meditated upon for the sake of liberation, there is no omission of them; rather, they must indeed be combined [in meditation]. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad, having first stated the knowledge of Brahman as qualified by attributes such as having true desires—saying, "Those who depart from here having understood the Self and these true desires, for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds"—then continues: "But those who depart from here without having understood the Self and these true desires, for them there is no freedom of movement in any world."

By thus censuring non-feeling (*avedana*), it demonstrates respect for feeling characterized by specific qualities. Likewise, in the Vājasaneyaka: "The controller of all, the lord of all," and "He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He..."

From the repeated instruction regarding sovereignty, such as "He is the protector of beings," it is understood that there is a regard for the qualities [of the body]. This is likewise elsewhere. Furthermore, the scripture—which is more affectionate than even a thousand parents—cannot possibly deceive those seeking liberation who are already wandering through the cycle of transmigration by respectfully teaching qualities that are non-ultimate, fit only to be discarded, and not established by any other means of valid cognition, like a deceiver.

The meaning of the statements "There is no diversity here whatsoever" and "It is to be perceived as one alone" has already been explained at length: having enjoined the perception of oneness because everything is of the nature of Brahman since it is an effect of Brahman, they negate the previously established perception of diversity based on the view that things are not of the nature of Brahman.

In the passage, "This Self is 'not this, not this' (neti neti)," the word "iti" refers back to the nature of the phenomenal world as apprehended through other means of knowledge; thus, it is established that Brahman, which is the Self of all, is distinct from the phenomenal world by stating that Brahman is not of such a nature. Immediately thereafter, the text provides the justification for this: "It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped; it is indestructible, for it is not destroyed; it is unattached, for it is not attached; it is untroubled, for it is not troubled; it does not suffer."

Because it is of a different nature from that which is graspable by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it does not disintegrate; this should be understood accordingly in what follows. In the *Chāndogya* as well—"It does not age with his aging; it is not slain by his slaying. This is the true city of Brahman; in it all desires are contained"—having established that Brahman is of a different nature from everything else, qualities such as having true desires are enjoined therein. (39)

But even so, since there is scriptural mention of a connection with worldly results for the knowledge of Brahman as qualified by attributes such as "true desires"—as in the passage beginning, "Those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires, for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds; if he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers..."—then Brahman with attributes should not be meditated upon by one seeking liberation who desires to attain Brahman. And the fruit of the higher knowledge (paravidyā) is precisely this: "Having reached the highest light, he appears in his own true form."

Therefore, [the opponent argues] that qualities such as "having true desires" (satyakāmatva) and so forth are not to be combined for one who seeks to attain Brahman; to this, the author reads the following reply:
"When [the meditation] is present, therefore, because of the statement regarding that. (Sūtra 3.3.40)

*Upasthitiḥ* means approaching (*upasthānam*), namely, attaining Brahman (*brahmopasampattiḥ*). When one has approached [Brahman] and is perfected in Brahman—that is, when the inner self (*pratyagātman*) has been manifested in its own form, being liberated from all bonds—it is for this very reason of attaining [Brahman] that "wandering at will in all worlds" is spoken of. As it is said: "Having attained the highest light, he is manifested in his own form"; "He is the Supreme Person"; and "There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing, with women, or with chariots, or with kinsmen, not subject to rebirth."

"Remembering this body," [it is said], "he becomes his own ruler; for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds. This will be demonstrated more thoroughly in the fourth [chapter]. Therefore, since the power of moving at will in all worlds is a fruit to be enjoyed by the liberated one, the qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth must be combined [from various texts] for the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*). The section concerning desire and so forth (*kāmādyadhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
There is no restriction regarding the determination of that [result], because it is seen as such; the fruit is established separately through the absence of obstruction. || 41 ||

Regarding such meditations as "One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha," which rely on the constituent parts of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), these are established as auxiliary elements of the ritual through the medium of the Udgītha and so forth—which are themselves parts of the ritual—just as the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood is an auxiliary of the ladle (*juhū*) and the like. Consequently, because it is impossible to conceive of a separate fruit for the present-tense injunction, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣad—that alone becomes more powerful"—analogous to the hearing of the verse concerning the absence of evil for one who uses *parṇa*-wood, these meditations on the Udgītha and so forth must necessarily be integrated into the sacrifices.

This being the case, we reply: there is no restrictive rule regarding this determination (*nirdhāraṇa*). "Determination" means the fixing of the mind through certainty; that is to say, meditation (*dhyāna*). This lack of restrictive rule regarding determination means that there is no fixed rule for the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth among the ritual acts. Why? Because such a practice is observed. For a lack of restrictive rule in the performance of meditations is indeed perceived from the statement: "Both perform [the rite], he who knows this thus and he who does not know," since this speaks of performance even by one who lacks knowledge.

Furthermore, if meditation were an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) [of the ritual], a fixed rule for its performance would not be logically tenable. Thus, once it is determined that meditation is not an auxiliary part, when the injunction for meditation requires a result, it is understood—according to the *rātrisatra* principle—that its fruit is "greater vigor" (*vīryavattaratva*), which is distinct from the fruit of the ritual action. What is this "greater vigor"? It is simply the non-obstruction of the fruit of the ritual action itself. For the fruit of a ritual action is indeed obstructed for a certain period by the fruit of another more powerful action.

The absence of that [obstruction] is non-obstruction. The fruit is indeed distinct from the fruit of ritual action characterized by heaven and so forth. This is expressed as: "For the non-obstructed fruit is distinct. Therefore, since even those meditations (*upāsanā*) such as the *udgītha* and others—which depend on the constituent parts of rituals—possess distinct fruits, they are not to be combined with the rituals in a fixed manner, just like the *godohana* vessel and similar items. Thus ends the section concerning the non-necessity of determining that [distinction].
That has been stated as being like a gift. 42.

In the *Dahara-vidyā*, after stating that the meditation on the *daharākāśa* as the Supreme Self is performed with the words, "Those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires," the separate meditation on the qualities (*guṇas*) themselves is also enjoined by the phrase, "and these true desires. Regarding this, there arises a doubt: when reflecting upon the qualities, must the reflection on the *dahara* Self—qualified by each respective quality—be repeated, or not?

Since the qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) belong to the small ether (*daharākāśa*) alone, and since that [ether] can be meditated upon all at once, the meditation for the sake of those qualities need not be repeated. This being the position reached, it is said: "It is just like the offering" (*pradānavadeva*). The meaning is that it must indeed be repeated, just like an offering. Although the small ether is the single substratum (*guṇin*) of the qualities such as freedom from sin, and it was meditated upon first; nevertheless, because the form qualified by the qualities is distinct from the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*), [the meditation on the qualities must be repeated]. "Freedom from sin... [and so forth].

Since [the Self] has been prescribed as an object of meditation by being qualified with attributes such as "free from evil, free from old age," and so forth, a repetition must be performed for the purpose of contemplating—as qualified by freedom from evil and other such attributes—that which was previously contemplated in its mere essential nature.

"Just as one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to King Indra," "to Indra the Overlord," and "to Indra the Self-Ruler"—even though Indra alone possesses the qualifying attributes such as kingship and so forth, the offering is repeated because the forms associated with those respective attributes are distinct. As it is stated in the *Sāṅkarṣaṇa*: "Or rather, [the offerings are] separate, because of the distinctness of the deities. (42) || The section concerning the offerings (*pradānādhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
On account of the plurality of indicatory marks, that indeed is stronger; and that too [is stronger]. (43)

In the *Taittirīyaka*, immediately following the *dahara-vidyā*, the following is studied, beginning with: "The thousand-headed God, the all-eyed, the source of all happiness, the universal Nārāyaṇa, the imperishable, supreme Lord," and ending with: "He is the imperishable, the supreme, the self-luminous. Regarding this, a doubt arises: Is the specific nature of the object of worship for the previously mentioned *vidyā* being determined by this [passage] as part of that same single *vidyā*; or is it the determination of the specific nature of the object of worship for the supreme *vidyā* taught in all the Vedāntas?

What is appropriate? It is the determination of the specific object of meditation in the Dahara-vidyā. Why? Because of the context. For in the preceding section, the Dahara-vidyā is the subject under discussion: "The lotus that is small, free from sorrow, the dwelling place of another, situated in the middle of the city; even there, the space within it is small and free from grief—that which is within it is to be meditated upon."

Furthermore, in this Anuvāka, the description of the heart-lotus through the passage beginning with, "The heart is like the interior of a lotus bud, facing downwards," etc., strengthens the conclusion that this Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka is intended to determine the object of meditation for the Dahara-vidyā.

This being the case, we reply: "On account of the abundance of indicatory marks. Since this [section] serves the purpose of determining the specific object of worship among all the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), many such marks are observed. For instance, the object of worship—which in other higher knowledges is indicated by terms such as *akṣara*, *Śiva*, *Śambhu*, *para-brahman*, *para-jyotis*, *para-tattva*, and *paramātman*—is here restated using those very same terms, and its identity as Nārāyaṇa is then enjoined.

By restating what has been heard in numerous scriptures (*vidyās*) and then enjoining that Nārāyaṇa is [the object], there is an abundance of injunctions regarding Nārāyaṇa-hood; this constitutes a very strong indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the specific determination that the Supreme Brahman—characterized by qualities such as bliss and specified as being "not gross" (*asthūla*) and so forth—is indeed Nārāyaṇa, the one to be meditated upon in all the *vidyās*. Here, the word *liṅga* is a synonym for a sign (*cihna*); the meaning is that there are many more sentences serving as such signs.

For that [direct statement] is stronger than context; as it was stated in the first section (Pūrva-mīmāṃsā): "In the case of a conflict between direct assertion, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name, each subsequent one is weaker because of its remoteness from the meaning. As for what was said—that the statement beginning with "resembling the interior of a lotus bud" supports its being a subordinate part of the Dahara-vidyā—that is not so. Since it has been established by a stronger means of proof that this serves to determine the object of worship in all meditations, that very statement is appropriate even in the Dahara-vidyā, as Nārāyaṇa alone is the object of worship therein.

Nor should one suspect a connection with the meditations mentioned in the preceding section on account of the accusative case in "thousand-headed," etc.; for since the object of meditation is already expressed as the grammatical object (*karman*) by the *kṛt* suffix in the word "to be meditated upon" (*upāsitavyam*)—as in the phrase "that which is within it is to be meditated upon"—an accusative case is inappropriate for that object of meditation. Furthermore, because of the nominative case in such passages as "All this is indeed the Puruṣa" and "That is Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme," the accusative should be understood here in the sense of the nominative.

"Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without," and "In the middle of that flame, the Supreme Self is established; He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Indra, He is the Imperishable, the Supreme Sovereign. Since it is determined by such indications that Nārāyaṇa alone, who is superior to all, is the object of worship everywhere, it is concluded that the second [case-ending] has the sense of the first. || 43 || The section on the Abundance of Indicative Marks (Liṅgabhūyastvādhikaraṇa) is completed.
The previous alternative [of the word "sacrifice"] may apply here due to the context, just as the action [is understood] in the case of the mental [sacrifice]. // 44 //

In the *Vājasaneyaka*, within the *Agnirahasya*, the fires consisting of mind (*manascit*) and so forth are heard: "The fire built of mind, the fire built of speech, the fire built of breath, the fire built of sight, the fire built of hearing, the fire built of action, and the fire built of fire. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Are these fires beginning with the *manascit* of the nature of knowledge (*vidyārūpa*) by virtue of being produced through meditation (*sāmpādikatvena*), yet taking the form of ritual action (*kriyārūpa*) through entry into a sacrifice consisting of action (*kriyāmayakratu*)? Or rather, do they take the form of knowledge alone through entry into a sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmayakratu*)? In this dilemma, [the author] first states that they have the form of ritual action, beginning with the words "The previous alternative... (*pūrvavikalpa*).
Of these [fires], such as the mind-fire (manaściti) and others, which have been identified with the city-fire, there is entry into the sacrifice.

For those who have expectations [of results], since there is no obstruction to the sacrifice in their own country, and because in the preceding passage—"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1)—the fire built of bricks (*iṣṭakacita*) is the subject under discussion, and because that fire is invariably connected with a sacrifice consisting of action (*kriyāmaya-kratu*), the sacrifice is present therein; therefore, the "mind-built" fires (*manaścit*) and others, being grasped within that context, must be of the nature of action (*kriyārūpa*) as they are optional alternatives to that fire built of bricks. Even though they are of the nature of knowledge (*vidyārūpa*), their status as action is established—just like the mental cups (*mānasagraha*)—by way of their entry into the sacrifice consisting of action.

Just as in the case of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, on the tenth day of which there is no recitation (*avivākya*), the *mānasa-graha*—though consisting of knowledge—is considered to be of the nature of action because it is an auxiliary (*kratvaṅga*) to a ritual characterized by action, through its being produced by the mind and its sequence of taking up, placing, chanting the hymn (*stotra*), reciting the litany (*śastra*), and consuming; so it is here as well. || 44 ||
And because of the extended application (atideśa). || 45 ||

For this reason as well, it is understood that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the fire built of bricks and those consisting of mind (*manaścita*) and so forth, and that they possess the nature of action (*kriyārūpatva*). This is because the power (*vīrya*) of the previously mentioned fire built of bricks is extended (*atidiśyate*) to the fires consisting of mind and the rest, according to the text: "Each one of these is as great as that former one. Therefore, because they perform an equal function, there is an option; and consequently, just like the fire built of bricks, the fires consisting of mind and the rest—which are its constituent parts—enter into the sacrificial rite (*kratu*) composed of action through the performance of that specific ritual (*tatkratu*), and thus they indeed possess the nature of action. || 45 ||
This being the case, we reply:
"But it is knowledge alone [that leads to immortality], because of the specific determination and because of scriptural vision. (Sūtra 46)

The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position; namely, that which was stated—that the mind-altars and so forth, by entering into a sacrifice consisting of action, are themselves of the nature of action—this is not so; the meaning is that these are indeed of the nature of knowledge, as they are connected with a sacrifice whose form is knowledge.

Why? Because of the specification (*nirdhāraṇa*) and because of the scriptural statement (*darśana*). First, as for the specification: "These [fires] are indeed built of knowledge (*vidyācita*); for those who know thus, these are built by knowledge alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.4). Since the operations of speech, sight, and so forth cannot be "built" in the same manner as bricks and other materials, it is established that they consist of knowledge (*vidyārūpa*) by virtue of being mentally constructed fires. Nevertheless, the restrictive emphasis—"they are *indeed* built of knowledge" and "by knowledge *alone*"—is determined to be intended to indicate their nature as knowledge through their connection with a sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmayakratu*).

Moreover, the remaining constituent of these [fires] is seen here to be a sacrifice in the form of knowledge: "They were studied by the mind alone; they were piled up by the mind alone; by the mind the cups were drawn for them; by the mind they praised; by the mind they recited; whatever ritual act is performed in a sacrifice, whatever sacrificial act there is—all that was performed for those made of mind as consisting of mind, even as something consisting of excellent mind."

Whatever sacrificial rite consisting of action is performed in fires built with bricks, that very same rite is to be performed as consisting of mind alone in the fires such as the "mind-built" (manaścita) which are accomplished by the mind; from this statement, it is understood that even the ritual sacrifice (kratu) here consists of knowledge (vidyāmaya).

[Objection: But surely, since no injunctive word is heard here and the connection with a fruit is not perceived, their nature as knowledge would be sublated by their connection with a sacrifice consisting of knowledge—rather than with the sacrificial context consisting of action established by the fire-altar built of bricks? [Reply: No; he says:
"And because of the superior strength of direct statement and so forth, there is no sublation" (Sūtra 4.3.47).

Since direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*) are stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*), the sacrifice and its connection [to the fires] as understood from direct assertion and the others cannot be sublated by the weaker context. Direct assertion is as follows: "These, indeed, are built of knowledge alone" (*te haite vidyācita eva*). He explains this: "By knowledge alone these become built for one who knows thus" (*vidyayā haivaita evaṃvidaścitā bhavanti*). The meaning is that the mind-altars (*manaścita*) and the rest, being connected with the sacrifice consisting of knowledge, become "built."

"The sign [indicative of this] is: 'All beings always gather for him who knows thus, even while he sleeps. And there is the sentence: 'They gather for one who knows thus. A sentence consists of co-occurrence [of words]. The meaning is: for one who knows thus—that is, for one possessing the sacrifice consisting of knowledge—all beings always gather."

The fact that [the sacrifice] has all beings as its agent, pervades all time, and is accomplished by the mind—being unable to find entry into a ritual consisting of limited agents, times, and actions through the medium of some localized effect—serves as an indicative mark for its entry into a ritual consisting of knowledge (vidyāmaya-kratu). || 47 ||

As for the argument that because no injunction (*vidhi*) is heard and because no connection with a fruit (*phala*) is perceived, no sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*) other than the sacrifice consisting of action (*kriyāmaya-kratu*) is possible here—the Sūtra replies:
"On account of the adjuncts (*anubandha*) and so forth, as in the case of the distinctness of other cognitions; and it is seen, and it has been stated. (4.1.48)

The sacrifice consisting of knowledge is understood to be distinct from the sacrifice consisting of ritual action—which is characterized by the piling of bricks—due to reasons for distinction such as the "connections" (anubandha) and others. The "connections" are the elements associated with the sacrifice, such as the cups (graha), hymns (stotra), and recitations (śastra), which are set forth in passages such as: "With the mind these cups were drawn; with the mind they praised; with the mind they recited."
