By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the previously mentioned *śruti* and so forth are included; the meaning is that by means of *śruti*, *liṅga*, and the rest, along with their respective adjuncts (*anubandha*), the sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*) is understood as distinct [from the ritual sacrifice]. Just as other forms of knowledge (*prajñāntara-pṛthaktva-vat*)—such as the Dahara-vidyā and others—are understood through *śruti* and the rest to be separate from the ritual sacrifice consisting of action (*kriyāmaya-kratu*), so too is this [knowledge-sacrifice]. And thus, when the sacrifice consisting of knowledge is understood as distinct through its adjuncts and other factors, an injunction (*vidhi*) is postulated for it.

Furthermore, when an injunction is inferred in passages that have the form of restatements (anuvāda), it has been stated: "But the statements [are injunctive] because they convey something not previously known" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.31). As for the fruit, from the extended application (atideśa) stating, "Of each one of these, the fruit is as great as that of the former," it is understood that whatever fruit belongs to the fire-altar built of bricks by way of its own sacrifice, that same fruit belongs to the mental fire-altars (manaścit) and others as well, by way of their respective sacrifices. || 48 ||

As for the argument that the entry [of the mantras] into the ritual consisting of action is understood because their function as instruments of comparison is known through extended application (atideśa), to that he says:
"Not even on account of similarity, because they are perceived [as independent], for there is no attainment of the worlds, as in the case of Death. (Sūtra 49)

It is not necessarily the case that because of an extended application (*atideśa*), the intermediate operation must also be identical, such that these [meditations] would enter into the ritual acts consisting of action (*kriyāmaya-kratu*). For an extended application is observed even from some mere commonality; indeed, in passages such as "That person who is in this orb is death itself," an extended application is observed based on the mere commonality of being a destroyer, yet there is no attainment of that world nor reaching that place for the person in the orb, just as there is none for Death.

In the same way here as well, although there is an extension of the nature of the mind-altars (manaścit) and so forth to be like the brick-built fire-altar, they should not thereby enter into the ritual action consisting of the form and place of the brick-built fire-altar. Therefore, it is understood from this extension that whatever fruit belongs to the brick-built fire-altar through its own ritual context, that very same fruit belongs to the mind-altars and so forth through the medium of the knowledge-based (vidyāmaya) ritual. || 49 ||
And the same nature applies to the subsequent [syllables] as well; however, due to their greater number, they are treated as a continuous sequence.

Moreover, from the subsequent passage by the Brāhmaṇa, it is understood that this word—which designates the fire-altars consisting of mind and so forth—is of such a nature, namely, that it conveys what consists of knowledge (vidyāmaya).

For in another passage, the Brāhmaṇa states: "This world indeed is this Agnicit; its enclosing stones are the waters," and so on, concluding with: "He who knows this thus attains this entire world as it is being filled. Thus, a distinct meditation (*vidyā*) with its own specific fruit is enjoined. Therefore, for one who maintains that the fire-altar consists of bricks, there is no restriction to ritual action alone. If that is so, why are the mental fires (*manaścita*) and others, which consist of knowledge, not connected in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* [Upaniṣad], but are instead connected here?

To this it is replied: "But [the designation] is due to the abundance [of parts]. Because of the abundance of the constituent parts of the fire-altar to be mentally constructed (*manaścita*) and so forth, the connection (*anubandha*) is made here in their proximity. The section concerning the prior alternative (*pūrvavikalpa-adhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
[The self is] one, because [cognition] exists in the body [of each individual]. (51)

In all the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), it has been stated that just as the nature of the object of meditation (*upāsya*) and the meditation itself must be known, so too must the nature of the meditator (*upāsaka*) be known;

for it is said, "And thus there is the presentation and the question regarding these three alone. Furthermore, the text will later state that this inner self (*pratyagātman*) is to be meditated upon as being identical with the supreme self (*paramātman*), in the passage: "But they approach [the Self] as the Self, and they cause [it] to be grasped as such. Now, should this inner self be meditated upon merely in its form as a knower, an agent, and an enjoyer capable of wandering here and there; or rather in its essential nature as described in the Prajāpati discourse, characterized by freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth? What is the correct view? Some maintain that it is merely in the form of a knower and so on.

Why? Because this self of the worshipper exists within the body. For one who resides in the body, such a form [of the self] is sufficient, since the attainment of the fruit is established through that much alone of mental reflection.

Indeed, for those entitled to ritual acts who desire fruits such as heaven, the form that exists at the stage of experiencing the fruit—distinct from the state of being a knower and so forth—is not the form that must be reflected upon at the stage of performing the means; for the performance of the means and the attainment of their fruit are accomplished by that much alone, and there is no purpose in reflecting on anything more, as there is no difference [in the result]. It is exactly the same here as well.

[Objection: But surely, in this context, because of the specific statement, "As a person acts in this world, so does he become after departing from here," it is understood that only the form characterized by freedom from sin and so forth is to be meditated upon; [we reply: not so, because that [statement] refers to the object of meditation in the words, "In whatever way they meditate upon him. This being the case, we state the following:
"There is a distinction [between the two forms], because [the soul] becomes that which it contemplates, but not as in the case of perception. (Sūtra 3.2.52)

However, it is not the case that only the aspect of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) and so forth is to be meditated upon. Rather, that distinction of this Self between the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and the state of liberation (*mokṣa*)—characterized by freedom from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and other qualities—is what must be meditated upon. The meaning is that at the time of meditation, the Self is to be meditated upon precisely in whatever form it possesses in the state of liberation.

Why? Because [the result] arises from the existence of that [object of meditation], and because one attains its very form. As it is said: "In whatever way a person intends in this world, so does he become after departing from here; in whatever way they meditate upon Him, so indeed they become. For it is heard in scripture that attainment occurs precisely according to the mode of meditation. Nor can it be argued that this [attainment] refers solely to the nature of the Supreme (para), since the inner self (pratyagātman) is also included within the category of the object of meditation by virtue of being the body of the Supreme Brahman which is the object of meditation. Therefore...

It is stated that for one who meditates on the Supreme Self as having the individual self (pratyagātman) as its body—possessing qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) as declared in the words of Prajāpati—the attainment is of that very same form; for this reason it is said, "Having such a resolve (*kratu*), having departed this world, I shall attain that world. Therefore, the individual self must be contemplated precisely in its form as the object of attainment.

"Like the apprehension of Brahman" (*upalabdhivat-brahmopalabdhivat*): the meaning is that just as the prescribed apprehension of Brahman has as its object the true nature of Brahman as it exists, so too the apprehension of the Self has as its object the true nature of the Self as it exists. The contemplation of the Self's nature is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to ritual action; for it is the performance of the ritual itself—such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice"—that is enjoined for the sake of the fruit. The realization of the Self in the form of a knower distinct from the body and so forth is intended for the qualification (*adhikāra*) to perform rituals that are the means to a fruit occurring at a later time; thus, only that much is required there, and nothing is lacking. || 52 ||
The section concerning the non-existence [of the soul] in the body is completed.
But those [rites] connected with the limbs [of the sacrifice] do not belong to the various branches (śākhās) for each Veda. 53.

"One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha"; "One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds"; "People say 'Hymn, hymn'; that very thing is this hymn, namely this earth"; "This world, indeed, is this built fire-altar"—such meditations based on the constituent parts of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*) arise. The inquiry is: are these restricted only to those specific recensional branches (*śākhā*) in which they are heard, or are they connected to the Udgītha and other elements in all recensional branches?

Even though it is established that all the Vedānta texts convey the same meaning, there arises a reasonable doubt: because the *udgītha* and other elements differ according to the specific accentuation (*svara*) in each Veda, should they not be restricted to their respective branches? What is the correct conclusion? That they should be so restricted. Why? Because the instruction "one should meditate on the *udgītha*" is heard in a general sense as being connected with the *udgītha*; therefore, since a particular *udgītha* endowed with a specific accent is present in that very branch, it is logical that the meditation should terminate in that particular instance. Thus, these [meditations] should be restricted to those very branches.

This being the case, we reply: "But those connected with the constituent parts [of the sacrifice]. The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position. For the meditations connected with constituent parts such as the *udgītha* do not remain restricted to their own respective branches alone; rather, they should be connected with every Veda—that is, in all branches. The word "for" (hi) indicates the reason: because by the very nature of the scripture, they are connected merely with the constituent parts such as the *udgītha*, therefore they should be connected wherever those constituent parts, such as the *udgītha*, occur.

Although individual instances of the *udgītha* differ according to variations in accent, nevertheless, by virtue of the common term "udgītha," all such instances are present; thus, there is no authority for any restrictive limitation. Furthermore, according to the principle of the "single sacrifice across all recensions" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*), the ritual is one and the same in all recensions. Consequently, since the ritual is present in all recensions, the *udgītha* and other elements that are constituent parts of that ritual are also present. Therefore, as there is no specific distinction in proximity for any single instance, there can be no restriction. || 53 ||
Or rather, there is no contradiction, as in the case of mantras and the like. || 54 ||

The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "and" (*ca*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), number (*saṅkhyā*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), order (*krama*), substance (*dravya*), and action (*karman*) are included. Just as there is no contradiction in the application (*viniyoga*)—according to direct statement (*śruti*) and other means—of mantras and the like, which are recited in individual branches (*śākhā*), to the sacrifice (*kratu*) that is their subordinate (*śeṣin*), since that sacrifice is one and the same across all branches; so too here there is no contradiction. The section concerning the connection with the subsidiaries (*aṅgāvabaddhādhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
The greater importance of the plenary [Self] is like that of the ritual; for thus the scripture shows. || 55 ||

Beginning with the words, “Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava,” the Vaiśvānara-vidyā is taught; therein, Vaiśvānara is heard of as the Supreme Self to be meditated upon, having the three worlds as His body, with heaven, sun, air, ether, water, and earth as His constituent parts. And in that context, heaven is the head and the sun is the eye.

Fire is the head, Vāyu is the breath, Ākāśa is the trunk (meaning the middle part of the body), Water is the bladder, and Earth is the feet—these are the specific limbs. In this regard, a doubt arises: should meditation be performed upon this body of the three worlds taken individually, or both individually and collectively, or only collectively? What is the proper view? That it should be done individually. Why? Because at the beginning, meditation on the individual parts is taught.

For it is taught as follows: "Aupamanyava and others, with Uddālaka as the sixth, having approached Aśvapati Kekaya, asked: 'You indeed know this Vaiśvānara Self; tell that very one to us. Thus they questioned him.

And for each of them, he described the meditation on his own respective objects of worship—Heaven and the others—as being distributed across the head and other parts of the body, as previously stated, and specified the fruit for each respective meditation, beginning with: "He who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food, sees what is dear, and possesses spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in his family; for this [Heaven] is the head of this Self," and "This indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self, named 'The Radiant' (*sutejas*)," and so forth. Furthermore, in each of those meditations, he declares that the object of worship is indeed Vaiśvānara.

Therefore, meditation should be performed upon [Vaiśvānara] alone as divided [into parts]. Elsewhere, in the passage, "But he who meditates on this Vaiśvānara Self, which is of the measure of a span and all-pervading," it should be understood that there is a summary conclusion regarding the meditation on the head and other parts, which was previously taught in relation to Vaiśvānara as delimited by the measure of two fingers and so forth.

Another says that in this very way, the meditation on the whole [Vaiśvānara] must also be performed, because of the mention of separate fruits: "But he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara as of the measure of a span, as the all-measuring, eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves. Nor does this much constitute a split in the sentence, just as in the Bhūmavidyā, the meditation on Name and so forth and its fruit are mentioned at the beginning.

Having introduced the knowledge of the Infinite (*bhūma-vidyā*) with the words, "But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of Truth," and so forth, [the text] designates its fruit with the words, "He becomes self-ruling; for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds. In that case, even though the sentence is devoted to the knowledge of the Infinite, the meditations on name and so forth, as well as their respective fruits, are nevertheless accepted as subordinate parts; so it is here as well. This being the position reached, it is replied: "The greater importance belongs to the Infinite. The meaning is that the greater importance—i.e., the authoritative status—belongs to the Infinite alone, which is vast and comprehensive, because the unity of the sentence is understood.

For instance, beginning with "Prājīnaśāla Aupamanyava," [the text continues]: "This venerable Uddālaka Āruṇi is currently studying this Vaiśvānara Self; come, let us approach him. Thus, five great sages, including Aupamanyava and others, desiring to know the Vaiśvānara Self, approached that Uddālaka. Finding no knowledge of the Vaiśvānara Self there, and together with him approaching Aśvapati Kekaya, who was a knower of the Vaiśvānara Self, [they said]: "This very Self..."

Having asked, "You are currently studying Vaiśvānara; tell that very one to us," they understood from his presence the Supreme Self as Vaiśvānara, whose body extends from his own world down to the earth, as the object of meditation, and they understood its fruit to be the experience of Brahman, which is the self of all worlds, all beings, and all food. Thus, from the conclusion of the passage, the unity of the discourse is understood.

Thus, when it is understood that there is a single unified statement, it is determined that the injunctions regarding meditation on specific parts and the mention of results are merely restatements of portions of the meditation on the whole. This is like a sacrifice (*kratu*): just as for the sacrifice enjoined by the rule, "Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara," its constituent parts are restated in passages such as, "Insofar as it is on eight potsherds," and so forth; likewise, meditation on the whole alone is logical, not meditation on the parts individually.

For this Śruti demonstrates the harm resulting from meditating on [the Self] in its separate parts by stating: "Your head would have fallen off had you not come to me," and "You would have become blind had you not come to me," and so forth. Therefore, that which was asserted—the equality of the meditation on Name and the others—is also refuted; for while no harm is heard of in those meditations on Name and the rest, the Śruti declares that the meditation on the *bhūman* (the Infinite) possesses a superior fruit compared to the meditations on Name and the others.

"But he indeed speaks beyond [the ordinary] who speaks beyond by means of the Truth. Therefore, even though that passage has the knowledge of the Infinite (bhūmavidyā) as its primary subject, the meditations on Name and so forth, along with their fruits, are intended to be taught; otherwise, it would be impossible to praise the knowledge of the Infinite by means of a "speaking beyond" based on its superior fruit. Consequently, the meditation on the whole is alone the logical conclusion. The section concerning the superiority of the Infinite (bhūmajyāyastvādhikaraṇa) is completed.
Because of the distinction between various sounds and so forth. || 56 ||

In this context, all knowledges of Brahman (brahmavidyās) have as their sole fruit liberation in the form of attaining Brahman; examples include the knowledge of Being (sadvidyā), the knowledge of the Earth (bhūmavidyā), the knowledge of the Dahara (daharavidyā), the Upakosala-vidyā, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, the Ānandamaya-vidyā, the Akṣara-vidyā, and others—whether they belong to a single Vedic branch or to different branches. Others, moreover, have as their fruit objects such as the vital breath (prāṇa). Here, a doubt arises: is there identity of the knowledge (vidyaikya), or is there a difference between the knowledges (vidyābheda)?

When their mutual distinction has been established in this very context, the principle of "cognition based on all Vedāntas" (*sarvavedāntapratyaya*) applies to a single meditation, such as the Dahara-vidyā. What is correct? That there is unity of knowledge (*vidyaikyam*). Why? Because the object of knowledge (*vedya*), which is Brahman, is one. For the object of knowledge constitutes the very form (*rūpa*) of the knowledge; therefore, due to the identity of form, there is unity of knowledge.

This being the case, it is replied: "They are distinct. The meditations (*vidyā*) are distinct. Why? Because of the difference in words and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), repetition, number, quality, procedure, and name are included. Here, through differences in words and other factors, we observe distinctions in the auxiliary elements (*anubandha-bheda*) which serve as the causes for the distinction between what is to be enjoined. Even though [the text says] "one should know," "one should meditate," and so on...

Words such as "that" (tat) denote repetition, and the resulting cognitions have Brahman as their sole object; nevertheless, the knowledge consisting of the repetition of those cognitions—which makes known the repetition of cognitions whose objects are Brahman as qualified by attributes such as being the sole cause of the universe and being free from sin, as proclaimed in that context—destroys [ignorance].

It is determined that the sentences in each respective section—which describe specific meditations connected to the fruit consisting of the attainment of Brahman and which are complete in themselves—teach distinct forms of knowledge (*vidyā*). Although this point is established by the aphorisms (*sūtras*) stated in the earlier portion [of the Vedas], such as "There is a difference of action when there is a different word," its restatement here is for the purpose of dispelling the false view that the Vedānta sentences are concerned solely with knowledge that is not subject to injunction. Therefore, it is settled that there is a difference between the knowledges. 56.
The section concerning the distinction based on sound and other [sensory qualities] is completed.
The option [is permissible] because the result is not distinguished [from that of the regular rule]. || 57 ||

The diversity of the various knowledges (*vidyā*) that have Brahman as their fruit—such as the Sadvidyā, the Daharavidyā, and others—has already been stated. Now, regarding the doubt as to whether these knowledges can be combined (*samuccaya*) within a single person because they serve a purpose, or whether there is only an option (*vikalpa*) due to a lack of purpose: what is the correct view? It is that combination is indeed possible. Why? Because we observe the combination even of different scriptural teachings that have a single fruit.

For it is observed that even for a single result such as heaven, there is a combination of its means—such as the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—within one person, depending on the desire for a greater measure of that very heaven; likewise, here too, a combination is possible depending on the desire for a greater measure of the experience of Brahman.

This being the case, we reply: there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*); a combination (*samuccaya*) is not possible. Why? Because the fruit is indistinguishable. For it is heard in scripture that the fruit of all knowledges of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)—the experience of Brahman as unsurpassed and infinitely superior bliss—is indistinguishable: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"; "That is one bliss of Brahman, and of the learned Śrotriya who is free from desire"; and "When the seer sees the golden-hued maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman."

This is known from such passages as: "Then the wise man, having shaken off both merit and demerit, being stainless, attains the supreme equality. For Brahman is that which, when experienced by oneself, constitutes an unsurpassed and infinite bliss for both oneself and others. Since such an experience of Brahman is attained through one single knowledge (*vidyā*), what need is there for another? Thus, there is no possibility of their combination (*samuccaya*).

For in the case of heaven and the like, because they are limited in terms of space, time, and essential nature, there is the possibility of "abundance" (bhūyastva) relative to those factors of space and so forth; thus, for one who desires them, a combination (samuccaya) of means is possible. But here, in the case of Brahman, whose nature is the opposite of that, such a combination is not possible. Furthermore, since all meditations (vidyās) have as their fruit the attainment of Brahman by way of dispelling the beginningless karma and ignorance that are opposed to the experience of Brahman, they possess an identical fruit; therefore, there is only an option (vikalpa) among them all. || 57 ||

However, those meditations (*vidyā*) whose fruits are distinct from the attainment of Brahman may be combined or optionally chosen according to one's desire, just like rituals that have heaven and so forth as their fruit; for, since their fruits are limited, there is the possibility of desiring more of them. Thus it is said: "But optional [meditations] may be combined or not at will, because of the absence of the previous reason. (Sūtra 3.3.58)
The meaning is: because there is an absence of being immeasurable *palas* in weight. || 58 || The section concerning optional alternatives (*vikalpādhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
In the case of the limbs, there is a state of being dependent upon their respective bases. || 59 ||

Regarding the meditations (*vidyā*) based on the auxiliary elements of the sacrifice, such as the *udgītha*—beginning with the text, "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*"—is there a doubt as to whether they must necessarily be undertaken within the sacrifices like the *udgītha* itself for the sake of the sacrifice, or whether they may be undertaken according to one's desire like the *godohana* vessel for the sake of the person? In this dilemma, it is reasonable that they must be undertaken as a rule. But was it not established in the sūtra, "The non-rule regarding their determination [is due] to the perception of that; for [the meditation] is separate, and its fruit is the absence of obstacles," that there is no fixed rule because these meditations serve the purpose of the person?

True; however, in order to confirm that very point, it will be examined through certain observations of indicative marks (*liṅga*) and reasoning. For in that context, because of the observation of non-restriction in the statement, "By means of that, both perform [the sacrifice]," the fact of having separate fruits has been stated. Just as with the *udgītha* and other elements which serve as the substrata for meditations (*upāsanā*), there are many reasons found for the rule of employing meditations as subordinate members (*aṅga*). Indeed, in this case, unlike the injunction "One desiring cattle should fetch water in a *godohana* vessel," no connection with a fruit is heard within the injunctive sentence of the meditation itself.

In the passage "One should meditate on the *udgītha*," meditation is understood as being connected specifically with the *udgītha* and so forth; for the connection with a fruit is known from another statement in the form of a present-tense description: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the *upaniṣad*, that alone becomes more powerful. Since the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice is already determined by its own sentence through its connection with the *udgītha* and so forth—which are invariably connected to the sacrifice—a reference in another sentence to a connection with a fruit in the present tense would be merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), like the mention of hearing "sinless verses" (*apāpaśloka*).

Therefore, just as the *udgītha* and other such elements, being the substrata for meditations (*upāsana*), are invariably adopted by virtue of the injunctions regarding their application as constituent parts of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), so too the meditations resting upon them must likewise be invariably adopted, as they become constituent parts of the sacrifice through those very substrata. || 59 ||
And because of the conduct of the learned. || 60 ||

Instruction (*śiṣṭi*) means teaching, that is, the imparting of knowledge. Furthermore, because of the injunction for meditation as a subordinate part of the *udgītha* in the passage, "One should meditate upon the *udgītha*," there is a rule of inclusion (*upādānaniyama*). This is because, unlike passages such as "One desiring cattle should fetch water with the *godohana* vessel," no specific qualification (*adhikāra*) is heard in the injunctive sentence; rather, it is understood that the very status of being a subordinate part of the *udgītha* and so forth is what is to be enjoined. || 60 ||
Because of their being combined. || 61 ||

"Even from the Hotṛ's station, one may indeed rectify a poorly performed Udgītha"—thus a rule for rectification through meditation is observed. A "durudgītha" is an Udgītha devoid of the knowledge [of its true nature]. By stating that there is a restoration by another when such knowledge is lacking, the text demonstrates that this knowledge must necessarily be employed. 61.
And because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of qualities.

Because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of the quality of meditation (*upāsanaguṇa*)—that is, the *praṇava* which is the locus of meditation—together with the meditation itself, namely, "By means of that, this threefold knowledge proceeds: 'Om' he causes [the Adhvaryu] to announce, 'Om' he recites, 'Om' he sings the *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.9), it is understood that there is a combination of the meditation. Since the word "by that" (*tena*) refers back to the subject under discussion, it follows that the *praṇava* accompanied by meditation alone moves everywhere. Therefore, because one observes the rule of the constant coexistence of meditation with the *praṇava*, meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth must necessarily be included, just like the *udgītha* itself. || 62 ||
This being the position reached, it is said: "Or rather not, because their coexistence is not heard [in scripture]. (63)

It is not the case that there is a rule of mandatory inclusion for the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth within the sacrifices, in the same way that the *udgītha* itself is included. Why? Because their coexistence is not enjoined; that is to say, because their status as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice is not enjoined. For a rule of coexistence applies only when there is a relationship of being an auxiliary part. Although no separate injunction (*adhikāra*) is perceived within this collection of words, "One should meditate on the *udgītha*," nevertheless, immediately following it, [the text says]: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), that alone becomes more powerful."

The status of knowledge as a means toward the greater efficacy of the sacrifice (*kratu*) is being established. Therefore, knowledge—which has a fruit distinct from the fruit of the sacrifice—is enjoined as something to be performed in the words, "One should meditate upon the *udgītha*. It is not logical that there should be an application (*viniyoga*) of knowledge as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *udgītha*, which already possesses a fruit distinct from the fruit of the sacrifice. Now, when the meditation requires a substratum (*āśraya*), the proximate *udgītha* serves merely as that substratum.

Since the *udgītha* is a constituent part of the sacrifice (*kratu*), this distinct qualification—undertaken with the desire for the sacrifice to become more powerful—is based on meditations (*upāsana*) that take the *udgītha* and other such elements as their substrate. Therefore, there is no rule requiring its inclusion within the sacrifices themselves.

Furthermore, "more power" (*vīryavattara*) has been explained as the non-obstruction of the fruit of the sacrifice by the fruit of another stronger karma; the meaning is that the sacrifice yields its fruit without delay.

However, in the case of the *parṇa*-leaf [ladle] and so forth, although it is heard that "whatever one performs with knowledge (*vidyā*), that alone becomes more effective," there is no scriptural statement regarding their being a direct means toward results such as hearing the hymns of the sinless; rather, since there is no contradiction in their application as subsidiaries to the *juhū* and other implements which are themselves subsidiaries of the sacrifice (*kratu*), it is illogical to assume that those things which are already subsidiaries [of the sacrifice] can be means toward a different result. Therefore, the mention of a result in that context must be merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). || 63 ||
And because it is seen [in scripture]. || 64 ||

Moreover, scripture demonstrates that there is no rule regarding the requirement of meditative knowledge (*upāsana*) for officiating priests. By stating, "The Brahman priest who knows thus indeed protects the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the officiating priests," it declares that through the Brahman's knowledge, everyone is protected. This is only possible if there is no such rule requiring the other priests, such as the Udgātṛ, to possess that knowledge. From this indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is understood that the previously mentioned marks—such as the combination of offices and so forth—are merely incidental. Therefore, it is established that there is indeed no fixed rule. 64.
Thus ends the section concerning the existence [of mental factors] in accordance with their basis.
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
"The human goal [is known] from this [Veda], according to the word; thus says Bādarāyaṇa. (Sūtra 1.1.4)

The inquiry into whether there is a combination or non-combination of qualities has been conducted based on whether the meditations (vidyās) are identical or distinct. Now, it is considered whether the human goal (puruṣārtha) results from knowledge itself, or from ritual action that is an auxiliary to knowledge.

What is the correct view? The venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the human goal results from knowledge. Why? Because of the scriptural word (śabda); for we see scriptural passages belonging to the Upaniṣads declaring that the human goal results from knowledge, such as: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and "I know this great Person, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness; knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here."

"There is no other path for going. "Just as rivers, flowing along, reach the ocean and lose their names and forms, so the knower, freed from name and form, attains the divine Supreme Puruṣa," and so forth. || 1 ||
On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) objects:
"Because it is a subordinate element (śeṣa), it is a statement of human purpose (puruṣārthavāda), as in other cases; so says Jaimini. (Sūtra 2)

It is not the case that the attainment of the human goal from knowledge is understood through the word [of scripture]; for this passage beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" does not convey the attainment of the human goal from mere knowledge, because its purpose is to establish the true nature of the Self as the agent in ritual actions. Therefore, for the agent...

The teacher Jaimini maintains that because knowledge (*vidyā*) is subordinate to the sacrifice by way of being a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), the mention of its fruit therein is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), just as it is in the case of other things such as substances and qualities. As it has been stated: "In the case of substances, qualities, and preparatory rites, because they exist for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit must be an explanatory praise."

But has it not already been established that in the Vedāntas, one other than the individual soul (jīva), the agent of actions, is taught as the object to be known for the sake of attainment by those seeking liberation? This was indeed demonstrated previously through such sūtras as: "The other [is Brahman], because of the impossibility [of the other]"; "And because of the designation of difference"; "But it is not the embodied soul, because of the impossibility"; and "If it be argued that it is so because of the reference to the other, we say no, because of the impossibility," and so forth.

The claim that this very Brahman is non-different from the individual soul (jīva) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such statements as "That art thou" (*tattvamasi*) has also been refuted by [the sūtras] beginning with "But [Brahman is] greater, because of the designation of difference" (*adhikaṃ tu bhedanirdeśāt*).

Furthermore, the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—as in "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*) and "All this is indeed Brahman" (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma*)—is common to both sentient and insentient things. This is based on the fact that [Brahman] exists as the very self of each respective entity, as understood from such passages as "He who dwells in the earth" and "He who dwells in the self," and this has been established by such [Sūtras] as "On account of abiding, [it is so] according to Kāśakṛtsna. Therefore, how could the words of the Vedānta be intent upon teaching the true nature of the self as the agent in ritual acts? Thus, how could knowledge be a subordinate part of ritual action?

It is stated [in reply]: The opponent's intention is that one must necessarily admit—on the strength of the indications (*liṅga*) in the Vedānta passages themselves which suggest the primacy of ritual action over knowledge, and by means of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) reinforced by those indications—that the words of the Vedānta are intent upon teaching the true nature of the individual soul as distinct from the body. But [it may be objected] that [the Vedānta texts] do so by way of purifying the agent...

It cannot be said that knowledge enters into the sacrificial rite (*kratu*), because the agent is common to both worldly and Vedic acts, and thus lacks an invariable connection with the rite. This is not so; for although the agent of a worldly action is not distinct from the body, such an interpretation is possible. However, since the nature of the Self—which is distinct from the body and subject to necessity—is useful only in the context of the rite, its exposition by way of establishing that nature does not contradict its entry into the rite. Therefore, since knowledge is subordinate to the rite, it does not result in the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) [independently]. || 2 ||

What, then, are those indicative marks (*liṅga*) by which, through their strengthening of the grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*), the words of the Vedānta are determined to refer to the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*)? To this, he says:
"On account of the observation of [specific] conduct" (Sūtra 3).

Among those who know Brahman, conduct is seen to consist primarily of ritual actions. For instance, Aśvapati Kekaya, who was indeed the foremost among those who know the Self, said to the sages who had approached him for that knowledge: "O venerable ones, I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice. Likewise, Janaka and others, the leaders among the knowers of Brahman, are seen in the Smṛtis as being established in ritual action: "Indeed, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone," and "He too performed very many sacrifices, relying upon knowledge."

Therefore, since it is observed that for those who know Brahman, action is predominant, and since knowledge consists in the cognition of the nature of the agent, knowledge is merely a subordinate part of ritual action; thus, the human goal does not arise from knowledge alone. || 3 ||
This is an inferential mark (*liṅga*); [the opponent] says, "Let the attainment (*prāpti*) be stated," to which [the author] replies: "Because of its being taught" (*tacchāteḥ*). || 4 ||

For scripture itself declares that knowledge is an auxiliary to ritual action: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣadic insight, that alone becomes more powerful. This scriptural statement cannot be restricted by context to refer solely to the *udgītha* chant, because scripture is more authoritative than context; indeed, this scriptural statement—"whatever one performs with knowledge"—has as its scope knowledge in general. || 4 ||
Because of the act of simultaneous grasping. || 5 ||

The coexistence of knowledge and action is also observed in the statement, "Knowledge and action both accompany him. And this coexistence is possible only if, according to the reasoning already stated, knowledge is a constituent part of action. || 5 ||
Because there is an injunction for one who possesses that.

Because the injunction for ritual action pertains to one who possesses knowledge (*vidyāvat*), it is understood that knowledge is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of ritual action. This is evident from such passages as: "Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher according to the prescribed rule, and having performed the service for the teacher with what remains [of his time], having returned home, [he should perform rites] in a pure place in the family circle," and so forth. By enjoining rituals for one who has "studied the Veda," the text enjoins them for one who has completed his study up to the point of understanding the meaning; for it has been established that study extends until the comprehension of the meaning. Therefore, since even the knowledge of Brahman is employed within the context of rituals, it cannot be considered to have an independent fruit. || 6 ||
Because of necessity. || 7 ||

Furthermore, the human goal does not arise from knowledge. Because of the injunction, "Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years," which assigns the entirety of a knower of the Self’s lifespan to actions as a rule, it is understood that the fruit belongs to action alone, while knowledge is merely an auxiliary to action. (Sūtra 7)
This being the case, we reply:
But because of the teaching of something additional, Bādarāyaṇa holds this view, for such is seen [in scripture]. (2.4.8)

By the word "but" (*tu*), the previous position is set aside: the human goal [is attained] from knowledge alone. Why? Because of the teaching regarding the object of knowledge (*adhikāra-upadeśāt*). For, among the rituals, there is the teaching that the Supreme Brahman—the object of knowledge who is distinct from the agent, the individual soul (*jīva*), and who is the source of infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities—is the one to be known. Thus, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa’s view is precisely that the fruit [of action] arises from knowledge. Let the indicative marks (*liṅga*) stand aside; for the teaching regarding the object of knowledge is certainly of that which is superior to the agent, the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

How so? Because [the Supreme Being] is seen in the scriptural passages teaching knowledge within the context of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), even though that self is impure; for He is the source of infinite qualities that are inconceivable even in the pure [self], the object of knowledge who has cast off all trace of sin, whose play consists in the arising, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe by His own volition, the omniscient, the omnipotent, whose bliss is immeasurable by word or thought, the Lord of the individual soul (*jīva*), and the sovereign ruler of all—this Supreme Brahman is thus perceived in the sentences that enjoin His realization.

"His evil has been struck down; he is free from old age, death, sorrow, hunger, and thirst; his desires are true and his resolves are true. "He thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. He emitted heat. "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving. "His supreme power is heard to be manifold indeed, as are His innate knowledge, strength, and action. "That is the one bliss of Brahman. "From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it—having known that bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing whatsoever. "This..."

"He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings; He is the bridge, the upholder. "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses, and there is no progenitor of Him, nor is there any ruler over Him. "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart. "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart. "Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear of Him the sun rises; out of fear of Him Agni and Indra [function]."

"...the fifth runs and dances," and so forth. Therefore, in words that teach [the nature of] experience (*vedana*), there is not even a trace of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as the agent—an entity comparable to a firefly, unfit for connection with things to be abandoned such as ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, it is well said that the human goal arises from knowledge (*vidyā*), because the immortality consisting of attaining Him, which is heard of here and there in the scriptures, is the fruit of the knowledge whose object is the Supreme Person. || 8 ||
The indicative marks are also set aside,
for the observation is the same.

As for the claim that knowledge is an auxiliary to ritual action because we observe the performance of rituals by those who know Brahman—that is not so; for such observation is equally applicable even when knowledge is not an auxiliary. The meaning is that the observation of the performance of rituals by those who know Brahman is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since we also observe their non-performance. Indeed, the renunciation of ritual action by those who know Brahman is seen in such passages as: "The Kāvaṣeya sages said: 'For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we sacrifice? and so forth.

Therefore, since those who know Brahman are seen to renounce ritual action, knowledge is not an auxiliary part of action. How is this [apparent contradiction] resolved—that those who know Brahman both perform and do not perform rituals? It is because ritual action such as sacrifice, when devoid of attachment to its fruits, is an auxiliary part of the knowledge of Brahman. Thus, the observation of the performance of such action is logically consistent.

And it will be stated [later]: "There is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. Since that very work, such as sacrifice, when performed for the sake of a fruit, is opposed to the knowledge of Brahman which has liberation as its sole fruit, the observation that such [fruit-seeking] work is not to be practiced is more appropriate. If knowledge were a subsidiary part of ritual action, the abandonment of action would not be possible in any way. || 9 ||
Regarding what was stated—that the fact that knowledge is a subsidiary part of ritual action is understood from scripture itself—it is replied: "That [rule] is not universal" (sūtra 10).

This scriptural passage does not concern all forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), but rather concerns only the Udgītha-knowledge. This is because the word "whatever" (*yat*) in the phrase "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (*yadeva vidyayā karoti*), being unspecified in its particularity, refers specifically to the Udgītha under discussion in the phrase "One should meditate on the Udgītha" (*udgītham upāsīta*). For it is not the case that "whatever one performs" is connected with "with knowledge"; rather, having pointed out by means of the word "whatever" that which is performed with knowledge—namely, "Whatever one performs with knowledge"—it is said that "that very thing becomes more powerful" (*tadeva vīryavattaram*), thus declaring the superior efficacy of that which is performed with knowledge. || 10 ||
As for the statement, "Knowledge and action both follow him," which suggests that knowledge is a constituent part of action because we observe their conjunction—regarding that, he says:
"There is a separation, as in the case of the hundred. (Sūtra 11)

According to the principle stated in the passage, "Knowledge and action both follow him," a distinction must be understood: since knowledge and action have different fruits, knowledge follows for its own fruit, and action follows for its own fruit. Just as when it is said that two hundred [pieces of money] follow a seller of land and jewels, the distinction is understood to be one hundred for the sake of the land and one hundred for the sake of the jewels; so it is here as well. || 11 ||
[The entitlement belongs] to one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda]. || 12 ||

As for the claim that because the injunction for ritual action applies to one who possesses knowledge (*vidyā*), knowledge is therefore an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of ritual action—this is not tenable. This is because the injunction "having studied the Veda" prescribes [the rite] for one who has merely completed the study. Furthermore, the injunction for Vedic study does not itself impel one toward the comprehension of the meaning, since, like the consecration of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the study culminates merely in the grasping of the mass of syllables. And once the *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic text) has been grasped, a person spontaneously engages in the inquiry into its meaning—which results in its definitive determination—because it is observed that the grasped text leads to the comprehension of rituals that yield fruits.

Therefore, one who seeks ritual action engages in the knowledge of action, while one who seeks liberation engages in the knowledge of Brahman; thus, knowledge is not a subordinate part of ritual action. Even though the injunction for Vedic study itself impels one toward the comprehension of the meaning, nevertheless, knowledge is not a subordinate part of ritual action, because knowledge is a distinct entity from the mere comprehension of the meaning.

Just as the performance of rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma—which serve as the means to attain results—is distinct from the mere knowledge of the nature of those rituals, so too is that which is called "knowledge" (vidyā)—expressed by terms such as meditation (dhyāna) and worship (upāsana)—a distinct entity from the knowledge of the nature of Brahman consisting of the understanding of its meaning; for this [latter] knowledge is the means to the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha). Thus, not even a trace of connection with ritual action exists in it. || 12 ||
Not so, because there is no distinction. 13.

As for the argument that the statement, "Only performing actions here... (Gītā 3.19) restricts the knower of the Self to the lifelong performance of action by diverting him from knowledge—this is not tenable. For there is no specific reason to hold that this injunction concerns only independent actions that serve as means to a fruit, since it is equally logical that it refers to actions that are auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of knowledge. Furthermore, [the Gītā states], "Indeed, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone," and because for the knower, meditative worship (*upāsana*) continues until the moment of death. (Sūtra 13)

Having thus resolved the objection by means of the intrinsic nature of the meaning, he states the meaning of the passage "performing actions here indeed," as either a commendation for the sake of praise: "Or [it is] permission for the sake of praise. (14)

The word "vā" (or) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Since this occurs within the context of knowledge (*vidyā*) in the passage "All this is to be enveloped by the Lord," this permission for the performance of ritual action at all times is intended as a praise of knowledge. For knowledge is praised by the fact that even while performing action at all times, one is not tainted by actions due to the majesty of knowledge. The remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) shows exactly this: "Thus it is with you; there is no other way than this; action does not cling to the man. Therefore, knowledge is not an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of ritual action. || 14 ||
And some [hold that it occurs] by one's own will. || 15 ||

Moreover, certain followers of other Vedic branches record the abandonment of the householder's state by one established in the knowledge of Brahman according to their own will: "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this world is the Self? This statement, by declaring the abandonment of household duties at will on the part of the wise man who has become dispassionate, demonstrates that the knowledge of Brahman is not an auxiliary element of ritual action. For if knowledge were an auxiliary to sacrifices and other rites, the abandonment of the householder's state at will by one established in that knowledge would be impossible.
Therefore, knowledge is not an auxiliary to ritual action. || 15 ||
And [the rule applies] to the suppression [of the preceding vowel]. || 16 ||

Furthermore, it is taught in every Vedānta text that karma—consisting of merit and demerit and being the root of all worldly suffering—is destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman, as in such passages as: "The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted when He, the Higher and the Lower, is seen. This [destruction] is not consistent with the view that such knowledge is a subsidiary part of ritual action.
And [the rule applies] to those who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), for there is a scriptural statement to that effect. || 17 ||

Since the knowledge of Brahman is seen among those in the stages of life where the vital energy is drawn upward (the *ūrdhvaretas* stages), and since rituals such as the *agnihotra*, *darśa-pūrṇamāsa*, and others are absent in those stages, knowledge is not an auxiliary part of ritual action (*karma*). [Objection]: But surely the stages of life for those who have drawn their vital energy upward do not exist at all, because of scriptural injunctions such as "one performs the *agnihotra* as long as one lives," which establish a lifelong obligation for the *agnihotra*, *darśa-pūrṇamāsa*, and other rites; and because Smṛtis that contradict Śruti lack authority. To this, he says: "For [it is] the Word [that is the authority]," etc. (*śabda hi iti*).

For these [stages] are seen only in Vedic texts, such as: "There are three branches of dharma," "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity," and "Desiring this very world, mendicants go forth into the wandering life. As for the scriptural injunction regarding lifelong [householder duties], it refers to those who are not yet dispassionate.
Jaimini [holds that there is] a grasping [of the self], because it is not enjoined; for [the scriptures] indeed reject [such a view]. || 18 ||

As for the claim that because the stages of life (āśramas) characterized by lifelong celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*) are seen in Vedic texts such as "There are three branches of dharma," they must therefore exist—this is not tenable. Why? Because in passages such as "There are three branches of dharma," there is merely a reference to those stages of life; the meaning is that it is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Why is this so? Because there is no injunction (*codanā*) here; for no word of injunction is heard in this context.

For by the passage beginning with "three aggregates of dharma," the meditation on Brahman by means of the *praṇava*, which is the subject at hand, is being praised; this is because of the concluding statement, "One who is firmly established in Brahman attains immortality. Therefore, in this context, there is merely a restatement of those stages of life (*āśrama*) for another purpose. Furthermore, in the passage, "And those who in the forest worship through faith and austerity," since the intent is to enjoin the path of the gods (*devayāna*), there is no possibility of an injunction for other stages of life there either.

Moreover, the collection of scriptural texts (śruti) indeed censures other stages of life, stating, for example: "He who allows the sacred fire to go out is a slayer of the heroes among the gods. Therefore, the teacher Jaimini maintains that there are no stages of life for those whose semen is drawn up (ūrdhvaretas). 18.
Vādarāyaṇa [maintains] that it should be performed, because of the scriptural statement of equality. || 19 ||

The venerable Bādarāyaṇa considers that even the other stages of life, which have the householder as their basis, are to be practiced. Why? Because of the scriptural statement of equality regarding their being intended for adoption.

For the equality of those other stages of life with the householder’s stage is indeed heard in scripture; beginning with the passage, "There are three branches of dharma," the mention of the householder’s stage and the others is equal insofar as they serve to praise the state of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃstha*). Now, if it is held that the restatement of the householder’s stage is only possible when it has already been established—and thus its prior establishment must necessarily be accepted—that view applies equally to the others as well, except for one's own personal bias.

Nor is it correct to claim that the duty of the householder alone is denoted by all these terms—“sacrifice, study, charity, austerity, and celibacy”—on the grounds that both celibacy and austerity are possible for a householder. This is because it would be illogical to speak of a division as “the first, the second, and the third” after summarizing them as “the three pillars of dharma. Therefore, “sacrifice, study, and charity” refer to the householder’s stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*). Here, the word “study” refers specifically to the practice of the Vedas.

By the word *tapas* (asceticism), both the state of the householder (*vaiśvānara*) and the life of the wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*) are included, because both have asceticism as their primary characteristic. For the word *tapas* is conventionally established in the sense of bodily austerity, and that is common to both. The duties of the student (*brahmacārin*) alone are designated by the word *brahmacarya*. The term *brahmasaṃstha*, however, is etymological (*yaugika*) and applicable to all stages of life (*āśrama*), since it is possible for members of all orders to be established in Brahman.

"Brahma-saṃsthatva" (being established in Brahman) is the state of being firmly established in Brahman; and that is indeed possible for all. Those belonging solely to the stages of life (*āśrama*) who are deficient in their steadfastness in Brahman partake of the worlds of merit; among those very same people, he who is steadfast in Brahman becomes a partaker of immortality. This has been clearly stated by the venerable Parāśara, beginning with "The world of Prajāpati belongs to the Brāhmaṇas" and ending with "That of Brahman is remembered for the renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*)," [thereby describing] the world of Brahman for the castes (*varṇa*) and the stages of life taken individually.

Having described the fruit ending with attainment, [the text] states: "For those yogins who are single-mindedly devoted and always meditate on Brahman, their supreme goal is that station which the wise indeed behold. Thus, it declares the attainment of Brahman for those established in Brahman among these very [orders]. Therefore, since the orders of those who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) are seen to be equal to the householder's order (gṛhasthāśrama), they too are to be practiced.

And because of the statement, "And those who, pure in the forest, worship through austerity," since the prescription of the path of the gods depends upon reaching the stage of life (āśrama) where austerity is predominant, it must be admitted that they too attain that [path]. || 19 ||

Having established that, whether on the view that this is a mere reference (*parāmarśa*) or on the view that it is an injunction (*vidhi*), these [stages of life] must be practiced just like the householder’s stage, he says the following in order to demonstrate that this is indeed an injunction for all stages of life and not a mere restatement:
"Or rather, it is an injunction, as in the case of wearing [the sacred thread]," (Sūtra 2.4.20).

The word "vā" (or) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). This is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding the stages of life (*āśrama*); it is like the case of "holding. Just as in the Agnihotra prescribed by the *diṣṭa* [rite], in the passage, "He should run along holding the fuel-stick below, for he holds it above for the gods," an injunction is accepted for holding it above because it was not previously established, even though the sentence has the appearance of a restatement (*anuvāda*); this is stated in the *Śeṣalakṣaṇa*: "But there is an injunction regarding holding, because it is something new (*apūrva*)."

Likewise, here too, because [the practice] has not been previously established, an injunction alone must be resorted to. This has been demonstrated: even though the Jābālas state the rule for the stages of life (*āśrama*)—namely, "Having completed the student stage (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; and having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce; or else, otherwise, one may renounce directly from the student stage, or from the householder stage, or from the forest-dweller stage; on whatever day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce"—and although these sentences have other primary purposes, it was established that the non-establishment of the basis [for renunciation] must necessarily be accepted.

Thus, it should be understood that the scriptural injunction regarding debts (*ṛṇa-śruti*), the injunction for lifelong [performance] (*yāvaj-jīva-śruti*), and the exception-injunction (*apavāda-śruti*) all pertain only to those who lack dispassion. Furthermore, other Śrutis and Smṛtis which enjoin the necessity of performing rituals until death for the knower of Brahman (*brahmavit*) concern the specific duties of their respective stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*). Therefore, since the knowledge of Brahman is enjoined even for those whose semen is drawn up (*ūrdhva-retas*), it is established that knowledge is an end in itself for man (*puruṣārtha*). || 20 ||
The section concerning the human goal (puruṣārtha) is completed.
If it be argued that [the passage] is merely a praise because it takes up [what is already known], we say no, because of its novelty (apūrvatva). || 21 ||

Now this is being considered: Are such passages as "This is the essence of essences, the highest, the supreme, the eighth, which is the Udgītha" intended merely for the purpose of praising the Udgītha and other elements that are parts of the sacrifice, or are they intended to enjoin the meditation (*dṛṣṭi*) upon the Udgītha and others as being the essence and so forth? Here, having accepted the fact that these passages are devoted to meditation (*upāsana*), it was stated that because meditation serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), there is no rule regarding its employment within the sacrifices. What is appropriate? That they are intended merely for praise.
Why? Because of the mention of the *udgītha* and so forth; for, having taken up the *udgītha* and other elements which are constituent parts of the sacrifice, [the text speaks] of them...

The state of being the most flavorful (*rasatama*) has been established. Just as a statement asserting that the *juhū* ladle and other implements are the earth and so forth—such as "This [earth] is indeed the *juhū*, the heavenly world is the *āhavanīya* fire"—is intended solely for their praise, so it is here as well. This is what is raised as an objection: "If it is argued that it is mere praise because of the mention [of the *udgītha*, etc.]. If it is argued that because of the mention of the *udgītha* and so forth, these sentences are intended merely as praise for them, the answer is: "No, because of the novelty (*apūrvatvāt*). It is not tenable that they are mere praise; [for they convey something new].

Why? Because they are unprecedented (*apūrva*) and have not been previously established. For the *udgītha* and other elements have not been apprehended by any other means of knowledge as being the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*) and so forth, such that they would need to be restated (*anūdya*) as being "most flavorful" for the purpose of generating a cognition of their excellence. Nor is there any injunction regarding the *udgītha* and so forth present here, by virtue of which one might resort to the view that this passage is intended as a praise of those [elements] through syntactic unity with some injunction—just as in the case of "This earth is indeed the *juhū* ladle; the heavenly world is the *āhavanīya* fire."

Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing results such as the potency of the sacrifice, it is indeed logical that the meditation on the *udgītha* and other elements as the "most savory" (*rasatama*) and so forth is prescribed.
And because of the word "bhāva" (existence).

Furthermore, because of words such as "should be meditated upon" (*upāsitavya*), it is logical that they are intent upon injunction; for a verbal root denoting action joined with an injunctive suffix conveys its own meaning solely as something to be enjoined. Therefore, these scriptural passages have the purpose of enjoining meditation. The section concerning mere praise (*stutimātra-adhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
If it be argued that [the Upanishads] have a varied meaning, we say no, because they are specified [as having a specific purpose]. 23.

In considering whether the narratives found in the Vedāntas—such as "Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, approached the beloved abode of Indra," and "Śvetaketu, the son of Aruṇi, existed"—are intended for the ritual performance of the *pāriplava*, or rather for the exposition of specific forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), [the following is established].

If it is argued that because of the injunction, "They recite the *ākhyānas*," these narratives are to be employed in the *pāriplava* ritual and thus it is not reasonable for them to have knowledge as their primary purpose—[we reply: no, for not all *ākhyānas* deserve to be employed in the performance of the *pāriplava*. Why? Because of the specific qualification of the injunction. Having stated, "They recite the *ākhyānas*," it is there itself specified by the passage beginning, "King Manu Vaivasvata," and so forth, that the *ākhyānas* of Manu and others are singled out. Therefore, it is understood that only those [specific ones] are to be employed there.

Therefore, not all narrative passages in the Vedāntas are intended for the performance of the *pāriplava* recitation; rather, they are intended for the injunctions regarding knowledge (*vidyā*). || 23 ||
And likewise, because of the connection within a single sentence. || 24 ||

Because the narratives are connected as forming a single syntactical unit with injunctions such as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," it is understood that they serve the purpose of the injunctions for knowledge (*vidyā-vidhi*); just as the passage beginning with "He wept" serves the purpose of an injunction for ritual action (*karma-vidhi*), and not for the purpose of mere recitation (*pāriplava*). || 24 ||
The section concerning the meaning of the *pāriplava* is completed.
And for this very reason, there is no dependence on fire, fuel, and so forth. //25//

In connection with the topic of praise (*stuti*), two matters have been considered by way of a specific intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*). It was stated in the sūtras beginning with "And among those who are perpetual celibates (*ūrdhvaretas*), because of the word [in scripture]" (*sū. 3.4.17*) that there exist ascetics (*āśramin*) who possess knowledge and are perpetual celibates. Now, raising the objection that since perpetual celibates lack sacrifices and other such rites, knowledge—which has those as its constituent parts—cannot possibly exist for them, the author says: "And for this very reason, there is no dependence on the kindling of the sacred fires and so forth. (sū. 3.4.25)

For this reason, those belonging to the stages of life in which the semen is drawn upward (the *ūrdhvaretas* stages) are embraced by scripture as being connected with knowledge, through such passages as: "One who is firmly established in Brahman attains immortality"; "And those who, in the forest, worship with faith and austerity"; "Desiring this world alone, mendicants go forth into the wandering life"; and "Those desiring which they lead the life of a student (*brahmacarya*)."

For this very reason, knowledge belongs to those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*) without dependence on firewood, fire, and so forth. "Firewood" means the kindling of the fire; the meaning is that for them, knowledge does not depend on rituals such as the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires), the *agnihotra*, the *darśa-pūrṇamāsa*, and others, but depends only on the duties prescribed for their own specific stage of life (*āśrama*). The section concerning firewood and so forth (*agnīndhanādyadhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. || 26 ||

If knowledge were to accomplish immortality independently of sacrifices and other such rites, then it ought to accomplish it for householders as well, without depending on them; furthermore, the scriptural injunction regarding sacrifices and so forth—in the phrase "they desire to know"—does not establish that ritual action is a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of knowledge. To this, he says: "Dependence on all."

Knowledge indeed depends upon all actions such as sacrifice for those householders who possess action; why? Because of the scriptural injunction regarding sacrifice and so forth: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting. For sacrifice and the rest are heard in scripture as being auxiliary to knowledge. The meaning is that they "seek to know" (vividiṣanti) by means of sacrifice and so forth—that is, they desire to know, or they desire to attain realization through sacrifice and the like.

Only when sacrifices and the like are means for attaining knowledge is the designation that "one desires to attain knowledge through restraints (yama) and so forth" logically justified; just as there is the designation "he wishes to kill with a sword" only when the sword is a means for killing. Therefore, it is understood that sacrifices and the like are means for knowledge. Furthermore, this knowledge—which is distinct from the mere understanding of the meaning of scriptural sentences—is what is denoted by terms such as *dhyāna* (meditation) and *upāsana* (devotional worship); it takes the form of a memory characterized by the utmost clarity of direct perception, is supremely dear, and, being purified by daily practice, continues until death as the means for liberation.

This has already been stated by us previously, and [the author] will state it again in such passages as, "Because of the repeated instruction" (*āvṛtti-rasakṛd-upadeśāt*). Knowledge arises through the grace of the Supreme Person, by means of meditations of this kind performed daily, and through obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites that constitute the worship of the Supreme Person. This is what is established by the scripture in the passage, "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice and so forth. Therefore, for householders who possess ritual actions, knowledge depends upon all the obligatory and occasional rites, such as sacrifice.

Just as a horse, which serves as the means for a person’s movement, requires the preparation and equipment of its own trappings, so too knowledge, which serves as the means for liberation, requires the equipment of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*). The Lord himself has stated this: "Sacrifice, charity, and the act of austerity are not to be abandoned; they must indeed be performed. Sacrifice, charity, and austerity are the purifiers of the wise. And: "From whom the activity of beings proceeds, and by whom all this is pervaded—by worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection. (26)
The section concerning the requirement of all [auxiliary means] is completed.
Nevertheless, he should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth; for since those are enjoined as auxiliary parts of that [knowledge], they too must necessarily be practiced. (27)

In considering whether tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth are to be practiced by a householder or not, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they are not to be practiced because the performance of ritual action consists in the operation of the internal and external organs, whereas tranquility, self-control, and the like are of a nature contrary to that. To this, it is replied: although the householder is engaged in actions consisting of the operation of the organs, nevertheless, that wise man should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and the rest.

Why? Because they are enjoined as its auxiliaries; that is, because they are enjoined as auxiliaries to knowledge (vidyā), according to the text: "Therefore, one who knows this, having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, should see the Self in the very Self. Furthermore, since the arising of knowledge consists in the concentration of the mind, tranquility and the other qualities serve as visible prerequisites for it; and since these qualities such as tranquility must necessarily be practiced for the accomplishment of knowledge, they too are to be practiced.

Furthermore, there is no mutual contradiction between ritual actions such as *karma* and spiritual practices such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*), because they operate on different objects: the engagement of the faculties (*karaṇavyāpāra*) is prescribed for those [actions] that are enjoined, while their cessation is prescribed for those that are not enjoined and are devoid of purpose.

Nor is it impossible for one engaged in actions consisting of the operation of the instruments [of body and mind] to adopt tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities by virtue of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); for prescribed actions, being forms of worship of the Supreme Person, serve as the cause for the eradication of all contrary impressions through His grace. Therefore, even tranquility, self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth must be practiced by the householder. The section concerning tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth is concluded.
And there is permission to eat all food when life is at stake, because that is seen [in scripture]. (28)

In the *Vājasaneyins* and the *Candogas*, regarding the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*), it is proclaimed that for the knower of the breath there is permission to consume all food, as stated: "Verily, nothing becomes uneatable that has been eaten by him, nor does anything become uneatable that is accepted by him"; and "Verily, for one who knows thus, nothing whatsoever becomes uneatable. Regarding the doubt as to whether this permission to consume all food for one established in the knowledge of the breath applies at all times, or only in the event of the risk of life being lost—since no specific qualification is mentioned, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it applies at all times; however, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated: "In the event of the risk of life being lost."

The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis, meaning "only in the event of the risk of loss of life. Why? Because that is seen; for elsewhere it is observed that even for those who know Brahman, permission to eat all kinds of food is granted only in the event of the risk of loss of life, let alone for one who knows the Prāṇa.

It is said that Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa, a preeminent knower of Brahman, while living in a village of wealthy merchants in the Kuru country—which had been devastated by locusts and afflicted by famine—fell into a life-threatening crisis due to starvation. Desiring not to let his vital breaths fail so as to achieve the perfection of the knowledge of Brahman, he begged from a man who was eating some boiled beans (*kulmāṣa*), for whom there were no other leftovers than those.

Thus addressed, he replied once more, "Give me some of these," and having accepted the sour gruel (kulmāṣa) which the merchant had given him from his leftovers, Cākrāyaṇa was requested by the merchant for a drink to accompany it. Saying, "What I have drunk would indeed be the leavings of another," Cākrāyaṇa was questioned by the merchant, "Are these sour gruels not leavings? He replied, "I certainly would not have lived without tasting these; my desire was for water. [He spoke thus] because, by tasting even that much, he faced a danger to his life.

Having stated that drinking the leftover water of one whose life-force (prāṇa) depends on ghee would be forbidden if done out of desire, [the text continues]: after giving what remained of his own food to his wife and having it preserved by her, he, desiring to go out the next day with the wish to earn a living through officiating at sacrifices, again encountered a danger to his life and ate those very leftovers—which were his own leavings, stale, and [otherwise] forbidden. Therefore, since the permission for all food is seen even for knowers of Brahman only when there is a threat to life, it is determined that the state of being able to eat all food mentioned here without distinction applies to the knower of the Prāṇa only in the event of a life-threatening crisis. 28.
And because there is no contradiction. || 29 ||

From the injunction for purity of food for the sake of the arising of the knowledge of Brahman—namely, "When there is purity of food, there is purity of being; when there is purity of being, there is constant mindfulness"—it is understood that even for those who know Brahman, the practice of eating all kinds of food applies only to times of distress. Thus, since even for those who know Brahman and possess extraordinary powers, the permission to eat all food is restricted to times of distress, it follows that for one who knows the Prāṇa and possesses only limited power, the permission to eat all food applies exclusively to times of distress. || 29 ||
It is also recorded in the Smṛti. || 30 ||

Moreover, the fact that those who know Brahman may eat any food whatsoever is recorded in Smṛti both for them and for others: "He who, having fallen into a life-threatening danger, eats food from whatever source it may come, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (30)
And the word "and" (ca) here [indicates] the absence of restriction. || 31 ||
