Since for the knowers of Brahman and others alike, the state of eating all kinds of food is restricted solely to times of distress, it follows that the scriptural injunction regarding the absence of acting according to one's desire (*akāmakāra*) is a prohibition against acting according to one's desire (*kāmakāra*). Indeed, there is a scriptural statement in the *Kaṭha Saṃhitā* which prohibits acting according to one's desire: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa does not drink liquor, lest he be defiled by sin. The meaning is that a Brāhmaṇa does not drink liquor with the thought, "May I not be touched by sin. || 31 || ||
The section concerning the permission to eat all food is concluded.
And because it is enjoined, the duty of the stages of life (āśrama) is also [to be performed].

It has been stated that the knowledge of Brahman has sacrifices and other rites as its constituent parts. Now, a deliberation arises as to whether those rites, such as sacrifices, must be performed even by one who is not seeking liberation (an mumukṣu) and belongs solely to a [specific] stage of life (āśrama), or not. In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since these rites are auxiliary to knowledge, if they were merely subordinate to a specific stage of life, there would result a contradiction between the obligatory and the non-obligatory; therefore, it is impossible for sacrifices and the like to be duties belonging exclusively to a particular stage of life. To this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated: "Even the work of the stages of life. This means that even the work of a stage of life is to be performed by those who belong solely to that stage of life.

Why? Because it is prescribed by such injunctions as "As long as one lives, one performs the Agnihotra," meaning that it is prescribed as obligatory (nitya) by virtue of being contingent upon life. || 32 ||

Likewise, because they are enjoined as auxiliary parts of knowledge by such passages as "This very [Self] by the study of the Vedas," etc., he says that they must also be performed as subordinate to knowledge: "And as being auxiliaries. (3.4.33)

The meaning is that, by way of the arising of knowledge and as a cooperative factor for knowledge, these [rites] are to be performed; just as in the case of the Agnihotra and other rites, which have both a qualification based on living and a qualification based on heaven, there is no contradiction in their serving both purposes due to the distinctness of their injunctions (viniyoga-pṛthaktva). || 33 ||
In the same way, he states that there is no distinctness of action either:
"In every respect, they are the very same, because of the dual characteristic. (3.3.44)

In every respect—whether for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*) or for the sake of the stages of life (*āśrama*)—it must be understood that those same sacrifices and so forth are intended; the meaning is that there is no difference in the essential nature of the ritual acts (*karma*). Why? Because of the evidence of both [texts], since in both scriptural passages they are recognized by the words "sacrifice" and so on and then enjoined, and because there is no means of proof for a difference in the essential nature of the ritual acts. (Sūtra 34)
And it demonstrates non-overpowering. || 35 ||

By stating, "One removes evil through dharma," and so forth, [the text] points to those very dharmas such as sacrifice and shows that knowledge is not overcome by them, meaning there is no obstruction to its arising caused by sinful actions. For when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been purified by sacrifices and other rites performed day after day, knowledge arises with increasing intensity every day;
moreover, this is observed even in the intervals. (Sūtra 3.4.36)

It has been stated that the four stages of life (*āśrama*) possess qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), and that the duties of these stages are auxiliaries to that knowledge. Now, regarding those such as the widower (*vidhura*) who live outside the stages of life, there arises the doubt: do they have qualification for the knowledge of Brahman or not? Since knowledge has the duties of the stages of life as its required procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and since those outside the stages lack such duties, the prima facie view is that they have no qualification. To this it is replied: "And also for those in between" (*antarā cāpi tu*).
The word *tu* (but) serves to set aside the previous position, and the word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis.

There is indeed eligibility for knowledge even for those who live in between [stages of life] and those who do not belong to any stage of life (anāśramin). Why? Because that is observed; for it is seen that Raikva, Bhīṣma, Saṃvarta, and others—who were not in any stage of life—were nonetheless established in the knowledge of Brahman. Nor can it be said that knowledge is favored only by the duties of the stages of life, since we see that acts such as giving—which are not restricted to the stages of life—are also means of favoring knowledge, as in the text: "By sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting."

Just as, since knowledge is seen to reside even in those who have cast off their sacred fires (udhvaretas), the favoring of knowledge is performed by means other than the Agnihotra and other such rites; so too, since knowledge is seen even among those not belonging to any stage of life (anāśramin), the favoring of knowledge can be effected by means not restricted to the stages of life, such as recitation (japa), fasting, dwelling in the forest, giving gifts, and the propitiation of deities. || 36 ||
Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti. || 37 ||

Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti that even for those who do not belong to any stage of life (āśrama), the favor of knowledge is attained through recitation (japa) and other such means: "A Brāhmaṇa may attain perfection even by means of recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.

Whether he performs other [duties] or does not perform them, he is called a Brāhmaṇa who is a friend to all. The meaning is that he becomes perfected—that is, accomplished—by means of knowledge assisted by recitation and the like. || 37 ||
And there is a special favor. || 38 ||

This point is not to be established by logic (*nyāya*) and traditional law (*smṛti*) alone; it is also declared that the favoring of knowledge (*vidyānugraha*) occurs through specific duties not restricted to the [four] stages of life (*āśrama*), as in: "One should seek the Self through austerity (*tapas*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), faith (*śraddhā*), and knowledge (*vidyā*). (38)
Therefore, however, the other is superior, also because of an indicative mark. || 39 ||

The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. Therefore, because of being without an *āśrama*, the other—namely, being in an *āśrama*—is indeed superior; being without an *āśrama* pertains to a state of distress (*āpad*), whereas for one who is capable, being in an *āśrama* alone is to be adopted. This is because actions with more extensive duties and those with fewer duties do not have equal results, and this is also known from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the Smṛti. Furthermore, the Smṛti records that for a capable person, the adoption of an *āśrama* is mandatory, as in: "A twice-born man should not remain without an *āśrama* even for a single day," and so forth.

For one who has completed his period of studentship and whose wife has died, the failure to obtain a wife while lacking dispassion constitutes an *āpad* (emergency). The section concerning the widower (*vidhura*) is concluded.
But for one who has become that [initiate], there is no non-becoming of that state, according to Jaimini as well, because of the restrictive rules and because of the absence of that [prior] form. 40.

In the inquiry as to whether there is eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman even for those who have fallen away from the stages of life (āśramas) of the perpetual student (naiṣṭhika), the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa), and the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka), or not—the prima facie view being that there is eligibility because, as in the case of the widower and others, the grace of knowledge can be attained through acts such as giving gifts even by those not restricted to a specific stage of life—it is replied: "But for one who has become that [stage], there is no non-becoming of that. The word "but" (tu) serves to set aside the prima facie position.

For one who has become that—that is, for one established in a lifelong stage of life (*naiṣṭhika*) or another—there is no "non-becoming-that. That is to say, it is impossible for him to remain in a state of being without a stage of life (*anāśramitva*). Why? Because of the restriction based on the absence of those forms; the meaning is that "those forms" refers to the dress and duties of these lifelong ascetics and others. "The absence of those forms" (*tadrūpābhāva*) means the non-existence of those [characteristics]; because of the scriptural restriction regarding them.

For the scriptures indeed restrain those who have entered the lifelong stages of life (naiṣṭhika) and others from turning away from the duties of their respective stages, stating: "The student (brahmacārī) dwells in the teacher's family; the third [the lifelong student] wears himself out completely in the teacher's family"; "He should go to the forest and from there not return again"; and "Having renounced the sacred fires, he should not take them up again. Therefore, since it is impossible for the lifelong students and others to remain in a state of non-belonging to any stage of life (anāśramitva)—unlike widowers and the like—the knowledge of Brahman does not qualify them. By showing that even Jaimini agrees with this, the author confirms his own intended position. || 40 ||

Now, it might be argued that for those such as perpetual students (*naiṣṭhika*) who have fallen from their vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), eligibility [for knowledge] is possible through expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and there exists an expiation described in the section on eligibility [in the Jaimini-sūtras]: "And the animal sacrifice of one who has broken his vow of chastity belongs to him who possesses that [vow]. Therefore, since expiation is possible for one who has fallen from celibacy, one who has performed the expiation will become eligible for the knowledge of Brahman. To this, he replies:
"Nor even that which pertains to eligibility [is restored], because of the inference of a fall [from all eligibility], due to its incompatibility. (Sūtra 3.4.41)

Even the expiation (prāyaścitta) prescribed by the characteristics of eligibility is not possible for those who have fallen from the state of a *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate) and others; why? Because of the inference of their downfall and because that [expiation] is incompatible with them. Since there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) regarding the downfall of those who have fallen from the state of a *naiṣṭhika* and others—stating: "I see no expiation by which that twice-born man, having ascended to the duty of a *naiṣṭhika*, might be purified if he falls away, for he is a slayer of his own self"—therefore, the expiation described according to the characteristics of eligibility applies to other types of religious students (*brahmacārin*). || 41 ||
Some say that even when preceded by the prefix *upa*, it expresses existence (*bhāva*), just like the word for food (*aśana*); this has been stated [in the Vārttika].

The falling away from celibacy by perpetual students (*naiṣṭhika*) and others constitutes a minor offense (*upapātaka*), since it is not enumerated among the major sins (*mahāpātaka*); regarding this, some teachers maintain that there exists—or rather, that there is—the presence of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). This is like the case of eating: just as there is a prohibition against eating honey and so forth, and likewise an expiation for it, [this applies] to those who perform preparatory rites (*upakurvāṇa*).

This is common to the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate) and others as well; thus it has been stated by the authors of the Smṛtis: "And this is not inconsistent for those who follow the subsequent stages. The meaning is that what has been prescribed for one dwelling in the teacher's house (*gurukula*) is possible for those in the subsequent stages of life provided it does not conflict with their own specific stage. The same applies here: since there is the possibility of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for a lapse from the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the fitness for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) still exists. || 42 ||
But outside [the village], it is in both ways, according to Smṛti and custom. || 43 ||

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of excluding other opinions. Whether they are minor sinners (*upapātakin*) or major sinners (*mahāpātakins*), these persons are indeed excluded from those who perform the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) and so forth; the meaning is that they are not qualified for the knowledge of Brahman. Why? Because of the Smṛti—that is, because of the aforementioned Smṛti concerning their fall.

Although there exists the authority for penance through certain statements for the removal of impurity, nevertheless, a penance that serves as a cause for purification corresponding to the eligibility for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*) is not possible; the meaning is that this is according to the Smṛti: "I see no penance by which that self-destroyer might be purified. Furthermore, from the conduct of the virtuous (*ācāra*): the learned indeed avoid those who have fallen from their vows—such as perpetual students (*naiṣṭhika*)—even if they have performed penance, and they do not instruct them in the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) and so forth;
therefore, they have no eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman. || 43 ||
The section concerning "That Being" (tadbhūtādhikaraṇa) is concluded.
Ātreya maintains that the fruit belongs to the master, because the scripture declares the fruit for him.

Regarding the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth, which depend upon the constituent parts of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), there arises the inquiry: are they to be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) or by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)? In this deliberation, Ātreya maintains that they are to be performed by the sacrificer. Why? Because of the mention of the fruit (*phalaśruti*). This means that in the meditations on *tadvara* and others prescribed in the Vedāntas, one observes that the fruit and the meditation have a single locus; and here too, it is heard that the fruit of the *udgītha* meditation—namely, the non-obstruction of the fruit of the sacrifice—is to be located in the sacrificer. Nor can it be argued [that the fruit belongs to the priest] merely because it depends on a constituent part of the rite, as is the case with the *godohana* vessel.

The impossibility of the sacrificer being the agent [of the meditation] arises because, in the case of the *godohana* vessel and similar items, it is impossible for anyone other than the Adhvaryu priest to employ the *godohana* as the support for the act of fetching water (*praṇayana*), which is performed by him. However, here, even though the *Udgītha* chant is performed by the Udgātṛ priest, the sacrificer himself is able to perform the contemplation of that *Udgītha* and so forth as the "sweetest essence" (*rasatama*). To this [objection], the following is stated: "Ātreya [says] it belongs to the sacrificer; Auḍulomi [says] it belongs to the priest, for he is hired for that purpose. (Sūtra 3.4.45)

The teacher Auḍulomi would consider that the work of the officiating priests consists of the application of the *ātmayājya* [the self-sacrifice] and the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth; for it is for that purpose that they are employed.

It is "prepared," meaning it is acquired for the sake of the sacrifice together with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), which serves as the means to achieve the fruit. In the injunctions regarding ritual acts, such as "he chooses the priests" (*ṛtvijo vṛṇīte*) and "he gives the sacrificial fee to the priests" (*ṛtvigbhyo dakṣiṇāṃ dadāti*), it is understood through the scriptural teaching that the priests are the agents, that the sacrifice—along with its constituent parts, which constitutes the means to the fruit—is to be performed by the priests; therefore, the physical and mental actions included therein are indeed performed by the priests. Nor are capacity and incapacity the determining factors in this regard.

Although meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), nevertheless, because it falls within the scope of those authorized for the sacrifice (*kratvadhikṛta-adhikāra*), and because the sacrifice along with its constituent parts is performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and because of the scriptural statement—"What one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful"—which shows that knowledge is useful for the action performed by the priest and implies a commonality of agent, these meditations are performed by the priests. However, in the case of meditations such as that on the *dahara* (the small ether), since there is no scriptural mention of them being performed by the priests, and according to the maxim "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer," they must indeed be performed by the person seeking the fruit. The section concerning the Master [of the Sacrifice] is concluded.
The injunction of another auxiliary is established as a third [case] by way of an alternative, like the injunctions for one who already possesses that [auxiliary]. (46)

Regarding the passage, "Therefore, a Brahmin, having desisted from scholarship, should remain in the state of a child; and having desisted from both childhood and scholarship, he then becomes a sage," is the state of being a sage (*mauna*) enjoined here just like childhood and scholarship, or is it merely restated? We must consider this doubt because the words "sage" (*muni*) and "scholarship" (*pāṇḍitya*) both signify knowledge. Since the knowledge already enjoined by the phrase "having desisted from scholarship" is what is restated in the phrase "then he becomes a sage," there is no word of injunction heard here.

This being the case, we reply: "There is an injunction for another auxiliary" (*sahakāryantaravidhi*). For one who possesses that—that is, for one who possesses knowledge—sacrifices and the like, as well as all the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*) such as tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth, are enjoined; these are what is expressed by the word "injunction" (*vidhi*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) are included. Regarding the phrase "injunction for another auxiliary": here too, it is called an "injunction" (*vidhi*) because it is enjoined (*vidhīyate*); thus, "another auxiliary" (*sahakāryantara*) and "injunction" (*vidhi*) together form the compound *sahakāryantaravidhi*.

This is what is meant: just as by such passages as "The Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, and through charity," and "He who is calm, self-controlled," etc., sacrificial rites and the like, as well as tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth, are enjoined as auxiliary factors; and just as by the statement "It is to be heard and reflected upon," hearing and reflection—which are already established by implication—are understood as auxiliaries to knowledge; [so too is the case here].

Likewise, by the passage beginning with "Therefore, a Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship," a triad consisting of scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), childhood (*bālya*), and silence (*mauna*) is enjoined as another auxiliary to knowledge. And he states that silence is something distinct from scholarship by saying "by way of a secondary sense" (*pakṣeṇa*). Since the word *muni* is seen to be used in its secondary sense for those such as Vyāsa who possess the habit of profound reflection, silence is the third [stage] following the two, namely scholarship and childhood. Even though no injunctive suffix is heard in the phrase "then [he becomes] a sage" (*atha muniḥ*);

Nevertheless, since silence (*mauna*) has not been previously established [as an obligation], it must be accepted as something to be enjoined by the words "then he shall be a silent sage" (*atha muniḥ syāt*). And this silence is distinct from reflection (*manana*), which serves to stabilize what has been heard; rather, it consists in the repeated cultivation of the object of meditation, taking the form of its constant contemplation (*bhāvanā*). Thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "A Brāhmaṇa [should possess] knowledge."

The meaning is that, having become weary of mere talk and scholarship, and having realized the pure and perfect reality of Brahman through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), one attains the knowledge not previously obtained; and that [realization] is brought about by the increase of the quality of goodness (*sattva*) produced through devotion to the Blessed Lord, as stated in the passage beginning with "I am not to be known by the Vedas... and ending with "...but can be known by exclusive devotion. And the Śruti also says: "Of whom..."

There is supreme devotion toward the Divine, as expressed in such passages as, "This Self is not to be attained by instruction," and so forth. One should abide in "childlike simplicity" (*bālya*), the nature of which will be explained immediately hereafter. Having realized both childlike simplicity and wisdom (*pāṇḍitya*), one should then become a sage (*muni*); that is, having properly adopted childlike simplicity and wisdom, one should become intent on contemplation (*manana*) regarding the pure and perfect Brahman for the sake of attaining knowledge in the form of meditative realization (*nididhyāsana*).

Thus, he says, "Having mastered both non-mauna and mauna, one then becomes a Brāhmaṇa," to show that knowledge is attained through the employment of this triad. *Amauna* refers to the entire collection of auxiliary factors other than *mauna*; the meaning is that by properly employing both that [non-mauna] and *mauna*, one attains the pinnacle of knowledge, which is accomplished solely by that [knowledge].

When it was asked, "By what means would one become a Brāhmaṇa?", and the question was raised whether there might be some other means besides the one already mentioned, the reply was given: "By that [means] by which one becomes a Brāhmaṇa, he is indeed such. This means that by that very means—culminating in silence (mauna)—one becomes a Brāhmaṇa; it is not by any other means. Therefore, for the knower established in any of the stages of life (āśramas), scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*) and the third, namely silence (*mauna*), are enjoined as another auxiliary to knowledge, just like the duties of one's own stage of life, such as sacrifice and the rest. || 46 ||

Now, it might be argued: if it is said that for the wise who abide in all the stages of life (āśrama), knowledge—accompanied by the duties of those respective stages and with silence as its third assistant—is the means for attaining Brahman; then how is it that in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, beginning with "Having returned home, [living] in a family in a pure place," and concluding with "He, indeed, living thus as long as life lasts, reaches the world of Brahman and does not return again," there is seen an instruction to remain in the duty of a householder for the duration of one's life? To this, he says:
"But because of the presence [of all virtues] in the householder, the conclusion is made with him. (Sūtra 4.1.47)

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the objection. Because of its presence in its entirety—that is, because knowledge exists in all stages of life—the conclusion is made by means of the householder, implying that [knowledge] exists for him as well. Therefore, the intention is that the conclusion is drawn by way of the householder in order to demonstrate the duties of all stages of life. || 47 ||

Likewise, in this passage as well—"A Brahmin, having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, then lives the life of a mendicant"—the text first establishes the exclusive dharma of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrajya*). Then, by stating "Therefore, a Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship," and so forth, it demonstrates the injunction of a third auxiliary factor, silence (*mauna*), which serves as the cause for abiding in the dharma of wandering mendicancy.
Thus he says: "Because there is an instruction of the others as well, just like silence. (Sūtra 3.4.48)

The instruction on silence preceded by the practice of begging alms for one who is liberated from all desires is intended to demonstrate the duties (dharma) common to all stages of life (āśrama). Why? Because, just as there is this instruction on silence, there is also an instruction for those in other stages of life—beginning with "There are three branches of dharma" and culminating in "He who is established in Brahman attains immortality"—which concerns the attainment of Brahman. Furthermore, it has already been established previously that the term "established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃstha) is common to all who belong to the stages of life.

Therefore, it has been well said: "Just as all the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma), such as sacrifice and the like, are prescribed as auxiliaries to knowledge (*vidyā*), so too are [the stages] beginning with silence (*mauna*) and scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*) prescribed as auxiliaries to knowledge. The section concerning the injunction of another auxiliary (*sahakāry-antara-vidhi-adhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
Because it does not manifest itself, following from the logical sequence. || 49 ||

"In that regard, a Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship, should remain in a state of childlike simplicity" (*tasmād brāhmaṇaḥ pāṇḍityaṃ nirvidya bālyena tiṣṭhāset*). Here, the "childlike simplicity" (*bālya*) of the wise is enjoined as something to be adopted. "Childlike simplicity" (*bālya*) refers either to the state of being a child or to the actions of a child. Since the specific stage of life (the physical condition of childhood) cannot be adopted, it is the action of a child that is understood here. In this context, a doubt arises: should the wise person adopt all the actions of a child, such as acting according to one's own whims, or only the absence of hypocrisy and the like? Since there is no specific distinction [in the text], it might seem that everything is to be adopted, and thus restrictive injunctions would be set aside by this specific injunction. [The Sūtra refutes this: "But [only] the absence of hypocrisy and so forth, because of the mention of 'simplicity' (*bālya*). (Sūtra 4.1.13). The word "but" (*tu*) serves to exclude the aforementioned view. Only the absence of hypocrisy and the like is to be adopted by the wise, not acting according to one's whims and other such behaviors. Why? Because of the mention of "simplicity" (*bālya*). For the word "simplicity" denotes the absence of hypocrisy and the like, based on its association with the natural state of a child. It is observed that in common usage, the term "childlike simplicity" refers to the absence of pride, deceit, and crookedness. Furthermore, acting according to one's whims and other such behaviors are not specifically prescribed for the wise; rather, they are prohibited by general rules. Therefore, since the general prohibitions are not set aside by this specific injunction, only the absence of hypocrisy and the like is to be adopted. Moreover, the mention of "scholarship" (*pāṇḍitya*) implies the exclusion of acting according to one's whims and the rest. For "scholarship" is the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas, and its opposite is ignorance. Acting according to one's whims and the like is included within that ignorance. Thus, when one is said to have "become disillusioned with scholarship," it follows that those very actions are excluded. Consequently, the wise person should remain in a state of childlike simplicity, characterized by the absence of hypocrisy and the like. This is the conclusion. This being the case, it is replied: "Remaining unmanifest. The wise man should proceed by undertaking that action which consists in not manifesting his own nature, as is characteristic of a child. Why?

Because of the connection with that very [state], i.e., because of its connection with that very [state]; for in this injunction, "One should remain in a state of childhood," only that [childhood] can logically be connected, since the others are heard to be opposed to knowledge, as in: "Neither one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not composed, nor even one whose mind is not at peace, shall attain Him by means of wisdom. Also in such passages as: "From purity of food comes purity of being," and so forth. The section concerning non-manifestation (*anāviṣkāra*) is concluded.
The result belongs to this life when there is no obstruction of what is currently undertaken, because that is observed. (4.3.50)

Knowledge is of two kinds: that which has prosperity as its fruit and that which has liberation as its fruit. Regarding the knowledge that has prosperity as its fruit, there arises a doubt: does it arise immediately after the meritorious actions that serve as its means, or not immediately, or at some later time—there being no fixed rule? For a knower is born on account of meritorious actions performed in the past, as the Blessed One has said: "O Arjuna, four types of virtuous people worship Me."

When the means of realization have been accomplished, since there is no cause for delay, it is reached immediately; this is what is stated [in the sūtra]: "The fruit belongs to this life, provided there is no obstruction of what is currently underway. Meditation that has prosperity as its fruit belongs to this life; if there is no obstruction, it follows immediately, but if there is an obstruction, it occurs at a later time—thus there is no fixed rule.

Why? Because that is seen; for it is observed in scripture that the fruit of an action can be obstructed by another more powerful action. This is evident from the statement regarding the Udgītha-vidyā: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣadic insight, that alone becomes more powerful," which teaches that the fruit of an action conjoined with the Udgītha-vidyā is not obstructed. (Sūtra 50). The section concerning actions performed in this life (*aihikādhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
Thus, there is no restriction regarding the fruits of liberation, because that state is not determined; because that state is not determined. || 51 ||

The meaning is as follows: even for meditation (*upāsanā*), which has liberation as its fruit, there is likewise no fixed rule regarding the time of its arising when it is produced by extraordinary ritual acts (*karma*) that serve as its own means; for, as in the previous case, its state is understood as consisting of the absence of obstacles and the cessation of obstacles, and the reason for this is the same here as well. There is, however, a further doubt: since the ritual act that is a means to the knowledge (*vidyā*) whose fruit is liberation is more powerful than all other ritual acts, there can be no possibility of obstruction.

Even in that case, the resolution is that the occurrence of bondage is possible due to the existence of powerful misdeeds committed in previous lives against those who know Brahman. The repetition [of the word] indicates the completion of the chapter. || 51 || The section concerning the fruit of liberation is concluded.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
There must be repetition [of the meditation], because of the repeated instruction. (Sūtra 1)

In the third chapter, knowledge (*vidyā*) was considered along with its means of accomplishment. Now, after first clarifying the essential nature of knowledge, the fruit of knowledge is being considered. In this regard, concerning Vedic passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," "Having known Him thus, one goes beyond death," "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and "When the seer sees the golden-colored one," is the knowledge enjoined as the means for attaining Brahman something that constitutes the purpose of the scripture when performed only once, or must it be repeated many times?

There is a doubt. What is the correct position? That it is performed once; for, according to the statement, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," only the act of knowing is enjoined, and there is no authority for its repeated performance. Nor can it be argued that repetition continues as long as the task remains, on the grounds that knowing is a visible means (*dṛṣṭopāya*) toward the direct realization of Brahman—like the act of threshing (*avaghāta*)—because knowing is not a visible means.

Ritual acts such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and the knowledge enjoined by the Vedānta—which consists of the supreme propitiation of the Supreme Person—result in the attainment of the human goals known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa from that propitiated Supreme Person; for this has been established in the sūtra, "The fruit [comes] from Him, because that is logical" (Brahmasūtra 3.2.38). Therefore, just like the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by performing it only once, according to the scriptural injunction.

This being the position, we reply: "There is repetition; [it must be] more than once. Knowledge that is repeated more than once is indeed the meaning of the scripture. Why? Because of the teaching; for knowledge is taught through synonyms such as *dhyāna* (meditation) and *upāsana* (worship). And that these are synonyms is understood from the usage of the roots *vid* (to know), *upāsti* (to worship), and *dhyai* (to meditate) within a single subject in those scriptural passages intended to teach knowledge.

For instance, the matter introduced by the verb "to meditate" in the passage, "One should meditate on the measure as Brahman," is concluded by the verb "to know" in the passage, "He who knows this shines and warms with fame, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge. Similarly, the knowledge of Raikva expressed by the verb "to know" in the introductory passage, "He who knows what he knows—that has been told to me by him," is concluded by the verb "to meditate" in the passage, "Sir, instruct me further in that deity which you meditate upon."

Likewise, in sentences of equivalent meaning to "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"—such as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ*)—the act of knowing (*vedana*) is denoted by the term "meditation" (*dhyāyati*). Meditation is reflection (*cintana*); and that consists of a continuous stream of memory (*smṛti-santati*), not mere memory alone. [Upā...]

The term *stuti* (praise) has the same meaning as that [of knowledge], because we observe its application in the uninterrupted flow of one-pointed mental activity; since both have the same purpose, it is determined that the continuous stream of memory which occurs repeatedly is designated here by words such as "knowing" (*vedana*) in passages like "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" and "Having known God, one is released from all bonds. || 1 ||
And because of an indicative mark. || 2 ||

The *liṅga* (indicative mark) is the *smṛti* (traditional scripture). And from this *smṛti*, the following meaning is understood: for knowledge (*vedana*), which is the means to liberation, is established as being of the nature of a continuous stream of recollection (*smṛti-santati*). As it is said: "And that meditation (*dhyāna*)—which consists of a single, continuous stream of cognition having that [Brahman] as its form, and which is free from longing for anything else—is accomplished by means of the first six limbs. Therefore, knowledge alone, when repeated, is the meaning of the scripture. The section concerning repetition (*āvṛtty-adhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
But they accept [the notion] "self" and cause others to grasp it as well. // 3 //

This is now considered: Is Brahman, the object of meditation, to be meditated upon as distinct from the meditator, or as the very self of the meditator? What is the correct view? That it is distinct. Why? Because Brahman is an entity other than the meditator’s inner self (*pratyagātman*). This state of being a different entity has been established in such passages as "But [Brahman is] greater, because of the mention of difference," "Because of the teaching of the superior," and "Not the other, because that is untenable. Furthermore, Brahman must be meditated upon exactly as it exists; for if one meditates on it incorrectly, even the attainment of Brahman would be incorrect.

According to the principle that "in whatever manner a person intends in this world, so does he become after departing from here," it must therefore be meditated upon as something distinct [from the Self].

This being the position reached, it is replied: "But [it is] the Self. The word "but" (tu) is used for emphasis. That which is to be meditated upon is indeed the Self of the meditator. Just as the meditator, who is the inner self (pratyagātman), is himself the Self of his own body, so too should he meditate on the Supreme Brahman as being his very Self. Why? Because the ancient meditators understood it thus: "O venerable deity, I am indeed you; you are indeed I."

To the question, "How can those who worship accept that Brahman, which is an entity distinct from the worshipper, is their very self (aham)? he says: "The scriptures cause them to grasp it; the meaning is that they establish this for them. [He cites: "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal."

Likewise, [it is said]: "O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support; all this has That as its self," and "All this is indeed Brahman, for it is born from It, dissolves into It, and breathes in It. Because all things—both conscious and unconscious—are born from That, dissolve into That, breathe in That, are governed by That, and have That as their body, That is the Self of all. Therefore, He is your Self. Consequently, just as one identifies with one's own body because it is one's own Self, thinking "I am a god" or "I am a human"; [so too should one identify with the Supreme Self].

Likewise, since the inner self (pratyagātman) is also the Self, it is logical that the Supreme Self should also be meditated upon as "I" (aham). Thus, those who accept that all words have Brahman as their sole referent—since all cognitions are established by the scriptures as being grounded solely in Brahman—have expressed this through the exchange: "Verily, O Blessed Deity, I am Thou; verily, O Blessed Deity, Thou art I."

And thus: "Now, he who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know; for this Self is incomplete—thus indeed should one worship. "Everything abandons him who [seeks] everything outside of the Self."

The prohibition of contemplating [the Self] as something other—expressed in the passage, "One who knows 'I am the Veda'"—and the injunction to contemplate distinctness—expressed in the passage, "Having known the Self and the Impeller as separate"—are not contradictory. The prohibition of contemplating [the Self] as other is maintained because one contemplates it as "I," that is, as one's own self. Furthermore, just as there is a contemplation of one's own Self as superior to one's own body, so too is there a contemplation of one's own Self as distinct from the Supreme Self; thus, the injunction to contemplate distinctness is also preserved.

It is protected [by the following reasoning]: Since the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is the Self of the superior Brahman, and since that [inner self] has Brahman as its body, it was stated in the prohibitory passage, "For this one is incomplete. Therefore, it is established that Brahman is to be meditated upon as the Self of the meditator. || 3 ||
The section concerning the meditation on the Self is completed.
Not in a symbol, for he is not that. || 4 ||

In the inquiry as to whether the contemplation of the Self (*ātmatvānusandhāna*) must also be performed in symbolic meditations (*pratīkopāsana*) such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" and "He who meditates on Name as Brahman," [the conclusion is]: because these share the commonality of being meditations on Brahman, and because Brahman is the Self of the meditator, one should meditate [on them] precisely as the Self.

This being the case, it is replied: "Not in the symbol" (na pratīke). One should not perform the contemplation of the Self (*ātmatva-anusandhāna*) with respect to a symbol (*pratīka*), for that symbol is not the Self of the worshiper. In the meditations on symbols, the symbol itself is the object of worship, not Brahman; Brahman is there merely as a qualifying attribute of the vision. For what is called meditation on a symbol is the contemplation of Brahman through the vision of Brahman in that which is not Brahman; since the symbol, which is the object of worship, lacks the nature of being the Self of the worshiper, it should not be contemplated as such. || 4 ||

But surely, even here it is Brahman alone that is to be meditated upon; for while Brahman can appropriately be the object of meditation, it is improper to resort to non-intelligent and limited entities such as the mind and so forth as the objects of meditation. Therefore, Brahman alone is to be meditated upon through the contemplation of the mind and other organs. To this, he replies:
"The contemplation of Brahman [is to be superimposed on them], because of its superiority. (Sūtra 5)

It is indeed proper to view the mind and so forth as Brahman, but not to view the mind and so forth as Brahman; for Brahman is superior to the mind and so forth, whereas they are the opposite. For to view a superior king as a servant brings about sin, while to view a servant as a king leads to prosperity. || 5 ||
The section concerning the symbols is completed.
And the meditations on the sun and so forth are [to be applied] to the limbs [of the sacrifice], because that is logical.

Regarding the meditations based on the constituent parts of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), such as the passage beginning with "One should meditate upon that which shines yonder as the Udgītha," a doubt arises: in the case of the Udgītha and other ritual parts, should one view them as the sun and so forth, or should one view the sun and so forth as the Udgītha and so forth? According to the principle that the vision of the superior should be applied to the inferior, and because the Udgītha and others—being constituent parts of the rituals that are means to results—are superior to the sun and others which bear no fruit themselves, one should view the sun and so forth as the Udgītha and so forth.

This being the position reached, it is replied: "And the meditations on Āditya and so forth [are] on the subsidiary parts" (Sūtra 7). Here, the word "and" (ca) is used in the sense of restriction. On the subsidiary parts of the sacrifice, such as the *udgītha* and others, meditations on Āditya and so forth alone are to be performed. Why? Because of logical consistency (*upapatti*); for it is only Āditya and the other deities who possess superiority, and it is by means of propitiating the deities such as Āditya that even ritual acts become instruments for attaining results. Therefore, the meditation on them [the deities] is to be applied to the subsidiary parts like the *udgītha*. The section concerning the meditations on Āditya and so forth is concluded.
[The meditation] is performed while sitting, because that is possible.

It has been stated that the knowledge enjoined by the Vedānta scriptures as a means to liberation—expressed by such terms as "meditation" (*dhyāna*) and "worship" (*upāsanā*)—consists of continuous recollection (*santatasmṛti*) through repeated practice. Regarding this, it might follow that one should perform it without restriction while sitting, lying down, standing, or walking, since there is no specific difference between these states; however, it is replied: "Sitting. One should perform worship while sitting. Why? Because of possibility (*sambhavāt*); for only while sitting is a one-pointed mind possible.

That [posture] is impossible; for standing and walking depend upon effort, and while lying down, sleep may occur. To cease the effort required to support the lower half of the body, one should sit with a backrest. (Sūtra 7) And because of meditation. (Sūtra 8)

Since the term "it must be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*) indicates that meditation (*upāsana*) is of the nature of *dhyāna*, one-pointedness of mind is necessarily required; for it has been stated that *dhyāna* is the continuous contemplation of a single object, uninterrupted by other heterogeneous cognitions. || 8 ||
Oṃ, and it is also with reference to immovability. || 9 ||

Furthermore, the expression "meditates" is seen applied to the earth, the intermediate space, and so forth, with reference to their immobility: "The earth meditates as it were; the intermediate space meditates as it were; the sky meditates as it were; the waters meditate as it were; the mountains meditate as it were. Therefore, like the earth, the mountains, and so on, the state of immobility resulting from one-pointedness of mind would be possible for the practitioner only while he is seated. || 9 ||
And they remember it. || 10 ||

And they record that meditation belongs to one who is indeed seated: "Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place—neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, antelope skin, and kuśa grass from bottom to top; having made the mind one-pointed there, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained, sitting upon that seat, one should practice yoga for the purification of the self. (6.10–12)
Wherever there is one-pointedness [of mind], there [the result follows] without distinction. || 11 ||

Since there is no scriptural injunction regarding place and time other than that which is conducive to one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*), whatever place and time are favorable to one-pointedness are precisely the place and time for meditation (*upāsana*).

The statement, "In a level, clean place, free from pebbles, fire, and sand," expresses the solitude required for one-pointedness; it does not restrict the location, because of the supplementary phrase, "in a place agreeable to the mind. The section concerning the seated posture (*āsīnādhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
For even there, it is seen [to continue] until the departure from the body.

Regarding this doubt—whether this meditation, which has been described as the means to liberation, is to be accomplished in a single day alone, or whether it is to be continued every day until death—it must be concluded after that much alone, since the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled within a single day.

This being the position reached, it is said: "Until death" (Āprayāṇāt). It must be continued until the time of death. Why? Because it is observed even there; for it is observed throughout the entire interval from the commencement of the effort of meditation until death, as seen in the text: "Practicing himself thus, he reaches the world of Brahman for the duration of his life. (12) The section concerning "until death" is concluded.
Upon the attainment of that [knowledge], there is the non-clinging of future karma and the destruction of past karma, because there is a designation of those two. (13)

Having thus purified the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*), he begins to contemplate the fruit of that knowledge. Upon the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman, the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of a person's subsequent and prior sins are heard in scripture: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this"; "Having found the path and known Him, his soul is not smeared by evil action"—this refers to the non-clinging of subsequent sin. [And: "Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk in fire..."

"Just as a single thread being burnt, all its impurities are burnt away; so too, when that which is both high and low is seen, his actions are destroyed and his sins are consumed. Thus, there is the destruction of prior [sinful] deeds. There arises a doubt: are these two—non-attachment and destruction—appropriately established as the fruits of knowledge, or not? What is the correct view? That they are not appropriately established. Why? Because it would contradict scriptural authorities such as: "Action is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of eons unless its fruit has been experienced."

Furthermore, the designation of "non-attachment" (*aśleṣa*) and "destruction" (*vināśa*) found in the supplementary portions of the injunctions for the knowledge that serves as the means to liberation is justifiable even by way of establishing a praise of that knowledge. Moreover, knowledge is not enjoined as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for past and future sins, such that the destruction of those sins would be spoken of through that expiation. For knowledge is enjoined as the means to the attainment of Brahman, according to such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself."

Therefore, this declaration regarding the non-clinging and destruction of past actions is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) of knowledge. This being the position reached, it is replied: "Upon the attainment of that [knowledge]. Upon the acquisition of knowledge, the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins become possible for a person through the majesty of knowledge. Why? Because such majesty of knowledge is understood from scriptural declarations such as, "In one who knows thus, evil action does not cling," and "Thus all his evils are consumed."

Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural teaching that "karma is not exhausted without being experienced," because their subject matters are different. For that [teaching] concerns the persistence of the capacity of karmas to produce results; whereas this [teaching] establishes the power of knowledge (*vidyā*)—once arisen—to destroy the capacity of previously performed sins to produce results, and the power to obstruct the arising of the capacity of future karmas to produce results. Thus, the subject matter of the two is distinct.

Just as there is no contradiction in the validity of two means of knowledge—such as fire and water—which possess respectively the capacity to produce heat and to remove it, because their objects are distinct, so it is here as well. The act of *adhas* (eating before the previous meal is digested) consists in creating an obstacle to the production of that capacity which causes unfitness for Vedic rites, the latent impression (*vāsanā*), and the sin (*pratyavāya*). For when *adhas* is performed, it renders a person unfit for Vedic rites, creates a desire to undertake other similar actions, and brings about sin. This is the nature of *adhas*.

The "causing of destruction" refers to the destruction of that power once it has arisen. Furthermore, this power is simply the displeasure of the Supreme Person. Thus, knowledge—being itself unsurpassedly dear due to its being dearer than the object of knowledge for the knower—and having as its very nature the propitiation of the Supreme Person who is the object of knowledge, destroys the displeasure of the Supreme Person produced by the accumulation of demerit from past deeds; that same knowledge also obstructs both the production of future demerit and the arising of displeasure toward the Supreme Person subsequent to its own birth.

Therefore, that statement regarding non-attachment should be understood as referring to cases of negligence, because scriptural texts such as "Not one who has not desisted from evil conduct [attains it]" demonstrate that knowledge—which arises day by day until death and possesses ever-increasing excellence—is produced by the cessation of evil conduct. || 13 ||
The section concerning the realization of that [truth] is concluded.
For the other [type of karma] as well, there is likewise no attachment; however, upon death, [it falls away].

The non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of both [types of karma] in the northern and eastern directions have been stated by means of knowledge (*vidyā*); this same non-clinging and destruction of the other [type], namely merit (*puṇya*), would likewise occur through knowledge according to the principle already stated, because of the commonality of its opposition to the fruit of knowledge and because of scriptural designation (*vyapadeśa*). There is indeed such a designation: having pointed out both good and evil deeds, it says, "All evils (*pāpmānaḥ*) turn back from here," and "He shakes off his good and evil deeds. Since even good deeds have undesirable fruits for one seeking liberation, they are designated by the term "evil" (*pāpman*).

This extension [of the principle] is intended to remove the doubt that there might be no contradiction with knowledge (*vidyā*), because even meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*) are prescribed by scripture, and because it is observed that the fruits of some of them are limited. Now, one might object: "Even for the knower (*vidvas*), rites accompanied by material offerings (*setikartavyatāka*) are indeed desired for the sake of accomplishing meditations (*upāsana*) that yield results such as rain and food; how then can it be said that they are destroyed due to contradiction? To this, he says: "But at the fall [of the body]. But at the fall of the body, their destruction occurs; the meaning is that after the fall of the body, those meritorious deeds which have visible results consistent with knowledge perish. || 14 ||
The section concerning the other [deities] is concluded.
But those [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], for that is their limit. || 15 ||

It has been stated that prior to the arising of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), there is both the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and the destruction (*vināśa*) of good and evil deeds occurring before and after it. Now, regarding the doubt as to whether the destruction of the good and evil deeds existing prior to that [knowledge] occurs without distinction, or only for those whose effects have not yet begun (*anārabdhakārya*): because the scriptural statement, "All evils are burnt away," indicates that the fruit of knowledge is uniform, and because the continued existence of the body after the arising of knowledge is possible even through the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), like the spinning of a potter’s wheel, [the destruction occurs] without distinction.

This being the position reached, it is said: "But only those previous [deeds] whose effects have not yet begun. Good and evil deeds prior to the arising of knowledge are those whose effects have not yet begun—that is, those whose fruits have not yet commenced—whereas the Agnihotra and other such rites are for the sake of that very effect, because of the scriptural vision thereof. (Sūtra 16)

By the statement, "In the same way, there is non-attachment even for the other," it was declared that by the power of knowledge (vidyā), there is also non-attachment to merit (sukṛta). Since the obligatory and occasional rites such as the Agnihotra, as well as the duties of one's own stage of life (āśrama-dharma), are also generally considered merit, it would follow that their fruits are not attached [to the knower]; thus, the possibility of non-performance arising from a lack of desire [for those fruits] is addressed by the sūtra: "But the Agnihotra and so forth... [Brahmasūtra 4.1.16].

The word *tu* (but) serves to distinguish [these duties] from other well-performed acts (*sukṛta*). Duties pertaining to the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*), such as the *agnihotra*, must indeed be performed, because there is no possibility of their fruits adhering [to the knower]. This impossibility exists because those duties have that [knowledge] as their purpose; for the performance of the *agnihotra* and so forth by the knower is solely for the sake of the effect known as knowledge (*vidyā*). How is this understood? From the observation [of scripture]; for we observe [in texts] such as, "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, through austerity, and through fasting," which shows that the *agnihotra* and other rites [serve this end].

Since knowledge is the means to [liberation] and because knowledge—being subject to the addition of excellence through practice—must be produced day after day until death, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) must also be performed daily for the sake of its production; otherwise, if the duties of the stages of life are neglected, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) would be defiled, and the production of knowledge itself would not occur. || 16 ||

If good deeds such as the *agnihotra* are for the sake of the arising of knowledge, and if the merit prior to the arising of knowledge is destroyed through experience—according to the texts "having dwelt there as long as the [results] converge" and "having reached the end of its action"—then what would be the object of the statement "friends [attain] his good deeds" regarding the remainder of what was enjoyed, namely that which has begun to bear fruit (*prārabdhaphala*)? To this he replies:
"Therefore, according to some, there is also another [kind of merit] for both. (1.2.17)

Therefore, even other meritorious deeds (*sādhukṛtyā*) such as the *agnihotra* and so forth, which are performed for the sake of the arising of knowledge, can indeed exist in infinite measure—both before and after the attainment of knowledge—as long as their fruit is not obstructed by more powerful karma. It is with reference to this that the statement of certain reciters of the Veda occurs: "His sons inherit his property; his friends [inherit] his meritorious deeds. And the scriptural texts concerning the non-clinging and destruction of karma also refer to that same subject. (Sūtra 17)

He recalls what was stated previously—that even for an action performed, there is the possibility of an obstruction to its fruit—by means of the scriptural passage: "For by knowledge alone... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10). || 18 ||

By the statement, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone is more powerful," which declares that the Udgītha-vidyā has as its fruit the non-obstruction of the results of sacrificial rites, it is indeed indicated that there may be an obstruction of the fruit even for a rite that has been performed. Therefore, the Śāṭyāyani text, "The friends [take] the good deeds," refers to the case of one who possesses knowledge but whose performed action has had its fruit obstructed. Thus ends the section concerning the Agnihotra and other rites.
But having exhausted the others through experience, he then attains [the state of liberation]. || 19 ||

Regarding the merit and demerit whose non-clinging and destruction have been mentioned, there arises a doubt: are the other merits and demerits that have already begun to bear fruit destroyed at the conclusion of the body born of knowledge (*vidyā-yoni-śarīra*), or at the conclusion of that specific body, or is there no fixed rule as to whether they end with another body? In this doubt, [the conclusion is] that they end with the liberation from that specific body, because of the scriptural statement: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in the Absolute]" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.14.2). Thus, it ends with the liberation from that body.

This being the position, it is said: "But by experience. The word "but" (tu) serves to set aside the previous view. The other two—merit and demerit whose effects have already begun—are exhausted by the experience of their own commenced fruits; immediately after the completion of that experience of their fruits, one attains Brahman. And those merit and demerit, if their fruits are to be experienced in a single body, [then they are withdrawn] from that body into speech and mind, because of the scriptural vision and the sacred word. (Sūtra 1)

Now he begins to consider the manner of departure for the wise person (*vidvan*). First, the process of departure (*utkrānti*) is considered; regarding this, it is recorded in scripture: "O Śvetaketu, when this person departs, his speech merges into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity. Here, concerning the scriptural statement that "speech merges into the mind," there arises a doubt: does this merging of speech into the mind refer merely to the function (*vṛtti*) of speech, or to speech itself? It is reasonable [to hold] that it refers merely to the function.

Why? Because speech cannot have the mind as its material cause (*prakṛti*), since it is impossible for the nature of speech to be fully realized therein. Since the functions of speech and the other organs are dependent on the mind, the scriptural statement regarding the perfection of their functions is somehow justifiable.
Therefore, [the text says], "all follow after it" (2).

Since "attainment" (sampatti) is merely the conjunction of speech with the mind and not its dissolution, for this very reason the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of all the senses in the mind follows speech; that mind [attains] the vital breath (prāṇa), according to what follows. || 3 ||

That mind, together with all the sense organs, merges into the vital breath (*prāṇa*); it is conjoined with the vital breath, not merely as a mental modification. Why? Because of the subsequent scriptural statement: "of the higher self [the mind] into the vital breath. However, a further doubt arises: from the statement, "The mind, my dear, consists of food (*annamaya*)," it is understood that the mind has food as its material cause; and since food is established as being composed of water by the text, "They created food," it follows that the mind is essentially watery. Furthermore, from the statement, "The vital breath consists of water (*āpomayaḥ prāṇaḥ*)," it is understood that the vital breath has water as its material cause.

Therefore, regarding the statement, "From this, the mind merges into breath," the word "breath" (prāṇa) refers here to the waters, which are the material cause of breath; thus, by establishing the merging of the mind into them, the expression "merging" (sampatti) is justified as meaning a dissolution into its own ultimate cause through a traditional succession. However, the rebuttal is as follows: in the passage, "For the mind, my dear, consists of food, and breath consists of water," what is stated is the nourishment of the mind and breath by means of food and water, not their being the material causes thereof. This is because the mind is derived from the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), and breath is a modification of space (ākāśa).
And there would also be an indication of the waters by the word "prāṇa. Thus ends the section concerning the mind (manodhikaraṇa).
He [is merged] in the presiding deity, because of such passages as "approaching that."

Just as, in accordance with the statement "Speech merges into the mind; the mind [merges] into breath," the merging of speech and mind occurs specifically into the mind and breath respectively, so too, by the statement "Breath [merges] into heat," the breath merges specifically into heat.

This being the position reached, it is said: "That [prāṇa] [merges] in the presiding [soul]. That prāṇa merges into the presiding soul, the individual self (jīva), who is the master of the instruments. Why? Because of its approaching that, and so forth. First, the approaching of the prāṇa to the individual self is heard in scripture: "In this very way, at the time of death, all the prāṇas gather around this self. Likewise, the departure of the prāṇa together with the individual self is heard: "As he departs, the prāṇa departs after him. And its staying together with the individual self is heard: "When whom has he departed shall I depart?"

"In what, then, established, shall I be established? Thus, having joined with the individual soul (*jīva*), the attainment of fire by means of that [soul] is here expressed as "the breath (*prāṇa*) in fire. This is not contradictory, just as when the Yamunā joins with the Gaṅgā and proceeds to the ocean, it is not incorrect to say that "the Yamunā goes to the ocean. || 4 || The section concerning the presiding deity (*adhyakṣādhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
Because of its existence among the elements. || 5 ||

In the passage, "The breath [merges] into heat," the merging of the breath, which is conjoined with the individual soul (jīva), into heat is stated. Regarding the doubt as to whether this merging is into heat alone or into all the elements combined, the sūtra states: "Into heat alone, because that is what is heard;
for [the scripture] shows [this] in one [element]. (6)

Not in one [element], because each one individually is incapable of producing the effect. Indeed, the Śruti and Smṛti demonstrate this incapacity: "Having entered with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me differentiate name and form; let me make each of them threefold. Thus, the process of triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa) is taught for the sake of making them fit for the differentiation of name and form. [The Smṛti says: "Possessing diverse powers and existing separately, they were unable to create offspring without a combination;
having come together in mutual union and being dependent on one another, they [were able to do so]."

"For by them—the [subtle elements] beginning with the Great One (mahat) and ending with the specific (viśeṣa)—the egg is produced. Therefore, in the passage "The breath [is merged] in heat," the word "heat" (tejas) denotes heat as already mixed with the other elements. Thus, the merging occurs only into the elements. || 6 ||
The section concerning the elements is completed.
And this [attainment] is equal [to that of the other path], starting from the departure [of the soul] until the attainment of immortality without having burned away [the subtle body].

In considering whether this departure [of the soul] is common to both the knower and the ignorant, or belongs to the ignorant alone, the initial position is that it belongs to the ignorant alone. Why? Because for the knower, there is no departure, since immortality is declared for him right here; for the immortality of the knower is proclaimed in this very context: "When all desires that dwell in his heart are cast away, then the mortal becomes immortal, and even here he attains Brahman."

This being the case, it is replied: "And [the departure] is the same up to the beginning of the path. Even for the knower, the departure is the same up to the beginning of the path—that is, up to the commencement of the journey, meaning prior to entering the channels (*nāḍī*). For even in the case of the knower, the scripture declares that his movement proceeds by means of a specific channel: "There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head. Going upwards by that, he attains immortality; the others serve for departing in various directions. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.6).

Thus, because the movement [of the soul] is heard of as being by means of a specific channel (*nāḍī*), the departure (*utkrānti*) of even the knower is unavoidable. And that departure is common [to all] prior to the entry into the channel, since no distinction is heard of at that stage. However, regarding the state of having entered that channel, a distinction is heard: "By that light, this Self departs—either through the eye, or through the crown of the head, or through other parts of the body."

Because of its agreement with the scriptural statement, "One hundred and one [channels] of the heart," the departure from the head pertains to the knower, while the other [departure] pertains to the non-knower. As for what was said—that immortality is declared here for the knower—it is replied: "And immortality without having burned away [the body]. The word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis. Without having burned away—that is, without having consumed—the connection with the body, senses, and so forth, that immortality which consists in the non-clinging of future and past karma exists until absorption [into Brahman], because the state of transmigratory existence is still designated [at that time]. || 8 ||

And it must necessarily be understood that immortality belongs only to one whose connection with the body has not yet been burnt away. Why? Because the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is described as persisting until the final dissolution (*āpīti*). *Apīti* means *apyaya*, which is the attainment of Brahman. And it will be stated later that this occurs after traveling to a specific location by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*). Indeed, until that state is reached, transmigratory existence—characterized by the connection with the body—is described [in scripture], as in: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be united. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2)

"And: 'Having shaken off evil as a horse shakes off its hairs, and having freed myself like the moon from the mouth of Rāhu, I—having shaken off the body and being perfected in self—attain the world of Brahman. (8)
And it is subtle by measure, because it is perceived as such. || 9 ||

Moreover, even for the wise one (*vidvas*), bondage is not burnt away here, because he continues to follow a subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*). How is this known? From authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for it is perceived thus. Indeed, the existence of a body is perceived from the statement regarding the dialogue with the moon by the wise one traveling along the path of the gods: "One should speak to him; one should speak the truth. Therefore, the subtle body continues to follow [him], and consequently, his bondage is not burnt away. || 9 ||
Therefore, it is not by means of suppression. || 10 ||

Therefore, the statement, "When all desires that dwell in his heart are liberated, then the mortal becomes immortal and attains Brahman here," does not declare immortality through the destruction of bondage. || 10 ||
And from this very same reasoning, there is heat. (11)

Since the existence of this subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*) is established in some instances, the heat of a wise person who has begun the process of dying is perceived in the gross body (*sthūlaśarīra*) prior to death. And this heat does not belong to the gross body alone, because it is not perceived elsewhere; therefore, it is understood that the perception of heat in certain cases is due to the departure (*utkramana*) of the wise person's subtle body. Thus, it is rightly said that for the wise person as well, the departure is the same [as for the ignorant] until the commencement of the path (*āsṛtyupakrama*). || 11 ||
Furthermore, raising the objection that the departure of the wise is not possible, it is refuted:
"If it be said [it is not so] because of the prohibition, we say no; for [the departure] is from the embodied soul, as it is clear from some [scriptural passages]. (12)

As for what was stated—that the departure [of the soul] is the same even for the knower—that is not tenable, because the departure of the knower is prohibited. For, after describing the manner of departure for the non-knower in the passages, "Taking these particles of light, he departs toward the heart itself," and "As he departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him," and then stating the assumption of another body in the passage, "He makes for himself another form, newer and more beautiful," [the text continues]: "Having reached the end of that karma which he has here..."

Having concluded the section concerning the ignorant with the words, "Therefore, he who desires returns again from that world to this world for the sake of action," the text then prohibits the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) for the knower: "But he who does not desire—being without desire, free from desire, whose desire is fulfilled, whose desire is the Self—for him the vital breaths do not depart; being Brahman, he goes to Brahman. Likewise, in the earlier question of Ārtabhāga, the prohibition of the knower's departure is seen in the statement, "He conquers death no more," referring to the knower.

Having introduced the topic, [Janaka] asked, "Yājñavalkya, he said, 'When this person dies, do his vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) depart from him, or not? To which Yājñavalkya replied, "No," saying, "They are absorbed right here; he swells up, becomes bloated, and lies dead."

If it is argued that, therefore, the wise man attains immortality even here [in this body], that is not so; for what is prohibited here is the departure of the vital breaths from the embodied self, the inner Self (pratyagātman), and not from the body. In the passage, "His vital breaths do not depart," the word "his" (tasya) refers back to the embodied self introduced in the phrase "now he who is without desire," and not to the body, which was not previously mentioned.

If it is argued that the embodied self (śārīra) is indicated by the genitive case in the word "tasya" as being related to the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), but not as the point of departure for their departure—since the body alone is the point of departure for the departure—we say no; for when there is a requirement for a point of departure, since the self mentioned as being related [to the breaths] is more proximate than the body which is not explicitly heard [in this context], the self itself must be understood as the point of departure.

Furthermore, since the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are already known to be related to the living self (*jīva*), there is no purpose in stating that relationship again; therefore, it is determined that the ablative case (*apādāna*) alone—denoting mere relation—is the specific meaning intended by the genitive case, as in the expression "he hears from the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*). Nor should one dispute this here, for in the recension of some, namely the Mādhyandinas, it is clearly stated that the embodied living self (*śārīra-jīva*) alone is the ablative: "He who is without desire, free from desire, whose desires are fulfilled, whose desire is the Self... (*yo 'kāmo niṣkāma āptakāma ātmakāmaḥ*).

Regarding the statement, "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) do not depart from him": if it is argued that this prohibition is untenable because there is no possibility of the vital breaths departing from the embodied soul (*śārīra*), we reply: no. Since the text states, "For him, the delay is only so long," which speaks of the attainment of Brahman by the knower at the time of separation from the body, it follows as a logical consequence that the vital breaths also separate from the embodied knower at that time. Consequently, the attainment of Brahman via the path of the gods (*devayāna*) would be impossible; therefore, "his vital breaths do not depart" prior to reaching Brahman by way of the path of the gods.

It is stated that even from a living person who possesses knowledge, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) do not depart. Even the question of Ārtabhāga, when it concerns one who possesses knowledge, has this very same resolution; however, that [question] concerns one who lacks knowledge, because in that case no connection with the knowledge of Brahman is seen in the question and answer. For there, the nature of the senses and their objects is described as "seizers" (*grahas*), the waters as the food of fire, the non-abandonment of the vital breaths by the departing soul, the persistence of the name for the deceased, and his— Please note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion. If you have the full passage, please provide it for a complete rendering.

The attainment of states of existence according to merit and demerit—these matters have been answered following the initial questions. In that context, the statement "he conquers death by means of apāna" refers to the conquest of fire itself as the conquest of death, based on the knowledge that apāna is fire and food; therefore, this does not apply to the knower. However, for the non-knower, the teaching regarding the non-departure of the vital breaths (prāṇas) is faultless, as it establishes that the prāṇas do not leave like the gross body, but rather depart embracing the individual soul (jīva), just like the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma). || 12 ||
And it is recorded in tradition.

Moreover, it is recorded that even for the wise man, there is an exit through the upper channel (mūrdhan-nāḍī): "One among them stands above; having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā, by that [channel] he goes to the supreme goal. Thus ends the section concerning the commencement of the path (āsṛtyupakramādhikaraṇa).
These [points] are [explained] by others; for thus it has been said: || 14 ||

It has been stated that at the time of departure, the individual self (pratyagātman), together with the collection of organs, along with the vital breath (prāṇa), and presiding over the organs, merges into the subtle elements such as fire and the rest. Having raised the doubt that this merging does not occur for the knower (vidvas), it was refuted. Now, regarding the question of whether those subtle elements, embraced by the living self, proceed toward their own effects according to karma and according to knowledge, or whether they merge into the Supreme Self—in this matter of doubt, because no effect in the form of the experience of pleasure and pain is observed upon merging into the Supreme Self, [the elements] proceed according to karma, in accordance with the suitability for that experience.
And they proceed according to their ignorance, for there is no distinction [among them], as stated in scripture. || 15 ||

Regarding this attainment in the Supreme Self, is it of the nature of merging into the cause—as in the dissolution of the material world—or is it of the nature of non-distinction—as in the case of the text "Speech [merges] into the mind"? Upon such reflection, because the Supreme Self is the source of all things, this attainment is of the nature of merging into the cause.

This being the position reached, it is said: "Non-separation" (*avibhāga*). This means non-distinctness, that is to say, a state of union (*saṃsarga*) which is not subject to separate designation.
