Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "The fire [is merged] in the highest deity. Here too, because of the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*) of the word "is merged" from the preceding passage, "Speech is merged in the mind," and because that term denotes a specific kind of union; furthermore, there is no evidence for a change in the meaning of a syntactically connected word, nor is there any purpose for the merging into its cause at the time of departure, and finally, because there is no mention of the creation of the unmanifest (*avyakta*) and so forth in that context. Thus ends the section on Non-separation (*Avibhāgādhikaraṇa*).

The flame at the tip of that [channel] blazes up; its door being illuminated by that, he—favored by the one dwelling in the heart through the power of knowledge, through the remembrance of what remains to be done, and through yoga—[departs] by means of the hundred-and-first [channel]. 16.

Thus, the manner of departure has been described as being identical for both the wise and the ignorant up to the point of setting out on their respective paths; now, the specific distinction regarding the wise is stated. In this regard, the following is recorded in scripture: "There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends upward to the crown of the head. Ascending by that, one attains immortality; the others lead to departing in various directions."

There arises a doubt as to whether this restriction—that the departure of the knower occurs through the single channel at the crown of the head (*mūrdhan-nāḍī*) alone, while the departure of the non-knower occurs through other channels—is tenable or not. What is the correct view? That the restriction is not tenable. Why? Because, due to the great number of channels and their extreme subtlety, they are difficult to distinguish and impossible for a person to identify.

It is therefore reasonable to regard the statement, "Going upwards by that [channel], he attains immortality; in other ways, there are departures in all directions," as a description of a random or accidental departure.

This being the case, we declare: "By [the path] consisting of more than a hundred. The knower departs through the hundred-and-first artery alone, which is the one leading to the crown of the head. Nor is it difficult to distinguish him from the ignorant person; for the knower is graced by the Supreme Person with a gracious glance, due to his practice of recollecting the path that is exceedingly dear as it constitutes the propitiation of the Supreme Person.

And therefore, that abode—the heart, which is the place of that individual soul—undergoes a "flashing forth at the front" (*agrajvalana*); that is to say, its illumination occurs first. By the grace of the Supreme Person, the door is illuminated, and the wise man recognizes that channel; thus, the departure of the knower by means of that channel is established. The section concerning "That Abode" is concluded.
Following the rays. || 17 ||

It is heard in scripture that for the wise man, having departed from the heart through the hundred-and-first artery at the crown of the head, there is a movement toward the solar orb by following the rays of the sun: "Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays.
To the objection that this does not apply at night, we say: no, because the connection [between the arteries and the rays] exists as long as the body lasts; and scripture also shows this. (Sūtra 18)

This is now considered: Is there attainment of Brahman for one who dies at night after having acquired knowledge, or not? Although a journey by following the rays is possible even at night because the rays of the sun exist then, nevertheless, because dying at night is censured in the scriptures, the attainment of Brahman—characterized as the supreme human goal—is not possible for one who dies at night. In the scriptures, dying during the day is praised, while dying at night is the opposite; [as it is said]: "The day, the bright fortnight, and the northern solstice..."
"For those about to die, [death during] the day is praised, but death at night is censured;
likewise for one in the southern solstice. (19)

Since the very same reason has been stated for the attainment of Brahman by a wise person who dies even at night, the attainment of Brahman is established for one who dies during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) as well. However, a further doubt arises from the scriptural hearing that one who dies during the southern course goes to the greatness of the ancestors and attains union with the moon: "Now, he who dies in the south, having gone to the greatness of the ancestors, attains union with the moon; and when that [merit] of theirs is exhausted, they return again by this very path. And regarding those who have attained the moon, it is said: "When that [merit] of theirs is exhausted, then they return again by this very path."

Because of the scriptural mention of returning [to earth], and because we observe that even Bhīṣma and others, who were firmly established in the knowledge of Brahman, awaited the northern course of the sun, it follows that the attainment of Brahman is not possible for one who dies during the southern course.

The resolution is as follows: it is only for the ignorant who have reached the moon by the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*) that there is a return; however, even for the knower who has reached the moon, his arrival at the moon while dying during the southern course of the sun is understood to be merely for the sake of rest, based on the supplementary statement: "From there he attains the greatness of Brahman. Even in the absence of such a supplementary statement, because the previously mentioned cause of bondage is absent, the attainment of Brahman by the knower who has reached the moon is unavoidable.

The conduct of Bhīṣma and others—who possessed the power of yoga and thus could die at their own will—was for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of the northern course of the sun (uttarāyaṇa) for the promotion of dharma. || 19 ||

But is it not observed that for those who know [the truth] and are about to die, there is an injunction regarding specific times as the cause for either returning or not returning? [As stated in the Bhagavad Gītā: "I shall declare that time at which departing yogis go to non-return, and that at which they go to return: fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice—departing then, people who know Brahman go to Brahman. Smoke, night, likewise the dark fortnight, and the six months of the southern solstice..."

And in that regard, it is said: "The yogin, having attained the lunar light, does not return; for these two paths, the bright and the dark, are considered eternal for the world. By one he goes to no return, by the other he returns again. To this, [the author] says:
"These two are recorded in Smṛti as referring to yogins, and they are indeed matters of Smṛti. (Sūtra 20)

In this context, no specific time of death is prescribed for those who are about to die; rather, it refers to the yogins—those established in yoga—for whom two paths known as the path of the gods (devayāna) and the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa), which are objects of memory within the scope of the Smṛti, are taught as things to be remembered daily as ancillaries of yoga. For thus is the concluding statement: "Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogin whatsoever is deluded. Therefore, at all times, O Arjuna, remain disciplined in yoga."

The phrases "Fire is light" and "Smoke is night" are recognized as referring to the path of the gods (*devayāna*) and the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*). Furthermore, at the beginning of the passage, the word "time" (*kāla*) in the phrase "at which time" refers to the presiding deities of time who act as guides (*ativāhika*), because fire and the other elements cannot themselves be time. Therefore, what is enjoined here for those established in this knowledge is the recollection of the path of the gods prescribed in the statement "they reach the light," and not a specific time of death for those about to die. || 20 ||
The section concerning the southern course is completed.
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
By the path beginning with light, because that [attainment] is well-known [therein]. || 1 ||

The commencement of the journey for the wise man who has departed, by virtue of the grace of the one dwelling in the heart through a specific channel, has been described. Now, the path of that departing soul is being determined. In this regard, various modes of the path are recorded in the Śrutis in many ways.

In the *Chāndogya*, beginning with the passage, "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this," and having taught the knowledge of Brahman, it is recorded: "Now, whether they perform funeral rites for him here or not, they pass into the light (*arcis*); from the light into the day; from the day into the waxing half-month; from the waxing half-month into those six months during which the sun moves northward; from the months into the year; from the year into the sun; from the sun into the moon; from the moon..."

"A non-human person [who is] that male [being] at the lightning leads them to Brahman; this is the path to the gods, the path to Brahman. Those who proceed by it do not return to this human whirlpool. Likewise, in the eighth chapter of this very [text], it says: "Then, by these very rays, he ascends upwards. And the Kauṣītakins study the path of the gods differently: "Having entered upon this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni; he [comes] to the world of Vāyu, he to the world of Varuṇa, he to the world of Āditya, he to the world of Indra, he to the world of Prajāpati, he to the world of Brahman."

Likewise, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship faith as the Truth—they pass into the light; from the light into the day; from the day into the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight into the six months during which the sun moves northward; from those months into the world of the gods; from the world of the gods into the sun; from the sun into lightning. A non-human person [emanating] from lightning leads them to the worlds of Brahman."

Furthermore, in that same passage, it is stated otherwise: "When a person departs from this world, he comes to the wind; there the wind gives way for him like the hole of a chariot wheel, and by that he ascends upward. He comes to the sun; there the sun gives way for him like the hole of a drum, and by that he ascends upward. He comes to the moon; there the moon gives way for him like the hole of a drum, and by that he..."

"He ascends upwards, he reaches the moon; for him, there the door opens as [the opening] of a drum," and so forth. In this regard, a doubt arises: Is the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) one and the same that is taught by these scriptural passages, such that the knower goes to Brahman by that very path?
[The answer is: From the year to Vāyu, because of both non-distinction and distinction. (Sūtra 2)

It has been stated that the knowers proceed by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*). Regarding that path beginning with light, the Chandogas study the year (*saṃvatsara*) as being situated between the months and the sun, [reciting]: "From the months to the year; from the year to the sun. The Vājasaneyins, however, [place] the world of the gods (*devaloka*) between those two very same [stages], [reciting]: "From the months to the world of the gods; from the world of the gods to the sun. Since the path is one and the same in both cases, both [the year and the world of the gods] are to be combined in both places.

In this regard, although the sequence prescribed by scripture (*śrauta-krama*)—which mentions the year (*saṃvatsara*) and the world of the gods (*devaloka*) after the month—is equal [in its status], we observe that longer periods are placed successively after shorter ones in the passage: "From the light [they go] to the day, from the day to the waxing fortnight, from the waxing fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves northward. Therefore, because the year alone comes to mind immediately after the month, the year itself must be placed after the month; and after that, [the world of the gods].

It is thus determined that [the soul goes] to the world of the gods (*devaloka*). Elsewhere, however, the Vājasaneyins study [the sequence] as follows: "When a person departs from this world, he comes to Vāyu; for him, Vāyu makes way there, like the hole of a chariot wheel; through that, he ascends upwards and reaches Āditya. Thus, they place Vāyu before Āditya.

The Kauṣītakins, however, read: "Having reached this path of the gods, he comes to the world of fire (agniloka), then to the world of wind (vāyuloka). Thus, they study wind as being after the flame (arcis) designated by the term *agniloka*. In that regard, although wind is obtained as being after the flame according to the order of the text for the Kauṣītakins, its entry before the sun is determined by the Vājasaneyins through the scriptural sequence indicated by the word "upwards"—namely, "By that [path] he ascends upwards; he comes to the sun"—for the scriptural sequence is more authoritative than the order of the text.

Therefore, does the knower reach the world of the gods and Vāyu after the year and before the sun according to his own preference; or rather, since they are not different things, does he reach Vāyu as being the world of the gods situated after the year? What is appropriate? That they have distinct referents, because that is well-known. And if they have distinct referents, then—since both are reached in the sequence of the scripture between the year and the sun by means of the word "above" (*ūrdhvam*) and the ablative case (*pañcamī*)—and because there is no distinction [between them], it may be according to one's preference.

This being the position reached, it is said: "Vāyu [is reached] after the year. He should go to Vāyu after the year. Why? Because Vāyu alone is indicated by both the general and the specific. For the word *devaloka* (world of the gods) denotes Vāyu in a general sense, in the form "the world of the gods. However, the word *vāyu* in the passage, "He goes to Vāyu; for him there... denotes Vāyu specifically.

Therefore, since the terms "world of the gods" (*devaloka*) and "wind" (*vāyu*) refer to the wind without distinction, one should go to the wind itself after the year. Furthermore, for the Kauṣītakins, the term "world of the wind" (*vāyuloka*)—derived through the analysis *vāyuścāsau lokaśca* ("that which is both the wind and the world")—denotes the wind alone, just like the term "world of fire" (*agniloka*).
And it is heard elsewhere that the wind is the dwelling place of the gods: "He who blows here—he is the house of the gods. || 2 || The section concerning the wind (*vāyvadhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
Varuṇa is connected with lightning because of their relationship.

In the Kauṣītaki [Upaniṣad], it is said: "Having entered this path of the gods, he comes to the world of fire (agniloka), then to the world of wind, then to the world of Varuṇa, then to the world of Āditya, then to the world of Indra, then to the world of Prajāpati, and then to the world of Brahman. Here, it is undisputed that the word *agniloka* is a synonym for *arcis* (light/heat) and thus occupies the first place. Furthermore, the placement of wind (*vāyu*) after the year (*saṃvatsara*) has been stated.

In this context, even for Āditya, his placement above Vāyu—designated by the term "world of the gods"—is established by the sequence of the Vājasaneyaka scripture which states, "From the world of the gods to Āditya, and from Āditya to the moon," thereby overriding the order obtained from the [Chāndogya] recension. Now follows the consideration regarding Varuṇa, Indra, and the others.

Should Varuṇa and the others be placed above Vāyu according to the order of the text, or rather below lightning? Regarding this doubt: since the sequence of the scriptural text beginning with "from light to day" (arcir-ahaḥ) must be respected for all stages starting from light, and because the person of lightning is heard to be the one who leads them to Brahman in the passage, "The person consisting of that [lightning], a Mānava, he leads them to Brahman," and because there is no room for these deities elsewhere in the sequence, their instruction would otherwise be rendered purposeless; therefore, some displacement of the order must necessarily occur.

In accordance with the order of recitation, Varuṇa should be placed immediately after Vāyu; since the sequence of Vāyu and Āditya is thus set aside, Indra and Prajāpati should likewise be inserted at this very point.

This being the position, it is said: "Varuṇa [is to be placed] after lightning. Varuṇa must indeed be situated above lightning. Why? Because of their connection; for the connection between lightning and Varuṇa—due to lightning being dependent upon rain—is well-known in both common experience and the Veda. What is meant is this: since Varuṇa and the others must be inserted somewhere so as not to render their instruction purposeless, and since the sequence of meaning (arthakrama) is more authoritative than the sequence of the text (pāṭhakrama), Varuṇa is to be inserted immediately after lightning.

Consequently, it is understood that his capacity for movement is accompanied by purification (*vyavadāna*). Because that [capacity] is accompanied by purification, and because Indra and the others who have been taught must necessarily be inserted, and because they are taught after Varuṇa, and because those belonging to the *Āgama* group must be inserted at the end, Indra and the others are to be inserted after Varuṇa. || 3 ||
The section concerning Varuṇa is completed.
The subtle bodies are [of that nature], because of the scriptural indication thereof.

This is now considered: Are the *arciḥ* (flames) and so forth signs of the path (*mārgacihna*), or are they places of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*), or rather, are they the bearers who carry the wise ones as they proceed toward Brahman? What, then, is reasonable? That they are signs of the path. Why? Because the instruction is of that nature.

Because it is observed in the world that travelers toward villages and other destinations receive such instruction from guides as: "Having departed from here, go to such-and-such a tree, then to such-and-such a river, then to the side of such-and-such a mountain, and finally go to such-and-such a village. Alternatively, these [days] may be grounds of experience (*bhogabhūmi*), because it is impossible for well-known periods of time like days and so forth to serve as markers on a path, and because nothing else that could serve as a path-marker is denoted by these [terms].

And their status as a land of enjoyment is established by the statement that the light and so forth are worlds: "These indeed are the worlds: the days and nights, the half-months, the months, the seasons, and the years. For this very reason, the Kaupītakins recite the light and so forth in accordance with the term "world," beginning with the words, "He comes to the world of fire."

This being the case, we reply: they are the *ātivāhika*s (conveying deities). These [deities] beginning with Light (*arcis*) are specific divine beings appointed by the Supreme Person for the conveying (*ativāha*) of the knowers. Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) thereof—that is, the indicative mark of conveying. For "conveying" means the state of causing those who travel to go; and this state of being a conductor, heard in the concluding passage—"A person, not human, leads them to Brahman"—indicates that he alone is the connection for all the preceding [deities] as well, since they are heard without distinction.
And they say that the words "light" (arcis) and so forth refer to specific presiding deities who have light and the rest as their self-nature, just as in the passage, "The earth spoke to him. || 4 ||

If this is so, since the scripture—"That person who is non-human leads them to Brahman"—declares that the person belonging to the lightning alone is the one who causes them to go to Brahman, how can Varuṇa and the others beyond the lightning be connected as conducting deities (ātivāhika)? To this he says:
"By the one belonging to the lightning alone, because of the scriptural statement to that effect. (Sūtra 5)

Beyond the lightning, the journey of the knowers proceeds by means of the superhuman, conducting deity (ātivāhika) belonging to the realm of lightning, until the attainment of Brahman. Why? Because of the scriptural statement to that effect: "He leads them to Brahman," for scripture declares that he alone is the conductor. As for Varuṇa and the others, they are merely helpers; thus, their connection as conducting deities is indeed established. || 5 ||
The section concerning the subtle body (ātivāhika) is completed.
Bādari maintains that it has the effected [Brahman] as its goal, because the attainment of that state is logically possible.

It has been stated that the knower goes by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*); that the group beginning with light and ending with the non-human (*amānava*) is the escort (*ativāhika*) which leads the knower to Brahman. Now this is being considered: does this group beginning with light lead those who meditate upon the effected (*kārya*) Hiraṇyagarbha, or those who meditate upon the supreme Brahman itself, or those who meditate upon the individual self (*pratyagātman*) as having the nature of Brahman?
Regarding this doubt, [the sūtra says]: "And because of the specification. (Sūtra 4.3.7)

By the word "worlds" (*loka*) and by the plural number, it is specified that the non-human being leads only one who meditates upon Hiraṇyagarbha, who resides in those particular worlds, as stated in the text: "A non-human person, having approached, leads him to the worlds of Brahman. Furthermore, the one who has traveled by the path of light and so forth realizes his arrival in the vicinity of the effected Hiraṇyagarbha, as expressed in the passage: "He enters the assembly hall of Prajāpati. (Sūtra 7)

But if this is so, the scriptural statement, "That non-human *puruṣa* leads them to Brahman," would not be tenable; for if Hiraṇyagarbha were being led, the statement ought to have been, "He leads them to Brahmā. To this, the Sūtra replies:
"But that designation [of him as Brahman] is due to proximity. (Sūtra 8)

The meaning is that, because Hiraṇyagarbha is the first-born and thus proximate to Brahman, his designation by the word "Brahman" in the passage "He who creates Brahmā" is determined by the reasons already stated, such as the impossibility of [the individual soul] being the goal and specific qualifying attributes. || 8 ||

Now, it might be argued that if the attainment of Hiraṇyagarbha occurs via the path beginning with light (arcirādi), then the scriptural designations of the attainment of immortality and non-return—namely, "This is the path of the gods, the path of Brahman; those who proceed by this do not return to this human whirlpool," and "Going upwards by those two, one attains immortality"—would be untenable. This is because scripture teaches the destruction of Hiraṇyagarbha at the conclusion of the period of two parārdhas, and because of the statement, "O Arjuna, all worlds up to the realm of Brahmā are subject to return"; thus, for one who has attained Hiraṇyagarbha, return is unavoidable. To this, [the author] replies:
Because it is stated that upon the completion of his duties, he departs from this world together with his supervisor.

Upon the dissolution of the effected Brahma-world (*kāryabrahmaloka*), he—having himself attained knowledge therein—attains the Supreme Brahman along with the presiding Hiraṇyagarbha, who has completed his office as the ruler. This is understood from the statement that for one who has traveled by the path of light (*arcirādi*) there is the attainment of immortality and non-return, and from the scriptural declaration: "But at the time of the final end, all those in the world of Brahman are completely liberated through supreme immortality. (9)
And because of the Smṛti. || 10 ||

This meaning is also understood from the following scriptural passage: "When the time for reabsorption has arrived, at the end of the highest [Brahmā], all those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state along with Brahmā. Therefore, it is the opinion of Bādari that the group beginning with light leads only those who meditate upon the effected (kārya) Brahman.
On this point, Jaimini objects by adopting an alternative position: "But Jaimini [says it is] the Supreme [Self], because of its being primary. (JS 4.3.11)

The teacher Jaimini maintains that it is only one who meditates upon the supreme Brahman that the path beginning with light leads; why? Because of the primary sense [of the word], for the word "Brahman" in the passage, "That non-human person leads them to Brahman," has its primary meaning only in reference to the supreme Brahman. Indeed, a figurative interpretation is only appropriate when the status of being an effect [the lower Brahman] has been established by another means of knowledge.

Nor is the impossibility of going a valid means of proof; for even though the supreme Brahman is omnipresent, scripture teaches that the cessation of ignorance occurs only for the knower who has gone to a specific place. Just as the arising of knowledge is understood from scriptures such as "This very [Self] by the recitation of the Vedas," etc., to depend upon caste, stage of life, dharma, purity, conduct, place, time, and so forth, so too the perfection of knowledge—which consists in the complete removal of ignorance—is understood from the scriptures concerning going to depend upon reaching a specific place.

As for the objection regarding the prohibition of the departure [of the soul] for the knower (*vidvan*), that has already been refuted previously. As for the argument that the mention of "the worlds of Brahman" (*brahmalokān*)—due to the dual indicators of the word *loka* and the plural number—suggests the perception of Hiraṇyagarbha as a created effect; that is incorrect. According to the maxim of the "chief carpenter of the Niṣādas," it is more appropriate to take this as a *karmadhāraya* compound, "Brahman itself is the world, the world of Brahman. Furthermore, since the meaning is determined to be a single entity, the use of the plural is justified by the scriptural usage seen in the passage, "Aditi [bound] the fetters" (*aditiḥ pāśān*). || 12 ||

Moreover, scripture shows the attainment of the Supreme Brahman by one who has departed through the channel at the crown of the head and traveled by the path of the gods: "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4) || 12 ||

As for what was said—that there is seen a reference to the effected [Brahman] in the passage, "I enter the hall and the dwelling of Prajāpati," regarding one who has gone by way of the light and so forth—the answer to that is:
"And there is no reference to the effected [Brahman]. (Sūtra 13)

And this intention is not directed toward the effect, Hiraṇyagarbha; rather, it is directed toward the supreme Brahman itself, because in the remainder of the passage—"I shall become the glory of the Brāhmaṇas"—the one who intends it intends a state of being the Self of all, preceded by liberation from all ignorance and so forth, as expressed in: "Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair, and freeing oneself as the moon frees itself from the mouth of Rāhu."

"Having shaken off the body, being one whose self is perfected (kṛtātman), I attain the uncreated Brahmaloka"—because of this scriptural hearing that the Brahmaloka to be attained is "uncreated," and because of the direct hearing of liberation from all bonds, Jaimini’s opinion is that the group of superhuman conductors beginning with Light leads only those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman. (Sūtra 13)

Now the venerable Bādarāyaṇa states his own settled conclusion according to his own view: "He leads those who do not rely on symbols," says Bādarāyaṇa; for there is a fault in both cases, and because of the nature of their resolve. (Sūtra 14)
The venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the group of conducting deities beginning with Light leads those who do not rely on symbols—that is, those other than those relying on symbols.

What is meant by this is as follows: the position that [the deities] lead only those who meditate upon the effected (kārya) Brahman is not tenable; nor is there a restrictive rule that they lead only those who meditate upon the supreme (para) Brahman; nor indeed do they lead even those who rely on symbols. Rather, they lead those who meditate upon the supreme Brahman, as well as those who meditate upon the Self—separated from primordial matter (prakṛti)—as being of the nature of Brahman.

He leads those who know both; however, he does not lead those who, like the perception of a lion in Devadatta and others, meditate upon objects such as names and so forth—which are included within the effects of Brahman—merely by means of the perception of Brahman, nor those who meditate on various such objects alone. Therefore, He leads those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman, and those who meditate upon the Self as being free from primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and having Brahman as its essence.

Why? Because there are faults in both cases. If one holds the position that [the path] leads those who meditate on the effected Brahman (*kārya-brahman*), then scriptural passages such as "Having risen from this body, having reached the highest light... would be contradicted. Conversely, if one maintains the restriction that it leads only those who meditate on the supreme Brahman (*para-brahman*), then the scriptural passage—"Those who know thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity, they attain the light"—which states that those who know the fire-sacrifice (*agni-vid*) are led by the group beginning with light (*arcis*), would be contradicted.

Therefore, there would be a fault in both positions; thus, [the Lord] leads those who possess both kinds [of knowledge]. This is what he states with the words, "and having that as his resolve" (*tatkratuśca*). The meaning is: "having that as his resolve"—that is, one who meditates in such a way attains exactly that, according to the principle: "As a person's resolve is in this world, so does he become after departing from here," and "In whatever manner they meditate upon him. Furthermore, because it is heard that even those who know the five fires proceed by the path of light (*arcir-ādi*), and because it is heard that for one who has proceeded by the path of light, there is the attainment of Brahman and no returning again.

Therefore, by the principle of "as is one's resolve" (*tatkratu-nyāya*), the meditative contemplation on the Self as identical with Brahman, which is free from its material nature (*prakṛti*), is established. However, for those who take as their support symbols (*pratīka*) ranging from Name up to the Vital Breath (*prāṇa*), since there is no meditation established by the two kinds of scriptural texts, their meditation consists of a mixture of the conscious and the unconscious; and according to the *tatkratu-nyāya*, neither the journey via the path of light (*arcirādi*) nor the attainment of Brahman exists for them. || 14 ||
The author says that scripture itself demonstrates this distinction:
"And it shows the distinction" (Sūtra 1.3.15).

The scriptural passage beginning with, "As far as Name extends, so far he has freedom of movement," shows that for those who meditate on symbols (*pratīka*) starting from Name and ending with Prāṇa, there is no journey [to Brahman] and their specific fruit is limited. Therefore, it is established that the group of conducting deities (*ātivāhika-gaṇa*) does not lead those who meditate upon non-sentient things mixed with sentient ones, or purely sentient objects, by viewing them as Brahman or by dissociating them from Brahman; rather, it leads those who meditate on the Supreme Brahman, and those who meditate on the Self as dissociated from Prakṛti and as having Brahman as its essence.
The section concerning effects is completed.
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
The manifestation [of the soul] occurs by its own nature, because of the scriptural statement. || 1 ||

For those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman, and for those who meditate upon the Self as being of the nature of Brahman and dissociated from primordial matter (prakṛti), a path beginning with the rays of light has been described, characterized by non-return. Now, he begins to consider the manner of the sovereignty of the liberated ones. This is recorded in scripture: "In this very way, this serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own true form."

Does this sentence teach that one who has risen from this body and attained the supreme light becomes connected with a form to be acquired, like the forms of the gods and so forth; or does it teach the manifestation of one's own natural essential nature? In the face of this doubt, it is reasonable to hold that there is a connection with a form to be acquired. Otherwise, the scripture concerning liberation would fail to communicate a human goal, for one’s own essential nature is seen to be not a human goal in itself.

For when the activities of the body and senses have ceased in deep sleep, no connection with a human goal (puruṣārtha) is observed for the mere nature of the Self. Nor is the mere cessation of suffering the human goal for one who has attained the supreme light, such that the manifestation of one's own nature alone could be called liberation. [As stated: "That is one measure of the bliss of Brahman; and of the learned Śrotriya who is free from desire," and "This is indeed the essence."

The meaning is "from the feet. For if an adventitious distinction were being accepted, the qualification "in its own form" would be purposeless; for even without that qualification, its status as having its own form would be established. || 1 ||
As for the objection that the statement "having attained, he manifests" (upasampadyābhiniṣpadyate) is purposeless because one's own nature is eternally attained, the answer is:
"The liberated one [is meant], because it is so declared. (Sūtra 2.3.2)

Being liberated from the connection with karma and the body and so forth produced by it, and abiding in its own natural form, one is said here to "manifest in one's own form. Therefore, although one's true nature is eternally attained, its manifestation here is said to be the cessation of that concealment which was hidden by ignorance in the form of karma. Why is this so? Because of the initial proposition; for that [nature] is proposed as the subject to be explained. How is this understood? From the reference to the inner self (pratyagātman) under discussion in the words, "That which is the Self... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).

In order to demonstrate that [the Self] is free from the triad of states beginning with waking and is also free from the body initiated by karma—which is the cause of what is liked and disliked—the text repeats, "I shall explain this very same thing further," and then declares, "In this very way, this serene being (samprasāda), having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own true form. Therefore, for one who was bound by karma, there occurs—upon reaching the highest light—a liberation consisting in the cessation of bondage.

It is said that "liberation is realized in its own form"; for even in the manifestation of one's true nature, the word *abhiniṣpatti* (realization/attainment) is seen used in such expressions as "this matter is accomplished by logic" (*yuktyāyamartho niṣpadyate*) and so forth. || 2 ||

As for what was said—that because the nature of the Self is seen to lack human purpose during deep sleep, the scripture on liberation would teach something that is not a human goal if it were merely the manifestation of that [sleeping] nature, and therefore "attainment" (*abhiniṣpatti*) must be understood as reaching another state connected with happiness, like the states of being a god or other beings—the answer to that is:
"The Self [is the one attained], because of the context. (Sūtra 3)

It is understood from the context that this Self, by its very nature, possesses attributes beginning with freedom from sin and ending with the power of true resolve; for the opening of Prajāpati’s discourse begins thus: "The Self which is free from sin, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, without hunger or thirst, whose desires are true, and whose resolves are true. And that this context concerns the inner Self (pratyagātman) has been established in the sūtra: "If it be argued that [the qualities belong] to the other [Self], [we say no], because [it is] the one whose nature has become manifest."

Therefore, this Self, whose very nature consists of such qualities as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*), has its true form obscured during the state of transmigratory existence by ignorance known as *karman*. Upon attaining the supreme light (*paraṃ jyotiḥ*), it becomes one whose true form is manifested. Consequently, the innate qualities of the individual self, such as freedom from evil, become manifest for one who has attained the supreme light; they do not arise anew. As it was stated by the venerable Śaunaka: "Just as the brilliance of a gem is not produced by washing away its impurities..."

"Knowledge is not produced for the Self by the removal of defects, in the same way that the space occupied by water is not produced by the making of a well; rather, that which already exists is brought to manifestation. How could there be the origination of what is non-existent? Likewise, through the destruction of the qualities to be abandoned, the qualities such as consciousness (avabodha) and the rest are made manifest, they are not produced; for these are indeed eternal attributes of the Self. Therefore, since the qualities such as knowledge and bliss—which, though existing in the Self, were contracted due to karma—become manifest upon reaching the Supreme Light when the bondage of the form of karma is destroyed, they are seen as being inseparable [from the Self]. || 4 ||

Is this individual self (pratyagātman), having attained the supreme light and being liberated from all bonds, experiencing itself as distinct from the Supreme Self? Or is it non-different from That, being a mode of it? Regarding this doubt, [the scriptures state]: "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman," and "When the seer beholds the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman; then the knower, having shaken off merit and sin, becomes stainless."

"he attains supreme equality"; and from such scriptural and traditional texts as, "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature; even at the time of creation they are not born, nor do they suffer at the time of dissolution," it is understood that the liberated one possesses equality with the Supreme through association and commonality of nature. Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that he experiences himself as separate [from the Supreme]. To this, it is replied: "In non-separation. The liberated one experiences his own self in non-separation from the Supreme Brahman. Why? Because it is so seen; for one who has reached the Supreme Brahman and whose concealment by ignorance has ceased, his own self is seen in its true state.

For the true nature of one's own self is indeed of the essence of the Supreme Self, as indicated by such grammatical coreferential designations (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as "That thou art," "This Self is Brahman," "All this has that as its Self," and "All this is indeed Brahman"; and also by such statements as "He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal," and "Another has entered [as] the ruler of all beings, the Self of all. Thus, [the individual self] exists as having that [Supreme Self] as its body.

That it is of the nature of a mode [of Brahman] has been established in the passage: "On account of abiding, [the individual self is Brahman], so says Kāśakṛtsna. Therefore, one experiences only "I am Brahman" without any distinction. The designations of equality and similarity indicate that the true nature of the inner self—which is indeed a mode of Brahman—is identical to that [Brahman]; they demonstrate that, by casting off the natural forms such as those of gods and others, it attains purity equal to Brahman.

However, the scriptural mention of [the soul] being together with Brahman in this manner establishes the experience of its qualities by the inner self (pratyagātman) as the possessor of those qualities; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. For, since the non-distinction from Brahman is stated through the latter's being the mode (prakāra), such passages as "By mere will he attains those [worlds]" are not contradicted; nor are passages such as "But the difference is greater because of the designation of difference" and "Because of the teaching of superiority. The section on "Being seen as non-distinct" is concluded.
Jaimini [holds that the soul is of] the size of the body, on account of the statements regarding its ascent and so forth. (Sūtra 5)

It has been stated that for the inner self (*pratyagātman*), upon attaining the supreme light, there is simply the manifestation of its own nature once concealment has ceased. In this regard, that very nature by which this self manifests is now investigated due to the diversity of scriptural statements: Is it merely the state of being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth?

Does he manifest in that form as his own essential nature (*svarūpa*), or as mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*) in that form, or, since there is no contradiction between the two, in the form of both? What, then, is the prima facie conclusion? The teacher Jaimini considers that [he manifests] "by means of the Brahman-nature" (*brāhmeṇa*). This means by means of such qualities as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth. For qualities such as being free from evil are heard in the *Dahara* section as belonging to Brahman. How is it understood that [the manifestation occurs] "by means of the Brahman-nature"?

Because of the mention [of qualities] and so forth; for the qualities of Brahman, such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and others, are indeed attributed to the inner self (*pratyagātman*) in the Prajāpati discourse by the passage beginning with "The Self which is free from evil" and ending with "whose resolve is true. By the word "and so forth," activities such as eating, which depend on qualities like having a true resolve, and the worldly dealings understood from passages such as "eating, playing, and enjoying," are included.

Therefore, according to the opinion of Jaimini, it is not possible for the inner self to have the nature of mere consciousness (*vijñānamātrasvarūpatva*) on account of these mentions and other such factors. (Sūtra 5)
"Audulomi [holds that the soul is] consciousness alone, because it has that as its essence. (6)

The teacher Auḍulomi maintains that the essential nature of this Self is pure consciousness alone, and that it manifests in that very form. Why? Because the inner Self consists of that—that is, its nature is nothing but that—as is understood from the restrictive declaration: "Just as a lump of salt has no interior or exterior but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior or exterior but is entirely a mass of consciousness, a mass of pure cognition. Thus, it is known that its essential nature is indeed pure consciousness alone.

Therefore, since there is no other quality in this [Self], words such as "freed from evil" (apahatapāpmā) are intended to exclude qualities consisting of ignorance, such as pleasure and pain which are subject to modification; thus, according to the view of Auḍulomi, there is manifestation in consciousness in its pure form alone. 6.
Now the venerable Bādarāyaṇa states the final conclusion according to his own view:
"Even so, because of the introductory statement and because of the prior existence [of the organs], there is no contradiction; thus [says] Bādarāyaṇa. (Sūtra 7)

Even so, although there is the establishment that the nature [of Brahman] consists solely of consciousness (*vijñānamātra-svarūpa*), the teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers that there is no contradiction with the previously mentioned qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth. Why? Because of their prior existence due to the introductory statement (*upanyāsāt*); for, based on the scriptural authority of the introductory passage from the Upaniṣads beginning with "The Self which is free from evil" (*ya ātmā'pahatapāpmā*), those qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) also exist—that is, they are present. The meaning is that it is not logical for mutually contradictory qualities to cancel one another out when they are established by equal means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, it is not logical that qualities such as being free from impurity (*apahatapāpmatva*) are merely imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) on the grounds of a contradiction with reality; for according to the principle that "in the absence of a distinguishing factor, why should the opposite not be the case?", when two positions are of equal strength, it is more reasonable to conclude that a statement which is otherwise impossible must have a different intended meaning. Thus, even while asserting that there is no contradiction, he considers that the meaning—that its essential nature is pure consciousness alone and nothing else exists—is not what is being propounded by passages such as "consisting of nothing but consciousness" (*vijñānaghana eva*).

What, then, is the meaning of the restriction “consisting of nothing but consciousness” (*vijñānaghana eva*)? This meaning—that the entire Self is excluded from insentience, is self-luminous, and that not even a minute portion of it has its luminosity dependent on anything else—is made perfectly clear by the very statement: “Just as a mass of salt has no interior or exterior but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior or exterior but is entirely a mass of consciousness. Nor is it thus...

Even though the entire nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is the subject of the attributes, consists of the wealth of knowledge, its connection with attributes such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*)—which is understood from other scriptural passages—is not contradicted; just as, although the essence of a lump of salt is its flavor, which is perceived by the sense of taste, the qualities of color, hardness, and so forth, perceived by the eyes and other senses, are not contradicted.

The intended meaning of the statement here is as follows: just as in juicy mango fruits and the like, although there may be a difference in taste according to the different parts such as the skin and so on, there is nevertheless a single uniform taste throughout the wood and the fuel; in the same way, the Self also possesses the nature of pure consciousness and the nature of self-luminosity everywhere. This is the meaning. || 7 ||
The section concerning Brahman is completed.
Because that [creation] occurs from mere volition alone. Sūtra 8.

It has been stated that the liberated one, having attained the Supreme Brahman, manifests as the very nature of knowledge, possessing attributes beginning with freedom from sin and ending with the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*). With reference to such a person, scriptural accounts of his activities resulting from that power of resolve are heard: "There he moves about, laughing, playing, and delighting, with women, or with chariots, or with kinsmen."

Is the attainment of kinsmen and so forth by this [liberated soul] dependent on other efforts, or does it occur through mere volition alone, as in the case of the Supreme Person? Regarding this doubt, since we observe in the world that even for kings and others who are conventionally described as acting by "will," the accomplishment of their tasks depends on other efforts, it follows that for this [soul] as well, it is dependent on such effort.

This being the position reached, it is said: "By mere volition alone. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers arise for him. For thus it is heard in scripture that the arising of his fathers and others occurs through volition alone. Nor is another scriptural passage seen which speaks of dependence on other efforts, by virtue of which this restriction—"by volition alone"—might be limited as [the restriction] in the case of the phrase "consisting of pure knowledge" (*vijñānaghana eva*). || 8 ||
And for this very reason, it has no other dominant influence. || 9 ||

Since he is liberated, his resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is true; for this very reason, he has no other superior (*ananyādhipati*). For "having another as a superior" consists in being subject to injunctions and prohibitions; indeed, if one were subject to injunctions and prohibitions, one's resolve would be obstructed. Therefore, by the scriptural statement of "true resolve" itself, "having no other superior" is also established. For this very reason, it is said: "He becomes self-ruling (*svarāṭ*). || 9 || The section on Resolve (*saṅkalpādhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
Bādari says it is non-existence, for thus [the scripture] declares.

Does the liberated one possess no body or senses, or do they exist according to his will? Regarding this doubt as to whether they exist or not, the teacher Bādari maintains that there is an absence of body and senses. Why? Because it is said thus: "For one who possesses a body, there is indeed no removal of pleasure and pain."

Having stated that pleasure and pain cannot touch one who is indeed bodiless—thereby declaring the inevitability of suffering when there is a connection with a body—the Śruti further declares the bodilessness of the liberated one: "Rising up from this body and reaching the highest light, he manifests in his own true form. || 10 ||
Jaimini [maintains that the soul exists] as a real entity, because of the mention of various alternatives. || 11 ||

The teacher Jaimini maintains that for one who is liberated, there exists the state of body and sense organs. Why? Because of the scriptural statement regarding manifoldness: "Manifoldness" (*vikalpa*) means a threefold variety of options, namely the three Vedas; for the scripture says, "He becomes single-fold, he becomes three-fold, he becomes five-fold, he becomes seven-fold," and so forth. Since it is impossible for the single, indivisible Self to possess a manifold nature, it is understood that its becoming three-fold and so on is dependent upon the body.

However, the statement regarding "bodilessness" refers to the absence of a body caused by karma; for it is that very body which is the cause of pleasure and pain. But the venerable Bādarāyaṇa states his own conclusion:
"Therefore, according to Bādari, [the soul] is of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice. (Sūtra 12)

The word "ataḥ" (from this) in the phrase "saṅkalpādeva" (merely from resolve) refers to this very point; for this reason alone—namely, from resolve—the venerable Bādarāyaṇa considers the liberated one to be of both kinds: embodied and disembodied. In this way, both types of scriptural testimony are justified. For example, regarding the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), there are the injunctions: "Those desiring prosperity should undertake the twelve-day sacrifice" (*dvādaśāham ṛddhikāmā upeyuḥ*) and "One should cause one desiring offspring to sacrifice with the twelve-day sacrifice" (*dvādaśāhena prajākāmaṃ yājayet*). Through these two injunctions—of undertaking (*upeyus*) and sacrificing (*yājayet*)—it becomes either a *sattra* or an *ahīna* based on the difference in resolve. || 12 ||

When there is possession of instruments such as a body, there is no rule that those instruments—body and so forth—are created by [the individual] himself; thus he says: "In the absence of a body, [the dream state] is possible as in the case of the intermediate state (saṃdhyā). (13)

Since enjoyment is possible through the instruments created by the Supreme Person even in the absence of instruments such as a body created by himself, he—though possessing true resolve—does not create them himself. As it is said:

In the context of dreams, beginning with "Then he creates chariots, horses, and paths," and continuing up to "Then he creates lakes, lotus ponds, and flowing streams; for he is the creator," and further, "He who wakes among these sleeping ones, fashioning desire after desire—that indeed is the Bright, that is Brahman, that alone is called the Immortal; upon it all worlds are supported, and no one transcends it"—it is understood that the individual soul (jīva) enjoys objects such as chariots created by the Lord. Likewise, even when liberated, the soul experiences the rasa of divine play through the worlds of the ancestors and others created by the Lord, who is engaged in His sport. || 13 ||
In the case of an existing entity, it is like being awake. || 14 ||

Just as a person in the waking state experiences enjoyment, the liberated one also enjoys the rasa of divine play (līlā-rasa) when there arises the manifestation of worlds such as the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka), created from his own volition (saṅkalpa) as bodies and so forth; and just as the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa), for the sake of play, creates for Himself the world of the ancestors such as Daśaratha and Vasudeva and enjoys the rasa of the play of human attributes through them, so too the liberated ones sometimes create the world of the ancestors and so forth by their own power for their own play, and at other times, because of their power of true resolve (satya-saṅkalpatva), the liberated ones [create them themselves].
Thus, it is entirely logical that they themselves create their own worlds, such as the realm of their fathers, which are included within the divine play (līlā) of the Supreme Person. || 14 ||

Now, it has been stated that the self is atomic; how then is the conceit of selfhood possible for a single atom within multiple bodies? To this, he says: "The penetration [of the self] is like that of a lamp, for so it is shown. (15)

Just as a single lamp, existing in one location, pervades other locations by means of its own light, so too it is not illogical that the Self, though situated in only one part [of the body], pervades the entire body through consciousness (*caitanya*), which is of the nature of its own light. And just as, even within a single body, there arises the conceit of "I" (*ātmābhimāna*) throughout the whole body due to the extension of consciousness—though [consciousness] resides in only one specific region such as the heart—it is the same in this case. This much, however, is the distinction: for one who is not liberated, whose knowledge is contracted by karma, [the Self's presence is limited to] the body...

In other cases, an omnipresence corresponding to the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) is not possible; however, for one who is liberated and possesses uncontracted knowledge, an omnipresence corresponding to the conceit of self according to his will, as well as a capacity for apprehension of objects as "this," is not untenable. For scripture shows this: "The individual soul (*jīva*) is to be known as a part of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold, and yet it is capable of infinity. The distinction is that for the non-liberated, karma is the regulator, whereas for the liberated, it is their own will.

[Objection: But does not the Śruti show the absence of both internal and external cognition for one who has attained the Supreme Brahman, stating: "Embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman), he knows nothing that is external, nor anything that is internal"? How then can omniscience be predicated of the liberated one? [Response: To this, the answer is:
"It refers to either deep sleep (svāpyaya) or union (sampatti); for it is made manifest [as such]. (Sūtra 4.4.16)

This statement does not refer to liberation; rather, it refers to either deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) or death (*sampatti*). Deep sleep is *suṣupti*, and death is *sampatti*, as seen from the scriptural passage beginning with "Speech merges into the mind" and ending with "Fire [merges] into the highest deity. In these two states, there exists both the attainment of the Intelligent One (*prājña*) and the absence of consciousness (*niḥsambodhatva*); therefore, this statement refers to one or the other of those two states.

Indeed, the state of being unawakened during deep sleep and death, as well as the omniscience of the liberated one, has been revealed by the Śruti: "Verily, he does not now know himself as 'I am this,' nor indeed these beings."

Having stated that at the time of deep sleep there is a state of non-cognition in the words, "He has gone to utter destruction; I see no enjoyment in this," the same text speaks of omniscience with reference to the liberated one: "By means of the divine eye of the mind, he beholds these desires and rejoices in them, which are in the world of Brahman. Likewise, omniscience is explicitly stated in the passage: "The seer sees everything; he attains everything in every way."

Likewise, regarding death, it is said: "Lacking consciousness, having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them"; "perishes" means "does not see. Therefore, the statement "by the conscious self" (prājñenātmanā) refers to either deep sleep (svāpyaya) or union with the Supreme (sampatti). || 16 ||
The section concerning non-existence is completed.
Except for the activity of moving about the world, because of the context and because of its non-proximity. || 17 ||

Is the sovereignty of the liberated one that which includes the creation of the world and so forth—the state of being the Lord of all, which is unique to the Supreme Person—or is it devoid of that, consisting solely of the object of experiencing the Supreme Person? This is the doubt. What is the correct view? That it includes the lordship over the world as well. Why? Because of the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of supreme equality with the Supreme Person, namely, "The stainless one attains supreme equality," and because of the scriptural statement regarding His possession of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*).

For indeed, supreme equality and the state of having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) are not possible without the governance of the world, which is unique to all the Lords (*sarveśvara*). Therefore, for the sake of establishing true resolve and supreme equality, the liberated one's sovereignty must also consist in the governance of the entire world. This being the position reached, we reply: "Excluding the activity of the world. The activity of the world is the governance of the nature, maintenance, and various functions of all conscious beings. Excluding that, the sovereignty of the liberated one consists in the unimpeded experience of Brahman, for whom all veils have been removed. Why? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

For the Supreme Brahman is traditionally taught in the Upanishads as the controller of the entire universe: "That from which indeed these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, and that into which they enter at death—desire to know That; That is Brahman. If this control over the entire universe were common even to the liberated souls (*muktas*), then this characteristic of Brahman—consisting in being the Lord of the world—would not be consistent. For a definition must be something that is unique to the thing defined.

Likewise: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second. It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted heat. And: "In the beginning, this was Brahman alone, one only. Being one, it did not flourish. It emitted that which is the form of excellence—the Kṣatra—namely these divine Kṣatras: Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna. And: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. He thought: 'Shall I now create the worlds? He...

"He created these worlds. "In the beginning, indeed, there was only Nārāyaṇa; there was no Brahmā, no Īśāna, no heaven and earth, no stars, no waters, no fire, no moon, and no sun. Being alone, he did not find delight. As he remained absorbed in meditation, one maiden and ten senses emerged from him."

Thus they said: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth," and so on, beginning with these and continuing with "dwelling in the self," etc.; in all such passages, the governance of the entire universe is heard as belonging exclusively to the Supreme Person. Furthermore, because of his non-proximity, the liberated soul has no presence in these contexts concerning the governance of the entire universe, by which the cosmic activity would also belong to him. (17)

If it be argued that [the Lord is not omniscient] because of the teaching concerning direct perception, we say no; for [the scripture] speaks of Him as residing in the spheres of those who hold specific offices.

"He becomes his own ruler; for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds," and "Moving at will through these worlds, assuming forms at will"—thus, by means of direct scriptural testimony, the activity of the liberated one in relation to the world is taught. If it is argued that [the liberated soul] is therefore not excluded from such world-activity, we say no; for this refers to those who abide in the spheres of authority (*ādhikārika-maṇḍala-stha*). Those who are appointed to offices are the *ādhikārikas*, such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others; their spheres are the worlds belonging to them.

The meaning of the statement, "For him there is freedom of movement in all worlds," and so forth, is that enjoyments located therein accrue to the liberated one who is no longer subject to karma. The sense is that the liberated one, whose knowledge is unimpeded by karma, experiences the worlds of transformation—which are the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of Brahman—and rejoices according to his desire. Thus, by this sentence it is stated that he experiences all enjoyments existing within the sphere of transformation and situated within the circles of those holding office (*adhikārika*), which are the manifestations of Brahman; it does not refer to the activity of world-creation (*jagad-vyāpāra*). || 18 ||

If the liberated one, like the one in saṃsāra, were to enjoy objects of experience that fall within the realm of transformation (vikāra), then, just as for the bound soul, even for the liberated one the range of enjoyable things would be limited and finite. To this he says: "And [the Lord] abides beyond the sphere of transformation; for thus He declares His state. (19)

Because it does not abide in modifications such as birth and so forth, it is called "non-abiding in modification" (*vikārāvarti*). The liberated one experiences the Supreme Brahman—which has shaken off all modifications, which is the sole repository of auspiciousness opposed to everything that is to be abandoned, and which is unsurpassed bliss—along with its manifestations and all its auspicious qualities.

Because they are included within its manifestation (*vibhūti*), even the worlds situated in the realm of transformation (*vikāra*) are objects of enjoyment for the liberated; for the Śruti declares that the liberated one exists as the experiencer within the Supreme Brahman—which is changeless and characterized by unsurpassed, infinite bliss—in such passages as: "When he finds fearless support in that which is invisible, incorporeal, indefinable, and without abode, then he becomes free from fear"; and "He is indeed the essence (*rasa*); for having obtained this essence, he becomes blissful. And so forth.

The world, which has become His manifestation, exists in Him alone, according to the Vedic revelation: "All worlds are supported by That; no one transcends That. Therefore, experiencing Brahman along with its manifestations, He enjoys even those enjoyments situated in the spheres of authority that exist within the realm of modifications; this is what is expressed in such passages as "He moves at will in all worlds," and so forth. However, the management of the world's affairs does not belong to the liberated soul. || 19 ||
And thus, perception and inference have been demonstrated. || 20 ||

It has been stated that for this liberated inner self (pratyagātman), who is subject to control, it is impossible for the activity consisting of the governance of the universe—which is unique to the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa)—to be submerged [in him]. Śruti and Smṛti demonstrate that the activity consisting of the governance of the entire universe is unique to the Supreme Person.

"Out of fear of him the wind blows; out of fear of him the sun rises; out of fear of him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run on. Likewise: "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and moon stand held apart. And so says the Śruti: "He is the Lord of all, He is the Sovereign of beings, He is the Protector of beings, He is the Bridge, the Supporter, so that these worlds may not be confounded. Smṛti also says: "Under Me as the Supervisor, Nature brings forth the world of the moving and the unmoving."

"For by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the world indeed revolves," and "Pervading this entire universe, I stand with but one portion. Likewise, the Śruti and Smṛti show that even for the liberated soul, the Supreme Person alone is the cause of bliss preceded by the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpa*) and so forth: "For He alone causes bliss," and "But he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion, having transcended these qualities, is fit for becoming Brahman."

"For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable, of the eternal Dharma, and of absolute bliss. Although the multitude of qualities beginning with freedom from sin and ending with the power of true resolve is indeed innate to the individual self (pratyagātman) and has become manifest, nevertheless, its very existence in such a state depends upon the Supreme Person; and its permanent abiding likewise depends upon Him. Since this permanence is eternally desired by the Supreme Person, it exists as something eternal. Thus [it is said]: "I am the foundation of Brahman... and so forth. Even though the group of attributes starting with being free from blemish and ending with the possession of true volition is natural to the inner self and has been manifested, nevertheless, its being of such a nature is dependent upon the Supreme Person, and its perpetual state is also dependent upon Him. Because the Supreme Person eternally wills its permanence, it exists as something eternal. Therefore, it is not [the case that the self's qualities are independent].

There is no contradiction whatsoever. In this very way, it is understood from the scripture that the instruments of enjoyment and the instruments of divine play of the Supreme Person exist in such a state precisely because they are eternally desired by the Supreme Person, as they are known through the scripture to be eternal. Therefore, the liberated soul possesses the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) and equality with the Supreme Person, with the sole exception of the activity of creating and governing the universe. || 20 ||
And because there is a mark indicating equality in respect of enjoyment alone. || 21 ||

Furthermore, from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that establishes the equality of the liberated one with Brahman through the mere experience of enjoyment consisting in the realization of the true nature of Brahman—as seen in the text, "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman"—it is understood that [the liberated one's power] is "devoid of the activity of the world. Therefore, the equality of the liberated one with the Supreme Person and their possession of the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) must be described in accordance with the scriptural texts concerning the governance of the entire universe, which are unique to the Supreme Person; thus, the sovereignty of the liberated consists solely in being devoid of the activity of the world. || 21 ||

If the sovereignty of the liberated depends upon the Supreme Person, then, because He is independent, there might be a suspicion that the liberated one could return again by His will; to this, he says: "Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement. (2.3.22)

Just as it is understood from scripture that there exists the Supreme Person—designated as the Supreme Brahman—who is the sole embodiment of auspiciousness opposed to all that is to be discarded, the cause of the birth and so forth of the world, distinct from all other entities, omniscient, whose will is ever-true, an ocean of singular affection for those who take refuge in Him, supremely compassionate, and beyond the possibility of any equal or superior; even so, He is perceived through the worship of Him, which consists of the adoration of that [Brahman] supported by the performance of the duties of one's caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama-dharma) day after day.

It is understood from the word "also" (*api*) itself that [the Lord], having turned back the ignorance consisting of the beginningless and endless accumulation of difficult-to-cross karma for those who sit in devotion (*upāsīna*), and having caused them to attain the unsurpassed bliss consisting of the experience of His own true nature, does not cause them to return again. And the scriptural text is such as: "He, indeed, living thus for the duration of his life, attains the world of Brahman and does not return again, he does not return again."

And thus it was said by the Blessed One himself: "Having come to Me, those great-souled ones do not undergo rebirth, which is an impermanent abode of suffering, for they have attained supreme perfection. All worlds, O Arjuna, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return; but having come to Me, O son of Kuntī, rebirth does not exist.

Furthermore, for one whose bonds of karma are severed, whose knowledge is uncontracted, whose very nature is the experience of the Supreme Brahman, who has that alone as his sole refuge, and who experiences the Brahman of infinite and unsurpassed bliss—since there is no possibility of dependence on anything else or of undertaking actions for its sake—[there can be no return].

The fear of returning. Furthermore, the Supreme Person, whose resolve is ever-true, having obtained a knower who is exceedingly dear to Him, will never cause him to return; for He has said: "For he is dear to Me, and I am dear to him. All these [others] are indeed noble, but the knower is My very Self—that is My view. For he, being disciplined in mind, is established in Me alone as the unsurpassed goal. At the end of many births, the man of knowledge takes refuge in Me."
"He who perceives Vāsudeva as all is a great soul, exceedingly rare. The repetition of the aphorism indicates the completion of the treatise; thus, everything is consistent.
The section concerning the exclusion of the world's activity is completed.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.
